FISCAL YEAR 1975 FOREIGN ASSISTANCE REQUEST TUESDAY, JUNE 4, 1974 HOUSE OF REPRESENTATIVES, COMMITTEE ON FOREIGN AFFAIRS, 

Washington, D.C.

The committee met at 9:45 a.m. in room 2172, Rayburn House Office 

Building, Hon. Thomas E. Morgan (chairman) presiding. 

We meet today to receive testimony from the Secretary of State on the President's foreign assistance message and on the situation in the 

Middle East. 

Mr. Secretary, we welcome you home from your long and difficult mission. I understand that you set a record as Secretary of State on your recent visit-at least for the number of takeoffs and landings. 

More important for history is the progress you made toward a Middle East settlement. We congratulate you, Mr. Secretary, and join you in hoping for a permanent peace in that important region of the world.

Before we go into detail on the results of your negotiations, I understand that you want to testify on the President's foreign assistance request for fiscal year 1975. That request includes the amount designed to help promote a permanent peace in the Middle East. (The text of the President's message, transmitting the proposed foreign assistance legislation, is in the appendix, p. 717.) 

Mr. Secretary, we hope that you will testify in open session until a little after 11 o'clock; then, with the committee's permission, we will go into executive session to hear in detail about your 32 days of negotiating in the Middle East. Since classified material is involved, I hope the committee will give permission to go into executive session. 

Mr. Secretary, you have a long statement and you may proceed as you wish.

STATEMENT OF HON. HENRY A. KISSINGER, SECRETARY OF STATE Secretary KISSINGER. Mr. Chairman, gentlemen, I appreciate this opportunity. I will, with your permission, testify first about the foreign assistance program, and then, if the committee approves, in cxecutive session I will discuss the details of the Middle East negotiations. 

I will not read the entire statement but submit it for the record and simply read some of the key sections of it in order to permit more time for questions, if this is agreeable to you. 

Chairman MORGAN. It is agreeable, Mr. Secretary. 

(1)

Secretary KISSINGER. Let me begin by placing the foreign assistance program within the context of our larger foreign policy purposes. 

The assistance program originated in a world so accustomed to cold war that even the most routine relations among nations were carried out in the shadow of global confrontation. The history of the postwar period was a never-ending effort to maintain peace through crisis management. Fundamental problems persist, but they no longer dominate the conduct of all international relations. 

It is now possible to envisage a peace sustained by the growing realization on the part of all nations that they have a stake in stability and that stability is insured by acting from a sense of justice and moderation. In such a world, all nations would share the benefits of stability and all would have an incentive to maintain it through cooperation. 

Americans have a vital stake in the realization of this prospect. In a world made interdependent by nuclear weapons, instant communications, and a global economy, Americans can preserve their security, their values, and their prosperity only by nurturing the shoots of stability and cooperation. 

U.S. POLICIES IN AN INTERDEPENDENT WORLD 

Our policies are shaped to that purpose: First, because there is an unprecedented opportunity for American diplomacy supported by Congress and the American people to make progress on the central issues which have threatened world peace for the past quarter century. 

Second, because the progress we have made toward the resolution of old issues in the Middle East, in Indochina, with the People's Republic of China, and the Soviet Union is only a beginning, and would be sacrificed should we fail to persevere. Third, because recent events, such as the energy crisis, have made us acutely aware that the problems of a global economy under stress, rampant inflation, raw-material shortages, the threat of mass starvation, could lead to new forms of confrontation and renewed tensions with unforeseen consequences for peace.

We in the United States cannot alone underwrite the success of the quest to resolve all issues or alone persevere in the face of continuing obstacles to peace. Nor can we assure that the imperative of cooperation will overcome nations' temptation to pursue short term advantage. But it is equally clear that hopes for a peaceful, cooperative, and just international order can only be realized with the strong participation of this Nation.

Our assistance programs are crucial vehicles for that participation. 

They are not handouts. They are not relics of the cold war. Security and economic assistance programs are essential instruments as we seek to shape a cooperative international order that reflects our interests. 

The foreign assistance and security proposals for fiscal year 1975 include programs for strengthening the peace in the Middle East and Indochina, assisting the poorest nations and the poorest within nations, supporting the efforts of our friends to defend themselves, giving substance to our efforts to build a new partnership in this hemisphere.

U.S. DIPLOMACY AND AID: KEY TO WORLD ORDER 

The program comes before you at a time when attempts are being made to divide the world anew-between north and south, developed and developing, consumer and producer. The United States must demonstrate through the concrete expression of our concern which the assistance program provides that all nations can achieve their aspirations for development and defense by a cooperative approach. As both the world's leader in times of crisis and the world's largest exporter and importer of raw materials, we have a clear responsibility and a clear self-interest to address this challenge with vision, realism, and compassion.

Our diplomacy and our assistance programs are key elements needed to help the world travel the right path. We will be available to your committee to further define what we perceive as a common endeavor. 

A substantial portion of this program, $2.3 billion, or about half, is devoted to two areas-the Middle East and Indochina. 

THE MIDDLE EAST 

This focus reflects our past involvements and continuing interests and the importance to global stability that these regions represent. In the Middle East we are witnessing one of the most arduous but also one of the most hopeful developments of the past generation. This process has involved major diplomatic changes. While we have maintained our steady support of Israel, we have also seen fundamental improvements in our relations with the Arab nations. 

Many of these countries have turned toward a moderate course, giving up exclusive reliance on a single outside power, and increasingly prepared to focus on development rather than dispute. 

The program we are requesting is designed to further the momentum that the peace process has now acquired. It recognizes that a settlement in the Middle East requires that Israel be confident of its own security and the Arab nations be confident that their legitimate aspirations will be realized.

First, the program will provide Israel with the assistance needed to maintain its own security, giving it resolve to persevere in the negotiations assured of its own strength and our support. Second, it would give tangible expression to our new and fruitful relations with various Arab countries and encourage those seriously prepared to work for peace. Third, it would foster the peaceful development of the area, reducing the incentives to violence and conflict, and deepening the interest of all the peoples in cooperation. 

More specifically, with this program we would make available to Israel $350 million in grants and credits to enable it to continue purchasing vitally needed military equipment from the United States and to relieve it of some of the burden of its defense costs; extend roughly $207 million in grants and credit to Jordan, both to enhance its security and to assist economic development; provide $250 million in economic assistance to Egypt; make $100 million available in the form of a special requirements fund to be able to seize opportunities to reinforce the peace process as we get further into negotiations. 

We have a vital stake in a lasting Middle East settlement. We are asking Congress for the resources which will enhance our ability to play a constructive role in this process.

INDOCHINA 

Now let me turn to Indochina. The Paris agreements of 1973 brought an honorable termination of direct American military involvement and the return of our prisoners, peace in Laos, and a substantial reduction of hostilities and casualties in Vietnam; a prevailing military balance of forces and a substantial lessening of the risk of confrontation among outside powers.

We have a moral obligation to persevere. Failure to sustain our purposes would have a corrosive effect on interests beyond the confines of Indochina. Our immediate objective in Vietnam is to consolidate the gains for peace and stability, which I have already noted. 

In economic assistance, our objective is the earliest possible development of a South Vietnamese economy which is self-sustaining. In military assistance, we seek to provide our friends with the minimum required to defend themselves and to deter a renewed North Vietnamese offensive. The achievements of recent years may hinge on sums that are small in proportion to the total effort that has already been made. 

Our request for $750 million in economic and humanitarian assistance is essential to maintain stability in Vietnam. Our programs are designed to do more than simply shore up the Vietnamese economy. 

They are shaped to bring about Vietnamese capacity for self-support by stimulating reconstruction and development, returning refugees to productive lives, and helping Vietnamese to defend themselves. 

By August 1 we will submit to the Congress a 5-year projection which will reflect our expectation of a gradually declining U.S. role. 

DEVELOPMENT ASSISTANCE 

Let me turn to development assistance.

The development assistance package before you has been importantly shaped by this committee, by the mandate of this committee to focus on food, education, and population programs. We offer it at a time when relations between developed and developing nations, and among developing nations themselves, are in rapid flux. The energy problem symbolizes this change, the dangers of confrontation between developed and developing nations, the severe plight of the poorest nations, as well as the potential for new forms of mutually beneficial cooperation. 

Now, consumers and producers, developed and developing, must join in meeting the challenges of global economic interdependence, not by creating restrictive blocs but by seeking higher levels of income and production for all nations, not by attempting to achieve unilateral advantage but by meeting the legitimate aspirations and interests of all people.

A nation's foreign policy must be rooted in its most basic beliefs. 

The economic assistance program of the United States is an expression of our moral values. Our people could not be fulfilled by a foreign policy devoid of concern for the survival of the 800 million people who must exist on less than 30 cents a day.

Assistance also is a device by which we pursue our national interests. The programs we are proposing will place us in a better position to enlist the developing nations' cooperation in sustaining an open global economy, to promote a long term balance between demand for

LO goods and their supply, and to be responsive to the concerns of countries and areas of importance to us. 

The development assistance program reflects congressional príorities, long term food, population and education programs. It places particular emphasis on helping developing nations increase their agricultural production; $675 million would be spent for that purpose. 

THE INTERNATIONAL DEVELOPMENT ASSOCIATION (IDA) 

Another crucial source of assistance is the International Development Association, which concentrates on the needs of the poorest. 

America's share of IDA funding has been significantly reduced as other nations have increased their contributions. But failure to contribute our share now would unravel the whole fabric of multilateral assistance.

I urge the House to follow the Senate and approve our $1.5 billion request for the U.S. share of IDA's fourth replenishment. 

WORLDWIDE SECURITY ASSISTANCE 

Let me say a word about our security assistance program, apart from those in Indochina and the Middle East. While our programs in those two areas demand our greatest attention in terms of resources, we must still buttress the security of friends in other parts of the world. 

We cannot claim that nations have achieved the capacity for selfdefense when they have not. Political and economic development can only take place in a secure world. Our military assistance programs and our foreign military sales credits help build such a world. These programs have been modified to encourage nations to bear the primary burden for their own defense.

As a result, countries are meeting more of their defense requirements through their own resources. But in specific situations, grant assistance must continue to major role. The bulk of this grant assistance, excluding Indochina, is directed to Korea, Turkey, and Thailand. 

In each we have very substantial interests. 

With respect to Latin America, we will consult further with the Congress as our long term approach to development and security assistance is more explicitly defined. But let me outline for you how our approach is taking shape in an area of special concern. The United 

States and the countries of Latin America and the Caribbean are together forging a new partnership. The initiative to create a new relationship came from Latin America. Our goal, however, is a common one: To make a global agenda of interdependence a program for cooperation in the Americas. To help us toward that goal, the administration is seeking $345.6 million in bilateral economic assistance, $500 million to complete our share of the last replenishment of the Inter- American Development Bank. We are asking also that the $150 million ceiling on credit arms sales be lifted.

GENERALIZED TARIFF PREFERENCES 

Finally, the generalized tariff preferences in the administration's trade bill are of particular importance and concern. I strongly urge

that the Congress consider them in the light of our interest in seeking a partnership with Latin America on the basis of trade, not aid alone. 

Let me conclude. This past decade has been difficult. We have witnessed the tragedy of assassination. We endured a long and costly war. We learned that our desire for a world which shared our institutions and prosperity was not always matched by our ability to bring about such a world. The impact of these events has been profound. But history is strewn with civilizations which interpreted the future only in the light of their fears.

The assistance package before you has been designed with opportunity and risk very clearly in mind. The United States can make a decisive contribution to building a more cooperative, more peaceful, more stable order. These proposals we have put forth for your consideration are vital tools in this effort. They will allow us to reinforce peace where it is threatened and build cooperation where it is needed. 

In your deliberations on our proposal I ask that you consider the world as it is and as it is becoming and as it might be. 

I hope that you will then agree that a strong American commitment to assistance is vital to our interests and to our values. 

Mr. Chairman, with your permission, the entire statement will be submitted for the record. 

 Your full statement will be made a part of the permanent record. 

[The prepared statement follows:] PREPARED STATEMENT OF HON. HENRY A. KISSINGER, SECRETARY OF STATE 

Mr.

Chairman and distinguished members of the House Committee on Foreign 

Let me begin by placing the foreign assistance program within the context of our larger foreign policy purposes, and the global situation in which America must pursue its national interests. 

The assistance program originated in a world so accustomed to cold war that even the most routine relations among nations were carried out in the shadow of global confrontation. The history of the postwar period was a never ending effort to maintain the peace through crisis management. Fundamental problems persist; but they no longer dominate the conduct of all international relations. 

It is now possible to envisage a peace sustained by the growing realization on the part of all nations that they have a stake in stability and that stability is insured by acting from a sense of justice and moderation. In such a world all nations would share the benefits of stability, and all would have an incentive to maintain it through cooperation. 

Americans have a vital stake in the realization of this prospect. In a world made interdependent-by nuclear weapons, instant communications and a global economy-Americans can preserve their security, their values and their prosperity only by nurturing the shoots of stability and cooperation. Our policies are shaped to that purpose:

First, because there is an unprecedented opportunity for American diplomacy supported by Congress and the American people to make progress on the central issues which have threatened world peace for the past quarter century.

Second, because the progress we have made toward the resolution of old issues in the Middle East, in Indochina, with the People's Republic of China-is only a beginning and would be sacrificed should we fail to persevere;

Third, because recent events, such as the energy crisis, have made us acutely aware that the problems of a global economy under stress-rampant inflation, raw material shortages, the threat of mass starvation-could lead to new forms of confrontation, and renewed tensions, with unforeseen consequences for peace.

We in the United States cannot alone underwrite the success of the quest to resolve old issues or alone persevere in the face of continuing obstacles to peace. 

Nor can we assure that the imperative of cooperation will overcome nations' temptation to pursue short term advantage. 

But it is equally clear that hopes for a peaceful, cooperative, and just international order can only be realized with the strong participation of this Nation. 

Our assistance programs are crucial vehicles for that participation. They are not handouts. They are not relics from the cold war. Security and economic assistance programs are essential instruments as we seek to shape a cooperative international order that reflects our interests. 

The foreign assistance and security proposals for fiscal year 1975 include programs for- Strengthening the peace in the Middle East and Indochina; 

Assisting the poorest nations and the poorest within nations; 

Supporting the efforts of our friends to defend themselves; and 

Giving substance to our efforts to build a new partnership in this hemisphere.

My recent intensive discussions in the Middle East, at the United Nations Special Session, and with the Latin America Foreign Ministers have strengthened my conviction that this program is fundamental to the achievement of our purposes as a nation.

The program comes before you at a time when attempts are being made to divide the world anew-between north and south, developed and developing, consumer and producer. The United States must demonstrate, through the concrete expression of our concern which the assistance program provides, that all nations can achieve their aspirations for development and defense by a cooperative approach. As both the world's leader in times of crisis and the world's largest exporter and importer of raw materials, we have a clear responsibility and a clear self-interest to address this challenge with vision, realism, and compassion.

Our basic point is not that of the 1950's and 1960's-that raising the living standards in individual countries will necessarily bring stability and peace-but to build a cooperative approach to the problems of economic growth and security which concern all nations. When you study our proposals, therefore, I ask that you remember that the basic philosophy behind them is to promote cooperation and to prevent confrontation and pressure on ourselves, our friends, and our allies.

The world can respond in one of two ways: 

It can choose the path of autarchy, of attempts to achieve unilateral and bloc advantage. That road leads to economic stagnation, and growing political tensions, which unravel the fabric of global security. 

Or it can choose the path of collaboration. A cooperative world will reflect the imperatives of technology and the necessities of economics. It will yield a secure peace.

Our diplomacy and our assistance programs are key elements needed to help the world travel the right path.

We will, of course, be available to your committee further questions to define what we perceive as a common endeavor. 

MIDDLE EAST 

A substantial portion of this program-$2.3 billion or about half-is devoted to two areas, the Middle East and Indochina. This focus reflects our past involvements and continuing interests, and the importance to global stability that these regions represent.

In the Middle East, we are witnessing one of the most arduous but also one of the most hopeful developments of the past generation. A lasting peace in this troubled area can only result from the decisions and actions of the parties directly involved. In previous years, the critical obstacle to that objective has been a deep lack of trust between Arabs and Israelis. Each side saw its vital interests in play with scant hope of compromise. For Israel, the issue was survival and physical security; for the Arabs, it was justice and sovereignty. And no third party was sufficiently trusted by both sides and willing to take the risks to help bring them together.

During recent months, the first crucial steps have been taken to break this impasse. Thanks to the farsighted views of key leaders in the region, and with the active role of the United States, we have seen important steps toward peace and the partial erosion of decades of hostility and mistrust among the parties. 

This process has also involved major diplomatic changes. While we have maintained our steady support of Israel, we have also seen fundamental improvements in our relations with the Arab nations. Many of these countries have turned toward a moderate course, giving up exclusive reliance on a single outside power and increasingly prepared to focus on development rather than dispute. 

These tendencies are in the interests of all people in the Middle East; they are in our own interest. We have an obligation to reinforce them. The program we are requesting is designed to further the momentum that the peace process has now acquired. It recognizes that a settlement in the Middle East requires that 

Israel be confident of its own security and that the Arabs be confident that their legitimate aspirations will be realized. 

First, the program would provide Israel with the assistance needed to maintain its own security, giving it resolve to persevere in the negotiations assured of its own strength and our support. 

Second, it would give tangible expression to our new and fruitful relations with various Arab countries and encourage those seriously prepared to work for peace. 

Third, it would foster the peaceful development of the area, reducing the incentives to violence and conflict, and deepening the interest of all the peoples in cooperation. 

More specifically, with this program we would- Make available to Israel $350 million in grants and credits to enable it to continue purchasing vitally needed military equipment from the United States and to relieve it of some of the burden of its onerous defense costs. 

This would be a significant demonstration of our steadfast support for 

Israel's security. 

Extend to Jordan roughly $207 million in grants and credits, both to enhance its security and to assist its economic development. This would strengthen Jordan's ability to hold to the course of moderation it has consistently followed in the Middle East; 

Provide $250 million in economic assistant to Egypt. There has been a dramatic turn in Egyptian foreign policy. Egypt has made the bold decision to move from confrontation to negotiation as a means of resolving the Arab-Israel dispute. Its leaders have shown a desire to substitute friendship and trust in the United States for the hostility and distrust which has so long divided us.

Make $100 million available in the form of a special requirements fund to be able to seize opportunities to reinforce the peace process as we get further into negotiations. We would consult closely with Congress on the use of this money.

We have a vital stake in a lasting Mideast settlement. We are asking Congress for the resources which will enhance our ability to play a constructive role in this process.

INDOCHINA 

Now let me turn to Indochina. The Paris Agreements of 1973 brought- 

An honorable termination of direct American military involvement and the return of our prisoners; 

Peace in Laos and a substantial reduction-though unfortunately not an elimination-of hostilities and casualties in Vietnam; 

A prevailing military balance of forces, despite the efforts of North Vietnam to upset the equilibrium ; and 

A substantial lessening of the risk of confrontation among outside powers. 

We have a moral obligation to persevere. It is rooted in the history of our involvement and the continuing efforts of our friends. Many American lives were lost and much American treasure spent in Vietnam. Now our allies have assumed the direct responsibility for their own defense. We owe them the opportunity to achieve economic progress and political stability. 

Failure to sustain our purposes would have a corrosive effect on interests beyond the confines of Indochina. Our willingness to bear vastly reduced but still vital burdens in the area will influence other countries' assessment of our resolve and stamina. And renewed warfare in Vietnam could put renewed pressure on relationships we are developing with other interested powers.

Our immediate objective in Vietnam is to consolidate the gains for peace and stability I have already noted. 

In economic assistance, our objective is the earliest possible development of a South Vietnamese economy which is self-sustaining. 

In military assistance, we seek only to provide our friends with the minimum required to defend themselves and to deter a renewed North Vietnamese offensive.

The achievements of recent years may hinge on sums that are small in proportion to the total effort that has been made. Including the separate legislation for military aid, our total Vietnamese assistance request is about what we spent in a single month in 1968 at the height of U.S. involvement. 

We hope that in time, North Vietnam will recognize the futility of its efforts to win a victory of arms, and it will turn to political accommodation within the terms of the Paris Accords. 

A stable military situation and eventual accommodation cannot be achieved if South Vietnam's economic problems are allowed to get out of hand. Our request for $750 million in economic and humanitarian assistance is essential to ward off that danger. In the past year, South Vietnam has experienced problems over which it had very little control-sharp decline in dollar revenue following the withdrawal of our troops, and world inflation:

At the peak of our involvement in the war, Vietnam's dollar earnings from U.S. Government activities ranged between $350 million and $400 million a year. Last year, following the withdrawal of U.S. troops this figure dropped to just over $100 million. 

At the same time, the costs of Vietnam's imports soared as global inflation boosted the prices of raw materials and semifinished products. 

South Vietnam has done an excellent job of adjusting to these challenges. It initiated a dramatic austerity program, increased tax collections, raised exports and dramatically cut imports. But its foreign exchange reserves have fallen dramatically.

Substantial assistance is still necessary. Our programs, however, are designed to do more than shore up the Vietnamese economy. They are shaped to nurture 

Vietnam's capacity for self-support by:

Stimulating reconstruction and development; 

Returning refugees to productive lives; and 

Helping the Vietnamese to defend themselves.

The country has made good use of our assistance. By August 1 we will submit to Congress a 5-year projection which will reflect our expectation of a gradually declining U.S. role. 

We are also seeking $362.5 million in military assistance and $110 million in reconstruction funds for the Khmer Republic. The Cambodians are fighting for their survival against forces aided and advised by the North Vietnamese. The country's economy has been shattered and the level of combat is intense. The people have paid a heavy price. A negotiated settlement of this war is the only responsible outcome. The government of the Khmer Republic has consistently affirmed its desire for a peaceful settlement through direct negotiations with its adversaries.

In Laos, a cease-fire has been achieved and the process of political accommodation begun. The country is shifting from war to rehabilitation and reconstruction. The $142 million assistance package we are seeking will help it to carry out that transition.

DEVELOPMENT ASSISTANCE 

The development assistance package before you has been importantly shaped by this committee to focus on food, education, and population programs. We offer it at a time when relations between developed and developing nations, and among developing nations themselves, are in rapid flux. 

The energy problem symbolizes this change the dangers of confrontation between developed and developing nations, the severe plight of the poorest nations, as well as the potential for new forms of mutually beneficial cooperation. 

No nation has an interest in prices that set off an inflationary spiral and economic recession which reduces income for all. For example, the price of fertilizer has risen in direct proportion to the price of oil, putting it beyond the reach of many of the poorest nations and thus contributing to worldwide food shortages. 

Confrontation can only drive prices up, production down, and nations apart. 

It will corrode the structure of global stability and peace. 36-333-74-2

Thus consumers and producers, developed and developing, must join in meeting the challenges of global economic interdependence-not by creating restrictive blocs but by seeking higher levels of income and production for all nations, not by attempting to achieve unilateral advantage but by meeting the legitimate aspirations and interests of all people. 

A nation's foreign policy must be rooted in its most basic beliefs. The economic assistance program of the United States is a faithful expression of our moral values. It reflects the humanitarian dimension of the American character. Our people could not be fulfilled by a foreign policy devoid of concern for the survival of the 800 million people who must exist on less than 30 cents a day. 

Assistance also is a device by which we pursue our national interest. The programs we are proposing will place us in a better position : 

To enlist the developing nations' cooperation in sustaining an open global economy;

To promote a long term balance between demand for goods and their supply; and

To be responsive to the concern of countries and areas of importance to us. 

The United States must pursue a comprehensive approach to our relations with the developing nations. Both aid and trade can play a major part: 

The development assistance program reflects congressional priorities; long term food, population, and education programs. It places particular emphasis on helping developing nations increase their agricultural production; $675 million would be spent for that purpose. 

Another crucial source of assistance is the International Development Association, which concentrates on the needs of the poorest. America's share of 

IDA funding has been significantly reduced as other nations have increased their contributions. But failure to contribute our share now would unravel the whole fabric of multilateral assistance. I urge the House to follow the Senate and approve our $1.5 billion request for the U.S. share of IDA's fourth replenishment-developing nations meet more of their foreign exchange needs through trade rather than aid. Congressional passage of the administration's trade bill would be a crucial contribution to the development process. 

The bill contains our request for authority to grant generalized tariff preferences which are of major economic and political significance to the developing nations.

SECURITY ASSISTANCE 

Let me say a word about our security assistance programs apart from those in Indochina and the Middle East. While our programs in those two areas demand our greatest attention in terms of resources, we must still buttress the security of friends in other parts of the world. 

We cannot claim that nations have achieved the capacity for self-defense when they have not. Political and economic development can only take place in a more secure world.

Our military assistance programs and our foreign military sales credits help build such a world. These programs have been modified to encourage nations to bear the primary burden for their own defense. As a result, countries are meeting more of their defense requirements through their own resources. But in specific situations, grant assistance must continue to play a major role. The bulk of this grant assistance, excluding Indochina, is directed to Korea, Turkey, and Thailand. In each we have very substantial security interests. The rest of the program will provide modest amounts of materials and training to nations in 

Latin America, Africa, the Middle East, and East Asia.

We must provide adequate credit levels to our friends and allies as we reduce direct government assistance. The foreign military sales program promotes the self-sufficiency we seek and our partners are pursuing. 

LATIN AMERICA 

We will consult further with Congress as our long term approach to development and security assistance is more explicitly defined. But let me outline for you how our approach is taking shape in an area of special concern for us all-Latin America.

The United States and the countries of Latin America and the Caribbean are together forging a new association-a new partnership. The initiative to create a new relationship came from Latin America. But our goal is now a common

one: To make the global agenda of interdependence a program for cooperation in the Americas.

To help us toward that goal, the administration: 

Is seeking $345.6 million in bilateral economic assistance. Our $267.5 million in development programs will focus on food production, rural development, and development of human resources; 

Is asking $500 million to complete our share of the last replenishment of the Inter-American Development Bank. This appropriation, originally authorized in 1972, would fulfill an agreement made more than 4 years ago, on which we are in arrears. The Bank is effectively promoting development and deserves our support. 

Is asking that the $150 million ceiling on credit arms sales be lifted.

Latin America spends a smaller percentage of its total product on arms than any other developing area except Africa south of the Sahara. The credit limitation has not worked to discourage arms purchases. It has worked to reduce our access, not the access of others, to governments in the area. It is, as well, unworthy of a relationship of equals; 

Finally, the generalized tariff preferences in the administration's trade bill are of particular importance. I strongly urge that Congress consider them in light of our interest in seeing our partnership with Latin America grow on a basis of trade, not aid alone. 

Let me conclude.

The past decade has been difficult. We witnessed the tragedy of assassination. We endured a long and costly war. We learned that our desire for a world which shared our institutions and prosperity was not matched by our ability to bring about such a world.

The impact of these events has been profound. But history is strewn with civilizations which interpreted the future only in the light of their fears. 

Victims of the past, they were blind to the opportunities and dangers before them.

The assistance package before you has been designed with opportunity and risk very clearly in mind. The United States can make a decisive contribution to building a more cooperative, more peaceful, more stable order. The proposals we have put forth for your consideration are vital tools in this effort. They will allow us to reinforce peace where it is threatened and build cooperation where it is needed. Our security and our well-being require nothing less. 

In your deliberations on our proposals, I ask that you consider the worldas it is and as it is becoming, and as it might be. I hope that you will then agree that a strong American commitment to assistance is vital to our interests and our values.

A successful American foreign policy cannot be the province of one branch of Government or of one party. Only if it reflects the bipartisan support of the 

Congress and our people will American diplomacy have the required constancy of purpose.

I ask you to support this legislation because it is what the Nation requires and because it is a worthy expression of America's purposes in the world. 

A 5-YEAR PROJECTION FOR INDOCHINA 

Chairman MORGAN. Mr. Secretary, the President has asked for $940 million in fiscal year 1975 for Indochina reconstruction. I have read that in the other body, the administration has been asked what total resources the U.S. Government plans to put into Indochina over the next 5 years.

Has the Executive any information for us on a 5-year program for Indochina? 

Secretary KISSINGER. Mr. Chairman, we are in the process of putting together a 5-year program projection for Indochina designed to demonstrate that if adequate funds are made available in the next 2 years, that a substantial reduction can take place over the remaining 3 years to a level which is very small in relation to what we are asking now.

SOUTH VIETNAM: WAR OR PEACE? 

Chairman MORGAN. Mr. Secretary, it seems to me that very little attention has been paid to the Paris agreements, especially by North Vietnam. Meanwhile, the fighting goes on and on. Under these conditions, are we talking about postwar reconstruction or are we really talking about South Vietnamese efforts to maintain their independence?

Secretary KISSINGER. We are talking about both, Mr. Chairman. We are talking about the efforts of South Vietnam to maintain its independence as well as undertake its reconstruction. Fighting is going on but it is going on on a relatively small scale, especially when measured against what had occurred before the signing of the Paris agreements. 

It is our judgment that, militarily, South Vietnam will be able to hold its own with the assistance that has been requested. The biggest danger to stability in South Vietnam is political dislocation caused by a decline in the level of economic activity. That decline is in part caused by rising prices of imports and by the decline in foreign exchange earnings occasioned by the withdrawal of American forces.

Therefore, we believe that the level of economic assistance or reconstruction assistance which we see requesting will be necessary to maintain the economic and political stability which are the essential ingredients in the defense of South Vietnam.

OPENING THE SUEZ CANAL 

Chairman MORGAN. Mr. Secretary, in the few minutes I have remaining, I see in the press this morning where we are spending $20 million on the Suez Canal. Is this operation proceeding according to plan? 

When do we expect the canal to be open? How much does the United 

States contribute to the opening of the canal? Is any other nation making a contribution to the opening of the canal?

Secretary KISSINGER. We have budgeted $20 million for the clearance of the Suez Canal for next fiscal year. I think there was something like $8 million made available for the operation that has just been concluded the removal of the mines. The other countries that are participating are Britain, and I think the Soviet Union has offered to contribute but there has not yet been a final decision. The sums that we have discussed represent the total that is involved in the clearance of the Suez Canal as far as the United States is concerned, but, of course, we are also requesting $150 million for the reconstruction of the cities along the Suez Canal. We believe that this will make a contribution not only to the development of Egypt and to the continuation of its moderate foreign policy, but also to the maintenance of peace in the area by giving all countries a stake in economic development rather than in military operations.

CONTRIBUTIONS OF OIL-RICH ARAB STATES 

Chairman MORGAN. Mr. Secretary, was any effort made to influence some of the rich oil-producing countries in the Middle East to make some contribution to opening this canal? It is going to be an economic advantage for the countries in that area, and Saudi Arabia and some of those countries have American dollars running out of their ears.

Is any effort being made to induce them to contribute some of their surplus dollars toward the costs of opening this canal? 

Secretary KISSINGER. Yes. An effort was made, and Iran is contributing $250 million. Also some other countries. I know Iran is contributing $250 million and some of the Gulf states are contributing lesser sums. The American share will be in percentage terms something in the order of less than 30 percent.

In addition, some of the European countries are making a contribution. Our economic assistance in Egypt, however, should not be seen merely in economic terms. It should also be seen in terms of the overall foreign policy objectives and in terms of our objectives in the Middle East, which I would like to discuss in greater detail in an executive session.

ISRAELI USE OF SUEZ CANAL 

Chairman MORGAN. Mr. Secretary, one final question.

Under section 220 (A) of the Foreign Assistance Act, the President is authorized to furnish financial assistance for the reopening of the Suez Canal. The law specifically says that this may be done after agreement has been reached by the parties involved which "provides for the use of the canal by ships of all nations, including Israel, on a nondiscriminatory basis."

In your discussions when you were in the Middle East, when you made your first agreement with Egypt, was the requirement in section. 

220 (A) of the Foreign Assistance Act that Israeli ships could use the canal agreed to by Egypt? 

Secretary KISSINGER. I think the particular provision to which you refer, Mr. Chairman, has been waived under section 614. With respect to cargoes, shipments to Israel, as part of the Egyptian disengagement agreement, an understanding was reached which was considered satisfactory by the parties. I would like to discuss that, too, in the executive session.

I would like, however, to point out not only with respect to this but with respect to other amendments that may be offered that the whole evolution of the Arab countries in a more moderate direction and toward greater reliance on the Western countries could be jeopardized if too many restrictive amendments are added to the economic assistance programs for the Middle East. These countries have a very strong sense of independence. 

 My time has expired. 

Mr. Frelinghuysen.

Mr. FRELINGHUYSEN.  

Mr. Secretary, it is a pleasure to join in welcoming you back to the committee. I should also like to congratulate you on the role you played in establishing the framework for a just settlement in the Middle East. I am sure that there are many obstacles ahead, but the role you played has certainly been absolutely essential. I have listened to your statement with much interest, having traveled both in the 

Middle East and Southeast Asia a few months ago.

I strongly support what you say about the importance of your recommendations, and I hope that it will not fall in deaf ears in Congress.

MORAL OBLIGATION IN INDOCHINA 

You talk about the moral obligation to persevere in Indochina, and I certainly say amen to that. It does seem to me that even though the amounts seem substantial they are relatively small compared to what we already have invested in that area. And the consequences of our sharp curtailment, I assume, would be disastrous not only to the 

Vietnamese but to our own interests in Southeast Asia.

Secretary KISSINGER. I agree completely. 

U.S. ROLE IN MIDDLE EAST 

Mr. FRELINGHUYSEN. I wonder about the kind of participation in the Middle East that you anticipate the United States will play. You refer to the importance of giving tangible expression to our desire to encourage the moderate elements and their focus on development. You suggested that the U.S. share of such support would be less than 30 percent. Does that mean that there is a clear definition already of the needs of a country like Egypt, and the role the international community will play in helping meet those needs?

Secretary KISSINGER. With respect to Egypt-Egypt, under the leadership of its President has undertaken a dramatic change in the orientation of its policies in the last year. Until last year, the general position of all Arab countries, including Egypt, was that their objectives could be realized only by sharp confrontation with the United States and total reliance on one of the other superpowers. This led to the polarization of the Middle East into competing power blocs, which in turn contributed to producing the energy crisis at the end of last year.

Since then, Egypt has chosen negotiations and is attempting to bring about economic development by inviting contributions from all countries. This change was executed extremely rapidly. Therefore a comprehensive program could not be developed by the time of the submission of our request to the Congress. However, we are confident by the time we come to the Congress again, the World Bank and other institutions will be able to put together a total package into which the individual contributions of other countries can fit in a coherent pattern.

For example, the Federal Republic of Germany, with our strong support, is engaged in the definition of a long term program for Egypt as well. We would say that what we have requested for this year represents the essential contribution by the United States to get the process started. By the time we return to the Congress next year, we hope to be able to put it within the framework of a comprehensive economics development program. 

Mr. FRELINGHUYSEN. Thank you.

AID: A "TIRED OLD BUREAUCRACY”

As long as it is going to be run by that same bunch of bureaucrats that have been running it for years and pouring money into funnels all over the world, it leaves me totally cold. 

COST OF OPENING THE SUEZ CANAL

ADMINISTRATION OF THE AID PROGRAM 

Secretary KISSINGER. They took a vote whether to give me the picture and it came out 50-50.

First of all, let me say that I know of the great contribution that you have made in helping us in the conduct of foreign policy whenever you have had an opportunity to do so. I understand the spirit in which these comments were offered.

Second, with respect to bureaucracy. I am not an excessive admirer of bureaucracy and I cannot pretend that I have had an opportunity to look into the details of the criticisms that you have made. We are making a major effort, however, with the really enthusiastic cooperation of Mr. Parker, at my right, to relate our foreign assistance program to the long-term foreign policy goals of the United States, and not to permit budget categories that were established 10 years ago be the determining factor in the operation of our program. 

Undoubtedly it will take us some time to achieve all of these objectives, but I think you will find in the present program we have attempted to emphasize high priority objectives, that we seek to justify them, and, I think can justify them, in terms of their contribution to long term American foreign policy. This is without any prejudice to your call for more efficient administration and a more purposeful overall program.

PURPOSE OF OPENING THE SUEZ CANAL 

I would like to make one comment, however, about the opening of the Suez Canal, which is often presented in terms of benefit to the Soviet Union. Obviously, our purpose in opening the Suez Canal is not to enable the Soviet fleet to enter the Indian Ocean. Our purpose in opening the Suez Canal is that to the extent that the Suez Canal becomes a peaceful artery, to the extent there is economic reconstruction in the cities along the Suez Canal, to that precise extent also the countries in the area will have an interest in maintaining peace and an interest in seeking their objectives, not by confrontation but through the moderate course that has already been advanced. 

I think this is an interest that is shared by all the countries in the area and has been expressed to us by all the countries in the area. 

With respect to the transit of Soviet ships through the Suez Canal, this is possible, but nothing is going to prevent us from having every Soviet ship followed by an American ship. If we are concerned over the increase in Soviet ships in the Indian Ocean, nothing prevents us from putting American ships into the Indian Ocean as well, assuming that political influence in the Indian Ocean is directly related to the number of ships in the littoral areas of the Indian Ocean about which 

I would also have some question.

It is our judgment that we can protect our strategic interests in the Indian Ocean, and the benefits of reconstruction of the Suez Canal area far outweigh the admitted strategic profits that are produced by the opening of the Suez Canal. Those strategic profits do not seem to us very decisive.

Mr. Broomfield.

Mr. BROOMFIELD.  

I too want to join with my colleagues today in welcoming you before the committee, and also congratulating you on your outstanding job in the Middle East.

PROSPECTS FOR OIL PRICE REDUCTIONS 

I wonder, Mr. Secretary, if you could comment as far as what possibilities we might expect from the Arab nations in reducing the price of crude oil? It seems to me this is a major problem throughout the world. 

Secretary KISSINGER. As you know, the United States has long held the view that the price of oil is exorbitant and is a threat to the economic stability of all nations-the developed as well as the developing nations—and, indeed, that it jeopardizes the position of the developing nations even more than those of the developed nations. 

To some extent, the prices have already come down from the panic. situation that existed last fall, but in auction prices went up to as high as $16 and sometimes above $20 per barrel. The prices have been dropping to some extent.

Unfortunately, from the price point of view, the oil-producing countries have increased their participation from 25 percent and have asked that the price for their 60 percent be at 93 percent of posted prices.

As a result, the price of oil has not come down as rapidly as we had hoped. It now looks as if it might stabilize at around $9, where we had thought it might stabilize at something around $7. 

There is a meeting of the OPEC nations in Venezuela next week. 

We believe that Saudi Arabia may exercise an influence in the direction of reducing prices. We hoped that over a period of time there would be a gradual reduction of prices, which the world economy can sustain and which are really to the long term interests of the oil-producing countries as well.

AID TO TURKEY AND POPPY PRODUCTION 

Mr. BROOMFIELD. I notice in your statement that we are prepared again to give substantial aid to Turkey. Could you tell us what progress we are making with the Government of Turkey with respect to the poppy situation?

Secretary KISSINGER. The poppy situation is a major domestic issue in Turkey, as well as, of course, a source of great concern to the United States. We have pointed out to Turkey the extreme sensitivity in 

American public opinion if they should resume poppy production.

I cannot say we have had a decisive impact as yet. We are attempting, first, to prevent them from resuming production and, secondly, if they should resume production, to do it by a method in which the product is easier to control. I think the second objective may be more easy to achieve than the first.

COMPLETION OF U.S. MINE CLEARING IN SUEZ CANAL 

Mr. BROOMFIELD. One final question with respect to the Suez Canal clearance. When will our men, who are over there assisting in the clearing of the Canal, be leaving that area? 

Secretary KISSINGER. Will you repeat that question?

Mr. BROOMFIELD. I was talking about the clearance of the Suez 

Canal. We have a number of people assisting there. 

Secretary KISSINGER. Yes. The American personnel that were involved in clearing mines in the Suez Canal have substantially completed their work and are in the process of leaving the area. The carrier Inchon, which was in Port Said, is paying a port call in Alexandria and will then depart from the area. This will end the involvement of American personnel in the mine clearing operation. 

Mr. BROOMFIELD. Thank you very much, Dr. Kissinger.

SPECIFIC COMMITMENTS TO MIDDLE EAST

Chairman MORGAN. Mr. Fascell. 

CEILINGS ON ARMS SALES TO LATIN AMERICA 

Mr. FASCELL. Thank you, Mr. Chairman. 

Mr. Secretary, welcome and congratulations.

I would like to shift gears for a moment and talk about Latin America and your efforts in this hemisphere. 

One of the suggestions that you have proposed in this bill is to lift the ceilings on arms sales in Latin America. I must confess that our policy and effort there, although well-intentioned, really hasn't paid off in terms of either control or reducing the amount of expenditures. 

I wonder if you care to express your opinion generally on that subject of lifting the entire ceiling? 

Secretary KISSINGER. First of all, the total expenditures on arms for Latin America are small, smaller than any comparable area in the world. We are not talking of a big arms sales. It is a fact that several of the countries in Latin America are governed by military rulers and that they believe, even those who have civilian governments, they have certain minimum independence needs which must be met. Our experience has been that the refusal by the United States to sell arms has not led to the shifting of resources away from arms procurement. It has merely resulted in the purchase of arms in other countries, including as in the case of Peru of some arms from the Soviet Union after the United States refused to furnish them. 

Therefore, we believe that it is a mistake for the United States to lose its traditional relationship with many of the groups in Latin America with which we have been associated by not furnishing the arms they desire. We would not contribute to lowering the levels of arms expenditures by doing so and we would merely be opening up these countries to the influences of other countries that will be prepared to sell arms to them.

In terms of our overall policy, while we are not favoring an arms race in Latin America and while, as you know, in the meetings of Foreign Ministers and at the OAS, we have supported all arms limitations agreements that exist in Latin America, we believe that the United States would be limiting itself to no purpose by the ceiling of $150 million.

CRITERIA FOR JUDGING ARMS SALES 

Mr. FASCELL. Mr. Secretary, the purchase of Soviet tanks by Peru has raised question marks both in Chile and in Ecuador. How does the 

State Department and at what point does State get into the balancing act with the various factors involved in a consideration of the request that would be coming to us both from Chile and Ecuador?

Secretary KISSINGER. Our general belief is that we should not conduct a reactive foreign policy. We should get into these discussions at an early enough stage so that we can shape the requests that come to us, rather than have to wait for an arms race to develop and try to manage it.

We therefore favor, on the one hand, an agreement among these countries, putting a ceiling on their military expenditures.

On the other hand, if Chile and Ecuador come to us with requests, we would hope to discuss them at a very early stage in the process so that we do not spark an arms race beyond what is already inherent in the situation.

Mr. FASCELL. Mr. Secretary, as I understand your approach to this new policy in Latin America, it is to resolve as promptly as possible whatever major items of dispute exist and in whatever countries on a bilateral basis.

Secretary KISSINGER. Exactly. 

Mr. FASCELL. And then try to proceed from there on diplomatic terms? Am I correct?

ELIMINATION OF VENEZUELA FROM SUGAR ACT 

Secretary KISSINGER. That is correct, Mr. Fascell.

Mr. FASCELL. Mr. Secretary, an effort will be made tomorrow on the floor of the House on the sugar bill to take punitive action against Venezuela by eliminating its sugar quota because of its alleged oilpricing policy. I believe that that is an unrewarding approach, both for the United States, otherwise which I won't bother to reckon at this point.

I would like to hear the Secretary's opinon of this kind of approach to diplomacy and politics. 

Secretary KISSINGER. I don't believe we can deal with the oil problem, the problem of oil prices, by taking punitive action against individual countries on a bilateral basis. 

We would like to deal with the problem of oil prices within the framework of the energy conference in which, through measures of conservation, development of alternative resources, and eventually a conference between producers and consumers, we will try to work out a price structure which is to the benefit of both. 

Venezuela is not in a position by itself to reduce oil prices and to take punitive action against one country. Because it is part of OPEC and not the decisive country of OPEC, it would seem to me to be a mistake.

MORAL VALUES AND FOREIGN POLICY 

Mr. ROSENTHAL. Mr. Secretary, I want to join my colleagues in commending you for an extraordinarily useful mission. 

In your statement, the following sentence appears, "A nation's foreign policy must be rooted in the most basic beliefs. The economic assistance program of the United States is a faithful expression of our moral values." Then you further define this expression as the humanitarian dimension of the American character. 

In our choice of countries to which we render economic or military assistance, do we take into account the maintenance of democratic institutions and the question of whether the governments of those recipient countries are democratically elected? 

Secretary KISSINGER. It is one of the factors. On the other hand, it is also true that some of the countries in which the need is greatest, such as the drought areas in Africa, for example, do not necessarily 36-333-74- -3

have democratic governments. In a number of instances we have to take into account the special necessities. 

Second, situations can exist where there are overriding American security and other interests and we will have to make the decision on the basis of those interests and not entirely on the basis of the democratic structure of the government, though we would have preferred it if the governments were democratic. 

Mr. ROSENTHAL. There seem to be at least three interests we consider before we approve recipient countries. One is the humanitarian interest, as in the drought areas, the second is military security interests, and the third is foreign policy and broad American interest areas. Each of these have relevant values on the scale. 

In a quick look at the countries that were recipients of international security assistance, including the training of troops, which brings in some European countries, there are 53 countries. Less than 10, which includes the European countries, have democratically elected governments. That distresses me. The training of military forces really has nothing to do with humanitarian considerations. 

Secretary KISSINGER. No. The training of military forces is ob viously not related to the drought problem. The training of military forces is in countries in which we believe that the American security is served by having a strong capacity for local defense. 

Now, it is of course a regrettable fact that if you took a survey throughout the world of the number of countries locally who have democratic government, I suppose you would find the proportion is about the one you described. 

AID TO NONDEMOCRATIC GOVERNMENTS 

Mr. ROSENTHAL. I don't know how we can continue to justify support for this bill to the American people over a period of years to nondemocratically elected governments. I can see temporary situations, drought situations, peculiar situations, but over a period of years we can't continue to maintain support of nondemocratically controlled governments.

Secretary KISSINGER. It depends, I think, on what American purposes are served by supporting these governments. 

First of all, we wouldn't look at it in terms of supporting these governments. We would look at it in terms of what specific purposes, either in terms of the peace of an area or in terms of the security of the United States, are served by the particular programs we are conducting.

We have no quarrel with your general proposition, that we would prefer to deal with democratically elected governments. But there can be overriding interests in terms of the maintenance of peace, either vis-a-vis the United States or vis-a-vis an area which affects American interests, where we will have to do it in terms of the results and where we have regretfully to work through nondemocratically elected governments.

Mr. ROSENTHAL. Eighty percent of the governments that we render assistance to have nondemocratic institutions. That, to me, is very distressing. It does violence to the statement in your own paper, that the

economic assistance program of the United States is a faithful expression of our moral values. 

Chairman MORGAN. Mr. Thomson. 

MILITARY AID TO SOUTH VIETNAM 

Mr. THOMSON. Mr. Secretary, I just have one question. When people ask us why we continue to provide military assistance to South Vietnam, what is the basic reason? Why are we doing that? 

Secretary KISSINGER. Military assistance for South Vietnam is not part of the bill about which I am testifying. We are doing it because the North Vietnamese are maintaining substantial military forces in South Vietnam in violation of the Paris agreements of 1973. 

The Paris agreements did not require them to withdraw their forces, but they required them not to reenforce their forces. So that as a result of the agreement, had it been observed, there would have had to take place a substantial attrition of North Vietnamese forces. 

In fact, the North Vietnamese had continued to infiltrate on a massive scale. Therefore the South Vietnamese are confronted with military aggression within their territory or military pressures within their territory.

The North Vietnamese are receiving assistance from both China and the Soviet Union, which makes it impossible for the South Vietnamese to defend themselves without American assistance. 

NATURE OF U.S. COMMITMENT TO VIETNAM 

Mr. THOMSON. Did we make any kind of a commitment to South

Vietnam to continue to support them in their war with the North? Do we have any obligation, moral or otherwise, for our continued assistance?

Secretary KISSINGER. We have a moral obligation produced by 10 years of association, by the large American investment that has taken place there over a period of years, as well as the American casualties that have been incurred there.

We do not have an enforceable legal obligation, but we have a moral and political obligation.

Mr. THOMSON. Did we give them some kind of assurance that we would continue to support them? 

Secretary KISSINGER. They had reason to suppose at the time of the conclusion of the Paris agreement that the United States would continue to support them in the form of military equipment. I do not believe that there is a formal legal obligation, but there certainly is a strong moral obligation. But it has always been the United States position that we would withdraw our own forces and that Vietnamization, as it was then called, would be an attempt by the South Vietnamese to take care of their own defense, a position which they in fact have achieved with the support of American equipment. 

It is, after all, the North that is making war in the South. What we are seeing in South Vietnam is the self-defense of the South 

Vietnamese against the North Vietnamese.

[Security deletion.] THE PRESIDENT'S ROLE 

Mr. FINDLEY. Mr. Secretary, the press and Members of Congress have given richly deserved tribute to you for your diplomacy in the Middle East, almost to the exclusion of the role of the President himself. I wonder, Mr. Secretary, if you would want to give us an insight into the role of the President in these deliberations. 

Secretary KISSINGER. Of course, the ultimate responsibility for the conduct of foreign policy is always the President. No Secretary of 

State, if he has any sensitivity to constitutional processes, would ever presume to pretend that he is conducting a foreign policy that is not guided by the President. When I am on a trip, and although I have worked with the President for 5 years and have a very detailed idea of what it is that he is trying to accomplish, I, nevertheless, communicate with the President at least once a day. I send him a report every night at least, unless there is some emergency development during the day that requires immediate communication. 

Given the difference in time zones, a report I send him at night reaches him late in the day and provides him an opportunity to give me his views or instructions before the opening of the business the next morning. I hear from the President, if not every day, at least frequently enough so that I know which direction he wants me to go. 

In other words, the basic responsibility for the conduct of foreign policy, obviously, is the President's. 

Mr. FINDLEY. Thank you, Mr. Secretary and Mr. Chairman.
