FISCAL YEAR 1975 FOREIGN ASSISTANCE REQUEST WEDNESDAY, JUNE 5, 1974 HOUSE OF REPRESENTATIVES, COMMITTEE ON FOREIGN AFFAIRS, 

Washington, D.C.

The committee met at 10 a.m., in room 2172, Rayburn House Office 

Building, Hon. Thomas E. Morgan (chairman of the committee) presiding. 

Today we continue our hearings on the President's foreign assistance request for fiscal year 1975. The witnesses are Hon. James R. 

Schlesinger, Secretary of Defense, and Lt. Gen. Louis T. Seith, representing the Chairman of Joint Chiefs of Staff. Also at the witness table is Vice Adm. Ray Peet, U.S. Navy, Director of the Defense Security Assistance Agency. 

Secretary Schlesinger and General Seith will testify about the international security aspects of our assistance program. 

Mr. Secretary, you both have prepared statements? 

Secretary SCHLESINGER. Yes, sir. 

Chairman MORGAN. You may proceed first, and General Seith next.

We will then address you as a team in the question-and-answer period. 

You may proceed.

STATEMENT OF HON. JAMES R. SCHLESINGER, SECRETARY OF DEFENSE 

Secretary SCHLESINGER. Thank you very much.

Mr. Chairman and members of the committee, the Secretary of 

State has already discussed with you the broad outlines of the proposed fiscal year 1975 security assistance program and the role it is expected to play in supporting the foreign policy objectives of the United States. My purpose, therefore, is to discuss somewhat more specifically the manner in which the two forms of security assistance administered by the Department of Defense-foreign military sales (FMS) credit and the military assistance program (MAP)—advance our objectives.

SECURITY ASSISTANCE IN CONTEXT OF STRATEGIC DOCTRINE 

I would like to begin, Mr. Chairman and members, by briefly placing our security assistance proposals into the overall context of our present strategic doctrine. 36-333-74- 4 (41)

Earlier this year, before the Armed Services and Appropriations Committees of both Houses of the Congress, I reviewed the fundamental strategic issues that we face and the policies and programs we believe are important for the long-run security of the United States. 

I pointed out that it was no longer sufficient, now that the Soviet Union had achieved nuclear parity, to rely for deterrence of nuclear war solely on the rhetoric of "assured destruction," with its implication of a relatively massive nuclear response. 

Accordingly, I have proposed changes in our targeting doctrine which will give us the wider response options necessary for continuing deterrence.

In addition, having in mind the aggressive development and testing of new ICBM's now underway in the Soviet Union, we are proposing to the Congress R. & D. programs that would be necessary to help assure essential equivalence between the U.S. and U.S.S.R. strategic forces-if the U.S.S.R. does not agree to essential equivalence in the 

SALT negotiations. 

A balance of U.S.-U.S.S.R. strategic nuclear forces is part, but only part, of the wider need to maintain a worldwide military equilibrium. 

Deterrence is greatly strengthened if there are regional military balances in critical areas of the world. 

In Europe, for example, we and our NATO allies are seeking to maintain a satisfactory long-term balance of forces. Similarly, we wish to maintain a balance of naval forces, for unlike the U.S.S.R., which is predominantly a land power, the United States and its allies have long and exposed sealines of communication. Access to vital supplies, such as oil and other overseas resources, is essential to the West. 

The United States, however, cannot by itself maintain adequate conventional forces to protect its larger interests and to insure stability in all potentially volatile areas of the world. The conflict in Southeast Asia has demonstrated the problems that can result from the direct involvement of American forces. Here is where security assistance has an indispensable role.

PURPOSE OF SECURITY ASSISTANCE 

It is the principal purpose of security assistance-both the grant aid and the military sales programs to strengthen deterrence and promote peaceful negotiation by helping our friends and allies to maintain adequate defense forces of their own. We believe that hostilities can often be avoided altogether; and when they cannot, then we aim to insure that our friends and allies have the capacity to defend themselves and to restore stability as soon as practicable. In this way we seek to achieve regional stability in crucial areas of the world without the need for direct intervention by American forces.

The Middle East is an excellent example. We have helped Israel maintain sufficient defense capability, thus, avoiding the need for great power military intervention and the dangers of confrontation. We have been free to pursue arrangements for stability and a more durable peace through diplomatic means. The recent initial success of the diplomatic process is apparent, and I am certain the Secretary of State would tell you-if he has not done so already-that the security as-

sistance program is essential to the success of our hopes for a greater measure of Middle East peace. 

The vast bulk of our military assistance and foreign sales programs recommended for fiscal year 1975 is aimed at two of the more unstable parts of the world-the Middle East and Asia. More than 80 percent of our proposed grant and sales programs is directed to the countries of these two areas. 

By far our largest credit sales program-$300 million-is for Israel, a country which only recently was required to mount a swift and sizable defense. By far the largest grant program-$362 million-is for Cambodia, a country now struggling to defend itself. 

THE MIDDLE EAST PROGRAM 

The Secretary of State will have reported to you on the progress of his recent negotiations in the Middle East. Nowhere do the efforts of the United States to reduce tension, encourage rapprochement, and preserve an incomplete and fragile peace have greater import than in the Middle East.

To limit the possibility of direct superpower confrontation, to provide the confidence needed for negotiation, and to permit Israel and certain of the moderate Arab States to have the capacity to defend themselves without the need for direct U.S. military intervention, we are recommending major grant and sales programs to certain Middle East countries. We are proposing credit sales programs of $300 million for Israel, $30 million for Jordan, $10 million for Lebanon, $71 million for Greece, and $90 million for Turkey.

We are recommending grant assistance programs of $94 million to Jordan, $80 million for Turkey, and a small ($150,000) program for Lebanon. Israel and Jordan are at the center of the present instabilities in the area, and their defense needs are paramount. Greece and 

Turkey are, of course, key members of the NATO Alliance, and the maintenance of adequate defense capabilities in both countries is crucial to the alliance.

In addition to the paramount importance of achieving and preserving the peace throughout the Middle East the United States recognizes an equally vital need to pursue policies conducive to continuing access to the area's tremendous oil reserves. Denial or curtailment of this access would represent a threat to the security and economic well-being of the United States and other free world nations. Judicious use of foreign military sales, both cash and credit, and grant military assistance as instruments of national policy toward deflecting that threat is thus clearly consistent with our national interest. 

SECURITY ASSISTANCE IN ASIA 

We have, in recent history, invested heavily in lives and fortune in Asia-first in Korea, and then in Indochina. Our prompt assistance. and continuing support to Korea have permitted that country to maintain its independence-an independence that almost vanished in 1950. 

The proposed military assistance to Korea for fiscal year 1975— $161.5 million MAP, $52 million FMS-is meant to help strengthen and to make more certain a satisfactory military balance there. A satisfactory military balance in that important meeting place of great

power influence is essential for deterrence and defense; it is also an essential underpinning for negotiations between North and South 

Korea. 

The large majority of our assistance to Asia is to Southeast Asia— $544.3 million in grant assistance, $150 million in FMS. The reasons for it are well known. When we withdrew American forces from Indochina, it was understood that we would provide the military tools to enable the people there to defend themselves. The need to do so has not lessened in the last year.

The flow of military equipment, supplies, and personnel from the north to positions endangering Cambodia, Laos, and South Vietnam continues. Cambodia is particularly hard pressed. The security requirements of Thailand, Indonesia, and the Philippines are continuing ones which they need help in meeting. It would be very wrong, in my judgment, to default on our obligation by failing to provide the help needed by these countries in this difficult hour. 

Another of our objectives in providing military assistance is continuing an uninterrupted access to bases and facilities important to the worldwide U.S. military posture. In all cases, however, DOD security assistance programs are designed to facilitate and encourage greater contribution by countries to their own and the common defense.

FOREIGN MILITARY SALES (FMS) 

The proposed allocation of FMS credit clearly indicates both the thrust and the progress of this effort. A striking case in point is the sharp drop in MAP grant aid programed for the Republic of China from almost $30 million in fiscal year 1973 to the $400,000 trainingonly program proposed for fiscal year 1975. During the same 2-year period, the FMS credit sales to that country nearly doubled-rising from $45 million in fiscal year 1973 to an expected $80 million in fiscal year 1975.

A similar transition from grant aid recipient to purchasing nations status is already well underway in Latin America. In less than 10 years, MAP grant aid provided throughout this region has dropped by approximately 75 percent from a total of almost $80 million in fiscal year 1966 to the less than $20 million proposed for fiscal year 1975. 

Less than $10 million in grant materiel is programed for all of Latin America.

Only 9 of the 18 countries in the region receiving assistance will receive grant materiel. The other nine will be provided training only, either in the United States or at U.S. schools in the Canal Zonetraining which serves our own interests as well as theirs and promotes the spirit of cooperation and partnership which is a basic objective of security assistance to Latin America. FMS credit planned for 16 of the 18 Latin American countries participating in fiscal year 1975 DOD security assistance programs amounts to $200 million-more than five times as much as in fiscal year 1966. 

MODERNIZATION OF FORCES IN LATIN AMERICA 

In this connection, I note the objection raised by some in the Congress and the public at large with respect to the sale of U.S. military

equipment to Latin American countries whose limited resources, they contend, could be better spent on economic development. 

Actually, the defense budgets of Latin American nations are generally modest and, by comparison, lower than those of equally advanced countries in other parts of the world. By comparison, the amount of national resources devoted to defense is quite low-an average of about 2 percent of the GNP.

The modernization requirements of their armed forces are not excessive. Latin American countries are obviously determined to modernize and replace U.S. equipment of World War II and Korean war vintage. It is and has been fruitless for the United States to dictate to the governments of such sovereign nations the extent to which they should satisfy what they have determined to be their military requirements.

By refusing to help them achieve modest modernization programs, we do not spur economic development or an alternative distribution of resources; we simply encourage them to make their military purchases elsewhere. This is inconsistent with a foreign policy which seeks strong regional associations with the nations of the Western Hemisphere.

I do not recommend major grant assistance programs to Latin America. I do not recommend selling arms there or elsewhere in a haphazard way, simply because there is someone willing to buy them. I endorse the strong congressional overview that is given to our program for Latin America. I do recommend, however, that we go ahead with prudent grant and arms sales programs to our Latin American neighbors where those programs make sense from our point of view, and not leave the supply of arms largely to those outside this hemisphere. 

This is the basis for our fiscal year 1975 programs. 

IMPORTANCE OF SECURITY ASSISTANCE 

Mr. Chairman and members of this committee, I have not tried to be all-inclusive today. There are programs I have not touched upon, although I would be glad to answer any questions you have about them. What I wanted to do and what I hope I have achieved is to establish at the outset the relationship between our security assistance programs and our broader strategic and defense policies, supplementing the views put forward to your committee by the Secretary of State.

I hope I have made clear that the MAP and FMS programs are part and parcel of our overall policy. We are succeeding in our efforts to adjust our strategic nuclear policies and programs to the conditions we can expect in the next decade. Similarly, we are giving substantially greater emphasis to the conventional forces of the United States, particularly our NATO and naval forces, for in a time of nuclear parity, deterrence is made more likely if there is a balance of conventional forces in key areas as well as a balance of nuclear forces. 

Where we do not have the forces to help maintain a conventional balance as is the case, for example, in the Middle East and in much. of Asia-we must rely primarily on the security assistance program. 

It is a low-risk, low-cost alternative to direct American involvement

in areas of great importance. The security assistance program thus makes an essential contribution to the security of the United States and to the protection of American interests, to the prospects for greater stability and a more durable peace in critical parts of the world.

Secretary SCHLESINGER.  

You may proceed, General Šeith.

STATEMENT OF ADM. THOMAS H. MOORER, U.S. NAVY, CHAIRMAN OF THE JOINT CHIEFS OF STAFF, AS PRESENTED BY LT. GEN. 

LOUIS T. SEITH, U.S. AIR FORCE, DIRECTOR, PLANS AND POLICY, JOINT CHIEFS OF STAFF General SEITH. Mr. Chairman and members of the committee, Ad miral Moorer asked me to express his regret that he is unable to be here. He is hosting General Sonyaro, who is Turkey's leading military officer, which was a longstanding commitment. 

He has asked me to present his statement and to be available to assist Secretary Schlesinger in responding to your questions. 

His statement follows here:

As I respond to your request to present a military assessment of the security assistance program for fiscal year 1975, I am not unmindful that this is my fourth such assessment. Under these circumstances, perhaps you will permit me to preface my remarks with a very brief review of the security assistance program over these past few years. 

From fiscal year 1972 through fiscal year 1974, the executive branch requested that the Congress provide $3.73 billion in regular military assistance and foreign military sales funds. 

COST OF PAST REDUCTIONS IN SECURITY ASSISTANCE 

Congress appropriated $2.63 billion. These reductions have not been accomplished without cost.

The armed forces of many of our allies remain far short of their defense needs as they perceive the threat to their nations. 

The reluctance of some of these nations to revert to complete peacetime civilian governmental arrangements may stem from reduced U.S. assistance.

Other nations whose military requirements have not been met find themselves still engaged in an armed effort to maintain internal security when, under other circumstances, the insurgency may have been eliminated. 

Some nations are turning elsewhere for security assistance. The lack of capital investment funds has precluded even others from achieving greater, if not complete, self-sufficiency.

The U.S. access to bases has, to some extent, been influenced by the security assistance program.

I am well aware of the agonizing and complex problem the Congress confronts in the apportionment of scarce resources among competing and compelling national needs.

These remarks are not intended as criticism. They are made simply to provide a backdrop for the current discussion of this year's pro-

gram- a program designed to protect the security of the United States, her friends and Allies. 

This program is being proposed during a period when the strategic balance is in dynamic equilibrium and where each unprecedented challenge to our global interests produces an equal and opposite unprecedented opportunity for peace. 

STRATEGIC APPRAISAL OF ASIA 

I believe that a brief strategic appraisal of the areas of the world. where we, by sustained effort, expect to demonstrate continued progress toward our ultimate goal of a peaceful, free, and secure world would be of assistance.

First, East Asia and Pacific. This area has, for hundreds of years, been beset by turmoil and aggression. The United States has substantial interests and deep historical involvement in the region. We have been and must remain a Pacific power. 

Yet, the President and the Congress have signaled clearly a need for a new form of American participation in Asian affairs. The first anniversary of the agreement on ending the war and restoring the peace in Vietnam has passed. Since 1968, one-half million U.S. military personnel have been withdrawn from the Asian mainland. 

It has been almost 9 months since the last combat mission was flown by an American airman; and yet, the war continues unabated in Cambodia, and South Vietnam remains under periodic attack.

MILITARY SITUATION IN VIETNAM 

The military situation in South Vietnam defies definition in the traditional terms of war or peace. It is an amorphous melange of the worst elements of both. Over 200,000 NVA personnel remain. The 

Government of Vietnam has suffered in excess of 63,000 casualties since the January 27, 1973, cease-fire.

The Khmer insurgency has grown to between 50,000 and 60,000 troops. NVA/VC combat forces in Cambodia are advising the insurgents and represent about one-tenth of this effort. 

In addition, North Vietnam continues to provide the major portion of the logistical support to the tactical units of the insurgents. The 

Government, in spite of many dire predictions, retains effective control of 55 percent of the population and 20 percent of the territory. 

The remainder is either under insurgent control or vacated. 

The insurgents have interdicted all of the major land lines of resupply to the capitol and are striving to crumble Phnom Penh's defenses and force a capitulation of the Government. 

If the North Vietnamese and their Khmer allies are successful in defeating the legal Cambodian Government, the entire fabric of peace in the area would be severely weakened. 

MILITARY SITUATION IN SOUTH KOREA 

In South Korea, where the interests of four major powers converge, there is also a formidable threat. The dialog between the two Governments, which began in 1972, has broken down, and North Korea has laid claims to the waters surrounding five U.N.-controlled and South 

Korean-occupied islands. The potential for conflict remains high.

The security assistance program for this areas amounts to $854 million for eight countries-almost two-thirds of which is for Cambodia and Korea. In Cambodia, 80 percent of the program is for basic ammunition essential to the survival of the Nation. 

In Korea, we are striving to assure that this staunch and loyal ally, which determinedly has resisted continued aggression both at home and side by side with U.S. Forces in Vietnam, is sufficiently strong to deter North Korean aggression and provide stability on the peninsula. 

In 1971, the United States undertook, with express congressional approval, a balanced 5-year force modernization program. Funding shortfalls amounting to almost $300 million have drastically slowed the pace of this effort. The goals remain valid. 

The distinguished House majority leadership recently has added his voice to those of the administration in support of the program. 

MILITARY SITUATION IN LAOS 

This program also includes $85.2 million for Laos and reflects the congressional dictated termination of funding within the DOD budget for this small nation, where it appears that peace may be returning after many bitter years of continuous conflict. 

We seek peace and security in the area. We are not engaged in a vain defense of the status quo. It is, however, important to U.S. interests that there be an environment which will permit the nonviolent process of change to unfold free of force.

There are nations in the area which have demonstrated a propensity to assume added risks in the face of weakness. Even with this program, no warranty of peace can be given; but without it, history's starkest military lesson will again be taught-when aggression is rewarded anywhere, it is encouraged everywhere. 

Concerning the Near East, strategically, the Middle East is important because of two major factors-one geographic and the other geologic.

THE MIDDLE EAST 

Geographically, the Middle East is the corridor connecting the Eastern Hemisphere's three major continents. It is the avenue through which another strategic line of Soviet communication to the Indian Ocean and the Far East may be established. The eastern Mediterranean is also vital to the defense of NATO's southern flank. 

Geologically, the primary resource of the Middle East is oil. Middle 

East oil supplied 13 percent of preboycott U.S. demand, 75 percent of Western Europe's, and 85 percent of Japan's. Within the next decade, there is not likely to be significant diminution in the dependence of the industrialized West and Japan on the Middle East's oil. 

One-third of the non-Communist world's supply of oil is projected to come from Saudi Arabia and Iran alone. 

Superimposed on these strategic considerations is the longstanding political commitment made by both the Congress and every President since Truman to the survival of Israel, most recently manifested in the 

Emergency Security Assistance Act of 1973.

The credibility of this commitment, like all other U.S. international obligations, depends on the proven past record of performance by the United States, including the performance of our Armed Forces. 

Further complicating the flammability of the situation is the fact that the area is the birthplace of three of the world's great religions. 

It is against this background that the varied, compound, and interdependent objectives of the United States must be viewed. Peace and stability are our principal national objectives, and defusing the Middle East crisis is central to global security. 

U.S. OBJECTIVES IN MIDDLE EAST 

This point, where the interests of major powers converge, has all the necessary ingredients for being the cockpit for great power confrontation; and yet, there are political and military forces at work well outside the scope of the usual "Communist" and "free-world" interface. 

The area threatens to be the "Balkans" of the late 20th century. We seek mutually beneficial and nonexploitative relations with all the nations of the area.

Second only to peace is the crucial need to insure access for both the United States and her allies to the energy resources of the area. Until substitute energy sources are established, we will remain dependent, in part, upon oil from the Middle East. 

Also present here is the potential for divisiveness, which could damage severely the cohesion of the Atlantic community and United States-Japanese relations; serious diplomatic efforts have reduced this potential divisiveness. These efforts are continuing. 

A further U.S. goal remains the denial of hegemony over this strategic area by the Soviet Union or any other power with interests inimical to the United States-ambitions not unknown to Russian history. 

TURKEY, GREECE, AND IRAN 

Encroachment into or domination of the area by such a power would endanger NATO's southern flank principally guarded by Greece and Turkey, reduce U.S. mobility, and endanger our lines of communication.

It also would sever the economic and military relationships we have nurtured so carefully in the interest of the region's stability, progress, and independence.

Turkey and Greece play an essential role in NATO's military force. 

Astride important straits and strategically situated on the southeastern flank, these nations demonstrate growing self-reliance. 

Their continued strength is essential to the process of deterrence, which, in the long run, alone will determine the durability of détente. 

I have just returned from a visit to several of the countries of the Middle East. I spoke at length with Arab leaders and with the Shah of Iran, and I can report to you today that there remains in these nations and their leaders a deep reservoir of respect and admiration for the people of the United States. They view our willingness to share with them our military technology as an important factor in the effort

to remove the incentive for war and to deepen the stakes for peace in the area.

SOVIET ARMS DELIVERIES 

From 1955 through 1973, the U.S.S.R. has delivered thousands of of tanks to Middle East and North African countries-a number approximately equal to our total inventory. 

Thousands of pieces of artillery also have been delivered-a level almost twice the U.S. inventory. To counter this and to further the cause of peace, we seek a program of $174.2 million in grant aid for 

Jordan and Turkey; $501 million sales credit for Greece, Israel, Jordan and Lebanon, and Turkey; and a training program of about $1 million for six other countries in the area. These costs may well be dollar-for-dollar our best investments in peace.

The threat to our NATO and other allies in the Near East may well have receded, but it has not ended. They require and deserve our assistance until such time as they have recovered fully their self-confidence and economic strength.

PORTUGAL 

Concerning Europe, for the most part, our Western European allies have demonstrated the vitality of this program and long ago have outgrown the material grant aid program. For this reason, it has been curtailed drastically.

Grant aid to Portugal of less than $1 million is all the material. assistance that is requested. This program will assist Portugal's 

NATO-committed forces primarily in meeting the highly sophisticated air and submarine threat.

I might add parenthetically that, without Portugal's cooperation, manifested by her consent to the use of the Lajes Airbase in the Azores, the resupply operation which made Israel's survival possible could not have been conducted without great hazard to the lives of the crews and almost prohibitive cost.

AFRICA 

Concerning Africa, of all the major areas of the world, Africa appears to offer the greatest hope of consensus in terms of policy goals. 

These are political stability; freedom from great power intervention; peaceful economic and social development; and bilateral relations founded on self-reliance, independence and forms of support sustainable over the long term.

Many Americans feel deeply their ancestral relationship to this vast and rich continent. The richness of African resources is demonstrated by accelerating direct U.S. private investment now in excess of $4 billion.

The over 40 African nations constitute almost one-third of the membership of the U.N. and other international forums. These nations are playing a major role in such diverse issues as the law of the sea, peacekeeping, the laws of war and environmental protection far beyond the scope of traditional African interests. They are intensely aware that, in these arenas, political influence is not tied necessarily to military strength or economic might.

They also know that without this strength and might, the political vitality and functional stability necessary to independence and survival soon may be lost to outside interference or internal subversion. 

If conflict is to be avoided, they must be able to protect their independence a fragile commodity in many countries-without regard to whether it is recent or ancient. 

The nature of the economic and political situation of the continent has not escaped the attention of the U.S.S.R. and the PRC. 

MILITARY ASSISTANCE TO AFRICA 

Military assistance to Africa from these countries has been widespread, if not massive. The equipment ranges from small arms to sophisticated surface-to-air missiles and fighter aircraft. 

It is estimated that more than 30,000 Communist technicians-an appreciable portion of which were military-served in Africa during 1973.

Over 2,000 African military personnel were trained in the U.S.S.R., East Europe or the PRC during 1973.

Again, the U.S. proposes a modest program designed to further the national goals noted above. A small training program involving a total of 344 students from six countries is requested, together with limited FMS credit in the amount of $24.5 million-$14 million of which is for Morocco's small, but efficient, army-and a grant aid program for Ethiopia and Tunisia amounting to $13.3 million. 

The Ethiopian program is designed to assist that nation to defend its historic status as a free and independent nation from externally supported attack. We seek to preclude the loss of the Horn of Africa to a nation or group of nations with interests hostile to those of the 

United States.

Tunisia, also, occupies strategically important territory astride one of the Mediterranean's most important chokepoints. The Tunisian security assistance program, composed primarily of spare parts for existing U.S. equipment and rifles, is designed to provide an adequate self-defense from both external and internal attack. 

The operation of hostile ships and aircraft from Tunisian bases could disrupt severely NATO's defense of Europe. This program will assist Tunisia in insuring her own independence. 

Any discussion of security assistance in Africa, in general, and in Ethiopia, Morocco, and Tunisia, in particular, without some reference to the considerable influence these three nations exercise in the political councils of the continent would be far from complete. 

Their moderation and frieindship for the United States transcend the military relationship carefully nurtured by all of us and include support for mutually beneficial programs in the U.N. and elsewhere. 

SITUATION IN LATIN AMERICA Finally, Latin America. The vital interface between the security interests of the United States and the countries to our south is much too well-known to require explanation here.

Our relations with the Latin American nations and their military establishments, however, have been in a state of transition and, at times, crisis since 1968. 

Secretary Kissinger, in a recent address to the OAS, termed this a transition from the "good neighbor" to the "good partner."

In October 1968, prohibitions on the sale of sophisticated weapons to underdeveloped countries were established by the law—a move that many Latin American leaders, military and civilian alike, perceived as not only preemptory, but also arrogant.

At the same time, our military presence in Latin America-long a symbol of our concern and our commitment-was caught up in the twin scoops of administration concerns for the balance of payments and congressionally directed reductions in such military presence abroad.

Other events roiled the troubled waters: Military leaders took on the surprising role of radical reformers; tuna boat seizures and the subsequent suspension of military sales led to the expulsion of the U.S. military presence in Peru and Ecuador; Salvador Allende was elected President of Chile and then deposed; Peru took delivery of 

Soviet tanks-the first Latin American nation other than Cuba to acquire significant military equipment from the Soviet Union; and 

Cuban potential for inciting insurgency remains, even if somewhat reduced.

NEED FOR U.S. ARMS PROGRAM IN LATIN AMERICA 

The inflow of European arms, including French Mirage aircraft and French and Soviet armor, has impacted upon our traditional relationship with Latin American leaders.

This has exacerbated further our already declining relationship, which flowed, in part, from the decrease in the security assistance program and the restrictions on sophisticated weapons systems. 

We must act now if we are to avoid, or at least mitigate, serious degradation of our lines of communication with Latin American leaders in furtherance of our strategic interests and overall security policy objectives.

The military assistance program of $18.2 million and FMS credit of $200 million will not solve, of course, these longstanding problems, but it should be sufficient if coupled with our best diplomatic efforts, to keep the door open at least while solutions are studied and prepared. 

From a military standpoint, we must give up totally any idea that Latin America is a "bloc" of nations beholden to the United States. 

They are not, and I doubt that they ever were. They are individual nations who perceive their defense needs from the perspective of their individual nations, not as seen from any part of the United Statesfrom the White House, the Capitol, or the Pentagon. 

SECURITY ASSISTANCE ESSENTIAL TO U.S. SECURITY NEEDS 

In conclusion, I would state simply that in my view, this program is essential to U.S. security needs. I believe the hard choices have been made to separate the incidental from the fundamental.

It is much more than a tangible indication of continuing U.S. concern. It is, in effect, a shield behind which the free nations of the world can build a stable military equilibrium. 

This will permit the development in the still undetermined future of a fabric of common concern, where the relations between States can be conceived cooperatively and not in conflict or competition. 

The relatively modest security assistance program is designed so that our allies and friends can develop the capability of defending their own vital interests without directly involving the Armed Forces of the United States.

It also should insure that we are not isolated in a hostile worldan isolation which is as susceptible of creation by a neglect of responsibility and power as from the abuse of power and authority. 

REASONS FOR INCREASE IN MILITARY AID Chairman MORGAN. Thank you, General. 

Mr. Secretary, the administration has requested $985 million in military grant assistance for fiscal year 1975. This is $300 million more than was requested last year. It is more than double the $450 million which Congress appropriated for fiscal year 1974. 

I have two questions: First, why do we need such a large increase in grant military assistance? And second, as you know, Congress over a period of years has shown its desire to phase out grant military assistance. Some of your predecesors as Secretary of Defense indicated to this committee that the Department of Defense over a period of years would like to phase out grant military assistance, but they never set a definite date.

Does the Department of Defense have any timetable in mind for phasing out grant military assistance? Is it going to be with us a long time?

Secretary SCHLESINGER. Mr. Chairman, to answer the last part of that question, I would expect grant military assistance will be around for a long time if we are wise. That does not mean its composition will not change or that we may not be able to reduce it in terms of total expenditures.

Turning to the earlier part of your question, "Why is the request for fiscal year 1975 larger than the request for fiscal year 1974 and double the appropriation of last year?" Mr. Chairman, I was not here last year at the time the amount of the request was determined, but the final appropriation of the Congress was regarded by some as not unduly generous in relation to the request or to the requirements abroad.

In order to live with the level of appropriations of last year, we used $250 million worth of drawdown authority in the Department of Defense, which funded some of the requirements of the ongoing contest in Cambodia.

So, in reality, the MAP program amount last year was $700 million rather than the $450 million.

In addition to that, Laos has been moved back into the MAP program this year and out of the MASF program and, as we are all

keenly aware, there has been a change in the situation in the Middle East which has resulted in significant increases in the requests for inilitary assistance to that area of the world. 

Those are the primary considerations. 

SECURITY ASSISTANCE REQUEST FOR LAOS 

Chairman MORGAN. Mr. Secretary, you are requesting $90 million for Laos. I understand the $90 million figure was set while there was still fighting in that area. Since that time there has been a cease-fire. 

So why is the $90 million still going to be required for Laos? 

Secretary SCHLESINGER. Yes, sir, this is assistance to the forces of

Laos, including the absorption within their armed forces of what have previously been referred to as irregulars. The funding for Laos, as you will recall, has been primarily through the Department of Defense budget. The force structure in Laos now has been substantially reduced. External forces are required to depart under the cease-fire agreement.

We are waiting for, and hoping fervently to see, the final departure of the forces of North Vietnam. That has not as yet been completed. 

While the contest in Laos has been terminated by the cease-fire agreement, there must continue to be a balance of force between the forces of the royal government and those of the previous insurgent groups. 

The total expenditures in Laos have gone down markedly since the time of the cease-fire.

STRATEGIC IMPACT OF OPENING SUEZ CANAL 

Chairman MORGAN. Mr. Secretary, as you are well aware, many would say that opening the Suez Canal will give the Soviets a military advantage in the Indian Ocean area. Has there been any disagreement in the executive branch as to whether or not we should aid in opening the canal? 

Secretary SCHLESINGER. I think not, Mr. Chairman. I think that the point you have just made is true that the reopening of the canal shortens the Soviet lines of communication to the Indian Ocean. In a narrow and technical military context, this is not advantageous for anyone other than the Soviet Union.

However, if we look at the conditions in the Middle East in a larger context, in terms of the economic benefits to Egypt of operating the canal; the ability of the Egyptian regime to flourish both in terms of external resources and the acquiring of foreign exchange; the selfesteem resulting from having the country's premier enterprise operating again; and the reorientation of Egypt's position in the Middle 

East-all this is beneficial overall to American foreign policy. 

Mr. Frelinghuysen.

EFFECT OF CONGRESSIONAL FUNDING CUTS Mr. FRELINGHUYSEN.  

It is a pleasure to see you here, Mr. Secretary. I would like to follow up the chairman's questions with respect to the grant assistance primarily.

You indicated that Congress was not unduly generous last year, and Admiral Moorer's statement indicated that over the last 3 years somewhat less than $1 billion was taken off the requests of the administration for aid generally. So if experience is any guide, there is going to be some severe slashing again. 

I cannot say I agree with this position, because it seems to me that in Southeast Asia, as an example, the stakes are very high, and we should recognize continuing obligations there. 

Could I ask you about Korea and Cambodia. They are scheduled to receive the largest amounts and, therefore, would be the likely targets for reductions if those should be necessary. I see $160 million is requested in grant aid to Korea. How much of this would represent force modernization? Admiral Moorer's testimony said the goals of force modernization remain. 

Secretary SCHLESINGER. Essentially, all of it will be for force modernization.

Mr. FRELINGHUYSEN. So if there should be a reduction, this would mean a continuing postponement of what has been in process since Congress agreed to a force modernization program? 

Secretary SCHLESINGER. Yes, sir, we have slipped considerably in terms of funding the 5-year program that was started in 1971. 

EFFECT OF FUNDING CUTS IN CAMBODIA 

Mr. FRELINGHUYSEN. The other big program is in Cambodia, which is scheduled to receive $358 million in grant assistance. As I understand, most of that is for ammunition.

Secretary SCHLESINGER. About 80 percent, as I recall. 

Mr. FRELINGHUYSEN. What would be the result if there should be a sharp reduction in the amount of ammunition that could be provided because of insufficient funds?

Secretary SCHLESINGER. The ability of the governments to survive would be severely compromised. As you recall, at the time of the cutoff of tactical air support last summer, there was some question whether the Government could survive. It pulled itself together, but it is dependent upon its own forces and the munitions that are supplied to these forces. Without such munitions, it is hard to see how it could survive.

MONITORING AID TO CAMBODIA 

Mr. FRELINGHUYSEN. In view of the sharp limitations on the size of our mission in Cambodia, and the fact that there are no advisers there, how can we tell whether our aid is being effective? Is this a limitation which circumscribes our assistance?

Secretary SCHLESINGER. It certainly does circumscribe our ability to monitor our assistance, and if Congress wishes to review that limitation, it is an appropriate subject for review. 

We are constrained in terms of total manpower to a figure of 200, which does interfere with our ability to follow the flowthrough of those resources and to assure they go into the places intended, and that the intended places are the right places. 

Mr. FRELINGHUYSEN. I was not suggesting by the question that 

Congress does wish to review this situation. It seems to me an arbitrary

kind of a procedure. If we are giving substantial aid, it would seem to me wise for us to monitor it effectively. So I would like to see a review, but I am not sure one is to be expected. 

Secretary SCHLESINGER. I agree with your observation. Under the present circumstances, we are in a position in which we have to spotcheck; and while the sampling technique does work to some extent, it does not work as effectively as a larger monitoring system. We are talking about trivial numbers of personnel. 

COMMUNIST AID TO AFRICA 

Mr. FRELINGHUYSEN. I notice in Admiral Moorer's statement that widespread assistance has been given to African countries by the Soviet Union and the Republic of China. Could you give us an indication of what countries get such aid and what kind of aid it is? 

Secretary SCHLESINGER. One principal recipient we keep in mind is 

Somalia, and in the past, Egypt. Assistance has varied over the years; 

Libya is about to receive military equipment from the Soviet Union. 

Algeria and the Sudan have in the past. The extent to which these states receive Soviet largesse depends upon their orientation. 

As a general proposition, the details of the Soviet military sales program are classified, and I would be prepared to send you a letter giving specifics on a classified basis. 

Mr. FRELINGHUYSEN. Thank you. [The information requested, which was supplied, is classified and is retained in the committee's files.] 

U.S. AIRDROPS IN CAMBODIA Chairman MORGAN. Mr. Zablocki. 

Mr. ZABLOCKI.  

I want to join in welcoming you, Mr. Secretary. If I may pursue the questions of Chairman Morgan and Mr. Frelinghuysen, in the testimony today, and certainly we are fully aware that Cambodia is a very serious situation. Many towns have been surrounded by the enemy.

It is my understanding that U.S. military transports are an integral part of airdrop operations to some of those enclaves and have averaged some 690 sorties per month over Cambodia during fiscal year 1974. 

Do you expect this kind of involvement to increase, and is the cost of these airdrops charged against the Cambodian MAP program? 

And more important a question. I think, is: What precautions are taken against the C-130 transports being shot down, thereby running the risk that American airmen will be prisoners of war in Indochina? 

Secretary SCHLESINGER. There is some risk but we are taking precautions to keep that risk as low as possible, Mr. Zablocki. Regarding the way in which we orient those operations, we have established a firm rule that American aircraft should be used for supplying towns and villages for which lines of communication have been interrupted, but there is no question that the Government under those circumstances is in firm control of those areas. Consequently, aircraft can approach without any undue risk.

We have firmly indicated that U.S. aircraft should not be used as an adjunct to the forces of the Khmer Republic and, if those forces should become isolated, they must be supplied, not by U.S. aircraft, but by Cambodian aircraft.

So we distinguish sharply between areas of the country and cities that have been isolated because of an interruption to lines of communication, and forces in combat which are isolated by the actions of the insurgents.

We feel there is limited risk in U.S. aircraft being involved in airdrops in the former case. Nonetheless, we are attempting to reduce and phase out the operations of the aircraft in this context and to have these operations taken over by Cambodian aircraft. 

Mr. ZABLOCKI. And the cost is funded from the MAP program? 

Secretary SCHLESINGER. Yes, sir.

COMPLIANCE WITH LAOS CEASE-FIRE 

Mr. ZABLOCKI. Turning to Laos, you stated that the North Vietnamese have not abided by the cease-fire agreement. You have not stated whether you expect them eventually to abide by the agreement and ultimately withdraw.

If they do not, what will be the impact on the survival of the new coalition government and what recourse is open to the United States in this situation? 

Secretary SCHLESINGER. I addressed that elliptically, Mr. Zablocki, in my earlier observations. I said we are hoping, we are watching and we are waiting. There has been some reduction of North Vietnamese forces in Laos, but there has not been a complete withdrawal. 

The continued existence of those forces would continue to shadow the existing coalition government and, therefore, to be a source of pressure against the non-Communist members of that coalition government.

To the extent that it was only a source of pressure, it might not overthrow the government, but that would depend upon events. It is not clear that we have any physical recourse that we can take under the circumstances, save to make use of diplomacy and apply pressure in that way on Hanoi to abide by the agreements into which she has entered.

Mr. ZABLOCKI. You imply, however, that our aid will therefore, be required for indefinite period in the future.

Secretary SCHLESINGER. I think we must expect that there will be a continuation of the Laotian program. 

MILITARY SITUATION IN VIETNAM 

Mr. ZABLOCKI. One question on involvement in Vietnam. I was there recently and there are conflicting views as to what the position of the 

South Vietnamese military may be. Some believe that the North Vietnamese will stage an allout attack on the South sometime within a year or even within 1974. Others believe that the present level of hostilities could persist for some time without concerted attack. 36-333-74---5

How do you see the military situation in Vietnam developing and how is it likely to be affected by levels of economic aid to be voted by 

Congress for the next fiscal year?

This is one area where there will be a concerted effort to shut off all aid.

Secretary SCHLESINGER. The level of aid contemplated is sufficient, so long as there is no major offensive by the North Vietnamese. Six or 7 months ago, the probability of such a North Vietnamese offensive seemed higher than it does today. 

At the present time we do not put a high probability on an allout offensive by the North Vietnamese. The Armed Forces of South Viet nam are giving an excellent account of themselves when there are flareups of hostilities under the cease-fire agreement. 

To many who observed the ARVN of 6 or 7 years ago, the account they are now giving of themselves is splendid. In something on the order of 70 or 75 percent of the engagements that occur, the ARVN is able to emerge on top. And this is quite a contrast to the situation of a half decade ago when frequently a company of North Vietnamese troops could scatter a battalion of ARVN forces.

So I think there is a great improvement in terms of their conditioning and their military readiness. The quality of the North Vietnamese forces is not as high as it was some years ago. By contrast, however, there continues to be a very impressive logistical operation-incidentally in violation of the agreement-in which vast floods of material and excessive manpower have been introduced into South Vietnam by North Vietnam.

If the appropriation level which is anticipated for this year holds up to, say, the level that was adopted by the House, it will permit military operations to be carried on by the South Vietnamese. It will require some shrinkage, in all probability, of the force structure of South Vietnam; but there will be the possibility of continuing operations.

The biggest problem South Vietnam has at the present time is the shrinkage of foreign exchange. This is coincident with the recall of 

U.S. forces which has resulted in reduction of about $400 million a year of foreign exchange flowing into South Vietnam. The South 

Vietnamese economy is not in good shape, and that is the greatest source of internal difficulty at the present time. I hope that the economic difficulties will not result in a decline in morale that would affect military operations.

Chairman MORGAN. Mr. Broomfield. 

ROLE OF U.S. AMBASSADOR IN COUNTRY TEAM 

Mr. BROOMFIELD. Mr. Secretary, in looking over the Congressional

Record for May 20, I notice the Senate has passed the State Department authorization bill and there are several sections of that bill which appear to me to impinge upon the Defense Department. 

If this assessment is correct, it causes this committee some jurisdictional problems with the Armed Services Committee. I wonder if you would comment and give us an opportunity to hear your feelings about what the Senator has done with respect to this legislation.

Secretary SCHLESINGER. I think, Mr. Broomfield, that the legislation passed by the Senate is based upon a misreading of a letter that was sent out by President Nixon, and by previous Presidents, to ambassadors. The various elements in what has been called the country team are all subject to the authority of the ambassador. The letter states that all U.S. Government activities overseas, including the elements of the Department of Defense, are subject to the overall supervision of the Secretary of State, a point of view with which we entirely concur. I would add that the President's letter also reserves for himself direct authority over the military chain of command to U.S. military forces under the command of a U.S. area military commander. 

The problem with the legislation is that in place of overall supervision it substitutes words like "full" supervision and suggests a degree of control that would interfere with the chain of command in departments having personnel in these countries. This would be, I think, detrimental to the effectiveness of these departments. 

We have suggested in a letter to the chairman of this committee-a letter I can put into the record that certain changes in wording be made that indicate once again what has been stated by President Nixon and prior Presidents with respect to subjecting the incountry organizations, including those of the Defense Department, to the direction of the Ambassador but not to the exclusive control of the Ambassador. 

Mr. BROOMFIELD. Thank you, Mr. Secretary. 

[The information requested follows:] THE DEPUTY SECRETARY OF DEFENSE, 

Washington, D.C., June 5, 1974.

Hon. THOMAS E. MORGAN, House of Representatives, Washington, D.C. 

DEAR MR. CHAIRMAN: The Department of Defense has noted with some concern Sections 8 and 16(b) of the FY 1975 State/USIA Authorization Bill (S. 3473) 

passed by the Senate on 20 May 1974 and now under consideration by the House 

Subcommittee on State Department Organization and Foreign Operations. 

Section 8 is based on a letter from previous Presidents to all U.S. Ambassadors, and renewed in December 1969 by President Nixon. The letter gives the Ambassador full responsibility to direct and coordinate the activities and operations of all elements of the U.S. Diplomatic Mission and refers to the responsibility of the 

Secretary of State for the overall direction, coordination, and supervision of U.S. 

Government activities overseas. Section 8 would assign to the Ambassador the full responsibility for the direction, coordination, and supervision of all U.S. 

Government officers and employees in the country other than personnel under the command of a U.S. area military commander. 

By adding "supervision" to the Ambassador's responsibility and by changing the adjective from "overall" to "full" as regards "supervision," Section 8 raises the following questions:

Whether non-Department of State civil service employees overseas should remain on the payroll of their parent departments and agencies; 

Whether the Ambassador would be responsible for personnel actions (assignments, promotions, separations, within-grade step increases) of such employees stationed overseas if they remain on the payroll of their parent departments and agencies; 

Whether DoD representatives would continue to write efficiency reports on MAAG military personnel and defense attaches of whether the Ambassador would assume the job of rating them; 

Whether the dual reporting system would be modified so that non-Department of State personnel and organizations would be permitted to report in parallel to their parent departments and agencies only with the permission of their "supervisor," the Ambassador.

In short, the concept of "supervision" may here suggest that the concept of "parent department or agency" would become inappropriate overseas, that the Department of State should request payroll funds for these people, and that military personnel would, while remaining in military service, be detailed to the Diplomatic Mission and solely responsible to the Ambassador for execution of his orders.

The President's letter can legally be modified in whole or in part as he or his successors choose whereas Section 8, if enacted as an Act of Congress, cannot. 

It is, after all, the President's Constitutional authority to conduct foreign policy which is involved, and if he decides to exercise it personally or through an agent other than the duly appointed Chief of Mission or Principal Officer in a particular matter or subject of concern, he may now without legal objection do so. For example, the President's letter reserves for himself "direct authorityover such military activities as I elect, as Commander-in-Chief, to conduct through military channels." Section 8 would not appear to permit a President in the future to employ alternative channels or individuals to conduct our foreign relations. Aside from Constitutional difficulties which such a law would face, common sense suggests that there will continue to be situations in which it will be desirable to use a less formal, more flexible means to propose or receive proposals than the Ambassador or those under his direction. 

The Defense Department suggests that these difficulties may be met by making two alterations of the wording of Section 8: 

Insertion of the phrase, "Under the direction of the President-" between "Sec. 16." and "(a)". Such a modification would parallel Sec. 622 (c) of the

Foreign Assistance Act of 1961 and Sec. 2(b) of the Foreign Military Sales Act (Title 22 United States Code, sections 2382 (c), 2752(b)); 

Deletion of the words "and supervision" from subsection 16 (a) proposed by Section 8 of S. 3473. 

Secondly, Section 16 (b) directs a 10 percent across-the-board reduction in the number of Department of Defense military and civilian personnel (other than foreign nationals) which could be assigned or detailed overseas as attachés or to various Military Assistance Advisory Groups or Military Missions, commonly known as MAAGS.

Since completing in September 1972 the 15 percent reduction in MAAG 

strengths mandated by Section 512 of the Foreign Assistance Act of 1971, the 

Defense Department has, through good internal managemnet procedures, further reduced the MAAGS by 8 percent and is continuing to examine MAAGS with a view to making additional reductions in FY 1975. This objective can be best accomplished by DoD without the mandatory reductions imposed in the State/ 

USIA Authorization Bill. 

Furthermore, the Report accompanying S.

3473 states that Section 16(b) would also include Technical Assistance Field Teams (TAFTS). These teams are not representatives of our government to foreign governments. Moreover, their services are fully cost reimbursed by the recipient foreign country pursuant to the 

Foreign Military Sales Act, as amended.

We also do not believe that there should be a numerical ceiling on U.S. military and naval attaches, who are diplomats in the full sense of the term, any more than there should be a ceiling by law on the number of First Secretaries of Embassy which can be accredited to foreign countries. Indeed, the Department of Defense urges deletion of the whole of Section 16 on the grounds that personnel ceilings should not be legislated. Sound personnel management practices suggest that changing personnel levels should be responsive to our changing personnel requirements rather than being imposed irrespective of our foreign policy needs as determined by the President. 

I trust that you will consider these suggestions during the examination of the Bill by your Committee. Sincerely,

NORTH AND SOUTH KOREA W. P. CLEMENT, Jr. 

Mr. BROOMFIELD. Now, in Admiral Moorer's statement referring to the situation in North and South Korea, I wonder if you could further elaborate on the tensions there, Congressman Frelinghuysen mentioned the importance of modernization, and I certainly for many

years have been supporting that and feel we have not been doing our maximum in keeping that up. 

Could you elaborate on the situation as far as North and South 

Korea is concerned?

Secretary SCHLESINGER. There is at the present time a period of enhanced tension. There is a retrogression, as it were, in the gropings of the two Koreas toward a greater harmony and toward-I hesitate to use the word "coexistence" or "accepted coexistence." These periods of tension succeed periods of greater harmony. I think that we ought not to become unduly concerned about such periods of tension, save to recognize the fact that the relationships between the two Koreas do fluctuate and that it is therefore necessary for South Koreans to have a military capability sufficient to continue to deter hostilities directed against her by North Korea.

In the larger context, the plan for the modernization of Korean forces was associated with the reduction of U.S. forces by 20,000 men in 1971. It holds out the prospect in the years ahead-although there is no immediate prospect of a further reduction of U.S. forces in Korea as that modernization program is completed. Such a further reduction would, of course, be wise overall in terms of economy. 

The presence of U.S. forces in Korea also serves a political purpose which is preeminent in that the interests of four major powers come together over Korea in an area in which there is this confluence of interests and tension: the mainland Chinese, the Japanese, the Soviet 

Union, and ourselves.

The changing relationship between the Soviet Union and China is reflected in the changing purposes for which in part American Forces are stationed in Korea. As that relationship has become more triangular. the mainland Chinese view the presence of those forces less in terms of a threat to mainland China and more in terms of the reassurance that they draw from the continued interest of the United States in the affairs in the Far East. The Japanese take a similar attitude. 

SOVIET AID TO NORTH KOREA 

Mr. BROOMFIELD. Could you comment as far as the Soviet Union's efforts in North Korea at the present time in assisting that country in military hardware?

Secretary SCHLESINGER. I believe we can submit a classified letter in this area. [The information, which was supplied, is classified and is retained in the committee's files.]

As a general proposition, there continues to be a flow of military equipment, including a flow of aircraft. While the balance between 

South and North Korea in terms of ground forces is quite satisfactory from our standpoint, there is an imbalance in the air, and there is a preponderance of North Korean air strength relative to the South, that continues to be enhanced by the programs of support by the Soviet Union. 

Mr. BROOMFIELD. Thank you, Mr. Secretary.

STATEMENT OF LT. GEN. LOUIS T. SEITH, DIRECTOR PLANS AND POLICY, JOINT CHIEFS OF STAFF 

General SEITH. I would like to place in the record a brief assessment of the Brazilian contribution to the Allied effort in World War II. 

[The information supplied follows:] BRAZILIAN MILITARY CONTRIBUTIONS WORLD WAR II 

In addition to the assistance furnished U.S. forces within the Hemisphere, Brazil organized an expeditionary force to assist the Allies in the war in Europe. 

After initial training at home, the Brazilian Expeditionary Force (FEB) began movement to Italy in June 1944. The FEB consisted of 25,334 troops, including an infantry division and a fighter squadron. The Brazilian ground forces were assigned to the IV US Army Corps, which was part of the US 5th Army under the command of General Mark Clark. The fighter squadron passed to the opera tional control of the US XXII Tactical Air Command in early October 1944. 

The first contingents of the FEB entered combat in Italy on 14 September 1944. 

On that date, Brazilians relieved embattled US forces in position in the Massaciuccoli-Filetole-Vecchiano area north of Pisa. Two days later, on 16 September, they occupied the town of Massarosa. 

In October 1944, Brazilian forces moved into the Serchio Valley, capturing the towns of Fornaci and Barga. During the night of 3-4 November, elements of the 

FEB were rushed to reinforce the left flank of the IV Corps line in the Reno Valley. Not only did the arrival of the Brazilian forces stabilize a precarious situation, but also this action marked the beginning of the employment of the 

Brazilians as a complete division force.

After spending the bitter winter months defending the Allied front in the Reno Valley of northern Italy, the tropically bred FEB attacked the hill town of Monte Castello in late February 1945. With air support from Brazilian aircraft, the FEB captured the town on 21 February, ending three months of stubborn German resistance there. From Monte Castello, the FEB moved on to take Castelnuovo on 5 March 1945.

In four days of hard fighting from 14 to 17 April, the FEB drove the entrenched Germans from the Montese massif. This battle was the most arduous of all the Brazilian actions during the Italian campaign. Lieutenant General Willis 

D. Crittenberger, Commander of the IV Corps, called the capture of Montese "one of the most prophetic battles of the spring offensive, pointing to our final 

Allied victory in the Panaro Valley."

With the war in Italy now moving rapidly, the FEB drove on to capture Zocca and Collecchio on 21 and 27 April, respectively. The fall of Collecchio protected the flank of an Allied attack on nearby Parma. On 28 and 29 April, the 

FEB engaged in heavy fighting at the town of Fornovo. Moving with great speed, the Brazilians surrounded and captured the 148th German Infantry Division with its equipment and remnants of two other German divisions. In all, 14,799 Germans, including two general officers, surrendered to the FEB at Fornovo. Captured German equipment included 1,500 motorized vehicles of various types, 80 cannons, and large ammunition stores. General Crittenberger said of the 

Fornovo victory: "This feat of arms was an indication of the combat effectiveness of the Brazilian Division at the end of the War-an achievement all the more striking when one recalls the division's inexperience and lack of battlefield training a few months earlier when it first landed in Italy." 

The Germans surrendered in Italy on 2 May 1945. In less than eight months of combat, the FEB suffered over 2,000 casualties amounting to approximately eight percent of the Force. The FEB began its departure from Italy on 6 July 

1945 and all Brazilian troops had returned home by early October 1945.

POST-WORLD WAR II 

In the post-World War II years, Brazil furnished a small number of military personnel for the United Nations emergency forces sent to Suez and the Congo. 

Particularly helpful to the United States and the cause of peace in the Hemisphere was Brazil's contribution of troops and high-level leadership to the Inter- American Peace Force (IAPF) in 1965 to maintain order in the Dominican Republic. On 6 May 1965, the OAS formally established the IAPF to take over the duties of enforcing a ceasefire. The U.S. forces already deployed in Santo 

Domingo were thus relieved of some of the hazards of the operation. Brazilian 

General Hugo Panasco Alvim was selected as commander of the force, with U.S. 

General Bruce Palmer as his deputy. By the end of May, Brazil had contributed over 1,100 men to the IAPF out of a total of 1,550 Latin American troops. The 

U.S. forces, which at one time had exceeded 23,000, were reduced to under 

13.000 by early June. While OAS, U.S., UN, and various Dominican representatives tried to formulate a workable government, the IAPF negotiated the details of a continued ceasefire.

They succeeded in preventing major strife between the competing factions until the Act of Reconciliation established a provisional government under Garcia Godoy on 31 August 1965. The IAPF was then reduced to 8,200 men, but it continued to play an important peacekeeping role until the new President, Joaquin Balaguer, was elected. The last of the IAPF troops withdrew on 21 September 1966.

Brazilian military forces have contributed to the cause of peace and security. 

They have made valiant sacrifice in the past and are prepared to again contribute if required.

CREDIT SALES TO ISRAEL 

Mr. GROSS. There are credit sales in your―you refer to $300 million worth of credit sales to Israel. 

Secretary SCHLESINGER. Yes, sir. 

Mr. GROSS. What do you think they are going to use for money to pay for those credit sales of arms?

Secretary SCHLESINGER. I think that it would be best for us to provide a statement for the record on that. 

[The information requested follows:] ISRAEL'S ABILITY TO PAY FOR ARMS 

We believe the Government of Israel is and will remain viable and credit worthy. While it does have large foreign debt obligations, Israeli foreign exchange reserves and anticipated earnings appear to be adequate to meet the repayment terms expected to be negotiated for this credit. 

Secretary SCHLESINGER. As your question implies, the foreign exchange position of the Government of Israel is not awe inspiring at this moment. 

Mr. GROSS. I would think not.

I doubt very much if they have paid us the $1 billion they owed us when we gave them $2,200 million for arms late last year and early this year. 

Secretary SCHLESINGER. Part of that was credit; part of that represented a release from contractual liability, Mr. Gross. 

Mr. GROSS. What commitments, if any, have we made with respect to Diego Garcia? 

Secretary SCHLESINGER. Diego Garcia would be funded in the military construction bill and is not a part of this bill. 

Mr. GROSS. And will not appear in this bill?

Secretary SCHLESINGER. No, sir. 

BURDEN OF FOREIGN AID ON U.S. ECONOMY 

Mr. GROSS. Mr. Secretary, you are a former professor of economics, and you wrote a book on the subject. 

Secretary SCHLESINGER. Yes, sir. 

Mr. GROSS. I have not read it, but I intend to.

How far can we stretch this rubberband of inflation in this country in our desire to continue to police and bankroll the world; how far can we go in stretching this rubberband? Do you have any idea?

Secretary SCHLESINGER. The question of our ability to fund these kinds of activities is primarily one of balance of payments, which has only a tangential relationship to inflation. I would think as long as the Congress of the United States and the public is prepared to make these kinds of assistance, which amount to about a quarter percent of the GNP available, we could continue to tolerate that kind of burden. 

Mr. GROSS. You lost me on that tangential, or whatever it is, relationship. What does that mean?

Secretary SCHLESINGER. It means that the largest part of inflation comes from domestic sources rather than from external sources, save in commodities of a unique nature, such as oil which created problems last fall.

Under normal conditions, inflation will be driven by excessive demands in which the expenditure of the Government for foreign assistance is a very minute part of the total, or it is driven by wage and cost increases in the United States which are generated by pressures within either the corporate structure of the United States or the labor union structure. 

Mr. Rosenthal.

Mr. ROSENTHAL. Mr. Gross seemed like he had another question on the tip of his lips, and I would not want to intervene. 

Mr. GROSS. I will stop there. Thank you, Mr. Rosenthal.

STATUS OF HOMEPORTING IN GREECE Mr. ROSENTHAL. What is the status of the homeporting proposal in 

Greece?

Secretary SCHLESINGER. The status of the homeporting proposal is that we are staying at the present phase and not moving on to the next phase until we have a better understanding of the developments and relationships as they impact on our own attitudes toward the desirability of that facility. 

Mr. ROSENTHAL. What developments and what relationships? 

Secretary SCHLESINGER. I beg pardon?

Mr. ROSENTHAL. What developments and what relationships? 

Secretary SCHLESINGER. Primarily those involving the terms and the considerations that would apply to such a facility, and our estimate as to the long-term durability of such a facility if we are able to consummate an agreement with the present Government of Greece. 

Mr. ROSENTHAL. What does that mean in simple terms? Are you having difficulty working out the terms of the arrangement or are there other considerations that you prefer not to talk about?

Secretary SCHLESINGER. I would say that there remain differences with regard to the terms of the arrangements, and that we are not pressing at this time for that reason, as well as for broader reasons. 

GREECE AND TURKEY IN CONFLICT Mr. ROSENTHAL. The rise of nationalism both in Greece and Turkey and some of the current disputes over the Aegean Islands and potential oil reserves-how does that affect our aid programs to both of these countries if they continue on what is potentially a collision course? 

Secretary SCHLESINGER. I missed the last few words.

Mr. ROSENTHAL. If both the countries continue on what appears to be a collision course, how do we relate our assistance to these countries and their relationship within NATO?

Secretary SCHLESINGER. The relationships between those two countries have not been characteristically harmonious and there have been periods of great friction between them. Our relationships with them are based on the following considerations:

First, that Turkey maintains a very substantial armed force and is located in a forward defense area. Therefore, continued assistance by the United States is appropriate for Turkey. 

In the case of Greece, we have eliminated the military assistance program as far as grant is concerned and they have been shifted over to a credit program. Anything beyond that program must be paid for in dollars and in full within 120 days after delivery, and will be reviewed in light of the overall relationship at that time between the two countries.

MORALE OF U.S. TROOPS IN EUROPE 

Mr. ROSENTHAL. Mr. Secretary, you recently visited our troops in

Europe. How did you find their morale, their attitudes, their understanding of their mission, their military efficiency, and so forth? 

Secretary SCHLESINGER. I am glad that you asked that question,

Mr. Rosenthal, and I am happy to be able to report to you that in contrast to the situation the last time we talked on this subject, there has been a marked improvement in the discipline, the combat readiness, the morale and the understanding of the mission that those forces are to serve.

There has been a dropoff, for example, in letters going to General Abrams with regard to complaints from Germany. They may resume. 

Reenlistment rates for the units in Germany are up. The drug problem is under control.

I recognize that these issues do not necessarily impact on the larger issue which you have raised about the desirability of continued U.S. presence in Germany at as extensive a level as at the present time. However, it is reassuring to note that whatever the level of that involvement, the morale of the forces is high and they have a strong sense of mission.

There are many reasons for this dramatic change that I could go into.

U.S. SECURITY INTERESTS IN CAMBODIA 

Mr. ROSENTHAL. I wonder if you could briefly state for us-in light of the fact that you are proposing to give Cambodia $362 million in grant military assistance-what the strategic interest to the United States is in Cambodia, what the national security interest for the United States is in Cambodia, what the national interest of the United States is in Cambodia, and what, if any, special relationships we have with the present Cambodian Government. 

In other words, why are we doing this? 

Secretary SCHLESINGER. Our relationships with the Cambodian 

Government are those we would have with any friendly government that is under attack by insurrectionist groups. 

The national interest in the preservation of a free regime in Cambodia, is based on two considerations: First, the impact that a fall of that regime would have on the security of South Vietnam; and second, the significance that might be drawn in a psychological sense if nobody were prepared to assist in the survival of a friendly government under attack from the outside.

I think U.S. involvement has occurred as a result of both this narrow geographic context and the larger context of providing assistance to those governments that are will context of providing for their own protection. to

Mr. ROSENTHAL. Is there a national security interest that the United 

States has in the preservation of the present Cambodian Government? 

Secretary SCHLESINGER. I have indicated that. I think it is in the national interest of the United States that South Vietnam survive and the value of Cambodia's survival derives from its importance to the survival of South Vietnam.

INCREASE IN ARMS SALES 

Mr. HAMILTON. Mr. Secretary, I want to direct your attention to the enormous jump in U.S. arms sales. As I understand the figures, U.S. arms sales to foreign countries in the past 3 years far exceed the sales in the previous two decades. 

I also understand that U.S. arms sales far exceed those of any other country in the world, the Soviet Union or any other state; and in the case of Iran our cash sales in the fiscal year 1974 exceed the total worldwide cash sales for all countries in fiscal year 1973. 

Now, all of these statistics-and I have just picked a few at random-show not just marginal increases in sales of arms but enormous quantum jumps in the amount of military equipment that we are selling abroad.

It is happening at the same time that the defense budget is not declining or even staying level but is going up rapidly or at least sharply. 

I guess the question on my mind is: Why, at a time when we talk so much about the spirit of détente, when we talk about the fact that U.S. troops have withdrawn from Vietnam and when we are in a period of negotiation rather than confrontation-why do we see this tremendous increase in arms sales across the world. 

Secretary SCHLESINGER. I have put a slide on here that illustrates the point you are making, Mr. Hamilton.
