STATISTICS ON ARMS SALES 

Secretary SCHLESINGER. In 1974, arms sales totaled approximately $8 billion. Presumably that will affect deliveries that will take place over a number of years, and I suspect that the figure may recede in future years.

The numbers are reflected on that chart. 

Now the military posture of the United States is established to maintain- Mr. HAMILTON. Mr. Secretary, if I may interrupt at that point, I also included in my figures, I think, the cash sales which the Government has to approve, although obviously it is not part of the Secretary SCHLESINGER. That is included in the $8 billion. 

Mr. HAMILTON. That includes the military assistance program? 

Secretary SCHLESINGER. That is both credit and cash sales. The credit sales of last year, less the Israeli portion, were approximately a couple of hundred million dollars, as I recall it, so the balance represents cash sales of which the Iranian sales are a very large part. 

Now yours was a complex question and it has required considerable testimony before the Armed Services Committee and Appropriations Committee to discuss the U.S. defense budget. 

REQUIREMENTS FOR DEFENSE EXPENDITURES 

Let me say briefly that the U.S. expenditures for defense are designed to maintain a worldwide military equilibrium in which the United States, with the assistance of its allies, maintains forces that provide a balance against other existing forces that could be hostile. 

This means that the force structure of the United States and our military expenditures depend upon the capabilities external to the United States rather than the atmospherics of détente. 

I think there is a good reason for that; détente depends upon an underlying balance of military forces. 

If one did not have that underlying balance, one would not have a hope for the progress of détente. I could go on at some length, but that is sufficient, I think, to indicate why we structure our forces as we do. 

Generally speaking, the rise in the defense budget is roughly approximate to the increased cost of doing business in this period of inflation to which Mr. Gross referred. Expenditures of the Department will rise by about $62 billion next year, which is about a 71/2-percent increase.

ARMS PURCHASES BY IRAN 

With regard to arms sales, each situation would have to be reviewed in its own terms. To take the most notable of these, the Iran purchase, the Government of Iran perceives external problems on its western border where there have recently been clashes with the forces of Iraq, armed with Soviet-supplied materials. 

Mr. HAMILTON. Mr. Secretary, every country perceives threats and problems, but we are pumping billions and billions of dollars worth of arms into Iran in sales and no other country in that area of the

world has anything like that kind of military equipment flowing into it.

Secretary SCHLESINGER. Correct. 

Mr. HAMILTON. What are we balancing against so far as Iran is concerned? You have Iraq. You are not pretending Iraq can match the kind of military arsenal we are putting into Iran?

Secretary SCHLESINGER. As a matter of fact, the Iraqis have more tanks and more aircraft than do the Iranians. 

Mr. HAMILTON. Are they getting those from the Soviet Union? 

Secretary SCHLESINGER. Yes, sir.

SOVIET ARMS TO IRAQ 

Mr. HAMILTON. Are you suggesting the Soviet Union is putting in comparable amounts of money for arms into Iraq that we are putting into Iran? 

Secretary SCHLESINGER. We are putting no money into Iran. These are cash sales.

Mr. HAMILTON. Let's face the question in terms of military equipment. Are the Soviets putting the type of military equipment into 

Iraq that we are putting into Iran?

Secretary SCHLESINGER. In the case of tanks, they are indeed. There is also a comparability in certain areas of aircraft. In the more sophisticated aircraft, the Russians do not have the kind of quality in the equipment that they provide. 

Mr. HAMILTON. Do you see this pattern of $8 billion or whatever the figure is—is that going to continue now over the period of, say, 5 years, or so? 

Secretary SCHLESINGER. AS I indicated, I would expect the number to be about $4 or $5 billion in 1975. 

The reason the number was as large as it was this year was because of the modernization of the Iranian Armed Forces including the purchase of the F-14 aircraft, which was a billion-dollar sale.

ASSESSMENTS OF THE NAVAL BALANCE 

Mr. HAMILTON. May I also have you comment, Mr. Secretary, on the-what looks to me as if differing assessments coming from the Defense Department with regard to the naval balance? 

Admiral Moorer said recently, and I am quoting him, I think, directly, "That the Soviet naval capabilities are becoming more formidable every year," and Admiral Zumwalt has said, "The lines have crossed and the United States could no longer control the sealanes in time of war."

At the same time, we read a Defense Department study concluding that old age is overtaking a lot of the ships of the Soviet Navy and will also reduce their number considerably by the end of this decade. It appears to me, at least on the surface, that there is a differing assessment coming out of the Pentagon with regard to the naval balance. 

Could you comment on that, please? 

Secretary SCHLESINGER. Yes, sir. I am not sure there is that great a difference in the assessment. I think there are different facets of the

problem on which different people would place different degrees of emphasis. For example, the Soviet naval forces, as we see them in terms of surface competence, will probably slip between now and 1980 by about 15 or 20 ships.

The number of major surface combat ships, could therefore decline by about 10 percent. What you have is a growth of the capability of individual ships because of the placement onboard of antiship missiles. 

Thus, one might refer to the growing strength of the Soviet Navy if one were evaluating the combat capability of individual vessels, which offset the decline in numbers. But one should not equate the growing strength of the Soviet Navy to the growth of numbers of combatant ships.

The second point is that the U.S. Navy itself has declined substantially in numbers of commissioned general purpose ships from 951 in fiscal year 1968 to 522 in this year's budget. This is a source of disquiet to the Navy. Consequently, as they look at the balance, they notice that it has tended to shift in a way not favorable to the United States, although it is not clear that the United States does not continue to retain some margin of superiority.

Third, the United States and its allies, as I indicated in my statement, are dependent on the sealanes of communication in a way that the Soviet Union is not. Therefore, the mere denial of the use of the seas would be a disaster from the standpoint of our country and our allies. Consequently, we are vulnerable to a greater degree, and that is the point, I think, Admiral Zumwalt was stressing.

Mr. Buchanan.

Mr. BUCHANAN.  

MILITARY AID AND MILITARY SALES FIGURES 

Mr. Secretary, if I could see your chart correctly a moment ago, I believe, it showed a picture of descending levels of military assistance and ascending levels of foreign military cash and credit sales, is that correct? 

Secretary SCHLESINGER. Yes, sir.

Mr. BUCHANAN. So, that would indicate that the trend is for this: program to cost the taxpayers less money and to mean more in terms of sales and in terms of balance of trade and payments and so forth, is that correct? 

Secretary SCHLESINGER. That is correct. That is quite along the lines of the question that the chairman raised earlier. The trend is downward for grant aid. In real terms, the program has cost typically less and less over a great many years. 

Mr. BUCHANAN. Mr. Secretary, is it in our power to dictate to other governments of friendly countries what their national security interests may be and needs may be? Can we tell them they don't need to make these military expenditures and have any controlling voice in that situation?

Secretary SCHLESINGER. We cannot dictate to any sovereign state.

POLITICAL INFLUENCE AND MILITARY SUPPLIES 

Mr. BUCHANAN. Are we in better position to influence to whatever extent may be possible a state that is dependent on us for military hardware or one that we have rejected because we feel they want to spend too much money in that area?

Secretary SCHLESINGER. The degree of influence of the supplier is potentially substantial, and typically, those relationships are long enduring. It is for that reason that, when states wish to buy hardware, we prefer that it be American supplied rather than supplied by some state that may be hostile or indifferent to the same kind of objectives of American foreign policy.

IRAN Mr. BUCHANAN. In the case of Iran, for example, we depend heavily on Iran as an important source of oil to us. It is in our vital interest that we continue to import substantial quantities of oil from them. 

Could one reasonably say that this military sales program creates some kind of reciprocity of vital interests, since this is something they at least feel they need that we can supply, or is that too simplistic? 

Secretary SCHLESINGER. I think that is a very significant aspect of the situation. The relationship between the United States and Iran with regard to arms supplies is symptomatic of a very close relationship between the two Governments. If that close relationship did not exist, the arms relationship would not exist.

If we refuse to go on with the arms relationship, I think that close tie between our two Governments with regard to the security of the Persian Gulf and the maintenance of a military balance in the Middle East would be subject to erosion. 

Mr. BUCHANAN. I would like to echo what my colleague, Mr. Derwinski of Illinois, said a few moments ago, Mr. Secretary. I really think we would err if we do other than encourage those countries that have security and defense needs and military needs and who_are friendly to us to do business with us rather than with the French or the Soviets. It seems to me it cannot be in our national interest for them to become dependent on some other country in an area of supreme national importance to any country. Where we have other vital interests, such as our need for oil from Iran and our need to continue that good and longstanding friendly relationship, it does make especially good sense to continue this kind of posture.

I would like to echo what he said in support of that program and that idea. I also would like to commend the idea of moving from assistance to sales and credit. I think that is healthy for the taxpayers. 

MILITARY ASSISTANCE IN DOD BUDGET 

May I ask you another question along this line? How much money is in the Defense budget for military assistance, not in this? 

Secretary SCHLESINGER. The request in the Defense budget for 

"Military assistance service funded," which this year includes only South Vietnam, was for $1.450 billion in new obligational authority. 

That number was reduced in the recent vote to $1.126 billion, I believe.

Mr. BUCHANAN. Mr. Secretary, how would that compare, taking that total, plus the total in this bill, to what we were spending at the height of our direct involvement in the conflict in Southeast Asia!

Secretary SCHLESINGER. It is approximately one-twentieth, or about 

5 percent of what we were spending at the height, in terms of current dollars.

If you take into account the rise in prices, it is probably about onethirtieth, or one thirty-fifth-about 3 percent.

Mr. Wolff.

TURKEY AND DRUG ABUSE 

Mr. WOLFF. 

Mr. Secretary, I would like to read a statement, a short statement, and get your comments on it.

Winning the battle against drug abuse is one of the most urgent national priorities confronting the United States. I consider keeping dangerous drugs out of the United States just as important as keeping the armed enemy forces from landing in the United States. 

Would you like to comment on that statement? 

Secretary SCHLESINGER. I think that those are strong words on an important subject. 

Mr. WOLFF. Well, would you agree with them? 

Secretary SCHLESINGER. I certainly agree with their thrust, yes, sir.

Mr. WOLFF. Those are the words of President Nixon. I would like to get to a point that Mr. Hays alluded to on the question of the value of Turkey to the United States. We heard what they did during the 

Korean war.

ROLE OF TURKEY IN MIDDLE EAST WAR 

What did they do in the last war, the Middle East war? Were we permitted to use our airbases, were we permitted to land in Turkey at our airbases during that war? 

Secretary SCHLESINGER. I believe there were one or two flights in which- Mr. WOLFF. We were prohibited from landing, were we not? 

Secretary SCHLESINGER. Landings were on an emergency basis.

Mr. WOLFF. In other words, where we had to abort a flight, but as to our contribution of resupply to that Middle East struggle, we were not permitted to land in Turkey. Were we permitted overflights of Turkey's airspace during that time? 

Secretary SCHLESINGER. We had the same rights as anybody else with regard to Turkey's airspace.

Mr. WOLFF. It is my understanding and the statement was made before our subcommittee that we were not permitted overflights of Turkey. 

Secretary SCHLESINGER. I am not sure that is correct. 

Mr. WOLFF. Could you furnish that for the record? 

Secretary SCHLESINGER. I will furnish that for the record. 

[The information requested follows:] OVERFLIGHTS OF TURKEY 

Throughout the Middle East crisis Turkey permitted the US normal usage of the common defense installations which we and Turkey maintain in accordance with our defense responsibilities under NATO. Recognizing, however, the uncomfortable position in which Turkey was placed by the Arab-Israeli war, and because there were alternative routes and facilities available to us, the US did not seek landing or overflight privileges in connection with the US supply opera-

tion to Israel. Landings and overflights unrelated to that operation were not affected.

Mr. WOLFF. It is my understanding that, the Soviets, however, were permitted the use of the airspace of Turkey during that struggle. Is that correct?

Secretary SCHLESINGER. I think, what the Turks attempted to do in that period of time was to abide by the Montreaux Convention and by other conventions.

Mr. WOLFF. We have an overriding treaty with Turkey-we have a mutual defense pact with Turkey have we not? 

Secretary SCHLESINGER. Turkey is a member of the NATO Alliance, and the NATO Alliance calls on one member to come to the support of other members under circumstances in which the nation is under attack.

TURKEY AND NATO 

Mr. WOLFF. I surely do not think you could say that Turkey was of help to us in that Middle East struggle by adhering to another act, the Montreaux Convention, when we have a NATO Treaty with them and we have bases in Turkey, specifically to support our efforts whereever our interests happen to be?

Secretary SCHLESINGER. No, sir. The bases in Turkey have been established strictly to support NATO activities. This was not a NATO activity.

THE SUEZ ORDNANCE REMOVAL PROGRAM

Secretary SCHLESINGER. The easiest part of the task was sweeping the canal, which was done in large part by the U.S. Navy. That is completed.

Over the period since 1967, literally tens of thousands of weapons-landmines and that sort of thinghave been placed deliberately on both sides of the canal and in the waters of the canal. BENEFITS FROM CLEARING SUEZ CANAL

Suez Canal?

But the main point, Mr. Winn, that should be stressed is that the potential benefit to the United States of this action reflects a calculated risk that there will be a reorientation of politics in the Middle East that will be beneficial to the stability of that area.

The committee stands adjourned until further notice by the Chair. [Whereupon, at 12:25 p.m., the committee adjourned, to reconvene at the call of the Chair.] [Subsequently, the following questions were submitted by Congressman Gilman to the Secretary of Defense, who supplied answers as follows:] 

Mr. GILMAN. Essentially, how is the determination made in defining and classifying security assistance as a "grant" program or a "military sales" program for a specific country? What are the criteria and how are the priorities aligned... are the political considerations the highest priority, or ability to pay? What other factors are considered?

How do we go about assessing the validity of need for military sales or grants?

Secretary SCHLESINGER. In deciding whether to provide security assistance in the form of grants or credit sales, the primary consideration is the receiving country's ability to pay. As you probably are aware, this Administration desires to shift from grant aid to FMS credits wherever and whenever recipient countries are able to assume this added responsibility for their own defense. This policy is in accord with the Congressional purpose manifested in sections 505 (c) and 635(a) of the Foreign Assistance Act of 1961, as amended, and section 1, of the Foreign Military Sales Act, as amended. The ability to pay varies markedly, of course, between the prosperous nations of Western Europe and the developing countries of Asia, Latin America and Africa. It is worth noting that 

Taiwan, which was previously dependent on large amounts of grant aid, has been able to shift over entirely to a program of FMS cash and credit purchases. 

A similar transition is underway in Korea, Greece and Turkey and we hope to see increasing evidence of this shift in other areas as the prosperity of our underdeveloped defense partners increases.

Political factors also are taken into account. For example, friendly regimes may be faced with extraordinary defense problems resulting from insurgencies or terrorism or threats from hostile neighbors. These problems must be weighed against the recipient's ability to pay, the urgency of the situation in terms of regional or global stability, and-most important of all-U.S. defense interests. 

We have several means to assess the validity of potential recipients' needs for military grants or sales credits assistance. Overseas, military advisory and assistance groups and our defense attache offices are in close contact with the host governments and are able to collect extensive information on the local military situation as well as the specific strengths and weaknesses of the host governments armed forces. Our Embassies have political and economic officers who are able to provide complementary information against which purchase requests must be weighed pursuant to section 622 (b) of the Foreign Assistance Act of 1961, as amended, and section 2(c) of the Foreign Military Sales Act, as amended. Similarly, we are in communication with the diplomatic and military missions that the host countries maintain here in Washington. No grant assistance or sales credit assistance is furnished without extensive interagency consultation within and between Washington and our overseas missions. Whether a grant or loan is large or small, routine or extraordinary, the interagency consultation process inevitably includes the Department of State and Defense and frequently the Department of the Treasury, the Office of Management and Budget, and the Arms Control and Disarmament Agency.

FISCAL YEAR 1975 FOREIGN ASSISTANCE REQUEST TUESDAY, JUNE 11, 1974 HOUSE OF REPRESENTATIVES, COMMITTEE ON FOREIGN AFFAIRS, 

Washington, D.C.

The committee met at 10 a.m., in room 2172, Rayburn House Office 

Building, Hon. Thomas E. Morgan (chairman of the committee) presiding. 

Today we meet to hear Hon. Daniel Parker, Administrator of the

Agency for International Development, who will testify in support of the President's foreign assistance request for fiscal year 1975. 

Mr. Parker is accompanied by Hon. John Murphy, who is AID 

Deputy Administrator; Hon. Robert H. Nooter, Assistant AID Ad ministrator for Supporting Assistance; and Hon. Philip Birnbaum,

Assistant AID Administrator for Program and Policy Coordination. 

Gentlemen, most of you have been here on previous occasions. We welcome you here again today.

Mr. Parker, while you have testified here before on other legislation, I believe this is your first appearance before this committee in behalf of the overall AID program since you have become Administrator. If you wish, you may summarize your statement. That will allow more time for questions and answers. 

STATEMENT OF HON. DANIEL PARKER, ADMINISTRATOR, AGENCY FOR INTERNATIONAL DEVELOPMENT 

Mr. PARKER. 

I would like to submit a more complete statement and discuss it briefly.

First of all, I wish to apologize for bringing this request before your committee so late in the fiscal year. There were, however, certain events outside of our control-such as the recent initiatives in the Middle East and the world food shortage-which affected the timing and the nature of this foreign assistance request. 

Second, I wish to express my appreciation for the consideration you will be giving this bill. I realize that consideration of an aid bill is a time-consuming matter, but I feel that the need and urgency for the passage of this proposal fully merits your attention. 

Finally, I wish to say that I am more concerned with offering an open and constructive presentation of this bill rather than presenting what many have come to know as the standard defense of the aid 36-333-74- -7 (89)

bill. This Agency finds itself in agreement with this committee in many areas, ranging from the need to channel development assistance into key functional areas to the need for such a coordinating body as the Development Coordination Committee. 

FOREIGN AID: ESSENTIAL TO U.S. FOREIGN POLICY 

The central theme of our request is that U.S. foreign assistance programs are essential components of our foreign policy strategy for strengthening world peace and for expanding international economic cooperation in a rapidly changing world environment. 

The challenge to world peace is immediate, direct and urgent in the Middle East and in Indochina. If new Middle East relationships among the countries of the area are to emerge, external resources are needed to help establish the framework for cooperation with the nations of that area. By contributing to the processes of reconstruction and development, the United States not only accelerates these processes, it helps to build a system of international cooperation. 

Our request for economic assistance to Indochina reflects our conviction that assistance is necessary to continue the momentum of peace and that world peace is inextricably linked to this area. A serious deterioration of South Vietnam's economy because of inadequate aid would jeopardize the process of political accommodation and the ultimate peace. Such would, in fact, have a corrosive effect well beyond. 

Vietnam and Indochina.

But economic stability alone is not enough. Our assistance request is also designed to provide resources essential to accelerate the development process that will allow Vietnam to stand on its feet economically, to solidify Laotian peace, and to encourage political-not military-reconciliation in Cambodia.

THE "CHALLENGE OF INTERDEPENDENCE" 

We are faced with the challenge of interdependence because world peace is indivisible and all nations are participants in a single international economic system. The events of the past year-the energy crisis, food and raw materials shortages, the rapid rises in pricesclearly demonstrate the mutuality of interest of all nations, rich and poor, in an open international system with increasing levels of trade, investment and economic growth. Our development assistance programs will be the U.S. contribution to working out resolutions of these problems.

It is in the light of these considerations that I would like to briefly describe the authorizations for which we are seeking your approval. 

THE MIDDLE EAST 

In regard to the Middle East I would like to stress that we are not proposing that the United States alone help Egypt. We expect that the United States will join with and encourage others to participate in this task.

As to our request for a special requirements fund to permit us to respond effectively in support of our foreign policy to the rapidly

changing political situation in this area, we will be consulting with your committee on concrete uses before committing these funds. We hope that you will authorize this fund in full at this time. 

INDOCHINA 

The peace we seek in Indochina remains a fragile and tentative one with sharply different situations in Laos, Vietnam and Cambodia. 

Our immediate objective in Vietnam is to consolidate the gains for peace and stability. A stable military situation and eventual political accommodation cannot be achieved if South Vietnam's economic problems are allowed to get out of hand. The aid we request in economic and humanitarian assistance is essential to the economic stability and growth of the economy.

While the level of assistance proposed for South Vietnam is substantial, I want to assure this committee that we are actively working with our colleagues in the Department of State to put forward a 5year schedule for the phasedown of economic assistance to this country. We will submit this to Congress by August 1. Our objective will be to attempt to provide sufficient assistance in the next few years to permit the economy to grow to the point where its own economic strength will be adequate to carry it on in the future. 

NEW DIRECTIONS: FOOD AND NUTRITION 

In regard to development assistance programs we are in full agreement with your basic position that participation by the poorest majority is necessary for successful development. We clearly share your objectives and welcomed the new legislation as support for a restructuring of our assistance programs along lines we fully endorse. I believe real progress has been made.

In our major development assistance program category-food and nutriition-we are seeking a significant increase. The food supply situation in the world has forced me to conclude that we must do even more than we planned last year. AID has and will continue to move forward on many fronts to help the less developed countries increase their food production. Our fiscal year 1975 program, for example, shows its biggest increase for rural roads and irrigation systems. 

To undertake the food and nutrition programs at the proposed level would have been possible with a relatively small increase in our authorization amounts were it not for the decision of the Congress last year to cut in half the development loan reflows available for the AID program. It is in part to replace these funds that we must request a higher authorization level.

DEVELOPMENT COORDINATION COMMITTEE 

Aside from the organization of our own programs the act requires the President to establish a Development Coordination Committee to advise him with respect to coordination of United States policies and programs affecting the developing countries. Plans for implementation of this requirement have received a great deal of intensive study and are now under discussion within the executive branch. I hope to be able

MA to report to Congress on the decisions reached before the end of July. 

In summary, I come before you today to urge your support of our programs in the Middle East, Indochina and the developing world. 

But it is not only your support I request; I need your response urgently. We have done our part in building a foreign policy leading toward peace; we have linked our foreign assistance programs tightly to that peace policy; and instead of sterile confrontations, we have built a momentum of constructive negotiations which our foreign assistance programs will encourage.

I know that you support these initiatives and share with us—and with the world-the hope that the thrust toward peace will be maintained and brought to a successful conclusion. 

URGES RAPID CONGRESSIONAL ACTION 

When the present fiscal year comes to a close, Congress will fund ongoing AID programs through a continuing resolution. A simple continuing resolution cannot support our new initiatives, however. 

Rather, to avoid losing the momentum we have managed to create in resolving international tensions and to move quickly to other areas of major U.S. concern, it will be necessary to have a continuing resolution which specifically takes account of our new programs in the Middle East and the funding levels necessary for Indochina and for food and nutrition. To permit us to urge such a course on the Appropriations 

Committees of the Congress, we must have the concrete demonstration of your policy support in the form of a completed authorization legislation prior to the end of the fiscal year. 

You have unique authorities, thus I suggest, the Congress also has unique responsibilities. It is both important and timely that the 

Congress and the executive branch join in a manifest consensus in support of foreign policies committed to peace. We are faced with a unique set of circumstances where the need is urgent and where your role is crucial to the accomplishment of our foreign policy objectives. 

I earnestly ask for your prompt and favorable action.

DANIEL PARKER, ADMINISTRATOR, AGENCY FOR INTERNATIONAL DEVELOPMENT Mr. Chairman and Members of the Committee: Last week Secretary Kissinger testified before you in support of the President's full request including security programs for new appropriations of $4.2 billion for FY 1975 under the Foreign 

Assistance Act. Today I would like to review with you those social and economic programs for which the Agency for International Development is responsible economic assistance components of the Middle East program, the Indochina Postwar Reconstruction program, and the worldwide development assistance programs and for which we are requesting a total of $1,685 million in new authorizations to permit a total program of $2,842 million. The Secretary of 

Defense has testified on the Military Assistance programs and the Foreign 

Military Credit Sales programs. 

The central theme of our request is that U.S. foreign assistance programs are essential components of our foreign policy strategy for strengthening world peace and for expanding international economic cooperation in a rapidly changing world environment.

The challenge to world peace is immediate, direct and urgent in the Middle East and in Indochina. If new Middle East relationships among the countries of

the area are to emerge, external resources are needed to help establish the framework for cooperation with the nations of that area. By contributing to the processes of reconstruction and development, the United States not only accelerates these processes, it helps to build the system of cooperation. 

Our request for economic assistance to Indochina reflects our conviction that assistance is necessary to continue the momentum of peace and that world peace is inextricably linked to this area. The serious deterioration of South Vietnam's economy which inadequate aid would cause would jeopardize the process of political accommodation and the ultimate peace. Such would in fact have a corrosive effect well beyond Vietnam and Indochina. But economic stability alone is not enough. Our assistance request is also designed to provide resources essential to accelerate the development process that will allow Vietnam to stand on its feet economically, to solidify Laotian peace, and to encourage political-not military-reconciliation in Cambodia. 

We are faced with the challenge of interdependence because world peace is indivisible and all nations are participants in a single international economic system. The events of the past year-the energy crisis, food and raw material shortages, the rapid rises in prices-clearly demonstrate the mutuality of interest of all nations, rich and poor, in an open international system with increasing levels of trade, investment and economic growth. And our development assistance programs will be the U.S. contribution to working out resolutions of these problems.

It is in the light of these considerations that we come to the Congress to seek authorizations for programs of the Agency for International Development for the fiscal year 1975 and appropriation of the necessary funds for their accomplishment. I would like to describe the authorizations for which we are seeking your approval.

THE MIDDLE EAST 

We are requesting a total of $477,500,000 in economic assistance in direct support of our foreign policy initiatives in the Middle East, including $100 million as a Special Requirements Fund. Of this amount $250 million is for Egypt. Most of these funds would be devoted to reconstruction in the war-damaged areas of the Suez Canal: $20 million to complete mine and ship removal from the canal and $150 million for reconstruction, notably of the devastated cities, in the canal area. The additional $80 million in loans will be used to finance essential imports from the U.S. to help Egypt restore its economy. 

I would like to stress that we are not proposing that the United States alone help Egypt. We expect that the United States will participate with others in this task. We expect, and are encouraging, the World Bank to provide a useful framework for coordination among a substantial number of donors including West Germany, Japan, Kuwait and Iran who have already indicated a willingness to participate. Of course, the Egyptians themselves will have to provide most of the funds for reconstruction; foreign assistance can only be a useful supplement. 

Our request includes $50 million for Israel in the year ahead, as in this year. 

These are economic funds, of course, and in addition to the military programs you have been discussing with others. The request also includes $67.5 million for budget support for Jordan and $10 million to be used to help further the development of the Jordan Valley. The national budgets of both Israel and 

Jordan have been distended by the costs of defense allocations. The addition of funds for development projects reflects Jordan's own desire to begin to shift from budget support to development. 

Finally we are requesting $100 million for a Special Requirements Fund to permit us to respond effectively in support of our foreign policy to the rapidly changing political situation in this area. As Secretary Kissinger has said, no commitment has been made to Syria for these funds, although some of them might well be used there. We will be consulting with your Committee on concrete uses before committing these funds, but we hope that you will authorize this Fund in full at this time. 

INDOCHINA POSTWAR RECONSTRUCTION 

We are requesting authorization for almost $940 million for Indochina, including $750 million for South Vietnam, $110 million for Cambodia and $55.2 million for Laos. This represents a significant increase compared with fiscal year 

1974 and I would like to explain why this increase is necessary. The principal

difference is a positive one-we believe that opportunities now exist for major productivity improvements in South Vietnam.

The peace we seek in Indochina remains a fragile and tentative one with sharply different situations in Laos, Vietnam and Cambodia. Our immediate objective in Vietnam is to consolidate the gains for peace and stability. A stable military situation and eventual political accommodation cannot be achieved if South Vietnam's economic problems are allowed to get out of hand. The aid we request-$750 million-in economic and humanitarian assistance is essential to the economic stability and growth of the economy. In the past year, South 

Vietnam has experienced problems over which it had very little control-sharp decline in dollar revenue following the withdrawal of our troops, and world 

At the peak of our involvement in the war, Vietnam's dollar earnings from U.S. Government activities ranged between $350 and $400 million a year. 

Last year, following the withdrawal of U.S. troops this figure dropped to just over $100 million.

At the same time, the costs of Vietnam's imports soared as global inflation boosted the prices of raw materials and semi-finished products. 

South Vietnam has done an excellent job of adjusting to these challenges. It initiated a dramatic austerity program, increased tax collections, and raised exports. But its foreign exchange reserves have fallen dramatically, and substantial assistance is still necessary. 

In South Vietnam, a major portion of the $228 million allocated for the recor.struction and development program will go to expand agricultural production through irrigation and fertilizer projects. Other funds will go for the importation of agricultural and industrial raw materials. Thanks to these importations, factories can continue to produce, farms can be returned to productivity, homes can be lit and meals can be cooked. In other terms, jobs will be provided and basic consumer goods will be available. 

South Vietnam clearly has the potential for economic growth. It has natural resources, extremely fertile land and an industrious population. It has been a net exporter in the past and could be one again. We are carefully directing our efforts toward that end.

At the same time, we hope to increase our economic assistance for refugees and children by more than 50% to $135 million, including an increase in our child care programs. Our goal is to assist South Vietnam to return refugees to economic productivity as soon as possible.

While the level of assistance proposed for South Vietnam is substantial, I want to assure this Committee that we are actively working with our colleagues in the Department of State to put forward a five-year schedule for the phasedown of economic assistance to this country. We will submit this to Congress by 

August 1. Our objective will be to attempt to provide sufficient assistance in the next few years to permit the economy to grow to the point where its own economic strength will be adequate to carry it on in the future. To accomplish this objective it will be necessary to ask and receive from Congress aid levels of the magnitude of this year's request only for a relatively brief period. But without rather sizeable inputs at this time, we do not believe it will be possible for the economy to grow enough to become self-sustaining within a reasonable period of time. Rather it will just "stagger along" year after year into the future. 

Our request for Cambodia will permit us to continue a commodity import program of $71 million and humanitarian assistance for refugees and others displaced by the continuing fighting. The $20 million for humanitarian assistance will support the activities of voluntary agencies such as CARE, Catholic Relief Services and the International Committee of the Red Cross in their activities on behalf of refugees and will also be used for refugee resettlement. Cambodia without the burdens of war has excellent prospects for development, given the high productivity of its agriculture sector, but little economic progress can be expected while the fighting continues placing a million or more of its people as refugees on welfare rolls because they are precluded from lives of productivity. 

Our assistance will help the economy survive the present difficult period. 

In Laos, the United States supports the political solution now evolving. We seek with our economic assistance to help Laos make a successful transition from the disruption of war to the fruits of peace. But Laos is a very poor country and

economic development will be slow at best. To assist we plan to continue our contributions to the multilateral Foreign Exchange Operations Fund which helps Laos finance its imports and to increase our humanitarian assistance for refugees. A substantial task of resettlement lies ahead as the Lao political solution evolves. Thus, $15 million is proposed for refugee and humanitarian assistance. 

We are also planning to use about $4 million for reconstruction. 

DEVELOPMENT ASSISTANCE 

This Committee last year went to great effort to spell out its views on development assistance programs. We are in full agreement with your basic position that participation by the poorest majority is necessary for successful development. Our foreign assistance policy has long been predicated on the belief that successful development will enhance the ability of developing countries to participate cooperatively in international systems of trade, finance, investment and other matters that are important to all of us and, in fact, indispensable in our present world of interdependence and mutuality of interest. To the extent that we can assist in giving both disadvantaged people and nations a sense that they are participating in and sharing the benefits of worldwide economic growth we are also contributing to the elimination of sources of international conflict and the potential for our involvement in them. At the same time, this "poorest majority," these hundreds of millions of villagers and urban slumdwellers are, of course, the people Americans have always wanted to benefit from our efforts in the developing countries. 

I would like to emphasize that little progress would have been realized in reorienting our programs if there were not a very large measure of identity of views between A.I.D. and the Congress. We clearly share your objectives and welcomed the new legislation as support for a restructuring of our assistance programs along lines we fully endorse. I believe real progress has been made. 

We do face some real constraints, however, in trying to move faster in the new directions. Overseas we cannot forget that basic decisions about development will be made by the developing countries themselves. We can persuade, but only they can decide. While many developing countries are convinced of the need to involve their millions of small farmers and businessmen in development, they are uncertain about how to proceed. 

At home we must try to resolve the dilemma posed by the fact that your Committee and we wish to follow directions which are inherently staff intensive while other forces upon us seek to impose reductions of manpower and support costs. Similarly, research designed to permit us to make significant breakthroughs in the principal assistance sectors is restricted by limitations on the funds we may allocate for this purpose. 

Nevertheless, we have made real progress in shifting the program content of 

A.I.D.'s Development Assistance program. In FY 1973, Food, Rural Development, and Nutrition accounted for only 24% of A.I.D.'s program, and this sector plus the other two new appropriations, Population Planning and Health and Education and Human Resources, accounted for only 50% of our total program. In 

FY 1975 Food, Rural Development and Nutrition is projected to be 60% of our program, and the three sectors together will be no less than 90%. The following table reflects these changes.

This leads me to our third requested authorization-an increase for Food and Nutrition to $546,300,000-an increase of $255 million. Knowing that your Committee had authorized funds for these programs for two years, I am naturally reluctant to ask you to reconsider and raise the amounts, but the food supply situation in the world has forced me to conclude that we must do even more than we planned last year. For the first time in the history of man, the totality of the world's ability to supply food has been challenged by the totality of the world's need to consume it. As Secretary Kissinger recently said at the 

United Nations: "For countries living near the margin of starvation, even a small reduction in yields can produce intolerable consequences." 

Because most of the arable land in the developing world is already being cultivated, increased yields will need to come from higher output per acre. This means involving a quarter of a billion small farmers in the Third World. But real progress is possible since in most developing countries foodgrain output per acre is less than 1,500 pounds and in some it is less than 1,000 pounds, even on land which could produce two or three times more. In Taiwan and South 

Korea, for example, foodgrain output averages more than 3,000 pounds per acre, which compares with productivity in the developed nations. 

A.I.D. has moved forward on many fronts:

Our FY 1975 program shows its biggest increase in funds for rural roads and irrigation systems, essential basic infrastructure for more productive agriculture.

Programs to improve local governments will continue in Latin America and Asia.

A.I.D. will support farmer cooperatives in countries in all three continents. 

Projects relating to the organization of local agricultural market areas and market towns will be implemented in nine countries in Asia and Latin America.

In addition, we have continued to pursue vigorously a number of other activities not specifically cited in the legislation but designed to contribute in other ways to increased food production now and in the future. These include improving access to seeds, fertilizer and pesticides, agriculture planning and management assistance and continued research. For all of these programs we intend to devote no less than 60% of our Development Assistance resources. We believe we should program $676 million for this purpose, compared to $285 in FY 1974. 

To undertake programs at that level would have been possible with a relatively small increase in our authorization amounts were it not for the decision of the Congress last year to cut in half the development loan reflows available for the A.I.D. program. It is in part to replace these funds that we must request a higher authorization level. To meet the program needs and undertake new initiatives in this area, we have determined to place all of these additional resources in the Food and Nutrition category. 

While we are not requesting any increase in our authorization for the other functional categories, I would like to report briefly on the other assistance categories. They have, in fact, important bearing upon the sector above in both direct and indirect ways.

Nearly half of the 2.5 billion people in the developing countries are under the age of 15 and have most of their fertile years ahead. The implications are clearthe present population of nearly every developing country will double in the next 18 to 30 years. Major efforts are needed now if the population assistance program's objective of sharply reduced population growth rates is to have any chance of realization.

The effects of rapid population growth are becoming more widely understood. 

Aside from the obvious impact on the availability of food, high fertility means poorer maternal health and higher infant mortality, slower growth in per capita income, labor force growth outpacing jobs, and ever increasing numbers outstripping all resources available for basic health and education services. 

A.I.D. with specific support and direction from the Congress has provided worldwide leadership in focusing attention on this most critical problem. 

Today A.I.D. provides population assistance directly or indirectly to 70 nations. We are working through bilateral, regional, and interregional channels and through multilateral and private institutions. Even so, the greatest challenges are yet to be met. Exclusive of China, less than 15% of the LDC population

is now reached by any kind of effective health-related services, and, more specifically, even less are reached with family planning services. 

To make population planning and also health and nutrition programs more effective, we are working hard on low-cost, integrated delivery systems aimed primarily at rural populations. These systems are based on the use of paramedical personnel working under the supervision of qualified physicians. Through training programs and the supervision of doctors, their skills and the quality of medical service can be raised considerably. A.I.D. expects to expand this program from 8 to 21 countries by the end of the fiscal year. 

The FY 1975 population program, in addition, supports country and interregional programs which concentrate on (1) assistance in collecting and analyzing demographic and social data as an essential tool for determining appropriate population policies and programs; (2) the training of medical and paramedical personnel, administrators and others in scientific, technical, managerial and informational aspects of family planning programs; and (3) essential research on fertility behavior and better birth control techniques adapted for LDCs. One area of special study is a better understanding of the economic, social, and cultural factors affecting decisions regarding family size. 

The Agency's health program, at $88 million, is focused on low-cost health delivery systems, health planning and environmental health. The impact of disease on productivity is often startling. Over two-thirds of the people in developing countries suffer from intestinal diseases. Such diseases frequently have debilitating effects. Onchocerciasis (river blindness) simply prevents the use of some of the most fertile river valleys in Africa, since people cannot live in them. A.I.D. programs will attempt to reduce the risk of these and many other diseases prevalent in the poor countries of the world. 

In the third of the new sectors, Education and Human Resources Development, A.I.D. gives special emphasis to devising techniques of non-formal education as a way of reaching tens of millions of people not now being reached through the formal school system. Several projects appear to offer great potential in this field. In Guatemala, for example, radio and picture posters are being combined to bring agricultural extension to illiterate farmers. In the Philippines, villagers themselves are being used as extension agents. They work with government officials in various technical fields and serve as the communications link between trained personnel and the village communities of which the agents are residents.

Hopefully, though the pursuit of such projects, we can meet the problem of expanding the impact of education of poor countries at less than the cost of formal education and at the same time make education more relevant to the needs of the developing countries. 

Not all activities which are essential for development fall precisely within our three main areas of program concentration, as you recognized last year by creating the Selected Development Problems category. There are some countries where electric power generation, railroad construction, industrial development or urban development may be the critical problems to be addressed. Science and technology support can be crucial in some areas. The continued possibility of addressing these problems-even with relatively limited resources-is clearly important to our shaping development programs to the specific needs of assisted countries.

In the Selected Countries and Organizations category we have sharply cut back our program lending. Instead, we are concentrating on increasing the contribution of U.S. private and voluntary organizations to economic and social development in the developing countries. For several months members of my staff and I have been holding extensive discussions with these private and voluntary organizations to develop new and fundamental concepts of organization of relationships. Recently over 150 of them met in Washington to assess these new ways of working better together. I have also approved the use of $5 million for strengthening the development capacity of these organizations and $6 million for overseas programs which they sponsor and manage. They can thus serve as development associates of A.I.D. Other funds in this category will be used to assist multilateral organizations, especially in Latin America, in their development programs.

Aside from the organization of our own programs, the Act requires the President to establish a Development Coordination Committee to advise him with

respect to coordination of U.S. policies and programs affecting the developing countries. Plans for implementation of this requirement have received a great deal of intensive study and are now under discussion within the Executive Branch. I hope to be able to report to Congress on the decisions reached before the end of July.

In summary, I come before you today to urge your support of our programs in the Middle East, Indochina and the developing world. But it is not only your support I request; I need your response urgently. We have done our part in building a foreign policy leading toward peace; we have linked our foreign assistance programs tightly to that peace policy; and we have built a momentum of constructive negotiations, instead of sterile confrontation, which our foreign assistance programs will encourage. I know that you support these initiatives and share with us-and with the world-the hope that the thrust toward peace will be maintained and brought to a successful conclusion. 

When the present fiscal year comes to a close, Congress will fund ongoing A.I.D. programs through a continuing resolution. A simple continuing resolution cannot support our new initiatives, however. Rather, to avoid losing the momentum we have managed to create in resolving international tensions and to move quickly in other areas of major U.S. concern, it will be necessary to have a continuing resolution which specifically takes account of our new programs in the Middle East and the funding levels necessary for Indochina and Food and Nutrition. To permit us to urge such a course on the Appropriations Committees of the Congress, we must have the concrete demonstration of your policy support in the form of completed authorization legislation prior to the end of the fiscal year. 

You have unique authorities, thus I suggest, the Congress also has unique responsibilities. It is both important and timely that the Congress and the Executive Branch join in a manifest consensus in support of foreign policies committed to peace. We are faced with a unique set of circumstances where the need is urgent and where your role is crucial to the accomplishment of our foreign policy objectives. I earnestly ask for your prompt and favorable action.

Chairman MORGAN. Thank you, Mr. Parker. 

INCREASED REQUEST FOR DEVELOPMENT AID 

Mr. Parker, last year the administration requested and Congress approved a 2-year authorization for development assistance, including nearly all that the administration requested for food and nutrition assistance. As you know, this bill has a very difficult time getting through the House on a 2-year basis. We were able to hold a 2-year authorization for the economic part of the bill in the Senate and in conference, and the President signed the bill into law last December 17.

Now it turns out that in the President's budget, submitted to Congress in January, AID was seeking a large increase in development assistance for fiscal 1975 above the authorized ceiling. 

Mr. Parker, when was this decision made-was it made in December last year, or January, or when-that AID would want to go above the fiscal year 1975 authorization ceiling? What do you think is the point of Congress setting a 2-year authorization, if you come in the second year with an increased request? Could you tell the committee why you are here asking for this increase?

Mr. PARKER. Yes, Mr. Chairman. 

The budget process, I think, explains a good part of it. I would like to point out that at the present time, we are sending to the field the request for our fiscal 1976 budget proposals. This same sort of cycle in leadtime existed before.

At that time, it was not known that the Foreign Assistance Act of 1973 as passed would include a 50-percent reduction in the utilization of revenues from prior loans. The difference in amounts requested is approximately that.

Second, the real effects, Mr. Chairman, of the world food crisis, were really being felt during that period when the minimal budget was being put together; when we were doing our debating within the administration on it, we were beginning to feel the real pressures of the price increases in some of the needed commodities such as fertilizer and the limitation of availability.

These are the principal factors, Mr. Chairman, that have led to this. 

We appreciate the fact of the 2-year authorization. I was naturally reluctant, I still am, and I apologize for having to come back and ask for an increase. But I think the circumstances warrant it.

FOREIGN AID FROM OIL-RICH ARAB STATES 

One more question: Last week David Rockefeller was quoted as estimating that the oil cartel countries will receive $100 billion a year for their oil exports, of which they will spend some $40 billion for goods and services.

This leaves $60 billion as a surplus for reinvestment. That is 15 times as much as the $4 billion they had in surplus in 1973. Has any effort been made to interest these oil cartel countries in reinvesting some of this money in an aid program, especially in the Near East? 

Mr. PARKER. Yes, sir. There have been many efforts, Mr. Chairman. 

I will be very candid with you; I think, at the present time there has been more effort than results. But I think we are getting closer. 

May I take a moment to put into perspective something I think we have to recognize in the oil producer's outlook and attitude toward this? This is something that is rather disanalogous to our experience as Americans, where we have grown up and lived lives on the premise that we have replenishable assets, and as we use them, we can look to other parts of the world, and that we are never going to run out of anything. While the oil producers look at their assets principally as the oil and knowing that this is a nonreplenishable asset, this, then, they consider to be their endowment for the future. 

So, first, I think, we have to recognize that they have a certain sensitivity as to how this asset is dispensed and as to how it is converted into their own future security.

Second, they simply have not had the experience of living within Western institutions. They happen to have the upper hand in these fund availabilities. But I think it is in the best interest of all of us to attempt to develop means whereby they can feel the confidence in institutions that will serve their long-term interest.

MEANING OF "MOMENTUM OF PEACE"

What do you mean by momentum of peace? What momentum of peace do you see in Indochina, and are you suggesting, if peace fails in Indochina, there will be a world war?

Mr. PARKER. Not directly. I suggest there is a momentum for peace. 

In Laos, for example, there is a status of political reconciliation. 

There has been an effective cease-fire, and I think, there is a great deal of basis for hope that that situation will continue. 

Most of the forces, foreign forces that were in Laos, have withdrawn. There has been a reduction in the levels of North Vietnamese, although far from a total withdrawal. The casualties in Vietnam are a third of the level that they were before. I think there is a momentum for peace, sir. 

Mr. GROSS. You say, at the bottom of page 2, "To encourage political, not military reconciliation in Cambodia." How is our aid going to encourage political reconciliation in Cambodia?

Mr. PARKER. By enabling the Cambodian Republic to remain in place and to resist the attacks of the Khmer Communists.

If they can

survive these attacks-which I suggest they are devastating in a humanitarian way, random fired rockets into cities-I am hopeful that the Communists and their backers in Hanoi and elsewhere will decide that they simply cannot afford to continue that kind of effort toward a military takeover.

THE MIDDLE EAST: DOLLAR DIPLOMACY

Mr. PARKER. Yes, sir, it has. There may be, just to be accurate, a pipeline of some public safety equipment, but I think they are all 36-333-74- -8

Mr. FRASER. Would you be able to provide a detailed response on this for the record? 

[The information requested follows:] TERMINATION OF POLICE AND PRISON ASSISTANCE IN VIETNAM 

After the signing of the Vietnam Ceasefire Agreement in January 1973, AID terminated all advisory assistance to the National Police (NP) and the Directorate of Corrections (DOC). By the end of CY 1973 all other AID support for 

DOC ended. Up to the date of the enactment of the FY 1974 foreign assistance legislation, AID's direct assistance to the NP was limited to training police personnel outside Vietnam and providing commodities in the pipeline financed from prior year funds.

Upon enactment of the legislation, AID immediately took a series of actions to conform with the legislative prohibitions on police or prison-related activities. 

AID terminated all advisory services to the Combined Telecommunications 

Directorate (CTD).

AID has terminated participant training of police personnel. 

The Prime Minister's Computer Center will no longer process police or prisonrelated data systems. 

AID terminated any further AID-financed Commodity support to the NP and CTD, except for commodities in the pipeline against which firm orders or contracts with suppliers have been placed which cannot be cancelled. 

AID is terminating its role as an agent for the DOD in the documenting, processing and monitoring of DOD-financed commodity and budgetary support to the NP and CTD. DOD is assuming responsibility for commodities in the pipeline against which firm orders have been placed which cannot be cancelled. 

All remaining funds are being deobligated and returned to the DOD. 

In sum, AID has terminated or is terminating all activities in support of police and prisons in Vietnam in compliance with the Ceasefire Agreement and the FAA of 1973. The detailed status of each activity follows. 

DIRECT HIRE ADVISORS 

1. Direct hire advisory assistance to the National Police (NP) terminated 3/28/73. 

2. At the time of the enactment of the FAA of 1973, AID had nine direct hire advisors working with the GVN's Combined Telecommunications Directorate (CTD). The last of these advisors departed post on 3/28/74.

CONTRACT ADVISORS 

1. At the time of the enactment of AID's current legislation, AID was managing six contracts in direct or indirect support of police or prison-related activities. 

The present status of these contracts is as follows. 

A. Quinton-Budlong, Inc. (AID 730-3231) provided 5 U.S. radio technicians to 

CTD, This AID-funded contract was terminated 3/21/74. 

B. Far East Technical Services (AID 730-3491) provided 20 TCN technicians who furnished operational and repair services to CTD. This AID-funded contract was terminated 3/31/74.

C. Computer Sciences Corporation (Navy 00600-71-D-1090) provided 37 U.S. 

and 11 Vietnamese computer system advisors to work with the Prime Minister's Computer Center. Only one task order, No. 7, assisted NP in development of 7 operational data systems. This task order was terminated on 5/20/74. The remaining task orders dealt with war veterans, Central Reconstruction Development Council, technical writing, contract management, etc., but were not related to NP activities in any way. This DOD-funded contract was terminated on 

6/13/74. Further, the GVN agreed to transfer all police and prison-related data systems from the Prime Minister's Computer Center to another computer facility which is not receiving AID assistance. It is anticipated that this transfer will be accomplished by 7/1/74.

D. South East Asia Computer Associates (SEACA AID 730-3618) provided 11 

U.S. advisors to assist the Prime Minister's Computer Center (PM/CC) in developing instructors capable of training Vietnamese programmers and systems analysts working in the PM/CC. This AID-funded contract which has no NP involvement terminates 11/8/74.

E. SEACA (AID 730-3519) provided 8 technicians to teach management to 

PM/CC staff. There is no involvement with the NP in this AID-funded contract which will terminate 8/20/74.

F. SEACA (AID 730–3486) provided 6 U.S. technicians to assist GVN agencies in transferring data systems to the PM/CC. There is no involvement with the NP in the remainder of this AID-funded contract which will terminate on 8/3/74. TRAINING 1. At the time of the enactment of the FAA of 1973, AID planned to train approximately 64 NP personnel in general police administrative subjects and 200 in computer system management. Only 26 of these 264 scheduled participant training programs were actually implemented. The last 2 NP participants completed their long term training program in traffic management and departed on June 17, 1974. All training of police personnel in the U.S. or third countries has ended. 

2. All English language and office skills training for police personnel at the 

USAID Staff Development Center in Saigon was terminated 4/10/74.

COMMODITIES 

1. At the time the current legislation was enacted, AID was scheduled to provide $520,000 in FY 74 for commodity support of the CTD, while the DOD was scheduled to finance a total of $10.6 million in commodity and budgetary support for the NP and CTD. Of this total, only $526,453 in DOD funds has not (and cannot) be deobligated. 

2. On 1/11/74, AID suspended the placing of both AID and DOD-funded commodity orders in support of NP and CTD except for commodities which were already in the pipeline prior to the enactment of the FAA of 1973. Aid is processing only those procurement actions against which firm orders or contracts with suppliers have been placed which cannot be cancelled. 

3. AID is terminating its role as an agent of the Department of Defense (DOD) in documenting, processing and monitoring DOD-funded commodity support for the NP and CTD. DOD is assuming responsibility for those commodities in the "pipeline" against which firm orders or contracts with suppliers have been placed which cannot be cancelled. All remaining DOD funds are being deobligated and returned to the DOD. 

4. NP, CTD and DOC have been removed from the list of eligible recipients of 

CIP-funded commodities. 

5. NP, CTD and DOC can no longer acquire in-country excess property. 

6. AID no longer serves as procurement agent for the GVN-funded procurement for NP, CTD or DOC. All remaining GVN-owned Dollar funds held in-trust by 

AID will be returned to the GVN as soon as confirmation is received that firm orders with suppliers have not yet been placed. 

7. NP can no longer receive U.S.-supplied commodities from the GVN's Medical Logistics Warehouse. AID has established screening procedures to prevent the NP from requisitioning U.S.-funded medical supplies. 

8. AID is terminating its commodity assistance to the GVN's Repair Parts Depot of the Central Logistics Agency and to the Province Maintenance System of the Ministry of Interior since the automotive spare parts provided to these facilities are used in the repair and maintenance of NP vehicles. GVN funds held in-trust by AID which were used to finance these parts are being returned to the GVN as soon as confirmation is received that firm orders with suppliers have not yet been placed.

BUDGET SUPPORT 

1. At the time of the passage of the FAA of 1973, the GVN had budgeted 1.2 billion piasters in support of NP and CTD with piasters which were to be purchased with DOD dollars. The GVN, DOD and AID agreed to delete these funds from the Foreign Aid Chapter (FAC) of the GVN National Budget for CY 1974. 

Thus, DOD-funded support for the NP and CTD was eliminated from the GVN's budget for CY 1974.

2. AID is terminating its role as agent for the DOD in documenting, processing and monitoring DOD-funded budgetary support for the NP and CTD. Funds budgeted for prior years will be reimbursed in accordance with existing agreements with the GVN. 

3. Early in CY 1973, well before enactment of AID's present legislation, AID agreed to the GVN's use of $100,000 worth of GVN-owned local currency generated from C.I.P. sources to support the budget of the DOC. This local currency assistance terminated 12/31/73.

Mr. FRASER. With respect to the police training program under the 

Office of Public Safety, what specific ways would you say that program has been helpful to the U.S. interests abroad? 

Mr. PARKER. Mr. Fraser, are you referring to the

Mr. FRASER. Police training program. 

Mr. PARKER. We are maintaining the International Police Academy, and I am proposing that you give specific consideration to the authorization of its ongoing function. As to its relationship to U.S. national interests, I think, it is basically related to our interests in civil and individual liberties and rights. 

I think that, the more professional a police force is, the less political it is, and the more effective it is.

POLICE TRAINING IN AUTHORITARIAN STATES 

Mr. FRASER. Would you agree, then, that police training in an authoritarian government is probably wrong for the United States to pursue, since such governments obviously are not according civil liberties and civil rights?

Mr. PARKER. I think, one has to look at each country on an individual basis as to the premise that you start with, as to whether it is an authoritarian government. Basically, I think individual rights are better assured through more professional police competence.

Mr. FRASER. In countries like Brazil and in Chile, there seem to be documented cases of systematic violations of human rights, and the police appear to be involved in this. Do you believe it is in the interests of the United States to be associated with the training of the police forces for those Governments? And if you do, I would like to have you tell me how you think it advances our interests.

Mr. PARKER. I think, from having looked at some of the curriculums of the International Police Academy, that it would be desirable for police anywhere to understand the emphasis that the curriculums give to individual rights and civil liberties. 

Mr. FRASER. Those civil or human rights are being deprived by the 

Government. What does it mean in these countries to have the U.S. 

Government train the army of the government to make possible, therefore, the deprivation of those rights? How does that advance our interests?

Mr. PARKER. I think, we start from different premises. I am starting from the premise that police who are trained and thoroughly understand the importance of these rights will be less willing to carry out such activities.

Mr. FRASER. If you have any evidence that in fact that is what happens in totalitarian societies, I would appreciate receiving it for the record.

Mr. PARKER. I would be glad to submit, for example, some statements that were made by some of the graduates. I would not restrict it to what you have said as to totalitarian governments. 

[The information requested follows:] STATEMENTS BY IPA GRADUATES ON EFFECTS OF PUBLIC SAFETY TRAINING Deputy Commander Ecoundayo J. Mahoney, Gambia, May 24, 1974 Graduation Ceremony, representing English General Course No. 46 stated: 

"Our course was well planned and covered practically all the principles of modern police activities. We soon realized that although our police forces may function differently because of the laws of our lands, the major concepts of good policing are universal, particularly with respect to the harmonious relationship which must exist between the police and the community. This Academy is making great strides in disseminating these fundamental principles. It is contributing to world's understanding by making it possible for a large number of countries to participate in its courses, and by advocating, above all, cooperation and mutual respect among nations. We do recognize, however, that the power of the police to fulfill their functions and duties is dependent on public approval of their actions, and on their ability to secure or maintain public respect. This we shall seek not by being overindulgent but by constantly demonstrating impartial service to all without regard to wealth or social standing; by being always courteous and friendly; and by ready acceptance of individual sacrifice in protecting life and property."

Deputy Chief of Police Tony Torralba Teves, Philippines, October 12, 1973 Graduation Ceremony, representing English General Course No. 42 stated: 

"I like to think that the training provided at the International Police Academy during the past four months, and the exchange which took place between the participants have not only imbued us with new knowledge, new experiences and a new wisdom but have also increased our capabilities as human beings and as policemen. For it is a truism that the best policemen of any law enforcing agency and of any race or country are those who, above all, are real human beings endowed with such virtues as honesty and integrity, a sense of fairness and justice, compassion and love for their fellow men; those who contribute to the realization of the dreams and aspirations of their countries and their peoples; those who believe that international peace can only be achieved through international friendship and understanding."

Lieutenant Felipe Pena, Dominican Republic, May 5, 1972 Graduation Ceremony, representing Inter-American General Course No. 59 stated: 

"Four months have elapsed since we came to this hospitable country-months of deep reflection on the mission and destiny of our law enforcement organizations which are so misunderstood by the citizenry whose security, life, and property we strive to protect. We became impressed here with the urgent necessity to establish a frank and effective dialogue with the public in order to express factually, but in a dignified way, our delicate task of controlling unlawful behavior within the framework of human rights and individual freedom." 

Assistant Commissioner Basdeho Tapesar, Mauritius, November 5, 1971 Graduation Ceremony, representing Senior Officer Course No. 13 stated: 

"I can therefore give you the assurance that all of us have benefited in no small measure from all that has been unfolded to us and I feel sure that when we go back to our respective countries, mindful of the welfare of our peoples, we will diffuse with renewed vigor and self-confidence the new ideas, techniques and concepts we have acquired here. Among these stands out the necessity for all the police forces of the free world to work together, and to establish a climate of mutual understanding between their organizations and the public they serve. 

This is perhaps the most important aspect of our responsibilities in our endeavor to make this world a better place for all of us to live in." 

POLICE POWERS AND U.S. INTERESTS 

Mr. FRASER. That is the point I am trying to make. One of the things that is important to people about government is the power the government exercises over their lives, the power to arrest, the power to enforce laws, the power to punish. When we train the instrumentality which carries out these policies of an authoritarian government which is depriving people of rights, how can that promote the interests of the United States? Mr. PARKER. As I said, I think we begin on different premises. I could cite, Mr. Fraser, the case in Thailand when the Government fell some months ago. There were many of the police officials who had received training through the U.S. assistance program. And I think there was general consensus throughout the world that Thai police were the most effective in achieving a balance in seeing to it that individual rights and liberties were protected not only those of demonstrators but of society in general. 

ROLE OF WOMEN IN DEVELOPMENT 

Mr. FRASER. Why is it that the agencywide working group established to accelerate AID's efforts to help the rural poor share in development had no women among those planning what to do in the developing countries?

Mr. PARKER. We are taking quite an assertive approach to the involvement of women in the objectives of a society under development.

We have worked quite closely with Senator Percy in the objectives which he espouses and quite genuinely so. I think the key premise that we operate on, which maybe indicates our feelings better than anything else, is that we have communicated to our missions and to our field staff, as well to our people in AID, Washington, that development programs should not simply assume that women are going to play the full and proper role in the society, but we must assertively see to it that women are given the opportunity to play a full role as development occurs.

INVOLVING SMALL FARMERS VERSUS IMMEDIATE FOOD NEEDS 

Mr. FRASER. One last question. Of the $675 million for food, rural development, and nutrition-which is the amount proposed for this coming fiscal year-how much of it will be for programs which were emphasized in the new AID legislation last year: Small farm agriculture and broad-scale rural development? How much for that purpose as against how much would be used for getting the most food grown over the next year or two? Is there a conflict here between the purpose of getting food grown and the desirability of involving small farmers in broad-scale programs? 

And how is this conflict resolved, if there is one?

Mr. PARKER. I would say the two are very compatible rather than conflicting. In certain instances there might be a trade off. When in doubt whether short-term food assistance is required, if there has to be a trade off against meeting the longer term development, I think our natural inclination is to trade off in favor of enabling people to survive. But the objectives are very complementary because basically many of the poorest of the poor are people who live on a subsistence basis. Now their subsistence is based on basically their own food production.

If we can address this problem which is the main thrust of the legislative directions which I think we both feel very strongly about, then we can begin to cure this problem not only for those people directly involved but for the rest of the people in their own societies. 

So these, in fact, are basically oriented toward the poorest of the poor and the increase in their capability to produce food.
