[The information requested follows:] OIL-PRODUCING COUNTRY CONTRIBUTIONS TO THE MIDDLE EAST 

Contributions of the oil producing countries to the Middle East, in the form of 1974 bilateral commitments and pledges to special multilateral institutions, as reported in the press, are estimated to exceed $3 billion. Egypt can be expected to receive at least $900 million of this total. A sizable share of these totals can be expected to be disbursed over several years, possibly as long as five or more years since the estimate includes pledges to newly proposed but not yet operational special multilateral institutions. 

Publicly announced contributions through bilateral assistance programs and funds amount to roughly $1 billion as of mid-June. Substantial additional unannounced amounts are believed to have been provided to the countries affected by the recent hostilities. Iran recently extended an $870 million aid package to 

Egypt for the reconstruction of the Suez canal area. Syria has received a $50 million loan from Iraq. The United Arab Emirates have announced loans of $36 million to Bahrein, Egypt, Mauritania, Somalia and Tunisia. The Abu 

Dhabi Fund for Arab Economic Development has approved a $22.5 million loan to Arab countries. Major beneficiaries include Syria, Egypt and Jordan. The 

Kuwait Fund for Arab Economic Development has extended loans of $10 million and $14 million, respectively, to Tunisia and Yemen. The Kuwait based Arab 

Fund for Economic and Social Development recently extended approximately $66 million in loans to Algeria, Egypt and the Sudan. Egypt will receive $22 million of this total. Saudi Arabia and Kuwait have been and may continue to be extending both balance of payments support and now reconstruction assistance to Egypt, Syria and Jordan on a substantial scale. 

Non-oil Middle East countries are also expected to be major beneficiaries of the proposed multilateral institutions such as the Islamic Development Bank and the OPEC Special Fund. Iran has pledged $150 million to the latter institu-

tion. The Islamic Development Bank with a proposed capital subscription of $1 billion is charged with the responsibility of promoting economic development in Islamic, mainly Middle East countries. 

Middle East countries can also expect to be major beneficiaries of the proposed $3.1 billion increase in the authorized capital of the Kuwait Fund for Arab 

Economic Development which is now under consideration.

[The following additional comments were supplied:] COMMENTS ON REPROGRAMING 

First of all, Mr. Hamilton, let me emphasize that we are very anxious to keep the Congress fully and completely informed regarding all aspects of our program. 

I appreciate your concern regarding what may appear to be unusually large swings in the program from the time it is presented to the final allocation of funds. This is also of concern to me and I am anxious to improve our ability to more accurately forecast our needs. However, I think it is important to note the numerous uncertainties which influence the composition of the program during the year. The budget cycle, as you know, is extremely long and many of the activities which we will fund in FY 1975 were developed up to two years prior to the date of final obligation. During this period there can be substantial changes in political and economic circumstances-the energy situation for example-and we need the flexibility to tailor the program to these circumstances. In addition there are technical uncertainties—a feasibility study may not prove out or an aid recipient may decide that it does not wish to support a project. Also, Congress may enact new provisions which require adjustment in program emphasis as was the case this year.

I believe it is also appropriate to point out that there are already restrictions on our ability to readjust our program without Congressional knowledge. For example, Section 114 of the Appropriation Act now requires that we notify the Appropriations Committees five days in advance before obligating funds for any activity. A major effect of the revised language is that the Congress must be notified in advance of all activities, loan or grant, that are to be undertaken with funds in any of the specified appropriations. Specifically, in all cases involving reprograming of funds for activities not contained in the Congressional Presen-

tation, descriptions of the activities are sent to the Appropriations Committees in both Houses of Congress. The Congress is thus informed before the fact of all activities undertaken. 

There are numerous other statutory requirements and restrictions which limit our ability to readjust our program. For example there are explicit limitations on both our research and population programs. There is also a limitation on the total size of the Agency's grant program. In addition to this distinction between loans and grants, we now have five functional categories based on program purpose. This is a substantially tighter appropriation framework than the old development loan, technical assistance matrix. I should also mention that last year 

Congress removed authority for the Agency to utilize the Section 610 transfer authority to move funds out of the five functional accounts. In addition, we are required to provide numerous and extensive reports to Congress on our activities. 

To mention just a few: each year we notify Congress of disposition of funds following appropriation action (the 653 Report) at the close of the year we provide a report comparing the actual to the proposed program for the year and explain deviations: (634d Report). We also notify Congress on the use of all funds generated from deobligations.

For all of the above reasons, I do not believe that further restrictions on our funding processes are necessary or desirable. Because the development assistance effort is inherently uncertain, we need modest flexibility to adjust to changing circumstance.

DISPROPORTIONATE AID DOLLARS TO INDOCHINA 

Mr. HAMILTON. I am struck by the percentage of our total worldwide economic assistance here that goes to Indochina. 

As I calculate the figures on the basis of your summary tables, the total worldwide economic assistance for fiscal year 1975 is something like $3.9 billion, and roughly $1.2 billion of that goes to three countries, Cambodia, Laos, and Vietnam, which is roughly 30 percent of the total amount, if my figures are roughly right, and I think they are. 

It strikes me that we are putting a very disproportionate amount of the total dollar into one relatively small area of the world, and I wonder how you react to that.

Latin America and Africa, for example, and other areas of the world where you may have really a better opportunity for development than you do in Southeast Asia today are therefore slighted. 

Mr. PARKER. Again I would have to say, Mr. Hamilton, you do not necessarily have better opportunities for development. Personally I have been very impressed with the potentials for development in South Vietnam. I would not want to have the impression left that I do not see these opportunities. I think the Vietnamese people are inherently productive and capable people. They have a productive land. It has been war-damaged. They have extraordinary needs, and I think that this is a commitment that we have, but more importantly than that I think the commitment is justified to make these investments there, and I think they will in fact, as I hope the figures we submit in August will show, that South Vietnam will move to a position of being much more capable of standing on its own feet. [Following are further questions submitted by Mr. Hamilton, together with answers supplied by Mr. Parker:] 

$900 PLUS MILLION AID PACKAGE 

Mr. HAMILTON. The Administration has introduced a $900 plus million aid package for the states involved in the Arab-Israeli conflict. What effort is the

State Department undertaking to encourage other states and international institutions to take part in the reconstruction effort? 

Mr. PARKER. Several other countries have already indicated their intentions to take part in the reconstruction effort. Among Middle East countries, Saudi 

Arabia, Kuwait and the United Arab Emirates have given Egypt and Syria grant assistance totalling at least a billion dollars. Iran has offered soft loans for various projects in Egypt. We are encouraging the IBRD to play a coordinating role for this assistance in addition to providing funding from its own sources. At the present time, the IBRD is actively seeking participation in a $188 million effort to provide equipment needed by the Suez Canal Authority to put the Canal into operation after clearing is completed. We expect the IBRD to finance $50-$70 million of this package. 

Mr. HAMILTON. Do you envisage another Middle East aid package that size next year?

Mr. PARKER. I would be frank to say that we do see this as a beginning. We have yet to reach any decisions at all on next year, but I would expect that we will be proposing further assistance. 

Mr. HAMILTON. What consideration is the United States giving to the creation of a Middle East Development Bank to coordinate international efforts and assure participation by others?

Mr. PARKER. We believe the IBRD is in the best position to coordinate participation among interested countries. The Bank can draw on its experience as a lending institution and on its experience in coordinating aid to a number of 

LDC's around the world.

SUEZ CANAL REOPENING 

Mr. HAMILTON. The U.S. has made a commitment to spend about $30 million in FY 1974 and 1975 to help open the Suez Canal. Some Pentagon officials, however, say that an open canal is a strategic plus for the Soviet Union. Why then, is it in our interest to help open the canal? 

Mr. PARKER. Secretary Kissinger commented on this earlier. We do believe that re-opening the canal should be viewed in the broader context of U.S. interests. It is a practical step toward an overall settlement in the area, and enhances both the interests of the U.S. and those of the other countries in the region as well.

RECONSTRUCTION OF SUEZ CANAL CITIES

But let me ask another question. You mention the $20 million and $150 million. Then you say there is an additional $80 million in loans. 

How do we decide, or how does your Department decide, what will be a grant-I presume these other amounts are grants. 

Mr. LAGOMARSINO. And what will be a loan?

Mr. PARKER. That is based on the assumption there is a distinction between productivity and reconstruction from war damage. These commodity imports are related to production and therefore should be able to generate over a period of time the capability of repayment of them. The war damage and the Suez cities area we believe should be on a grant basis at this time.

Mr. LAGOMARSINO. Was there a commitment to Egypt for this money?

Mr. PARKER. No, sir, there was not a commitment, but it was discussed openly in the press when the budget was sent over. I think it is certainly not a commitment at all.

Mr. LAGOMARSINO. There was not a commitment as far as you know between Secretary Kissinger and the President of Egypt? 

Mr. PARKER. I can say that Secretary Kissinger is quite well aware of the authorities of Congress, and he has told me he did not make a commitment. 

$100 MILLION "SPECIAL REQUIREMENTS FUND" 

Mr. LAGOMARSINO. Could you tell us a little more about this $100 million for a special requirements fund? What would that be used for?

Mr. PARKER. First, let me put it into the context of the nature of negotiations within the Middle East. As Secretary Kissinger described it, it is a step-by-step negotiation. The area has become so entwined in its emotional difficulties that a decision was made some time ago that it would be impossible to try to settle the entire complex. 

Therefore, the focus was to be upon issue by issue at the time to avoid, frankly, having to delay the submission of this budget. We did not know what the next step was going to be.

I don't know at the present time, and I don't think Secretary Kissinger knows, what the next step after this is going to be. 

This is the reasoning underlying it. We simply don't know. We have seen success in the utilization of the step-by-step approach. 

First, the Egyptians and the Israelis, and now the Syrians. 

Mr. LAGOMARSINO. Last week Secretary Kissinger told this com mittee, and he made the statement elsewhere, that no commitment was made to Syria, but my recollection was that there is some money in the bill of Syria. Am I correct in that?

Mr. PARKER. Well, there is none in the bill, and there was none designed into the bill for Syria, and there was no commitment made to

Syria, but this does not mean that if you do authorize these special requirements funds and if Syria were to request it, and if they were to comply with conditions which would make it logical and resultful for stabilizing the area, then some might be directed to that. 

Mr. LAGOMARSINO. I understand that, but my understanding had, been that we were being asked for $100 million for Syria. 

Mr. PARKER. No, sir, that is not corrcet.

A 5-YEAR PLAN FOR SOUTH VIETNAM 

Mr. LAGOMARSINO. You talk on pages 5 and 6 about a 5-year plan for 

South Vietnam, for Southeast Asia in general, I guess. Do you have any idea now as to what that schedule is going to be, what you are going to recommend?

Mr. PARKER. We are in the process now of making this. This is the result of an amendment offered by Senator Humphrey to the State Department authorization bill, and with which we are in agreement. 

We have indicated that we would respond to this. 

I think it is important and desirable, frankly, to put this into perspective. I don't see it as hopeless, and I think it would give us an opportunity to expose and explain why. 

You must, of course, realize that it has to proceed from certain assumptions, one of which is the level of military activity and another is the assumption of the initial inputs. I could discuss either of these at greater length if you would like.

SPECIAL REQUIREMENTS FUND: BLANK CHECK? 

Mr. GROSS. What then is the purpose? If the $100 million special requirements funds is not for Syria, what is the purpose of this blank check?

Mr. PARKER. It is not a blank check because we are firmly committed to consultation with the Congress before it is committed.

Mr. GROSS. So you want the money, and then you will come to Congress later and tell us what the hell you want it for, is that correct?

THE SPECIAL REQUIREMENTS FUND Mr. DU PONT.  

Mr. Parker, I would like to go back to this $100 million fund if I could and talk a little about what your restrictions are. You could use that for Egypt, am I correct? 

Mr. PARKER. Yes, sir, it could be used for Egypt. 

Mr. DU PONT. Could it be used for Syria as well?

Mr. DU PONT. Libya? 

Mr. PARKER. By definition we have tried to or by lack of definition we have tried to leave it open to those components of the Middle East where it might be most effective in assisting in the step-by-step process of negotiation to reduce the hostilities and focus on peace. 

Mr. DU PONT. But you basically could use that for any Middle Eastern country that you felt could contribute to a stabilization in the 

Middle East?

Mr. PARKER. Yes, I presume it would be subject to the same prohibitions on trade with Cuba and North Vietnam and other such countries. 

Mr. DU PONT. You cannot use it outside the Middle East? 

Mr. PARKER. No, sir, that is correct.

Mr. DU PONT. Mr. Parker, I don't have any objection to the administration having available funds to use on a quick response basis in this area or that where it would be helpful, but I do wonder about using funds like that to start up brand new programs, that is, programs with countries to which we have no commitment now and give no aid to now. Don't you think under those circumstances that before you commit that money, you ought to come back to Congress?

Mr. PARKER. Yes, sir, and this is provided for in what I said and 

Secretary Kissinger has said. We expect to have a program of continuing consultation about the entire area. 

"CONSULTATION" ON NEW PROGRAMS 

Mr. DU PONT. Your word "consultation" makes me uneasy. You still have the money if we appropriate it. 

Mr. PARKER. Yes, but I think we know where it comes from and if we ever want to get more, we know we have to be responsible for it. We do intend to keep the Congress involved and we intend prior notification and consultation, not of just the specific, but as well of the general circumstances leading up to any utilization of the funds. 

Mr. DU PONT. So you think you can say that before starting a new program with an additional nation such as Syria or Libya, to take two examples, that you would come back to this committee?

Mr. PARKER. This is our intent, Mr. du Pont. 

U.S.-OWNED EGYPTIAN CURRENCY 

Mr. DU PONT. If I could explore another area, how much Egyptian currency does the United States now own, roughly? 

Mr. PARKER. About $270 million.

Mr. DU PONT. Can't this currency be used without a further appropriation by Congress to do such things as reconstruct the cities around the Suez and so forth?

Mr. PARKER. We have to look at what local currencies really are. I don't know the technicalities, but I could certainly find out. From a practical economic standpoint, unless these resources were to attract new resources or be augmented by additional resources, their use would simply be inflationary. In some cases, they would be able to be used, but I think not significantly in major amounts. In some local situations

I think some things could be accomplished using those funds, like labor and reconstruction efforts, but obviously they would not cover the cost of imports, unless you can find somebody who would accept Egyptian pounds as payment. 

Mr. DU PONT. I would appreciate some perhaps further investigation by your staff to see how much of the work proposed to be done with the $250 million for Egypt might be done with currency that we already own.

Mr. PARKER. The thrust of your question is very appropriate and we certainly will and do in all cases look at how we can utilize U.S.-owned local currencies.

MULTILATERAL AID AND OPENING SUEZ 

Mr. DU PONT. One final question before my time expires. Isn't the opening of the Suez Canal a perfect place to use multilateral aid? 

Mr. PARKER. Yes, sir, and this is going to be required. You have to look at this in three stages. The first stage, which is essentially complete now, is removing the unexploded ordnance and the things that actually preclude people from using the area. 

Second is raising of the ship hulks that were sunk in the area. 

Third is the dredging where the banks have fallen in and where the bottom has shallowed to enable the canal to get back to the pre-1967 level of capacity.

Now that third stage is the costly one. The current estimates-and I don't know how precise they are-I think they have been made by the World Bank, range up to $400 million. At the present time we are not indicating any contributions beyond phases I and II from the United States. I believe something over $200 million is already firmly pledged by the World Bank, by Japan, by Germany-there may be some others, such as Kuwait, so this estimate up to the $400 million investment is required to get it back to pre-1967 capacity. 

Mr. DU PONT. These commitments have already been made?

Mr. PARKER. I don't know if they are signed documents, but they are certainly pledges.

AID TO INDIA 

Mr. Parker, how can we justify $75 million for India based on their poverty plea when they just spent $175 million to explode a nuclear device?

Mr. PARKER. Let me, first, say I would be the last one in this town to debate the fact that the Government of India is a debatable government. I think they have done a number of things that a number of people would not agree with. 

Mr. WILSON. Can you think of one friendly gesture they made toward the United States in the last 5 years?

Mr. PARKER. I can think of a lot of things the Indians have done. 

I am not sure I am prepared to answer about the Indian Government, but the focus I would like to put on our aid intentions would be to help

the Indian people, who are fine people. They are people burdened with terrible poverty. There are over 580 million of them and I think that we are possibly going to see some very significant shortages of food in their country.

Mr. WILSON. Did you notice they are about to enter into some sort of agreement with Egypt to build arms and munitions factories in Egypt? 

Mr. PARKER. No, sir, I did not know that. 

Mr. WILSON. Do you think that might be relevant to this, their real chauvinistic attitude they developed the last couple of years. They are no longer the passive peaceful society down there it once was. I think we had better realize that.

Mr. PARKER. No response. 

Mr. WILSON. I think we had better get back to the nuclear device, too. 

Mr. PARKER. I do not endorse the fact they have exploded a nuclear device. 

Mr. WILSON. You don't think there is any conflict between us, our

Government giving them this money and them expending $175 million to set off a nuclear device?

Mr. PARKER. I don't think there is interchangeability of the funds. 

So if that is an implication, I would debate that. 

If our request were approved and appropriated, the assistance we propose for India would be rather directly related to their food production and improvement in their fertilizer production. 

Mr. WILSON. Then that would free other funds they might have to use for their own food for them to spend on perhaps a delivery vehicle for the nuclear device.

Mr. PARKER. I am not so sure our aid is fungible in that way. Our commitment of funds for development also draws Indian money into development. Further, I think there are other constraints which would naturally apply to developing a delivery system which would be very expensive. I think the diversion of plutonium is certainly clearly within their capability, but any that might be supplied by the United States is clearly controlled under international safeguards. 

I am sure others are going to be quite mindful of controls on diversion of any plutonium generated from their supplied atomic materials. 

Mr. WILSON. Are we absolutely certain that no heavy water of plutonium or anything furnished by the United States, are we certain this did not go into this nuclear device?

Mr. PARKER. I have inquired and been told our controls which follow the ground rules set by the International Atomic Energy Agency are sufficiently tight that this is virtually impossible. I cannot personally attest to that.

REPROGRAMING FOR FISCAL YEAR 1974 

Mr. WILSON. Would it be possible for you to furnish this committee for the record a reallocation that took place in line with Mr. Hamilton's questions on 1974; in other words, tell us the countries that did not get the funds that were appropriated and tell us which ones did get the funds? 

Mr. PARKER. Yes, sir, you will get quite a list, because when you go from the budgetmaking process to the actual final appropriations

there are many, many changes. It might be more confusing than helpful. Would you like to specify what areas you really would like to know about, so we can isolate those or give you the whole thing? 

Mr. WILSON. I particularly would like to know what Cambodia, Laos, and South Vietnam got over and above what was appropriated and which countries they essentially came from? 

Mr. PARKER. That is the problem that we get into, because if you look at all of the reductions and all of the increases, I can show you where it comes out. But as to a direct linkage-this simply does not exist.

Mr. WILSON. But if we furnished you with a list of specific countries that we thought got less than Congress intended, you could tell us how much they got? 

Mr. PARKER. Yes, sir, I think it would be best to give you the full list of changes, increases and decreases, and then proceed from there. [The information requested was supplied subsequently and is in the appendix, see pp. 949–53.]

INCREASES FOR ISRAEL 

Mr. WILSON. One final question or subject. I generally support, I think, the $250 million for Egypt for the reasons you stated and that Mr. du Pont brought out, but the basis for that is the damage and the strain on the economy caused by the war essentially? 

Mr. PARKER. Yes, and damages actually incurred in war. 

Mr. WILSON. Israel's economy suffered seriously because of this war too. I notice that there is no increase whatsoever for Israel. The same $50 million that is sort of the usual procedure, whereas there is a significant increase for Egypt, $100 million for contingency funds which everybody assumes will go to a serious increase for Jordan. This does not seem to me to be an evenhanded approach. 

Mr. PARKER. I think we have to look at it in perspective. There is a significant amount of military assistance proposed this year. Second, I think we have to look at it in perspective of the large amount that was provided additionally last year.

Mr. WILSON. But that was all arms. We are talking about the economy now and Israel's economy probably suffered as much as Egypt did because of this war. It was seriously stalled. It would seem to me that there should be some notice made of Israel's economic loss due to the war. 

Would your Department, do you think, object seriously if this committee were to perhaps raise the amount of money that Israel is to receive somewhat equal to that of Egypt?

Mr. PARKER. No. I would have to say that, on the basis of our analysis of the economic situation in the entire area, we do believe this is an adequate amount. I would also point out the projection for the future would indicate that Israel with a considerably smaller population and its resource base will probably require increasing amounts in years ahead.

BUDGET ACCOUNTING FOR VIETNAM 

Mr. WHALEN. It seems you are asking here for $750 million, so on that basis it would appear that very little of that is raised locally by the Government of South Vietnam; is that correct?

Mr. PARKER. Not all of that goes to Government expenditures. A significant portion of what we are proposing will go into refugee resettlement, into the private sector, financing rural agricultural financing institutions.

Mr. WHALEN. Do I understand you then, Mr. Parker, to say this is not considered a part of the efforts which otherwise would have to be taken by the Government of South Vietnam? Let me put it another way. If the Government of the United States did not undertake this effort, would it not then fall to the Government of South Vietnam to do so? 

Mr. PARKER. I am afraid they could not do so if it requires revenues which they do not have and foreign exchange availabilities which they do not have.

Mr. WHALEN. From an accounting standpoint, then, should we not add this to the total budget of the Government of South Vietnam because, indeed, it is a governmental effort while in part these funds

may be handled by private organizations. Certainly they come from government; namely, our Government. 

Mr. PARKER. I would not debate that money is fungible. 

Mr. WHALEN. Let's go back, then, and recompute this figure of $873 million. If you add what the United States gives to the private sector of the economy, what would the total be?

[The information follows:] VIETNAM BUDGET 

In CY 1973, total Vietnamese governmental expenditures were 504.1 billion piasters. Of this amount, the Vietnamese government provided 328.1 billion piasters from its own sources, while the U.S. contributed 176.0 billion piasters. 

The GVN's share was primarily raised through striking gains in domestic tax collections which comprised about 80 percent of total government revenues and consist of various kinds of excise and income taxes. In CY 1973, collections in this category rose in terms of current prices 149 percent over 1972. During the first four months of this year there was a 100 percent increase computed on the same basis. Adjusted for inflation, the 1973 increase was 50 percent and the increase so far in 1974 comes to 25 percent.

[The information requested follows:] AID COMPLIANCE WITH HELMS AMENDMENT RE ABORTION The so-called "Helms Amendment" and the A.I.D. Policy Determination to implement it follow. Generally, we feel that the Policy Determination covers both the intent and spirit of the amendment. That is the way we will implement it. 

POLICY DETERMINATION RELATIVE TO ABORTION-RELATED ACTIVITIES INTRODUCTION 

Section 114 of the Foreign Assistance Act of 1961, as amended, adds for the first time to this legislation restrictions on the use of funds relative to abortions. 

The new provision read as follows: 

"Section 114. Limiting use of funds for abortion-None of the funds made available to carry out this part (Part I of the Act) shall be used to pay for the performance of abortions as a method of family planning or to motivate or coerce any person to practice abortions."

The indicated policy positions represent the best legal and policy judgment in A.I.D. on a desirable stance the Agency should have at this time relative to this subject. The A.I.D. policies relative to abortion dealt with here involve the following programmatic aspects-Procurement and Distribution of Equipment; Institutional and Program Development; Motivation, Promotion, and Training; 

Research; Fees for Abortion Services; and Coercion. 

1. Procurement and distribution of equipment 

A.I.D. policy. No funds available to carry out the Foreign Assistance Act will be used to procure or distribute equipment provided for the purpose of inducing abortions as a method of family planning. 

2. Institutional and program development 

A.I.D. policy.-A.I.D. funds will not be used for the direct support of abortion activities in LDC's. However, A.I.D. may provide general population assistance

A program support to LDC's and institutions so long as A.I.D funds are wholly attributable to the permissible aspects of such programs. 

3. Motivation, promotion, and training 

A.I.D. policy.-A.I.D. does not and will not fund information, education, training, or communication programs that seek to promote abortion as a method of family planning. A.I.D. will finance training of developing country doctors in the latest techniques used in OB-GYN practice. A.I.D. will not disqualify such training programs if they include pregnancy termination wth the overall curriculum. However, A.I.D. funds will not be used to initiate or expand the pregnancy termination component of such programs, and A.I.D. will pay only the extra costs of financing the participation of developing country doctors in existing programs. Such training is provided at the election of the participants. 

4. Research

A.I.D. policy.-A.I.D. will continue to support research programs designed to identify safer, simpler, and more effective means of fertility control. This work includes research on both foresight and hindsight methods of fertility control. 

5. Fees for abortion services

A.I.D. policy.-A.I.D. funds are not and will not be used to pay women in the less developed countries to have abortions as a method of family planning. Like wise, A.I.D. funds are not and will not be used to pay persons to perform abortions or to solicit persons to undergo abortions. 

6. Coercion

A.I.D. policy.-Pursuant to the Foreign Assistance Act and A.I.D. policy, A.I.D. 

activities in family planning and population assistance to developing countries cannot incorporate coercive features relative to the practice of family planning or any mode thereof.

Mr. ZABLOCKI. I am sure we have your assurances that no substitutes or changes will be made in the Helms amendment without consultation with Members of Congress who are particularly interested in the matter. Am I correct? 

Mr. PARKER. You are correct. You have my assurance that we will consult with interested Members of Congress in the event that any important change in this policy is contemplated. 

IMPLEMENTING CONGRESSIONAL REFORMS IN AID 

Mr. ZABLOCKI. There was mention by others of the new directions that were contained in the foreign aid legislation passed during the last session of Congress. I am sure you are personally committed to carrying out the approach developed and embodied in the legislation passed last year which seeks to involve the poor in the development process. Can you tell us generally what you have already done and what you are planning to do, to translate the congressionally mandated policy and the rhetoric into full program changes? Can you submit for the record a more detailed explanation of the steps you are taking along these lines? 

Mr. PARKER. Yes.

Chairman MORGAN. Without objection it is so ordered. 

Mr. PARKER. I appreciate the opportunity to do so. 

[The information requested follows:] TRANSLATION OF NEW DIRECTIONS ASPECT OF LEGISLATION INTO ACTUAL PROGRAM CHANGES 

We certainly agree that simply broadcasting the new approach contained in our legislation will not have a significant impact on our programs. A wide range of actions is necessary. These include policy guidance in each of the

three major functional areas ranging from general guidelines to specific changes in operating procedures, covering the first steps in the design of projects and programs in the field through the Washington review process, to implementation and evaluation. It also involves taking the new approach into account in the selection, orientation and training of AID staff, consultants and contractors. We have issued general strategy papers and more detailed policy guidance in several of the functional areas and we plan to follow this up with additional guidance. We have also established special task forces charged with recommending changes affecting the full range of Agency operations indicated above. 

The budget guidance that was sent to the field in the spring of 1972 and which started the program currently being implemented in the current fiscal year stressed program concentration and some of the themes which Congress emphasized in the FAA of 1973. In October, 1972, we issued a Policy Determination on 

Employment and Income Distribution Objectives for A.I.D. Programs and Poli cies. This was followed by FY 75 Program Guidance in spring, 1973, which stressed the three functional areas and quite specifically endorsed the approaches that the Congress was deliberating. In the summer of 1973 we instituted an Accelerated Program Development effort to assure priority funding to field missions submitting new programs in these areas. Strategy papers have been issued for education, health and nutrition and more detailed policy guidance messages have been issued for education, health, family planning and small farmer credit programs. These initiatives received strong reenforcement from the new legislation and from the recently issued FY 1976 field budget submission guidance.

Three task forces charged with making recommendations on AID policies and operations dealing with various aspects of the new directions have been estab lished. These groups are (1) a New Initiatives Task Force, (2) a Working Group on the Rural Poor, and (3) a Percy Amendment Working Committee. The recently created New Initiatives Task Force is charged with examining and recommending ways in which the operational policies and procedures of AID can be changed so as to more effectively implement the legislation's call for emphasis on programs addressing the needs of the poorest majorities in developing countries for improved food and nutrition, health and family planning, and education and manpower development. This task force is directly responsible to our Senior 

Operations Group headed by the Deputy Administrator, Mr. John Murphy.

The Working Group on the Rural Poor was established earlier this spring to make recommendations on how AID programs can more effectively and directly address the needs of the rural poor, who typically constitute both the largest population group and the poorest of the poor in developing countries. The working group, composed of rural development experts drawn from every bureau of the AID Washington organization, is divided into subcommittees addressing such aspects of the problem as organization, staffing, research, policy and analysis. The subcommittee dealing with policy and analysis has obtained the assistance of experts from U.S. universities and research institutions to help draft strategy and policy papers dealing with the various aspects of rural development mentioned in both the House Foreign Affairs Committee Report on the new legislation and our FY 75 Congressional Presentation. These papers are to be completed by the end of this summer in order to guide our field missions as together with host countries they develop projects and programs for FY 76. 

The Percy Amendment Committee is finalizing a report which contains recommendations for my consideration and action on program, staffing and organizational changes designed to implement the Percy Amendment's call to take into account in our programs the integration of women into national economies. 

Finally, as I have already noted in my statement, we have been involved in an intensive effort to inform and strengthen the capability of AID-assisted private and voluntary organizations to focus their programs in developing countries on the objectives set forth in the new legislation. 

"NEW DIRECTIONS" AND THE AID BUREAUCRACY 

Mr. ZABLOCKI. I wonder if you would, on the record, advise the committee what problems AID is having with the bureaucracy in Washington and in the field, with the new directions? Are they generally accepting the new directions or are they treating them as some-

This is not-the word "mandate" has been used and I don't dispute that except the implication that we have to be forced to do what we already want to do. Then there are some problems in implementing these new directions. I think this might be indicated by the fact that about 5 years ago, I think, the staff levels of AID personnel were something over nine per million dollars of programing. 

In our projection for fiscal 1975 it is down to about three and onethird AID employees per million dollars of programing. I think this is progress, but I must say it is difficult as well because the new directions are inherently more staff-intensive in implementation. It is much more complex to engage in the development of a rural electrification project than it is to buy engineering design of a thermo generator. 

This is the type of problem that we have in carrying them out. 

We also have some difficulties in different skill categories because in the past the agency did, in fact, go out into the field and undertake directly the work of a lot of projects. A part of the new directions which we share is to help others to learn how to do and replicate their programs. This takes two different kinds of people. 

I admit that in certain of the more traditional professional categories we have some redundancy. We are trying to engage in retraining programs to enable these people to take on new professional capabilities.

Mr. ZABLOCKI. In order that we may understand to what extent the agency has gone in this direction, could you supply for the record the guidelines or directives that you have sent to the field?

[The following was subsequently submitted for inclusion in the record.] Problems 

NEW DIRECTIONS IMPLEMENTATION PROBLEMS 

As indicated in my statement to the committee, we do face some real constraints in trying to move faster in the new directions. While the response we have received so far from governments to the new approach appears favorable, there are limits to our ability to shift their priorities. We can persuade but only they can decide. While many developing countries are convinced of the need to involve their small farmers and businessmen in development, they are uncertain about how to proceed. 

A second problem has to do with the pioneering nature of the task we have set for ourselves. While we share the belief of some experts that the successful experience of such countries as Taiwan and South Korea in involving the broad majorities of their populations in the tasks and benefits of development contain lessons applicable to other countries, we also find complex problems in various countries and regions which make successful involvement of poor majorities extremely difficult. In some cases, it is a matter of technology. The state of development of highly productive technology suitable for dry-land agriculture and accessible to small farmers, for example, is not as well as advanced as for irrigated agriculture. Many countries do not have conditions suitable for irrigation. In other cases, existing forms of organization and sociocultural traditions tend to inhibit the adoption of new technologies or the retention of their benefits by small farmers and businessmen. 

AID is not alone, of course, in facing these problems. The entire development community is seized with the same challenges and problems. We engage in frequent exchange on these questions with other bi-lateral donor agencies through expert meetings of the Development Assistance Committee of the OECD, through staff level contacts and exchange with counterparts in the IBRD and other international organizations, as well as with practitioners in developing country governments.

I might add, in this regard, the observation I made in my statement to the Committee that the new directions imply an inherently staff intensive effort as well as additional research designed to permit us to make significant breakthroughs in the new directions areas. It is, however, difficult to respond to these needs when at the same time we are being enjoined to reduce manpower and support costs and our research efforts are restricted by limitations on the funds we may allocate for this purpose. Guidelines We have prepared and issued policy guidelines to the missions for submission of proposed programs for FY 1976 funding which explicitly treat each of the new directions areas (food and nutrition, health and family planning, education and manpower). These guidelines stress the objective of reaching the poorest of the poor in each category and, to the extent possible in a relatively brief message and given the current state of the art and knowledge, indicate the considerations which need to be taken into account when developing projects and programs designed to meet this objective in these fields. [See Appendix p. 889.] 

As indicated above, we have created three special task forces, a task force on the new initiatives, a working group on the rural poor, and a working committee on the Percy amendment, to accelerate the implementation of the new approach embodied in the legislation. One of the tasks of the working group on the rural poor is to develop more specific guidance in the area of rural development to reach missions in time to be useful in developing projects and programs intended for funding in fiscal year 1976.

Acceptance 

The great majority of AID staff in Washington and in the field appear to have accepted the substance and the spirit of the new directions. We have brought the new approach to the attention of the staff in a variety of ways: widespread distribution of the legislation and committee reports, field mission and regional workshops and conferences attended by AID Washington staff, and regular orientation and training sessions provided by our personnel office. 

The problem arises, as I observed in my reply to the first part of your question, in the implementation of the legislative mandate. Many in our staff are very

concerned about this problem and are searching for more detailed and concrete guidance. We are therefore giving urgent priority to the work of the abovementioned task forces charged with developing such guidance. 

RECEPTIVITY OF GOVERNMENTS TO FOREIGN AID REFORMS 

Mr. ZABLOCKI. My final question-and it is related to the material that will be supplied for the record-has the agency encountered any problems as far as the recipient governments understanding the new directions? Are there situations where it is not clear that a government is willing to involve the poorest majority in development? My question really is threefold. Do they understand, are they willing to follow the new directions and if not, what can we do to encourage them?

Mr. PARKER. I think it would be safe to say almost all governments are oriented to the masses of the population and in the case of developing countries these are the objectives that we are working toward. 

Second, as to whether they understand the thrust of our new directions, I think it is safe to say the vast majority of them do. Within any government how much down this goes in their own bureaucracy may vary from case to case. As to whether they know how to do it, Mr. Zablocki, is the next question.

In many cases they are somewhat uncertain about how to undertake programs like this from their own administrative- Mr. ZABLOCKI. One of the criticisms of AID in the past has been that the rich in the LDC's were getting richer and the poor were getting poorer. What we intended with the new directions was to reach the poor. 

 [Subsequently, Mr. Parker responded to Mr. Zablocki's questions as follows:] LDC GOVERNMENT RESPONSE TO NEW LEGISLATION Mr. ZABLOCKI. What is AID doing to discuss the new legislation with govern ments overseas?

Mr. PARKER. Every time there is a change in our aid legislation our field missions discuss the change with governments where we provide assistance. 

These discussions take on particular importance for the new legislation in view of the significant changes in sector and program emphases embodied in the legislation. We have expressed to governments our special interest in the food and nutrition, population planning and health, and education and human resources sectors.

Mr. ZABLOCKI. What sort of response are we getting from governments about our new approach to aid?

Mr. PARKER. The response so far has been generally favorable. Many countries have already re-oriented their development strategies along the lines of the emphases contained in the new legislation. In many Latin American countries a coincidence between our programs and the emphases of the new legislation has existed for several years. In Asia and Africa, where many countries still need further major investment in capital infrastructure, governments have recognized that AID is no longer a primary source for such help. 

Let me give you a few specific examples of reactions from individual countries. 

In the Philippines, U.S. assistance was already concentrated in the new emphasis sectors. Therefore, when an AID officer discussed the new emphases with several top (cabinet level) Philippine officials, they responded very favorably, and assured us of their support of such programs as the "Masagana 99" project to increase rice production, the child-feeding nutrition program and the project to improve living conditions in rural areas. In Afghanistan the A.I.D. Mission ini-

tiated a series of discussions with top Afghan planners on our legislation and the Afghan Government's revised developmental priorities. The result of this intensive dialogue will be a significant restructuring of the A.I.D. program in favor of new activities designed for more rapid impact on the rural poor. In Indonesia the new directions in AID's legislation have been discussed with the Government at various levels. The reaction has generally been favorable, since the priorities of Indonesia's new development plan accord closely with the new directions. The 

Government, however, has expressed some concern that as most donors begin emphasizing agriculture, education and health there may be inadequate development financing for projects in other sectors. 

Similar reactions have come from African countries. In Ethiopia the reaction of the Government has been particularly favorable. This reflects the major shift in priorities toward rural development, employment and equity as embodied in the new Ethiopian development plan. A high official of the Cameroons Government has asked for copies of the House Committee Report so that he and his staff might study them. But the new legislation has also caused a few African governments to express some concern about the new approach. Tanzania, for example, has been very committed for several years to reaching its poorest majority, but it and many other African countries are still very deficient in such basic infrastructure as roads, power and dams for irrigation. Without such infrastructure, the rural poor in these countries cannot be involved in the development process. Officials in Tanzania and several other African countries have expressed concern that there will not be adequate development financing for basic infrastructure. 

Mr. ZABLOCKI. In situations where it is clear that a government is unwilling to involve its poorest majority in development, do you think the United States should try to help? What can the United States do in such a situation?

Mr. PARKER. Our experience has been that we usually find a sufficiently common ground of interest with an LDC government to develop programs in a collaborative way. We believe this will continue to be possible as we increase the emphasis of our program in the new directions areas. By and large, most governments are interested in the same areas as we are programs in food and nutrition, health and family planning, and education-and in reaching the poor with these programs. Even where a government does not have a major emphasis on reaching the rural poor, for example, there is often considerable scope for supporting projects and programs which reach the rural poor. In such circumstances, we may through our assistance be able to encourage the government to expand its commitment of its own resources to such programs.

[The information requested follows:] INVENTORY OF PROPOSED DEVELOPMENT ASSISTANCE OF THE OIL EXPORTING NATIONS TO THE DEVELOPING COUNTRIES 

The amounts of development assistance which the oil exporting countries are contributing to the developing nations cannot be precisely defined and are subject to a continuing revision. The data is accumulated mainly from press reports and similarly based compilations that are more vague than precise with respect to sums, completeness of coverage, names of institutions and definitions of terms. 

It is further noted that the summing of pledges to non-operational mutlilateral special funds and bilateral commitments in several instances would best be viewed as an inventory of potential development assistance that is likely to require an extended period for assuring full disbursement of the specified sums. 

With these caveats in mind, it is possible to estimate very roughly the magnitude of the potential inventory of accumulated development assistance based on the announced bilateral commitments and pledges of the oil exporting nations to existing and proposed international institutions. 

The amounts of development assistance which the oil exporting countries are potentially willing to contribute to the developing nations could well exceed $13 billion based on announcements during the first five months of this year. The bilateral development assistance which the oil exporting countries are currently providing or proposing, including commercial credits, amounts to roughly $4 billion but several years will be required to fully disburse these commitments. 

Pledges to support proposed increases in either the subscribed or authorized capital of existing, newly established and proposed Arab financed development funds, are believed to exceed our estimate of $5 billion. Other actual outlays and pledging activities, amounting to roughly $4 billion, include IFI borrowings of $0.5 billion, the $3.2 billion IMF Oil Facility and $0.5 billion in Special Fund 

Activities. Benefits to the developing nations are likely to be somewhat diffuse and limited with respect to the IMF oil facility.

Bilateral Government-to-Government commitments of the oil exporting nations during the first six months of 1974 have been directed mainly to non-oil Middle East developing countries. Egypt, Syria and Jordan may well have received actual or pledged assistance in excess of $2.0 billion mainly from Kuwait ($700 million), Abu Dhabi ($200 million) and Saudi Arabia ($1.3 billion). Assistance from Saudi 

Arabia includes commitments from a proposed $1 billion Rehabilitation Fund. 

Egypt has also received commitments from Iran ($870 million). Iran has extended to India roughly $800 million in credits, and $150 million to Syria. 

Pakistan may also receive assistance from Iran. Assistance from Iraq to India and Syria is believed to exceed $100 million but be less than $200 million. 

Development assistance is also being extended on a bilateral basis to other, mainly African developing countries. Nigeria has offered Zambia almost $1 million in emergency assistance. Talks are believed to be underway between 

Venezuela and those several Latin American countries requiring assistance to meet higher oil import bills. A number of bilateral aid commitments to, or agreement with, African countries south of the Sahara and amounting to more than $300 million have been announced by Kuwait, Libya, Saudi Arabia, the United Arab Emirate and Algeria. Other loans are under consideration. The 

Kuwait Fund has extended a $14 million loan to Yemen and is likely to approve a $10 million loan to Tunisia. 

Bilateral and Special Multilateral Development Funds, existing, newly estab lished and proposed, are expected to provide additional assistance to developing nations over the next half decade. The Kuwait Fund is considering the increase in its authorized capital from $0.7 billion to $3.3 billion. Extending access to non-Arab LDC's is also being considered. The subscribed capital of the recently established $100 million Abu Dhabi Fund for Economic Development will be paid up over a six-year period and may be increased. The Arab Fund for Economic and Social Development has extended approximately $95 million in loans during the first half of 1974 mainly to Middle East and North African Muslim countries. 

The authorized capital of the newly established Arab Bank for Agricultural and Industrial Development in Africa is expected to reach $500 million and that of the Special Arab Fund for Africa $220 million. The subscribed capital of the newly established Islamic Development Bank and the proposed Libyan-United Arab Emirate Fund for African Development amounts to roughly $1.3 billion. 

Iranian pledges to the proposed OPEC Special Fund and the New Development 

Fund amount to $300 million but the extent of Arab participation in these institutions continues to be uncertain. The subscribed capital of the Arab Technical 

Assistance Fund for Africa amounts to $17 million. 

IFI-Type activities are likely to yield a less direct and more diffused benefit to the LDC's but are estimated to roughly total $4 billion, including a $3.2 billion participation in the IMF Oil Facility. IBRD borrowings from the oil rich countries during CY 1974 amounted to $385 million or almost 44 percent of 

IBRD totals. Purchases of IDB, ADB and the Caribbean Development Bank bonds by the oil exporting nations have been, respectively, $23 million (Venezuela), $17 million (Kuwait) and $24 million (Venezuela). Kuwait, a Part I member of IDA since the mid-sixties has negotiated a $27 million subscription to IDA IV. Venezuela is considering a $500 million pledge to a Special Fund of the 

IDB and a sizeable contribution to the UN Emergency Assistance Fund.

Mr. FOUNTAIN. Now, in our report on the disaster assistance bill, I think the committee noted an amount which originally had been programed for Pakistan in fiscal 1974 but was shifted to the amount programed for Vietnam. Can you tell us how much, all told, was shifted to Indochina in fiscal 1974 from amounts which in your presentation had been programed for other parts of the world? 

Mr. PARKER. I would like to discuss it. I cannot give you a specific answer for the reason I will explain. No. 1, at the beginning of the year

there was a development loan shift of $50 million. My understanding of that is that it really was for fiscal 1973 carried into fiscal 1974 and shown in the accounts for fiscal 1974. 

Second, the operational year budget submission indicated an additional $60 million from development loan funds to go to Vietnam. I would have to tell you this decision has not yet been made. I have been instructed by Secretary Kissinger to see to it that the economy of South Vietnam does not collapse. He has indicated to me if we need to, we should be prepared to increase the amounts allocated there by the amount of $60 million from 1974 development loan funds. 

I will be candid and say I have been reluctant to do this. We are calculating the requirements in South Vietnam almost more than daily. 

We are doing it almost hourly.

Mr. Gilman.

AID TO MALTA 

Mr. GILMAN. Mr. Parker, as part of the $477 million for the Middle 

East you recommended $9.5 million for Malta. It seems a little strange that Malta should be included in the Middle East proposal. Can you tell us what these funds are being utilized for in Malta? 

Mr. PARKER. I don't believe we have it in what we call the Middle 

East Fund. We have it in what we call the supporting assistance fund. This is the U.S. share of the combined assistance to Malta for the utilization of port facilities. These are base rights and their connection to NATO, our responsibilities in NATO. 

Mr. GILMAN. Did we have any utilization of those bases during the 

October war?

Mr. PARKER. I don't know the extent to which the U.S. Navy has used it. The British Navy is the one that operates the base. 

Mr. GILMAN. Do we have any military installation at Malta?

Mr. PARKER. I don't believe we have one. I think it is a British installation as part of the NATO system.

Mr. GILMAN. Essentially we are paying the $9.5 million for the British utilization of the Malta base; is that it? 

Mr. PARKER. I think we are paying about one-quarter of the total required to maintain that base. 

Mr. GILMAN. We do not utilize that base at all?

Mr. PARKER. I don't know, sir. I would assume we do call on it. As to whether we have the U.S. Navy there, I don't know. 

Mr. GILMAN. At this point in the record could you supply information for us?

Mr. PARKER. Indeed.

[The information requested follows:] UNITED STATES UTILIZATION OF MALTA BASE 

The agreement between the Maltese and the UK gives the UK full use of military facilities on Malta. Under the agreement, the Government of Malta will not permit Warsaw Pact forces to use military facilities there. The agreement provides that the use of facilities by all other countries, including other NATO members and the U.S., shall be subject to the concurrence of the Government of Malta. However, the access to these facilities by a NATO member is important to the NATO presence in the Mediterranean.

AID TO ISRAEL 

Mr. GILMAN. Mr. Parker, in support of the aid you are recommending for South Vietnam of some $750 million, you recite that economic and humanitarian assistance is essential to the economic stability and growth of its economy. In the Middle East you are recommending some $477 million, of which you are recommending $250 million for Egypt, $100 million for a special requirements fund for Syria and some $77 million for Jordan. We have received reports of the cost of the war to Israel amounting to approximately $10 billion and that it had a massive impact and imposed an enormous burden on its economy.

In your report you recommended $50 million in supporting assistance for Israel. I believe in response to my colleague, Mr. Wilson's inquiry you stated that there was substantial money being given to Israel for military equipment. Why is your recommendation so modest for economic assistance for this country that has had such a burden as compared to what is being recommended for the other Arab nations on which you are basing on which your recommendations are based primarily upon economic assurance and stability?

Egypt is $250 million, Jordan $77 million, the contingency funds for Syria are $100 million. Can you explain that vast difference between these recommendations? 

Mr. PARKER. Mr. Gilman, one minor point, the $100 million Special

Requirements Fund is not necessarily earmarked as Syria. This was discussed earlier. Some may go to Syria, but I just passed that quickly in the interest of getting to your discussion of your full question. 

Specifically on the matter of Israel and the amount of that we are proposing, there has been a significant increase in military assistance. 

This is what we have calculated on the basis of study and analysis of their budget

NONMILITARY AID TO ISRAEL 

Mr. GILMAN. Mr. Parker, if I might interrupt, I am comparing the amounts being appropriated for assistance, nonmilitary assistance. I have not pursued the military assistance to the other countries. Can we discuss just the nonmilitary assistance being proposed? 

Mr. PARKER. Surely. I think it is appropriate to begin by noting that the population of Israel is about 3.5 million. The Arab neighbors are about 64 or 65 million. I think we have to recognize that the balancing,

both economically in terms of power and military and economic resources, is a very complex thing. 

Rather little of Israel was damaged in war. A great deal of Egypt was damaged in war. Over a considerable period of time it has lain fallow. The Suez cities since 1967 are an example. There is a great deal of damage there.

It is our belief that assisting the Egyptians to reconstruct these will stabilize the peace.

AID TO JORDAN 

Mr. GILMAN. Mr. Parker, if you are utilizing the population figures and the destruction, how do you explain the $77 million for Jordan? 

Mr. PARKER. Jordan's economy was badly distended by the cost of bearing expenses for defense and to maintain a military capability in support of their moderation, which is reflective of the cost upon their budget. 

Mr. GILMAN. Shouldn't the same criteria apply to Israel? That is what I am suggesting. If you are going to base criteria for Jordan on that economic strain, shouldn't the economic strain be considered when you consider the needs of Israel?

Mr. PARKER. Yes, I think the same factors have to be taken into consideration. Our calculations thus far have indicated this is the amount required to attain this balance.

AID TO INDIA 

Mr. BINGHAM. 

I would like to join in welcoming Mr. Parker and compliment you on your presentation and your knowledge of the program. I think it is quite extradordinary. I would also like to compliment you on recruiting John Murphy as your deputy. I share the distress of some of my colleagues about the proportions of the aid program, the disproportionate amount for South Vietnam and, in particular, the comparatively inadequate provision for Israel. 

I will pass the point as to Israel. I think others have made that point. 

I would like to ask you if you consider the amount for India adequate in terms of the threatening food shortage there and the fact that we may be confronted with a major disaster in the next 2 or 3 years there in terms of famine?

Mr. PARKER. Mr. Bingham, I don't know how to quantify what the 

Indian needs are. I know they are going to be large. Even to attempt to bring food production into balance with consumption is going to be a vast undertaking. They have crowded their land and overburdened their land for centuries. How to make the land more productive and the economy more viable is just going to be a tremendous job. As to specifics of what their food import needs are going to be next year or the year after, estimates vary a great deal, depending on how effective the monsoon season is, the extent to which new seed varieties are planted, and the amount of fertilizer they get. There

have been in the past couple of years substantial requirements for food imports, involving, this past year, about 5 million tons of grains. 

Mr. BINGHAM. You certainly would not, I trust, argue that because you are asking $750 million for South Vietnam and $75 million for 

India that South Vietnam is 10 times as important?

Mr. PARKER. I do not think the two are quite comparable in that way, Mr. Bingham. I think that there is a unique importance to any area in which so many Americans have given their lives, in which such vast American investment has been made in economic terms. 

Mr. BINGHAM. Let me just say for the record that I agree with the comments my colleague from California made about some of India's policies. I am appalled personally by their having devoted these resources to nuclear devices and I have certainly been greatly distressed by their consistent support of the Arabs against Israel over the years. 

On the other hand, I agree with the implications of your answer that we must be concerned primarily with India's people and that we always respond generously when there is a question of famine or major disaster. What we are engaged in here, I take it, is an effort to forestall that in India.

It is not politically related. I take it you would agree with that? 

Mr. PARKER. Yes, indeed. One of the main thrusts of the new directions we are undertaking is to help people build their own productive capability which would obviate having to come in with massive emergency aid.

PROHIBITIONS ON AID 

Mr. BINGHAM. I like your discussion of the new direction. I think that is reassuring. Let me ask you a special question. You may not be in a position to answer it now. 

The legislation on which we are operating still prohibits any aid to be extended to a country which allows ships under its registry to trade with Cuba or North Vietnam. What would be the attitude of the administration toward an amendment to either repeal those subsections under section 620 or to give the President discretion to make exceptions in the national interest?

Mr. PARKER. I have not discussed it with the President. I have not discussed it directly with Secretary Kissinger in specific terms. I can on my own comment say that I think that the fewer the automatic trigger-type mandates that there are, the better.

Mr. BINGHAM. Could you get us a definitive administration statement on your position with regard to section 620 (A) (3) and section 

620 (N)?

Nam Ngum, Phase Two On May 30, 1973 the AID Assistant Administrator for Supporting Assistance approved a U.S. pledge of $5 million toward construction of the Nam Ngum, Phase two project. On May 31, 1973, in Bangkok the U.S. Representative to a special pledging session for this project, in the context of a multilateral pledging session where other donor nations made similar commitments, made the above commitment, subject to the availability of funds and other conditions. 

All conditions having been met, and a suitable Fund Agreement having been prepared by the Asian Development Bank, the Assistant Administrator for

Supporting Assistance authorized a loan of $5 million for the implementation of Nam Ngum Phase Two on June 4, 1974. The multilateral Fund Agreement is expected to be signed on June 29, 1974, and the U.S. loan to Laos in support of this project will be signed on or about June 30, 1974. For additional information regarding this project see the AID FY 1974 Submission to the Congress, Indochina Postwar Reconstruction Assistance, page 86. Malta

A new defense agreement was concluded between the United Kingdom and Malta on March 26, 1972 which provides that the Government of Malta will receive an annual payment of 14 million pounds sterling (about $37 million) for a seven year period.

The members of the North Atlantic Treaty Organization (NATO) have agreed that a continued British presence on Malta and a concomitant exclusion of Warsaw Pact Forces warrant a substantial outlay by members of the Alliance.

The U.S. has agreed to provide $9.5 million as its annual share of these payments to Malta under the NATO Agreement. The U.S. commitment is to 

NATO. AID has provided these funds in FY 1972, FY 1973 and FY 1974. For additional information regarding this agreement see the AID FY 1975 Submission to the Congress, Middle East and Security Supporting Assistance 

Programs, page 25. Spain

During the 1968/69 negotiations for renewal of the original United States- Spanish Defense Agreement of 1953, the Spanish Government expressed a strong desire that the new Agreement should include provisions for U.S. assistance in the fields of education, agriculture, environment, economics, space, science and technology. The United States concurred and components for such assistance were included in the five-year Agreement of Friendship and Cooperation between the United States and Spain, commonly referred to as the base agreement, signed August 6, 1970. The agreement is for a period of five years, with an option for extension, if both Governments agree, for another five years. 

The U.S. annual payment is $3 million. Payments were made in FY 1972 with 

Department of Defense funds and in FY 1973 and FY 1974 with AID Support ing Assistance funds. For additional information regarding this agreement see the AID FY 1975 Submission to the Congress, Middle East Peace and Se curity Support Assistance Programs, page 27. 

Cambodia Exchange Support Fund (ESF) 

Under the auspices of the IMF, a multilateral Exchange Support Fund is in its third year of operation. It finances (a) commodities for which Cambodian reserves and earnings are insufficient, and (b) services and commodities required in connection with capital projects or technical assistance. 

At a November 1973 review with other donors and Cambodia for calendar year 1974, the United States indicated its intention, subject to authorization and appropriation of Funds by Congress, to match the contributions of others up to a limit of $17.5 million. The U.S. contribution for calendar year 1974 is planned to be $17.5 million, or half of the estimated total of about $35 million. Along with 

Cambodia and the United States, Japan, the United Kingdom, Thailand, New Zealand, and Malaysia will also contribute. 

Our CY 1974 contribution is being financed with $8.75 million from FY 1974 funds and $8.75 million from FY 1975 funds. For additional information regarding this Fund see the AID Submission to the Congress, Indochina Postwar Reconstruction Programs, page 53.

Laos-Foreign Exchange Operations Fund (FEOF) 

A similar economic stabilization fund also recommended by the International Monetary Fund exists in Laos. 

The fund was created in 1964 and has been renewed annually since then. On 

April 30, 1974 the most recent agreement was concluded in which the United States pledged subject to the availability of funds $16.1 million for calendar year 

1974. Approximately $3.05 million of FY 1975 funds will be needed to meet our commitment for calendar 1974.

Other contributors to the fund are Australia, France, Japan, the United Kingdom, and, since 1972 the Lao Government. For additional information regarding this Fund refer to the AID FY 1975 Submission to the Congress, Indochina Postwar Reconstruction Programs, page 61.

Africa-Cameroon 

At a donor's meeting held in Brussels on March 26, 1974, A.I.D. representatives met with representatives of FED and the Government of Cameroon concerning contractor claims on the Trans-Cameroon Railroad, Phase II project. 

The A.I.D. representatives indicated to the parties present that A.I.D. is prepared to participate, subject to the availability of funds, to the extent of 25% of the claims paid on the basis of a settlement agreement or arbitration award In addition, the A.I.D. representatives stated that A.I.D. would be willing to provide, subject to the availability of funds, as additional amount equivalent to the devaluation loss on the $2 million of the A.I.D. loan used to meet local currency expenses. This would continue A.I.D.'s position of maintaining a 25% participation in the overall project. 

African Development Bank During the spring of 1974, President Labidi of the African Development Bank visited the United States and, among other things, discussed A.I.D.'s contribution to the Bank. During these discussions, A.I.D. officials indicated to President 

Labidi that A.I.D. would be prepared to favorably consider a $2 million grant for feasibility studies related to investments in the Sahel upon enactment of the 

FOREIGN DISASTER ASSISTANCE ACT of 1974. 

Burma-Narcotics Control

Korea-Letter dated October 16, 1971 from Ambassador David Kennedy, U.S. 

Ambassador to Korea, to His Excellency Lee Nak-Sun, Minister of Commerce and Industry of Korea 

This letter commits the United States to make available subject to Congression appropriation, 100 million dollars in development loans through U.S. FY 

1975 as well as increasing the value of PL 480 programs to Korea over 5 years by $275 million. The commitment was made in consideration of the Government of Korea's agreement to limit Korean exports of textiles to the United States over a 5 year period. A report on this Agreement was presented to Congress by the General Accounting Office (GAO Report No. B-179-342, May 1974). 

Fiscal year 1975 is the final year for fulfilling the U.S. commitment for development loans. It is expected that AID will obligate 25 million dollars in fiscal year 1975. While it is more difficult to compute the exact amount remaining under the PL 480 commitment pursuant to this agreement, fiscal year 1976 is set as a target date for fulfilling this portion of the commitment. 

Indus Basin Development Fund Agreement of 1960 (Tias 4671), and Supple mental Agreement 1964 (Tias 5570).

The 1960 Agreement commits the United States Government to make a contribution to the fund, subject to Congress appropriation, of U.S. $177,000,000 and $70 million in loans to the Government of Pakistan to assist the fund in the construction of water related projects for effective utilization of waters assigned to the Government of Pakistan pursuant to the Indus Waters Treaty. amendment increases the U.S. commitment to $118,590,000 in grants and $51,- 

220,000 in loans to the Government of Pakistan.

Turkey Poppy Memorandum of Understanding of July 16, 1972. 

In consideration of the Turkish Government's issuance of a decree on limiting and promise to enact legislation banning poppy growing in Turkey, the United States agreed to provide, subject to Congressional Appropriation of funds, up to 35.7 million dollars in assistance including a minimum of 15 million dollars in grants over a five year period, and an additional $10 million in grants in FY 72 and $10 million in FY 73, to be utilized to assist Turkey's efforts to redirect economic life in the areas affected by the Poppy ban. The Understanding also provided that the United States will send agricultural experts to Turkey to advise on the development of a agrarian reform program. 

The General Accounting Office is presently preparing a report to Congress on this Agreement.

Of the 35.7 million dollars pledged to Turkey pursuant to this agreement, $15,608,260 have already been transferred to Turkey. An amount of $5,091,740 has been obligated under a 10.4 million dollar grant agreement, but has not yet been released to the Government of Turkey. The U.S. has not as yet committed $20,091,740 to the Turkish Government. 

Organization of American States (OAS) 

Annual pledges are made to contribute to development programs administered by OAS. They are made with the clear understanding that they are subject to the availability of funds.

The United States pledges to match payments made by Latin American and Caribbean nations on a 66:34 basis. Pledges now outstanding total up to $17.7 million for payments to be made by the U.S. in FY 1975. A more complete description of the OAS programs appears in the FY 1975 Congressional Presentation for Latin American, beginning on page 231.
