U.N. SPECIAL SESSION PROPOSAL Chairman MORGAN. Mr. Parker, the United States proposed at the United 

Nations Special Session this spring a $4 billion, 18-month aid program to poor countries on top of existing programs. As you know, the U.S. proposal was not accepted and the UN General Assembly did not adopt a specific aid target figure. 

Could you tell us please:

How much of this $4 billion would have come from the United States? 

Second, if A.I.D. wants to go above the two-year authorization ceiling, why don't you wait until the UN decides on a target figure for 1975 so we will know how any extra American assistance would fit in and what others will be contributing?

Mr. PARKER. The proposal that the Special Session of the General Assembly focus on the need of the poorest countries for about $4 billion was advanced informally by the United States as a possible basis for discussion looking toward a concerted effort by the oil-exporting countries and the developed countries, both 

Socialist and Western.

In his major address to the Special Session, Secretary Kissinger indicated that the oil producers have a major responsibility to use some of their new wealth to help the poorest countries and that the developed nations also have an obligation to help. He indicated that the United States intended to continue its development assistance program and to endeavor to find other means of helping. 

Specifically, he expressed the hope that we would be able to increase our food aid program above last year's level and that we would be able to join in supporting the expanded International Development Association Fourth Replenishment. 

Our request for an increase in the two-year authorization level for our food and nutrition program long preceded the UN initiative and is based on the clear importance of increased attention to enlarging LDC food production. This is needed regardless of whatever efforts may be made at the UN or elsewhere. 

AID LEVEL FOR VIETNAM Chairman MORGAN. Mr. Parker, I understand that the Administration orig inally planned to ask for $600 million for South Vietnam in fiscal 1975. I also understand that the South Vietnamese Government budgeted for $670 million in foreign economic assistance for fiscal 1975, of which about $80 million would be supplied by others than the U.S. That leaves South Vietnam's proposed U.S. aid figure at $590 million. Now you are asking for $750 million. 

Could you explain to me, in more detail than you have in your statement, why you are asking for so much more than the $600 million originally planned? 

How much of the $150 million increase is based on the theory that it will spur 

South Vietnam's economy to "take off" on its own?

Mr. PARKER. In our analysis and formulation of the FY 1975 program levels for Vietnam, we concluded that $600 million would do little more than keep Vietnam where it is now in economic terms, with a small but clearly insufficient amount of funds available for the investment required to build a momentum for sustained economic growth. On the other hand, we believe that the $750 million we are requesting will provide not only the required funds for the immediate welfare requirements of the people but also the initial major injec tion of capital investment funds required to expand Vietnam's productive base. 

The government of Vietnam also believes that a figure less than $750 million would not enable it to move forward on the path of self sustaining development. 

It was with these considerations in mind that our Congressional Presentation sets forth a $219 million requirement for capital investments. 

CARTEL PRICE JACKING 

Chairman MORGAN. Mr. Parker, your statement speaks on P. 9 and elsewhere about the need for cooperation in an interdependent world. 

I assume you include cooperation between producing and consuming countries. I assume you are against deliberate price hiking—especially when we here at home are suffering from high inflation. 

Now for our part in the U.S., in products like wheat our prices went up because of demand. But the price has been coming down because we have done our best to increase production.

Let's leave oil aside for the moment, and I will ask you about some deliberate price Kiking by countries including some getting U.S. AID. 

For instance, the news reports last week said Jamaica's Senate passed a bill which will more than quadruple the money Jamaica gets from American companies for bauxite.

Four Latin American countries recently imposed export taxes on bananas, which can mean higher banana prices for American housewives. 

My question is, why should we give aid to countries which are deliberately jacking up prices against us-and what is A.I.D. doing to make sure that cooperation in fair prices is a two-way street? 

Mr. PARKER. The U.S. government does not condone these measures and has expressed its serious concern. The State Department is discussing these issues with the appropriate governments and export restrictions such as the bauxite and banana tax issues are being raised in various international forums, including GATT and the IMF. The U.S. companies are also engaged in direct negotiations with these governments. These efforts will continue, hopefully resolving many of the issues.

A major difficulty, of course, is that as a result of the rapidly rising costs of petroleum, food, fertilizer, and capital goods, many LDCs are facing critical balance of payments problems this year. In response to mounting deficits and the so far uncertain prospects for significant additional external capital flows from the oil producers or elsewhere some LDCs have instituted export tax measures as a means to help them earn additional foreign exchange to finance their immediate import costs.

A.I.D. assisted LDCs are attempting to solve basic development problems. 

These problems have been exacerbated by the current economic crisis. It is our hope that A.I.D.'s help in these countries will encourage more viable economies which will not have to rely as extensively on massive imports of expensive commodities and on the export of only one or two products. This a a long-term effort, but we believe it is important in helping to assure that all countries recognize and accept the need for a cooperative and interdependent relationship. 

PROPOSED INCREASE OF $255 MILLION FOR FOOD AND NUTRITION IN FISCAL YEAR 1975 Chairman MORGAN. Mr. Parker, the Table on p. 11 of your statement shows how your Food and Nutrition program is proposed to jump in fiscal 1975 about 2½ times above the 1974 program. 

This figure does not include the additional food amount in the Disaster Assistance Bill now in House-Senate conference which will be available in fiscal 1975. 

Now on p. 9 and 10, you speak of "some real constraints in trying to move faster in the new directions."

In view of this-and with the recommendations of the World Food Conference not coming until November-I wonder if you are trying to do too much too fast.

Since you already have an increased amount for food in 1975, without the extra $255 million, could you be satisfied with just doing a better job with what we have already voted?

Mr. PARKER. We believe that the full increase of $255 million is extremely important. The constraints that I mentioned were taken into account in proposing this level.

It is evident from the preparatory meetings for the World Food Conference that major emphasis will be placed on increasing agricultural production in the developing countries. The United States must be in a position to take a leadership role, particularly if we are to join with other nations in a cooperative effort. 

The proposed increase will demonstrate the seriousness with which the U.S. views the world food situation. We give a high priority to the programs proposed-provision of rural roads and irrigation systems, assistance to small farmers, and projects relating to the organization of agricultural markets, to mention a few important areas.

[Following are questions submitted by Mr. Fraser and the answers subsequently supplied by Mr. Parker:]

STUDIES ON INVOLVING THE POOR IN DEVELOPMENT Mr. FRASER. What kinds of studies or experimentation is A.I.D. undertaking, financing, participating in, or collecting the results of: (a) to test the proposition inherent in last year's authorization bill that involving the poor in development can accelerate economic growth and (b) to translate this general strategy of development into practical terms that are appropriate for specific country situations?

Mr. PARKER. In response to the first part of your question, A.I.D. is supporting and planning a wide range of research projects and evaluative studies intended to increase our understanding of ways in which the poor can be involved in the development process through making a greater contribution to economic growth and receiving a greater share of its benefits. 

AID-supported research projects currently underway which deal with various aspects of this question include studies on employment, unemployment and technology choice in LDC's being conducted at the Economic Growth Center of Yale University, studies on income distribution, economic growth and public policy in LDC's at Rice University, Princeton University and the Brookings Institution, and studies on rural employment and income in Asia and Africa at Cornell University and Michigan State University, respectively. We are planning to support research projects on the role of public works programs in providing employment and creating useful assets for the poor in developing countries and on the relationship between income distribution and investment in human resources (health, education and nutrition) in LDC households. 

In addition to these research projects, we have and are conducting evaluative studies of projects and programs intended to benefit the poor. These studies include a large number of papers prepared last year by experts within and outside AID on various aspects of small farmer credit programs in LDC's. We are currently initiating a series of evaluation studies of selected A.I.D. capital and technical assistance projects with the objective of developing better means for identifying and defining who are the intended beneficiaries of assistance and the factors which determine whether intended beneficiaries are, in fact, actually helped as expected.

In response to the second part of your question concerning translation of these studies into practical guidance, we try to do this in various ways. These include widespread dissemination of research reports and findings to our field missions and to LDC governments, an airgram sent to our missions in June which synthesizes the policy implications resulting from the studies produced by our 1973 "Spring Review of Small Farmer Credit," and a series of strategy and policy papers dealing with the various aspects of rural development mentioned in both the House Foreign Affairs Committee Report on the new legislation and our FY 75 Congressional Presentation. These rural development papers are to be completed by the end of this summer in order to guide our field missions as together with host countries they develop projects and programs for FY 76. 

Planned longer term efforts include an Agency Review on Rural Poverty and AID-supported research on developing and refining a methodology for devising rural poverty strategies for LDCs. 

COLLABORATIVE STYLE OF OPERATIONS 

Mr. FRASER. What steps are you taking to ensure that A.I.D. missions and regional bureaus understand that instructions they may receive to put our aid into activities that involve and benefit the poor are not meant as a license to try to browbeat and force other countries into accepting a particular economic point of view?

Mr. PARKER. A.I.D.'s development assistance programs, aimed increasingly at involving and benefiting the poor through concentration on problems relating to

basic human needs, are carried out in collaboration with the countries to which the aid is given. The emphasis on a collaborative style has been repeatedly stressed to field missions. As an example, the Administrator's central guidance message to Mission Directors for FY 1974 contained the following statement: 

Collaborative Assistance Style.-LDCs over the past decade have increased their capacity to play a greater role in development programs. Progress has not been uniform, and developing countries still vary widely in management capacity and growth potential. Nonetheless, the nature of relationships between donors and recipients is changing everywhere. LDCs are intent on setting their own priorities and taking responsibility for planning and managing their development programs. Accordingly, Missions should continue to move toward organizational and programming approaches that are less directive and provide for greater LDC participation and responsibility. 

Most of the countries with which we deal in the development process are also concerned about problems affecting the poor, such as equity and income distribution. While performance is uneven, many of these countries have established development plans and policies that are generally consistent with A.I.D.'s new approaches, so that, rather than forcing them into directions that they may resist, A.I.D. is frequently responding to the stated needs and interests of developing nations.

A.I.D. has long accepted the basic premise that development assistance activities, to be meaningful and lasting, must involve the participation of each recipient country to the maximum extent. The application of self-help criteria, including the financial participation of the recipient country in A.I.D.-funded development activities, is an indication of the collaborative nature of our programs. If a recipient country does not accept the approach that is to be taken in an A.I.D.supported program or activity, that country usually is not willing to contribute its own resources. In such cases, A.I.D. cannot undertake the activity, because the new Sec. 110 of the Foreign Assistance Act requires that the country must contribute at least 25 per cent of each "program project or activity" that A.I.D. finances.

In summary, A.I.D.'s legislation and our central guidance to operating staffs have made it clear that A.I.D. projects are joint ventures with developing country governments. The message has gone out that focusing of the program on the needs of the poor is in no way a license to force these countries into accepting our approaches to economic and social development. 

REVIEW OF LDC POLICIES ON PARTICIPATION OF THE POOR 

Mr. FRASER. Has there been any review of the countries to which AID development assistance is provided in the light of their policies toward greater participation of the poor in the development process? 

Mr. PARKER. While we have not had a review focused exclusively on policies affecting participation of the poor in A.I.D. countries, we do expect an appraisal of these policies, along with an appraisal of other policies affecting social and economic performance, in the Development Assistance Program documents which we require from each of our major field missions. The purpose of these documents is to provide a framework for our development assistance program in each country for the next four or five year period. When we come to discussing and developing with the host country actual projects and programs we might assist. participation of the poor is an objective we strive to incorporate. In these discussions and reviews we again assess the consistency of host country policies with the objective of involving the poor in development. 

LDC GOVERNMENT ACCEPTANCE OF NEW LEGISLATION 

Mr. FRASER. Have you run into any difficulty with host country governments by moving toward greater sensitivity to social justice in your programs? Have there been any countries that have said, we'd like your aid, but not under those conditions?

In other words, have you run into any practical problems resulting from the potential conflict between the need to follow the approach to development endorsed in last year's act and the need to refrain from telling other countries what to do?

Mr. PARKER. The reaction so far to this aspect of our legislation has been favorable from most host country governments. However, as I indicated in my state-

ment to the Committee and as your question suggests, there are limits to our ability to shift the priorities of sovereign governments. We can persuade but only they can decide. Our experience has nevertheless been that we are usually able to find a sufficiently common ground of interest with an LDC government to develop programs in a collaborative way. We expect this to continue to be possible as we increase the emphasis of our program on reaching the poorest majorities in LDCs. 

Another factor which makes it easier to discuss this kind of emphasis with host governments is that other donors are by and large attempting to shift their priorities in the same direction. But this kind has also caused a few governments to express some concerns about the new approach. These tend to be primarily African countries which are still very deficient in such basic intrastructure as roads, power, and dams for irrigation. Without such infrastructure, the rural poor in these countries cannot be involved in the development process. As most donors increase their emphasis on agriculture, education and health, these countries have expressed concern that there will not be adequate development financing for basic infrastructure.

NEW DIRECTIONS 

Mr. FRASER. Have you made or do you plan to make any changes in the structure or operating procedures of the Agency to make it better able to undertake programs designed to involve the poor in the development of their countries? 

Mr. PARKER. Yes, we are taking a number of actions which will enable the 

Agency to improve its response to this important objective. These actions include policy guidance in each of the three major functional areas ranging from general guidelines to specific changes in operating procedures, covering the first steps in the design of projects and programs in the field through the Washington review process, to implementation and evaluation. It also involves taking the new approach into account in the selection, orientation and training of AID staff, consultants and contractors. We have issued general strategy papers and more detailed policy guidance in several of the functional areas and we plan to follow this up with additional guidance. We have also established special task forces charged with recommending changes affecting the full range of Agency operations indicated above.

The budget guidance that was sent to the field in the Spring of 1972 and which started the program currently being implemented in the current fiscal year stressed program concentration and some of the themes which Congress emphasized in the FAA of 1973. In October, 1972, we issued a Policy Determination on Employment and Income Distribution Objectives for A.I.D. Programs and 

Policies. This was followed by FY 1975 Program Guidance in spring, 1973, which stressed the three functional areas and quite specifically endorsed the approaches that the Congress was deliberating. In the summer of 1974 we instituted an Accelerated Program Development effort to assure priority funding to field missions submitting new programs in these areas. Strategy papers have been issued for education, health and nutrition and more detailed policy guidance messages have been issued for education, health, family planning and small farmer credit programs. These initiatives received strong re-inforcement from the new legislation and from the recently issued FY 1976 field budget submission guidance. 

Two task forces are charged with making recommendations on A.I.D. policies and operations dealing with aspects of the new directions designed to involve the poor in the development of their countries. These groups are (1) a New Initiatives 

Task Force and (2) a Working Group on the Rural Poor. 

The recently created New Initiatives Task Force is charged with examining and recommending ways in which the operational policies and procedures of AID can be changed so as to more effectively implement the legislation's call for emphasis on programs addressing the needs of the poorest majorities in developing countries for improved food and nutrition, health and family planning, and education and manpower development. This task force is directly responsible to our 

Senior Operations Group headed by the Deputy Administrator, Mr. John Murphy. 

The Working Group on the Rural Poor was established earlier this spring to make recommendations on how AID programs can more effectively and directly address the needs of the rural poor, who typically contitute both the largest

population group and the poorest of the poor in developing countries. The working group, composed of rural development experts drawn from every bureau of the AID Washington organization, is divided into subcommittees addressing such aspects of the problem as organization, staffing, research, policy and analysis. The subcommittee dealing with policy and analysis has obtained the assistance of experts from U.S. universities and research institutions to help draft strategy and policy papers dealing with the various aspects of rural development mentioned in both the House Foreign Affairs Committee Report on the new legislation and our FY 1975 Congressional Presentation. These papers are to be completed by the end of this summer in order to guide our field missions as together with host countries they develop projects and programs for FY 1976. BUT RI 

Finally, as I have already noted in my statement, we have been involved in an intensive effort to inform and strengthen the capability of AID-assisted private and voluntary organizations to focus their programs in developing countries on the objectives set forth in the new legislation. 

PROGRAMS BENEFITING THE POOR 

Mr. FRASER. On page 11 of the summary presentation book there is a tablesimilar to the one that appears in your prepared statement, also on page 11showing that the percentage of the program proposed for food and nutrition for FY 1975 is nearly double the percentage estimated for FY 1974. The table also shows that amounts proposed for all three main functional categories-food and nutrition, population and health, and education—are higher than the FY 1974 figures, while the amounts proposed for the two miscellaneous categories are down sharply.

The introductory statement in the presentation book asserts that the table reflects the new direction of last year's legislation, according "greater priority to policies and projects that can can directly improve the living standards of the majority."

Now, since agricultural, health, population and education programs can benefit the rich and bypass the poor-as many of A.I.D.'s past activities in these fields seem to have done I find it difficult to understand how your table proves your point.

Mr. PARKER. The shift of emphasis from infrastructure and balance of payments, support to activities in agriculture, population, health and education does not, in of itself, guarantee that the A.I.D. program is reaching and affecting the poorest people. This shift in emphasis must be seen in the context of a range of other actions that the Agency has undertaken. For example, in order to ensure that activities in the three main categories do, in fact, benefit the poorest majority, A.I.D. has issued and will continue to issue a series of global sector strategies and guidelines for field missions that directly incorporate the new direction of last year's legislation for each major area of program concentration. Our budget guidance to the field mission for Fiscal Year 1975 which was sent out last spring emphasized the basic approaches contained in the FAA of 1973 and our budget guidance for next fiscal year-Fiscal Year 1976-refines and continues this emphasis. Also, the Agency has instituted multi-year country program plans which explicitly consider how A.I.D.'s activities can best meet the needs of the poorest majority.

We have made it abundantly clear at all levels of the Agency that programs which directly affect the poorest majority will receive priority funding. A system for central review and approval of projects is well established and it is through this mechanism that we enforce stated Agency policy. While I agree that the data is only indicative and while I would certainly concur that we have a great deal more to do, the Agency is making a real and determined effort to refocus its program.

EXAMPLES OF ASSISTANCE TO SMALL-FARM AGRICULTURE 

Mr. FRASER. On page 12 of the summary presentation book, it says all of the additional funds requested for FY 1975 for food, rural development, and nutrition will go for "increasing the productivity of small producers." Could you tell us specifically some of the things you have in mind to do with the extra funds that would in fact benefit small-farm agriculture?

Mr. PARKER. I would be happy to do so. We plan a rapid increase in activities which will benefit small farmers, including programs for rural roads, irrigation, rural electricity, and farmer cooperatives. 

For instance, fifty thousand farm families in Sri Lanka will be able to carry out more intensive farming and multiple cropping because of an $8 million irrigation project.

In Haiti, the most impoverished nation of the hemisphere, A.I.D. will help increase small farmer production of basic food crops. 

In Guatemala, a loan is proposed for new programs in land resettlement and conservation, small-scale livestock production, and the creation of a seed bank. 

In Tanzania, an agriculture sector loan is planned to assist cooperatives and district development corporations to finance farm inputs such as seeds, fertilizer and machinery for small farms, and to improve water development, and farmto-market transport.

Of course, these are only a few examples of the many programs for small farmer which A.I.D. has planned.

SMALL FARMER NEEDS 

Mr. FRASER. Mr. Parker, the summary presentation book states, on page 19, under the heading of research on agricultural production-“Increased attention is being given to ensuring that technologies are developed in a manner best meeting the needs of the small farmer and to working out crop systems that are job creating and applicable to small scale operations."

Please submit for the record a detailed account of what is being done along these lines.

Mr. PARKER. One of the principal Agency criteria in scrutinizing all agricultural research support proposals is their potential contribution to job creation and small farmer needs. Where projects appear to have some such potential that is not being adequately realized, action is taken to bring about the necessary reshaping. For example: 

AID has been encouraging action by the international agricultural research centers to strengthen their social science analysis units and to have these work

A closely with the agricultural scientists in systems type analysis of the small farmer environment. This would identify factors inhibiting fuller use of improved technologies and what can be done to improve the situation by R&D work of the centers or by efforts elsewhere that complement or supplement the centers' work. For example, AID proposed and led the organization of a major seminar last summer on how to strengthen this aspect of the centers' work. The seminar was run at the World Bank under the auspices of the IBRD/FAO/UNDP sponsored Consultative Group on International Agricultural Research (CGIAR) which includes 20 national, international and private development assistance agencies that finance the centers' programs and also developing country representatives. 

The seminar included the Directors, Board Chairmen, and principal economists of the individual centers, the CGIAR members, and invited experts from developing and developed countries. This and prior and subsequent efforts are having the intended type of influence on the centers' work. To illustrate, the International Rice Research Institute is organizing a major cooperative research effort at the farm level among a series of Asian countries to identify differences between actual technology applied by the mass of small rice farmers and available higher yielding technologies, what factors explain the differences and what is needed to reduce the differences-including changing the technologies as needed to fit actual farm situations better. This will involve multi-disciplinary work by social and agricultural scientists. The corn and wheat center in Mexico (CIMMYT) is carrying forward a similar multi-country activity on corn. And so on. All of the centers are expanding their capabilities and efforts in this general area. 

Closely related are efforts to make labor intensity and low risk, along with high yields, principal purposes of the research work at the centers and in AID's own research projects. Small farmers gain more of their income than large farmers from labor inputs by their family, as compared to land or capital use. Labor intensity also increases employment for landless farmers. Small farmers need low risk technology packages even if these give smaller average yields over a period of years than other available technologies, as they can be wiped out or suffer severely from short term crop losses. Thus increasing efforts are being made to provide technologies that yield substantially more than those now used by small farmers but that minimize risks of crop failure from poor weather or other environmental hazards (disease, pests, etc.), and that also reduce risks by requiring low capital investment and comparatively simple management skills. Some illustrations of technology efforts along these along these lines are: 

A very successful AID conventional research project to introduce better weed control technology to LDC's has now shifted its attention to R&D work in LDC's that seeks new control systems that use more labor and less herbicides and have simpler management requirements for successful use. 

The international centers are shifting research attention more to total han cropping systems employed by small farmers, and how to increase yields from the composite systems under the farmers actual conditions, as distinguished from work to find maximum yield systems for individual crops which may not fit efficiently into the small farmers total system needs. 

A recent AID research breakthrough is introducing a new and far more effective method of eliminating heavy cattle losses from rabies carried by vampire bats. The new method requires much less capital investment than the inoculation systems now in use. 

Similarly, research on controlling losses from cattle blood diseases is introducing a low cost and much more effective inoculation system in lieu of current dipping and spraying practices. 

The international centers are experimenting with more labor intensive cultivation systems in lieu of capital intensive reliance on fertilizers, herbicides, etc.

The centers are putting increased stress in their genetic research on greater resistance to prevalent plant diseases and pests and climatic stress, in order to obtain lower risk plant varieties. 

An AID research project conducted at IRRI is developing low cost, simple machinery for small rice farmers that meets their needs much better than developed country type equipment and that permits fuller use of their land over the year thereby increasing labor demand. 

The quality of life of the small farmer and his family, and of the other rural and urban poor, is affected strongly by the nutritional quality of the cheap, mass

consumed staple foods. Thus AID is giving research priority to achieving radical increases in the protein and other nutrient value of these foods, both by breeding and fortification routes. For example, major genetic breakthroughs have been achieved for corn and sorghum, the two most important foods of the poor in Latin America and Africa and in parts of Asia. Promising experiments are being run on village level fortification of wheat, corn, rice and cassava. 

More broadly, priority for crop improvement research is being given, through AID and international center programs, to crops that are the most important sources of employment calories, protein and other nutrients for poor producers and consumers. All of the principal crops being researched have at least one of these characteristics and most have all three. (Crops are rice, wheat, corn, sorghum, barley, cassava, potatoes, soybeans, dry beans, chickpeas and cowpeas.)

AID's agricultural economics research, through a sizeable set of projects, is working on methodologies for analyzing employment and capital requirements and income distribution effects of alternative farm policies and programs, and is identifying development strategies (including technology selection) that improve these factors and the position of small farmers. 

These technology related efforts to improve the position of the rural poor are reinforced by other projects to develop local organizational capabilities, to foster area development in poor regions, and to develop systems for mass rural delivery of health and learning services at costs that the developing countries can afford. 

MALNUTRITION IN THE DEVELOPING COUNTRIES 

Mr. FRASER. We hear a lot about malnutrition both in this country and abroad, but not many people are aware of the true extent and nature of the problem as it applies to people in the poor countries. 

Can you tell us how many people in the poor countries are malnourished and what this really means in human terms? 

Mr. PARKER. The Food and Agricultural Organization of the United Nations estimates very reliably and repeatedly that there are about one and a half billion hungry people in the poor countries of the world today. 

Children are most vulnerable to the consequences of malnutrition. It is estimated that in 1975 more than 800 million children in the developing countries will be malnourished. More than half of these will be preschool age children and two-thirds of these will develop disabling diseases attributable to malnutrition. The steady increase in the number of malnourished children is shown in the following table.

NUMBER OF MALNOURISHED CHILDREN IN DEVELOPING COUNTRIES, 1966-75 

[Rough estimate in millions] 

Number of children by age group 1966 1968 1975 0 to 6 

7 to 14 342 350 425 325 338 390 

Total 0 to 14. 667 688 1 815 

1 From "The Protein Gap," Agency for International Development, Bureau for Technical Assistance, Washington, D.C 

20523, 1970. 

Malnutrition and mortality are inseparable. In Brazil, eighty-percent of all deaths are in the under-five age group. In India, it is sixty-five percent, in Egypt, sixty-eight percent. Malnutrition is the direct or associated cause for at least fifty-seven percent of all these deaths. The price of malnutrition is high for those who survive. Malnutrition in the infant and preschool child retards physical and mental development. The effects persist throughout life. The malnourished school child cannot concentrate or learn. He lacks curiosity. He is irresponsive to stimuli, listless and apathetic. He becomes a "non-achiever" first in school and then in life.

Malnutrition in women during pregnancy can lead to stillbirths and low birth weight babies whose survival chances are poor. Impaired lactation may result

in premature weaning of infants and enhanced infant morbidity and mortality. 

Adults, in general, living on suboptimal calorie and protein intakes and on diets deficient in vitamins and minerals lack physical strength and precise muscular coordination; work output is low and achievement poor. A malnourished child in a developing country may survive only to face a submarginal existence dominated by hunger, illness and poverty. 

FERTILIZER SHORTAGE 

Mr. FRASER. There are a lot of reports in the newspapers and elsewhere that the shortage of fertilizer due in part to the oil embargo and oil price rises will make it impossible for some developing countries to grow even as much food as they were able to in recent years, despite their growing populations. There has even been a lot of talk about famine affecting millions of people. 

Is the problem as serious as it sounds, and what is A.I.D. doing about the fertilizer shortage in the developing world to try to prevent this kind of famine from occurring?

Mr. PARKER. The fertilizer shortage is an extremely serious problem for the developing countries. The most recent estimate we have is from the UN: the 

ECOSOC Working Group on fertilizers estimated in May that the LDCs will be about 12 million metric tons short in 1974/5 and 1975/6, resulting in a food grain drop of 12 million tons. Not only is fertilizer supply insufficient, the prices are now so high that some LDCs cannot afford to buy what little fertilizer is available. 

In addition to supporting a return to larger PL 480 grain export programs to meet LDC urgent short term needs and increased stress on programs designed to build a better long-term base in agricultural development, A.I.D. is proposing a 200% increase in financing for fertilizer procurement in 1975 over 1974. In 

FY 1974, we financed 569,000 product tons of fertilizer at a total cost of nearly $65 million. In FY 1975, we propose to finance 703,000 product tons of fertilizer at an estimated total cost of $210 million. In addition, we will indirectly finance at least $10 million in fertilizer purchases through agricultural development projects where host country government agencies will purchase fertilizer in small quantities for projects such as agricultural credit schemes. We also are planning to join in funding two fertilizer production projects which will help Pakistan and Bangladesh become more self-sufficient in fertilizer production. 

These two projects will involve about $50 million in AID funds. 

In total we expect to finance about $270 million in fertilizer procurement and production in FY 1975, assuming our Congressional Presentation budget request is met. To do more would cut deeply into our planned agricultural production projects which are contributions to the long-term agricultural self-sufficiency of the LDCs. 

BOND GUARANTEE PROPOSAL 

Mr. FRASER. I understand that A.I.D. is studying a proposal to guarantee bonds issued by developing countries, so that countries which have been unable to borrow in the U.S. capital market on their own would be able to issue their bonds without risk to the bondholder. 

Where does that proposal stand? Will you submit for the record an analysis of the proposal, and include discussion of the possibility of providing subsidized interest rates for countries that need foreign exchange but can't afford market rates of interest.

Mr. PARKER. A.I.D. has been studying the question of what the U.S. Government might do to help developing countries gain access to the U.S. long-term capital market. In recent years very few developing countries have been able to borrow from the American insurance companies and other financial institutions, or the general bond-holding public, who together constitute the largest market for long-term lending in the world. While private direct investment by U.S. corporations has of course provided substantial resources for many developing countries, long-term "portfolio" borrowing by LDC goverments or enterprises has been extremely limited and restricted to only a handful of countries. mostly in Latin America. Many credit-worthy LDCs should be able to borrow long-term in the U.S., but are hampered by a number of institutional and knowledge barriers which have proved difficult for them to overcome by themselves. AID staff has been examining how the U.S. might help facilitate the access of credit-worthy LDCs to the U.S. private capital market through the provision of technical assistance and some form of guarantee.

The purpose of the U.S. guarantee would be to help such countries overcome these institutional barriers and establish their name and credit-worthiness, encouraging long-term lenders to acquire the bonds of the initial borrowing of these countries by greatly reducing, or possibly eliminating, the risks to the bondholder. At what could be a very small cost to the U.S. Government, these countries would be helped to enter the private capital market which is the mainstream of investment financing under the U.S. economic system. 

At this time, the approach developed by A.I.D. staff toward this problem of LDC market access is being discussed with officials of other interested agencies and with members of the securities industry. The possible role of guarantees to facilitate LDC access to long-term capital markets in Europe is also being discussed with the other aid donor countries who are members of the Development Assistance Committee of the OECD. The governments of many developing countries have a strong interest in gaining access to the U.S. long-term capital market. For example, improving such access was one of the questions raised by the Latin American Foreign Ministers with Secretary Kissinger at the meeting of Foreign Ministers in Mexico City in February. At this stage. we are pursuing technical discussions to determine the feasibility of the particular approaches A.I.D. has been considering. 

The guaranty provision should effectively reduce the interest rate on the LDC bonds to a level that would be moderately lower than the current commercial rates obtainable by these countries. A.I.D. has in this context reviewed the question of subsidizing interest rates in order to lower interest rates still further to a level which would be in line with the financial position of the lower Income LDCs. The cost of such a subsidy program was, however, considered to be not only too high but also only indirectly related to the purpose of the guaranty program.

A more detailed analysis of the proposal is submitted for the record. 

DEVELOPING COUNTRY ACCESS TO THE U.S. CAPITAL MARKET 

This paper briefly sets out a proposal designed to help selected less developed, countries (LDC's) gain access to the U.S. long-term capital market, by providing them with U.S. Government guarantees for two or three initial issues. The proposal is being developed by staff of the Agency for International Development, and as of this writing is only in a technical discussion stage. 

The developing countries' continuing long-term need for capital inflows has now been greatly increased in the short-run, due to the petroleum and food/ fertilizer situation. In their great need to supplement the capital inflows they have been receiving from private investment and official development assistance, many LDCs have borrowed from the Eurocurrency market in the past three years (despite the fact that the terms and nature of this market are not well suited to the financial requirements of most LDCs). It would clearly be in the interest of many LDCs to be able to borrow in the U.S. long-term market: interest rates and maturities would be better than in the Eurocurrency market; an additional major source of funds would be opened to them; the funds would be available more flexibly than is the case in IBRD or IDB project lending; their credit-worthiness in all other money markets would be enhanced. If the 

U.S. capital market turns out to be a major recipient of excess foreign exchange earnings of the major oil-exporting countries, access to the U.S. capital market will be one important way for LDCs to obtain "recycled" oil money. 

There are many LDC governments which should be able to borrow in the U.S. long-term market (as have Mexico, Brazil and Argentina), based on their credit-worthiness, but have been unable due to a variety of institutional, knowledge and other barriers. Such barriers could be overcome through a guarantee mechanism whereby the U.S. would guarantee payment of principal and interest to the bond-holders in the event of default. The LDC bonds would thus be virtually legally equivalent to USG obligations in the eyes of the American insurance companies and trust funds which would be the principal initial buyers of the guaranteed obligations. In the process of flotation and subsequent interest payment, a participating LDC government would be getting to know the operations of the U.S. capital market, and would be establishing its name and bona fide's for later borrowing on its own without USG help.

LIMITED EXTENT OF PRESENT ACCESS 

A mechanism for increasing LDC access to the U.S. long-term capital market should be of considerable interest to many LDCs. LDC external bond issues in the period 1960-72 were small, representing less than 5% of their total external sources of funds. For only two countries, Mexico and Argentina, did external bond issues provide as much as 10% of total external financial sources. And there has been no consistent trend of such LDC issues to rise (or fall). 

In the U.S. market, LDC issues comprised only 4.6% of all foreign issues in the period 1960-1972, and as a percentage of total bond issues ranged between 

0.4% in 1965 to .02% in 1970.

Absolute amounts of LDC bonds issued in the U.S. in recent years were as follows: 

1965 1967 1969 1970 Millions $130 70 98 13 46 1971 1972 76 Distribution by country has been very skewed. The lion's share of issues and volume of funds borrowed has gone to four Latin American countries, with most of the other 19 LDCs that issued bonds (publicly or privately placed) between 1962-1970 borrowing only three times or less, and raising miniscule amounts. If all external LDC issues in 1972 had been placed in the U.S. market, they would have amounted to less than 1% of all money raised in the American bond market. Thus with only two real exceptions, the U.S. long-term capital market has not been an important source of financial transfers for LDCs; for most LDCs it has not been a source of any capital flow whatsoever. 

NEW MODERATELY CONCESSIONAL ASSISTANCE OVER THE NEAR TERM 

Borrowing long term at rates very close to USG rates would constitute a degree of concessionality in relation to Eurocurrency market or short-term bank loan borrowing costs which are the major alternatives. While the guarantee would not extend to the poorest countries (by virtue of their need for highly concessional aid and their poor credit-worthiness prospects), it would provide moderately concessional resources to the middle-income LDC's that need to increase the availability of external resources for their development. 

HIGHLIGHTS OF THE PROPOSAL 

AID would seek authority for five years, with an initial cumulative ceiling on outstanding gurantees. Provision of a guarantee could be linked with technical assistance on access and operations in the highly regulated U.S. money market. 

Issues would of course vary by size by country. 

Eligibility for assistance into the long-term commercial market would be set by economic and financial criteria which would in effect define a set of middleincome LDCs, compare with the IDA countries which need concessional, not commercial, terms, and richer LDCs able to borrow from this market without guarantee assistance.

Budgetary cost could be quite minimal. The contingent liabilities to the U.S. created by extending guarantees could, if necessary, be "backed" by a reserve fund only some fraction (10%?) of the size of these liabilities. The reserve could be increased over time from the proceeds of a small premium charged to the borrower.

There are several precedents for USG guarantees of foreign debts to American creditors. AID's Housing Investment Guarantee authority, OPIC investment guarantees, and EXIM Bank guarantees all serve to guarantee private U.S. creditors. DOD has authority to guarantee credits to foreign governments for sales of American military equipment.

Except for determination of eligibility and extension of the guarantee (and monitoring), implementation would be handled entirely by the investment banking and underwriting community as an ordinary operation of the market.

TECHNICAL ASPECTS 

Administration of a guarantee would involve the following: 

Technical assistance for finance ministry and central bank officials unfamiliar with the institutions, legal requirements, etc., of the U.S. market. 

Preparation of economic-credit-worthiness appraisals by AID both to back up extension of each guarantee and to provide the potential lenders with the information they need for an investment decision. 

Problem of late data generation to meet registration needs may need special attention.

Information requirements will be greater to meet legal requirements of a secondary market, than will be required initially for private placements; the borrowing country should supply this with the help of its investment broker. 

Information requirements, registration requirements and form and marketing of issues will vary depending on whether an issue is for private placement, public issue, aimed at eligibility for the secondary market, aimed only at U.S. market or designed to be linked with parallel issue in Europe, etc. These are issues primarily between the LDC and its investment banking advisors, but AID will have an interest in guiding these choices in directions consistent with ultimate objective of LDC ability to borrow without the guarantee. 

AID will have to monitor payment of principal and interest, and sinking fund deposits if called for, in view of USG legal obligations under the guarantee. 

A.I.D.'s POPULATION PROGRAM AND LESTER BROWN'S BOOK, "IN THE HUMAN INTEREST" 

Mr. FRASER. Lester Brown, of the Overseas Development Council, has just written a book on population control called "In the Human Interest"; I am sure you have seen it. One of the book's more startling points is that with the right set of policies it might be possible to stabilize world population at 6 billion-a far lower figure than even the most optimistic estimates that have been made. 

Do you agree that it might be possible to keep population down to such a low figure? What is A.I.D. doing about the population problem? Are there any of the proposals Brown makes in his book that you think A.I.D. might be able to help implement?

Mr. PARKER. The essential point Lester Brown makes in his book is that if world population is to be limited to six billion, a major effort will be required by all countries. Rich countries will further need to reduce their own fertility and to provide resources to the poor countries to assist them in their efforts to reduce fertility. LDC's will need to work especially hard to provide family planning services and to create the conditions for rapid family planning acceptances. 

The annual cost of providing family planning services to the populations of noncommunist LDC's would be about $2 billion, a figure Brown obtained from the 

United Nations' Fund for Population Activities. Half this sum would come from donor countries, the remainder from internal LDC sources. Brown states that the present flow of funds into LDC's from both public and private funds is about $250 million, a quarter of what would be needed.

A.I.D. believes that with strong population policies and vigorous action on the part of all nations, the goal of population stabilization at 6 billion would be attainable. A lot of hard work will be required, however, if that goal is to be realized, and substantially larger funds will need to be provided from the U.S. and other donors. If nations do not immediately make a much stronger effort to reduce fertility, it is unlikely that stabilization will be reached before the present population is doubled to about 8 billion, and perhaps not even then. 

A.I.D. has a comprehensive program which is described in some detail in the 

Congressional Presentation. In brief, A.I.D. is assisting LDC's on a bilateral basis as well as through multilateral channels to assess the implications of their population growth, to plan and execute programs to deliver family planning services, to supply these programs with needed contraceptives and other commodities, and to evaluate the effectiveness of these programs.

Brown makes several suggestions for activities which A.I.D. is already doing. 

For example, he believes commercial distribution of contraceptives to be potentially very important. Actually, some of the data he cites on existing commercial distribution was taken from marketing studies carried out under an A.I.D. 

---

Brown also talks about creating the social conditions for fertility decline. 

A.I.D.'s three main program emphases are Food and Nutrition, Population Planning and Health, and Education and Human Resources. These programs are tackling many of the problems Brown cites as impediments to more rapid acceptances of family planning.

DEVELOPMENT ASSISTANCE POLICY CONFERENCE 

Mr. FRASER. A.I.D. recently co-sponsored a major conference on the role of private and voluntary agencies in development, and I commend you for moving quickly to implement the provisions of last year's bill that call for greater participation of private institutions in development programs. 

What were the main results from that conference, as you see them, and what do you plan to do now in this area?

I understand a summary of the conference has been prepared. Could you submit a copy for the record?

Mr. PARKER. In line with the objectives of the legislation, A.I.D. has been developing improved ways for increasing the participation of private and voluntary organizations (PVO's), including cooperatives in development activity in the LDC's. We are also seeking ways to improve, at all levels, day-to-day operations which involve PVO's. We have been interested in finding ways in which the staff and organizational effectiveness of PVO's could be enhanced in their efforts to do this added work. 

The Conference proved a very useful first step in carrying out these objectives. 

The participants understood their respective objectives, potentials and limitations as a result of the frank exchanges which occurred. 

At the Conference we announced A.I.D.'s new policy of setting aside funds to facilitate greater PVO participation in overseas development. During FY 1975, $5 million will be available for Development Program Grants, designed to support qualified, interested PVO's in planning and negotiating LDC developmental activities, providing, where appropriate, assistance to augment their staffs and other capacities to enable them to plan, design, manage, and evaluate programs. It is also contemplated that $6 million will be set aside to fund specific projects involving PVO activity in the field. 

Additionally, we are planning again in collaboration with the private and voluntary agencies, a series of smaller follow-on conferences and workshops. 

These will be technical level discussions to help A.I.D and PVO staffs share ideas and perspectives about the new emphases in the Foreign Assistance legislation. Our expectation is that the staff involved will be able to focus better on programs and projects in such fields as LDC food production, better nutrition, low cost health-related services, etc., where our overall objective is to help the LDC's improve the lives of the poor majority. We have already held one meeting with PVO representatives to seek ways to improve the planning and execution of P.L. 480 food distribution program. 

The Conference Report is not yet completed. We anticipate it will be finished the week of June 29 and we will submit it for the record at that time.
