Report, April 29-30, 1974," was furnished Mr. Fraser and also for the committee's file.] 

COMMUNICATIONS SATELLITES 

Mr. FRASER. In your statement, you mention some of the ways you are trying to bring relevant education to tens of millions of people in the poor countries at low cost, through non-formal methods. Will you also be using the new education satellite that was just launched a couple of weeks ago, as a means of reaching a great many people who cannot be reached by any other means? 

Mr. PARKER. No, sir for several reasons. The ATS-6 TV satellite (known as the ATS-F in all pre-launch documents) is fully scheduled for the first two years of its three years of estimated useful life. The first year is committed to concurrent educational experiments in three geographic zones of the United 

States: Appalachia, the Rocky Mountain area and Alaska. The satellite is then to he moved. in mid-1975, to a suitable location over the Indian sub-continent where it will be, for a year, at the service of the Government of India for educational experimentation involving more than 2,000 villages in different parts of the country. Third year plans are not yet firm.

A.I.D. has no financial involvement in the launching or operation of this satellite. India and the National Aeronautics and Space Administration of the 

United States agreed in 1969 to the year of satellite use for that country's experiment.

A.I.D. has been very active, however, in policy development and research on the use of communication satellites. We have been very active in the Department of State's Inter Agency Working Group on Direct Broadcast Satellites (DBS). We participated in the UN Working Group meeting in Geneva in March 

1974. We have been aware of the apprehensions and the cultural sensitivities of nations to the "intrusion" of communications not under their control, and have made great strides by limiting ourselves to sharing technological know-how, and stimulating as well as conducting studies and research whose findings we also share.

At our May 1974 conference in Denver on Educational Broadcast Satellites, we distributed copies of studies of the planned experiments in Brazil, India and the United States. We financed these studies, among others. We will observe and share the ATS-6 results. 

The Denver conference was attended by representatives from India, Indonesia, Brazil, the Andean States, Iran, the Economic Commission for Africa and the League of Arab States, as well as delegates from Canada, New Zealand, UNESCO, and the three areas of the United States which will be involved in the 

ATS-6 first year experiments.

We feel that we have achieved acceptance in a leadership role in assisting other natious to use satellites to reach segments of their population previously unreachable.

DEVELOPMENT COORDINATION COMMITTEE Mr. FRASER. Section 102(b) (7) of the Foreign Assistance Act, enacted as part of last year's bill, gives A.I.D. responsibility for "coordinating all United 

States development-related activities." This section is independent of the Development Coordination Committee, but that Committee presumably is meant to be the main mechanism for carrying out that responsibility. 

I realize that the Development Coordination Committee has not yet been established, but I wondered if you could tell us whether you have begun to take a look at some of the areas you will be dealing with as development coordinator. 

For example, would it be worthwhile examining the role of the Peace Corps in development, to see if there are appropriate ways of using Peace Corps experience as a means of helping bring the poor into the development process? 

Or are there ways of estimating the development impact of trade preference for developing countries and mechanisms that might be established if preferences are adopted to ensure that development goals are considered as preference provisions are implemented?

Are questions like these being examined to see where the attention of the development coordinator and the development coordination mechanism might best be directed?

Mr. PARKER. The Agency has spent considerable time in the last several months trying to think out the kinds of issues which might best be examined by the Development Coordination Committee. We have been anxious to get the 

Committee, once it is set up, off to a good start by involving it in vital issues which need ventilation and which are not currently being aired by other bodies within the United States Government. 

Both of the examples which you have cited occurred to us also as suitable subject matter for the Development Coordination Committee. How best to use the Peace Corps experience is a most likely Committee subject; I think I can say that without qualification. The question of trade preference needs to be qualified somewhat. As far as the Less Developed Countries are concerned probably the most important thing which needs to happen is the passage of the Trade Reform Act of 1973. As you know this was passed by the House of 

Representatives as PL 10710 and is being considered by the Senate. The bill establishes a generalized standard of preference which includes provision for duty free entry into the United States of manufactured goods, and some other goods as well, from the Less Developed Countries. After passage of the bill,

however, I do believe that the Development Coordination Committee will wish to keep this as an item on its agenda for further consideration. 

OPS PROGRAM AND U.S. INTERESTS ABROAD 

Mr. FRASER. In what specific ways would you say that the OPS program has been helpful to U.S. interest abroad? In what ways harmful? 

Mr. PARKER. The Public Safety effort, like all other U.S. programs abroad, has intended and unintended effects that go beyond its more immediate and specific objectives of assisting friendly nations to establish their systems of justice. Each program has had some effect on broader U.S. objectives and interest in Asia, Africa and Latin America to provide the structure for development of emerging nations. Specifically, assistance in this sector is calculated to enhance the efficiency, capability and professional character of the civil police establishment and to instill within the police the concept of service to the community. 

There are various examples which can be cited to demonstrate the effectiveness of this approach. As a result of Public Safety efforts, a Coast, River and Lake 

Guard Force was created in Zaire. In the past year, this organization has been commended for rescuing numerous persons on Lake Tanganyika during violent storms. The image of the U.S. as well as the police cannot help but be improved. 

During the catastrophic floods in the Philippines, police units played major roles in rescue operations and providing aid for refugees. These units had been partially equipped and trained by U.S. police assistance efforts. The police telecommunications network was the only functioning system in the Philippines during the crisis and played a major role in reducing human suffering. The police performed well during the crisis, bringing distinction to the civilian police units.

Major efforts have been made since the earthquake of 1972 in Nicaragua to reestablish the police organization and facilities which were almost totally destroyed. The Public Safety advisors worked through the disaster, side-by-side with their police counterparts, to assist in relief of the victims. The U.S. image was enhanced by the efforts of these individuals. Since the earthquake, a new police headquarters and 14 of 17 precincts have been constructed and placed into operation. Prior to the earthquake, police duties were performed by National 

Guardsmen utilizing military uniforms and weapons. The total organization of the police has now been restructured and a separate force with distinctive uniforms and carrying only sidearms is operational. Some of these efforts were initiated prior to the earthquake but have taken final form since. 

In addition to pursuing its basic objectives of strengthening the civil police, the OPS has become involved in three other specific and growing U.S. interests abroad in recent years: (1) to help other police forces to protect Americans overseas; (2) curb international terrorism; and (3) fight illicit narcotics traffic. 

As to the question of in what specific ways the program has been harmful, I have no details. I would only note that assistance in this or any other area has the immediate effect of strengthening the regime that receives it. The element of risk that it may be misused has existed and continues. 

OPS IMAGE IN LATIN AMERICA 

Mr. FRASER. What kind of image does the OPS program have among Latin Americans?

Mr. PARKER. My impression is that A.I.D.'s Office of Public Safety enjoys an image of professionalism in those governments with which they have been associated. These countries have expressed appreciation for the assistance that has permitted them to develop their capabilities to maintain a stable and orderly atmosphere in which development can occur. 

STATE OF SIEGE 

Mr. FRASER. Have you seen State of Siege? Regardless of whether it was accurate and honest, do you think it was a convincing film? 

Mr. PARKER. Yes. Mr. Fraser, I did see State of Siege. It struck me as a tendentious film and did not convince me of its basic premises. I found it impossible to view our operations abroad in the context the director insisted upon.

[The following article on the movie was submitted for inclusion in the record :] [From the Sunday News, Detroit, Mich., Aug. 12, 1974]

SUNDAY VIEWPOINT "STATE OF SIEGE": HOW MARXISTS USED THE BIG LIE AGAINST THE UNITED STATES IN DOCUMENTARY (By Ernest W. Lefever) 

Dr. Ernest W. Lefever, 53, is a senior researcher on the foreign policies studies staff of the Brookings Institution in Washington. A recognized authority on U.S. policy toward the Third World, he has made research trips to the 

Congo and other African states, Asia and Europe in the last decade. He has written or edited eight books in the fields of world armaments, politics and foreign policy. He also has served as an international affairs consultant to both governmental and private agencies 

WASHINGTON.-At 4:15 a.m. Monday, Aug. 10, 1970, the body of a stocky, unshaven 50-year-old man was found in the back seat of a stolen Buick convertible parked on Calle Lucas Moreno in Montevideo, Uruguay.

Blood was dripping through the floorboard and running toward the curb. 

He had been shot twice in the head and twice in the body. His eyes were bandaged. His left armpit bore deep bruises close to a half-healed gunshot wound. 

His inner arms were pitted by 16 needle punctures.

This 12th murder and fifth kidnap victim of the Tupamaro terrorists was Dan A. Mitrione, former police chief of Richmond, Indiana, a devoted Catholic father of nine who was a U.S. public safety adviser in Uruguay. 

Kidnaped 11 days earlier, Mitrione had been "tried" by a Tupamaro "peoples court" and accused of being a CIA or FBI agent, of teaching Uruguayan police advanced torture techniques, and of organizing a campaign of repression against "revolutionary" leaders. For these "crimes," he had been condemned to death. 

Three years later, Dan Mitrione's good name has been besmirched and his family anguished by a viciously anti-American film designed to malign him and what he stood for, and "prove" that the Tupamaros who killed him were justified. "State of Siege”—a widely applauded "documentary" now making the rounds of U.S. "art" movie houses (it played in Detroit in July at the Studio-4 and 

Studio New Center)-is a skillful and plausible but profoundly fraudulent version of the death-and lifeof Dan Mitrione. "State of Siege" was authored by two apostles of Europe's intellectual left- Constantin Gavras (who now calls himself Costa-Gavras, a craggy-faced film director of Russian-Greek parentage, and Franco-Solinos, a gifted Italian Communist scriptwriter. It was reportedly bankrolled by Donald S. Rugoff, Madison 

Avenue film distributor, who has a taste for radical themes and whose wife plays a role in "State of Siege."

Costa-Gavras, "the Hitchcock of the Left," has spared little effort in his attempt to convince American critics and the world that his film is a factually accurate account of the kidnaping, and death of Dan Mitrione. 

Varying his words only slightly. Costa-Gavras made this claim a score of times in New York and Washington interviews with newspaper and TV people. Still further attention was focused on this documentary question by an 11th-hour decision to withdraw "State of Siege" from its scheduled showing last April at the gala opening of the American Film Institute's new theater in Washington's Kennedy Center by the Institute's director, George Stevens, Jr., because it "rationalizes an act of political assassination.” "The events in this film actually took place in a South American country," says the opening line, followed by a close-up of a light green Cadillac with a Montevideo license plate. "State of Siege," like Costa-Gavras' previous box-office hit, "Z" (which Rugoff also reportedly underwrote to the tune of $600,000), makes use of a documentary format. Costa-Gavras and Solinas (who wrote "Battle of Algiers") intended it to be dramatic journalism, accepted as fact not 

To underline their point, the two authors published a 214-page book in France and the U.S. (Ballantine Random House, 1st edition, 150,000 copies) containing 36-333-74-12

the screenplay and 80 pages of what they call "the authentic documents that inspired the script" of this "exact documentary." 

During promotional encounters in America, Costa-Gavras has repeatedly emphasized how diligently he pursued evidence through reading and two field trips to Uruguay before filming in Chile. "We verified our facts," he said, "by talking to Uruguayan journalists" and consulting “books about AID. We wanted to use only the facts we could be sure of by research." "We built a rigorous construction of events," added Solinas, "without inventing anything, and above all without foisting on Mitrione a culpability which was not proved by facts.

This claim that "State of Siege" is factual, at least in essentials, has been accepted at or near face value by many American reviewers. A few took the opposite view, but most critics never faced the issue directly. 

Judith Crist (New York Magazine) saw the film as an authentic document. 

Costa-Gavras, she says, performed "a public duty that the American media has failed in by informing us of a situation of which, I would say, 99 percent of the public is completely ignorant." 

Noting that the co-authors "researched and documented their case," Miss Crist is horrified at "revelation heaped on revelation" by this "brilliant expose of American imperialism in Latin America." She is upset by AID's role in "suppressing political dissent" in Uruguay, "a land of total repression," by providing "instruments of torture (shipped under diplomatic cover)." "Is Costa-Gavras telling it like it was in Uruguay?" asked Leonard Harris on

WCBS-TV. He answers his own question. Reporting on a panel held after the 

April 12 New York premiere, he says. "No one on it suggested he wasn't. I'll give 'State of Siege' five out of five camera eyes.' (Had WCBS-TV's panelists been critical, it would have been a surprise. The panel included Costa-Gavras and Solinas themselves; the militant ex-Congressman Allard Lowenstein; Jose Yglesias, Latin book reviewer for the Communist journal New Masses; liberal historian Arthur Schlesinger Jr.; and Nat Hentoff, editor of New York's Village Voice, who moderated.)

Some critics called the film dishonest and distorted. "For all is hyped-up drama and feverish social consciousness," said Paul Zimmerman of Newsweek, "it is just a tract on dirty Yankeeism in Latin America. Like Costa-Gavras' other films, 'Z' and 'The Confession'," he added, it is a "melodramatic left-wing restaging of history." 

This mixed reception raises two questions: (1) Is "State of Siege" an honest documentary, a fictional thriller, an anti-U.S. propaganda tract, or a combination? (2) Will it exert, as Judith Crist and others have suggested, a constructive impact on Washington's policy toward Latin America by shocking U.S. citizens into awareness of "torture and repression" that the Agency for International Development (AID) already carries out in their name?

These questions can be answered only by comparing the film with the factsthe flashing, disjointed, confusing images of "State of Siege" with the straightforward march of events that led to the murder of Dan Mitrione. 

In 1970, Uruguay was, to begin with, anything but the reactionary police state pictured by Costa-Gavras and Solinas. On the contrary, it was one of the most democratic and open societies in the world. Its president and parliament were popularly elected. Its two major parties and political groups to the right and left were free to debate, criticize, publish and organize. The 37,000-member Communist Party was represented in parliament and published El Popular, a widely circulated daily.

Uruguay had no death penalty, the maximum for any crime was 30 years, and the prisons were run by the ministry of culture and education. Though the economy was stagnant, Uruguay's per capita income was twice that of Brazil and more evenly distributed. The government operated a cradle-to-grave welfare system.

With one of the most permissive governments of modern times, Uruguay was a marshmallow state.

Liberty had lapsed into license. Communist-dominated unions and other radical groups took advantage of this vulnerable situation to seek their objectives through strikes and violence.

The most notorious troup was the Tupamaro Liberation Front, a small paramilitary terrorist organization dating from 1962, similar to the Weathermen in America and the Black September killers in the Mideast. In 1970 there were fewer

than a thousand Tupamaros, with about 150 in prison or awaiting trial. Their social goals were not clear, but they seemed to seek a revolutionary order a la 

Castro or Mao. 

Like other terrorist extremists in Colombia, Venezuela and Argentina, the

Tupamaros were an amalgam of idealists, romantics, nihilists, misfits, dropouts, and common thugs. They pursued their immediate aim of social demolition through bank robberies, auto theft, bombing, kidnaping, and murder. The Tupamaros killed their first policeman on Dec. 16, 1966, shooting him in the back with a submachine gun. By last May, their murder victims numbered 45.

As of mid-1970, when Mitrione was kidnaped, they had looted a naval armory, stolen explosives from a quarry, held up banks, burned the Montevideo General Motors offices, and raided the town of Pando. The raid resulted in the murder of one policeman and the death of a bystander. A peasant who stumbled onto a 

Tupamaro hideout in Pan de Azucar was murdered. Witnesses to terrorist crimes were threatened with death and suffered reprisals. One was rubbed out for giving information to the police. Some of these incidents depicted in "State of Siege." 

In early years the Tupamaros enjoyed a Robin Hood image, which Costa Gavros attempts to perpetuate. But the Tupamaros never gained wide support: 

At the zenith of their influence the political faction nearest theri view, Partido 

Erro, polled only 4.3 percent of the popular vote.

The day after Mitrione's murder, a Uruguayan Communist leader denounced the Tupamaros as "insane fanatics." In 1971 Moscow called them "pseudo-revolutionaries" and "loud-mouthed thugs," and "gangster tactics."

In Chile (where "State of Siego" was made with the blessing and encourage- Iment of Marxist President Salvador Allende) orthodox Party film-crews nonetheless walked off the lot during shooting because of the disapproval of Communist Party leaders for the wild, and, in their view, counterproductive Tupamaro terrorists of Uruguay.

Through interrogation, flashback, inference and published "documents," Costa- Gavras portrays Dan Mitrione as a CIA super-agent willingly serving U.S. political and financial interests by installing reactionary, repressive, semifascists regimes in Latin America. "Your methods are war, fascism, and torture," cries his interrogator.

Mitrione is presented in the film as a ruthless, calculating, deceitful man "who never had any sentiments." He is the over-patriotic self-righteous immigrant, a kind of "convinced Stalinist" of the right, in contrast to "good immigrants like Sacco and Vanzetti,' as Yves Montand, who plays Mitrione, says in the book. 

He is armed at all times. The cover of the Ballantine Random House paperback, "State of Siege," shows him with dark glasses, shoulder-holster gun, and a 

Humphrey Bogart drooping cigaret.

Yet the real Dan Mitrione's background and temperament hardly prepared him for the James Bond role Costa-Gavras and Solinas cast for him. 

Dan Mitrione did not smoke cigarets nor carry a gun and he seldom drank. 

Despite the film, it is unlikely that he ever saw the inside of a nightclub during his year in Montevideo.

Mitrione was a home-centered man of simple tastes-"a staunch family man," recalls a fellow adviser in Uruguay, "and unusually compassionate. He was considerate. Brutality was foreign to his nature. The Uruguayans who got to know him held him in affection and respect." 

The Hollywood Reporter said in its review of "State of Siege" : "The film explicitly charges the United States with training South American policemen to torture, terrorize and murder political activists working against the status quo."

Mitrione was born in Italy in 1920. The following year, his parents emigrated to Richmond, Indiana, where he grew up and attended public and parochial schools. From 1942 to 1945, he served honorably in the Navy as an aviation machinist's mate. In 1943, he married Henrietta Lind, and they had nine children (not seven, as the film). Out of the Navy in 1945, he joined the Richmond police force as a patrolman and 11 years later had risen to be its chief. In Richmond he was active in youth, social service, church, and other charitable work. 

According to "State of Siege," Mitrione was well prepared for alleged "secret missions in Brazil, the Dominican Republic, and Uruguay by special training and extensive traveling in Latin America.

The film pictures him arriving in Brazil, descending the first-class steps of a Pan American plane with his wife and children. They are whisked away in two

spacious AID limousines to their two-story home where "a huge basket of exotic fruit" and "three black domestic" await them. Mitrione slips off his coat, exposing "a gun and holster discreetly at his waist."

His double mission in Brazil, says Costa-Gavras, is to overthrow the "undemocratic" (read left-leaning) Goulart regime with the help of the Brazilian military and substitute a regime with the "blessings" of Cardinal Spellman and "the American God;" and to teach sophisticated torture techniques to military officers. Mitrione is directly linked to a lurid scene showing nude males being tortured by electric shock before an audience of army officers. 

During his alteed two years in the Dominican Republic, he is portrayed as responsible for installing, with the help of "40,000 U.S. Marines," a reactionary junta "financed by the CIA."

In real life, however, Mitrione never had any training to be a secret or any other kind of agent. He traveled very little in Latin America and never set foot on Dominican soil. The Dominican involvement depicted by "State of Siege" is a total fabrication. (So, incidentally, are the "40,000 U.S. Marines" supposedly occupying the country from 1965 to 1967. The peak number of Marines at the height of the 

Dominican intervention was 3,500, every single Marine had left Santo Domingo. by June 6, 1965.)

In July 1960 Mitrione joined the Agency for International Development as a public safety adviser, spending his first seven years in Brazil, five in the provincial city of Belo Horizonte and two in Rio de Janiero. His job was to help local police upgrade their quality and efficiency by providing technical advice, modern gear, and, when in Washington, to train them in AID's International Police 

Academy. 

The film's picture of Mitrione's arrival in Brazil is as phony as its portrayal of his work there and elsewhere. 

He arrived alone, tourist class (AID officials aren't authorized to travel first class). His wife followed with the children by ship, also tourist class, and the family went to a modest motel in two taxis. There was no gun; he never carried one in 10 years overseas.

Mitrione had nothing to do with the unscheduled overthrow of Goulart. Before. and after this coup, which occurred while he was in Brazil as a police training adviser, he worked to encourage civil law enforcement by "legal and humane. means. ." Costa-Gavras' nude torture scene appears to be a figment of imagination. 

On the side, Mitrione arranged visits by 34,000 children to police facilities in 

Belo Horizonte and organized little league baseball. After his murder, grateful citizens named a street in his honor. 

The primary action in "State of Siege" is confined to 11 days, from the kidnaping of Mitrione on July 31, 1970, until his body is found on Aug. 10. Much of this time, in film and in fact, he was being questioned by his captors. This interrogation is frequently interrupted by violent and lurid flashbacks to supposed events in Mitrione's past. 

Throughout this process his Tupamaro questioners are portrayed as young,. virile, intelligent, competent, and possessed of a dream of justice and compassion for the poor. They are also cast as the vanguard of liberation from facist repression. The Tupamaros has "a perfect organization" and are "held together by serious passionate idealism," says Costa-Gavras. 

The real Mitrione, alas, was not treated gently by the real Tupamaros. 

When abducted, his car was rammed, not blocked as the film has it, and his driver stunned. Mitrione was beaten, kicked, cursed, and shot from the back while lying down, helpless and unarmed. The film makes no reference to this rough handling or the beating by a blunt instrument at that time or shortly thereafter. The kidnapers' blows broke the skin and left three distinct wounds: near his left armpit that matched the shape of the butt of a .38 colt revolver, a number of which the terrorists had recently stolen. 

The film, however, generally follows Mitrione's official autopsy report (which was inaccurate in two significant respects). 

Made by a coroner said to be sympathetic to the Tupamaros, the report failed to note the three armpit wounds and erroneously recorded the first bullet as: entering the middle of the chest. The report correctly notes the two entry and one exit wounds in the head (which the picture omits), and the presence of "injec tion marks" on the arms but does not mention that there were 16. (It is not. known what drugs were administered-the coroner did not specify-or why.)

Mitrione was also subjected to intense interrogation while still suffering from the trauma of his initial gunshot wound and manhandling. 

Every person I interviewed believes the film sequence showing Mitrione being smuggled into the hospital was a fabrication since the terrorists had their own medical personnel and X-ray equipment. Contrary to the film, no black dye was in his hair when the body was found. 

Besides falsification of the central facts of Dan Mitrione's life and death, "State of Siege" propagates a long litany of untruth and distortion ranging all the way from the Catholic church to AID's International Police Academy. 

Costa-Gavras conveys the impression that the Tupamaros enjoyed widely based support from significant elements in the Catholic church. In the film's faked cathedral funeral scene, for example, the archbishop of Montevideo is portrayed as sympathetic to the Tupamaros and hostile to the U.S. by panning a shot into the archbishop's conspicuously vacant chair. In the Random House Ballantine book Costa-Gavras says the Pope denounced "the systematic torture put into effect" by Mitrione.

Contrary to "State of Siege," the terroists never had the support of the Catholic hierachy. The archbishop of Montevideo did celebrate the catherdral memorial mass on August 22. (The film portrayal of the coffin draped with an oversized American flag, the distraught widow, and Mitrone's medals on display, was also pure fabrication: Mitrone's body was flown home on Aug. 11, he was buried at Richmond, and he had no medals.)

The Urguayan Catholic hierarchy also explicitly condemned the murder. On 

Aug. 14. Reuters moreover quoted the outspoken leftist Brazilian bishop, Helder 

Camara, as saying that the crime was "absurd and inhuman." During the ordeal while her husband was captive, Mrs. Mitrione was given a sacred medallion by the Papal Nuncio. 

One of Costa-Gavras' misleading techniques was to twist and transpose times and events to vilify Mitrone and justify Tupamaro terror. 

For example, Mitrione is shown as pay-off man and instigator behind the "death-squad" shooting of a Tupamaro on "a very beautiful beach."

Actually, the murdered adviser had nothing to do with "death squads," torture, or any other illegal activities—except to express strong disapproval of such tactics.

On July 31, 1971, however, a year after Mitrone was kidnaped, the body of Manuel Ramos Filippini, a Tupamaro terrorist recently out of prison, was found on a beach. Leaflets left by the body suggest that he was killed by anti-Tupamaro 

Uruguayan vigilantes. These illegal groups, widely condemned in the Uruguayan press, received no American support. 

In another scene Mitrione is associated with the alleged police "assassination" of a leader in a student strike. Yet the episode a radical student engaged in a shakedown was apparently shot accidentally by an armed comrade-actually occurred on July 24, 1971, with Mitrione 11 months in his grave. 

AID's International Polic Academy appears in "State of Siege" as the center of a global network for a U.S. program to eliminate "democratic forces" in the 

Third World, for which Mitrione was supposed to have recruited Latin American police officers as U.S. agents.

Costa-Gavras and Solinas show the police academy as teaching terror tactics, elimination of "progressive" leaders by bombing, shooting, and planned "accidents." Lurid scenes of a "specialized course" in Texas, "in a deserted town near the Mexican border" are flashed on the screen. "Mitrione-recruited" Uruguayan policemen are shown blowing up old cars, refrigerators, and dummies at "a political rally." In interrogation scenes Mitrione is accused of training anti-revolutionary terrorists and provocateurs. 

By contrast, the real police academy teaches a wide spectrum of above-board skills-administration, management, communications, logistics, weapons, records and identification, investigation procedure, traffic management, narcotics control, VIP protection, community relations, and identification of explosives. To date, some 4.500 police officers (including 119 Uruguayans) have taken courses at the academy.

Like U.S. advisers in other countries and fellow instructors at the academy, Mitrione (who taught there in 1968-1969) emphasized that mistreatment was unprofessional and unethical and that, on practical grounds alone, a fingerprint or a chip of paint provided more reliable evidence than a useless confession beaten out of a suspect.

(One former assistant secretary of state for inter-American affairs, Covey T. 

Oliver, spoke for all informed observers when he dismissed a "stupid and untrue" charges that AID police advisers have taught or advocated torture. "No inheritors of the Iberian-Roman tradition," he said, "seem to need much instruction from representatives of other cultures.") "State of Siege's" allegedly "documented" picture of Dan Mitrione as a "torturer" is a good example of left-wing truthtwisting. 

Costa-Gavras and Solinas apparently base their torture charge on a headline story that appeared first in the Jornal do Brasil in mid-August 1970, allegedly quoting Captain Alejandro Otero, a Montevideo police official, as confirming that "Mitrione used methods of repression, violence, and torture." Independent research, however, discloses that the story was surreptitiously inserted in the paper without the knowledge of any of its three Montevideo correspondents, let alone Otero.

Subsequent denials by Otero and the three correspondents that any such interview took place were later run in a disavowal by Jornal do Brasil. 

Mitrione is shown by "State of Siege" as an agent of FBI or CIA. In the film a task force of 100 FBI agents is flown into Uruguay after Mitrione's kidnapping. Yet Dan Mitrione never worked for either agency (though as an Indiana police chief he was one among a total of 6,800 American senior law officers who have taken 12-week courses at the FBI Academy). The U.S. sent no FBI agents to Uruguay in connection with the Mitrione affair and no FBI agent was stationed, there. "State of Siege" is in fact a cynical propaganda tract masquerading as a documentary.

A documentary should bear substantial resemblance to reality and it should advance more truth than error, yet "State of Siege" omits the most important facts, distorts other facts, and invents "facts" to serve its single-minded purposes. 

It adds up to a massive massacre of the truth. 

The arson, robberies, bombings, assassination attempts and murders committed by the Tupamaros go virtually unmentioned in the film. There is not a single scene of a Tupamaro murder-out of 45 to date. The viewers are even spared the details of how the principal character was killed. When asked why he omitted the scene, Costa-Gavros lamely said he lacked "the verifiable data," this in the face of an avalanche of facts in the public domain. The lack of "data" didn't deter him from fabricating or twisting scenes of "official violence" as he called it, to blacken the image of Mitrione or of the U.S. or Uruguayan governments. 

The facts on these and many other issues raised by "State of Siege" were available from reliable documents and disinterested observers. But Costa-Gavras and Solinas were not interested in truth. Only a contrived mix of fact and falsehood would serve their propaganda purpose.

The reason for the film's existence, admitted Solinas, is "American imperialism, with its mechanisms of repression, its murders, its tortures. The occasion for the film was the capture and death of a person who symbolized this mechanism." Costa-Garvas added: "We also felt we had to make a movie" that would prompt the audience never again to regard "an American Embassy as just an embassy, but as a center for espionage, surveillance, and political pressure." 

Given the Marxist commitment of Costa-Gavras and Solinas (the latter avowed by Communist Party membership, the former by his own admission), seeing “eye to eye" with Solinas it was inevitable from the start that Mitrione would be found "guilty" and that his kidnapping and murder would be, to use George Steven's word, "rationalized;" although Solinas appears to have had some misgivings about the political efficacy of assassination. 

The Tupamaros, Solinas said, "like the Black September fighters at Munich," did not want to kill their hostage, but they were "forced to execute him." Costa- 

Gavras goes further-in a rhetorical question he asks: "Who killed him? The

Tupamaros with three or four bullets, or the government, backed up by the 

American Embassy, which decided not to free the 150 prisoners?" 

Has "State of Siege" any redeeming value?

From the tone of many reviewers, the answer would be yes. 

To Penelope Gilliatt (New Yorker) it was a "thoughtful new political film:" to Liz Smith in Cosmopolitan, "the most important political film of this decade:" to Donia Mills (Washington Star-News) "powerfully reasoned:" and to Archer

Winsten (New York Post) "of inestimable value." "State of Siege lives up to its claim of authenticity," wrote Joy Gould Boyum (Wall Street Journal) "insofar as the events we witness can be verified."

Miss Boyum added that the film had "not fallen prey to its own fierce partisanship. It has recognized... the moral ambiguities of its world; it has allowed those it sympathizes with the agonies of self-doubt; it has granted those it disagrees with humanity and intelligence. Most impressive of all, it treats its audience with respect."

But what value can anyone extract from this grotesque caricature of U.S. policy toward Latin America? With its vivid and titillating fare of small facts and big lies, this political pornography neither informs the intellect nor quickens the conscience. Laced with tired Marxist cliches and symbols calculated to discredit America-Cardinal Spellman, United Fruit, and "Rockefeller interests"- "State of Siege" plays on the ignoble qualities of alienation, anger, withdrawal, cynicism, and of course (as can readily be perceived from many of its reviews) of credulity.

The guilt-ridden, ashamed of American power and wealth, may find perverse satisfaction in the whiplash of two professional America-haters. The film will "be greeted with ecstasy wherever the premise that America is the world's No. 1 imperialist power is accepted without reservation," said Edward Behar (Newsweek.)

To angry, idealistic, frustrated students, the hypnotic simplicity of the virile, romantic Tupamaros may suggest a way out of their helplessness and alienation. 

To the Arthur Bremers and Sirhan Sirhans, it may suggest one final act of political violence that will enshrine them for immortality.

Just as Solinas' "Battle of Algiers" was used as a training film by the Black Panthers and Weathermen, his new apology for revolutionary violence may help to incite terror in American streets. If this happens, "State of Siege"-to borrow a slogan from Students for a Democratic Society-will be "playing midwife to murder."

The film may not have these dire consequences, but, even in the best possible light, it will hardly move viewers to a more thoughtful or rational consideration of America's troubled relations with the world's weaker and poorer countries. 

Were "State of Siege," however angry, rooted in fact and honestly argued, it might encourage constructive self-examination. But this fraudulent fabrication can claim no such redeeming value.

CIA PERSONNEL IN OPS MISSIONS ABROAD 

Mr. FRASER. Has OPS been used by CIA abroad? Have any CIA personnel ever worked in OPS missions abroad?

Mr. PARKER. Yes sir, A.I.D. OPS has had a cooperative arrangement with the 

CIA missions abroad. Further details of these arrangements should be solicited from that Agency.

ELIGIBILITY FOR INTERNATIONAL POLICE ACADEMY TRAINING 

Mr. FRASER. If a government wants to get IPA training, in Washington, for its police, and is willing to pay the expense, how does it go about making application?

Can any government obtain such training in Washington? Would we give such training to Soviet police? Why not?

Would we give such training to the police of, say, South Africa, Brazil or Chile?

Mr. PARKER. Regulations governing the acceptance of independently funded 

Public Safety training applications, and procedures for entering the International

Police Academy (IPA), are incorporated in Department of State Circular A-384 

of May 22, 1974, titled "Public Safety Training, International Police Academy and AID/W Worldwide Public Safety Training Fund, FY-75." 

Approval of government applications for independently financed public safety training is based on whether, at the time of application, such training would be in the best interest of the United States and whether it would meet the test of the Foreign Assistance Act of 1961. If such training were requested by the 

Soviet Union, we would not and could not provide such training. If requests were received from South Africa, the response would be the same. In cases of 

Brazil and Chile, we would not provide such aid.

DEPARTMENT OF STATE 

MAY 22, 1974. 

To: AIDTO circular A 384 From: Washington 

E.O. 11652: N/A 

Subject: Public Safety Training, International Police Academy and AID/W Worldwide Public Safety Training Fund, FY-75 Reference: 

(A) STATE 000841, (B) AIDTO Circular A-1182 (C) AIDTO Circular A-725, 6-29-73 

I. WORLDWIDE PUBLIC SAFETY TRAINING FUND 1. Establishment of fund: 

a. A worldwide Public Safety Training fund has been established for FY 1975. 

These funds, as available, will be used to finance fully or in part, training for police officers from LDC's, excluding narcotics training which will be funded through NCAP's. The worldwide training fund has been established to provide training for those LDCs listed in Attachment A. In addition, AID/W will consider candidates from those countries listed in Attachment B on the basis of independent funding only. b. Allocation of spaces will be based on requests from AID Missions. Where 

AID Missions do not exist, U.S. Embassies and Consulate Generals may forward requests to AID/W for consideration. Training requirements will be coordinated with the respective AID Country Desk and other appropriate officers. 

2. Operation of fund: 

a. AID/W will control the fund through the Office of Public Safety (OPS), Washington, D.C. b. Funds, as available, will be used to finance training for police officers from 

LDC's. Obligation of funds will be based on allocation of spaces to meet training requirements. c. Funds will not be used to finance cost of narcotics training; nor for participants from those countries who are able to pay for such training; however, participants from such countries may be trained at the International Police Academy (IPA) or at any other institution through facilitative assistance of OPS/W, provided the countries concerned bear the full cost of training (See 

Section IV, below.) 

d. International travel should be borne by the host country whenever possible, unless stipulated otherwise in Project Agreements or other agreements with the countries involved. If action addressees request that the Worldwide Public 

Training Fund should bear the cost of international travel, such recommendation should include full justification therefore. e. AID/W will issue PIO/P's and calls forward. 

II. TYPES OF TRAINING AVAILABLE 

1. International Police Academy.-please refer to referenced Circular A-1182 and attached program guide for Public Safety Training (Attachment C). 

2. Training at Other Institutions.-this can be arranged through OPS/W (see 

Circular A-1182 for some of the courses previously arranged). Courses not listed in the circular may be requested, but action addressees should provide full particulars pertaining to the training, accompanied by full justification for con sideration by AID/W. 

III. ADMINISTRATIVE PROCEDURES 1. Forecast of Training Requirements for FY 1975:

ATTACHMENT C PUBLIC SAFETY CODE 710 

Public Safety training is predicated on the principle that the security, stability, and progress of any country are contingent upon the laws of the land and the ability of its police agencies to enforce those laws fairly, justly, and in a humane manner.

Training in the United States is offered, primarily, at the International Police 

Academy, Washington, D.C., a function of the Office of Public Safety (OPS), Agency for International Development.

Public Safety training in the United States as provided at the International Police Academy, include police executive programs and technical specialist programs. Comparative police administration, management and operations proce dures are dealt with in course presentations; thus allowing problem solving against specific conditions the participant will find in his country. U.S. laws and enforcement procedures and pertinent U.S. court rulings are not used as a basis for curriculum development or presentation. The International Police Academy is the pivotal institution providing police training for cooperating nations of the free world. It provides a forum for overseas police officers to discuss common problems and to increase their individual and their organizations' professional capabilities. 

The principal purposes of Academy training are to impart to police leaders of emerging countries democratic concepts of responsible and humane police administration; provide them with professional knowledge that will assist in strengthening their police forces for the purpose of enforcing the law and maintaining the peace with full attention to individual civil rights; prepare them more effectively to counter criminal violence; encourage them to improve the character and image of their forces, thus binding them more closely to the community. 

Available training programs and guidelines are detailed in this document. 

A worldwide Public Safety training fund has been established for FY 1975. 

These funds, as available, will be used to finance training for police officers from LDCs, excluding narcotics training. These funds will not be used to finance training of participants from those countries who are able to pay full or in part for such training. However, participants from such countries may be trained at the 

International Police Academy or any other institution through the facilitative assistance of OPS/W provided the countries concerned bear the full cost of training. 

Training costs will be determined under the provision of AIDTO Circular A-725, dated 6-29-73. The rates do not include costs for international travel, but cover maintenance allowances, including per diem, miscellaneous expenses connected with training (books, postage, transportation for field trips), normal tuition costs when enrolled at some other institution (U.S. Coast Guard Academy, U.S. Navy School, Northwestern University, etc.), and reception centers (New

York, Miami and San Francisco) as well as the one-week orientation at the 

Washington International Center and hospitality (COSERV). The International 

Police Academy does not charge any tuition for its courses. 

Additional information concerning qualifications and selection processes will be covered in each course announcement. When appropriate, AID/W will consider waiving certain requirements (i.e., age, education and experience), provided addressees furnish full data and recommendation that a waiver be granted. 

TITLE AND CODE: INTERNATIONAL POLICE ACADEMY-SENIOR COURSE-710-1 

(Offered in English and Spanish Languages) 

Duration: 12 weeks; enrollment limited to 30 officers.

Locale: International Police Academy, Washington, D.C. 

Begins: Conducted once annually in each language. Exact dates to be announced. 

ESTIMATED FISCAL YEAR-1975 STANDARDIZED COST: (EXCLUDING INTERNATIONAL TRAVEL) 

English-$3,750 ($1,250X3 man/mo).

Spanish-$4,350 ($1,250x3 man/mo plus $200 interpreter fee X3 man/mo when required).

DEVELOPMENT OBJECTIVES 

To acquaint senior police and law enforcement officials with the techniques of police administration, operations and management; current international trends in criminal justice procedures; to enable them to discuss these methods with other police officials of the free world and to upgrade police operations and management; and to encourage increased cooperation between police organizations of the different countries.

H 

TRAINING PLAN 

Comparative police administration; police organization, management, operation, research and development; police/community relations; communications; administration of justice; crime prevention; criminal investigation management; control of criminal violence. Leadership, command and management science are studied in the widest police context. Visits to federal, state, and municipal law enforcement agencies and other U.S. institutions are included. Students are required to prepare and submit a research paper. 

CANDIDATE REQUIREMENTS 

The position occupied in the country police hierarchy, professional knowledge and proven leadership capability, rather than rank title, will govern the selection of participants to this course. These officers should command a national police force or major operational element at national, provincial, or municipal levels, or hold executive positions with responsibility for the establishment of policy or staff planning. Also eligible are chiefs of divisions and their deputies, and those in charge of major administrative functions provided they meet previously established criteria. Candidates should be at least 25 and not more than 50 years or age, have at least a high school diploma or its equivalent, and five years of experience in law enforcement. A minimum English language proficiency of 75-75 is required for the English language course.

TITLE AND CODE: INTERNATIONAL POLICE ACADEMY-GENERAL COURSE-710-2 

(Offered in English, French and Spanish Languages) 

Duration: 15 weeks; enrollment limited to 40 officers.

Locale: International Police Academy, Washington, D.C. 

Begins: Detailed announcements are distributed three months in advance of each course. (Conducted twice each year in French, and several times annually in both English and Spanish.)

ESTIMATED FISCAL YEAR 1975 STANDARDIZED COST: (EXCLUDING INTERNATIONAL TRAVEL) 

English-$5,000 ($1,250×4 man/mo).

Spanish and French-$5,800 ($1,250×4 man/mo plus $200 interpreter feeX4 inan/mo when required).

DEVELOPMENT OBJECTIVES 

To enable intermediate grade officers to study police organization, administration, operations and leadership; to improve these functions in their countries; to acquaint them with current trends and new procedures and enable them to discuss these methods with other police officials of the free world; to upgrade police operations and management and encourage increased cooperation between police organizations of the different countries. 

TRAINING PLAN 

The syllabus of the course includes: Police administration, organization and operations; investigations; scientific and technical aids; border and customs control; crime prevention; public relations; internal security; control of criminal violence; defense tactics; firearms; instructor training. Visits to federal, state and municipal law enforcement agencies and other U.S. institutions are in iuded. A research project is required. 

During the last four weeks of the course, specialized training is provided for each student in one of the areas listed below. Three specializations are normally offered for each course. The class is divided into groups of from 8 to 12 for each of the specializations given. The choice of the specialization to be attended by each participant is determined by his own law enforcement organization and the Mission. Since not all of the specializations discussed below can be offered for every course, those to be offered for a particular course will be listed in the course announcement.

1. Criminal Investigation Management.-A management level course designed to develop an understanding of the techniques involved in the investigation of criminal matters which include preservation and identification of evidence, crime scene searches, and laboratory aids to investigation. 

2. Criminal Violence Control.-Defines the nature of the criminal violence threat, its motivation, significance, objectives, achievements and potential. Delineates the forms and methodology of criminal violence with emphasis on current modes. Discussion of current control measures and identifying problem areas in criminal violence control, including airline security, bomb threats, kidnapping, extortion and assassination. 

3. Defense Equipment Training-Management and Safety.-Designed to qualify officers as firearms instructors in their own countries. Includes theory and practical work, instruction in reloading equipment, familiarization with police weaponry, marksmanship, instructor methods encompassing fabrication and use of training aids, and preparation of lesson outlines. 

4. Immigration/Customs Control.-Covers organization and functions of the immigration and naturalization service, philosophy of border control, immigration inspection, and other related activities of border and immigration control. 

5. Instructor Methods.-Designed to develop an understanding of the principles of learning and skill in the methods and procedures of the teaching process, including fundamental lesson planning, training aids, methods of instruction, tests and questioning techniques, development and supervision of police training programs. 

6. Police Community Relations.-Emphasizes the need and importance of public and community relations in modern police operations. The scope includes the study of the role of the police in democratic society, psychological and sociological aspects of police community relations, techniques for written and verbal communication, police press relations, organization and administration of an effective police/public community relations program and production and utilization of visual aids in the publications field. 

7. Police Patrol Operations.-A management level course designed to develop an understanding of modern patrol techniques and procedures for administration of patrol activities. Provides instruction on planning for effective patrol, distribution of the force, forms of patrol, supervision of patrol force, patrol records. and crime prevention. 

8. Protection of Dignitaries.-Covers the techniques, procedures, equipment and training of personnel who are responsible for the personal security of officers, visitors, and dignitaries. The scope includes general protection techniques, planning, organization, selection and training of personnel, surveillance, protective devices, emergencies, crowd control, and communications. 

9. Records and Identification.-A management level course designed to develop an understanding of techniques of police records management and identification procedures. The scope includes functions of police records, organization and administration of records, types of police reports, report writing and reporting procedures, classification of incidents and other pertinent matters. 

10. Traffic Management.-Designed to provide some knowledge in all major aspects of a traffic management program including the broad field of traffic control, emphasizing methods and techniques of traffic control. as well as the police relations to other agencies and groups involved in traffic management. This specialization is directed towards police commanding officers who will have the responsibility for assisting in improving traffic control in their countries. 

CANDIDATE REQUIREMENTS 

Officers of commissioned status with rank up to and including that of a major, or of equivalent civilian rank. (Both male and female, but any country sending female officers should send two for any one course.) They must occupy supervisory positions in the operational or administrative-support elements of a law enforcement organization, or they must have instructional responsibilities which will enable them to disseminate the knowledge acquired through United States: training. Any deviation from these prerequisites must have AID/W approval.. 

Candidates should be at least 21 and not more than 45 years of age, have at least a high school diploma or its equivalent, and three years of experience in law enforcement. Other A.I.D. participant criteria apply.

Application of entire civil police resources to narcotics and dangerous drug control and enforcement effort will be discussed. TRAINING PLAN This course consists of the following curriculum:

B. Executive management: Principles of management underlying planning, organizing, integrating and measuring the functions of the Public Safety Tele communications Branch.

On-the-job observation: Practical assignments for each participant, tailored to his specific needs in appropriate police organization to study/observe communication systems in use, and the appropriate electronic equipment manufacturing plants to study/observe the latest models of communication equipment being produced.

INTERNATIONAL POLICE ACADEMY CURRICULUM 

Mr. FRASER. Does IPA training include interrogation methods? Do you think that in some cases that might conceivably help the police of an anti-democratic government smash the democratic opposition?

Mr. PARKER. The subject "Interviews and Interrogations" is taught as part of criminal investigation specialty courses given at the IPA. It is our view that this course is one element in helping to build effective, civil police institutions and, in turn, that such institutions are one of the necessary conditions for development. The means are neutral and it is quite possible that at some later date the police trained here may participate in repression. But I would deny that the contents of the Academy curriculum bear on the causes of such repression. 

The IPA curriculum and presentations continually emphasize the importance of civil liberties and human rights as they relate to the responsibilities of professional law enforcement officials to their citizens. This philosophy is not presented in a pedantic classroom atmosphere only, but as part of the give and take learning and conditioning experience in a free society with a heterogeneous group of U.S. and foreign professionals.

TRAINING OF POLICE OF A GOVERNMENT WHICH SANCTIONS TORTURE 

Mr. FRASER. Do you think we should train the police of a government which sanctions torture, even though we ourselves do not teach them torture? 

Have we not taught the police of such governments in the past (even though we did not teach them torture)? Do we not plan to continue to do so in the IPA? 

Mr. PARKER. I do not believe we should train the police of a government which sanctions torture. Public Safety training is predicated on the principles that the security, stability and progress of any country are contingent upon the laws of the land and that the ability of its police agencies to enforce these laws fairly, justly and humanely determines the effectiveness of these laws. Police torture is abhorrent to these processes.

The principal purposes of the International Police Academy training are to impart to the police leaders of emerging countries democratic concepts of responsible and humane police administration; provide them with professional knowledge that will assist in strengthening their police forces for the purpose of

(a) All (၁) None (b) Part (one-way), enforcing the law and maintaining the peace with full attention to individual rights; prepare them more effectively to counter criminal violence, encourage them to improve the character and image of their forces, thus binding them more closely to the community. 

The USG has no control over the internal activities of any foreign government. 

Allegations have been made regarding torture tactics being used by certain governments, which include some for which Public Safety training has been provided. Often these are isolated cases contrary to the policies of that government or may be deliberate misrepresentations. 

But rather than discuss the past, I believe that you and we should consider techniques for assuring mutual understanding of the circumstances of our training programs and the criteria which guide its operations. 

VIOLENT OVERTHROW OF GOVERNMENTS 

Mr. FRASER. I gather that one of the basic assumptions behind the OPS program is that the violent overthrow of democratically elected governments is undesirable. Am I correct?

In that case, were A.I.D. and OPS unhappy with the overthrow of the Allende Government?

Mr. PARKER. You are, of course, correct in your statement that one of the basic assumptions of U.S. foreign policy and A.I.D.'s public safety programs is that

3 the violent overthrow of democratically-elected governments is undesirable. A.I.D. was not happy at the overthrow of the Allende Government. 

OPS PRIORITIES IN TRAINING 

Mr. FRASER. Is it not clear from your answers, and from our records, that OPS has given a lower priority to such ideals as stability and peaceful development than it has to simply helping and strengthening our friends and allies, regardless of whether they are undemocratic and repressive? 

Is it not true that in deciding whether or not to give training to the police of any given country our primary consideration has been whether a government is friendly to us, and that in some cases our police training program has actually served to strengthen repressive governments?

Mr. PARKER. I do not believe that the pattern which emerges from our answers and records is that which you suggest, that we give a lower priority to peaceful development and stability than to simply help in strengthening friends and allies without reference to their repressive tactics. 

But I am less concerned with a discussion of that which has come before than I am with that which we should do in the future. 

As my other answers have indicated, I believe strongly that the function of aid for police institutions is a perfectly legitimate one. The need for political stability in the less developed world is great and through the training which we will be able to offer at the International Police Academy we can, I believe, make a contribution to this process.

It is of course quite correct that before we give aid to any nation, we are required by law to determine that the government is not hostile to us and, as you know, there are certain limitations as to who can receive aid under the For eign Assistance Act. 

It may be that in some instances police training programs under A.I.D. have been misused to strengthen repressive governments. I do not know of any specific instance. But far more important is that you of the Congress and we of the 

Executive Branch agree on the purposes and the criteria of programs which we mount in support of helping those newly independent nations to establish their own institutions. And I look forward to working with you to this end. 

OPS AS A PART OF A.I.D. 

Mr. FRASER. Do you think OPS should be a part of A.I.D.?

Mr. PARKER. Mr. Fraser, the conceptual answer is yes, it should be part of 

A.I.D. If foreign nations wish help in the improvement of their techniques for establishing systems of justice, we should be prepared to help and such help certainly would fall within A.I.D.'s competence.

In practice there is, of course, a variety of problems dealing with differing judgments on the value and effectiveness of these activities and the effects these have upon other elements of the program. Consequently, I would not be concerned if we could assure the establishment of an institute, either within or outside the U.S. Government, which could serve as a source of training, consultation and research on that whole complex of questions which arise under the rubric of systems of justice.

WOMEN IN DEVELOPMENT 

'Mr. FRASER. How will AID make sure that women at home and abroad will be fully represented in planning foreign aid programs whose very success depends in good part upon whether women in developing countries take part in the program? 

Mr. PARKER. AID is committed to improving its utilization of women in AID, particularly in professional positions, which are directly involved in program areas both in AID Washington and Overseas. The Percy Amendment Working Committee report contains the following recommendation: That AID show measurable improvement in employing women, particularly in professional positions, as a continuing policy and practice. Increasing the number of professional women in AID/W and overseas not only serves as a model for others, but such utilization of women brings valuable insights to the problems of disadvantaged groups in developing societies, and provides opportunities for linkages to women in developing countries.

Finally, the report concludes that AID should also appoint more women as participants to internal committees and to conferences and donor meetings. 

Where feasible and natural, AID should encourage the delegates to international meetings to seek out and establish continuing communications with LDC and other donor women leaders, delegates, and professionals and their organizations in attendance at such meetings. AID can and will encourage developing countries to utilize more women but AID cannot insure such success. AID can improve its own posture as an example and where appropriate suggest the host countries do likewise. 

FEMALE VERSUS MALE EMPLOYMENT IN AID 

Mr. FRASER. Has the percentage of women in the middle and top levels of AID been increasing each year? Despite the size of AID, the mix of men and women should be equitable if the Agency is going to plan the kinds of programs the American public expects. I would like a report on the numbers of men and women in each grade since 1971, with percentages reported for the grades from year to year to show the trend.

Mr. PARKER. Since June 1971 through March 1974, the percentage of women in the Agency has remained essentially stable. The proportion of women, as shown in Table I, in the Top and Clerical levels has similarly remained constant. In the 

Junior level, which includes GS 07-11 and comparable grades in the Foreign Service System, the percentage has risen from 60 to 80. In the Middle level, GS 12-14 and comparable grades in the Foreign Service System, the percentage has risen from 13 to 15.

RURAL INFRASTRUCTURE AND UTILITIES 

Mr. FRASER. The report of the Foreign Affairs Committee called for special emphasis on institutions of participation. Yet, on p. 17 of the A.I.D. Summary presentation, it states that the largest amount of funds are to be devoted to rural infrastructure and utilities. 

How do you explain this?

Mr. PARKER. Mr. Fraser, while this is admittedly the largest of the subheadings, it amounts to less than half the amount requested for Rural Development which in turn is only 25% of the amount requested in the Food and Nutrition Appropriation. All of the program included under the Food Production and 

Nutrition appropriation are intended to support the Foreign Affairs Committee Report which called for increasing productivity and improving the quality of life in rural areas through concentration on inter alia, "local infrastructure and utilities; farm-to-market roads, small land improvement, rural electrification,

= = storage facilities, water supply, and sanitation." Building institutions of participation was one aspect of this development program which was specifically stressed and which A.I.D. fully supports. 

Although we have included a large amount of funding under the subheading of "Rural Infrastructure and Utilities," these programs clearly contribute to the report goals. For example, the $20 million we are requesting for a Rural 

Electrification Loan in the Philippines will not only provide the financing of materials and constructions costs to extend the benefits of electricity to reach some of the 73% of the Philippine people who presently do not have electricity but will do so through the institutional framework of establishing 22 additional rural electric cooperatives. 

In this subcategory we have also included an illustrative attribution of $25 million of a possible $75 million Rural Development Loan proposed for India. 

The resumption of an A.I.D. program for India would be dependent on the outcome of discussions between the India and U.S. Governments. The proposed loan would be to help the lower 30% of the rural farmers through provision of needed agricultural inputs and possibly through support to projects improving rural infrastructure. Due consideration to institutions of participation will be given when we design the specifics of this loan. 

Similarly, the $15.5 Rural Development Loan for Turkey will help finance infrastructure projects in selected low-income areas of that country. In addition to helping to provide basic social service in the rural areas, the project will focus on activities which should result in substantial employment generation and a more equitable distribution of income. In Sri Lanka, fifty thousand farm families will benefit from the proposed $8 million loan for the rehabilitation of minor irrigation systems. All of these projects meet the criteria outlined in the Report of the Foreign Affairs Committee in aiding small farmers and helping reduce income disparaties.

EXAMPLES OF PROJECTS BENEFITING AND NOT BENEFITING MOST RURAL PEOPLE 

Mr. FRASER. Of the proposed programs or projects, list examples of those which would incorporate and benefit most rural people throughout the country. List examples of those that would not.

 As examples of projects which would incorporate and benefit most rural people throughout the country: In Panama, a proposed $11 million sector loan will assist the Government to improve the agriculture marketing system by developing a national market news service, establishing a price incentive system and setting up easily accessible produce assembling centers. 

Loan funds will be used to expand facilities for training agronomists and extension agents including training for and organizing of cooperatives. Loan funds will be used for research to adapt crops for subsequent planting by Panamanian farmers;

In Honduras, a proposed agricultural cooperatives project-part of a sector strategy involving both grant and loan funds-will provide technical assistance to an Honduran effort to organize and operate a network of cooperative societies; 

In Rwanda, a proposed $2.5 million grain storage and marketing loan would provide for the design and construction of storage warehouses such that all producing areas would be within 30 kilometers of a storage facility. The project is designed to stabilize agricultural prices and increase remuneration to the farmer;

In Bangladesh, a proposed $15.0 million sector loan will support the Government's Integrated Rural Development Program through in-country training for cooperatives and rural development, the expansion of agricultural credit and construction of facilities needed to implement the cooperative credit program, and support for a labor intensive Rural Works Program; 

In the Philippines, a proposed Small Farmer Income and Production project will assist the Government to increase agricultural production and small farmer income by providing technical assistance on adaptive research systems for development and analysis of planning data, and advice on grain pricing and credit policies.

As examples of projects which would not incorporate and benefit most rural people throughout the country:

In Haiti, a proposed rural community development project will attempt to institutionalize community action efforts in North-Western Haiti by installing

area service centers for medical, public health and family planning teams. The project will provide agronomists and engineers to advise on crop improvement and rural infrastructure;

In Zaire, a proposed $5 million River Transport loan would help to improve the efficiency of river transportation between the Northern region of the country and the urban markets to the Southwest by expanding port facilities and providing equipment for dredging operations. Waterways in Zaire serve as the main link between scattered rural populations and the country's commercial centers; 

In Ethiopia, the Ada District Development project is designed to increase the agricultural production of small farmers in the district, to develop institutions to stimulate a market-oriented economy, to promote cooperative societies, and to improve local infrastructure. The project will try to demonstrate a manageable and replicable method for increasing the income and improving the living conditions of large numbers of Ethiopian small farmers; 

In Afghanistan, a proposed $8 million loan will assist a government rural works program to develop farm-to-market roads, small-scale irrigation works, village water supply systems, and other rural community facilities in the most economically depressed provincial areas of the country. 

PROPOSED FY 1975 RURAL INFRASTRUCTURE AND UTILITIES PROJECTS 

Mr. FRASER. Would you provide a list of Rural Infrastructure and Utilities

Projects by cost and country of location? 

Mr. PARKER. We will be happy to furnish such a list. A.I.D. is presently attempting to resolve issues of appropriate sub-categories for activities and placement of activities within such sub-categories-so the list should not be considered precise in an accounting sense. For example, it probably makes as much sense to include construction of grain storage facilities in agricultural production as in rural infrastructure. Further, elements of several sector loans should be included in rural infrastructure.
