Mr. FRASER. Which of these projects are planned and executed by the central government and which by people in a local agency? 

Mr. PARKER. Most of these activities will be planned and executed by central governments. Several-for example the Afghanistan and Bangladesh loans-will involve affected residents in project selection and will employ local workers in the use of labor-intensive construction techniques; but the fact that resource transfers are based on bi-lateral agreements between governments tends to encourage project planning and implementation through the central government of the less developed country. A.I.D. recognizes that this limits the involvement of those it is trying to assist and has begun to consider ways in which local planning and execution of projects can be incorporated into the design of Agency activities. We have established a Working Group on the Rural Poor which is examining procedural and structural changes in A.I.D.'s programming system which will facilitate "bottom-up" planning and execution.

NEW APPROACHES FOR REACHING DISADVANTAGED PEOPLE 

Mr. FRASER. What work is under way in A.I.D. to determine which development programs and projects are most successful in assisting disadvantaged people in a country? Is the Agency identifying approaches which have the potential of accomplishing that objective?

Mr. PARKER. The Agency is tackling this question on a broad front. We are taking some administrative measures to focus attention on the problem, we are intensifying research already under way and initiating new research and evaluation programs to identify promising approaches in reaching poor people, and we are developing training programs to improve our capability for dealing with this question. Our efforts include the following: 

An Agency-wide Working Group on the Rural Poor has been recently established and is attempting to establish a framework for a program of inquiry, exchange of information and policy development and coordination relating to programs for the benefit of the rural poor. This group plans to produce a series of conceptual papers this fall dealing with regional development, institutional development, and local financial institutions. These papers should help provide the basis for operational guidelines for project design and for project review to be developed later on. 

The Agency has prepared the design for a research contract or grant to develop a methodological capability for systematically selecting sound rural development strategies that will effectively and efficiently help to alleviate the poverty of the various groups of rural poor. 

As a concommitant to this research, AID plans to carry out a comprehensive evaluative study of experience in programs and projects aimed at the rural poor. 

This study is intended to identify the causal factors/impediments which underly rural poverty, to assess the strategies which have been employed to attach the causal factors and to weigh the relative effectiveness of the strategies by evaluating the impact of operational programs on the rural poor. 

In addition to the above, the Agency is undertaking a study of measures of benefit incidence. The intent of the study would be to develop a methodology for formulating benefit incidence indicators and applying them to individual programs and projects. When completed the work should enable us to design projects with increased probability of affecting the targeted low income groups. 

The Agency also has under way a research study expected to be completed at the end of CY 1974 to examine the feasibility and the effectiveness of different policies in dealing with problems of income distribution and poverty. These studies look, for example, at the role of agricultural policy and of education in reaching the poor.

AID is also intensively planning a manpower management development program for early initiation which would sensitize AID personnel to the issues involved in reaching disadvantaged groups and provide them with the analytical tools in economics, sociology and anthropology they need to accomplish this objective. 

In July 1973, the Agency completed an Administrator's Spring Review on the role of agricultural credit for small farmers. This review, worldwide in scope, produced policy and program guidance for the integration of credit elements into the design of rural development projects. The findings addressed such questions as alternative low cost institutional credit delivery systems, alternative sources of non-official, informal credit, and alternative approaches to self-sustaining credit systems, including remedial methods. In addition to the publication of findings, a series of field workshops were held to test and communicate the findings with project planners in the United States and in developing as well as developed countries. 

In the health area, AID initiated a project in 1972 for the Development and Evaluation of Integrated Delivery Services (DEIDS) which calls for pilot projects in four countries to test different approaches for reaching large masses of the population in poor countries with integrated health services.

FISCAL YEAR 1975 FOREIGN ASSISTANCE REQUEST' WEDNESDAY, JUNE 12, 1974 HOUSE OF REPRESENTATIVES, COMMITTEE ON FOREIGN AFFAIRS, 

Washington, D.C. 

The committee met at 10:18 a.m., in room 2172, Rayburn House

We are meeting again to continue the hearings on the President's foreign aid message.

Today we will hear testimony on one of its most important parts, which deals with the Middle East. The leadoff witness will be Hon. 

Joseph J. Sisco, Under Secretary of State for Political Affairs. 

With Mr. Sisco are Hon. Robert H. Nooter, Assistant Administrator for Supporting Assistance, Agency for International Development; 

Mr. George S. Vest, Director, Political-Military Affairs, Department of State; and Rear Adm. Brian McCauley, who was in charge of the U.S. Navy minesweeping of the Suez Canal. 

I understand Admiral McCauley has just returned from the Middle East. He has no prepared statement but he will be available to answer any questions concerning the Suez minesweeping operation. 

Mr. Secretary, you have been before this committee many times.. 

It is a real pleasure to have you with us again. We are grateful for your assistance to Secretary Kissinger in the 33 days you have just spent in the Middle East. We are glad to have you back here in 

Washington again. 

Mr. Secretary, you have a prepared statement. I see it is rather short. You may proceed with it.

STATEMENT OF HON. JOSEPH J. SISCO, UNDER SECRETARY FOR POLITICAL AFFAIRS, DEPARTMENT OF STATE 

Mr. SISCO. 

I appreciate the opportunity of being here again. 

As you know, the Middle East problem is one that has occupied my attention for many years. Throughout the period of my involvement the peoples of the area have been locked in incessant struggle a cycle of wars followed by uneasy cease-fires, followed again by bloodshed and tragedy. Thus, two peoples who lived and worked together peacefully for centuries were thrown together in what history will undoubtedly record not as a series of wars, but as one long war broken by occasional armistices and temporary cease-fires. 36-333-74 -14 (201)

The area's progression from conflict to conflict has been written in death and suffering for the peoples of the region. But the effects of the 

Middle East struggle transcended the local issues. When chronic tension erupted into war, world peace was threatened. The interests and concerns of two global powers meet in the Middle East. It is an area of vital interest to the United States. A stable and lasting peace in the world requires a stable and durable settlement in the Middle East. 

Now for the first time in my memory, it is possible to hope, if not see, a time when the Arab-Israeli war will be punctuated not by an armistice but by a secure and lasting peace. Ironically, the progress had has its origin in the ferment resulting from yet another Arab-Israeli warthe war of October 1973 which changed the objective conditions in the area and the perception each side has of the other. 

If I may, therefore, I would like to trace for you briefly the situation we faced before that war; the results we sought when that war began; and what we have accomplished in the months that followed. I do this so that you can have a better understanding of what we mean when we refer to a momentum for peace in the Middle East. 

THE MIDDLE EAST: THE PAST 

For many years this was the panorama that presented itself to us in the Middle East:

The Arabs and the Israelis shared only a distressing legacy of mutual distrust and suspicion. The Israelis, as a result of their experience, have stressed security and survival the primary issues. The Arabs, as a result of their experience, have underscored justice and national sovereignty as the primary issues. Nations who shared borders had almost no real understanding of each others problems, motivations and concerns.

The area was dominated by a trend toward polarization between Israel strongly tied to the United States and certain Arab States increasingly dependent upon the Soviet Union. 

It was clear that a final settlement in the Mideast could only come about primarily by the actions of the parties themselves. But the participants were too deeply divided to begin the process of compromise and no third party was in a position to bring them together, although the United States more than any other nation made major efforts to do so between 1969 and 1973. 

ST THE MIDDLE EAST WAR AND ITS AFTERMATH 

PAT When the October 1973 war came again to the Middle East, we had two immediate objectives. First, to bring about a cease-fire and second, to do so in a manner that would leave us in a position to play a constructive role with both Arabs and Israelis in shaping a more secure peace in the area. It was evident that the search for that peace would be arduous and that a lasting settlement could only be approached through a series of discreet steps in which the settlement of any particular issue would not be dependent on the settlement of all issues. 

What we have accomplished in the past 8 months.

I think it can be said that for the most part guns are silent. Disengagement agreements between Israel and Egypt and Israel and 

Syria have been completed.

I believe we have demonstrated that the United States can maintain its undiminished support for Israel's survival and security and have relations of trust and understanding with Arab nations. We have reopened channels of communication with Syria and reestablished diplomatic relations with Egypt. We have deepened our relationships with Jordan and Saudi Arabia. We have helped both the Arabs and 

Israelis to move toward mutual understanding. 

The focus of discussion is now on progress on a step-by-step basis toward peace. Countries in the area are no longer dependent on a single outside power. Most but not all have adopted a more moderate course. Instead of concentrating solely on preparation for war, they are ready to consider, however tentatively, the possible fruits of peace. 

We, of course, did none of these things alone. Progress to date has been possible only through the courage, vision, wisdom, and statesmanship of the key leaders in the area-on both sides of the conflict, I might emphasize.

But it is apparent that none of the progress that has been made would have been possible without the United States. 

It is equally clear to me that a will to achieve peace has emerged and is gathering strength in the area, challenging those forces still opposed to a peaceful settlement based on mutual accommodation. The challenge to all parties concerned with the Middle East is to build. a bridge between current realities and a future vision—a vision of peace.

BUILDING A PEACE 

Now if there is to be such a transition, I believe the United States once again will have to play a critical and decisive role. The steps ahead are clear:

There must be further stages in the diplomatic process. It will be even more difficult as we approach the more fundamental issues of an overall settlement. This is not a question, Mr. Chairman, where you solve a difficult problem and you move on to a series of less difficult problems, but rather as you get closer to the basics of a fundamental settlement progress becomes even more difficult. 

It is important in the first instance that the disengagement process on the Syrian-Israeli front continue to proceed smoothly in accordance with the agreement. Each day of effective implementation, hopefully will help build the kind of confidence which will at least begin to break some shackles of past suspicions.

There is continuing need to maintain Israel's security. For Israel to persevere in the negotiations it must possess the confidence of our support for its security.

There is an urgent need to make a start on reconstruction and development in the entire area. Leaders have made the bold decision to move toward moderation in the belief that their aspirations for a life free of tragedy with security, justice, and decency for their peoples can best be realized in conditions of peace. 

The agenda is a full one. We have come a good distance toward our overriding objective in the Middle East-a comprehensive and lasting peace as a framework for durable U.S. relationships with all the nations of the area. The obstacles are obviously formidable. Yet, it must be stressed that these are only first steps, important as they are. 

We still have a very long way to go.

THE SIGNIFICANCE OF AID PROGRAM 

Congress is now considering a major program which can contribute to our overall objectives. We do not pretend that the assistance program you are considering can buy peace. Nor can we purchase constructive relations in the area. Peace and good relations are not for sale-in the Middle East or anywhere else. 

Rather, the program is an essential adjunct to our broader diplomacy, though not sufficient to bring success. 

As you consider the program, I ask you to bear in mind that the sums involved are not large when compared to what this Nation has spent over the past 25 years in the area-25 years in which peace remained an elusive goal.

We believe that the program that is before you will: Contribute to 

Israel's security; help sustain the growing belief in the area that peace is an essential condition for modernization-an aspiration shared by all the peoples of the area; reinforce our diplomacy as we move toward the most difficult aspects of Mideast negotiations. 

Mr. Chairman, Secretary Kissinger has already outlined for you this program, therefore, I will not repeat the specifics which are part of the record. 

"A MOMENTUM FOR MIDEAST PEACE" 

Let me merely conclude with one final thought. We believe that a momentum for Mideast peace has been established. In our view, this program is essential to the maintenance of that momentum. 

Opportunities such as the one before this Nation in the Middle East do not come often. They are not easily hoarded. In fact on the basis of my experience in this volatile region, I would say that opportunities for creative diplomacy are especially perishable in the Middle East.

Thus, it is our hope that Congress can act expeditiously on our request. I believe we need to demonstrate that Congress supports the initiatives that we have taken. We need to encourage those who are seriously interested in the area in working for peace. And we need to do these things in a timely manner. 

This program bespeaks our unremitting concern for the security of Israel. It points the way toward a new and mutually rewarding relationship of friendship with Egypt and other Arab countries. We trust these are objectives the Congress supports, as it has supported our search for a Middle East that contributes to a stable world order. 

The promise of a just and lasting settlement is closer today than in the past-a past made up of lost opportunities. It has taken great and sustained effort by many to come so far. Still greater courage and effort will be required to reach a secure and durable peace. It is in our interest that there be such a peace. We must do what we can to see that that goal does not elude us and the people of the area once again. 

AID BY OIL-RICH COUNTRIES  

Mr. Secretary, the question of what the rich-oil exporting countries are doing to help in development assistance has been raised a

number of times in these hearings. With respect to the Middle East area, what are the Arab oil-producing countries contributing toward economic development of their sister states? Also will you tell us what other countries are making any contributions to economic development in the Middle East?

Mr. Sisco. Mr. Chairman, I have prepared a paper which includes both the Middle Eastern donors as well as the others as you have asked. 

I will put the entire paper into the record with your permission, but let me just cite some illustrations as it relates to the Arab countries in particular.

Take, for example, Saudi Arabia in relationship to Egypt where, as you know, our program calls for $250 million. The Sandis have been giving, since the 1967 war, on the average of $100 million annually of budget support to Egypt. 

Kuwait, for example, in this past year for Suez Canal reconstruction equipment alone, $35 million. 

Abu Dhabi and Qatar-small sheikdoms-for a Suez-Mediterranean pipeline, $200 million.

The Gulf States have under consideration projects relating to fertilizer, refineries, cement, textile plants, all joint ventures with Egypt. 

We estimate roughly about $170 million worth. 

In terms of IDA and IBRD, they are interested in the Suez Canal reopening and various agricultural and industrial products. We have no specific amount, but these are illustrative in terms of what Saudi Arabia in particular, and Kuwait, and the sheikdoms are doing in relationship to Egypt.

AID FROM IRAN 

Now let me say a word about Iran. As far as Port Said reconstruction, the amount is roughly $250 million in loans. The Iranians are involved in a Mediterranean free port facility project, an ammonia plant-I am still talking about Egypt, Mr. Chairman-a phosphate fertilizer plant, a plasticizer plant, and a cotton spinning plant. We estimate the totality of this to be roughly about $400 million. 

The Iranians have indicated an interest in the Suez-Port Said oil pipeline, but there is no specific amount of money that has been designated as yet.

There is also a project for a joint Egyptian-Iranian Investment Bank, and our estimate here is roughly an investment of about $10 million in the first instance from the Iranians. 

Then they are involved in chemical, paper, tires and tubes, cotton and synthetic yarn industries-credits of roughly $100 million on a loan repayable basis.

Credits for machinery, equipment, machine tools, roadbuilding equipment, buses, consumer and durable goods, another $100 million loan.

We estimate roughly that Iran is either committed or is in the process of discussing overall commitments to Egypt alone, of $860 million. 

I will put all these into the record, Mr. Chairman. [See p. 207.] 

SAUDI ARABIAN PAYMENTS TO IRAN 

There are some other figures that I can also insert as it relates to the fact that Jordan, for example, has been receiving a regular subsidy payment from the Saudi Arabians consistently. Likewise

Kuwait has been giving financial support to Jordan rather consistently. So I think the indications are that they are doing a great deal actually in terms of helping a number of these other Arab States who do not have the oil capacity that say Saudi Arabia or Kuwait has. 

To be very precise, Saudi Arabia gives Jordan $47 million a year, and Kuwait gives Jordan a similar amount per year. 

In addition, I mentioned Iran in terms of these specific projects as they relate to Egypt. You will also recall that just perhaps 6 or 8 weeks ago Iran made an offer of $1 billion to help the countries of the less developed area who are suffering in their foreign exchange standing principally resulting from these higher oil prices.

USE OF U.S.-OWNED EGYPTIAN POUNDS

STATUS OF PAST AID TO ISRAEL

Mr. Sisco. All of it will have been committed by the end of June, and in fact all of this has been actively and currently in the pipeline. NEEDS FOR RECONSTRUCTION AID IN EGYPT 

Mr. FRELINGHUYSEN. I just hope you don't move even higher in the ladder.

Mr. Sisco, having been to Egypt and Israel in February, I certainly would like to underline the importance of developments in the area. 

I think we have all appreciated the headlines. We know what the 

Secretary and what you have done in setting the stage for progress toward peace, and I think we all want to acknowledge the significance of that, and yet at the same time I think there really is perhaps a failure to understand why we are asking for the kind of economic assistance that you are supporting here today with respect to the Middle East, and I think this does need to be underlined. 

When I visited with President Sadat, he certainly was concentrating not on the past but on the needs of the present. 

I would like to ask you about what you described as the urgent need for reconstruction and rehabilitation. How does that fit into the peace building process? Why is it so urgent? Is it one of the ways in which we can expect progress eventually in Geneva if there is movement in this direction?

Mr. Sisco. Let me put it this way, because I think it is a critical question, and I think it is critical in relationship to the program that, as you say, we have before the Congress.

I happen to believe that a rather decisive change in the psychological mood and attitude in the Middle East has occurred, and I think the forces of moderation have the upper hand. I say this with a good deal

Tell teel Ni 1 of trepidation, simply because for me personally having been involved in this area 20 years, it has been 20 years of lost opportunities. I think people in the area are tired of war, and I think people are looking toward trying to find ways to coexist between the Arabs and the Israelis.

AIMS OF PRESIDENT SADAT OF EGYPT 

President Sadat in particular in the Arab World, has taken the lead. in moving in the direction at a political solution on a step-by-step basis, and now President Assad has certainly made a decision that is significant in terms of at least a major first step in separating forces. 

This means that these leaders intend and want to turn to development and reconstruction in their own countries. 

Let's take Egypt, for example. President Sadat is very interested not only in the clearing of the canal, and the opening of the canal, but more importantly the reconstruction of cities on the Suez Canal. 

This is a peaceful pursuit that is important to the Egyptian people, and it is a peaceful pursuit that is important politically in that country. Egypt is a country that has great resources. What it needs more than anything else is technical know-how, management, administration, organization-the kind of input that helps to organize and harness the very, very considerable capacities that this country has. So this program, in my judgment, is only a very modest beginning, but it can help psychologically, and in a concrete and in a practical way, in turning the focus of these leaderships away from war and to meet the needs of the people. Because in reality, no matter how many pieces: of paper are signed, real peace is going to come to the Middle East, if ever, when there is interaction and movement between these people, where there is security in terms of the kinds of jobs that they have, and in the kind of a life that they can look forward to. 

I happen to believe, as important as the peacemaking process has been, that what we are going to try to do to be helpful in reconstruction-and we are not the only ones to help-in the long run is going to help establish hopefully the kind of social and economic underpinning that is essential to a real and a durable peace and coexistence between two sides in what has been a climate of suspicion and mistrust. 

This is what I think this program is all about, Mr. Congressman, and 

I think that in terms of gaging it against the abstract standard of a need, it is miniscule. What is important is that it gives psychological hope. It shows these people in the area that America is interested not only through its peacemaking process in achieving the peace finally in the area, but in helping these people to stand on their own two feet and to create peace on their own. We cannot create that peace for them, but we can be helpful in terms of them standing on their own two feet. 

U.S. FUTURE ROLE IN MIDDLE EAST 

Mr. FRELINGHUYSEN. How do you envisage the future U.S. role in progress towards peace? You say that we must continue, or should continue, to play a critical and decisive role. One of those ways would be to provide some psychological support through economic assistance, I assume. It is easy to see why we have been playing a decisive role, but what will be the nature of our role once the Geneva negotiations

start? Will it still be as decisive as it has been? How do you see it developing?

Mr. Sisco. Well, first of all, as you know, there has been no decision as to when Geneva will reconvene, but my assumption is, as the Secretary indicated to this committee, that at some point this year the 

Geneva process will probably begin.

Our whole philosophical approach to the Arab-Israeli dispute over the years has been that while outside powers can be helpful as intermediaries, as catalysts, in the last analysis a peace can only come primarily through the efforts of the parties themselves. So, therefore, to the degree to which we will have finally helped to achieve a framework and a forum in which the parties themselves can focus on these issues in the first instance, this is all to the good. 

Now our role will always be a critical one, quietly or in shuttle diplomacy, or on the fringes of the Geneva conference, simply because of the fact that this is the desire of both sides-and let me emphasize the desire of both sides, the Israelis and the Arabs. I think our posture today is one that is recognized by both sides efforts being directed at trying to find a fair settlement that meets at least the minimal conditions of the two sides. Therefore, I expect that we will have a role in the context of the Geneva conference, but bearing in mind that our thrust will continue to be that it is the parties in the first instance that have to resolve this problem and have to live with it. 

THE SOVIET ROLE IN THE MIDDLE EAST 

Mr. FRELINGHUYSEN. Do you think the Soviets are going to be satisfied with a role on the fringes of the Geneva conference, or do you think they are anticipating that they are going to be able to play a more active role once the discussions begin? 

Mr. Sisco. My judgment is that the Soviets want to play as active and as direct a role in these negotiations as is possible, but the kind of role that they can play, and for that matter the kind of role that the United States can play, is primarily dependent not on the Soviet attitude or the American attitude, it is primarily dependent on the attitude of the parties in the area. If one says, well, why has the United 

States played the kind of prominent almost unilateral role in bringing about the Egyptian-Israeli disengagement agreement and the Syrian- Israeli disengagement agreement, the answer is very simple: This was the desire of the parties on both sides-that the United States, and the United States alone, play that role. 

Mr. FRELINGHUYSEN. Thank you.

THE UNRWA DEFICIT 

Mr. Sisco, the UNRWA Agency for Palestine Refugees has a deficit of about $12 million. The request in the AID bill is for $25.2 million, but I understand that the amount requested will cover only the regular 

U.S. contribution and not the deficit. 

Mr. SISCO. That is correct.

E. 

Mr. FRASER. What does the United States intend to do with respect to the UNRWA deficit? What are other countries doing about it?

Mr. SISCO. One, in recent weeks we have discussed the matter not only with the Director of UNRWA, but we have also discussed the matter with certain countries in the area with the hope that they can increase their own contribution. These are under consideration, and I cannot report any dramatic specific increases on the part of these countries as yet, but we are doing this diplomatically and we will continue to do so.

Second, we have looked ourselves at what more we could do, and quite frankly within the constraints of our own budgetary situation, we have not, Mr. Fraser, found it possible to make an additional contribution going beyond our regular contribution. Our regular contribution this last year, as I recall, is roughly the same $23 million figure as we have put in for the coming year. 

Now it could lead to a situation where some of the services may very well have to be curtailed. I hope that any curtailment that might be required will not be of such a serious character so as to jeopardize this agency, because you know for well over 20 years this agency has played, I think, a very significant role in maintaining stability in the area by taking care of roughly 1.3 million refugees. I don't have a very good answer to your question because we have not found a fully satisfactory answer to the short fall this year of roughly $12 million. 

VOCATIONAL TRAINING FOR UNRWA 

Mr. FRASER. The $2 million for vocational training for UNRWA in fiscal 1974, why is that not shown in the 1975 estimate? 

Mr. Sisco. Vocational education is a very important element because what you want to do is to provide a number of these people with the wherewithal so that they can be trained to get on and make their own living and get off the rolls. However, as you may recall the addition of this authorization was a congressional initiative. It was not an administration proposal. Second, I for one would want to look at the legal aspect of this because this is not normally, as you well know, the account from which this kind of a cost has been defrayed.

CLEARING OF THE SUEZ CANAL 

Mr. Chairman, we have Admiral McCauley here, and I wonder if we could take a moment or two and ask him to give his observations of the clearing of the Suez Canal. 

Chairman MORGAN. Yes. 

STATEMENT OF REAR ADM. BRIAN MCCAULEY, COMMANDER, MINE WARFARE FORCE 

Admiral MCCAULEY. Well, I think the most obvious thing in this whole episode from the sweeping was the attitude of the Egyptian people. There was absolutely no question from the highest down to the lowest person that they had a tremendous warmth for the Americans. Everything I wanted I was given. The cooperation from everyone, the tremendous protestations of a desire for peace in the future— I think what Mr. Sisco has said about their wanting peace and not war, I had from the Minister of Defense through every military chief of staff tell me specifically that Egypt had had enough war, they wanted peace, and I think this was most significant. 

The sweeping which I have just completed went along beautifully, and the reason it did was because there was total and complete cooperation, aid, and friendship from the Egyptians with whom I dealt, and these observations are based on over 3 months of almost day-today association with the Egyptians.

MINE SWEEPING OF NORTH VIETNAM 

Mr. BROOMFIELD. Were you also involved with the sweeping of 

North Vietnam? 

Admiral MCCAULEY. Yes indeed, I was.

Mr. BROOMFIELD. How did that compare? 

Admiral MCCAULEY. Well, I fought every day there, and negotiated every day. Here I just asked for things and created some tremendous friendships.

PROTECTIVE OPENING OF SUEZ CANAL 

Mr. BROOMFIELD. When do you expect the Suez to be opened? 

Admiral MCCAULEY. That is a difficult question. The sweeping is completed. They are now working on the clearance of ordinance from the bottom of the canal, and also on the banks. It is hard to predict a time here because as you move through a battle area, for instance, there is a lot of ordinance in there. So my guess is that that portion of it will be finished within about 6 months. 

The other operation going on as you know is the salvage of the ten ships blocking the canal, and they are estimating 3 to 6 or 8 months. 

It is hard to really predict, but then of course there is a lot of reconstruction to do, and I would think perhaps in a year we will see the

canal opened. The Egyptians are thinking by October 6, but I am not sure of that one.

Mr. BROOMFIELD. Are all of our people out of there now, the U.S. personnel? 

Admiral MCCAULEY. No, we still have a couple of hundred people there involved as advisers in the clearance of the dead ordinance from the canal itself and advising on the banks. We have Army people advising the Egyptian engineers in the use of our equipment in the clearance of those minefields on the banks. In addition, of course, we have Murphy Pacific with some Navy supervisors working on the salvage, and they will be there at least for this period that I talked of. 

Mr. BROOMFIELD. Thank you very much. 

Chairman MORGAN. Mr. Hamilton. 

ARMS INTO THE MIDDLE EAST 

Mr. HAMILTON. Mr. Secretary, the title of your presentation to the committee is "Building Peace in the Middle East." I notice that in the total amount of money for the countries in the Middle East, which I think is roughly $900 million, at least half of that figure, if not more, is for military-related items. I am just wondering if this is the best way to build peace in the Middle East, to pour so many arms into the area?

Mr. Sisco. I think that is a very good question, and I would respond in this way: I think the Middle East is an area in transition at the moment. I make no claim other than the part of this program that is dedicated to reconstruction and development is a real beginning. My hope is that as confidence is built between the two sides this balance that you have cited can move more rapidly in the direction of development and reconstruction. I think that is a very cogent point. I think our objective ought to be that as confidence is built in this area to move more and more in that direction.

Mr. HAMILTON. I was not sure of your response to the chairman's question about the attitude of the Department toward a proposal that we increase the amount of security supporting assistance to Israel. 

Are you for or against that proposal?

Mr. Sisco. I gave you a diplomatic answer, Mr. Hamilton, which I will repeat.

Mr. HAMILTON. That is the way I understood it. 

Mr. SISCO. My response was that we felt that this $350 million program with respect to Israel was our best judgment based on consultations with them; and obviously if the members of this committee or the Congress seek to increase it, obviously we would have to look at what the considerations are.

INCREASED ARMS AID TO JORDAN 

Mr. HAMILTON. We have a very sharp increase here for military assistance to Jordan. Could you tell us why that is necessary? In fiscal year 1974, U.S. aid was about $91 million, and it has moved up to something like $202 million in this request, a large portion of

which is military aid. Why the necessity for such a sharp increase in military aid to Jordan? 

6 Mr. ŠISCO. Well, I think there are a couple of reasons. First it is a continuation of the modernization program of the armed forces, both in weapons equipment and training. Second, the kind of equipment that is involved has increased in cost. Third, both we and the Jordanians feel that during this past year we would have hoped to have been able to do something more than we have done and were unable to do so. 

So basically it is a question of this modernization process continuing on the basis of increased costs and involving items that have kicked up the amount.

STATUS OF PALESTINIANS 

Mr. HAMILTON. Mr. Secretary, there is a statement in your AID presentation booklet referring to the $100 million special fund which 

I would like to quote to you. It is as follows:

These projects are likely to be of special urgency as large numbers of Pales-tinians look to reestablish regimes-rather than the revolutionary organizations to help them fulfill their aspirations. 

Do I understand from that that the United States is against any of the Palestinian organizations representing the Palestinians? 

Mr. Sisco. First let me say I have not seen this sentence, and I would not say it is the most felicitously written sentence I have come across.

Mr. HAMILTON. I wouldn't either. 

Mr. Sisco. Let me just say that at the outset.

Now insofar as your question is concerned, we obviously have made no substantive decision whatsoever in terms of how the so-called legitimate interests of the Palestinians will be met in the context of any peace agreement. We are convinced that there can't be a durable peace in the area unless the interests of Israel, the Arab States, and the Pales-tinian people are taken fully into account. I would not want you to read into that particular statement that we have adopted any new policy in this regard.

We have not even made a decision, Mr. Hamilton, as to what our position will be if and when the question of the representation of the 

Palestinians at any Geneva conference will arise. For example, the

Palestinians themselves have not been able to make this kind of a decision. They have just concluded 4 or 5 days of meetings in Cairo, for example, with what I would term very inconclusive results as it relates to the possible participation of Palestinians in the Geneva conference.

PALESTINIAN REPRESENTATION AT GENEVA 

Mr. HAMILTON. I am under the impression, Mr. Secretary, that as a result of that conference in Cairo that Mr. Arafat would like to go to Geneva.

Mr. SISCO. I have the same impression, and likewise I have the impression that a principal decision which arose from that particular meeting is a disposition to participate, but on conditions that are dif-

ferent than the present substantive framework of the Geneva conference. The Geneva conference framework is based on Security Council 

Resolution 242, the November 1967 Security Council Resolution. This resolution has not been accepted as a matter of formal decision by the Palestinian Liberation Organization. So that I have read these reports and I am not sure this is in fact the decision, but if we are talking about participation on the basis of different conditions, then this is a matter that the parties themselves will have to decide, including, by the way, the cochairmen of the conference.

U.S. POSITION ON PALESTINIANS 

Mr. HAMILTON. Would the United States accept the PLO as a representative of the Palestinians at the conference, or haven't we made that decision?

Mr. SISCO. We have not made that decision, and obviously we are not in a position to. I am certainly not going to cross that bridge here this morning. 

Mr. HAMILTON. Would you consider the discussion of the "legitimate rights of the Palestinians" as an item on the agenda of the Geneva conference?

Mr. Sisco. Our position has been that the legitimate interests of the 

Palestinians have to be taken into account in any peace agreement. We have not gone beyond that, Mr. Hamilton.

Mr. HAMILTON. Thank you.

USE OF EGYPTIAN POUNDS 

Mr. BUCHANAN. Let me ask you a couple of questions about this aid. 

First of all, would not the Egyptian pounds have to be authorized and appropriated? 

Mr. SISCO. No, Mr. Buchanan. U.S. holdings of Egyptian pounds were generated primarily under Public Law 480 and are excess to our needs. Section 104(f) of Public Law 480 authorizes use of foreign currencies owned by the United States generated under Public Law 480 sales to promote multilateral trade and agricultural and other economic development. Under the Mondale amendment, the final proviso of section 104, Public Law 480, excess foreign currencies may be used for various development purposes without an appropriation. In addition, under section 614(a) of the Foreign Assistance Act, up to $100 million of foreign currencies held by the United States may be used without appropriation for any Foreign Assistance Act purpose if the President himself determines that the use is important to the security of the United States.

Mr. BUCHANAN. Thank you, sir. 

ASSISTANCE PROGRAM "CANNOT BUY PEACE" 

You have, I think, very accurately described the situation in your written statement in saying, and I quote:

We do not pretend that the assistance program you are considering can buy peace. Nor can we purchase constructive relations in the area. Peace and good relations are not for sale in the Middle East or anywhere else. Rather, the program is an essential adjunct to our broader diplomacy-necessary to the success of that diplomacy, though not sufficient to bring success. 

Would you say that in the scale of things as a matter of priority the Middle East assistance included in this bill is of very great importance to the process of peace?

Mr. SISCO. I would say it is, and in my judgment the sentence that you just read is probably the most important sentence in this entire brief statement of mine. The reason why I say this is that I have a very strong feeling, Mr. Buchanan, that we must not approach the 

Middle East from the point of view of making progress toward peace on the basis of what moneys we can contribute. 36-333-74- -15

Now this may sound like an argument against the program. Not at all. I happen to believe that this is a very modest program, and I think that the process of peacemaking and peacebuilding can be helped. 

I can think of certain countries 10 and 15 years ago where we felt that if we poured enough money into this situation that this would solve the problem. This is the wrong psychology, and I want to avoid this in the Middle East because it stimulates undue expectations on the part of the people as well as the states in the region. We cannot carry on that kind of a major resource program. We help them to help themselves.

RECEIPT OF MIG'S BY IRAQ 

Mr. BUCHANAN. Thank you very much, Mr. Secretary.

There are press reports that Iraq is now receiving the latest model MIG's. I wonder if you would have any comment on Iraq's role, or possible role, in any settlement? 

Mr. SISCO. Well, first of all, insofar as the negotiations are concerned, the Iraqis have not played any kind of a role. The focus obviously has been on the principal parties concerned, but I would add that in time if the kind of evolution that we see developing will continue to be nurtured, extended, intensified, one would hope that this would begin to embrace a number of other states in the Middle East. 

The Iraqis are not direct combatant states as the others are. They did, of course, participate in a minimal sort of way on the Syrian front during the recent war, but I think the winds that are blowing in the Middle East are affecting all of the countries in the area, and one would hope that in time this would have an impact toward a more moderate course in a country such as Iraq. 

I find it particularly significant that Syria has made this agreement, and the fact that Syria has made this agreement I think has an important psychological impact on other Arab countries, particularly those Arab countries that are particularly proud of their so-called radical credentials. 

Mr. Yatron.

IMPORTANCE OF GREECE TO MIDDLE EAST STABILITY 

Mr. YATRON. Mr. Secretary, I would like to ask a question about the importance of Greece to the stability of the peace in the Middle East. 

Is it important?

Mr. SISCO. Well, Greece, of course, is an important member of 

NATO, and is an important element in the southern flank of NATO itself and, therefore, from a strategic point of view the kind of relationships that we are maintaining with Greece are of significance. 

Greece has not played any active or direct role in the Arab-Israel process itself; it enjoys good relationships with countries in the area, but in terms of pronouncements or having any direct impact on the process that is going on, I think the preoccupation in Greece today is largely internal. 

Mr. YATRON. Thank you.

EGYPT AND SYRIA MOTIVES FOR PEACE 

Mr. LAGOMARSINO. Mr. Sisco, in your opinion what was the major reason why Egypt and Syria finally decided that peace was a nice thing to have?

Mr. SISCO. Well, it is a very good question, I must say, and I don't know how good of an answer I can give.

First of all, I think Egypt in the first instance made up its mind that ever since the 1967 war that all of the attempts at peacemaking that were made, whether it be in big power context or the Security Council at the U.N. basically resulted in political support in the form of a Security Council resolution or a public pronouncement, but it had no practical effect on the reality of negotiations, on the reality of making progress toward the peace. 

I happen to believe that the most fundamental thing that happened is the result of the objective conditions having been changed in the area resulting from the October war of 1973. 

Mr. LAGOMARSINO. You mean like Israel crossing the Suez Canal?

Mr. Sisco. I mean that the perception of each side of the other has changed. There is a realization on each side that, if there is a resumption of hostilities, the likelihood would be another war of attrition with an inconclusive result. Therefore, I think that the diplomatic position became the far more attractive alternative both to Egypt as well as Israel in these circumstances, and I think it is directly a result of the changed objective conditions following the October war of 1973.

NO MILITARY AID TO SYRIA IN BILL 

Mr. LAGOMARSINO. Is there anything in this bill that would provide military aid to any of these countries other than Israel? 

Mr. Sisco. No; this is the totality. There is Jordan and Israel. Aid to Egypt is nonmilitary.

Mr. LAGOMARSINO. Anything given to Syria under that $100 million provision would be nonmilitary?

Mr. SISCO. No decisions have been made. 

Mr. LAGOMARSINO. But that would be nonmilitary?

Mr. Sisco. It would not be military in any event. 

ISSUE OF TERRORIST ACTIVITIES 

Mr. LAGOMARSINO. I wonder if you would care to comment on the question of terrorist activities. As I understand it most of these take place from Lebanon, but some from Syria as well. Was this a part of the negotiations?

Mr. Sisco. There is nothing in either the formal agreement or the 

United Nations protocol that is attached to the agreement that deals with the question of terrorism per se. However, we did make a public statement in the context of this overall agreement while we were in the area, and this statement was as follows: That the United States would consider terrorist action across these borders as abridging the cease-fire and this agreement, and that if this occurred-that if Israel were violated against in this respect-Israel could expect political support from the United States. So there is nothing as part of this

agreement, but certainly the whole terrorist problem is in the outer climate, if I can put it that way. 

This is a personal judgment that I am expressing now. I am convinced that it is absolutely essential that terrorist acts be controlled from the Syrian side, because otherwise it could obviously jeopardize what has been achieved. The difficulty on the Lebanese side you have put your finger on, and that is that they have not been fully able to control it, and that is where the problem primarily is at the present time.

Mr. LAGOMARSINO. Thank you.

NUCLEAR EFFORTS OF ISRAEL AND EGYPT 

Mr. ZABLOCKI. In the process of the consideration of this bill some concern was registered that the $75 million to India should be scrutinized because of the nuclear device India has produced. Is there any similarity to the nuclear efforts being undertaken by Israel? 

Mr. Sisco. Not that I am aware of, Mr. Chairman.

Let me say this, that both Egypt and Israel have long been interested in power reactors to be used for generating electricity in their countries. In addition to electricity as far as the Israelis are concerned they have always been interested in power reactors for projects on desalinization.

Let me say that we have had, and I think you are aware of this, a long and detailed study that has been developed in the executive branch. We have gotten to the point where we think basically we ought to respond positively to this kind of a desire on the part of Egypt and Israel; however no final decision has, in fact, been made.

​I 

INDIA'S NUCLEAR DECISION 

Insofar as the Indian matter is concerned, let me just say one word. You know what our position has been, Mr. Zablocki. We are a signer of the Non-Proliferation Treaty. We have been against these peaceful explosions, and that is basically our position. Without making a long speech about India-about this $75 million that we have in-we have not been involved in any kind of an economic aid program with India since 1971, since the war. We are talking in terms of hopefully a new economic relationship within the context of an improved relationship between India and the United States. I think this is very modest by comparison to what we did 10 and 15 years ago, and I would hope that regardless of the developments of recent weeks that the members of this committee would focus on the continuing humanitarian need. There are people there that are starving that need food and need help. 

I can understand why there might be a questioning attitude with respect to the decision taken, but regrettably I don't think this obviates the need of the people themselves, so I hope that the members of this committee will look at it from that point of view as well as the fact that this is a very modest sum indeed. 

INTERNATIONAL WEAPONS SALES BY ISRAEL 

Mr. ZABLOCKI. Mr. Secretary, and according to the recent press reports, Israel is now selling weapons in international trade. If this is so, what possibilities are there that Israel could make use of its own arms production and have the U.S. phase down its aid? If Israel is selling munitions, why should we 

Mr. Sisco. First, the kind of thing that they are selling, let me say, is not firstline equipment which the Israelis are using primarily in their own defense, but that is not really the response that I want to make to you.

I think if we can continue to make progress toward the achievement of a durable peace, one can at least begin to have a glimmer of hope that the whole arms supply in the entire area can be reviewed and looked at in that context. I happen to believe that the kind of military balance that has been in the area has been conducive to the peace efforts that we have been pursuing as well as at least the minimal stability that we have in the area today. 

I don't think a disequilibrium is going to be helpful either through the process or through the long-term goal, but my hope is that as you make progress on these disengagement agreements if we can get at the fundamental elements of a settlement certainly one would want to look at the whole arms situation in that context, but I don't see us able to do that, Mr. Zablocki, before we reach that point. 

Mr. ZABLOCKI. It would be helpful to the committee to get better understanding of your response if you would supply for the record what munitions, what conventional arms, the State of Israel is selling in international trade. U.S. POSITION ON PALESTINE REFUGEES 

What is the position of the United States with respect to the Palestine refugees?

Mr. Sisco. I said a moment ago, Mr. Zablocki, there is no durable peace that is possible unless it meets the concerns of Israel, the Arab 

States and the Palestinian people.

You cannot settle with Israel and the Arab States on the one hand and leave as a sore the unrequited interests and concerns of the Palestinian people who are quite numerous in the Middle East. 

What form that solution is going to take, I am frank to say, I don't know.

The Arab States have differences of views on that, and the Palestinians themselves have differences of views on this question. 

So our objective is to help diplomatically in terms of stabilizing this area where all of the peoples are coexisting and living alongside one another, and when you say that it obviously includes-

RUSSIA AND PEACE IN MIDDLE EAST 

Mr. FOUNTAIN. Let me ask you, what is Russia doing to help bring about peace in the Middle East?

Mr. SISCO. Well, the Soviet Union and the United States, as you know, are cochairmen of the Geneva conference.

In analyzing the Soviet role over the last 2 months, I would say that on the whole they have not been unhelpful. 

You see, they have not played a direct role in the negotiations. The fact of the matter is that the Soviet position in the Middle East is a reality; they have capacity, they have good relationships with Syria, they have good relationships with Iraq, and so on. 

I have no doubt in my own mind that there is a recognition on the part of the Soviets that there is a parallelism of interest between the United States and the Soviet Union that the cease-fire serves not only 4

the interests of the area but peace generally, as well as the overall relationships between the United States and the Soviet Union. 

Insofar as the actual process of progress toward peace, I think basically they have not intervened in any unhelpful way without at the same time playing any direct role as catalysts as we have.

MILITARY BALANCE IN THE MIDDLE EAST 

Mr. FASCELL. Is the basic assumption in the Middle East a military balance which will lead to progress for an ultimate decision and that the military balance exists?

Mr. SISCO. I think it does. I think both sides feel in the aftermath of the October war in particular, Mr. Fascell, that if either side starts another war, it is apt to result in an inconclusive result, and I think that is one of the realities which at the present time has been helpful to the peacemaking process. 

Mr. FASCELL. Is part of that assumption also economic?

Mr. SISCO. We feel that as we begin to achieve greater stability in the area you can have the beginnings-and they are reflected, I think, in this program-of a turnaway from war and some of the preparations. Not all of them obviously, because insecurity still remains, but they can begin to move toward reconstruction and development. 

ASSUMPTIONS ABOUT SOVIET ACTIONS? 

Mr. FASCELL. Is part of that assumption also that the principal parties, the Soviet Union and the United States, will not during this period of progress, whatever period of time it takes, unduly jeopardize the situation by providing additional arms so as to create an imbalance? 

Mr. SISCO. There is no explicit understanding, Mr. Fascell, between us and Mr. FASCELL. No, I didn't mean there was an understanding but it is a basic assumption that if the Soviets keep pouring arms into the Middle East it will certainly not help maintain a balance. 

Mr. Sisco. I could not disagree with that.

Mr. FASCELL. It seems to me fundamental to consideration of your program proposal before us to determine whether in fact such a balance exists.

Mr. SISCO. Well, I think there is a balance. 

Mr. FASCELL. I am not asking you to comment on it at this moment until you are prepared to give specifics. I may be willing to go with the assumption, but I want to know more about it. For example,

whether there is going to be a $500 million grant out of the previous money; whether there will be $300 million given in economic aid for Israel; and whether you are advocating $550 million in economic aid in other countries in the Middle East, I would like to know whether, in fact, there is such a balance as you suggest, and it seems to me that the time has come to lay that on the record. 

NEED FOR INFORMATION ON ARMS 

The United States only has certain information but I don't think it helps the situation at all to say, well, I think the Syrians are getting new airplanes, I think the Israelis are getting some, we don't know what the Egyptians have gotten. We must know all facts to the best of our ability to obtain them.

Does the $2.2 billion really offset the balance that was used up in that war? Did the $5.6 billion that the Russians put in there really create an imbalance? We need to know all the information you have and the factors you considered in submitting a "balanced proposal."

Until we can review that it seems to me we are just making an educated guess with respect to the matters before us. 

Mr. SISCO. Let me make two very brief observations on that. I think you would agree that whatever balance or equilibrium exists in the area, that this is not a static thing. 

Mr. FASCELL. Agreed.

Mr. SISCO. And it is one that obviously has to be watched. 

Second, in terms of what you said, I think I should supply to the members of the committee on a classified basis-you ought to know what we think is going in from the Soviet Union, what they have been doing with country X, Y, and Z. 

Mr. Chairman, I think this is a very valid question and with your permission I would like to put that into the record and send it over to the committee on a classified basis. [The information requested was received, but is classified and is retained in the committee files.]

[The information follows:] ECONOMIC POSTURE 

ISRAEL 

1. Gross National Product: At 1972 prices, GNP reached over $7.1 billion in 

1973, up $300 million (4%) from 1972. For 1973 the pre-war predicted GNP growth rate was 8%, but will probably be about 6%. Per capita GNP runs about $2,200. 

2. Broadening Productive Sector: Industrial exports for 1971-72 were up almost 200% over pre-Six Day War years, indicating significant growth in nontraditional production areas. Europe absorbed 45-50% of Israel's total exports while the U.S. bought less than 20%. Exports will fall but, except for tourism, will likely drop less than 12-15% as a result of the war. 

3. Trade and Payments Imbalance: Current account in 1973 showed a deficit on goods and services of about $1.

6 billion ($500 million above 1972) due pri-

marily to defense imports. Imports totalled $2.9 billion against $1.4 billion in exports during 1973. Balance of payments surplus for 1974 probably will increase due to foreign remittances increasing faster than the deficit on current account. 

Remittances and bond sales abroad amounted to almost $700 million during prewar 1973 and reached about $1 billion by the end of the year. 

4. Foreign Exchange reserves: Israel's foreign exchange reserves were about $1.5 billion representing 6.2 months of imports, at the end of 1973, up from $1.2 billion at the end of 1972. Reserves rose to $1.5 billion in August 1973, prior to the latest war, and reached a peak of $1.8 billion during the war in October before trailing off toward $1.5 billion. 

5. Budget and Revenues: The 1973 GOI budget was about $7.65 billion, up from $3.63 billion in 1972. Revenues, excluding aid, were 56% of total expenditure ($3.93 billion) in 1973 and 63% ($2.60 billion) in 1972. The 1974 budget may reach $5.0 to $6.0 billion. 

6. Prices: Consumer prices rose at an annual rate of about 9% during 1970 and 1971, 13% for 1972 and 15% for 1973. The 1972 and 1973 increases were primarily due to foreign exchange injections. 

7. At the end of 1972, the GOI had a record-breaking foreign debt of $3.6 billion. This was up from $2.9 billion at the end of 1971, $2.3 billion in 1970, and $1.9 billion in 1969-105% increase in 36 months. Debt service payments have risen substantially since 1970 and amount to approximately 15% of foreign earnings. On a population of 3 million people, the per capita foreign debt burden is over $1,000. This debt climbed to $4.5 billion by the end of 1973. 

Israel's public debt terms are quite favorable. These terms reflect in part the large subscription to GOI bonds, most of them in the U.S. These bonds total $1.3 billion, or 1% of Israel's total foreign debt. The bonds have maturities ranging up to 15 years and commonly carry a 4% annual interest rate. They are generally "rolled over", as the aggregate amount of publicly issued debt outstanding has constantly increased. Additionally, the foreign exchange proceeds from redemption payments are often converted into Israeli Pounds, making the terms even more favorable.

The mass of loans extended to Israel by the United States Government in recent years, mainly for the purpose of arms purchases, brought Israel's outstanding debt to the U.S. at the end of 1973 to over $1 billion. This makes the 

U.S. Government Israel's second largest creditor following GOI bond holders. 

At the end of 1971, included in the above debt to the United States were funds from PL 480, $174 million; A.I.D., $116 million; the Export-Import Bank, $35 million military sales and other miscellaneous resources of between $600 and $700 million.

Since 1969, the U.S. has granted very concessional terms on government loans. 

Long maturities and low interest rates characterize four-fifths of Israel's debt to the U.S., both military and economic. PL 480 loans carry interest rates of about 3% and maturities of 20 years. EX-IM Bank loans, both medium and long term, bear a 6% interest rate. It should be said that Israel has also increased its use of costly sources of external finance such as long-term borrowings from financial institutions.

Direct obligations to the U.S. Government represent a large and increasing segment of the total foreign debt, rising from 20% in 1966 to about 50% at the end of 1973.

Other large creditors are the World Bank to which Israel owed approximately $100 million as 1972 ended, and the German Federal Republic to whom Israel still owes $410 million on previous loans. 

8. Economic Impact of the War: Israel emerged from the 1973 war and its aftermath in relatively good financial and economic condition. Foreign exchange reserves increased through 1973 because foreign remittances continued to rise more rapidly than the current account deficit. Authorized U.S. military assistance, if fully used, would provide a military establishment considerably stronger than at the outset of the war. In the longer term, the economic situation will be critically dependent on the political and military settlement, the amount and terms of arms purchased, the duration of the mobilization and, finally, the willingness of the Israeli people to endure some further economic sacrifices in order to control a growing inflation and support continuing large defense expenditures.

EGYPT Gross National Product: The Egyptian GNP for 1972 was $8.3 billion, or $243 

per capita.

Agricultural Production: The Egyptian economy is heavily agricultural, rely ing primarily on cotton, rice, corn and wheat. Overall agricultural production has risen 8% since 1969. 

Foreign Trade: In 1973 exports totaled $1.1 billion, up 36% from 1972. Imports for 1973 were $905 million, up 4% from a 1972 level of $877 million. 

Budget: The 1973 Egyptian expenditure budget was $4.2 billion ($1.4 billion for defense), up 18% from a 1972 budget of $3.5 billion ($1.3 billion for defense).

Domestic revenues for 1972 and 1973 were $1.7 billion and $1.8 billion respectively.

Prices: The CPL has risen at an average rate of about 4% since 1969 but rose almost 30% during 1973.

Foreign Exchange: Egypt's FX reserves rose dramatically during 1973 ($390 

million) as a result of one time contributions by other nations supporting the Egyptian war effort. This asset will likely be disbursed quickly in reconstruction programs.

Balance of Payments: The loss of Suez Canal income, a decline in tourism, a falling-off of long-term loan disbursements from other Arab countries, heavy loan repayments, and a continuing trade deficit, characterized the adverse balance of payments picture in Egypt from 1967 war through 1971. The shortage of foreign exchange led to the imposition of several restraints on imports of raw materials and replacement equipment, resulting in substantial idle industrial capacity (now estimated as high as 35% of the total).

Beginning in 1972, the balance of payments picture improved with a rise in transfer payments and capital inflow, coupled with continued curtailment of vital imports. The overall balance of payments estimates for the last three years, furnished by the Egyptian Ministry of Economic Planning to the AID team, are as follows: 

Balance of payments deficit/surplus.. 

Gross foreign exchange reserves.. [In millions of dollars) 1971 1972 1973 -141 161 +3 +309 149 301 The balance of payments surplus in 1973 provided at least a temporary rise in foreign exchange reserves. However, this can be accounted for in large part by massive support payments from the Arab world in late 1973, coming too late in the year to permit relaxation of import controls. Thus, the 1973 surplus does not reflect any basic economic trend changes. To restore industrial production, Egypt estimates it will need to increase purchases of essential raw materials and spare parts by some $200 million per year. This will require substantial inflows of additional foreign exchange if Egypt's balance of payments is not to fall back into severe deficit.

External Public Debt: Of the total medium and long-term debt and suppliers' credits outstanding at the end of 1972, slightly more than half was owed to IMF members and the IBRD, with the United States, Kuwait, Germany and Italy being the largest creditors in this group. In the Eastern bloc, the USSR is the largest creditor, followed by Czechoslovakia and East Germany. Although half the outstanding debt was to be repaid by 1976/1977, rescheduling arrangements have been reached with most creditors. 

JORDAN 

Gross National Product: GNP is about $760 million, counting the West Bank, giving a per capita income of about $286. 

Narrow Productive Sector: Agriculture and industry, including mining, account for only 25 per cent of GNP.

Trade Imbalance: CY 1972 imports of $274 million were five times larger than exports of about $48 million.

High Ratio of GOJ Spending: Governmental spending equals about 74 per cent of GDP at factor cost, excluding the West Bank. 

Extensive Budget Deficits: Domestic revenues of about $143 million in CY 1973 covered only about 44 per cent of government spending. 

Dependence on Foreign Aid: External budget support accounts for about 37 

per cent of governmental spending, and about 50 per cent of foreign exchange receipts.

High Liquidity: Money supply has grown faster than the economy and at the end of CY 1973 stood at the equivalent of over $430 million. 

Relative Price Stability: Annual price rises in recent years have averaged 7 per cent, without the large amounts of foreign aid and the apparent liquidity preference, prices would undoubtedly have risen faster. 

Foreign Exchange Reserves: Reserves stood at $312 million at the end of 1973, a growth of $41 million over the year, and a level equivalent to about 12 months worth of imports.

Debt Servicing: Foreign debt servicing costs in CY 1973 were about $14 million approximately 26 per cent of export earnings.

What are they? You have got the whole question of the West Bank which is a very sensitive issue because it is close to the populated areas of Israel. TERRORISTS AND TERRORISM 

Mr. KAZEN.  

Mr. Secretary, I also want to congratulate you and the Secretary on what you have all been able to achieve.

I am delighted that you are still around because now the many years of labor that you put into this field are beginning to show results. 

Mr. SISCO. Thank you. 

Mr. KAZEN. There is one thing that bothers me. That is the terrorist situation. As I understand it very, very few, if any, of the terrorist raids into Israel have come from Syria. 

Mr. Sisco. That is correct. 

Mr. KAZEN. Most of them have come from Lebanon. If any more come in the future they will come from Lebanon. Are you satisfied that Lebanon's Government is doing everything possible to contain the terrorists?

Mr. Sisco. Mr. Kazen, this is a very difficult question for me to answer particularly in open session. I think the Lebanese Government has made clear to us that they view this problem seriously both from a military and a political point of view. 

They have said to us that they are really doing all that is possible within their physical capacity. I happen to believe that terrorism will continue over the next year or two for the simple reason that these individual groups or even these individuals, these isolated cases are quite strangely almost impossible to control. 

Why do I think they are going to continue? Because I think basically these dramatic grandstand acts of violations are acts of desperation and they are antipeace acts-they are performed by people who are against the achievement of a political solution and a settlement that permits the Israelis and the Arabs to coexist alongside one another. 

CONTROLLING TERRORISM ON LEBANESE BORDER 

One would have hoped that even more could be done to control this situation along the Lebanese border. I reveal no secret when I say to you that the Israeli Government does not agree with the Lebanese Government that the Lebanese Government is doing all that it can. 

I am not expressing the Israeli point of view. 

So, you have got the dual problem of where, for example, while we were in the Middle East you had the tragedy of Maalot which resulted in a very substantial retaliation. 

The Arabs on the one hand make a distinction between the acts of an organized government and the acts of individual terrorists or small groups of terrorists.

Israel does not make this distinction, arguing that our people are no less dead whether they are at the hands of an individual terrorist group or otherwise.

Candidly it is a very serious problem for both sides. I think that the only solace that I can take is that as the atmosphere improves you don't today, in the Arab world, get statements from prominent Arab leaders that you got 2, 3, and 4 years ago, in effect endorsing if not complementing these individual acts of violence.

I think the individual Arab States have made it very clear that they do not want to have this kind of thing occur, and it is now less a problem of attitude but more a practical problem of how you control it. 

INNOCENT PEOPLE KILLED IN LEBANON 

Mr. KAZEN. The thing that worries me is that if this continues, the retaliatory action will continue and there will also be innocent people killed in Lebanon.

Mr. Sisco. Absolutely; it is tragic on both sides. 

Mr. KAZEN. It is, and if the Government of Lebanon is doing everything it can within its present capabilities, the retaliatory acts and their dead are just as dead as the ones on the other side. 

Mr. SISCO. Sure. 

Mr. KAZEN. And just as innocent as the ones on the other side. 

Mr. Sisco. That is correct.

Mr. KAZEN. Is there any place that this situation can be worked out? 

Mr. Sisco. Well, we have not found the answer. We have taken the lead in the world in trying to cope with the whole terrorist problem, and on the assumption that this is a global problem that requires a global attack. Its serious manifestations are along the Lebanese-Israeli border.

In the Security Council of the U.N. itself we have tried to inject the political element. We have tried to support propositions in the 

Council which condemned violence from whatever quarter; in other words not only the individual terrorist act but the retaliation as well. 

We have not intended to make a distinction between the individual terrorist action and the governmental action for the reason that we have given, but we don't have a satisfactory answer to this, and unfortunately neither do the Arab or the Israelis in the area have a satisfactory answer.

U.S. POSITION ON ISRAELI RETALIATION 

Mr. KAZEN. I don't know what the agreement was between those countries on retaliation, but apparently from what I read in the press the United States in the future will not condemn retaliatory action. 

Mr. SISCO. No. 

Let me do this. I will put in the record this statement that was made in the Middle East while we were there and I will paraphrase it for you here very precisely, Mr. Chairman, in a moment.

I would like to put this statement in the record.

Mr. Gilman.

CRITERIA FOR ALLOCATING U.S. AID 

Mr. GILMAN.  

Mr. Sisco, we welcome you here and I join my colleagues in thanking you for your analysis of the problems that are confronting us in the Middle East.

Yesterday I expressed some concern about the allocation of the funds for the various countries in the Middle East under the security supporting assistance program and again today I would like to raise the issue with you.

Some $250 million is being recommended for Egypt, $77 million for Jordan, and $50 million for Israel under the security and supportive assistance program. Can you discuss with us the criteria that have been developed for allocating these amounts for the various countries! 

They seem to me to be a bit out of balance when we consider some of the economic stresses that have been placed on some of these countries and the populations involved.

U.S. AID TO EGYPT 

Mr. SISCO. Well, first, with respect to Egypt, what we have in mind is roughly $20 million that would go into the work on the Suez Canal which Admiral McCauley described here this morning. 

We have in mind roughly $150 million for reconstruction, largely in the cities that were destroyed in and around the Suez Canal during the recent war, Ismailia and others.

And roughly $80 million for commodity imports, and this is a program which will finance essential imports such as fertilizers, pesticides, grain handling equipment, and newsprint-the whole purpose being a stimulation of the agriculture and industrial production. 

Let me put it literally. This is just a drop in the bucket as far as 

Egypt is concerned. It represents no more than really a beginning, an important beginning I might add, and a manifestation that we would like to be helpful as they turn toward reconstruction and development.

U.S. AID TO ISRAEL 

Now, insofar as Israel is concerned, I think the figures have to be considered in the background and in the backdrop of the $2.2 billion which the Congress authorized this past year. The $300 million figure for foreign military sales is military security, and it basically was arrived at through consultations with the Israeli Government itself. 

The supporting assistance component is really the continuation of a commodity import program for Israel, and it is intended quite frankly because it is the direct support to help alleviate the financial burdens.

I said a bit earlier in my testimony this is really our best judgment in terms of our discussions with the Israelis, and this, like the rest of these programs, obviously will have to remain under continuing review.

U.S. AID TO JORDAN 

On the Jordan side again, it is $207.5 million, $77.5 million of which is in the form of supporting assistance and $67.5 million cash grants, because they need on a continuing basis to be giving their budgetary deficit a good deal of direct support. 

Much of this money is going into a modernization of the Jordanian Armed Forces, and at the same time going toward development itself. 

We want to put these numbers together and equate them on a parallel basis. We tried really on its merits to determine what would be sensible in the context of Egypt and Israel and so on, and this is what we arrived at.

ECONOMIC IMPACT OF WAR ON ISRAEL 

Mr. GILMAN. I assume that in these considerations, you consider the economic strength and the economic needs of each nation? 

Mr. SISCO. Yes. - Mr. GILMAN. I understood that Israel suffered a $10 billion cost as a result of the October war that the war inflicted $10 billion of expenditures to that small nation.

Mr. Sisco. They have. On the other hand, if you look at the foreign exchange position of Israel, it still, I must say, is pretty good. 

Mr. GILMAN. I would assume that if this committee were to recommend additional areas of support for the various countries, that there may not be too much objection raised by the administration. 

Mr. SISCO. Mr. Gilman, I am responding with a smile. This seems to be the very favorite question I am getting this morning. We will look at whatever the committee in its wisdom decides in this regard.

Mr. GILMAN. Thank you.

SECURITY COUNCIL RESOLUTION ON ISRAEL 

Mr. BINGHAM. Very well.

Many of us in Congress and, of course, elsewhere were dismayed at the U.S. vote in the Security Council following the terrorist attack at 41

3 1 Kiriyat Shmoneh on a condemnatory vote that did not contain a balance in that it seemed to be a departure from previous votes. 

First of all, I would like your comment on that, your explanation, if any, and also what assurance can we have that that type of vote will not be repeated? 

Mr. Sisco. One, let me say very candidly that that resolution was not as balanced as we would have desired, but let me say with equal force that that resolution was as strong a resolution in terms of dealing with acts of violence from all quarters, including the terrorist acts, as any that has been adopted by the Security Council, and I think I can document that on the basis of every Security Council resolution that has been adopted on this matter. 

As I say, it was not as balanced as we would have liked, but if you look at operative paragraph 2 of that resolution, we said explicitly it referred to all acts of violence and innocent victims. 

You go on to paragraph 3 of that resolution-and I will forgive your U.N. background and mine at this particular point-which called upon all states to assume their obligations under the charter and international law.
