[The information requested follows:] FISCAL YEAR 1975 SUPPORTING ASSISTANCE FOR ISRAEL 

The decision to request $50 million in FY 75 supporting assistance funds for Israel was based on several factors, among which were: (1) the economic and financial impact of the totality of U.S. assistance provided in FY 74; (2) a forecast of Israel's balance of payments situation in FY 75 and (3) an assumption that there would not be a resumption of active hostilities in FY 75. 

Since FY 1971 total annual U.S. assistance to Israel has averaged about $500 million. In addition to $300 million in FMS credit and $50 million in supporting assistance, our assistance has included grant assistance to help offset the costs of Jewish emigrants from the USSR, PL 480 credits and housing guarantees. 

One significant result of the substantial level of U.S. assistance was a very considerable increase in Israel's foreign exchange reserves, which increased from $528 million in 1971 to $1,515 million in September, 1973.

The October 1973 war triggered a vast increase in Israel's military expenditures in the U.S. Consequently, the President requested and the Congress authorized an emergency appropriation of $2.2 billion. $1.5 billion of this was made available on a grant basis and the balance of $700 billion on long term, low interest repayment basis. We anticipate that the actual financial impact of this massive injection of assistance will be felt over a period of about three years. 

There are two critical measures of the impact of the war on Israel's economy, insofar as U.S. assistance is concerned: changes in its foreign exchange reserves and changes in its foreign debt position. At the end of 1973 Israel's foreign exchange reserves were about $1.5 billion, up from $1.2 billion at the end of 1972. 

The GOI's foreign debt has been rising steadily. In recent years, it has increased as follows: $1.9 billion-1969; $2.3 billion-1970; $2.9 billion-1971; $3.6 billion-1972. By the end of 1973, Israel's foreign debt amounted to $4.5-$5 billion. There has been a concomitant increase in debt service payments and they now amount to approximately 15% of foreign exchange earnings. However,

Israel's public debt terms are quite favorable. They reflect in part the large subscription to GOI bonds, most of them in the U.S. These bonds total $1.3 billion, or of Israel's total foreign debt. The bonds have maturities ranging up to 15 years and commonly carry a 4% annual interest rate. They are generally "rolled over", evidenced by the fact that the aggregate amount of publicly issued debt outstanding has constantly increased. Also, the foreign exchange proceeds from redemption payments are often converted into Israeli pounds, making the terms even more favorable. Finally, the debt service ratio is still less than it was in the mid-sixties.

Since 1969, the U.S. has granted very concessional terms on government loans. 

Long maturities and low interest rates characterize four-fifths of Israel's debt (over $1 billion) to the U.S., both military and economic. PL-480 loans carry interest rates of about 3% and maturities of 20 years. Ex-Im Bank loans, both medium and long term, bear a 6% interest rate. 

The economic significance of the heavy and growing debt burden depends on the future ability of Israel to service them and that, in turn depends on Israel's future growth and future balance of payments situation. It was our judgment that in FY 75 Israel's balance of payments, after allowing for U.S. assistance, would show an increased surplus, mainly because we anticipated that financial remittances to Israel would increase more rapidly than its deficit on goods and services. If that forecast is accurate, there would then be a further addition to 

Israel's foreign exchange reserves. This would occur, despite continuing high levels of military purchases abroad.

Admittedly, there is no certainty in forecasting. What we have given you represented our best judgment at the time, based on past performance of the Israeli

economy and our estimate of how we believe it will perform in the year ahead. 

We are of course keeping these factors under continuing review to see whether subsequent revisions of our estimates may be desirable.

STATEMENT OF HON. ROBERT S. INGERSOLL, ASSISTANT SECRE- TARY OF STATE FOR EAST ASIAN AND PACIFIC AFFAIRS Mr. INGERSOLL.  

Mr. ZABLOCKI. I understand you will summarize your statement.

Mr. INGERSOLL. Yes. 

Mr. ZABLOCKI. The entire statement will be placed in the record.

Mr. INGERSOLL. Thank you, Mr. Chairman. 

Mr. Chairman, members of the committee, you have received the full text of my statement this morning. I suggest that, in order to save more time for your questions, I simply present a summary of that statement now. I would like to speak of our assistance programs for 

East Asia, and particularly toward Indochina, in terms of their relationship to our major policy objectives in the region. Following this 

I will be glad to answer any questions you may have either with re- (245)

spect to our overall policy or concerning specific programs in our request. 

The primary goals of U.S. policy in East Asia are on the one hand to reduce tension among the major powers involved in the region, and on the other to promote a condition of peaceful, evolutionary change among the small nations. Our assistance programs, by helping to make available much needed resources, contribute to the second of these goals; and-insofar as they are a tangible manifestation of our continuing and important interests in the region-they also work to enhance the equilibrium which has begun to emerge among the major powers. 

An important corollary objective of the United States in East Asia is to move, as circumstances allow, from a primary to a supporting role in meeting the defense and development needs of friendly and allied nations of the region.

The Nixon doctrine concept of burden sharing challenges those nations to concert their efforts as never before in developing their own resources and in making the most effective use of outside assistance. 

Their response has been gratifying, they have, in fact, assumed a larger share of the burden, and we have been able to reduce our role and our responsibilities accordingly. 

However, despite encouraging progress, the economic imperatives posed by overpopulation, food shortages, and disease-and the lack of investment capital and technical expertise with which to attack those problems-means that outside assistance still has a vital role to play. For many nations of the region the obstacles to develop have been compounded in the last year by the energy crisis and worldwide inflation which have further strained scarce resources. Thus, our economic assistance programs in the coming year are designed to sustain, in the face of these continuing problems, the heartening progress which has already been made. 

Similarly, the legitimate self-defense needs of a number of East Asian nations cannot be met without a measure of outside assistance. 

In providing such assistance our aim is to enhance the sense of security which has begun to emerge in East Asia and which has brought in its turn self-confidence and an increasing tendency toward regional cooperation. Only in this way can further adjustments in our own role in East Asia take place without threatening the stability of the area. 

U.S. AID FOR INDOCHINA 

The largest portion of our request is for Indochina. Why is this so? 

Why are we still required to devote such great attention and so many resources to this area?

The contral objective of our assistance programs in Indochina is to support and preserve the rough balance of forces there. That balance has made possible the movement toward peace, and toward great power disengagement, which has thus far taken place in Indochina and which is vital to the worldwide structure of peace we are seeking to build. These programs also give substance to our desire to fulfill our obligations in Indochina and help to sustain the purposes they reflect. I fully share Secretary Kissinger's observation before this:

1 1 the M ​ΤΟ committee last week that failure to uphold those obligations and those purposes would have a corrosive effect on our interests far beyond the confines of Indochina.

It is my strong conviction that reduced aid to South Vietnam would not bring us closer to a complete peace. It is North Vietnam, not the 

South, which has blocked full implementation of the Paris agreement. And it is Hanoi, not the people of South Vietnam and not the cause of a just peace, which would benefit from reductions in our aid. 

The need for higher aid levels for South Vietnam in the coming year is acute. That country is in a deepening economy crisis not of its own making. The crisis stemmed initially from the destruction wrought by the 1972 offensive. It has been perpetuated, and intensified, by North Vietnamese military pressures since the Paris agreement, the marked decline in U.S. assistance-and U.S. military expenditures and the effects of worldwide inflation. With adequate security and economic assistance the prospects are that major North Vietnamese offensive actions will be deterred, the level of violence will decline, and the evolution toward political settlement can go forward. 

Without such assistance these desirable prospects are unlikely. 

CAMBODIA AND LAOS 

Cambodia is engaged in a war for survival, combating a foe which has scorned repeated offers of negotiation apparently in hopes of winning a military victory. We believe that as the prospects of military solution diminish the insurgent leadership will see the logic of negotiation. In the meantime, however, military assistance-and economic aid to ease the burdens placed on the civilian population-is urgently required.

In Laos our assistance is vitally necessary to assist that country's hopeful transition from a long era of warfare to one of peace. The transition will not be without difficulty and success could be jeopardized should we give less attention to the needs of peace than we for so long devoted to the requirements of war. 

Mr. Chairman, members of the committee, we do not envisage foreign aid as a burden to be borne perpetually by the American people. 

On the contrary, our economic assistance programs are intended to hasten the day our aid will no longer be required. Similarly, we expect that our programs of military assistance will gradually decline and that we will shift from grant assistance to credits and, eventually. to cash sales. I do not seek to minimize the cost to this Nation of programs such as those for which we are requesting funds in the coming year. I firmly believe, however, that these programs are important and effective-in advancing the larger goals of America in East Asia, and I ask you to consider them in that light. 

[Mr. Ingersoll's prepared statement follows:] STATEMENT OF HON. ROBERT S. INGERSOLL, ASSISTANT SECRETARY OF STATE FOR EAST ASIAN AND PACIFIC AFFAIRS 

Mr. Chairman, distinguished members of the committee, I am pleased to appear before you this morning in support of our request for economic and security assistance funds for East Asia in the coming fiscal year. I would like to speak briefly of

our assistance programs, particularly those in Indochina, within the context of the major objectives of U.S. policy toward this region, after which I will be glad to answer your questions.

U.S. POLICY IN EAST ASIA 

The two major goals of American policy in East Asia, as defined in the Nixon Doctrine, are the reduction of tension among the major powers involved in the region and a condition of peaceful, evolutionary development among the smaller nations in which those nations are able to provide increasingly for their own economic and defense needs. Our ability to contribute to the achievement of those goals is, to a very large degree, premised on continued American interests in the region-of which our assistance programs are an important tangible manifestation. Thus, with respect to those smaller nations, United States assistance is an essential ingredient in the accelerated economic, political and social development which they need and which continued regional stability requires. By the same token, our ability to shift gradually from a leading to a supportive defense role in the region, reducing our own military presence and role as the nations of the area become more able to assure their own security, is heavily dependent on military assistance. Were such assistance to be curtailed drastically, adjustments in our role-particularly in terms of our military presence could not be made without damaging effect upon the peace and stability of the area.

The Nixon Doctrine precept of shared responsibilities for development and defense presents a challenge to governments associated with us, whether in formal treaty relationships or only by informal ties of friendship. They are called upon to exert greater efforts, not only in identifying and developing their own talents and resources and bringing these to bear on the problems they face, but in putting to use in the most effective manner possible the assistance we provide. The nations of East Asia have responded impressively to this challenge, they have in fact assumed a larger share of the burden, and we have been able to reduce our role and our responsibilities accordingly. For example, American forces in Asia have been reduced by more than 600,000 in the past five years-and by 110,000 even excluding our withdrawals from Viet-Nam.

As East Asian nations provide increasingly for their own defense and developmental needs, which our assistance has helped them to do, they have grown in self-confidence. This in turn has fostered a trend toward regional cooperation as the nations of the area-confident of their political identities, their economic prospects and their secure independence are willing to subordinate nationalistic considerations in order to seek common solutions to common prob lems. Our assistance has obviously not been the sole determinant of this encouraging trend, but it has contributed toward it, and the enhanced prospects for regional stability which that development portends are an important indirect result of the economic and security assistance programs the U.S. has maintained in the region. 

However, despite a generally encouraging picture throughout the area, the economic imperatives which continue to confront a number of East Asian nations require that aid continue to be provided. Over-population, pervasive porerty, food shortages, illiteracy and disease persist in many areas, as do shortages of investment capital and technical expertise with which to combat these problems.

The economies of the region have recently had to contend with a new difficulty as well-the precipitate rise in oil prices-as a result of which, capital needed for domestic investment must be spent for fuel requirements, and developmental objectives must be revised downward. Food production goals may also go unmet because of fertilizer shortages resulting from the energy squeeze. Thus, foreign aid remains essential to the orderly growth of many of the national economies of East Asia, and drastic reductions in outside assistance would not only imperil future prospects, but could vitiate progress already achieved. 

Similarly, despite reduced tensions in the region and the major efforts made by East Asian nations themselves, the legitimate self-defense needs of many nations of the area can only be met by a measure of outside assistance. A failure on the part of the U.S. to provide such assistance would, at the very least, undermine self-confidence and, eventually, regional stability. I should add that it is my firm belief that our programs of security assistance do not contribute to tensions in East Asia. On the contrary, insofar as such programs demonstrate our con-

they alt tinuing concern for the security of our friends and allies in the area, the likelihood of aggressive and destabilizing actions by unfriendly powers, from within the region and without, is reduced. This is particularly evident in Korea. There, U.S. security assistance to the ROK has reassured it of our support and enabled it to take constructive initiatives towards stability of the peninsula. 

INDOCHINA 

By far the largest portion of our request is for Indochina. I would like to speak for a moment of the situation there: Why is it in our interest to provide this aid? Why is more needed this year than last? What are the prospects for the future?

Our continuing aid to the Indochina countries is designed to support and preserve the rough balance of forces in Indochina which made possible the movement toward peace and toward great power disengagement-which has taken place over the past two years. This is in turn vital to the worldwide structure of peace we are trying to build. Our assistance is also necessary to fulfill our moral commitments to the governments and peoples of these countries.¹ Failure to honor these obligations, and to sustain the purposes they reflect, would corrode the value and credibility of our commitments everywhere and thereby reduce our ability to conduct effective worldwide diplomacy. I strongly believe that we have a moral obligation-rooted in the history of our involvement and the continuing efforts of our friends-to see the struggle through. Our huge investment of human and material resources, and our encouragement through two decades of these governments and peoples in their efforts to achieve selfdetermination—which we believe redounds to our interests as well as their own-demands that we persevere. 

Some maintain that eliminating or sharply cutting our aid to South Viet-Nam will bring peace by forcing the South Vietnamese to negotiate a settlement. This may be true if the kind of peace desired is that of abject surrender to Communist aggression, or the peace which would follow a bloody Communist military victory. But this is not the kind of peace for which we have invested so much all these years, nor the kind of peace which would be in our interest or in the interest of the South Vietnamese people. In fact it has not been the South Vietnamese 

Government which has been blocking implementation of the Paris Agreement and further progress toward peace, but rather the North Vietnamese. Consequently, short of forcing their surrender or military defeat, there is no way we can pressure the South Vietnamese alone to make a real peace. The best hope for genuine negotiated settlement and eventual reconciliation in Viet-Nam is to main the balance of forces which has permitted the progress made thus far. 

The need for a higher aid level, especially in Viet-Nam, has become increasingly evident in recent months. South Viet-Nam is in a deepening economic crisis not of its own making. The crisis stemmed initially from the 1972 North Vietnamese offensive which caused widespread disruption and left in its wake a new influx of refugees into already crowded urban areas. The crisis has been perpetuated since the Paris Agreement by the continuing North Vietnamese military build-up and failure to observe the cease-fire. It has been exacerbated by the sharp decline in real terms in the past two years in the value of U.S. economic assistance and by the economic impact of U.S. troop withdrawals. And it has been further compounded by rapid increases in the price of major South Vietnamese imports, primarily petroleum, fertilizer, and foodstuffs. 

South Vietnam must look to others for the wherewithal to reverse this economic deterioration and begin the reconstruction and development effort necessary for movement forward toward economic viability and self-sufficiency. It is therefore imperative that we increase our assistance. Continuing aid at or below the present level would at best postpone the day when South Viet-Nam can stand on its own; at worst it could facilitate a violent Communist takeover. 

On the other hand, in spite of its present economic problems, South Vietnam is stronger militarily and politically than ever before, and it has excellent longrange prospects for economic self-sufficiency. Its military forces have demonstrated their ability to defend the country; its government is politically strong and stable and controls well over 80 percent of the population; and-if they 

1 The word "moral" was added subsequent to the hearings at the request of Mr. Ingersoll and pursuant to a question by Congressman Gross, (See p. 271.) 36-333-74- -17

can be developed-its adequate natural resources, including good prospects of major oil discoveries, give it the possibility of an economic takeoff comparable to that of Korea and Taiwan.

Consequently, provided we continue for the next two or three years to provide the military support necessary for self-defense and the economic support necessary to begin serious reconstruction and development, there are good prospects that North Vietnam will be deterred from launching all-out offensives; that further reductions in the level of violence can be achieved; that South Vietnam can move steadily toward self-sufficiency thus permitting a gradually declining U.S. role in that country; and, that over the long run, evolution toward peaceful accommodation and reconciliation will be possible. As Secretary Kissinger mentioned in his recent appearance before this Committee, we will submit to Congress by August 1 a five-year projection which will reflect our expectation of a gradually declining U.S. role. However, if we do not provide adequate assistance now, these desirable prospects will be improbable, if not impossible. 

In Cambodia, a war for survival goes forward against forces aided and advised by the North Vietnamese. The level of combat remains high, and the Cambodian economy has been shattered. The Government of the Khmer Republic has constantly affirmed its readiness to seek a negotiated solution of the conflict. Insurgent forces have as consistently rejected negotiations, apparently in the belief that a military victory was possible. It is our hope that, as the prospect of miliary solutions becomes more obviously remote, the insurgent leadership will accept the compelling logic of negotiations. In the meantime, continued military assistance and economic aid to ease the burden of warfare for the people of Cambodia-is an unavoidable and urgent necessity. 

In Laos, an effective ceasefire has been maintained for well over a year, and the process of political accommodation has progressed to the point that a coalition government has been formed and is functioning. The country is thus in a transition from a period of prolonged warfare to one of peace and reconstruction. 

The assistance we are seeking for Laos will help it to carry out that transition 

SECURITY AND DEVELOPMENT ASSISTANCE 

We are also requesting security and development assistance funds for four other countries in East Asia-Korea, Indonesia, the Philippines and Thailand. 

These nations have legitimate self-defense needs which continue to require a measure of outside assistance. Such assistance, by increasing the sense of confidence and security of these nations, increases their readiness to deal openly and cooperatively with their neighbors and to negotiate with their adversaries. 

The maintenance of a strong militarily capable Republic of Korea, for example, is essential to the avoidance of hostilities and, indeed, contributes significantly to the process of accommodation on the Korean peninsula. For the nations of 

Southeast Asia, military assistance is an important element in their efforts to achieve self-sufficiency in their defense, in line with the Nixon Doctrine concept of burden sharing, and reinforces the encouraging trend toward cooperation and stability in the region. Our programs of military assistance thus do not contradict our espousal of détente and reduced tensions, but in fact contribute to the hopeful evolution from an era of confrontation to one of cooperation in East Asia. 

Similarly, each of these countries has made major and sustained efforts to overcome the obstacles to progress posed by underdevelopment. The Republic of Korea has developed a strong industrial base, and has emerged as an impor tant trading nation. Indonesia has continued a steady recovery from its severe economic problems of the mid-60's, and its mineral and energy resources have, of course, assumed new importance. The Philippines, despite natural disasters in 1972, has achieved steady economic growth and is attracting private foreign investments at a substantial rate. Thailand, too, has maintained an encouraging 

GNP growth rate in recent years, has accumulated ample foreign exchange reserves, and has developed a healthy production base. Nonetheless, in order to sustain the progress they have made, each of these countries stand in continuing need of outside assistance. They have shown an ability to use such assistance effectively, and we can be sure that additional aid will be sharply focused upon their most critical developmental needs. 

CONCLUSIONS 

Mr. Chairman, Members of the Committee: We do not envision economic or security assistance to East Asia as a burden to be borne perpetually by the 4

251 INI American people. The economies of many of the development countries of the region have performed impressively in recent years; we wish to sustain that progress and thereby hasten the day our aid will no longer be necessary. U.S. economic assistance to the Republic of China has already been terminated, as I am sure you are aware, and other programs have been reduced as the need has diminished. Similarly, it is our expectation and the long-term policy of the U.S. that the levels of our security assistance will be gradually reduced, and that we will continue to move from grant MAP to FMS credit and ultimately to cash sales of military equipment as circumstances permit. 

Let me take note of one additional concern which you and many of your colleagues have expressed, and which we share; the indisputable fact that many of the governments to which the U.S. provides economic and security assistance pursue internal policies in conflict with American democratic values. Our assistance programs do not constitute an endorsement of such policies, nor even of the governments which pursue them. Our aid is designed to promote the economic well being of the people of recipient nations, and, in the larger sense, to promote a secure, stable and relatively prosperous environment in which their interestsand the cause of peace-can be advanced. As the President stated in his June 5 address at Annapolis, our foreign policy must reflect our ideals and purposes. 

We continue to adhere firmly to certain humane principles, not only in appropriate international forums, but also in our private exchanges with other governments-where this can be effective. We believe we can achieve more results through diplomatic action than through hundreds of eloquent speeches. 

Mr. Chairman, Members of the Committee: I spoke earlier of the major objectives of American policy in Asia as being two-fold: on the one hand a reduction of tensions among the great powers whose interests interact in the region, and on the other situation of stability and evolutionary change among the smaller nations in which the largest responsibility for development and defense is assumed by those nations themselves rather than the U.S. These two goals are complementary and mutually reinforcing. Reduced tension among the major powers helps to establish an atmosphere of stability and confidence which encourages the smaller nations to devote their attention, their talents and their resources to the tasks of peaceful development. In turn, confidence, security, and relative prosperity among the smaller nations reduce the likelihood that local tensions and conflicts may arise which would engage the major powers, undermine the nascent understanding which has emerged among those powers, and which could thereby threaten the peace of Asia and the world. It is therefore important-for our own interests in this age of interdependence and in the interests of the Asian peoples-that we remain steadfast in our determination to help these nations help themselves. 

I would like to urge, in closing, that these programs be given early-and I hope favorable consideration and action. If this is possible, these countries will be much better able to plan ahead and to make the best and most effective use of our assistance.

I appreciate being able to discuss these matters with you, and I will be pleased to answer your questions. 

Mr. ZABLOCKI. Thank you, Mr. Secretary. 

If you will proceed, Mr. Nooter.

STATEMENT OF HON. ROBERT H. NOOTER, ASSISTANT ADMINIS- TRATOR FOR SUPPORTING ASSISTANCE, AGENCY FOR INTER- NATIONAL DEVELOPMENT 

Mr. NOOTER. Mr. Chairman and members of the committee, it is a privilege to appear before you this morning to present the program of economic assistance for South Vietnam, Cambodia, and Laos. 

In the interest of time, I will just read portions of my statement and summarize other parts supplementing what Mr. Ingersoll has already said.

Mr. ZABLOCKI. Very well. Your entire statement will be made part of the record.

Mr. NOOTER. 

The South Vietnamese economy is beginning to adjust to the economic impact caused by the withdrawal of U.S. military forces. The response to that withdrawal has been very excellent over the last several years. Domestic tax collections during the first 4 months of this year, for one example, were almost 25 percent over last year in real terms, which in turn followed a 50-percent increase in tax collections in 1973 compared to 1972. Exports have increased 100 percent in those comparable periods. The refugees in camps, who numbered 489,000 on July 1, 1973, have now been reduced to 85,000, the lowest number in Vietnam since 1971. However, much remains to be done, and an adequate level of U.S. assistance is necessary for the task to be accomplished successfully.

The cutbacks in aid levels over the last several years and the sharp increase in world commodity prices have put a continuing downward squeeze on Vietnam imports during the past 5 years. In real terms, imports in fiscal year 1974 are only 55 percent of imports during the peak year of 1969 and are about the same now on a per capita basis as they were in 1964 and 1965.

I would particularly like to address your attention to the attached charts which show what it is that is putting Vietnam in the economic squeeze which Mr. Ingersoll described and which is the background for the press reports that you see about the economic difficulties out there. In real terms after discounting for the inflation in import prices, they have been contracting their imports at a fairly severe rate over the last 4 or 5 years.

This sharp drop in imports has led to severe strains on the Vietnamese economy, producing growing unemployment and severe economic hardships on substantial portions of the population. The urban population and government employees have been particularly hard hit, with growing cases of malnutrition and misery on the part of those unable to find jobs. Statistics are not precise, but unemployment appears to be in the range of 800,000 to 1 million persons.

The Vietnamese are a resourceful and hardy people, and they are adjusting to these reductions with great fortitude. However, there is a limit to endurance, and they are approaching that point now. Further reductions would impose intolerable burdens on a people who have already suffered enough.

PURPOSES OF U.S. PROGRAM IN SOUTH VIETNAM 

Our program proposes to do three principal things: (1) To supply the humanitarian needs of the population through a series of programs in child care, health care, and refugee aid; (2) to meet the ongoing needs of the economy by the importation of fertilizer, pesticides, industrial raw materials, and petroleum products to maintain current Vietnamese production at about present levels; and (3) to undertake a greatly expanded program of capital investment projects so that the Vietnamese economy can begin to grow at a more rapid rate and hence to achieve economic self-sufficiency in the shortest possible time. 

While the numbers seem large, this is nevertheless a relatively austere program. It will only maintain general imports at the current

level, which is already greatly reduced as mentioned previously. Nevertheless, it will provide the possibility for Vietnam to begin to expand production, to create jobs in order to relieve the growing unemployment, and to increase its capacity to feed and supply its own people without having to rely forever on foreign assistance.

We are in the process of making some long-range projections of economic requirements in the coming years. While these projections have not been fully completed, the general outline is now clear. The $750 million request this year should, in constant prices, be the peak request which we will present to the Congress. If the Congress grants this request, U.S. economic aid to Vietnam will decline steadily over the next 5 years, beyond which any further economic aid would be at normal levels. This process cannot begin, however, unless we can make a sizable infusion during fiscal year 1975. The sooner we begin, the sooner the Vietnamese economy will be restored to normalcy.

HUMANITARIAN PROGRAMS IN VIETNAM 

I would like to say a word about the humanitarian programs. The $135 million request is needed not only to resettle refugees located in refugee camps, as we have done in prior years, but also to begin a program to resettle those refugees who fled or migrated to the cities during the war years and who now find they cannot make a living there any longer.

We have also greatly expanded and accelerated our assistance to children under a new program to improve nutrition, living conditions in orphanages, and to provide more day care centers. We have increased support for out-of-country adoptions of war orphans. In all of these new programs for children, we are relying very heavily on the services of American voluntary agencies. I have attached a short paper on our child welfare program, identified as attachment I. 

Members of Congress have frequently expressed their support for the humanitarian element in this program, which we appreciate. However, it does not make any sense to be generous in our support for refugees and war orphans while cutting back on general economic support which provides the livelihood and means of support for the general population. The reports of misery and hardships which are coming out of Vietnam recently are not related to refugees which are being fed 'under U.S. support programs; rather, they are average Vietnamese who have lost their jobs because of the general economic hardship being imposed on the country. Thus, in the broadest sense, virtually the entire economic program can be thought of as humanitarian in nature. 

"COMMERCIAL IMPORT PROGRAM": TERM ELIMINATED 

We have eliminated the term "commercial import program" this year due to the consistent misunderstanding that the term has engendered in the past. In spite of our frequent explanations to the contrary, the general public has tended to identify the CIP with the importation of Hondas or consumer goods, which it never was. Therefore, this year we have identified the imports which we plan to finance by the purposes for which they are being used.

Thus, fertilizer, pesticides, and other imports required for the production of food has been identified as "Food and nutrition," as would be the case in other aid-recipient countries. Industrial raw materials such as yarns and fibers, chemical products, iron and steel, and wood pulp are being requested under the category called industrial production, and those inputs needed to provide the inputs to operate Vietnam's transportation system have been so labeled. The control system developed under the CIP in past years, including close U.S. review and auditing, will, however, be retained in order to assure that goods are ordered and used for their intended purposes. 

Before I leave Vietnam, I would like to call attention to the success of the land reform program there which has really been a major success. I have attached a short paper on this which may interest the committee, identified as attachment II. 

THE LAOS PROGRAM 

To go on now to Laos, the formation of a Provisional Government of National Union (PGNU) this past April represents a bona fide political resolution of Laos internal differences. I will not read those; they are in the statement. 

Ön Cambodia, I would like to say that our humanitarian assistance has increased from a level of $1.2 million in fiscal year 1973 to $13.4 million in this fiscal year and an estimated $20 million in fiscal year 1975. Almost all of this aid is being administered through voluntary agencies.

We also have a short statement, giving a description of the $9.4 million regional program and $18.7 million in support costs. 

In closing, I would like to comment on the impressions I have. Never have I seen the present South Vietnamese Government look stronger or more competent and more able to deal with the problems it is facing than now. We are closer to achieving a self-sufficient Vietnam than most Americans realize. The cost to continue this effort is considerable, but it is no longer an unbearable burden. We urge your continued support. 

Thank you. 

[Mr. Nooter's prepared statement follows:] STATEMENT OF HON. ROBERT H. NOOTER, ASSISTANT ADMINISTRATOR FOR SUPPORTING ASSISTANCE, AGENCY FOR INTERNATIONAL. DEVELOPMENT 

Mr. Chairman and members of the committee, it is a privilege to appear before you this morning to present the program of economic assistance for South Vietnam, Cambodia, and Laos. 

There has been continued progress toward peace in Indochina during the past year, even though that progress has been somewhat uneven and more gradual than we would have liked. Nevertheless, a political solution has now been achieved in Laos with the formation of a coalition government and the complete cessation of hostilities. In South Vietnam, a political solution has remained elusive, but the level of fighting has declined so that military casualties have been about one-third of the 1965-1972 period. The South Vietnamese Government has demonstrated that it can cope with both its military and civilian problems so long as a reasonable amount of U.S. assistance is available. In 

Cambodia, fighting remains at a high level, and any serious discussions leading to a political settlement must await a clarification of the military situation. 

The aid which we are requesting today is one of the elements needed to continue this gradual but steady momentum toward peaceful solutions in Indochina.

7 An adequate level of economic assistance is an absolutely essential ingredient in order to preserve the degree of stability and peace which has been achieved, and to provide the humanitarian support desperately needed by the people of Indochina after many years of war. 

Progress toward rehabilitation and reconstruction has been slower than we expected, for several reasons. First, the level of military activity in South Vietnam and Cambodia has been somewhat higher than anticipated. This in turn has slowed down the economic support which we had expected would be forthcoming from other donors, although some, such as Japan and France, have increased their contributions. Also, the level of U.S. economic assistance approved by the Congress for FY 1974 was not adequate to undertake the capital development projects which are an essential part of moving these countries to a state of economic self-sufficiency, and the real value of this assistance was even further diminished by sharp increases in the cost of the goods which Indochina imports.

Nevertheless, much progress was made. The South Vietnamese economy is beginning to adjust to the economic impact caused by the withdrawal of U.S. military forces. Tax collections during the first four months of 1974 have increased in real terms by almost 25% over last year. Exports have jumped 100% in the same period. Refugees in camps, who numbered 489,000 on July 1, 1973, have now been reduced to 85,000, the lowest number since 1971. However, much remains to be done, and an adequate level of U.S. assistance is necessary for the task to be accomplished successfully.

The refugee population has exploded during the past year, and while earlier refugee groups were able to provide for themselves, this is becoming increasingly difficult for refugees now. We plan to use $20 million for humanitarian assistance.

REGIONAL DEVELOPMENT 

We are requesting $9.4 million in Indochina Postwar Reconstruction Funds for a variety of regional projects particularly focused on the Indochina countries, in addition to $5.8 million in other A.I.D. funds for regional development projects broader than Indochina.

The Indochina funds will be provided as a mixture of loans and grants. The largest of the grants, $2.2 million, is for the Mekong Basin Development Planning Project for a variety of activities including delta water systems and soils

management, fisheries, navigations aids and dredging. The proposed loan, $4.5 million, is to increase the existing power generation at the hydro-electric plant at Drayling on a Mekong tributary in Vietnam.

The program which we are presenting today is essential to maintain the progress toward peace in Indochina. The task has been a long and arduous one, but we are closer to achieving our goals than ever before. The costs to continue the effort in Indochina is considerable, but it is no longer an unbearable burden. 

Sharp reductions now would guarantee the loss of the considerable effort and investment we have made in the past. We urge your continued support.

Orphanage Support and Improvement: Food and clothing allowances, health care, equipment, improvement of facilities and staff training. ($1,736,000)

On the other hand, the children of an unemployed adult can suffer just as much as the children in an orphanage with inadequate resources. 

ATTACHMENT II-LAND REFORM IN SOUTH VIETNAM 

South Vietnam recently marked the 4th anniversary of the signing of its revolutionary Land-to-the-Tiller Law of March 26, 1970, which set off one of the major non-communist land reform programs of the 20th century. 

The land reform was begun under the most difficult conditions imaginable. 

Widespread fighting was continuing on a major scale, and the administrative structure was creaky, so far as it existed at all. 

Further, this was not the reform of relatively few, very large estates. The tenancy rate on Vietnam's rice-land was among the highest in the world, roughly 60 percent, but on many middle to small sized holdings.

If the catalog of problems was endless, the land reform was pressed and the goal of 2,200,000 acres (1,000,000 hectares), which had seemed visionary, was in fact reached three years later in March 1973. By comparison, the often and rightly lauded land reform on Formosa distributed one-quarter of the acreage under conditions of peace and a full three years were taken simply for planning. 

When the goal was reached last year, tenancy was virtually eliminated in South Vietnam and ownership of half of the country's rice land had changed hands. The program has continued over the past year and title to another 330,000 acres has changed hands. To date, some 750,000 farm families, composed of almost 

5,000,000 members, have become property owners. 

Apart from the political reasons for land reform and considerations of equity, it has brought economic benefits to Vietnam's countryside. Tenants who once paid 25 to 35 percent of the crop to their landlords now have this to invest in better farming, seeds, fertilizer, improved irrigation, and there is much evidence that they have been doing so. 

South Vietnam's most significant social reform has received scant public attention. In fact, recent News stories referred to landlords reclaiming land previously granted. These stories were carefully checked and found to be largely erroneous.

ATTACHMENT III-EMERGENCY RELIEF AND RESETTLEMENT NEEDS IN CAMBODIA 

Cambodia's refugee problems accelerated rapidly in FY 1974 as the fighting moved closer to the populated areas around Phnom Penh and the province capitals. Registered refugees now total 885,039 compared to 662,000 at the beginning of the fiscal year. 

A number of emergency relief programs begun in FY 1973 were expanded at a rapid rate as Cambodia's refugee needs escalated. A.I.D. does not directly conduct emergency relief programs in Cambodia, but utilizes the services of a number of U.S. and International Voluntary Agencies as well as supporting Cambodian efforts to provide relief assistance. 

We have: 

1. Increased A.I.D. funding of the refugee programs from $1,175,000 in FY 

1973, to about $14 million this fiscal year. 

2. Provide ten Packaged Disaster Hospitals for use in the areas with the greatest numbers of refugees. 

3. Provided grants to the Catholic Relief Services (CRS), the World Vision 

Relief Organization (WVRO) and the Indochina Operations Group (IOG) for the establishment and operation of four of the ten hospitals. 

4. Provided additional grants to CRS, WVRO, CARE, and the IOG to enable them to supply emergency food, shelter and in-camp medical care to refugees and to begin a refugee resettlement program. 

5. In addition, A.I.D. has begun this year to support the operations of the new 

Resettlement and Development Foundation which the Cambodian Government has established to manage refugee resettlement. The largest part of our FY 1974 refuge/humanitarian aid, about $8 million, is to assist the Cambodians to resettle refugees in situations where they can grow more of their own food and can be reasonably self-supporting.

The voluntary agencies have done an outstanding job is responding to these needs on short notice in an extremely difficult and frequently dangerous situation. 

For FY 1975, these refugee/humanitarian assistance programs will continue to expand. About half of our $20 million request is needed for the voluntary agency programs, to provide food, medical attention, housing and other emergency relief assistance. The other half is needed for the Cambodian's own resettlement programs primarily around Phnom Penh, to clear and prepare land, help refugees construct simple houses, and prepare land, and provide the tools, seeds and some animals these people will need to lead more productive and self-reliant lives.

PROSPECTS FOR OIL IN VIETNAM

To what extent is the oil expected to be a factor in self-sufficiency for South Vietnam?

Mr. INGERSOLL. Well, it is practically impossible to discuss what oil may be found any place where exploration takes place, but the geology of the area would indicate that oil may be found, it is expected that drilling will take place or at least begin before the end of this year, so that in a relatively short time we will know at least whether finds are possible, and then as development drilling goes on we will begin to know the scope of the find. HOPE FOR NEGOTIATIONS 

Mr. ZABLOCKI. Mr. Secretary, on page 9 of your statement you state that, in Cambodia, it is our hope that as prospects for a military victory dim, the Khmer Communists will accept the idea of negotiations. Is it possible to build

1:|:ཀུན :|: a foreign policy on hopes? What hard evidence do you have that the other side will be willing to negotiate in the next few months?

Would you expect them to begin negotiations before the next United Nations session in which a move will be made to oust the Lon Nol government and seat a regime headed by Sihanouk? 

Would you expect them to begin to negotiate before another dry season?

Is it not true that the earliest we can reasonably expect some move toward negotiations by the other side would be at the end of the next dry season-about one year from now-and only if the Khmer Communists had failed to win significant new military victories?

Mr. INGERSOLL. It is our policy to provide material and diplomatic support to help the Khmer Republic defend itself and by this demonstration of strength move its opponents to negotiate an end to the war. It is our hope that the Khmer 

Communists will realize sooner rather than later the impossibility of imposing their will on the Khmer Republic through a military victory. 

Any policy contemplating the future rests in part on hope. However, it is our considered judgment that unless we furnish the Khmer Republic the weapons and supplies to defend itself, a minority hostile to compromise in Cambodia and to stability in Indochina will impose its will on the majority of Cambodians now under the control of the Khmer Republic. There is now clear evidence that the GKR is willing to negotiate and able to defend itself. This combination offers the best hope that a reasonable compromise solution helpful to stability in Cambodia and in Indochina can be found. However, U.S. material and diplomatic support are essential to obtaining these policy objectives. As you note, it is difficult to predict in any precise way when the Khmer Communists will move to the negotiating table. Our support of the GKR's army and its economy and our strong endorsement of its peace proposals are designed to encourage this development as soon as possible.

ICCS FINANCING 

Mr. ZABLOCKL. I am concerned about the financing of the International Commission for Control and Supervision in Viet-Nam. 

As you know, the North Vietnamese and the Viet Cong both have refused to pay their shares of the cost of the ICCS. 

What representations have we made to the Communists to pay up on the ICCS? 

I have heard a report that members of the ICCS have been told by Le Duc 

Tho of North Viet-Nam that he has had assurances from the American Secretary of State that the United States will shoulder the burden of the ICCS costs, since the Communists are refusing to.

Is that report true? Should we pick up the tab for the ICCS and thus let the 

Communists off the hook so easily?

Mr. INGERSOLL. The two Communist parties to the Paris Agreements have made some financial contributions to the International Commission of Control and Supervision (ICCS) in Viet-Nam, but their payments have been well below their fair share of the costs of the Commission. We have made strong representations to North Viet-Nam, directly and through third parties, on this issue of delinquent contributions. While such representations have had little or no effect to date, we will continue every effort to induce the Communist parties to make their prescribed contributions to the ICCS.

We too have heard reports that the North Vietnamese are alleging that the United States has assured them it would shoulder the burden of ICCS costs because of the failure of the Communists to make their full payments. We have given the North Vietnamese no such assurances that they are to be "let off the hook." However, in the light of the deficiency of the Communist contributions, we have in fact had to contribute more than our share of ICCS expenses in order to keep the Commission in business. 

It is clear that the Communist parties, through their lack of financial support, are seeking to bring about a reduced role or even a termination of the ICCS. 

The United States, on the other hand, believes it essential that the ICCS be kept operational. While the performance of the ICCS has never matched its potential, the Commission remains an essential part of the peace structure established by the Paris Accords. The presence in South Viet-Nam of several hundred foreign personnel charged with overseeing the military situation does, we believe, help deter a resumption of all-out warfare. If the ICCS is to survive, the United States must be prepared to assure an adequate level of funding for the essential costs of the Commission.

LONG-RANGE ECONOMIC PROSPECTS IN SOUTH VIETNAM 

Mr. FRELINGHUYSEN. I would like to ask about a statement that 

Ambassador Ingersoll made, with respect to the prospects of South Vietnam. On page 8 you say, "It has excellent long-range prospects for economic self-sufficiency." You also said that you did not envisage aid to East Asia as a burden that should be borne perpetually. 

I think one of the problems is that many people think of aid as a bottomless pit, and the long-range prospect worries me. I would assume that if there could be peace, that the prospect would be quite short range for improvement. As I understood Ambassador Martin's explanation, he feels that we need to give a relatively large infusion of assistance now, somewhat less next year, and perhaps substantially less the third year.

I would suppose this is what we would hope to see in the 5-year projection that you are preparing, that is, a reasonably early scaling down of aid. Would you care to comment on what you meant by long-range prospects?

Mr. INGERSOLL. Well, I think the prospects so much depend upon the military situation, and when I mention long range we are trying to be realistic that we do not know when the military confrontation will be reduced. We are estimating that the level of activity may continue at the present level for 2 to 3 years.

We believe that somewhere in that time frame the North may realize, as they did prior to the Paris peace agreements, that they cannot achieve their objectives by military means. They, as you recall, demanded that the Thieu government be replaced for many years, and finally after the 1972 invasion was not successful they concluded that they should agree to a peace, or an agreement anyway without the removal of Thieu. We think that as they are confronted by successful South Vietnamese forces in the next 3 or 4 years they will again find that they cannot achieve their military objectives and then will seek a political accommodation.

This is why I say long range, and it is difficult to project when they might make that decision. We believe it is ultimately going to be made.

As far as economic aid, it would not take too long to have this country become self-sufficient if there were no hostilities and if there were not insecure areas where the people could be self-sufficient in producing their own food, and this is why I use that term “long range," trying to be realistic and not overly optimistic.

We give a very high priority to food aid for this area, which has been torn by war and contains a high proportion of refugees. Vietnam and Cambodia are among those countries most seriously affected by the energy crisis and are facing severe balance of payments problems. 

Our presentation book also shows about $5 million in food aid specifically earmarked for the Sahel for FY 1975. This approximates the annual quantity programmed to the Sahel in non-drought years. The presentation also contains a $35 million reserve for emergencies and disasters. In October we should have a much better idea of the food aid requirements for the Sahel. In any case, we anticipate that substantial emergency shipments will be required in FY 1975. The U.S. gives such assistance a high priority and we fully intend to do our fair share.

The planning levels shown in our Congressional Presentation books were developed by A.I.D. and the State Department. 

The Inter-Agency Staff Committee (ISC) chaired by the Department of Agriculture normally determined PL 480 program levels. Other agencies represented include State, A.I.D., Treasury, Commerce and OMB. In addition PL 480 program priorities for FY 1974 and FY 1975 are being reviewed by a policy level group chaired by OMB. In addition to ISC members, representatives of the Council of Economic Advisors, the Cost of Living Council and the NSC have been included in this group.

[The information requested follows:] VIETNAM (COMMODITY IMPORT PROGRAM) RECORD AUDITS The AID office of the Auditor General, Area Auditor General/East Asia 

(AAG) performs systematic audits in Vietnam on selected groupings of commodities imported under the CIP. This function is performed with the mandate of protecting the integrity of the program. The objectives are to determine whether commodities are procured according to agency regulations and procurement documents, received in Vietnam and cleared through customs in the quantities invoiced, and properly received and used or sold by the importers. 

Goods not used by end-users or sold by importing wholesalers or retailers within one year are subject to corrective actions. 

A few examples of audit findings follow: 

1. In July 1973, the AAG reported finding 45 gasoline engines that had been stocked for more than one year. This finding was brought to the attention of the GVN and the importer and the engines were sold and put to their intended use. 

2. In August 1972, the AAG discovered that 10 tractors valued at $71,000 had been purchased but had not been put to use. The tractors were moved to the provinces and were sold for use by farmers whose bonafides had been verified by the Ministry of Economy. 

3. An AAG report on chemicals made in June 1973 recommended a claim for reimbursement for excessive handling losses in a shipment of sodium trypolyphosphate. The same report noted the presence of 180 metric tons of calcium carbide costing $21,000 that had been stored for over one year. The Mission issued a bill for collection and received the full recommended amount of $2,500 for the handling losses and took steps which resulted in the sale and proper use of the calcium carbide. 

4. An AAG report of July 1973 covered iron and steel transactions costing $17 million. Sales by importers/dealers were traced to 40 end-users and retailers in the Saigon/Cholon area and Gia Dinh Province. One importer/dealer had not disposed of steel pipe valued at some $69,000 and which had remained in his inventory for more than one year. This individual was given 60 days to dispose of his stock and he did so within the required time. 

5. During an April 1974 audit performed on yarns and fishnets the AAG noticed seeming variances in the ocean freight rates of eighteen shipments costing $46.000 of yarns imported between December 1972 and April 1973. The recommended AID/W follow-up, however, revealed that the rate were not at variance with applicable tariffs. 

6. Bills of collection totalling $45,000 have been issued in response to the 

September 1973 AAG report that uncovered the improper use of 119 room air conditioners, intended for industrial uses. 

The preceding cases are representative of AID's regular on-going surveillance activity and although fairly substantial money is involved in each, we would 11 11

not classify them as "excesses" given the size of the overall program and the fact that each discrepancy is pursued until satisfactorily resolved. 

Although you have specifically directed your question to audits and actions taken on recommendations contained therein, we would like to call your attention briefly to continuing operational efforts to avoid excesses in the Vietnam CIP. We have regular data print-outs on licenses issued for all AID-financed commodities. Trends are constantly observed by Mission and AID/W staff. One result of such vigilance earlier this year revealed licensing of yarns and fibers at a rate far in excess of last year. This fact was called to the attention of the GVN and to the yarn importers. Realizing that they were risking the accumulation of stocks which they might find slow-moving when received, the importers began reducing or cancelling import licenses. As a net result sufficient licenses have been cancelled to reduce the total licensing of yarns and fibers by $4 million dollars this fiscal year. This is an example of efforts to keep imports in pace with requirements.

POLITICAL PRISONERS AND THE FOREIGN ASSISTANCE ACT 

Mr. FRASER. Thank you, Mr. Chairman.

My question I guess could be directed to any of our witnesses. 

Section 32 of the Foreign Assistance Act deals with the problem of political prisoners. Mr. Secretary, are you familiar with that provision? 

Mr. INGERSOLL. Yes, sir. 

Mr. FRASER. What do you understand the thrust of it to be? 

Mr. INGERSOLL. That the President should consider withdrawing aid from those countries who have proven to have political prisoners. 

That is essentially the gist of the thing. 

Mr. FRASER. Can you tell me to what extent there has been an implementation of that provision in the law? 

Mr. INGERSOLL. I know of none. 

Mr. FRASER. You know of none?

Mr. INGERSOLL. No. 

Mr. FRASER. In other words, that provision has had no consequence in the executive branch at least in your area?

Mr. INGERSOLL. Well, I think it is a matter of definition of political prisoners, sir. 

Mr. FRASER. Well, let's not get to that yet.

Let me read section 32 of the Foreign Assistance Act. 

It is the sense of Congress that the President should deny any economic or miiltary assistance to the government of any foreign country which practices the internment or imprisonment of that country's citizens for political purposes. 

IMPACT OF "POLITICAL PRISONERS' "" SECTION 

What you are saying is that that section, however you may interpret it, has not had any impact on our policies in Asia?

e Mr. INGERSOLL.

As far as I know it has not, although it has been reviewed continually.

Mr. Nooter, do you have any comment?

Mr. NOOTER. No. 

Mr. INGERSOLL. Mr. Fraser, as I pointed out we have been reviewing this question. It does come down to the matter of definition, and how you come out on the definition. One could possibly say that there is no country in the world that does not have political prisoners, depending on who makes the definition. I think even some people say in this country we have political prisoners and it certainly is true in the differing regimes around the world, and East Asia, or Asia is no exception. 

So we are continuing our evaluation of this section and have not yet determined how we should implement it.

DEPARTMENT MEMOS ON SECTION?

EXECUTIVE BRANCH ACTION ON SECTION 32 

Following the passage of the Foreign Assistance Act of 1973 on December 17 and its signature by the President on January 2, 1974, the Department and AID considered what steps should be taken to respond to that provision. A circular telegram was sent to all posts in aid-recipient countries informing them of the content of Section 32 and asking their views as to the applicability of that provision to their countries. This cable, dated April 4 was sent to a total of 68 posts. 

The text of that message follows: 

"1. Summary.

This message provides information on a new provision of the 

Foreign Assistance Act (FAA) of 1973 and requests affected Missions to cable appropriate response prior to April 22. 

"2. Section 32 of the FAA of 1973 is as follows: 'It is the sense of Congress that the President should deny any economic or military assistance to the government of any foreign country which practices the internment or imprisonment of that country's citizens for political purposes.' "3. Embassies are requested to provide assessment of how this legislation could affect the status of assistance programs in their countries. Specifically, we would appreciate assessments of the extent and nature, if any, of the internment or imprisonment of citizens for political purposes; whether through legislation and/or practice, there is a consistent pattern of reliably attested violation of the right to be free of arbitrary detention and certain other closely related rights (see para 5(b) below), and the position of the host governments on this matter. No representations to host governments should be made in developing this information. Previous reports may be referenced. If it appears to Embassy that condition at which Sec. 32 directed may exist, it is requested to suggest any opportunities for appropriate U.S. action or representation to improve the situation, including comments on appropriateness and probable effect of denying economic or military assistance on basis of Sec. 32. "4. For your background, other FAA provisions, showing related Congressional concern and intent are Section 102 (Statement of Policy) Sections, 201 (B), 211 (A), and 251 (B) dealing with the responsiveness of governments to the concerns of their people, rule of law and individual freedoms, Section 207 (A) calling for 'the encouragement of strong economic, political, and social institutions needed for a progressive democratic society', and Section 501 describing one objective of military assistance as 'creating an environment of security and stability in the developing friendly countries essential to their more rapid social, economic and political progress.' "5. A. 'Political prisoners' is not defined. An amendment to require cutting off assistance failed of adoption after debate in which difficulty of definition noted and from which it would appear that in order give effect of totality of Congressional purpose embodied in Act, Executive should proceed case by case on basis of all facts and with regard to all purposes of Act, giving full and due weight to interest in promoting respect for rule of law and human rights where eroded or violated by political imprisonments. "B. In effort to give effect to sense of Congress expressed in Section 32, we believe difficulty in defining 'political prisoner' can best be dealt with by reference to standard enjoying already established international approval and respect. Accordingly, in appraising degree to which particular situations may come within Section 32, Embassy should consider (A) whether persons have been arrested, detained or imprisoned arbitrarily in the sense of 

Article 9 or UN Declaration of Human Rights (Article 9 reads: 'No one shall be subject to arbitrary arrest, detention or exile.' For text of declaration, see 5 Whiteman Digest 237-242.) (B) whether by law or in practice such persons are deprived of (1) rights under Articles 10 and 11 of Universal 

Declaration Relating to Proper Charges and Trial and/or (2) rights under 

Articles 18, 19, 20 and 21, relating to such fundamental political freedoms as freedom of thought and conscience, or opinion and expression, or peaceful assembly and association and participation in self-government. While such tests might include persons arbitrarily imprisoned because of race or religion or some other factor rather than strict politics, this result appears reasonable and not inconsistent with Congressional purposes. Authority of universal 

Declaration of Human Rights as international standard is evidenced by its adoption by UN General Assembly in 1948 by overwhelming majority in furtherance UN's duty under Articles 55 and 56 of UN Charter to promote human rights and fundamental freedoms-a duty in the discharge of which

all members are pledged under Article 56 to cooperate. "(C) Finally, AID/ 

State believe Congress principally concerned about substantial and, continued violations of above standards occurring as matter of official policy or of gross negligence on part of government. "6. Since, in accordance Section 32, 'political prisoners' factor as above discussed will be evaluated in connection new of continued assistance programs, posts should review past reporting and present situation in light standards outlined above and provide such additional information, analysis and recommendation as may be helpful to ongoing evaluation. In any event, appropriate acknowledgement present telegram and cable report of any Embassy assessment would be appreciated by April 22, since Congressional hearings on FY 1973 assistance programs are scheduled to start in early May, and this subject may well be raised in hearings. "7. In providing any detailed analysis in light standards above outlined, posts may find following considerations relevant: (1) The legal/judicial processes which relate to the arrest, detention and trial of the country's citizens. (2) Whether the country's law prohibits arbitrary arrest and detention. (3) What remedies (defenses, opportunities to challenge in court, opportunities to secure redress) the law provides to a person who may be arbitrarily arrested or detained or denied fair and open trial with reasonable promptness. (4) Specific facts relevant to cases which have given rise to a political prisoner issue with attention to whether there is a consistent pattern or reliably attested violation of the right to be free of arbitrary arrest, detention or imprisonment. (5) As discussed above, any opportunities for appropriate U.S. action or representation to improve the situation, and comment on the appropriateness and probable effect of denying economic or military assistance because of the political prisoner issue. (6) Factors in the political and economic environment of the country which are relevant to the encouragement of the rule of law and the strengthening of freedom and opportunity for its citizens. "S. Although Foreign Military Sales Act credits do not under FMSA legally constitute 'military assistance', response from Athens also requested. "9. Defense concurs."

To date responses have been received from about sixty posts, describing in some detail conditions existing in those countries, and commenting on appropriate U.S. response. We are carefully reviewing these responses on a Department-wide basis, in close cooperation with AID, and on that basis are attempting to evaluate what additional steps we might take to ameliorate conditions in those countries giving most cause for concern. In the meantime, posts in aid-recipient countries in the East Asia and Pacific region have been instructed to inform host governments of the text of Section 32 and the Congressional sentiment which it reflects. These posts have been instructed to inform the Department when they have taken this action and to report the reaction of the host government. Consideration of similar steps is pending for other areas. 

With respect to South Korea, on April 23 Embassy Seoul responded to the April 4 telegram, referring to its considerable earlier reporting and observing that Washington agencies were in the best position to define whether or not there were "political prisoners" in South Korea within the context of Section 32. 

The Embassy referred especially to recent emergency measures prohibiting actions which are political in nature, e.g., demands for constitutional revision and student demonstrations, and to arrests, trials and convictions in this connection. It also referred to the domestic legal basis for such actions. The Department has authorized the Embassy to discuss Section 32 with the ROK 

Government and report its response. [Subsequently, the following letters were submitted to amplify the remarks of the witness in addition to the information supplied:] 

DEPARTMENT OF STATE, 

Washington, D.C., June 27, 1974.

Hon. THOMAS E. MORGAN, Chairman, Foreign Affairs Committee, House of Representatives, Washington, D.C. 

DEAR MR. CHAIRMAN: On June 13, in testifying before your Committee on the

President's Foreign Assistance Message, I replied to a number of questions

1 Fa ntis 

Ted s

Tatia Lati 2 ยุ di relating to Section 32 of the Foreign Assistance Act of 1973 and I said I would amplify my remarks. Several insertions have been made in the record of the 

June 13 hearings. Additionally, I would like in this letter to address some of the broader policy questions which are involved and would be grateful if this letter could be made available to other members of the Committee. 

I think it is important at the outset to set forth a few basic considerations which underlie our general foreign policy toward human rights questions. Firstly, we take seriously our obligation under the United Nations Charter to promote respect for and observance of human rights and fundamental freedoms for all. 

No matter where in the world violations of human rights occur, they trouble and concern us and we make our best efforts to ascertain the facts and promote respect for human rights and fundamental freedoms. At the same time, it must be recognized that the United Nations Charter does not prescribe how to fulfill that obligation in respect to particular violations by others. Thus there are usually complex questions of policy and tactics to be considered in deciding whether and how the United States can best seek to discharge its obligations in a particular case consistent with its commitment to other goals, including that of maintaining international peace and security. Such questions include the seriousness of the violation, the various options for United States action, and the consequences of inaction.

With particular reference to Section 32, the sanction of cutting off assistance does not seem to me necessarily to be the most effective or appropriate response to violations of human rights in other countries, whether or not the violation involves the holding of political prisoners. A cut-off is a one-time thing, the implementation of which removes the restraint its possible invocation may have induced. I believe the Congress recognized the difficulty of formulating such a general rule as well as the difficulty of defining who is a political prisoner by expressing the sense of the Congress in Section 32. It is thus open to the President, as it should be, to cut off aid, if in all respects this is the best course, or to cut down aid or particular elements of it, or to indicate that such options must be considered or, and most importantly, to move in any of a considerable number of other ways having as good or better prospect of actually promoting human rights in the particular situation. 

Following considerable discussion and study of Section 32, AID and the Department prepared and, on April 4, 1974, sent out an instruction to various posts including all those in countries receiving military or economic assistance. The text of this cable has now been incorporated in the transcript of the hearing. 

Replies have been received from about sixty posts. For the most part the replies have been helpfully informative, although in some cases amplification will be needed. We have followed this initial cable with a second cable requesting our 

Embassies in East Asian aid-recipient countries to transmit the text of Section 32 to the governments of those countries with our explanation of the seriousness with which we regard this section. We expect to receive reports of the reactions of those governments which may be helpful to us in our further review of problems presented. Consideration is also pending on a similar message to aidrecipient countries in other areas. 

Suppose a consistent pattern of human rights violations appears to emerge in a particular country? There are, as I have indicated above, a whole range of options which may be available in a given case ranging from quiet diplomacy to public condemnation, termination of assistance, and, in extremis, international sanctions. Very important are the United Nations Commission on Human Rights with the procedures established under it for consideration, fact finding, and recommendations in particular cases, and, in the American Republics, the Inter- American Human Rights Commission with roughly comparable features. Generally, where it has some promise of effectiveness, the preference is naturally for quiet diplomacy combined in varying ways with appropriate utilization of international fora for fact gathering and debate as well as cooperation with private organizations and groups active in the promotion of human rights and fundamental freedoms.

An important aspect, of course, is keeping the Congress informed of the facts concerning the observance or non-observance of human rights, and we will attempt to do so on an unclassified basis where this will not prejudice our objectives. In this regard. we have just supplied for the record of the June 13 hearing a statement on the state of human rights in Korea. It is our intention to keep the Committee advised as matters develop further, both generally with respect to Section 32 and specifically in regard to Korea.

I should also add that the Department is now considering several organizational proposals designed to improve its capability to discharge its human rights and humanitarian responsibilities, and keeps under continual review these issues and our policies to deal with them. 

I trust that this letter helps to clarify some of the matters relating to human rights and foreign policy brought up in the course of my recent testimony. If I can be of further assistance, please do not hesitate to call on me. 

Sincerely yours,

ROBERT S. INGERSOLL, 

Assistant Secretary for East Asian and Pacific Affairs.

Fraser plans to conduct on July 30 on human rights in Korea.

At this point, our experience under section 32 of the Foreign Assistance Act 1973 permits us to conclude that it would be wise, at least provisionally, to ensure that reporting and review features such as are growing up under that section are a continuing and permanent part of our fact finding and decision making processes with respect to all countries. To this end through further instruction we will meld the special section 32 requirements of aid recipients with the general human rights requirements affecting all countries.

We propose to use the facts collected and our evaluations of them to assure that human rights considerations are taken into account in the formulation of our foreign policy including our assistance programs. I am asking that early next year the geographic bureaus and others concerned report to me on significant human rights developments, by country and by important international bodies, with their recommendations for any desirable modifications of policy, new steps or new procedures. By then we will have received the second annual post reports and will have the benefit of another year's experience with the United Nations and Inter-American Human Rights Commissions. Such bureau reports should be an important indication of how we are doing at the international level in seeking to discharge our obligation to promote respect for and observance of human rights and fundamental freedoms.
