HUMAN RIGHTS IN KOREA 

For the past two years the trend in Korea has been toward an authoritarian mode of government. Institutional means of dissent have been rendered powerless and efforts to express opposition have been suppressed through a series of severe emergency decrees.

The Constitution was amended by referendum in 1972, concentrating all effective power in the office of the President and diminishing protection of human rights. The referendum was carried out under martial law and no debate of the proposed amendments was permitted.

Under the amended Constitution the President may be elected for an unlimited number of six year terms: election is made without debate by a body known as the National Conference for Unification which is itself popularly elected. The President is the Chairman of the Conference. One third of the legislative body, the National Assembly, is nominated by the President and elected by the National Conference for Unification.

The Constitution recites many of the human rights and fundamental freedoms found in the Universal Declaration of Human Rights and recognizes the existence of liberties and right of citizens not expressly enumerated in the Constitution. This makes it clear that Korea acknowledges the existence and impor tance of human rights. However, in amending its Constitution in 1972, Korea removed certain fundamental rights previously respected. For example, the new 

Constitution deletes paragraphs 5 and 6 of Article 10 of the old Constitution, which established the right to habeas corpus.

Moreover, Article 53 of the new Constitution vests in the President the power to take "necessary emergency measures" in time of "natural calamity or a grave financial or economic crisis, and in case the national security or the public safety and order is seriously threatened or anticipated to be threatened" (Article 

53 (1)). These emergency measures may be taken "in the whole range of the

State affairs, including internal affairs, foreign affairs, national defense, economic, financial and judicial affairs" (Article 53 (1)) and may include measures which temporarily suspend individual constitutional rights and measures affecting the rights and powers of the Executive and the Judiciary (Article 53 (2)).

Article 73 of the old Constitution granted the President similar but generally more restricted powers. For example. Article 73 (2) limited the President's power to issue ordinances having the effect of law by the requirement that this be done "only when it is necessary for the national security under the state of armed hostilities." The new Article 53 does not include this limitation. Rather, it defines the President's power to take emergency measures as being "in the whole range of the State affairs, including internal affairs, foreign affairs, national defense, economic, financial and judicial affairs." 

Finally, Articles 53 (4) prohibits judicial review of measures taken pursuant to paragraphs (1) and (2) of this Article. 

In early 1973 the press was placed under strict censorship with ROK CIA monitors in the editorial offices. The monitors have since been withdrawn but effective indirect controls remain. There are reports of government intimidation and police questioning and harassment. 

The opposition candidate in the 1971 Presidential election, Kim Tae Chung, was kidnapped from Tokyo in August 1973 and returned to Seoul by persons unknown. He was kept under house confinement for several weeks, his movements since have been subject to surveillance and he is now on trial for alleged violation of the election laws in 1971 and 1967. He has applied for a passport to come to the United States to accept a fellowship at Harvard but the government has not acted on his application. 

Several emergency measures have been issued this year: violations are tried under special courts martial rather than the regular courts. Presidential Emer gency Measure Number One proclaimed on January 8, 1974 under Article 53 of the Constitution makes it an offense punishable by imprisonment up to fifteen years to advocate amendment of the Constitution by petition. Members of the 

Christian community and student groups have been outspoken critics of the government. More than a score of persons have been convicted, a dozen of whom have received twelve to fifteen year sentences.

Emergency Measure No. 4 of April 3, 1974 requires punishment by death, life imprisonment, or not less than five years imprisonment for, inter alia: (a) Any student who engaged in any political activity (Articles 5 and 8); (b) Any person who defames the action of the Education Minister in (a) expelling a student or (b) dissolving an organization or abolishing a school to which violators of the measure may belong; (c) Any person who refuses to attend classes or examinations "without justification"; (d) Any person who communicates with a member of the National Federation of Democratic Youth and Students "or any related organization."

Emergency Measures No. 4 provides for arrest, detention, search or seizure without warrant. Fifty-four persons are presently on trial under this measure. 

From the above it is clear that the Government of the Republic of Korea acknowledges the existence and importance of human rights but has limited the exercise of important rights, citing the threat to national security it perceives from a hostile North Korea. The situation, that is both the security of the peninsula and the emergency measures taken by the Republic of Korea Government, is a matter of real concern to us. We have expressed this concern on appropriate occasions and will continue to encourage full restoration of human rights.

81 At the same time we intend to continue supporting efforts of the Republic of Korea Government to reduce tensions and contribute to a lasting peace on the peninsula.

RECONSTRUCTION AID TO SOUTH VIETNAM 

Mr. HARRINGTON. After listening to Congressman Fraser, I am not sure who I should address some of these questions to, but first let me give you some background. 

Last year by a vote of 12 to 12, if my memory is correct, I guess I was looked on-as unusual for me as it was--as the deciding vote on whether to keep the level of economic aid to South Vietnam where it was, or to accept an effort made by Congressman Bingham to reduce it. I argued, at that point, that it seemed difficult for those of the philosophic spectrum that had been vocal about ending our part in the war, to take as a target the only potential, if perhaps symbolic effort, that had been made by the U.S. Government to relieve some of the misery that was either unintentionally or intentionally created as a result of the war.

My first question is really broadly put-and I have a number of narrower questions in other areas. Why should I continue to maintain that posture of support for economic aid? I read language in the prepared statement which is almost reminiscent of a gap from 1948 to 

1973 in thinking-I am quoting on page 6. I won't read it all.

This may be true if the kind of peace desired is that of abject surrender to Communist aggression, or the peace which would follow a bloody Communist

military victory. But this is not the kind of peace for which we have invested so much all these years, nor the kind of peace which would be in our interest or in the interest of the South Vietnamese people. In fact it has not been the 

South Vietnamese Government which has been blocking implementation of the Paris agreement and further progress toward peace, but rather the North Vietnamese.

NORTH AND SOUTH VIETNAM 

Now, if there is any kind of redeeming quality distinguishing between the North and South Vietnamese, as far as the respective governments are concerned, it is hard to see it. It is this kind of statement that makes it hard for me to really believe in at least the broad enunciation of the doctrine of pluralism, which I think is perhaps unique and perhaps the only contribution of the administration in the area of foreign affairs, and one of the more valued as far as I am concerned. 

If I could see the differences between the two governments, I suppose I could adjust myself to the schizophrenia which runs all through the foreign policy of this administration and much of the generation that has characterized it. But for the life of me, I don't see what you understand as a reason to worry at all about what happens to the South Vietnamese Government as such. What reason would you want to continue to give us this kind of rationale of an intellectual underpinning for the continuation of aid?

What is so different about the approaches of these Governments that you want, as a matter of philosophy, to continue this kind of aid? 

Why should I continue to support it with the knowledge that, at best, a small portion of it may get to the people, in a naive expectation that we can help them in some fashion, and when I know that an enormous amount of this aid, whether it be in the "food for peace" program or in some other form, ends up in a quasi-military usage? 

HUMANITARIANISM OF U.S. AID TO VIETNAM 

Mr. NOOTER. Mr. Harrington, we not surprisingly agreed with the position you took last year for precisely the reasons you stated at that time; that is, and as I reaffirmed this year in my statement, while we have a section of this economic assistance request which we label humanitarian, nevertheless virtually the entire economic assistance request is in one way or another humanitarian in the sense that it does go to people in need and helps to support them. 

Now in the past, some of the counterpart funds generated from the commercial import program, some 30 percent or so, was attributed to the military budget, and it has been claimed, therefore, that this was indirect assistance for military purposes. That will not be true in fiscal year 1975. All of the fiscal year 1975 money, even counterpart funds, will be attributed to civilian purposes, to the civilian part of the economy. A cutback in the economic side of the bill has direct impact on necessary humanitarian concerns. Now, that does not answer your broader question. 

Mr. HARRINGTON. It certainly does not, no.

Mr. NOOTER. It does not answer the political questions and the military questions. I will still say that your statement last year and my statement, and in fact a statement in the Kennedy committee report, which we don't agree with in all other respects, all make the same

point; that is, that economic aid beyond the purely narrow humanitarian aid is necessary in order to provide the Vietnamese people with a way to make their living until this transition period can be seen. through.

CHARACTER OF THE THIEU GOVERNMENT

NEED FOR STABILITY IN ASIA

ECONOMIC AID Mr. HARRINGTON. The World Bank has estimated that by 1980 South Viet- 

Nam will still require $770 million in economic assistance each year. Ambassador 

Graham Martin, on the other hand, has stated that South Viet-Nam will need a large infusion of economic aid only over the next two years. Do you believe that the requirement of economic assistance will end in two years, or do you agree with the World Bank that the United States can be expected to provide hundreds of millions of dollars annually for the foreseeable future?

IT 5 Mr. INGERSOLL. We do not agree with the World Bank estimate that South 

Viet-Nam will require hundreds of millions of dollars annually in economic assistance from the United States Government for the foreseeable future. If for the next two years we can provide economic assistance for the Republic of Viet- Nam at the levels we have requested for FY 1975, we believe that a substantial reduction in aid can take place over the remaining three years of a five-year program to a level which is very small in relation to what we are asking now. The aid projections that we will submit to the Congress will reflect that expectation. We envisage a changing focus on our aid from war-related support to programs which will foster the economic development needed by the Vietnamese to move toward self-sufficiency. I would emphasize, as has Ambassador Martin, the necessity of high levels of aid in the initial two years of this program in order to provide the momentum to the South Vietnamese economy which will permit it to progess as we reduce the level of our support in subsequent years. 

FOOD FOR PEACE 

Mr. HARRINGTON. In fiscal 1974, Congress showed a clear intent to cut economic aid to Indochina, reducing “postwar reconstruction aid" from the $632 million request to $450 million. But the Administration actually managed to increase economic aid-by increasing Food For Peace from $208 million to $507 million, for South Viet-Nam, and by obtaining an additional $99 million development loan.

Can you give us any assurance that the Administration will not this year again use Food For Peace funds to effectively increase the economic aid to Viet-Nam and Indochina over what is specifically approved by Congress for that purpose? 

Mr. INGERSOLL. Our Food For Peace programs for Viet-Nam are managed in close consultation with and the approval of appropriate Congressional Committees. The statement that the program for Viet-Nam increased in FY 1974 from $208 million to $507 million is not correct. The value of Title I agreements with 

Viet-Nam in FY 1974 amounts to $269 million. This compares to our original estimate of $176.4 million contained in the FY 1974 Congressional Presentation.

This increase in the dollar value of shipments is due to the sharp and unexpected rise in commodity prices and freight costs. In fact the commodity volume of shipments in FY 1974 will be smaller than originally planned. In FY 1975 we anticipate that the volume of Title I shipments to Viet-Nam will be about the same as this year. The FY 1975 program will of course be carried out in consultation with and approval of the Congress.

The Development Loan provided to Viet-Nam in FY 1974 was $50 million, not $99 million as stated. It too, was reviewed by the appropriate Congressional Committees.

GKR CONTROL Mr. HARRINGTON. What percentage of land does the Lon Nol government control?

Mr. INGERSOLL. The Khmer Republic controls about 15 percent of the total territory of Cambodia, all of the major urban centers and about 70 percent of the population. About 56 to 60 percent of Cambodia is in communist hands, either occupied by the North Vietnamese or under the Khmer communists. The remainder is either contested, deserted or uninhabitable. 

USE OF U.S. AIR FORCE C-130 AIRCRAFT 

Mr. HARRINGTON. Secretary Schlesinger has reported before this Committee that US Air Force C-130 aircraft are being flown from Thailand on resupply missions to besieged Cambodian villages and towns. Are these aircraft ever fired upon by the Khmer Rouge? What kind of precautions are being taken against the loss of these transports? Are these aircraft being flown into situations where their involvement in hostilities is imminent? 

Mr. INGERSOLL. We have no reports of any of the C-130's being fired on. The 

USAF commander in charge of the C-130's assesses possible risks in advance and takes care to plan all flights to minimize any risk that might exist. The airdrops take place only to areas controlled by the Khmer Republic and flights are conducted at altitudes well above the capability of known hostile anti-aircraft weapons in Cambodia.

Given the non-combat nature of the C-130 flights, the fact that they are unarmed and the precautions taken to minimize any risk to the plane or crew,

the air-dropping of supplies to Cambodian forces does not place the USAF personnel in imminent involvement in hostilities. Mr. ZABLOCKI. Mr. Biester.

ECONOMIC PROGRESS IN VIETNAM 

Mr. GILMAN. 

Gentleman, as part of the purposes of the Indochina post war reconstruction fund, you set forth an objective of making Vietnam economically independent and expanding its economy. Has any headway been made in the past few years in that direction?

Mr. NOOTER. The reduction in real imports that I have referred to earlier, and is graphically shown in the charts which accompany my statement, does represent a move toward normalization of that economy. They are getting by with less outside assistance in real terms. 

Now, they have done that at some considerable sacrifice in terms of domestic consumption and so on. We think now what is needed is a bigger effort to build production. There has been some progress, however, in moving them toward the production of the new high-yield varieties of rice. Twenty-five percent of the rice crop is in the highyield varieties. Rice production, in spite of the military situation, is now about 20-percent higher than it was in the peak year of 1964. 

There have been increases in production of poultry and swine. Sorghum has been introduced as a new crop. It was not grown there before and is now making a considerable impact as animal feed and so forth. 

So this technical progress has been going on. There has been some readjustment to lower the import level, and now what is needed, we think, is a substantial increase in capital investment in irrigation and fertilizer production and some incentives to expansion. 

FUNDS FOR INDUSTRIAL EXPANSION IN VIETNAM 

Mr. GILMAN. What portion of the $750 million that has been proposed for Vietnam is earmarked for industrial expansion? 

Mr. NOOTER. $228 million is earmarked for capital investment. Most of that is in agriculture, though perhaps a third of it or less is in the industrial area. Most of it is either for irrigation or for fertilizer plants in support of agriculture. 

Mr. GILMAN. And approximately $80 million is being utilized for economic development?

Mr. NOOTER. No. All of the $228 million is for economic development. 

Of that, $50 million would be for industrial purposes directly, because the urea plant, which is listed on page 9 of the presentation book, is really in support of agriculture. 

Mr. GILMAN. Aside from the agriculture expansion, there really has not been any industrial expansion in Vietnam, is that correct? 

Mr. NOOTER. It has been rather minor during the war. There has been some expansion of their textile capacity; some in electrical production and the plastics industry has grown to some extent. But it is still a relatively modest industrial sector. We expect that that economy should move ahead more on the agricultural side given their agricultural base. They have good agricultural land.

THE ESF IN CAMBODIA Mr. GILMAN. Can you explain the Multilateral Exchange Fund? 

I think in Cambodia there is a $17.5 million contribution to the fund. 

Could you explain that to us?

Mr. NOOTER. Yes. This is a fund designed to help stabilize the econ omy similar to the Foreign Exchange Operations Fund in Laos. 

There are other donors. We agree to put up funds in large part for the financing of imports. The mechanism is a free market mechanism to make foreign exchange available for things that cannot be imported under the commodity import program. 

A technician on loan from the International Monetary Fund advises on operation of the fund. The IMF helped to set it up, designed the program, and gives technical advice in regard to its implementation. 

Mr. GILMAN. Is it loan money? 

Mr. NOOTER. It is grant money. 

Mr. GILMAN. Grant money.

CHILD WELFARE FUNDS IN VIETNAM

Mr. GILMAN. It is an outright grant? 

Mr. NOOTER. This is a grant; yes.

[The prepared statement follows:] STATEMENT OF VICE ADM. RAY PEET, DIRECTOR, DEFENSE SECURITY ASSISTANCE AGENCY 

Mr. Chairman and members of the committee, as Director of the Defense 

Security Assistance Agency, it is my privilege and responsibility to participate in the presentation to this Committee of the proposed FY 1975 Security Assistance Program. Previous witnesses have already addressed the relationship of that program to the national interest in terms of both U.S. foreign policy and the military requirements associated with our national objectives. My part in this presentation is, therefore, to speak to the content and management of the security assistance portion of the program, which is administered by the Department of Defense, and to answer any questions you may have as to past performance, present status, or future plans. 

Whereas the Secretary of State is responsible for determining whether there shall be a Military Assistance Program of a credit sale for a particular country, the actual execution of the Defense-administered Security Assistance Program is a function of the Secretary of Defense on whose behalf I serve as manager of the programs. His responsibilities with respect to the Military 

Assistance Program are, as you know, specifically stated in the Foreign Assistance Act. They provide a clear and concise description of the major military assistance functions assigned to the Defense Security Assistance Agency. These include the primary responsibility for: 

The determination of military end-item requirements: the procurement of military equipment in a manner which permits its integration with service programs; the supervision of end-item use by the recipient countries; the supervision of the training of foreign military personnel; the movement and delivery of military end-items; the establishment of priorities in the procurement, delivery, and allocation of military equipment. 

In overseeing the performance of these and similar, closely related functions for which the Secretary of Defense is also responsible, my primary role as manager is to ensure that the security assistance programs administered by the Department of Defense are efficiently implemented. I must be certain that the program is in accordance with applicable provisions of the Foreign Assistance and Foreign Military Sales Acts and other governing legislation, as well as within the established policy guidelines and the best interests of the United States.

What it all boils down to in actual practice is that our job is to manage the security assistance programs in a way which will provide each recipient country with the kind and amount of material and training needed to strengthen its armed forces and thereby encourage and enlarge their contribution to free world common defense. Occasionally, of course, the military goods and services we furnish a particular country may be designed to promote other different, but equally important, objectives associated with broad U.S. foreign policy goals.

We have two forms of Defense-administered security assistance to work with in developing those individual country programs. They are. as you know: (1) Foreign Military Sales (credit and credit guarantees); and (2) the Military

Assistance Program (including excess defense articles and military-related training programs).

One of the key factors taken into consideration in the development of individual country programs is the optimum "blend" of these three types of security assistance. Other influential factors include:

The relationship of the recipient nation's defense capability to U.S. security interests: a realistic force level based upon what is needed, what the country can sustain and what can be provided; economic and political conditions within the country; and the scope and phasing of actions leading to its self-reliance. 

The details as to how we propose to make use of the authority and appropriations we are asking for in FY 1975 are set forth in the regional and country pages of the Congressional Presentation Document which you have before you. I would like to highlight certain key elements of the program which I believe are especially pertinent to your consideration of our proposals. 

The proposed fiscal year 1975 credit program is requested at the level of $872 million to facilitate anticipated sales to our friends and allies during the coming year. Our request includes $555 million in new obligational authority for

of the 10% forar If I the! ​both direct DOD credit and to guarantee private financing (estimated at approximately $353 million in fiscal year 1975). We anticipate a need of $520 million for direct funding. This mix of direct and private financing is a key element in our program request. Many developing countries among our free world friends and allies are seldom able to expend substantial sums of cash for the purchase of modern weapons systems or to obtain credits from private sources on reasonable terms. Of course, all requested funds for direct credits will be repaid in full to the U.S. Treasury with interest by the governments to which they are made available. But credits provided by direct means or through private guaranteed funds in accordance with the provisions of the Foreign Military Sales Act are essential if such countries are to purchase the military equipment and services they need.

Comparing the FY 1975 request with that of last year, we are asking only a slight increase in grant assistance authorization from what has been available this past year. In FY 1974 Congress appropriated $450 million in new obligation authority. Adding to this the Laos program, which will be transferred from the 

Defense budget to the military assistance program as of the beginning of FY 1975, and the $250 million FY 1974 drawdown authority, together with the $69 million payback funds which were made available in FY 1974, the total FY 

1974 funding is within 10 or 12% of the $985 million requested for FY 1975. 

As for our request for grant military assistance, I am sure that you will note with satisfaction that only 20 countries will receive grant materiel assistance whereas 10 years ago 52 countries received materiel grant assistance. As the economic capabilities of many of the original major recipient countries have improved, their programs have been reduced and finally eliminated. Chief among the countries which have assumed responsibility for meeting their own defense requirements are the Western European NATO nations and Japan. 

Approximately 85% of the military elements of the security assistance prothe! gram will be allocated to only 10 countries, 7 of which will receive a major portion of this assistance in the form of credit funds under the provisions of the 

Foreign Military Sales Act. The Chairman of the Joint Chiefs of Staff can pro vide you with a military assessment of the need for these programs, but I wish to review for you the requirement, as I see it, for these programs in the 10 selected countries during fiscal year 1975 at the levels proposed by the administration. 

The recent war in the Middle East and the U.S. strategy for peace in that area of the world are in the forefront of the news and interest of the American people, but the situation in the Middle East in no way diminishes the military problems that continue in East Asia. Five of the selected countries are located in the East Asian and Pacific Region, so I will begin there, and come back to the 

Middle East later.

EAST ASIA AND PACIFIC REGION 

U.S. interests in the East Asia and Pacific region derive from the vast population, natural resources, industrial capacity, U.S. investments and markets, as well as the importance of the area's sea and air lines of communication to U.S. global strategy. The fragile truce between the governments of North and South Vietnam and the accord between the belligerents in Laos have permitted an extensive reduction of U.S. military forces in the region. The substantial security assistance programs proposed for the region will provide tangible evidence of the mutual interest we have with our friends and allies of the region in security and stability in the Far East.

The immediate threat to the realization of our security assistance objectives in the Khmer Republic is the continuing state of hositlities and high level of combat being experienced in that country. The continued ability of the Government of the Khmer Republic to maintain its present active opposition to communist aggression essentially depends upon U.S. military and economic aid. Because of active hostilities, the content of the program places more emphasis on operations and maintenance costs, essential for daily combat, than on investment items. 

Primary emphasis is being placed on maintaining a balanced Khmer force of Army, Navy, and Air Force elements. The Khmer Republic will be the largest grant recipient of the total Military Security Assistance Program. 

U.S. Security Assistance objectives in the Republic of Korea are to assure that 

ROK armed forces are sufficiently strong to deter North Korean adventurism and provide stability on the Korean Peninsula. To meet these objectives, the U.S. in 

FY 71 instituted a balanced Korean force modernization program, to be accom-

plished within five years. Primarily because of reduced Military Assistance Program appropriations, the modernization program has lagged behind, and the FY 1975 proposed program is focused on effective continuation of the modernization program at an austere level. The level of FMS credit proposed for Korea in 

FY 1975 reflects growing ROK financial capabilities, and represents, in our judgment, an amount which the Republic of Korea can undertake given its overall economic condition. The Republic of Korea will receive the next largest percent age of the total Military Security Assistance Program in the East Asia Region. 

The security objectives of U.S. Security Assistance to Laos are to support a balanced force which is of sufficient size and strength to maintain the survival of the politically neutral Royal Laotian Government and the independence of the people; and encourage pursuit by Laos of objectives compatible with U.S. interests. Laos will receive approximately 5% of the total military security assistance program. The amount indicated in the FY 1975 presentation documents represents a decrease in the amount provided last year from the DOD budget under the military assistance service-funded program. As you know, the Foreign Assistance 

Act of 1973 directed that service-funded military assistance for Laos be terminated as of June 30, 1974; and the $85.2 million required for materiel and training must be MAP-funded in FY 1975. 

The Republic of China on Taiwan remains an important link in the allied defense structure stretching from Korea to Southeast Asia. The Military Security 

Assistance Program for the Republic of China is now essentially on a sales basis. 

A small, continuing grant training program is also proposed to help maintain close professional ties between U.S. and Republic of China military personnel. 

Within the overall program, emphasis remains on force development and ROC self-reliance associated with resources management and defense production capabilities. Formerly one of the largest grant recipients, the Republic of China will receive only FMS credit funds in FY 1975, which will be fully repaid to the 

United States.

U.S. Security Assistance remains an essential element in the stability of 

Thailand. As a leader of the Association of Southeast Asian Nations, Thailand occupies a key position in the affairs of this region. We anticipate reducing our grant military assistance to Thailand as the capabilities of the Thai Armed Forces improve and Thai-financial capabilities increase. However, for the present our military assistance continues to be important. For FY 1975, our security assistance will continue to provide grant materiel and training to upgrade the armed forces in such vital areas as resources management, logistical support, and combat training. Force modernization will continue, with emphasis on aeronautical modernization, communications, and vehicles. Thailand will receive less than 4% of the total military security assistance program. 

Our proposed programs in Indonesia. The Philippines, and Malaysia make up the balance of the East Asia and Pacific regional programs which constitute nearly half of our worldwide FY 1975 programs. The increased security assistance funding requirements for the region in FY 1975 are necessary to offset the transfer of support for Laos from DOD funding to the military assistance program, and to supply minimum support for the continuing high level of combat activity in the Khmer Republic.

NEAR EAST AND SOUTH ASIA 

Recent events have made obvious our continuing, strong security interests in the Near East and South Asia region. These include not only our interest in the independence and security of Israel, Iran, Lebanon. Saudi Arabia, and Jordan, and support for the truce negotiations, but also include our interest in the im portant U.S. facilities in Greece and Turkey. 

The military capabilities of both Turkey and Greece are essential for the protection of NATO's southeastern flank, and to help contribute to stability in the eastern Mediterranean area. We are pressing the NATO nations to provide more military forces so that the relative scale of American contribution shrinks. But we should not underestimate what they are presently doing (or overestimate what they are capable of doing).

Although improvement in the Turkey economy has enabled Turkey to undertake the financing of a significant portion of the costs of improving her armed forces, a mix of U.S. military assistance and Turkish resources will be required to provide fiscal balance while maintaining the maximum possible effectiveness of her forces in being. The increasing ability of the Turks to utilize their own resources is reflected in a gradual transition from grant aid to foreign military

f the sed fr 

LATES 

​re a ther ing sales credit to the extent that we now propose to lend her more than we give her through grant aid. Turkey will be the fourth largest participant in both the grant and FMS credit programs. She too will repay the principal and interest on the sales loan we propose. 

The decision of the Government of Greece in January 1973 to forego further grant military aid reflects her increased self-sufficiency. Foreign military sales credit is, however, required to permit Greece to purchase essential items to meet valid military requirements. Greece, the eighth largest participant and formerly one of the largest grant recipients will receive only foreign military sales credit funds, which are fully reimbursable to the United States. 

The support of Israel's existence has been a cardinal tenet of American policy in the Middle East. In practical terms, this means the extension of large foreign military sales credits and grants to assure that the military balance does not go against Israel. The FY 1974 emergency request for $2.2 billion in mixed grant aid and credit sales prevented an upset in the military balance as a result of the most recent war. The regular program level of $300 million in foreign military sales credits is again needed in FY 1975 to allow Israel to continue to purchase the military equipment necessary to maintain the military balance in the Middle East, and to insure that Israel has the capability of defending herself. Although Israel will be the second largest participant in the total military security assistance program, she will repay the principal and interest on the credit sales program proposed.

Jordan is a moderate Arab State which maintains close ties to the West. 

Jordan has generally supported a peaceful settlement of the Arab-Israeli dispute. Jordan has demonstrated a willingness to use her armed forces to counter penetration of the area by radical and disruptive elements. The military assistance proposed for Jordan will assist her to meet critical modernization needs and help maintain the country as a bulwark against disruptive elements seeking to erode the negotiated peace settlement in the Middle East. 

LATIN AMERICA 

The largest participant in the security assistance program in the Latin American Region, which rounds out the 10 countries constituting 85% of the program, is Brazil.

Brazil has a tradition of international cooperation with the United States and its allies and is a potential world power. It is therefore in the U.S. interest to reestablish and maintain the traditional U.S. role as Brazil's primary source of military equipment; to nurture the favorable military-to-military influence inimical to U.S. interests in the hemisphere. Brazil will be the ninth largest participant, and will receive foreign military sales credit funds and grant military training, primarily in the United States, under grant aid. The credit funds will, of course, be repaid to the United States.

In conclusion, Mr. Chairman, the programs through which security assistance supports the defense efforts of other free-world nations are essential elements of U.S. foreign policy and make a significant and substantial contribution to the successful implementation of that policy. The security assistance programs help maintain a military balance in the Middle East conducive to restraint and to success of U.S. efforts to bring about a lasting peace in the area. These programs are the essential element in U.S. efforts to create conditions requisite for a truce and ultimate settlement in the Khmer Republic. And, in the case of Latin 

America, security assistance is an important factor in the development of new relationships and an improved sense of community between the United States and other nations of the Western Hemisphere. Considerations such as these explain the need for, and wisdom of, continued use of security assistance as a carefully controlled and selectively applied instrument of national policy. 

In this context, I urge this committee's support for appropriations of new obligational authority in the amount of $985 million and total obligational authority for $1.024 billion, upon which the fiscal year 1975 military assistance program is based. These funds, which represent approximately 1/20th of 1 percent of our annual gross national product, and approximately 1% of our own defense budget, are a reasonable price to pay to help strengthen the security of the United States and help promote world peace. 

I also urge this committee's support for $555 million in new obligational authority to be used for direct credit and/or guaranty of commercial credit, and a $872.5 million total credit program during fiscal year 1975.

fthet ​2E26E 

STATEMENT OF BENJAMIN FORMAN, ASSISTANT GENERAL COUN- SEL FOR INTERNATIONAL AFFAIRS, DEPARTMENT OF DEFENSE 

Mr. FORMAN. Yes, sir. 

As you undoubtedly know, Mr. Broomfield, the drawdown authority has been used by the President only four times since it was first enacted in 1961. It was utilized twice for Vietnam in the mid-sixties and twice during this current fiscal year for Cambodia. It is a very valuable authority to meet contingencies which might arise. It is, in effect, comparable to the contingency fund on the AID side which is a direct appropriation. Here it is not an appropriation, merely an authority to drawdown on stocks.

As Admiral Peet has indicated, we frequently find that we are half way through the fiscal year without having a statute enacted for that year and therefore during that interim we do not have available to us this drawdown authority; in fact, in fiscal year 1973 I believe no bill at all. We operated the whole year under CRA and therefore did not have the drawdown authority available to us for any emergencies. 

Now so far as Cambodia is concerned we do have that budgeted for in the fiscal year 1975 budget but should an emergency arise for some other country between July 1 and the time the Congress enacts the authorization act we would be completely without any flexibility to meet that emergency. This amendment is designed to take care of that problem in fiscal year 1976 and later fiscal years.

THE MILLER BARTER AMENDMENT 

Mr. FORMAN. Mr. Chairman, may I may make one comment about the Miller amendment as long as you have brought it up. 

We do have one difficulty with the amendment as he has drafted it; namely, that he has provided that the amounts received from the sale of the bartered material-the coffee which was Mr. Gross' illustration or oil-would be deposited to "Miscellaneous receipts." This to us appears impractical. 

For example, if we are selling airplanes, we need dollars to pay for those airplanes. Where are the dollars going to come from? If the proceeds from the sale of the oil or coffee go to miscellaneous receipts, there won't be any dollars to pay the manufacturer. Similarly, if what we were selling came from our own inventory and the resulting proceeds went into "Miscellaneous receipts," the military departments would not have any money to go out and buy replacement aircraft. We think there are technical problems in the way he has drafted it.

THE SECURITY ASSISTANCE PROGRAM REVIEW COMMITTEE (SAPRC) 

Admiral PEET. In working with the Department of State, yes. When we put the program together there is what we call SAPRC, a Security Assistance Program Review Committee, to which we have an input, as does AID, as does the NSC staff, as do OMB and others. 

Mr. FRASER. In other words, this is an interagency committee that establishes the basic policy that you then intend to implement? 

Admiral PEET. Yes, sir, it is an interagency committee; but it does not establish the policy. It is a sort of forum for presenting our views to the Department of State. The Secretary of State has the final say. 

Mr. FRASER. When the policy is decided upon with respect to a given country, how does that come to you? What does the policy say before you undertake to put together the particular elements? 

Admiral PEET. Well, when we put together the program, as shown in the Congressional Presentation Document, it is based on certain objectives; and insofar as possible the policy with respect to a given country is stated in the narrative covering that country. I find that policy comes to me with the individual decisions that are made. For example, whether or not we are going to sell a particular weapon to a particular country depends upon State Department approval.

IMPLEMENTATION OF THE “POLITICAL PRISONER” PROVISION 

Mr. VEST. I did not have that information the last time I was here. 

I can say that we did prepare in the State Department a message on this section of the act and sent it out to our Embassies in all the countries which received foreign assistance. We did this early in April and asked for a detailed analysis of the relevant legal standards, the practices in each country, the method of life which prevailed there. 

We have received about 50 replies to this message. The problem, as 

I think Mr. Ingersoll began to say, was that political prisoners is a very delicate matter, a deeply difficult one to deal with to try to achieve results. It is one thing to condemn and to take an action to isolate a party and then not be able particularly to influence them. 

Mr. FRASER. What you are saying, Mr. Vest, if I understand you correctly, and I don't mean to cut you off, is that you in the Department-you are with the Department, aren't you? 

Mr. VEST. Yes, sir. 

Mr. FRASER [continuing]. Are deciding for yourselves whether or not the congressional policy which is enacted into law should be implemented. 

Mr. VEST. No, sir. 

Mr. FRASER. Well, that is what you are saying. You are saying it is a very delicate matter.

Mr. VEST. We are finding out how best to carry out the intent of the act.

Mr. FRASER. Well, so far you have done nothing with respect to policy for implementing it. That is fair to say, isn't it?

Mr. VEST. So far we have not cut off absolute aid with any of the countries which I believe you mentioned last time. 

Mr. FRASER. And you have not diminished the aid to any?

Mr. VEST. I cannot speak to what changes there may have been as a result of this.

Mr. FRASER. Well, in each country an increase is proposed, isn't that right? 

Mr. VEST. I cannot speak to that, sir. I don't know.

SITUATION IN SOUTH KOREA Mr. FRASER. Well, there is in Korea. 

Mr. VEST. In Korea, we have a situation where we have a balance of interests there.

Mr. FRASER. But Mr. Vest, the congressional statement says there should be no military aid in that kind of a country. Now, what you are saying is that you are going to bring a lot of considerations to decide whether or not you are going to carry out the provisions of the law. Is that what you are telling the committee?

Mr. VEST. I am telling you, sir, that we are concerned. We have begun the process to try to establish how we can best carry out the intent of the act. We have certainly privately made our views known and the views of Congress known to a number of the countries concerned. The question is how best to achieve the end that you want, sir. 

Mr. FRASER. Well, let me try to state the problem this way. If we want to achieve implementation of the policy guideline laid down in the law, perhaps we should change it from a policy statement to a mandatory provision. Would that be helpful?

Mr. VEST. I would not say anything like that would be helpful, sir, but I don't have anything else. I don't have any more details on this other than what I have just mentioned this morning, sir. 

Mr. FRASER. Why is it that since the law was enacted last December, that communication only went out in April? 

Mr. VEST. I don't have an answer to that, sir. 

Mr. FRASER. Have you had an answer with respect to South Korea?

Mr. VEST. I don't have information on the exact answers from any country. 

Mr. FRASER. Despite the fact that the issue was raised last week, you have now discovered there are 50 responses, but you don't know if there was one for Mr. VEST. Sir, if you recall, we said last week we would get the details on this and make it available to the committee. We are in the process of preparing that now.

Mr. FRASER. Will that include a summary of each country's response? 

Mr. VEST. I am sure whatever information the committee wants we will try to prepare it. I am not involved in this at the present time. I merely wanted to tell you what I could at this time, but we are trying to prepare an answer to meet the committee's inquiries as made clear to Mr. Ingersoll last time (see p. 283).

Mr. FRASER. Do you disagree with the views expressed by Ambassador Reischauer?

Mr. VEST. Sir, it is one thing to be an Ambassador responsible, and it is another thing to be an ex-Ambassador and not responsible. When you have to weigh off the balance as to how best to carry out your Nation's policy, sometimes it looks different. 

Mr. FRASER. It surely must. 

Mr. VEST. It does, sir.

Mr. FRASER. And it does not help to write a policy statement into the law either, apparently.

Mr. VEST. Right. 

Mr. FRASER. 

Chairman MORGAN. Mr. Derwinski.

I ST EFFECTS OF MAP IN ISRAEL Mr. DERWINSKI.  

Admiral, I would like to direct my questions to a few stray geographic points rather than get all excited about a sense of Congress section of the bill. 

Could you tell us if the military assistance program for Israel in 1975 in addition to the $2.2 billion provided last year fully replaces the material losses Israel suffered in that October 1973 war?

Admiral PEET. There is $300 million for credit in the 1975 program. That $300 million is the same amount they have been receiving for the last several years.

Mr. DERWINSKI. So I assume the emergency is over in terms of resupply. 

Admiral PEET. Yes, sir, I feel that the emergency is over. I would like to expand my answer off the record. 

MAP FOR ETHIOPIA 

Mr. DERWINSKI. I can appreciate that.

Now, I realize that basically you have a naval background. I am just wondering though if you would feel equipped to discuss the status of our military aid program to Ethiopia. It is my understanding that the AID program we have for Ethiopia which is primarily for the Army was a quid pro quo for the use of the Asmara Air Force facilities. Since we are phasing out of that, does this have any effect on our aid program to Ethiopia?

Admiral PEET. It certainly has effect as far as the rationale for a program for Ethiopia is concerned, which I consider to be a political one primarily. They are having difficulties with their neighbors, the 

Somalians, who are receiving aid from the Communist world. 

Mr. VEST. That is the problem of Ethiopia. 

Mr. DERWINSKI. What about their instability? Do you have a reevaluation of what effect this has had on their ability to defend themselves from Somalian incursions?

Admiral PEET. There is no question but that this is a time of turmoil over there. The latest readings I have had indicate that the situation is improving, and they are coming back to a stable from of government. We are interested in making sure that it remains stable. That is an area of the world of great interest to us. It is of great interest to the Russians also, and we are trying to maintain a balance in the area.

THE KOREAN MODERNIZATION PROGRAM 

Mr. DERWINSKI. Mr. Broomfield neglected to discuss in any detail the Korean modernization program. I was wondering if you could tell us your evaluation of the timetable and the need for the moderniza tion program of the Armed Forces of South Korea. 

Admiral PEET. Well, as you know, we have had a modernization plan. Some people talk of it as a commitment, but it has never been any more than a plan. We can implement that plan various ways with grants and with loans, and that is what we are trying to do. Korea has good prospects of being able to phase out its need for grant aid, and of becoming self-reliant in the next 2 or 3 years. I think we are making progress along that line.

MILITARY ASSISTANCE FOR ZAIRE 

Mr. DERWINSKI. I have been intrigued by the fact that we are developing a military assistance program for Zaire, and I appreciate its size and location and so on. Would you care to elaborate in any way on our military assistance program for Zaire? 

Admiral PEET. Yes; for 1975, we are proposing about $300,000 to provide training in the United States only. Mr. Broomfield asked (see p. 308) about the size of the total training program worldwide and I have that answer now; it is about $34 million all told, and $300,000 of it is earmarked for Zaire. It enables us to bring key people from that country to the United States and train them in our ways and improve mutual understanding. Also, we are proposing for Zaire $3.5 million credit. She has been using precious credit to buy C-130 aircraft, for example. These aircraft serve primarily a military purpose, but they can also be put to good economic use. We believe it is a good thing for 

Zaire to buy them and I think it is particularly desirable that they buy them in the United States.

Mr. DERWINSKI. Is Zaire still basically dependent on Belgium military advisers and equipment for a good part of its military needs? 

Admiral PEET. Belgium does have a sizable amount of money invested in Zaire, and I believe their in-country activities are much greater than ours. 

Mr. DERWINSKI. Thank you. 

Chairman MORGAN. Mr. Hamilton. 

MILITARY SUPPLY POLICY TO PAKISTAN 

Mr. HAMILTON. Admiral, are we contemplating any kind of a change in our military supply policy toward Pakistan and South Asia? 

Admiral PEET. Not to my knowledge. The policy was changed 1½ years or 2 years ago. I know of no further change being contemplated now, but I would defer to the State Department on that question. 

MILITARY AID TO INDOCHINA 

Mr. HAMILTON. Let me read some figures to you with regard to the extent of our aid in some of the Indochina countries and ask your reaction to them. The figures that I will give are rounded off, they may not be precise but they are approximately correct. 

We are going to be giving total aid to Cambodia in excess of a half billion dollars and a very large proportion of that is military aid. 

That is a country that has less than 8 million people, and total domestic revenues of about $42 million. The per capita GNP in that country is $90 and the per capita U.S. aid, if you take the total aid and divide it by the number of people, is $72 which is just under the per capita GNP. 

If you switch over to Laos you find statistics that are similar. We are going to be putting in about $150 million of aid into Laos, a large portion of which is military. There is a population of a little over 

3 million people in that country. The per capita GNP of that country is about $65 and the per capita U.S. aid is about $46.

ate Then the third country in Indochina is Vietnam and we are going to be putting something like $2.4 million into Vietnam in total aid, a major proportion of which is military. That is a country with a popu lation of just under 20 million and it had a per capita GNP in 1972 of about $150. The U.S. aid per person under the program you are proposing to us is $121.

Now all of this represents a lot of statistics but what emerges is that in countries that are very small in population we are putting enormous sums of money, most of which is military assitance. It seems to me this aid is far beyond any reasonable allocation of fund for countries that are so very small. It raises real questions in my mind about the ability of those countries to absorb that kind of aid. 

I just wonder, and maybe this question goes to Mr. Vest as much as to you, how you really react to programs of this enormity and whether or not you think this is wise policy. Now there are political and military factors mixed up here but the extent of these programs is just enormous. How do you respond to that?

AMMUNITION EXPENDITURES IN CAMBODIA 

Admiral PEET. Mr. Hamilton, I do think there is a mixture of political and military considerations. Given a political decision to have programs for these countries, as manager of the program I have been concerned about the size of the programs. As you say, aid to Cambodia this past year amounted to over $400 million on the military assistance side. Most of that was used only to provide consumables so that it would not go down the drain for the want of ammunition or other consumables.

The cost of just ammunition expenditures by that country varies from a half a million to $12 million a day, so you can see it takes a sizable program to keep it from going under. 

Here again I would defer to Mr. Vest, of the State Department, to address the political aspect which I think is your primary concern. 

RATIONALE FOR CAMBODIA AND LAOS AID 

Mr. VEST. Mr. Hamilton, it is a troubling thing for any of us, for the taxpayers and we are all taxpayers-as well as to what is right and in the interest of our country to be doing in this area. I would only say that we have reached that delicate moment when the effort to find stability there, and we are working for this, we hope will move to the peacemaking phase.

Now you have to have two sides to work out a negotiation and we think in each of these we are working in each area to move to this. We think in Laos we have reached the stage where we may within the next year have moved to some type of accommodation there. We have budgeted to carry on the trends that we have there but we think that has moved. In Vietnam we have a never-never land at the moment but we have a South Vietnam which is more and more taking over its own responsibilities. In Cambodia, we have a Cambodia with a Phnom 

Penh which has been trying to get the other side to negotiate. 

Now the alternative would be to say we are not going to bother, we are going to let these people go on their own way. We have invested

an immense amount in a war, whether we liked the war or not, and it seems to me that the question we have is whether we want to try to carry this thing through terminal phases that have a chance of opening the way to peace.

Mr. HAMILTON. Mr. Vest, I don't know that the sole alternative is a complete turning away from these people and denying them everything. I think there may be alternatives other than nothing on the one hand and billions of dollars on the other. 

Let me go on to some other things.

INCREASED AMOUNTS IN JORDAN AID 

Admiral Peet, we are giving a substantial increase in military aid to Jordan. Why precisely are we requesting such a large increase for 

Jordan? What does the modernization program there involve?

Admiral PEET. Jordan has a need for modernizing its armed forces in the area of tanks, APCS, TOW antitank missiles, and equipment of that sort. It is pretty hard to keep up the morale of an army when they see that all their neighbors have more modern weapons. I think our program for Jordan has been a rather successful one in the past few years. Jordan has played a very responsible role in the Mideast, and our objective is to encourage its continuing to do so. 

Mr. HAMILTON. Are you projecting the level of assistance that you are requesting for 1975 as the level for Jordan in the next few fiscal years or will we go back to the figure that we had, say, last year in fiscal year 1974?

Admiral PEET. It remains to be determined, what our future year program will be, we contemplate a high level the next 2 years certainly 2 to 3 years.

STATUS OF EMERGENCY AID FOR ISRAEL 

Mr. HAMILTON. Could you tell us the status of the $2.2 billion in emergency aid for Israel? Has all of that money been committed?

Admiral PEET. Yes. As we indicated earlier, $1 billion of it has been authorized to waive contractual liability for cash dependable undertakings by Israel. The other $1.2 billion is credit except for $17.3 million which was used to support the U.N. Emergency Force. 

Mr. HAMILTON. When will all the deliveries of equipment be completed?

Admiral PEET. A good share of them have been completed. However, in the case of some equipment which they ordered from the production lines, it will take as long as 18 to 24 months to complete delivery. 

Mr. HAMILTON. There has been talk in the papers recently about putting Israel on a long-term aid footing. 

Mr. HAMILTON. Evidently the President said something about that while he visited there. Do you have any knowledge of that, and if you do, what do you know about it? 

Admiral PEET. No, sir; I have no knowledge of any specific offer.

Chairman MORGAN. Mr. Thomson.

NUMBERS OF COUNTRIES RECEIVING MAP Mr. THOMSON.  

Admiral, I would like to know whether more countries are receiving military aid than were, we will say, 10 years ago or 3 years ago. 

Admiral PEET. Well, 10 years ago, the grant material and military credit sales programs included 61 countries; and the 1975 program includes 50 countries. Ten years ago, 43 countries, for example, received grant materiel; and today only 20 countries are scheduled for grant materiel.

DOLLAR VOLUME ON MAP 

Mr. THOMSON. What about the dollar volume 10 years ago and today, or 3 years ago and today?

Admiral PEET. I can give you some examples. MAP grant aid programed for Latin America has dropped by about 75 percent in less than 10 years for a total of almost $80 million in 1966 to less than the $20 million proposed for 1975. 

The FMS credit plan for 16 of the 18 Latin American countries participating in the 1975 security assistance program amounts to $200 million-more than five times as much as it was in fiscal year 1966. 

I think there is a definite trend around the world to go toward the credit side and reduce the grant.

Mr. THOMSON. Well, can you give us examples of countries that are increasing their credit purchases and decreasing their grant aid? 

Admiral PEET. Yes. Greece, of course, is one; she has phased out her grant entirely and has made the transition to credit. Korea is decreasing its MAP and relying more on credit, China has zeroed out its grant program except for training and is depending almost entirely on credit. 

Most countries are moving in that direction, sir.

MILITARY AID FROM COMMUNIST COUNTRIES 

Mr. THOMSON. Are we the only nation that provides military assistance? Do the Communist countries have such programs?

Admiral PEET. No, sir, we are not. The Communist world provides military assistance, and the free world provides military assistance. 

The last check I made indicates that the respective amounts are roughly equivalent. 

Mr. THOMSON. Is the amount of military sales by other free world countries increasing?

Admiral PEET. Yes, sir, it is; significantly. In fact, a few years ago it was practically zero and now it is about 15 percent of the total military hardware sales. 

Mr. THOMSON. Fifteen? 

Admiral PEET. Fifteen; yes, sir.

MAP IN CHILE 

Mr. THOMSON. What are we doing in Chile?

Admiral PEET. We are offering Chile a credit program. In fact, we are asking for about $20.5 million credit for Chile in 1975. We also

propose a small grant training program for that country. Our interests in Chile are threefold, I would say. One is access to its copper supply and another access to the waters and the straits around that section of Latin America. Quite obviously, we would also like to deny influence in that area to potentially hostile countries, and to maintain our own relations with Chile.

Mr. THOMSON. Where are we conducting the training program, in this country or in Chile?

Admiral PEET. Most of it is done in Panama, sir, in our Canal Zone schools.

Mr. THOMSON. And this is the only military grant money that is going to Chile? 

Mr. THOMSON. Thank you.

MANAGEMENT OF FOREIGN MILITARY SALES 

Admiral, your responsibility extends to the management of all sales made under the Foreign Military Sales Act-both cash sales and credit sales? 

Admiral PEET. Yes, sir.

Mr. BINGHAM. So far as I am aware, we don't have any figures before us on cash sales under the act either for the current year or for the coming year. Do you have those figures? 

Admiral PEET. Yes; and I can provide them for the record.

Mr. BINGHAM. Would you please, the total? 

Admiral PEET. At page 84 of the CPD we indicate the cash, credit, and commercial sales. I can give you some numbers. 

Mr. BINGHAM. Are those figures all classified? 

Admiral PEET. Some are. I can give you ball park figures. 

Mr. BINGHAM. Please. 

Admiral PEET. Most of them are releaseable. You will see in that book which ones are and which ones are not. The ones that are shaded are classified, and the others are not.

Overall the FMS cash and credit total for fiscal year 1973 was close to $4 billion. For the current year, it will probably run closer to $7 billion.

Mr. BINGHAM. So it would be fair to say then that the cash sales are far larger than the credit sales? 

Admiral PEET. Yes, sir; they are; much larger.

Let me give you the totals. The estimate for this year, as I said, is close to $7 billion for cash. As far as the credit is concerned, it will be about $2.9 billion, a great deal of which is for Israel. 

REPORTS TO CONGRESS ON LARGE FMS SALES 

Mr. BINGHAM. Last year in the debate on the floor of the House I proposed an amendment that would have required the Department to report to the Congress in advance of executing large sales in excess of $25 million, for example, so that the Congress might have a chance to review those sales. Would you have any objection to such a provision?

Admiral PEET. It would create many problems as far as managing the program is concerned. Mr. Forman and I did some work on this a little while ago, and we found that the transactions involved were in the hundreds. 

Would you want to comment, Ben?

Mr. FORMAN. Individual transactions of $25 million or more on the sales side last year. Our estimate is 19 such sales cases. If you add into that the credits and guarantees, you get up to 28 instances. The basic problem is not that that is a tremendous number for the Congress to consider but the problem of implementing these transactions. In many cases we have a time critical situation where if we don't place the actual procurement contract with the supplier by a fixed date the production line will be interrupted or will terminate and you incur considerable startup costs to again go ahead with the transaction or the manufacturer may have quoted a price which is valid only until a certain date and if you don't place your contract with him the price will increase.

Mr. BINGHAM. But the text of the Foreign Military Sales Act quite clearly reflects the fact that the Congress is concerned with policy matters and has laid down certain criteria for cash sales that apply just as much as they do to credit sales, is that not correct? 

Mr. FORMAN. I believe that is correct, sir.

Mr. BINGHAM. I understand now that we really have no information on which to determine whether the Department is carrying out the provisions of the act as laid down. We have no effective oversight over the program, is that not correct?

Admiral PEET. No, Mr. Bingham. We will provide whatever information is desired on this subject; and, in the CPD, we have provided quite a bit of detail.

CONGRESSIONAL PRESENTATION FIGURES: AN ESTIMATE 

Mr. BINGHAM. Let me pass to another aspect of this. You have asked for $872,500,000 of new authority for foreign military credit sales and you have broken that down in your presentation book so much for each country. 

Admiral PEET. Yes, sir, these are estimates.

Mr. BINGHAM. Is it not a fact that you have the authority to change that any way you want to within that ceiling, you are not bound at all by what you gave up in the presentation books? 

Admiral PEET. I think that is true.

Mr. FORMAN. That is pretty generally true for MAP funds until 30 days after the Appropriation Act is passed at which time we have to report to the Congress our detailed distribution of the MAP funds. 

Mr. BINGHAM. That is under the Appropriation Act?

Mr. FORMAN. No; it is a provision in this statute, sir. It is section 

653, I believe. Section 653 requires that 30 days after the appropration is passed we must then report to the Congress what we are going to do with the MAP funds, and we can't make any adjustments in that report after that by more than 10 percent.

Admiral PEET. And cannot increase country programs more than that without coming back to you.

Chairman MORGAN. Mr. Biester. 

REDUCTION IN LAOS MAP Mr. BIESTER. Thank you, Mr. Chairman. 

I wonder if I might pick up from the question that Mr. Fountain asked with respect to Laos. I believe, Admiral, you said that there would be a contemplation of a reduction of that figure down. I am wondering what the rationale of any moneys might be under the circumstances of a coalition government. My understanding is that previously this money had gone into the Royal Laos Government. 

Now since it is a coalition, what is the rationale of sending any support in?

Mr. VEST. Mr. Chairman, Mr. Biester, we are contemplating a reduction. The essential rationalization of providing support is the simple fact that you don't have a fully workable integrated Laotian government as yet, which mean that you don't have a single army, a single government, a truly integrated government and a national sense of confidence.

Mr. BIESTER. And, therefore, what we are pointing toward is that moment when there is a genuinely unified military force at which time this would not become necessary? 

Mr. VEST. That is correct.

MAP TRAINING FOR PORTUGAL 

Mr. BIESTER. With respect to the moneys for Portugal, I note that there are training moneys of some $500,000 to $550,000. Can you tell. me where that training takes place and what sorts of activities are. involved in that?

Mr. VEST. While more Portuguese students are trained overseas, we also bring the key Portuguese officers to this country where they attend senior war colleges, things of that sort. For example, we have a war college up in Newport, and then they attend some of the Army staff colleges, and they associate with our military and learn some of our techniques. It is a program that in my view is probably one of the most beneficial to us. 

Mr. BIESTER. Does that include to any extent training of counterinsurgency?

Mr. VEST. Not to my knowledge, Mr. Biester.

INCREASES IN KOREAN MAP 

Mr. BIESTER. I noticed that the amount for Korea is up-and my percentage computations are undoubtedly well rounded off and probably not accurate-approximately 30 percent for Korea, up about 40 percent for Thailand, up about 25 percent for Indonesia. These seem like fairly substantial increases in each of those countries. I wonder if there is any special circumstances that calls for that? 

Mr. VEST. Well, they are requests over what we received last year, and we were cut back significantly last year. In Korea, it is merely an attempt to get further along with the modernization plan so we can phase out entirely there. In Thailand, we are phasing out there also. 

INCREASE IN THE INDONESIA PROGRAM 

Mr. BIESTER. Indonesia up 25 percent. Is there any particular reason for that?

Admiral PEET. It is up 25 percent over last year's program-in the neighborhood of $20 million. I can provide the details for the record, if you wish.

Mr. BIESTER. Very well. 

[The information requested follows:] FISCAL YEAR 1975 MILITARY ASSISTANCE PROGRAM FOR INDONESIA 

The FY 1974 proposed Military Assistance Program for Indonesia was $20.8 for materiel and $2.0 million for training, a total of $22.8 million-almost exactly the level of the FY 1975 request. So there is no increase in the amount requested for FY 1975 as compared to the FY 1974 request. In comparing the FY 1975 request with the FY 1974 estimated program, the 1975 request would provide [security deletion]. Overall, the program is significantly higher in "investment" items, and the funds allocated for operating costs are actually reduced. 

FMS GOVERNMENT VERSUS PRIVATE FUNDING 

Mr. BIESTER. I note that in terms of financing that there has been quite a shift in fiscal year 1974 and fiscal year 1975 private financing. 

For example, on page 22 of this pamphlet, I noticed that private financing was some $540 million in fiscal year 1974 and U.S. Government direct credit was $190 million, and the shift in fiscal year 1975 is $353 million for private financing and a jump of up to $520 million in U.S. Government direct credits. Is there an explanation for that?

Admiral PEET. We develop a total program, and it is much easier for the underdeveloped countries to shift from grant aid to credit if we can offer them direct credit at the cost of money to the United States. If we have to go out on the money market, the interest rates are pretty high-close to 10 percent or more. We are trying to work out the best combination we can.

Mr. BIESTER. So that the reason may very well lie in the fact that interest rates have jumped considerably over the last year. Would that be correct? 

Admiral PEET. Yes, sir, that is certainly a major factor.

Mr. BIESTER. And not a reflection in terms of the interest to the private sector or private financing? 

Admiral PEET, Yes, sir.

Mr. BIESTER. Thank you very much, Mr. Chairman.

Chairman MORGAN. Mr. Yatron. 

Mr. YATRON. 

NATO AND THE EASTERN MEDITERRANEAN

FUNDING BY NATO ALLIES 

Mr. YATRON. Is anything being done, Admiral, in terms of finances with our NATO allies? I know that the United States is contributing approximately $17 billion per year as our share toward NATO and the other 14 countries collectively are spending approximately $30 billion. 

Is anything being done to encourage our NATO allies to start assuming more of the costs of their own defense?

Mr. VEST. Sir, just in a general sense this is really a continual effort that is being carried out by our Ambassador in NATO and by our general relationships with the key NATO allies. This has been a program that has been going on throughout the year. We have just concluded a meeting of the NATO defense ministers in Brussels at which the representative for our Secretary Schlesinger, Assistant Secretary

Ellsworth, who was a former NATO ambassador, was there. This is a continual program. We have reached the stage where we have them forming for themselves something called a Eurogroup and that is group of the European countries themselves in which they meet to get together to take on individual additional expenses and take a larger military effort.

As you know, they are a bunch of separate countries, many small, and this is an effort to get them to work together and do more. It is a sustained program, however, not a separate thing that happens at one time. General Goodpaster who will be in here later I am sure will be in a position to testify in even greater detail because he as Supreme Allied Commander is the recipient of any of the efforts that any of the countries manage to work out together. 

Mr. YATRON. Mr. Vest, I am aware of the fact that Germany, as an example, just announced they were going to implement the program by approximately $2 billion per year.

Mr. VEST. Yes; the Germans are participating, along with the other members of the Eurogroup, in a $2 billion force improvement program. 

Mr. YATRON. Do you have any knowledge of any other countries besides Germany who are planning to implement the program? 

Mr. VEST. I don't have information on this particular subject, sir. 

We would be glad to get more for you if you wish.

Mr. YATRON. Thank you. 

[The information requested follows:] DEFENSE BUDGETS OF NATO ALLIES 

The total defense expenditures of all our 14 NATO Allies in calendar year 1973 was approximately $39 billion. That compares with an estimated $17 billion of NATO-related expenditures in fiscal year 1974 for the United States. In 

1968, all of the European Allies with the exception of France, Iceland and Portugal formed the Eurogroup in order that the European Allies could play a more active role than in the past in improving the Alliance's defense posture. 

Since 1970, the Eurogroup has planned and coordinated specific European force improvement projects in response to the President's pledge that "given a similar approach by the other Allies, the U.S. would maintain and improve its forces in Europe."

The original European Defense Improvement Program (EDIP), which was announced in 1970, has been followed each year by a Europackage of specific force improvement projects added to the defense budgets of all the Eurogroup countries. The Europackage announced in December 1973, to which all Eurogroup countries will contribute, represents a total increase of $2 billion in the defense budgets of the Eurogroup countries as a whole for calendar year 1974. These funds will bring the following equipment into service in 1974: 

Army: 

474 main battle tanks. 

1,079 other armored vehicles. 

199 antiarmor weapons.

Navy: 

5 destroyers/escorts. 

15 submarines (including one nuclear-powered). 

10 fast patrol boats. 

33 maritime helicopters.

Air Force: 

195 modern combat and maritime patrol aircraft. 

140 land-based helicopters. 

820 antiaircraft guided missiles. 

853 antiaircraft guns.

Chairman MORGAN. Without objection, it is so ordered. [The information requested was subsequently supplied as follows:] 

PROGRAM FOR ISRAEL 

The $300 million in FMS credit requested for Israel was based on a judgement that took into account several factors, among which were: (1) the economic and financial impact of the totality of U.S. assistance provided in FY 1974: (2) a forecast of Israel's balance of payments situation in FY 1975 and (3) an assumption that there would not be a resumption of active hostilities in FY 1975. 

Some of the more important facts were: a substantial increase in Israel's foreign exchange reserves (from $528 million in 1971 to about $1.5 billion at the end of 1973), in large measure made possible by the roughly $500 million in assistance we have made available annually to Israel since 1971; our estimate that the

financial impact of the $2.2 billion emergency assistance to Israel Congress authorized in FY 1974 would be felt over a period of about three years; our forecast that Israel's FY 1975 balance of payments, after allowing for U.S._assistance, would show a surplus and therefore result in a further addition to Israel's foreign exchange reserves. This would occur despite continuing high level of military purchases abroad.

Admittedly, there is no certainty in forecasting. What we have given you represented our best judgement at that time, based on past performance of the Israeli economy and our estimate of how we believe it will perform in the year ahead. 

We are, of course, keeping these factors under continuing review to see whether subsequent revision of our estimates may be desirable.
