[The letter referred to follows:] DEFENSE SECURITY ASSISTANCE AGENCY, AND DEPUTY ASSISTANT SECRETARY (SECURITY ASSISTANCE), OASD/ISA, 

Washington, D.C., June 19, 1974.

Hon. GAYLORD NELSON, 

U.S. Senate, Washington, D.C.

DEAR SENATOR NELSON: I observed in my reading of the Congressional Record of June 6, 1974 that you have proposed an amendment (No. 1399) to the Foreign

Assistance Act of 1974. The stated purpose of this legislation would be to trigger a written report from the President to the Congress on certain proposed sales, credit sales or guarantees to any country under this Act prior to their implementation. In order to assess the possible impact of this proposed legislation on the operation of my Agency, I asked my people and the Office of the General Counsel, OSD, to provide me a memorandum giving their views on this matter. 

I am forwarding to you with this letter a copy of the memorandum which I received in reply to my request. I wish to record my opposition to your amendment for three reasons: (1) A reporting system such as you have proposed appears administratively impractical because of imprecision in the determination of the execution of sales transactions which can be forecast. (2) In accordance with section 35 (b) of the Foreign Military Sales Act, Congress is provided an annual forecast of anticipated sales transactions in the Congressional Presentation Document furnished the two authorizing and two appropriations Committees of the Congress. (3) The 30-day congressional review period for sales cases considered to be in excess of the dollar threshold levels indicated in your amendment might well be considered contrary to the national interests of the United States. Our ability to respond to the needs of friendly governments in their times of crisis, as we were recently able to do with Israel, might be severely compromised by the legislative restrictions you have offered. 

I hope you will accept my comments on your proposed amendment not as criticism of your intent but in the spirit that I view such a restriction as counterproductive to the United States Government's interest in the matter of foreign military sales. 

Sincerely yours,

RAY PEET, Vice Admiral, USN. 

MEMORANDUM FOR VICE ADMIRAL RAY PEET, DIRECTOR, DEFENSE SECURITY ASSISTANCE AGENCY Subject: Nelson Amendment No. 1399. 

Reference is made to your request for my views of the amendment number 

1399 to S. 3394, 93d Congress, "the Foreign Assistance Act of 1974," which was introduced by Senator Nelson on June 6, 1974 (Cong. Record, S. 9851-S. 9858).

I have discussed this amendment and the statement made by Senator Nelson upon its introduction with personnel in the Defense Security Assistance Agency, and this memorandum presents our combined comments. 

In pertinent part, Senator Nelson stated to the Senate that "the total number of reports that would have been submitted for congressional consideration in fiscal year 1973 had the Nelson amendment been in effect is approximately 30." 

That number came from a Library of Congress memorandum, printed at page S. 

9855, which was based on answers to questions posed to your office by the Library of Congress.

In the context of Senator Nelson's proposed Amendment to the Foreign Assistance Act, it is now apparent that there was a misunderstanding among your office, the Library of Congress, and his office as to the scope of the inquiry. 

Consequently, the number of 30 sales instances recorded in the Library of Congress memorandum is inaccurate in the context of his amendment. 

In particular, question No. 3 was understood as having reference to single sales transactions of $25 million or more each in a country which had already

ད་ T. AD PAST Ja purchased a cumulative total of $50 million. We now understand that question in the context of the amendment as having reference to sales transactions of any dollar amount which caused cumulative sales to any country to reach thresholds of any multiple of $25 million in excess of $50 million, i.e., $75 million, $100 million, $125 million, $150 million, etc. The estimated answer to that different question is 57 sales instances. The answer is an estimate inasmuch as the computer data base is not structured in such a way as to permit us to retrieve the actual number. For example, a single $35 million sales case might have crossed only one threshold figure or, on the other hand, it might have crossed two threshold figures, e.g., from $70 million to $105 million. Parenthetically, it is noted that if the amendment were so drafted as to require all sales cases for each country to be reported to the Congress after passing the threshold aggregate of $50 million for each such country, the estimate of the reports that would have been required during the fiscal year 1973 for sales transactions is 1,002. 

Further, with respect to all three questions, the Library of Congress neglected to ask about FMS credits and guaranties as distinguished from sales. 

As to question No. 1. the records show that during the fiscal year 1973 there were two interim credit agreements (the first fiscal year in which we made interim credit agreements and hence not necessarily representative of later fiscal years), four credit agreements, and three guaranties, which each involve an amount of $25 million or more. Such credit agreements or guaranties in any particular fiscal year might or might not be duplicative of the previous answer to question No. 1 of 19 sales transactions of $25 million each or more. For example, a credit or a guaranty agreement of $25 million may be used (a) to finance wholly a single FMS agreement of $25 million, a number of separate FMS agreements which aggregate $25 million, or a combination of FMS and commercial agreements which aggregate $25 million; or (b) to finance partially a single FMS agreement aggregating in excess of $25 million, a number of FMS agreements which aggregate in excess of $25 million, or a combination of FMS and commercial agreements which aggregate in excess of $25 million. Also, since an interim credit agreement is superseded in due course by a credit agreement and a guaranty agreement, any data relating to an interim credit agreement of $50 million or more might be duplicative of the separate credit agreement and/or guaranty agreement data, depending on their respective amounts. 

Insofar as concerns question No. 2, the addition of credits and guaranties does not change our prior answer that 11 countries purchased $50 million or more (cash and credit) during the fiscal year 1973.

With respect to question No. 3, the addition of credits and guaranties to the sales cases does increase the number of times that the incremental thresholds of $75 million, $100 million, $125 million, etc., was reached during the fiscal year. 

The estimate of that additional number, which might be duplicative in part for the reasons expressed above, is 14; the total is thus approximately 71 with respect to question No. 3. 

Thus, the outside limit of the number of sales, credit sales, and guaranties during the fiscal year 1973 which would have been reported to the Congress had the Nelson Amendment been in effect in 110, rather than 30, i.e., question No. 1, 28; question No. 2, 11; and question No. 3, 71.

In passing, I should point out that although we are able on au after-thefact basis to retrieve estimates of the factual information Senator Nelson has requested, it does not appear to us that the amendment as drafted can be administered in a practical fashion or that the reports which would be required by the amendment would necessarily be meaningful to the Congress. Specifically, the amendment raises questions in our minds in the following respects: 

In the operation of the foreign military sales program, a number of offers of sale are made upon request of foreign countries which are never accepted by the foreign countries. Offers may be outstanding for periods of from 30-90 days before acceptance or rejection. Are offers "proposed" sales within the meaning of the amendment? If so, which offer must be reported to the Congress-the offer which would, if accepted, cause a threshold figure to be reached or the offer which would upon acceptance, cause a threshold figure to be reached only if all prior pending offers to that country were also accepted prior to acceptance of the reported offer? If the latter, suppose that the reported offer is accepted prior to one or more of the previously pending unreported offers? In either event, which offer must be reported to the Congress if more than one offer is made on the same day to a country by one or more of the three military departments and any one of them would, upon acceptance, cause the threshold

to be reached? Further, what are the legal implications under the amendment if a reported offer, which is not disapproved by the Congress, is not thereafter accepted by the foreign country, e.g., would offers made thereafter be exempt from the reporting requirement until the next threshold level is reached or must implementation of all subsequent cases be held up until the passed-by threshold is in fact satisfied by an accepted offer which goes through the review process? 

Similar operational problems might also arise if the amendment is applicable only to offers which have already been accepted, e.g., if more than one offer is accepted on the same day by a foreign country and two or more of those accepted offers would each cause a reporting threshold to be reached. Further, contrary to the Senator's assumption that a 30-day Congressional review period prior to implementation of a sales contract would not cause serious interference with normal procedures, there are many instances in which the letting of the implementing production contract is time-critical, e.g., to prevent interruption of a production line, to get the advantage of a price quote which is good only for a specified time, etc.

Finally, even assuming that these operational problems could be overcome, it might well be that the case which caused a threshold level to be exceeded is of no significance either to the Executive Branch or to the Congress, i.e., that particular case may be for a small amount of money for items such as spare parts or consumables, or for training, or for routine repair and overhaul serv ices. Admittedly, the threshold sale might be a major one of significance not only to the United States but also to other arms export countries. But in that event, once the detailed terms are made public as a consequence of the review procedures, it is not inconceivable that another arms export country might seek, for political or economic reasons, to persuade the purchasing country to withdraw its acceptance of our offer and to purchase a substitute weapons system on better terms from that other country. Consequently, since neither the United States nor the purchasing country would be legally bound by the sales contract during the review period. Congressional debate of the sale under review might well turn out to be on a moot issue. 

There is also an apparent misapprehension as to the scope of the reports required to be made to the Congress under section 657 of the Foreign Assistance Act and under the Hathaway Amendment to section 414 of the Mutual Security Act of 1954. In the Senator's statement at page S. 9851 of the Congressional 

Record, he alleges that those reports include "data only on commercial sales which are approximately one-eighth of total American arms sales abroad" since the government-to-government sales "do not require an export license." 

In fact, government-to-government arms sales are exempt from the export license requirement only in those instances where the United States government actually effects delivery and transfer of title outside the United States. In the majority of our government-to-government arms sales, delivery and transfer of title occurs in the United States and the purchasing country is required to obtain an export license. It may be that this misapprehension as to the requirement for export licenses for government-to-government arms sales arises from the dollar difference between the amounts reported to the Congress under the sections referred to above and DOD reports on foreign military sales. A major reason for that difference, however, is that our reports on foreign military sales are on an order basis whereas the other reports are on an export, i.e.. delivery, basis and there is, of necessity, a lag between the time an order is placed and the time the items ordered are manufactured and delivered. Further, it should be noted that the section 657 (a) (4) report on exports of "significant" defense articles is required to cover all such items irrespective of whether exported under an export license.

With respect to Senator Nelson's contention that there is no statutory re quirement to ensure that Congress receives up-to-date information on foreign military sales, his attention should be called to section 35(b) of the Foreign Military Sales Act. In accordance with that section, the Congressional Presentation Document for the fiscal year 1975, which has been furnished to the two authorizing committees and to the two appropriation committees, contains at pages 84-86 our forecast for the fiscal year 1975 for FMS cash orders, FMS credits and guaranties, and of commercial transactions. 

As to the "waiver" provision of the amendment, the 30-day limitation on the duration of the waiver--when combined with the 30-day Congressional review period after lapse of the waiver-could prove to be substantially detrimental to the national interest of the United States. For example, if the

H TX

TA amendment had been in force at the time of the October war in the Middle East and a waiver made by the President at the outset of the war, it is not inconceivable that the Arab belligerents would, in the knowledge that no significant arms sales could be made to Israel by the United States Government after the end of the 30-day waiver for the succeeding 30 days, have refused a cease-fire or that Israel, because of the impending 30-day embargo period, would have substantially increased the scale of the hostilities during the first 30 days. I note in this connection that the Congressional review period cannot be shortened except by a motion to discharge filed by an opponent of a proposed sale.

Senator Nelson's statement that Congress and the public were not timely informed of the Administration's intention to resume military sales to Ecuador by implication charges a failure to implement the law. That implication is in error. As you know, the Presidential Determination restoring the elig ibility of Ecuador for foreign military sales was made on January 21, 1974, was promptly reported to the Chairman of the Senate Foreign Relations Committee, as required by law, and was printed in the Federal Register on 

February 11, 1974.

U.S. MILITARY ASSISTANCE TO AFRICA 

Mr. DIGGS. Please delineate all U.S. military sales and assistance to Africa (proposed assistance as well as assistance over the past year), as this does not seem to be mentioned in your statement. 

Admiral PEET. I will concentrate first on what we did during fiscal year 1974. 

We arranged Credit Agreements totalling $20 million for four African countries as follows: Ethiopia, $11 million; Morocco, $3 million; Tunisia, $2.5 million and

Zaire, $3.5 million. The grant aid program for Africa totalled $13.98 million, the bulk of it ($11.3 million) going to Ethiopia. Tunisia received $1.2 million; and the balance, to cover training, went to six other countries. There were FMS cash sales of $7.5 million to Morocco, Nigeria, Tunisia and Zaire. Commercial sales to African countries were $5.5 million for the same period. 

In fiscal year 1975, we plan credit sales of $24.5 million to Africa and anticipate that cash sales will be on the order of $15.8 million. Based on prior year activities, it is expected that commercial sales to Africa will reach $13.8 million. 

SOUTH AFRICA: AN ARMS EMBARGO? 

Mr. DIGGS. What does the U.S. plan to do in complying with the arms embargo with South Africa? Have any non-military items which can be used for military purposes been sold to South Africa?

Admiral PEET. Ever since the UN Resolution of an Arms Embargo against the 

Republic of South Africa in 1963, the United States has refrained from military cooperation with South Africa in accordance with the pledge we made to the United Nations through Ambassador Stevenson on August 3, 1963. Accordingly, the Department of Defense makes no sales of military equipment to the Republic of South Africa.

In addition, the Foreign Military Sales Act, as amended, requires a Presidential Determination be made in order to provide a basis for sales of U.S. military equipment or training to any country. No such determination has been made for the 

Republic of South Africa, and none is contemplated. 

As for nonmilitary items, export licenses to U.S. industry are controlled by the U.S. Department of Commerce. We are informed by that Department that all such items are subjected to pre-licensing investigations as to their end-use, and licenses are restricted to items intended for civilian purposes only.

DIEGO GARCIA 

Mr. DIGGS. There has been no mention made of Diego Garcia in your statement. 

What is U.S. policy to be concerning an American base there? What military assistance would be made in connection with this policy? 

Admiral PEET. The Administration has requested a total of $32.3 million for additional construction of military facilities on the small British island of Diego Garcia. There is currently a communications facility on the island. Implementation of plans to enlarge the harbor, lengthen the runway, increase fuel storage capacity, and expand the available quarters and other facilities would enhance our capability to periodically deploy military forces into the Indian Ocean area and maintain them without relying heavily on the littoral states for support and assistance. There is, however, no military assistance of any kind being contemplated or offered in connection with this requested authorization. 

CONVERSATION WITH SOUTH AFRICAN MINISTER

Was the topic of military assistance to South Africa discussed and how was it resolved? Please provide any transcripts or reports of these meetings. What are your specific responsibilities in the area of cordinating defense strategy? (The information requested was supplied but is classified and therefore is retained in the committee files.) 

DEFENSE COOPERATION: UNITED STATES AND SOUTH AFRICA 

Mr. DIGGS. Please explain and list all areas of defense cooperation between the 

United States and South Africa. Please explain the extent to which the United 

States gave assistance contributing toward the opening of a $21 million communications complex near Capetown by the South African Navy. 

Admiral PEET. Since 1963. the United States has maintained a comprehensive arms embargo against South Africa, with the exception of contracts ante dating the embargo. Defense cooperation between the United States and South 

Africa is primarily limited to (a) a USAF tracking station near Johannesburg. established in 1960, which is the terminal tracking station on the USAF's South Atlantic Test Range; (b) a U.S./S.A. exchange of unclassified maps and aeronautical charts and reciprocal reproduction of each country's hydrographic charts of coastal waters; (c) an exchange of military attachés; and (d) a U.S. 

Navy program of collecting magnetic information in the Southern Hemisphere by specially instrumented aircraft. The United States has provided no assistance toward the communications complex near Capetown, South Africa. 

COMMUNICATIONS EQUIPMENT TO SOUTH AFRICA 

Mr. DIGGS. How much communications equipment does the United States export to South Africa each year? What is the end use of this communications equipment?

Admiral PEET. Since the imposition of the arms embargo, the Department of 

Defense has not provided any communications equipment to South Africa. Commercial sales may be licensed for export by the Departments of State and Commerce, but only when the purpose and end use is for nonmilitary functions. 

AIRCRAFT TO SOUTH AFRICA 

Mr. DIGGS. To what extent does the United States allow its aviation industry to sell South Africa aircraft it declares nonmilitary? Please list all such nonmilitary items, and what is the end use by South Africa of this aircraft?

Admiral PEET. The Department of Defense does not assist South Africa in its commercial purchases of nonmilitary aircraft from the aviation industry of the United States. Nonmilitary aircraft sales permitted to South Africa are strictly controlled within the licensing jurisdiction of the Department of Commerce. 

That Department has informed us such licensing is subject to careful prelicense checks as to end use and has been limited to light civilian helicopters, light civilian aircraft, and larger civilian passenger transports and commerical cargo transports for civilian purposes.

INDIAN OCEAN POLICY 

Mr. DIGGS. The United States' Indian Ocean policy is planned and developed in 

DoD's International Security Affairs office. What is the current status of such strategy?

Admiral PEET. Last November, Secretary of Defense Schlesinger announced that the U.S. intended to return to a policy of more frequent and more regular deployments to the Indian Ocean area. That policy has been implemented in the succeeding months by a series of deployments from the Pacific Fleet, including both carriers and surface combatant units. These deployments are in addition to the three ships of Middle East Force, a small naval command which has operated in the Persian Gulf and Indian Ocean areas for nearly a quarter of a century.

In support of this policy of periodic deployments, the FY 75 military construction budget includes a request for funds to expand the facilities on Diego Garcia, as I mentioned previously. The requested additional support facilities on Diego Garcia would improve our capability to maintain forces in the Indian Ocean by reducing the length of the logistical "tail" which now extends over 4,000 miles to Subic Bay in the Philippines. However, there is no intent to base any operational forces at Diego Garcia, and the facilities there would not imply any given level of U.S. military presence. On the contrary, as Secretary 

Schlesinger pointed out in testimony before the House Armed Services Committee, "To development of further facilities at Diego Garcia provides us only with the option of moving into the Indian Ocean if the need should arise." 

NATO AND DEFENSE PLAN FOR SOUTH AFRICA 

Mr. DIGGS. A NATO official has recently admitted that NATO has issued orders or directives to SACLANT to begin secret contingency planning for the defense of southern Africa.¹ What is the nature of these plans? Why has the Defense

Department denied that this planning has occurred or that directives have been given for this planning while NATO has admitted to this planning? To what extent has a commitment been made by any NATO members to defend southern Africa?

Admiral PEET. The apparent difference between the Department of Defense answer to questions posed and the statements attributed to the NATO officials is caused by a substantive difference in the questions raised in each case. 

In the question originally posed to the DoD, it was alleged that in June 1973 NATO instructed SACLANT to draw up plans for a force to stand ready to assist South Africa. The DoD replied that there have been no NATO instructions to 

SACLANT or any other NATO Command for the planning of such assistance to the Republic of South Africa or any other country in southern Africa. That is still correct.

On the other hand, the questions answered by the NATO official addressed the fact that the NATO Defense Planning Committee (DPC) authorized SACLANT 

to undertake contingency planning for protection of shipping and sea-lanes outside of NATO's boundaries, including the South Atlantic. This authorization involved no country or land areas. In authorizing the sea-lanes protection planning, the DPC specified that any such plans: (1) would require approval by the 

NATO Military Committee; (2) would not be implemented or exercised without 

DPC approval; (3) would give special attention to protection of oil supply routes; and (4) should in no way be interpreted as removal of NATO's southern 

Atlantic maritime boundary nor as acceptance by individual NATO nations of additional maritime commitments. SACLANT has meticulously adhered to those constraints and no non-NATO nation has been contacted relative to such planning. 

Accordingly, the Department of Defense reaffirms that there has been no planning involving a defense of southern Africa or any country in it, and there have been no NATO commitments concerning a defense of southern Africa.

Chairman MORGAN. Admiral, I have some questions which I am going to submit to you to answer for the record. [The following information was supplied in response to questions submitted by Chairman Morgan:] SALES OF NOTES TO THE FEDERAL FINANCING BANK 

Mr. MORGAN. Admiral, section 10 of the proposed bill contains several amendments to the Foreign Military Sales Act including authority to sell promissory notes to the Federal Financing Bank.

What is the purpose of selling promissory notes to the Federal Financing Bank?

Will this in any way increase the size of the military sales program? 

Admiral PEET. The Federal Financing Bank is a corporation established by an act of Congress last year-P.L. 93-224-as an instrumentality of the United 

States Government. The Secretary of the Treasury is the Chairman of the 

Board of Directors of the Bank. The purpose of creating the Bank, as stated in the Act, is to assure coordination of federal and federally assisted borrowing programs and to assure that such borrowing is financed in a manner least disruptive of private financial markets and institutions. 

Section 6 of the act provides that the Bank is authorized to purchase and sell any obligation which is issued, sold, or guaranteed by a federal agency. 

It further provides that any federal agency which is authorized to issue, sell, or guarantee any obligation is authorized to issue or sell such obligations directly to the Bank. On its face, accordingly, the language of section 6 of the act would appear to supersede section 24 of the Foreign Military Sales Act, enacted in 1968, which excludes U.S. Government agencies from obtaining guaranties under section 24. However, since repeals by implication are not normally to be presumed, we think it prudent to request the Congress to amend section 24 of the Foreign Military Sales Act to conform with the later language of the 

Federal Financing Bank Act of 1973.

The reason for the exclusion of guaranties to U.S. Government agencies in section 24 of the Foreign Military Sales Act was the consensus in the Congress in 1968 to discontinue the pre-1968 procedure under which the so-called "country" loans were made by the Department of Defense and the Export- 

Import Bank. Under the "country" procedure, DOD advanced credit to a purchasing country with funds it obtained from the Export-Import Bank; the Bank was assigned the repayment rights on the credit extended; and the 

Department of Defense, through its guaranty, protected the Export-Import Bank from default by the purchaser. The congressionally perceived defect in this procedure was that these loans were not identified on the books of the Export-Import Bank by the name of the country concerned; rather, the books of the Export-Import Bank showed these loans as being made only to "country a". 

Neither we nor the Treasury have any contemplation of reverting to this abandoned "country r" loan procedure. Rather, it is proposed that the Federal 

Financing Bank would sign loan agreements directly with the country concerned, and that DOD would issue its guaranty to the Federal Financing Bank. 

This procedure would be no different than the procedure which has obtained since 1968 under which DOD issues its guarantees to private banks. Further, the direct loans made by the Federal Financing Bank would not involve any cost to the taxpayer. The Federal Financing Bank would obtain funds to finance these DOD guaranteed loans by issuing its own obligations to private financial institutions. The end result would be the same as if the loans extended to the foreign countries had been made in the first instance directly by the private financial contributions.

The interest rate charged by the Federal Financing Bank to the foreign countries would be set by the Bank at a rate which covers the cost of the money borrowed by the Bank from private financial institutions on its own obligations and its handling costs. In addition, the Bank is authorized to charge commitment fees adequate to cover all expenses. 

In summary, it is expected that the participation of the Bank would result in lower interest cost to foreign countries, at no expense to the federal taxpayer: would bring about greater participation by private financial institutions; and would assure that the FMS guaranty program is implemented in a manner which is fully coordinated with the debt management operations of the Treasury. 

Under existing procedures, in contrast, because of the current high prime interest rate and the substantial spread between the going rate for Treasury and other federal agency obligations on the one hand and FMS-guaranteed obliga tions on the other hand. recent borrowings during fiscal year 1974 by foreign countries from private financial institutions under FMS guaranty have been at interest rates averaging 10.85 percent. Moreover, for various reasons (political, economic and financial) the number of private financial institutions willing to make such guaranteed loans has been very small during fiscal year 1974 ranging from a high of nine bidders in the case of one country to a low of one bidder in the cases of two countries-despite the fact that approximately 400 banks were solicited by the Treasury to bid on such loans and that the solicitations were also published in the Federal Register.

மன 22 STE Insofar as concerns the amendment we have also requested to subsection (b) of section 24 of the Foreign Military Sales Act, we have no present plans, in view of current market conditions, of selling to the Federal Financing Bank, or indeed to private banks, the promissory notes received by DOD from foreign countries under credits directly extended by DOD under section 23 of the act. 

At some future date, however, it might be in the best interests of the United States to sell such notes in order to raise revenues for the Treasury. In that event, the Federal Financing Bank could prove to be a useful means of securing such revenues from private banks. Any such sales-whether directly to the public by DOD or indirectly to the public through the Federal Financing Bankwould in no way affect any current fiscal year ceiling on foreign military sales or credits under the act. As provided for in sections 24 (c) and 37(b) of the act, the proceeds from the sale of DOD of such notes to the Federal Finance ing Bank (less the amount required for the guaranty reserve) would go to the miscellaneous receipts of the Treasury. 

RESERVE GUARANTY REQUIREMENT 

Mr. MORGAN. You are requesting that the reserve guarantee requirement be lowered from 25 percent of the principal amount of the contractual liability to 

10 percent of that amount. What is the purpose of this request?

Admiral PEET. Our history of repayment for the guaranty program has been excellent; there have been no defaults in repayments in the history of the program. We feel that we now have sufficient experience to indicate that a reserve of 10 percent of each guaranteed loan is sufficient to cover the risk of each individual loan. The continuance of requesting 25 percent for this purpose therefore would result in an unnecessary inflation of the annual budget. 

Further, by lowering the guaranty reserve requirement we obtain additional financing flexibility during any given fiscal year. 

RESERVE REQUIREMENT FUND 

Mr. MORGAN. Section 24 (c) of existing law requires that 25 percent of the principal amount of the contractual liability be set aside as a reserve against default. Any funds in excess of this amount are required to be paid into the 

General Fund of the Treasury. In this bill you are requesting that the reserve requirement be reduced to 10 percent of the contractual liability, but are at the same time asking for authority to maintain the reserve guarantee fund at the full principal amount of the contractual liability of all outstanding guarantees. 

It seems to me that this could result in a substantial increase in the reserve guarantee fund since the authority would exist to maintain a fund at the full principal amount of all outstanding guarantees instead of 25 percent of that amount. What is the purpose of this request and why is it necessary? 

Admiral PEET. Your question, sir, proceeds upon the erroneous premise that the President's proposed bill constitutes a request for an increase in the guaranty reserve fund. In fact, the amount of the reserve fund would slowly decline as a percentage of the total principal amount of contractual liabilities related to all outstanding guaranties issued since the Foreign Military Sales Act was enacted in 1968, assuming a continuation of the FMS guaranty program in future years at a level comparable to the current level. Only if the FMS guaranty program were sharply curtailed or terminated in the future would the possibility provided for in the President's bill to which you refer occur. 

To illustrate this point, the following assumptions and estimated figures may be used. At the close of fiscal year 1974, approximately $948 million in outstanding principal of private loans guarantied under the FMSA since 1968 were on the books, for which a 25 percent reserve fund of $237 million was obligated. 

Approximately $150 million of principal should be repaid during each of the next 5 years (about 15%-16% of the $948 million, assuming the average private loan repayment period is between 6 and 7 years). Assume also that $352 million in guaranties are issued in fiscal year 1975 as the President proposes, and that $400 million in guaranties are issued in each of fiscal years 1976, 1977, 1978, and 1979 (i.e.. an FMS guaranty program level comparable to the current level). If the 

President's bill is enacted, approximately $35.3 million will be obligated for the reserve fund in fiscal year 1975 and $40 million would be obligated in each of the following 4 fiscal years. TRAINING OF CIVILIAN AND MILITARY STUDENTS IN THE UNITED STATES Mr. MORGAN. Section 510 of the Foreign Assistance Act limits the number of foreign military personel eligible for training in the United States annually to the number of civilian students brought in under the Mutual Educational and Cultural Exchange Act of 1961 in the preceding year. a. How many civilian students were brought in last year and how many military trainees will be brought in in fiscal year 1975? 

Admiral PEET. We estimate that, in fiscal year 1974, 5,494 civilian students will be brought in under the Mutual Educational and Cultural Exchange Act of 1961. There are 4,835 military trainees scheduled to undergo training in the 

United States under the military assistance program in fiscal year 1975. b. What has been the impact of this provision of law on the military training program?

Admiral PEET. Except for the initial fiscal year 1970 when this provision of the law was introduced, necessitating a reduction in the already scheduled number of students in order to fall within the newly established ceiling, the provision has not had an adverse impact on the program. 

REPEAL OF CEILING ON LATIN AMERICAN MILITARY SECURITY ASSISTANCE 

Mr. MORGAN. Section 10 (a) would repeal the ceiling of $150 million in military assistance, sales guarantees, credits and vessel transfers to Latin America. 

Last year the Congress agreed to exclude cash sales from counting against the ceiling. What is the reasoning behind repeal of the ceiling with respect to Latin America?

Admiral PEET. The repeal of the ceiling on Latin America would abolish a legislative restriction [security deletion]. Latin American countries, because of strong historic ties with the United States, desire to satisfy their military needs from us. Our ability to plan for and respond to legitimate requests for military equipment is restricted by a regional ceiling. 

DEFENSE ARTICLES PURCHASED BY LATIN AMERICAN COUNTRIES Mr. MORGAN. What quantity and type of defense articles did Latin American countries purchase for cash in fiscal year 1975 from the United States? 

Admiral PEET. Since fiscal year 1975 has not started, I assume you mean fiscal year 1974.

Total cash sales to Latin America in fiscal year 1974 were $119.8 million. These sales consisted of F-5E aircraft, destroyers, submarines, 105mm howitzers, 155 mm howitzers, T-41 aircraft, radar, landing vehicles, amored personnel carriers, recovery vehicles, torpedoes, ship overhauls, ships spares, aircraft overhaul, aircraft spares, engineering equipment, communications equipment, ammunition and training. 

Mr. MORGAN. What quantity and type were purchased from other countries either for cash or credit? 

Admiral PEET. During 1973 Latin American countries purchased over $425 million worth of military equipment on credit or cash terms. The purchasers and sellers and the value of their contracts follow: [Security deletion.]

AFRICAN CEILING 

Mr. MORGAN. Section 10 also requests authority to waive the regional limitation of $40 million on the amount of assistance and sales that can be provided to African countries. Has the United States ever provided over $40 million in military assistance and sales to African countries? As you remember, the Congress deleted the authority last year. Why are you asking for it to be restored?

Admiral PEET. Yes; pursuant to the previous waiver authority under section 

33 (C) of the Foreign Military Sales Act, as amended, the President made the necessary determination that it was important to the security of the United States to waive the $40 million ceiling in fiscal year 1971. 

We believe that the Congress should consider reinstating the waiver authority in order to give the President the flexibility to respond to stiuations where it would be important to the security of the United States to provide limited assistance. Although U.S. policy continues to attempt to discourage unnecessary defense expenditures for African countries, experience has shown that being unresponsive to reasonable military requirements has not necessarily resulted in reducing defense expenditures; the countries frequently turn elsewhere for their

requirements and often purchase more expensive and advanced equipment than originally sought from the United States. Some of these countries are increasingly turning to the United States, particularly those with whom we have had a military relationship, those whose economic growth is facilitating a weaning from their former colonial relationships, and those where we have important strategic interests. The African ceiling was established more than 7 years ago, and when viewed against inflationary trends since its inception-let alone the evolution of U.S. interests and relationships-is not reflective today of the legitimate defense requirements of those countries or U.S. interests. In fiscal year 1974 we had to seriously constrain the total program at about $39 million and are planning at about the same level in fiscal year 1975. [Security deletion.] In order to insure that we would have the flexibility to increase the size of those programs if it was found to be important to U.S. security we need to have the waiver authority restored.

Chairman MORGAN. Thank you, gentlemen.

FISCAL YEAR 1975 FOREIGN ASSISTANCE REQUEST WEDNESDAY, JUNE 19, 1974 HOUSE OF REPRESENTATIVES, COMMITTEE ON FOREIGN AFFAIRS, Washington, D.C. 

The committee met at 10:18 a.m. in room 2172, Rayburn House 

We will proceed today with our hearings on the President's foreign assistance request for fiscal year 1975. 

Our witness today is Adm. Noel Gayler. Admiral Gayler is the 

Commander in Chief of our Pacific Forces. 

Admiral, you have a prepared statement, and you may either summarize your statement or read it, as you wish.

STATEMENT OF ADM. NOEL GAYLER, U.S. NAVY, COMMANDER IN CHIEF, PACIFIC Admiral GAYLER.  

I think the statement is available to the members and has been for a couple of days, so if I may, I will just touch briefly on the principal points.

Chairman MORGAN. Your statement will then be made a part of the permanent record. 

Admiral GAYLER. Thank you, sir.

Then, of course, I will stand ready to answer questions after that. 

If the committee is interested, I am prepared to talk to the total Pacific position and strategy as well as directly to the security assistance aspects.

The first point that I would like to make is that I am very glad to be here, particularly because I think there is a very important relationship between security assistance in the Pacific countries and our total national position in the Pacific, and the first point that my statement makes lies in that area. 

I also would like to say that it has been a great pleasure to me to meet some of the members of this committee in my headquarters in Hawaii, and I would hope that any time any of the members come through there I would have that opportunity again. 

The first thing that I touch on then is what our interests are in the Pacific. These, of course, run to peaceful trade, control of the vital sea lines of communication and air lines of communication and peaceful evolution of the countries there people often say "stability." I don't like to use that word very much because it implies a status quo, and in some of those countries the status quo is not what it might be. We (349)

would like to see evolution, but of a peaceful rather than a warlike kind, and it is particularly important in the interest of our national security that the area not become dominated by any one power. 

It has been our consistent view that our presence, which is military, political, economic, and even sociological, all together is a good thing. 

And the Security Assistance complements that presence, and that is the next point that I wish to make.

SECURITY ASSISTANCE: HIGHLIGHTS IN PACIFIC COMMAND 

Then I talked to some of the highlights of the program in the Pacific Command Region as we have experienced them, and I think it is useful to talk about the countries which are sort of "graduates" of our assistance program. We can look back and see what it did for them, or near "graduates"-the countries that unfortunately still have combat within their borders-and the countries at peace. 

SECURITY ASSISTANCE "GRADUATES" 

In talking to the graduates, as I call it, I place Japan, and Korea, and the Republic of China in that category. Japan, of course, is perhaps the most important of our allies in the Pacific. It is a very weighty nation in terms of its economic potential, in terms of its political potential, in terms of its mass. The Japanese certainly have achieved a great comeback and a great success since the end of the war through a combination of their total economic and political policy, their enlightened leadership, and hard work. They also are, however, a military assistance "graduate"; and without assigning too much importance to the help that we gave them, I think it has been an important component of bringing Japan forward into the strong, stable, and peacefully inclined Japan that we see today. I look for a maturing and mutually useful security relationship with Japan, which is going to be very helpful to us, and we certainly will be happy to enlarge on that if the committee is interested.

In Korea there is a somewhat similar story. My statement goes through some of that history, talks about the 5-year modernization plan-what our hopes were for it and how it now stands-and makes particularly the point that the modernization of the Republic of Korea armed forces has been a major consideration in preserving the armistice, in providing the stability necessary for their remarkable and continued economic growth and in essence, the point that assistance and modernization drive toward stability in that country. 

The Republic of China (Taiwan) I think of as being another success story with respect to military assistance. This is a graduate country. There is a modest training program of $400,000, but outside of that, the grant aid ended in fiscal 1974, and the Republic of China has developed capabilities to repair and rehabilitate facilities, to coproduce aircraft and helicopters and is doing this through a mix of local financing and foreign military sales credit. So I think that they are increasingly able to take on the burden of their own defense. 

PROGRAM IN INDOCHINA 

I don't talk very much about the assistance to Vietnam since this is not a program under the Foreign Assistance Act, but I would say-

​VA and I am prepared to enlarge on this-that the continued U.S. support is, in my judgment, an essential element in the capability of South Vietnam to defend itself and in the prospects for a permanent peace.

The Cambodian assistance, I think it would be correct to say, is vital to the continued existence of the Khmer Government. They have made great progress. The forecasts of many people last fall that they would not be able to survive the loss of direct U.S. military support, particularly by bombing, have not been borne out. They have had their losses as well as their successes. I think that we are entitled to believe that they have defended themselves successfully during this last dry season, and that our general objective of helping them to be in a position for the negotiated peace, which I am sure all Khmers really want, has been successful. I am particularly happy about the success of our supply and support operations. 

In Laos, of course, there is a political settlement. The country is still in the state of flux; it is still shaking down. It is too early, in my judgment to make a definitive reassessment of the degree of continued support to the neutralist and government armed forces necessary to maintain the right balance, political and military, in that country so that it can remain truly neutral. The disappointment, of course, is that the North Vietnamese have not seen fit to carry out their part of to bargain to leave the country, but I think it is too early to assess fully the significance of all of that. 

PHILIPPINES AND THAILAND 

In discussing the Philippines, relatively modest support there has been helpful to that government and, I think, should be regarded in the light of our perceptions with the Philippines of our mutual interest in security and stability in that area of the world. I think it is the development of that mutual interest and mutual understanding which is the real underpinning of our absolutely vital base setup and our capability to protect the long sea lines our communications as well as stabilizing that part of the world. 

The political situation in Thailand is in a state of considerable flux since their quasi-revolution. The government of that country is still evolving. In my judgment, however, the basic Thai need, or the basic 

Thai perception of our common interest, still persists, and the ability to work with the Thais with an evolution of our presence, I think looks pretty good.

TRAINING PROGRAMS 

We have modest training programs in a number of countries: 

Afghanistan, $200,000; India, $100,000; Malaysia, $285,000; Nepal, $35.000; Pakistan, $280,000; and Sri Lanka, $15,000. I think it is important to keep these modest programs going. They improve the military professionalism in those countries and they retain the U.S. influence. I think we get high dividends from a relatively small investment.

PACIFIC COMMAND: RAPIDLY CHANGING SITUATION 

Looking at the command as a whole, of course, we are seeing a rapidly changing situation. Our allied and friendly capabilities are in-

creasing and there is a shift from grant aid to foreign military sales and sales credits that help offset reduced grant aid. I welcome this; I think it is a good thing from the standpoint of those countries and of our own. The important thing, of course, is not to be disruptive or precipitous in going from one system to another, but to take full account of the interests of those countries as well as our own. 

Finally, I will touch very briefly on the point that I have a lot of association with. Planners in these various countries on the whole do their best, I think, to make good sensible plans from their standpoint, so they have to rely on a certain stability in what they can expect from us in the way of assistance. So, when it is consistent with policy and consistent with resources, I would like to make a strong plea for reliability, if you will, in the assistance programs as we afford them. 

That is a very brief summary of my prepared statement, Mr. 

Chairman, and I am ready to answer any questions and also to enlarge on the general situation if it interests any of the members. 

[The prepared statement of Admiral Gayler follows:] STATEMENT BY ADM. NOEL GAYLER, U.S. NAVY, COMMANDER IN CHIEF, PACIFIC Chairman Morgan and Members of the Committee: I welcome this opportunity to discuss with this distinguished Committee the Security Assistance Program in the Pacific Command for Fiscal Year 1975. I would like to cover my perceptions of America's role in the Asian/Pacific region, and the importance of Security Assistance in establishing a structure for peaceful evolution. 

U.S. ROLE IN ASIAN/PACIFIC REGION 

What are present U.S. interests in the Pacific? We want a peaceful Pacific area where all nations are free to develop and to trade with each other and the world. 

No country should be vulnerable to the use or threat of external force. We should play an active role in maintaining balance in the Pacific to prevent any hostile nation from establishing a preponderant position. 

A consistent and reliable Security Assistance Program is an important tool in reaching these goals. We do not want to become involved in the internal affairs of our Allies. The capability of Allied and friendly countries to counter local threats removes the need for direct involvement of American forces, and furthers peaceful change as against violent. Our presence and our Security 

Assistance Programs have made major contributions to stability in those Pacific countries that face internal or external threats, and have played an indispensable role in their economic and political growth. As you know, that growth has been impressive.

SECURITY ASSISTANCE IN THE PACIFIC COMMAND 

Let me review some of the highlights of the Security Assistance Program in the Pacific Command region. In talking about specific nations, I think these categories can be distinguished: military assistance program graduates, or near graduates; countries at war; and countries at peace. 

In the first category of successful military assistance graduates, or near graduates, I place Japan, Korea and the Republic of China. Those nations most intimately concerned with hostilities are South Vietnam, Cambodia and Laos. 

Finally, I'll touch briefly on the other nations; the Philippines, Indonesia, Thailand, Malaysia and Singapore.

Within thirty years of a military defeat in World War II, Japan has emerged as the third largest economy in the world and one of our most important allies in Asia. The Japanese have achieved their economic success through a combination of total economic and political policy, enlightened leadership, and hard work. 

Japan is a U.S. military assistance graduate. For the most part, our grant aid was no longer necessary after 1967. We have a strong and stable Japan peacefully inclined. I look for a maturing and mutually useful security relationship.

1 Part of this Japanese success story can be attributed to our military assistance. 

Japan should not be forgotten in considering the utility of the whole MAP. 

SOUTH KOREA 

Korea has a similar history. In the early fifties, it lay in ashes. After the 

1953 settlement there was a long period of bitter hostility, violence, and confrontation. Then recently there has been a limited North and South détente and some moves towards each other through talks. I can't predict what will happen next. What matters is the attitude of North Korea. It is unchanged politically under Kim Il Sung, and is the toughest kind of military dictatorship. 

I do know that our substantial assistance, coupled with South Korean deter mination and strength, has deterred aggression from the North and sparked economic growth to the point where South Korea is now approaching self reliance. The Five Year Modernization Plan has formed the basis for the Security Assistance Program since 1971. This year's budget request is for MAP, 

$161.5 million, and FMS, $52 million. It provides the ROK Air Force with additional modern tactical aircraft, modern air control systems and radar equipment. It also provides the ROK Navy with ships for a positive deterrent against infiltration from the sea by North Korea, and the naval marine forces with improved communications and ground combat support equipment. I think that modernization of ROK armed forces has been a major consideration in preserv ing the armistice, providing the stability necessary for continued growth, and the wherewithal to deal from a position of strength with North Korea in the changing international climate in Asia.

REPUBLIC OF CHINA ON TAIWAN 

The Republic of China on Taiwan is another success story. It has moved from grant materiel aid to sales and self-reliance. Except for a modest training program of $400,000, American grant aid ended in FY 1974. The Republic of China has developed impressive capabilities in repair and rehabilitation facilities, as well as co-production of F-5E fighter aircraft and UH-1H helicopters. The major cost of these programs is borne by the Republic of China through local financing and U.S. foreign military sales credit for United States equipment requirements. 

Let me now turn to countries where fighting still goes on, SOUTH VIETNAM 

In South Vietnam, Vietnamization has worked. We have replaced our armed forces with military assistance, without the loss of Vietnamese independence. 

North Vietnamese goals haven't changed, and thus the fighting continues. Talks remain deadlocked, and I see no early chances for a breakthrough. Since 1966, military assistance for South Vietnam has been funded through our own Service budgets. Since this is not a program under the Foreign Assistance Act, I will not deal with it in depth in this statement. The South Vietnamese efforts to conserve U.S. supplied war materiel have been persistent and successful. With continued American support, South Vietnam can defend itself against aggression. 

CAMBODIA 

Our logistics assistance to Cambodia has given it the means to resist aggression by the Khmer Communists supported by North Vietnam with men and materiel. 

Since the resumption of U.S. assistance in 1970, the Khmer Armed Forces have grown from a small, primarily ceremonial force of 35,000 to a partially trained combat force of about 200,000. Training provided the Khmer Armed Forces emphasizes effective maintenance and use of U.S. furnished equipment without 

U.S. assistance .The government does not have the money, materiel, and skill as yet to defend itself. Their armed forces are improving, and I believe will continue to improve. Continued American materiel and training support is essential for Cambodia's survival and the creation of conditions for an ultimate settlement. They are fighting for the survival of their traditional and peaceful way of life and their religion. They are doing far better than most prophets predicted when American bombing support ended last August 15. We are asking for $362.5 million for Cambodia in FY 1975. Without this assistance, I doubt the Khmer

Government would be able to survive. Most of the $362.5 million will be applied to ammunition, largely related to Khmer combat activity, with only a relatively small amount ear-marked for training and replacement of equipment lost in battle.

LAOS 

Laos is moving from war to peace. Our main objective for Security Assistance to Laos is to support a balanced force of sufficient size and strength to assure Laotian survival, independence, and neutrality. There is a cease-fire in 

Laos, and I don't expect renewed major fighting there. Our grant aid has made possible the survival of an undeveloped country. Continued assistance is needed to maintain a neutral Laos, bolster its economy, and develop the self-sufficiency needed for this little nation to stand alone and on stable terms with its neighbors. Our FY 75 Laos program identifies requirements of $85.2 million and is designed to stress self-sufficiency. The situation in Laos is rapidly evolving and requires our careful attention. 

In Southeast Asia, the line between peace and war is narrow and fragile. 

We want to strengthen it on the side of peace. 

THE PHILIPPINES 

In the Philippines, history has presented us with a special responsibility. Our bases there are vital because of their strategic location. There is no other place so well situated to protect our security interests. Replacement costs in any case would be staggering. Our aid has contributed to stability by supporting internal security needs and disaster relief. In its effort to move from grant aid to sales, the Philippine Government will make use of U.S. military sales credits during FY 75 to finance the planned M-16 rifle co-production venture. 

Other useful projects can be foreseen. This year's budget request is for $17.9 million. It's aimed at improving air, ground, and sea mobility, communications, and coastal patrol.

The Philippine Government has problems with insurgency, smuggling, and piracy, made especially troublesome by the fact that this country of 7,000 islands is spread over an area greater than 700,000 square miles. All services suffer from obsolescent equipment and poor maintenance facilities. 

Continued Security Assistance will encourage the further development of self-sufficiency on the part of the Armed Forces of the Philippines. They are working hard on it. They have the message that they must do it, and I think they feel they will be better off for being self-sufficient as soon as possible. THAILAND The Thais are concerned about their insurgency problem and North Vietnamese capabilities.

Our Security Assistance bolsters their defense, and manifests that the United States continues to value them as an ally. Thailand understands and appreciates the interrelationship of its self-defense with the military situation in the neighboring countries of Indochina: Laos, Cambodia, and Vietnam. 

We should understand that however unlikely the need to use them may be, the USAF capabilities based in Thailand add a major element of uncertainty to North Vietnam, and therefore an important deterrent to an all-out offensive. 

The $56 million budget request for Thailand covers replacement aircraft, combat tactical support vehicles, patrol boats, communications upgrade, and shop equipment to help the Thai Armed Forces develop self-sufficiency in aircraft/ automobile engine overhaul. Security Assistance to Thailand will help provide the Thais a capability to maintain internal security.

INDONESIA Indonesia, with 134 million people, rich in natural resources, lies astride strategic lines of communication between the Western Pacific and the Indian Ocean. 

Our Security Assistance is designed to assist Indonesia to achieve self-reliance without overextending its resources at a time when the government still grap ples with difficult economic problems. We together have put major emphasis on improving communications, and logistics and maintenance facilities. Introduc tion of military sales credit. now, helps in the transition from grant aid. Indonesia, hostile only a few years ago, is a friendly country today. The modest Secu-

SE 1 rity Assistance Program we've established there has made a major contribution to this friendly relationship.

The $22.7 million required for Indonesia in FY 75 provides needed vehicles and weapons. Priority is also placed in the maintenance of materiel furnished by the United States. Project INDOCOM, the nationwide communications network scheduled for completion in FY 77 and wholly funded by MAP, will for the first time enable the central government in Jakarta to communicate effectively throughout this 3,000 mile archipelago. This huge nation needs technology badly, and we have been helping. 

TRAINING PROGRAMS 

I would like to emphasize the importance of one part of the Security Assistance Program-training. We have grant aid training programs in Afghanistan ($200,000), India ($100,000), Malaysia ($285,000), Nepal ($35,000), Pakistan $280,000), and Sri Lanka ($15,000). These programs are helpful in two ways. 

They improve their military professionalism, and they retain U.S. influence. 

Experience shows that military training programs provide high dividends for a small investment.

Within the Pacific Command, we are witnessing a rapidly changing situation with regard to Security Assistance. Because of an increase in allied and friendly capabilities, there is a shift from grant aid to foreign military sales. Sales credits help offset reduced grant aid. Foreign military sales fill valid security requirements of our friends. The record of repayment of loans is excellent. But the basic benefits are not economic; they relate to security. The Security Assistance 

Program fosters regional stability. It builds self-reliance. Allied military capability increases while the need for U.S. military involvement decreases. Security 

Assistance also provides the earnest for necessary rights, authorizations, and facilities. It is useful for working both military and political problems together. American training assures friendly contact with Asian military, many of whom will be the leaders of tomorrow. 

We need a Security Assistance Program that our friends can count on. They must be able to plan effectively and integrate efficiently our assistance with their own efforts towards national security and economic growth. 

Chairman MORGAN. Thank you, Admiral. 

U.S. COMMITMENT: TIED TO FUNDING LEVELS? 

Admiral, I would like to ask a general question concerning the level of American assistance to countries in the Pacific area. Many people argue that if we make any substantial reductions in our assistance in these Asian countries they will interpret that as a sign that the United 

States is giving up on Asia.

Is this attitude fair to the United States, and what do we have to do to convince our friends in that area that we are still interested in their survival even if aid is cut some? I question whether it is wise to allow political interest to be measured in terms of how much military assistance we give. What is your view of this?

Admiral GAYLER. I think it does have great symbolic importance in some countries. You cannot generalize about so many diverse sovereign nations. I know personally all the chiefs of state on our side of the bamboo curtain in the area, together with the foreign ministers, defense ministers, and many other senior officials; I think their general concern is of the kind you have described. They are concerned that the 

United States may be losing interest in the area. They tend to overdraw conclusions from the redeployment of our own forces and interpret this as a political signal. I tell them,

No; it is not a political signal; it is not so intended. What we are doing is reacting to costs and force level problems that we have to take care of. 

However, it still gives the impression of U.S. disinterest and withdrawal.

The security assistance level is part of it too. In countries like 

Thailand and Indonesia, I think they do regard the level of security assistance as being a symptom or measure of U.S. interest, therefore, it too, has symbolic significance. 

JAPANESE DEFENSE FORCES 

Chairman MORGAN. I notice, Admiral, that on page 2 of your statement you refer to Japan as a success story and a graduate of U.S. military assistance. You speak of a mutually useful security relationship between Japan and the United States in the future. 

Now, of course, under the Japanese Constitution Japan has only a rather small defense force. But some Japanese and some American military leaders believe that Japan should increase her forces, which would be of help to us. What is your attitude about an increased 

Japanese defense force?

Admiral GAYLER. Of course, it is something to which I have given a great deal of thought. I think that what we want to do is to work with the Japanese to develop a mature security relationship along lines that meets Japanese needs and perceptions as well as our own needs and perceptions. We have some troubles having to do with language. 

We also have some troubles in understanding each other for many cultural reasons, but very fortunately we have a great deal in common. 

We are both interested in the security and the stability of that part of the world. We are both interested in the security of the long sea and air lines of communication, which are absolutely vital to Japan, and extremely important to the United States.

Japan is a democracy. They have a democratic system of government, and we share their interest in preserving that. They have, in general, a quasi-private enterprise economic system and we have that in common together with an interest in world trade. We seek to develop our mutual security relationship so that we support each other. I think that is entirely possible.

I think that the Japanese assumption of full responsibility, for example, of the air defense of the Japanese Islands and for local antisubmarine defense is in our mutual interest. Access to satellites and the like would be extremely helpful to the United States, and very much in the Japanese interest. On the other hand, we would continue to supply the long-range capability and the umbrella of deterrence, and continue to enjoy the use of the limited number of Japanese bases. 

This type of complementary defensive relationship cannot be reasonably considered to threaten anybody. There is nothing threatening about antisubmarine forces or air defense forces. At the same time, these can help immeasurably both the United States and Japan in areas where we perceive we have a common interest, and we have a common interest in a great many areas. 

MILITARY ASSISTANCE TO VIETNAM: MAP OR MASF? 

Chairman MORGAN. Admiral, on page 4 of your statement you refer to South Vietnam. You note that military assistance for Vietnam has been funded through the DOD budget since 1966. Last year and the year before there were efforts in Congress to return this aid to the

military assistance program. These efforts were made particularly in the other body, not in the House. I expect there will be further attempts this year. 

Would you please tell the committee what the impact on South

Vietnam's military strength would be if our military assistance to South Vietnam were returned to the Foreign Assistance Act? 

Admiral GAYLER. Well, I think two general things have to be considered, Mr. Chairman. One is how much it is, and the other is how it would be administered. As to the latter, we have already planned to go on July 1 of this year to military assistance procedures with respect to the administration of that aid even though the money is still being provided in the service budgets. The effect of that, among other things, is to: First, place some restrictions on flexibility and freedom of action with respect to within a given ceiling, which I am not sure is helpful and, second, put the Pacific Command in the business of making military judgments about the efficacy of the aid and the use of the aid that we are providing to them and that is helpful. It is the position that the command is in with respect to all other assistance programs, and I welcome its being applied to Vietnam. I think it will be very helpful, although it is more work. 

Chairman MORGAN. Admiral, do you believe that as long as the present situation as it now exists in Vietnam continues it would be almost impossible to incorporate this assistance in the military assistance program? 

Admiral GAYLER. That is correct, sir.

Chairman MORGAN. We are going to have a difficult time this year with this bill at its present figure. Incorporating that amount of military assistance in the DOD budget is a lot easier than bringing it into this bill. I am afraid that this legislation would be in serious trouble if we listened to some of our friends on the other side of the Capitol. 

Thank you, Admiral. 

Mr. Frelinghuysen.

Mr. FRELINGHUYSEN.  

EFFECT OF MAP FUND REDUCTIONS 

It is a pleasure to welcome you to the committee, Admiral. Having been one of those who did pass through Honolulu I know that it is an interesting experience to go to your headquarters, and I hope some members of the committee will be able to avail themselves of your offer.

Admiral GAYLER. Thank you. 

Mr. FRELINGHUYSEN. I would like to begin by asking about your emphasis on a consistent reliable foreign aid program which will enable the recipients to, as you put it at the very end of your statement, integrate efficiently our assistance with their own efforts. 

Admiral GAYLER. Yes, sir.

Mr. FRELINGHUYSEN. About the only thing we seem to be sure of is that we are not going to be consistent, we are not going to be particularly reliable. I hate to be a prophet of gloom, but there seems to be an inevitability about a substantial reduction of what is being requested.

What is going to be the result if there is a drastic cut? I feel very

strongly that we should not cut too much, but there is the suspicion, especially as the dollar figures look big, that for a country like Cambodia we have earmarked too much. What would be the result if there should be substantial reductions in your opinion? 

Admiral GAYLER. It would depend on the country. In Korea, for example, it would create a good deal of difficulty with respect to proper planning for the improvement of South Korean forces, which we all think is a necessary part of a stable situation there. 

In other countries the effect would be, as the chairman mentioned a while ago, to cause questioning of our bona fides, of our reliability and of our intention to stay the course.

EFFECT OF REDUCTIONS IN NORTH VIETNAM 

In Vietnam a substantial reduction would, I think, weaken what I believe is a principal deterrent to the initiative of full-scale hostilities again from North Vietnam. In my judgment there are really about four factors which happily have dissuaded the North Vietnamese from resuming a full-scale offensive this year. 

There is a division in the Lao Dong Party between the "pragmatists," who want to rebuild up in the North, and the "hawks," who want to attack and give it another go-full-scale-in the South. The pragmatists, at least for this year appear to be in ascendency because they are still a little bit uncertain about what our reaction would be. 

I think that is good and ought to be maintained. 

In addition, they are uncertain, I believe, about the degree of support that they would get from the Peoples Republic of China and the U.S.S.R. in the event of another real major rekindling of the war. 

I think that they are also deterred by the realization that South Vietnam is a "tough nut to crack." In that connection, I think that our continued assistance to South Vietnam is very necessary. They must be kept a "hard nut to crack" in order to deter the DRV. 

Now so far as Cambodia is concerned, I think without much qualification that a significant cut in the programed assistance would put the Cambodian Government in very tough straits. They need ammunition; they need food; and they need POL. Particularly they need ammunition to defend themselves. I don't think that we could possibly cut that ammunition supply without taking on all kinds of grave consequences.

ROLE OF THE UNITED STATES IN CAMBODIA Mr. FRELINGHUYSEN. What is the role of the United States in 

Cambodia? I would suppose that a very substantial program like that really would need to be watchdogged. Do we have anything like an adequate staff there? 

Admiral GAYLER. As you know, sir, we are under an imposed ceiling of 200 people in the country which the Ambassador administers, carefully, and personally. We comply with the law in that respect as we do in every other respect. 

A good deal of our effort is, in fact, a monitoring of the end use of our equipment. We do what we can to see that it is efficiently used, to see that waste is cut down. I think the Khmers, General Fernandez, and others have made progress in the efficient use of their forces and in

HI the ammunition that we supply them. Beyond that we are not as a result of the ceiling in a position to do much for them. 

Mr. FRELINGHUYSEN. I don't see how as small a group as that could do much even in the way of monitoring the end use. It must be a very difficult operation, I should think, to have any meaningful kind of- Admiral GAYLER. I would agree with that. I have visited that mission several times and I am really impressed by the dedication with which both the military and the civilian side work the problem. They work long hours, get around as much as they can, and do a remarkable job under the circumstances. 

Mr. FRELINGHUYSEN. Thank you.

Chairman MORGAN. Mr. Zablocki.

PROSPECT OF REDUCTIONS IN MAP 

Mr. ZABLOCKI. No less than a Saturday morning on both occasions.

In view of the fact that for our own defense expenditures the authorization and appropriations we have at least attempted to hold to the level of the last fiscal year, granting an increase for inflation and other necessary costs, it would appear that we should also practice some economy in our overseas military expenditures. However, I am not for a drastic cut.

I think we must either be prepared for a cut or we will have no authorization at all. It is going to be difficult to pass a foreign aid bill this year in Congress and the military portion of it in the other body particularly.

It appears that particularly in your area there are increases over fiscal 1974, and particularly over fiscal 1973. I realize that in fiscal 1973 and 1974 there were additional countries that were not in the pre- 1973 period-Laos, for example, and the Khmer Republic. Nevertheless, overall there is an increase. Comparing it to fiscal year 1973 the request has almost doubled.

REQUEST FOR LAOS MAP 

So my questions are intended to ask where, really, can we cut the amount responsibly. For example, the administration request calls for $90 million military assistance in Laos for fiscal 1975. That is $12 million more than is being spent in Laos for the same purpose during the current fiscal year, despite that fact there is supposedly a ceasefire in Laos. We are informed by reliable sources that the U.S. MAP mission personnel in Laos believes that the funding requirements could be greatly reduced next year, and, indeed, they could live with a program of $50 million. 

My question, therefore, is: Can we indeed responsibly cut $40 million in Laos? What is your comment?

Admiral GAYLER. With respect to Laos, the money request relates to the situation as it was best perceived at the time the authorization was prepared. That situation is evolving. We don't know exactly what is going to happen. We can be hopeful, but, we must be prudent. In my judgment, however, it looks as if we may be able to make a pretty substantial cut if things go the way we would like to see them.

AMMUNITION EXPENDITURES IN CAMBODIA 

Mr. ZABLOCKI. I would like to pursue the questions of my colleague from New Jersey on the Khmer Republic. Almost 90 percent of the $362.5 being programed for Cambodia is for materiel, particularly ammunition. The reports from that country are that the ammunition is being wasted by the Cambodians because they are content to sit in defensive positions and fire rather than take the offensive. 

Are the Cambodian military leaders being convinced and advised by us that they must conserve ammunition, and that one way to do this is to become more aggressive militarily and not waste ammunition? What are our plans, for example, to ration ammunition in Cambodia?

Admiral GAYLER. I have considered recommending that alternative many times, Mr. Zablocki, but after rather careful consideration have decided against it. We continuously point out to General Fernandez and his other military leaders the fact that this support is not inexhaustible. They know that. They also know that unless they take conservation measures which will increase their military effectiveness they will have severe problems. 

Mr. ZABLOCKI. Maybe we in Congress can help in that respect, Admiral. 

Admiral GAYLER. I think that message has taken hold. I know General Fernandez assembled his principal commanders not too long ago and really read them the riot act. We have seen some statistical reaction to that. We have, in fact, slowed down the supply of ammunition up the Mekong, a very visible thing to the Cambodian leaders. They have not missed that signal. 

I have been reluctant to go to rationing because it is very serious to put ammunition constraints on a man fighting for his life on the battlefield. To get them aboard is, I think, the way to go, and I will not tell this committee that they are totally aboard in this respect. 

They have an awful lot to learn about the military life, but I think they are getting there.

Mr. ZABLOCKI. Well, I imagine we could be helpful to this, Admiral, if we cut back there a little bit on the basis that they must cut costs and conserve ammunition.

[The information requested follows:] USE OF MAP FUNDS FOR REIMBURSEMENT 

During FY 1974, the President exercised his authority under Section 506(a) Foreign Assistance Act (FAA) of 1961, as amended, and determining that it was in the security interests of the United States, authorized the provision of up to $250 million in defense stocks and defense services as additional military assistance to Cambodia. Reimbursement of the military departments must, under that section, be made from subsequent appropriations. None of the funds requested by the President for MAP in FY 1975 is proposed to be used for such reimbursement. The DOD has requested permission to seek such reimbursement, but the 

Office of Management and Budget has not yet taken action on DOD's request. 

I might add parenthetically that in these circumstances, Section 506(b) FAA of 1961, as amended, already authorizes the appropriation of the $250 million. Thus, only Appropriations Committee action is necessary to provide funds for the draw down reimbursement.

MILITARY ASSISTANCE TO INDONESIA
