Chairman MORGAN. Mr. Thomson. 

Mr. THOMSON. 

Admiral, in line with the questioning of Mr Zablocki, do you contemplate a modernization program in Indonesia similar to the one in Korea?

Admiral GAYLER. No, sir. The levels of effort there are not at all comparable. I think what we are doing in Indonesia is simply providing a catalyst and helping them with their most urgent requirements. 

It is largely an undeveloped country and such things as countrywide communications, such things as a minimal capability to observe what is going on in their own territorial waters, are essential. That is the sort of thing we have been concentrating on. Indonesia has an external threat not at all comparable to Korea. It would not be appropriate to go to Korean levels of support unless that condition existed.

THAILAND: MILITARY AID AND BASES 

Mr. THOMSON. Now in Thailand is the use of bases there dependent on military aid or is that a quid pro quo, or are they willing to have us there without regard to the level of assistance? 

Admiral GAYLER. I think the Thai perception is that we are allies, and that we have common interests. They are nervous about the domination of Southeast Asia by North Vietnam. They always have been.

They also are concerned about the outcome of events in Cambodia. 

They have for years seen and believed that our interests paralleled theirs and, therefore, they were happy to let us use their territory. 

The assistance that we have given them over the years is perceived as an earnest of our common endeavor. When it is cut down too much and too fast-and particularly unexpectedly-it gives a signal which they interpret as lack of further U.S. interest in their country. I think that is unfortunate.

DISCUSSIONS TO REDUCE PERSONNEL 

Mr. HAMILTON. Do we have underway at the present time any discussions with foreign governments in your area to reduce U.S. personnel?

Admiral GAYLER. Yes; we have ongoing almost continuous discussions with the Thai Government, for example, on the rate of redeployment of the American Air Forces in Thailand. Of course, in Vietnam, Laos, and Cambodia we don't have any forces anyway. 

There are no ongoing discussions in Korea of that nature to my knowledge, and no intent to reduce significantly our capabilities there.

In Japan, we don't have discussions of that direct kind. They tend to be more discussions between us and the Japanese in the light of evolution of our security relationship-land availability, base usage, and things like that.

In Taiwan, we are, of course, in close discussion with the Chinese with respect to a gradual drawdown of U.S. forces there. 

Mr. HAMILTON. Do you foresee any sizable reductions in troop reductions in the next year?

Admiral GAYLER. In Taiwan? 

Mr. HAMILTON. In any country under your command where we have forces.

Admiral GAYLER. Well, there is a prospect for some continued drawdown of Air Force personnel in Thailand. Other than that, no. 

INDIAN OCEAN NAVAL DEVELOPMENT 

Mr. HAMILTON. I understand that since the October war in the Middle East, we have deployed, on a regular basis, ships in the Indian Ocean. Has this deployment caused any particular problems for the 

7th Fleet?

Admiral GAYLER. It has really been more on an irregular basis than a regular basis. I make that point not to quibble but because I think that is probably our most effective presence there. Effective capability there can best be demonstrated by irregular visits in some strength rather than attempting to keep a force there regularly. 

To answer your question, yes; it does put the 7th Fleet under strain.

It is a long logistic chain. It keeps people at sea a long time. That is one of the reasons we would like to have some relief on that with a small operation at Diego Garcia.

Mr. HAMILTON. Has the U.S. Government received any word from the British Government on the status of our request to expand facilities there?

MIDEASTFOR 

Admiral GAYLER. I don't think so. To my knowledge no formal reply. All the indicators are pretty good, I understand.

Mr. HAMILTON. IS MIDEASTFOR under your command?

Mr. HAMILTON. If the Bahraini Government holds firm on its decision not to let MIDEASTFOR stay in the Persian Gulf, will that mean that more ships will have to be deployed by you in the Indian Ocean?

Admiral GAYLER. It will mean more than that. It will just be a little tougher to do the job of showing the flag over there with a very small force. I lived in and around Bahrain for a year some time ago and in my judgment it is only the pressure of other countries which led them to do this. I am quite hopeful that as things simmer down and peace is established in the Middle East, they may reconsider. 

SITUATION IN CAMBODIA 

Mr. HAMILTON. Admiral, I was interested in what I construed to be unfairly optimistic comments with regard to Cambodia, and I must

E withi the say I have a different impression. I have an impression of steady deterioration there in almost every respect. Politically we have had a 

Minister of Education who was killed, we have student protests, and you have inflation running at 300 percent in that country. You seem to find the situation improving. the te Admiral GAYLER. I don't know that I intended to exhibit too much optimism. The sands of Southeast Asia are littered with the bones of prophets. Prophecy is pretty tricky in this area. I think that the negative things that you have talked about are all true. There are, however, some positive things also.

On the military side, while I still would not designate the Cambodian Armed Forces as an example to anybody, they have pulled up their socks to a considerable extent. Their coordination and the effectiveness of artillery, for example, is clearly better. While it is true that their forces are not often the most offensive minded in the world, they still are considerably better than they used to be. They found some leaders.

I think General Fernandez himself and other leaders, particularly in the Navy, like Commander Vong Sarendy, are aggressive combat leaders.

KEEPING THE MEKONG ROUTE OPEN IN CAMBODIA 

The most important strategic fact, I think, is that the Mekong supply route remains open. The capital has food, ammunition, and oil. 

Most of the beleaguered enclaves in the countryside have survived. 

The push to take over the capital on the run last fall didn't succeed. The push to terrorize the inhabitants by rocketing and shelling them did not bring about the fall of the government.

Admiral GAYLER. Well, that sort of depends, of course, on the development of the political situation in the two Koreas. In addition, however, it is a pretty good place from some aspects to keep an American force, the training facilities are good, and it affords the capability to keep military readiness high. 

The presence of U.S. forces there is a plus. Frankly, I would like to have them available for potential use elsewhere.

Mr. Bingham. 

Mr. BINGHAM. 

NORTH AND SOUTH KOREA: BALANCE OF FORCES 

I did have one or two questions I would like to ask the Admiral. 

Referring to Korea, could you give us some picture of the relative strength of the North Korean forces and the South Korean forces? 

Admiral GAYLER. When you talk about strength, you should also,

I believe, talk about disposition; that is to say, the military deployment of the forces. The North Korean forces are comparable to the 

South Korean forces. On the ground they are numerically somewhat smaller with a near numerical equality in artillery. They have considerable armor. They have what is generally recognized as a superior air force. They have vessels in their Navy which are not matched by 

South Korea-the missile firing vessels.

On the whole, I would say that the military forces are a near standoff except in their air. Under the present circumstances it is the North 

Koreans who have the advantage of concealment and surprise if they chose to initiate an offensive. This results in part from the closed nature of that society and in part from the terrain. It is the estimate of all of our commanders that they could indeed achieve a strategic surprise which would be important. 

The other important point is that the capital of South Korea is very close to the border, and so the country does not have the usual time, the usual options of trading space for time, they must concentrate a defense all along the line of attack. Placing all of these things together, you would have to say that the superiority lies largely in the circumstances that we are talking about of a North Korean attack. 

U.S. RELATIONSHIP TO SOUTH KOREA 

Mr. BINGHAM. What is the nature of our relationship with South 

Korea in terms of a commitment to be involved militarily in the event of an attack by North Korea? 

Admiral GAYLER. I don't know of any commitment to do anything outside of our constitutional processes. We have a mutual defense treaty with South Korea which is the basis of our commitment. The command is still a United Nations Command and has an American commander.

Mr. BINGHAM. I have heard it said that the North Korean Army is about half the size of the South Korean Army. Is that an exaggeration?

Admiral GAYLER. That is an exaggeration, yes. A good deal depends on how you count it, of course, but if you are talking about organized combat ready divisions, that certainly is an exaggeration. 

Mr. BINGHAM. You said it was somewhat smaller. Could you give us some ratio? 

Admiral GAYLER. Yes, I think I can give you some figures. We are reporting a little better than a dozen North Korean divisions deployed along the DMZ instantly combat ready and something like twice that

number in their total ground forces. The comparable South Korean ready forces amount to 20 percent more.

TRANSFERABILITY OF MAP FUNDS 

Mr. BINGHAM. Admiral, as far as you are concerned, what would be your reaction if the program funds that you are asking for were to be specified country by country in the amounts that you are asking for with perhaps some limited amount of transferability?

What I am getting at is this. In the legislation the amounts are requested in a lump sum. In both the presentation book and in your statement you give they country by country. Would you feel impeded if the legislation were to specify those amounts country by country with a limited degree of transferability?

Admiral GAYLER. Yes. It has been my consistent position as U.S. 

Pacific Commander that the entire set of programs should be looked at from an area basis or a theater basis, not country by country. There is considerable interdependence. You can do a better job by looking at the total strategic picture and the influence of the assistance than you can by looking at it more narrowly on a country-by-country basis. 

In addition, I think that the Congress certainly should exert any controls that it wishes over the allocation but freezing levels in advance makes it administratively pretty difficult. There should be better ways to make sure that we can maintain flexibility and at the same time allow the Congress to oversee the operation to the extent that you desire.

LINE ITEM AUTHORIZATION FOR MAP 

Mr. BINGHAM. It was pointed out yesterday by, I think, counsel for the Defense Department, that in any event 30 days after the appropriation bill has been passed the administration is required to give us a firm breakdown of the funds and how they will be used country by country. To specify it in the authorizing legislation would simply be

AMERICAN POLICY IN CAMBODIA 

Chairman MORGAN. Admiral, I want to ask you some questions about Cambodia and about the general situation there. American policy in Cambodia appears to me to achieve a military stalemate which we hope will lead to some political negotiations. In that a fair assessment of our operation now in Cambodia? 

Admiral GAYLER. I don't think that anybody deliberately advocates a stalemate, Mr. Chairman. What we are advocating and hoping for is enough survivability, enough tenacity, enough resilience to put the Khmer government in a reasonable position to negotiate a peace, and to give the Khmer Communists, the inurgents, a strong and compelling motive to do that. We should strive within the limits of what

we and they can do to get some kind of negotiating position, position for the Government that will permit a just and fair peace. 

Chairman MORGAN. Admiral, we read in the press that there are about 50,000 or 60,000 Communist troops active in Cambodia in comparison with about 200,000 troops on the Government side. Yet the Communists control more than 60 percent of the land and seem to have more military initiative than the Government troops. How long can this situation exist? Could there be some military stalemate, and would it lead to negotiation? How long do you think the present

Government of Cambodia can hold out? 

Admiral GAYLOR. As I said before, sir, it is very difficult to make prophesies. A lot of people have tried, Southeast Asia has, I think defeated most of the prophets. I will say only that I think the relative position of the Khmer Armed Forces compared to the Khmer Communists has improved slightly in recent months. Most of the disasters which were forecast have not happened. 

There have been some encouraging military things of which the most important, I guess, is the demonstrated ability to keep the Mekong open even though it has been a major enemy objective to close it. There is, however, a balanced picture. The government has not been able to keep the roads open. They have had limited offensive initiatives. Until recently, most of the battles they have won have been defensive battles. The political situation on the government side is still not what we would like it to be, but on balance I think that there is quite a reasonable chance that this course of action will lead to a negotiated settlement.

1 

INCREASED DRAWDOWN AUTHORITY FOR CAMBODIA ¹ The President requested in the Emergency Security Assistance Act of 1973 

$200 million for Cambodia military assistance and $300 million in drawdown authority. The $200 million for Cambodia was omitted from the Emergency 

Security Assistance Act, but Section 506 (2) of the Foreign Assistance Act 

(FAA) of 1961, as amended, authorized the President in FY 74 to drawdown $250 million in defense articles in inventory and defense services from the Department of Defense to augment the military assistance program. 

Section 506 (a) permitted recourse to the draw down authority in FY 74 if the President determined it to be "in the security interests of the United States." 

The language of the conference report for the FY 74 FAA indicates that as of November 27, 1973, the Committee of Conference intended that up to $200 million of the 506 (a) authority be used for Cambodian emergency military assistance requirements. The Committee, in this conference report, anticipated that the use of the drawdown authority under Section 506 would be to meet the then foreseen needs for which funding had been requested in the 

Emergency Security Assistance Act. This marked a departure from normal practice. Traditionally, Section 506 (a) has been considered as an extraordinary authority for meeting unforeseen emergency MAP requirements. The remaining $50 million in Section 506 (a) was, therefore, available to serve the traditional purposes of Section 506(a)-worldwide unforeseen needs. 

The military assistance requirements of the Cambodian Government are directly related to the level of combat activity. In actuality, the enemy was able to sustain a much higher rate of combat than initially foreseen. The enemy mounted major offensive actions not only in Kampong Cham and Phnom Penh areas, but throughout the country. The Cambodian Government was able to withstand these attacks but only at severe and unforeseen increases in ammunition expenditures and combat equipment losses above the needs anticipated by either the President or the Congress. This ammunition and equipment had to be replaced on an emergency basis if the Cambodian Government was to survive. 

It became clear that additional funds beyond the $200 million were required to meet these unexpected requirements. Accordingly, the President decided that the use of Section 506 draw down authority was imperative to save the Cambodian Government and in the security interests of the United States. Prior to personally making the necessary determination reserved to him alone under 

Section 401 (c) of Executive Order 10973, the President notified the Speaker of the House and the Chairman of the Senate Foreign Relations Committee of his intention to invoke Section 506 in accordance with Section 652 of the FAA. 

No objection was received from the Congress, and the $50 million drawdown authority was used. Presidential Determination 17-19 was also published in the 

Federal Register. 

It therefore follows that the use of this authority by the President was both in strict compliance with the law and with the intent expressed by the Committee of Conference.

LINES OF COMMUNICATION THROUGH PACIFIC 

Mr. ZABLOCKI. Very important, Mr. Chairman, are the communication lines through the Pacific. It is my understanding that our forces in Korea and Thailand help to keep open our lines of communication in the Pacific. Would you advise us, Admiral, how do our forces in Korea and Thailand help to keep open our lines of communication in the Pacific, and how important it is? Would you comment, sir? 

1 Source: Legal Adviser to the Chairman, Joint Chiefs of Staff.

! 

Admiral GAYLER. "To keep open the line of communication," is a shorthand manner of talking about the protection of the sea traffic from military interference, or what is almost equally important, the threat of military interference. When you look at the map of Eastern 

Asia it is perfectly clear that the submarine threat must be based principally in Siberian Maritime Russia. Access to the oceans and to the sea lines of communication must be down to the eastern shore of Asia. Korea and Japan, taken together or separately, stand right on the flank of any such movement. 

In the antisubmarine business and in the antiaircraft business, geography is everything. Access to Japanese bases and to Korean bases is very important from the standpoint of air defense and potentially very important from the standpoint of antisubmarine defense.

Mr. ZABLOCKI. Admiral, it is argued that we do not need the level of American Forces present in that area, particularly in Thailand and Korea. It follows, as you well know, that there will be attempts to cut back our forces in that area of the world. Do we need the present level of U.S. Forces in Thailand and Korea to indeed secure our lines of communication? 

Admiral GAYLER. Those forces are there for several reasons: They contribute to regional security and protect our lines of communication. I would not tell you that we need them all for that sole purpose. 

The forces in Thailand are, in my judgment, an important part of the deterrent against a major offensive by the North Vietnamese. 

They are also there because of their access to the Indian Ocean, an important part of sea surveillance. In Korea our forces are there primarily as an additional deterrent to offensive action by the North Koreans. They, too, particularly the Fifth Air Force, lie on the flank of any movement to the south. 

There are two problems in keeping open the lines of communication: Sea control and that is principally, but not entirely, the submarine problem-and air control a contribution can be made from all three of the places that you have named.

FISCAL YEAR 1975 FOREIGN ASSISTANCE REQUEST THURSDAY, JUNE 20, 1974 HOUSE OF REPRESENTATIVES, COMMITTEE ON FOREIGN AFFAIRS, 

Washington, D.C.

The committee met at 10:15 a.m. in room 2172, Rayburn House Office 

Building, Hon. Thomas E. Morgan (chairman of the committee) presiding. 

Today we will hear from Gen. Andrew J. Goodpaster, Commander in Chief, U.S. European Command, and Supreme Allied Commander in Europe.

General Goodpaster's appearance will conclude the testimony by executive branch witnesses here on the foreign assistance request for fiscal year 1975.

Next week, following our markup session on other bills on Tuesday, the Chair's intention is to continue the foreign assistance hearings with testimony from Members of Congress and public witnesses. Members will be sent a notice of next week's hearings today. 

General Goodpaster, it is good to have you before us again. We received your prepared statement yesterday and it has been distributed to all members' offices in advance of the meeting this morning. You may read your statement, or summarize it if you wish. Then we will go to questions and answers. You may proceed, General. 

STATEMENT OF GEN. ANDREW J. GOODPASTER, COMMANDER IN CHIEF, U.S. EUROPEAN COMMAND, AND SUPREME ALLIED COM- MANDER, EUROPE General GOODPASTER. Mr. Chairman, members of the committee: I 

appreciate the opportunity to come before the committee again in support of the military assistance program, a program which I feel has served, and continues to serve, the interests of the United States, NATO, and other allies. My remarks will be made primarily from the standpoint of my U.S. command responsibilities as Commander in 

Chief of the U.S. European Command. 

Much has occurred in our command area since my last appearance before this committee on this specific subject in June 1971. The geographic area of responsibility of the command for the administration of security assistance programs has been expanded to include areas in the Middle East and Africa south of the Sahara. The latter pre- (381)

viously was administered by the U.S. Strike Command. The outbreak of Arab-Israeli hostilities and the subsequent moves toward settlement have had significant influence on security assistance programs in this area.

In keeping with the conviction that, in the long run, self-help is the best help, the number of countries in the European Command receiving grant aid for both defense articles and services has been reduced progressively from 11 to 5. This is an indication of the progress that has been made by friendly nations in achieving selfsufficiency. The type and the quality of assistance rendered by our military assistance advisory groups have been refined. Our MAAG's are evolving from a time of assisting primarily at the unit level to a role which includes counseling and helping to promote effective resource management at the level of the General Staffs and Ministries of Defense. 

ROLE OF MAAG'S IN EUROPE 

In Western Europe, the role of the MAAG's has changed to respond to the economic and political growth of the European community. They help to foster continuing close orientation to U.S. systems and doctrine. At the same time, they support a thrust toward standardization, which often will mean a cooperative involvement of friendly countries in development and production. 

A high degree of compatibility and interoperability of U.S. weapon systems with those of the allies and a commonality of weapons doctrine could prove of critical importance to success in theater-level combat operations. The Warsaw Pact countries already possess the advantage of a high degree of standardization in their weapon systems. 

Before proceeding to discussion of the proposed programs, I would like to review some of the significant recent changes in the Warsaw Pact forces that confront the United States and its allies in the European Command area-in military shorthand, the "threat" that we face.

GROWTH OF SOVIET MILITARY CAPABILITIES 

Even while attention is centered on détente and the current activities surrounding our negotiations in both the mutual and balanced force reduction and the conference on security and cooperation in Europe, it is still a matter of hard fact that the threat is undiminished. 

The last few years have been marked by a continuing-and disturbing-growth in Soviet and Warsaw Pact military capabilities. Soviet ground forces have carried out substantial improvements in firepower, equipment modernization, and logistical support. There has been an increase in the number of Soviet divisions comprising a threat to the European Command, while the numbers of East European divisions have remained unchanged. At the same time, qualitative improvement of the Pact Ground Forces has continued apace, with the introduction of late model tanks, better armored personnel carriers, and better artillery.

Warsaw Pact air operations against countries in the European Command area could be carried out by more than 6,000 fighters, bombers, and tactical reconnaissance aircraft. The Soviets continue to

modernize their Air Forces with new generation fighters and fighter bombers. The pact is augmenting and modernizing its air defense forces, emphasizing mobile systems to support rapidly moving field armies. Soviet naval power is a subject in itself. As the result of a tremendous effort the Soviet Union is able to project its sea power into the North Atlantic, the Mediterranean, the Indian Ocean, and in fact to all the areas of the world. This expanding facet of Russian combat power, capable of concentrating anywhere in the world, has ramifications that are far-reaching. 

SOVIET ARMS IN MIDDLE EAST 

You well know of the activities of the Soviets throughout a period of almost two decades, in North Africa and the Middle East, and of their efforts to supplant Western influence with their own. Principal recipients of past Russian military assistance have been Egypt, Syria, and Iraq. The Soviet Union has demonstrated a willingness to supply late model weapons. Examples of equipment furnished prior to last year's war include the latest model T-62 tank; the SCUD short range surface-to-surface ballistic missile, the SA-6 mobile surface-to-air missile system, the SA-7 hand-held surface-to-air missile launcher, MIG-21 jet fighters, TU-22 medium bombers, and Komar and OSA class guided missile patrol boats. Most recently Soviet deliveries to 

Egypt have been curtailed. Offsetting this decline, however, the Soviet aid program has become even more generous in aid commitments and deliveries to Syria and Iraq.

These activities continue to demonstrate the importance which the Soviet Union places on maintaining a presence and an influence in connection with military matters in this area of the world. During the 

Middle East war, these efforts were very much in evidence. 

In terms of security assistance, the Middle East war had new lessons for us, but for the most part it proved again some old maxims. In general it was shown again how essential is the expert integration of the combined arms involved in ground attack-tanks, infantry, tactical air, artillery, and air defense to an effective fighting force. At the same time we have seen that the expenditure of ammunition and equipment during intense modern warfare quickly reaches very high levels. Rapid availability and quick replenishment become keys to success.

The Soviet and Warsaw Pact capabilities, the continuing Soviet aid to certain countries, the demonstrated value of well-trained, wellequipped conventional forces, the need for good equipment on hand, and the importance of logistical planning are considerations that have been applied to the U.S. security assistance effort. 

I would like to review the principal programs before the committee, and comment both on regional considerations and on individual country programs.

SECURITY ASSISTANCE IN EUROPE 

Security assistance in continental Europe, except for Spain and Portugal, is in the form of military cash sales, with token grant training for Austria and Finland. Grant aid and foreign military sales credit are no longer required for other continental European countries. 4)

The program as now proposed for Portugal, of somewhat less than $1 million, would provide half a million dollars for training of personnel and limited support for MAP-provided equipment of NATO committed forces. The strategic importance of Portugal and the value of the Azores for aerial resupply in support of NATO or unilateral U.S. activities were dramatically demonstrated during the recent 

Middle East war. It is my hope that the policies being pursued by the new government may result in Portugal's assuming an enhanced role within the NATO structure. 

The proposed $1.6 million training program for Spain fulfills the final terms of the 1970 Agreement of Friendship and Cooperation, which has given the United States the use of certain bases and facilities in Spain.

SECURITY ASSISTANCE IN MEDITERRANEAN LITTORAL 

Proposed programs for countries around the Mediterranean littoral involve several types of security assistance, and demonstrate, I believe, both the value and the versatility of the program. By offering modest security assistance programs to nonalined Mediterranean nations, we provide them a reasonable alternative to alinement with more radical Arab States or the U.S.S.R., without encroaching on their national prerogatives. We thereby help to strengthen stability, security, and peace in the area.

The grant aid requested for Morocco is limited to $860,000 for training. The proposed $14 million in credit will improve ground mobility and enhance border defense capabilities. This moderate Arab State occupies an important position on NATO's southern flank at the Strait of Gibraltar. The U.S. Navy operates a communications station at Kenitra.

Tunisia has indicated its resolve to maintain its autonomy and to develop a military capability to assure internal order. The proposed $2 million in grant aid and $1.5 million in foreign military sales credit will assist Tunisia in achieving a modest degree of force modernization and training of personnel. 

SECURITY ASSISTANCE IN GREECE AND TURKEY 

In the Eastern Mediterranean, our NATO partners, Greece and Turkey, represent a substantial military capability for forward defense on NATO's southern flank. However, these countries are equipped for the most part with aging World War II and Korean war equipment and weapons systems. Although recent economic progress has enabled both Greece and Turkey to devote greater resources to legitimate defense needs, their requirements far exceed their funding ability. These requirements derive not from the creation of additional forces, but from the need to modernize and improve existing forces in order to approach a balance with the opposing Warsaw Pact forces and insure a credible deterrent posture.

The proposed program for Turkey includes fighter aircraft. helicopters, and armored personnel carriers to improve mobility, tank/ antitank capability, tactical communications equipment, and war reserve materiel. Of the combined total of $205 million in grant aid.

credit, and excess defense articles requested for Turkey, $90 million, or almost half, is in credit for the purchase of U.S. defense articles and services for modernization of the Turkish Armed Forces. 

Turkey has announced a 10-year modernization effort for which the Turkish Parliament has authorized more than a billion dollars over and above the regular defense budget. This is a major undertaking, particularly when it is recalled that until 2 years ago Turkey was almost totally dependent on outside aid for force modernization. 

The military requirements for Greece are of comparable magnitude and priority. The Hellenic Armed Forces are presently equipped in major degree with U.S. arms, and their general orientation toward cooperation with the United States within the NATO framework continues. They are accomplishing much of their planned modernization by purchase of U.S. equipment. Even though they have terminated their grant program, they still require credit assistance of sufficient. levels for this purpose.

SECURITY ASSISTANCE IN THE MIDDLE EAST 

Turning to the Middle East, the security assistance programs requested are considered an important part of the overall U.S. initiatives to achieve peace and stability in the area. 

Jordan has demonstrated a strong national will for survival as an independent nation. This independence, and confrontation with the 

Fedayeen, has resulted in the loss of sizable subsidies from wealthier Arab states, and Jordan has been dependent on U.S. aid in maintaining its autonomy. The proposed program of $94 million in grant aid and $30 million in credits has been developed as the minimum necessary to achieve adequate improvements in air and ground mobility and firepower of the Jordanian Armed Forces. 

Lebanon is another example of a moderate regime for which assistance in maintaining its independence and internal order is deemed desirable. The proposed $10 million for credit and $150,000 for training will facilitate modest improvement in ground forces to support those goals.

Continued assistance for Israel accounts for a large portion of the total funds requested for countries in the European command area. 

Since this program is not administered directly by my command, J will not comment on the details of the program. 

IRAN AND SAUDI ARABIA 

The October war emphasized the dependence of the free world on Middle East oil, and the opening of the Suez Canal will further link the interests of the European and Mediterranean nations to those of the oil-producing States. As an aid in sustaining U.S. interests in this area and to protect continued access to area oil resources, we consider it essential to continue, and improve, security assistance efforts in Iran and Saudi Arabia. I believe it is important to continue assisting Saudi Arabia in attaining a modernized defense force. Such a force is considered necessary, along with that of Iran, to maintain stability in the gulf area, and to prevent incursion of outside powers into the gulf.

While the proposal before you contains no funds for Iran, I would like to comment on the importance of the security assistance efforts there. The Shah has made clear his dedication to building first-rate armed forces, and is relying primarily on the assistance of the United States in achieving those forces. There is an accelerated requirement for both civilian and military expertise in Iran. To satisfy these needs the United States provides technical assistance field teams, which provide instruction in specific areas for a limited period of time. All costs associated with these teams are funded by Iran. In this way it has been possible to limit personnel increases in the MAAG and avoid increased costs to the United States. 

SECURITY ASSISTANCE IN SUB-SAHARAN AFRICA 

Turning to sub-Saharan Africa, the only sizable program proposed is for Ethiopia, taking account of its Western orientation and its influence among the nonalined African states. Ethiopia's defense budget is not adequate to provide the degree of force modernization required to maintain internal security and territorial integrity. The proposed program of $11.3 million in grant aid and $5 million in credits will permit modest modernization and force maintenance. The continuation of historically close ties with Ethiopia promotes stability in the African area of increased importance in view of the eventual opening of the 

Suez Canal. 

Three and a half million dollars in credit is requested for the Republic of Zaire to assist in equipping an armed force capable of maintaining internal security. It is anticipated that these credits will help promote a favorable bilateral relationship. 

Also proposed is a total of $295,000 to support appropriate personnel training programs in the sub-Saharan Africa countries of Ghana, Liberia, Mali, Senegal, and Sudan. We consider that these dollars spent on training will reap substantial benefit to the United States in the future.

SECURITY ASSISTANCE PROGRAMS SERVE U.S. INTERESTS 

Mr. Chairman, I believe that the proposed security assistance programs as they are presently configured will serve the interests of the United States. These efforts are in consonance with, and in support of, prudent policy objectives for the area. They are dynamic programs which have been adjusted continually to meet requirements in an efficient and effective manner. We have given continuing effort to seeing that the U.S. dollars in this field have been well spent. I solicit your support for the programs as I have outlined them." 

Let me again express, if I may, my appreciation for the opportunity to appear here today and state my views. I am prepared to address any questions that you and the members of the committee may have. 

THE FUTURE OF NATO Chairman MORGAN. Thank you, General. 

General, this year we are observing the 25th anniversary of NATO. 

Back in 1949, I was one of the sponsors of the founding of NATO.

Without NATO, we might have had World War III breaking out in Europe. However, General, times have changed, and now we have been hearing some criticism of NATO. For instance, NATO was formed as a defense against the Soviet threat. Now, our President is going to Moscow again next week and we have many negotiations going on, and trade deals with the Soviets. 

We have heard proposals on both sides of the Capitol to cut our troop strength in NATO, and complaints that our fellow NATO members in Europe are not carrying enough of the burden. So, General, I would like to ask you a three-part question.

First, could you tell us why you think NATO still will be needed in the years ahead? I noticed you speak, on page 3 of your statement, of a continued Soviet threat. 

Second, why can't we make some substantial cuts in our troop levels in Europe?

Third, what are our copartners in NATO doing to carry their fair share of the burden of the costs? Is the German offset agreement announced recently really fair to the United States?

OBJECTIVES OF NATO General GOODPASTER. Mr. Chairman, I think the purposes to which 

NATO is dedicated and which, I believe, NATO serves give the basis for a response to your first question, "Why is NATO needed in the years ahead?" The first objective of NATO-to which my command makes its contribution-is deterrence; that is, the prevention not only of war and the use of military force, but also the maintenance of a situation of stability, confidence, and security which dissuades the other side from efforts to threaten the use of military force as a sanction or a lever in forcing changes in the security situation or the independence of the member Nations. This deterrence can be effective only if it is founded upon a sound capability for defense. 

The second purpose is defense. NATO is a defensive alliance, It has no offensive plan or capability. We believe that we have organized our collective military capability into a "respectable posture of defense," in the words of President Washington.

The third objective that is served by NATO solidarity. The nations work together, not perfectly, not completely, but in a way far beyond anything that has ever been seen. They work with a high degree of cooperation, and with a considerable degree of harmony, particularly in matters of basic importance to security. They deny anyone outside the opportunity to play one off against the other. This "opportunity" has been the forerunner to many of the wars of this century. They are obliged by the NATO system and the degree of solidarity that exists to suppress ancient quarrels-again not completely, not perfectly, but far beyond anything that we have ever seen in the past. 

The final objective that we serve, and I think NATO serves, is the objective of détente; that is, a true détente predicated upon the reduction of tensions between the East and the West-a reduction of tensions which is founded in a desire to move, as President Nixon put it, into an era of negotiation and out of an era of confrontation.

DÉTENTE: TRUE OR ILLUSORY? 

I say a true détente. Détente carries some risks with it. You could have an illusory détente. Unless détente is coupled with a sound defense capability on our side, it would lead to instability rather than stability. The test and the measure of success is found in the fact that 

Europe and the Atlantic area have now enjoyed more than a quartercentury of peace and mutual confidence-something that Europe has not seen in many centuries. 

There is nothing in sight that can take the place of these NATO efforts in pursuit of deterrence, defense, solidarity, and détente. That is what to my mind defines NATO. I think NATO will continue to be necessary in the years ahead, particularly during a time when the Soviets continue to maintain, to modernize, and to strengthen at least the quality and effectiveness of their forces.

AMERICAN FORCES IN EUROPE: NO SUBSTANTIAL CUTS 

Why cannot we make substantial cuts in the American forces there? 

These American forces provide at the present time an essential component to the collective military force that exists in Europe. I have summed it up in the past in a three-part proposition:

That NATO or something like it is essential to the security interests of the United States just as it is to the security interests of every other member nation:

That an organized collective force in place on the continent of Europe is essential to a viable NATO; therefore, without the organized collective force, NATO would in time become no more than a scrap of paper like other treaties before it; and 

That a U.S. force contribution not substantially less than what is there today is essential to organized collective force, therefore to a viable NATO, and therefore to American security interests. 

This American contribution in General Eisenhower's terms in the early days of NATO "put the glue into NATO." It continues to do that. It is a modest contribution, but it is an absolutely indispensable one. I do not see any margin for significant cuts in the American contribution unless these are accomplished in the context of the mutual and balanced force reductions negotiations that are now going on. or in the longer term, as a result of Europe's gathering itself into a greater condition of unity, through technological, administrative, military organization, power, and decision.

I want to comment briefly on the costs, which run in the order of $3 billion to $4 billion a year for the American forces maintained in the area. In my judgment, Mr. Chairman, the United States derives a tremendous return in terms of security, stability, and a world climate which permits progress and concentration on progress in the economic and political spheres.

EFFORTS OF NATO COUNTRIES TO CARRY THEIR SHARE 

You also ask, "What are the NATO countries doing to carry their share?" You can measure the sharing of the burden in a number of ways. The single criterion that has seemed most meaningful to me is to

ith t d ilin the 

Lat I 

compare the defense effort in percent of gross national product country by country with the per capita income in each country. If you do that for NATO as a whole, and for the United States, you find that the other countries are very much on a par with the United States in that regard.

Now there are some laggards and I think that has to be recognized Fortunately, there are others who are carrying at least a full share, and perhaps somewhat more.

The balance-of-payments area has been an area of great concern to me in the past. It was made very clear to me that unless some resolution of the balance-of-payments problem were found, cuts would simply be forced upon the American force in Europe. I am happy to say that in the past few years there has been a much greater recognition of the need for action in this field. I understand the expeciation is that the requirements of the Jackson-Nunn amendment will be met satisfactorily. The offset negotiations with the Germans have contributed to that in a major degree. I personally cannot make any judgment, but I believe it is the view of our Government that the German agreement and commitment was forthcoming and equitable. 

I would like to sum up by saying that here we have what is, in my opinion, a success story. It has not been achieved without effort. Many commitments and much work have gone into it in the past. There has been support from the resources of our country. Our country can take satisfaction in what now exists. 

[The prepared statement follows:] STATEMENT OF GEN. ANDREW J. GOODPASTER U.S. ARMY COMMANDER IN CHIEF, U.S. EUROPEAN COMMAND, AND SUPREME ALLIED COMMANDER, EUROPE Mr. Chairman and Members of the Committee: I appreciate the opportunity to come before the committee again in support of the military assistance program, a program which I feel has served, and continues to serve, the interests of the United States, NATO, and other allies. My remarks will be made primarily from the standpoint of my U.S. command responsibilities as Commanderin-Chief of the United States European Command. Much has occurred in our command area since my last appearance here on this specific subject in June 1971. The geographic area of responsibility of the command for the administration of security assistance programs has been expanded to include areas in the Middle East and Africa South of the Sahara previously administered by Strike Command. The outbreak of Arab-Israeli hostilities and the subsequent moves toward settlement have had significant influence on security assistance programs in this area.

In keeping with the conviction that, in the long run, self-help is the best help, the number of countries in the European Command receiving grant aid for both defense articles and services has been reduced progressively from eleven to five an indication of the progress that has been made by friendly nations in achieving self-sufficiency. The type and the quality of assistance rendered by our military assistance advisory groups have been refined. Our MAAG's are evolving from a time of assisting primarily at the unit level to a role which includes counseling and helping to promote effective resource management at the level of the General Staffs and Ministries of Defense. 

In Western Europe, the role of the MAAG's has changed to respond to the economic and political growth of the European community. They help to foster continuing close orientation to U.S. systems and doctrine; at the same time, they support a thrust toward standardization, which will often mean a cooperative involvement of friendly countries in development and production. A high degree of compatibility and interoperability of U.S. weapon systems with those of the allies, and a commonality of weapons doctrine could prove of critical importance

to success in theater-level combat operations. The Warsaw Pact countries already possess the advantage of a high degree of standardization in their weapon systems.

Before proceeding to discussion of the proposed programs, I would like to review some of the significant recent changes in the Warsaw Pact forces that confront the United States and its allies in the European Command area-in military shorthand, the "threat" we face. Even while attention is centered on détente and the current activities surrounding our negotiations in both the mutual and balanced force reduction and the conference on security and cooperation in Europe, it is still a matter of hard fact that the threat is undiminished. 

The last few years have been marked by a continuing-and disturbing-growth in Soviet and Warsaw Pact military capabilities. Soviet ground forces have carried out substantial improvements in firepower, equipment modernization, and logistical support. There has been an increase in the number of Soviet divisions comprising a threat to the European Command, while the numbers of East European divisions have remained unchanged. At the same time, qualitative improvement of the Pact Ground Forces has continued apace, with the introduction of late model tanks, better armored personnel carriers, and better artillery.

Warsaw Pact air operations against countries in the European Command area could be carried out by more than 6,000 fighters, bombers and tactical reconnaissance aircraft. The Soviets continue to modernize their Air Forces with newgeneration fighters and fighter bombers. The Pact is augmenting and modernizing its air defense forces, emphasizing mobile systems to support rapidly moving field armies. Soviet naval power is a subject in itself. As the result of a tremendous effort the Soviet Union is able to project its sea power into the North Atlantic, the Mediterranean, the Indian Ocean and in fact to all the oceans of the world. This expanding facet of Russian combat power, capable of concentrating anywhere in the world, has ramfications that are far-reaching. 

You well know of the activities of the Soviets throughout a period of almost two decades, in North Africa and the Middle East, and of their efforts to sup plant Western influence with their own. Principal recipients of past Russian military assistance have been Egypt, Syria, and Iraq. The Soviets have demonstrated a willingness to supply late model weapons. Examples of equipment furnished prior to last year's war include the latest Model T-62 tank; the SCUD short range surface-to-surface ballistic missile, the SA-6 mobile surface-to-air missile system, the SA-7 hand-held surface-to-air missile launcher, MIG-21 jet fighters. TU-22 medium bombers, and Komar and OSA class guided missile patrol boats. Most recently Soviet deliveries to Egypt have been curtailed. Offsetting this decline however, the Soviet aid program has become even more generous in aid commitments and deliveries to Syria and Iraq. 

These activities continue to demonstrate the importance which the Soviet Union places on maintaining a presence and an influence in connection with military matters in this area of the world. During the Middle East war, these efforts were very much in evidence. In terms of security assistance, the Middle 

East war had new lessons for us, but for the most part it proved again some old maxims. In general it was shown again how essential is the expert integration of the combined arms involved in ground attack-tanks, infantry, tactical air, artillery, air defense-to an effective fighting force. At the same time we have seen that the expenditure of ammunition and equipment during intense modern warfare quickly reaches very high levels. Quick availability and quick replenishment become keys to success. 

The Soviet and Warsaw Pact capabilities, the continuing Soviet aid to certain countries, the demonstrated value of well-trained, well equipped conventional forces, the need for good equipment on hand, and the importance of logistical planning are considerations that have been applied to the U.S. security assistance effort.

I would like to review the principal programs before the committee, and comment both on regional considerations and on individual country programs. 

Security assistance in Continental Europe, except for Spain and Portugal, is in the form of military cash sales, with token grant training for Austria and Finland. Grant aid and foreign military sales credit are no longer required for other Continental European countries. 

The program as now proposed for Portugal, of somewhat less than one million dollars, would provide half a million dollars for training of personnel and

limited support for MAP-provided equipment of NATO committed forces. The strategic importance of Portugal and the value of the Azores for aerial resupply in support of NATO or unilateral U.S. activities were dramatically demon- 

Istrated during the recent Middle East war. It is my hope that the policies being = pursued by the new government may result in Portugal's assuming an enhanced role within the NATO structure. 

The proposed 1.6 million dollar training program for Spain fulfills the final terms of the 1970 Agreement of Friendship and Cooperation, which has given the U.S. the use of certain bases and facilities in Spain. 

Proposed programs for countries around the Mediterranean littoral involve several types of security assistance, and demonstrate, I believe, both the value and the versatility of the program. By offering modest security assistance pro- 

I grams to non-aligned Mediterranean nations, we provide them a reasonable alternative to alignment with more radical Arab states or the U.S.S.R., without the encroaching on their national prerogatives. We thereby help to strengthen stability, security and peace in the area. exi Ca eds The grant aid requested for Morocco is limited to 860,000 dollars for training.

GREECE AND NATO OBLIGATIONS Mr. BROOMFIELD.  

General, in the Washington Post, the 19th of this month, there appears an article by Rowland Evans and Robert Novak regarding some comments you recently made. It said:

Goodpaster praised Greece for "maintenance of her forces to an excellent level of training and to a high degree of readiness" and stressed Greece's strategic importance in NATO plans.

Given the internal friction that exists in Greece, do you think that they would be able to fulfill their NATO obligations?

General GOODPASTER. Here I will speak of the Greek Armed Forces.

the! di the in I, of course, follow their condition very closely. I was addressing their training and their readiness and the strategic role that the territory and the forces of Greece have in that NATO area. The state of their training is high, as I stated. They train hard and their soldiers are fit. They are dedicated to their country and to the independence of their country.

I have no question in that regard. They maintain a high state of readiness that is tested, insofar as their air forces are concerned, through various evaluation procedures. It is tested, insofar as their ground forces and their navy are concerned, through exercises and through other means. 

We are aware, of course, of the mutiny in the navy that occurred during the past year. No one would claim that this would be without effect. Even taking that into account, the capability that they have developed and maintained in their armed forces is, I think, a solid and sound one.

Their strategic role is important to the area. The forces of Greece in that area are important to the control of the eastern Mediterranean. 

The maintenance of a stable security situation there is very much dependent upon the continued participation in the NATO structure of our ally, the Greek nation.

You referred to the internal political situation. As an allied officer in the relation to Greece that I have been discussing here, it is incumbent upon me, my commanders, and my staff to avoid and keep clear of involvement or interference in the internal political affairs of Greece or any other NATO nation. We attempt to do that. Those attempts are not always wholly successful. However, we attempt as best we can to meet our obligations in good faith and to avoid being caught up in internal political situations.

Mr. BROOMFIELD. I guess my question was more to the fact that because of this internal problem, does it not reduce the effectiveness of 

Greece in the NATO program?

General GOODPASTER. To attempt to link those two factors would be speculative on my part. I think that I must confine myself to a description of the conditions of their forces as I perceive them.

WITHDRAWAL OF U.S. TROOPS FROM EUROPE Mr. ZABLOCKI.  

General Goodpaster, I want to join in welcoming you before the committee.

I want to pursue the line of questioning of the chairman. Certainly, as you well know, there are continuing pressures for the reduction of U.S. forces in Europe. I asked yesterday what would be the maximum number of troops that could be safely withdrawn from Southeast Asia and Asia. I would like to ask you, General, what in your opinion would be the maximum number of U.S. troops in Europe whose removal would not be damaging to our national security posture?

Perhaps you would prefer to reply for the record rather than in open session. 

General GOODPASTER. May I say what I can in open session on that, and if you like, augment my opening remarks with a reply on a classified basis.

If you are thinking of unilateral reductions, that is, reductions by the United States that are not balanced on the other side, this has been examined very thoroughly in NATO from the level of my command, from the level of my subordinate command in the Central European Area, and on up through the echelons of NATO to the highest political level.

Uniformly, the conclusion is very strongly, broadly, and definitely held that there simply is no margin for unilateral reductions, and

that if unilateral reductions were made we would lose the leverage necessary to attain mutual and balanced force reductions. 

MUTUAL AND BALANCED FORCE REDUCTIONS 

Now, if we are talking mutual and balanced force reductions, I have long felt and I feel now that there are major substantial opportunities for reduction on both sides. This, in my opinion, is what gives reality to the negotiations that are going on in Vienna. It is very early to attempt to say in detail what those reductions could be. This is the substance of the negotiations and, of course, I would not wish by premature comment to complicate in any way the process of negotiation. However, I think it is known that a proposal to reduce a common ceiling on the two sides, resulting in total reductions in the range of the better part of 100,000 on the Western side, and somewhat more than that on the Eastern side, could be contemplated if they are mutual reductions.

SOVIET DIVISIONS IN EUROPE

Are you referring to divisions in the satellite countries-in Czechoslovakia, Poland, Hungary, et cetera? Would you supply and amplify for the record your statement on the increase in the number of Soviet divisions and the threat to the European Command? 

General GOODPASTER. Yes, I would be very happy to do that. I can give you specific numbers on a classified basis. The numbers will demonstrate why we feel that there is no prudence in unilateral reductions. [The information requested was supplied as follows:]

INCREASE IN SOVIET DIVISIONS IN EUROPE 

Since about 1960, the Soviet forces in East Germany, Czechoslovakia and Poland have been increased by the equivalent of approximately [security deletion.] This program has accelerated during the past three to four years and now also includes augmentation with new and sophisticated weapons systems which have greatly increased the combat power of these Soviet forces. 

NATO AND THE MIDDLE EAST WAR 

Mr. ZABLOCKI. In further reference to your disappointment with our

NATO allies, particularly with regard to the October war in the Middle East, none of our NATO allies were really cooperative except for Portugal. Were you personally disappointed by the attitude of the NATO countries during the Middle East war? 

General GOODPASTER. I would like to say that I believe that there was a failure in NATO to consult and to try to determine the widest possible area of common position. To the degree that failure occurred, it can only occasion disappointment. That disappointment has been alleviated in the period since the October war by the fact that these shortcomings have been recognized very widely. In fact, much of the effort in NATO at the political level in formulating the socalled new relationship has been devoted to clarifying the possibilities

for consultation, not only on matters within the NATO area but also on matters that have an impact within the area of the alliance. 

I think the alliance was caught short when the Middle East war occurred. That kind of problem had not been faced in the past in a way that had resulted in the development of consultation procedures. 

I think that is where the shortcoming occurred. This, in my opinion, was a conclusion generally felt by all, that it could and should be done better in the future.

PAYING FOR MAAG'S IN EUROPE 

Mr. ZABLOCKI. Mr. Chairman, may I ask one final question.

In the presentation books, General, it states: 

There are U.S. civilian military security assistance personnel in several de veloped countries in Europe and the Middle East countries including Saudi

General GOODPASTER. I would like to supply the details of this on a classified basis, if I may. As I think you are aware, in general, many of the countries now meet a considerable part of the expenses of maintaining these MAAG's. In many cases, the MAAG's are very small in size. One of their main responsibilities is the supervision of the end use of items that have been provided in the past. Their role has been reduced. The amount of the cost that is borne by the host nation has risen, in some cases to a complete or nearly complete bearing of that cost.

I will provide that for the record. 

[The information requested follows:] U.S. CIVILIAN MILITARY SECURITY ASSISTANCE PERSONNEL OVERSEAS Military Assistance Advisory Groups, Military Missions and Military Groups in Europe, Saudi Arabia, and Iran commonly referred to as MAAGS are key elements in the system through which military assistance and foreign military sales requirements are identified and the resulting grant aid programs and sales arrangements are developed and implemented in a manner insuring their maxi mum contribution to U.S. security objectives. The DOD security assistance per sonnel assigned to the MAAGS plan, administer and manage the Military Assistance Program (MAP) and the Foreign Military Sales (FMS) programs as well as perform other functions of equal importance to the U.S. interests. In carrying out their responsibilities, MAAGS: 

1. Establish and maintain liaison between the U.S. defense establishment and that of the host country. 

2. Establish and maintain a relationship of mutual trust and confidence with the host country's military establishment. 

3. Under the supervision of the Commander of the Unified Command and consistent with the "Total Force" concept and country objectives and financial guidelines, develop security assistance plans and programs in coordination with the Chief of the U.S. Diplomatic Mission and other elements of the Country Team for submission to the Unified Command. 

4. Keep the Assistant Secretary of Defense (International Security Affairs), Defense Security Assistance Agency, Joint Chiefs of Staff, Unified Commands,

223.2.8.58 and Military Departments, as appropriate, informed of security assistance activities in country. 

5. Report on the utilization by the host country of, defense articles and services provided as grant aid, as well as personnel trained by the United States. 

6. Assist the host government in arranging for purchase of defense articles and services to meet valid country requirements through foreign military sales (FMS)' and commercial sales. 

7. Assist the Defense Security Assistance Agency and the Military Depart ments, as requested, in carrying out FMS negotiations with foreign governments. 

8. Cooperate with and assist representatives of U.S. firms in the sale of U.S. defense articles and services to meet valid country requirements. 

9. Assist U.S. Military Departments and their subordinate elements in arranging for the receipt, transfer, and acceptance of security assistance materiel, training, and other services for recipient countries. 

10. Assist the host government in the identification, administration, and proper disposition of security assistance materiel that is excess to current needs, including the reporting of (a) any dispositions made which are not in accordance with applicable understandings, agreements, and authorizations; and (b) the unauthorized transfer of defense articles of U.S. origin to third countries. 

11. Provide appropriate advisory services and technological assistance to the host country on security assistance matters. In less developed countries, provide advisory services, technical assistance, and training to develop a realistic capability to plan, program, budget and manage the military resources of the host country. 

12. When requested by appropriate authority, act as channel of communications for the Assistant Secretary of Defense (Installations and Logistics) (and the U.S. Defense Advisor to U.S. Mission NATO) regarding production and other logistical matters between the United States and the government to which accredited. 

13. When requested by appropriate authority, act as channel of communications for the Director, Defense Research and Engineering, regarding research and development matters between the United States and the government to which accredited. 

These personnel, therefore, establish and maintain rapport with the military of the host country to provide channels of communication, dialogue and influence which are valuable to the U.S. government for diplomatic and commercial as well as military reasons.

The annual operating costs of the MAAGS are composed of two parts-the DOD and the MAP annual operating costs. The DOD annual operating costs consist of items such as U.S. military salaries, allowances and permanent change of station costs to the host country. The MAP annual operating costs consist of items such as local civilian salaries, travel, rents, utilities and communications. 

In an effort to have the host government pay an equivalent to these DOD costs, a program of contributed currency is in effect. The host government contributes local currency which is available to meet the costs of these security assistance programs. In many cases, the amount contributed by the host government meets or exceeds the DOD annual operating costs. For instance, the following data are appropriate for FY 75.

Country DOD annual operating costs

Any excess of contributed currency more than needed to meet the DOD annual operating costs is used to meet the MAP annual operating costs.

HOST COUNTRY CONTRIBUTIONS

IRAN SECURITY PLANS Mr. WINN. Thank you, Mr. Chairman. 

General, on page 10 of your report you say that:

The Shah (of Iran) has made clear his dedication to building first-rate armed forces and is relying primarily on the assistance of the United States in achieving those forces.

Is there any country over there that does not have the same desires and the same demands on the United States? 

General GOODPASTER. I think the terms on which the U.S. assistance is provided varies from country to country. In the case of Iran, the expenses, as I indicated, are wholly borne by Iran. Now that is not true, of course, in some of the other countries. The assistance in Iran consists primarily of advice as well as facilitating and assisting in the process of the purchasing of the right kind of arms to do the military task that is involved. In other countries, some degree of credit assistance or grant aid still is required. 

Now, with regard to the dedication, the countries with which we are associated have shown their dedication to maintaining their own independence. This is shown in different ways. There is no doubt that that basic dedication is there. In the case of Iran, what is shown is a sense on the part of the Shah that he must assume a wider burden if there is to be stability and security in that whole area. 

The Shah is very conscious of that. He has dedicated a lot of this effort, not in a narrow way simply to maintain the immediate security of Iran, but on a wider scale. This is based on the conviction that if the area becomes unstable, in that it becomes a field for contesting by

1 outside powers to gain position and dominance in various parts of the area, this would work against the interests of his country over the long term.

The problems are certainly there. He can see in Iraq, for example, an instability. Through the acceptance of large amounts of outside assistance in South Yemen, many of the same kind of conditions exist. 

These are nations whose forces and whose weapons inventories constitute a threat to their neighbors and, in turn, a threat of instability to the area. This is what gives the special character to the program that the Shah has determined to follow.

THE SITUATION IN GREECE Mr. ROSENTHAL. Thank you, Mr. Chairman. 

General, it is good to see you again. 

I want to expand a little bit on the subject of Greece. 

On March 27 of this year John Zighdis, a former and leading member of the Center Union Party, testified before the Subcommittee on Europe. Among the things he testified to, he said that, The net result of the present government in Greece has been the weakening of the Greek armed establishment because practically all the senior officers with war experience and modern professional education have been removed for political reasons.

And he asserted that the naval situation of May 1973, had also led to some disintegration of the armed forces. 

INTERVIEW WITH GENERAL GOODPASTER 

Thereafter you presumably granted an interview to a Greek journalist, and that interview appeared in all of the Greek press in Athens on April 20, 1974, in some papers on four column headlines, and in other papers on eight column headlines. 

On April 21 Athens News, which is the English language newspaper, quoted the pro-junta newspaper, Acropolis, as follows: 

The significance of General Goodpaster's statement is manifold because- (a) those who may be plotting against the national interests of Greece are warned that the country's armed forces are strong and ready to protect them from any provocation: (b) a severe blow is dealt against those who in their effort to serve selfish political aims have not hesitated to claim that the Greek armed forces have been weakened as a former official of the Center Union Party did while testifying be fore the United States House of Representatives on March 27: 

(c) the Greek people's belief that the country's armed forces are strong and at a high degree of readiness is strengthened further by General Goodpaster's ascertainments. 

I gather that your statement unfortunately was used in a political context against Zighdis and subsequently Ziohdis did return to Greece and is now confined in some type of prison establishment.

I am also advised that Ambassador Tasca was distressed at your interview, and that your statements, while you intended no political ramifications and I am absolutely certain that that was your desiredid in fact have serious political ramifications and were used against Zighdis. 

What I am really interested in is the procedure. Is there anything that can be done about the procedures in NATO headquarters for clearing such interviews so that the political ramifications are not used to the detriment of the U.S. policy. Perhaps there is also something else you want to tell us about the incident. What if anything went wrong, and can anything be done to avoid this kind of situation in the future?

REMOVAL OF SENIOR MILITARY OFFICERS IN GREECE 

General GOODPASTER. First, may I say that in addition to my earlier comment concerning the Navy, I should have reference to this point of the removal of senior officers. These are officers of experience and ability. Inevitably in a situation of this kind there is a period of time before their successors have gained fully the level of leadership effectiveness. This is a fact of military life. These changes occur constantly in all services and all forces. When a considerable number of changes occur at the same time, there is an inevitable adverse consequence. I would like that there not be any misunderstanding or misperception in relation to what I have said about training, readiness, and the incidents in the Navy.

Now let me turn to the broader question that you have raised and add to my prior comments in order to respond to the additional points that you have raised.

The principle that we try to follow is clear. We try to do our military job, to carry out our military responsibilities, and to do that in the context of respect for our ally, the people and the nation of Greecea very sturdy and valued NATO ally. 

NATO OFFICERS AND INTERNAL POLITICAL AFFAIRS 

We try to do this also in a way that keeps clear of internal political affairs. I assure you of our effort to avoid interference, involvement, or influence either pro or con with regard to any particular regime or its opposition within any NATO country. It would be quite improper for us as holding allied responsibilities to so involve ourselves. 

We attempt to act correctly and to make our actions correct in these matters. That is the principle. The difficulty comes in assuring that that principle is reflected in practice and in the practical affairs that come up. Obviously, it is difficult because military matters do impinge, can be made to impinge, or can be made to appear to impinge on domestic political differences. Nevertheless, we try to hold to a neutral line. 

I must say in this regard that I am chagrined to hear that my interview, which was given in good faith and prepared very carefully to stick to the military and NATO aspects of the matter, may have been used in a way that had some influence on a domestic political situation. 

I can say only that should this question arise in the future, we will take account of the experience that we have had here. 

I do not want to overstate that because I don't believe that we could do our military job if we took a stance of refusing to give an evaluation.

of the role and the success of military efforts in a particular country. I regard that as part of my obligation. I try to do that carefully. 

With regard to procedural actions, I believe that what I have just said suggests the kind of additional consideration that we will have to give to requests of this kind if they are repeated in the future.

TENSIONS BETWEEN GREECE AND TURKEY Mr. FRELINGHUYSEN. Thank you, Mr. Chairman. 

I assume that the chairman has explained the delay in the arrival of two of us. We were being briefed at the White House by the President and the Secretary of State or we surely would have been here at the outset of your remarks.

It is a pleasure to welcome you back to the committee, General 

Goodpaster. I don't know what you have been asked. I will ask a brief question and hope it hasn't been asked previously.

There have been repeated questions about increased tension between Greece and Turkey. Would you care to comment on both the nature of that tension and its possible significance? In other words, do you think there is any likelihood of an outbreak of hostilities? I understand there has been some interest in the purchase of arms and so on. 

General GOODPASTER. I am aware of various issues that concern these two countries. This is a matter to which obviously I give thought and attention. I have had the opportunity to discuss some of these concerns with senior military leaders in each country. My view has been that these are issues arising in the framework of NATO and that solutions ought to be found through consultation and through the development of mutually satisfactory accommodations. 

Many of these issues have very complex backgrounds. With the best will in the world they will be extremely difficult to resolve. I have counseled restraint. I have been very gratified at responses assuring me that such restraint will indeed be exercised. This is of particular importance insofar as the military structure of the two countries is concerned. The problems are difficult enough without adding to the tension through arousing concerns, particularly concerns of an emotional nature within the military forces.

I might say in this regard that NATO gives us a very valuable framework within which to press for the processes of consultation to go forward. Secretary General Luns devotes his attention to this. All of us who bear senior responsibilities in NATO work in that direction. 

The specifics of these issues are very complicated. They have long historical precedents. Some aspects of them, particularly new problems, are arising that complicate and disturb the situation. It is my very deep hope that solutions will be found by the governments directly concerned and found through these processes of consultation. 

The other effort to which I have devoted myself is to try to keep the focus in both countries on what I regard as the greater issuethe maintenance of a stable secure situation in the eastern Mediterranean. There must be harmonious and cooperative action by these nations and the other NATO allies if that objective vis-a-vis the Warsaw Pact is to be attained.

I am hopeful that wisdom and the benefit of the NATO association will result in restraint.

NATO MECHANISM FOR CONCILIATION 

Mr. FRELINGHUYSEN. I assume from what you say that there is no formal mechanism in NATO or elsewhere that would provide for a process of conciliation. Is it basically an expression of concern by Secretary General Luns and yourself and others in the establishment? 

General GOODPASTER. It is part of the established practice and understanding within NATO to use the Council in particular as a forum within which these matters can be considered. The fact that each country is represented by experienced men of high position in the NATO Council imeans that they have constantly open channels of consultation. 

Along with that, from time to time the Secretary General is given a watching brief. Also, where he sees a problem area arising he traditionally has exercised initiative to bring the matter under discussionsometimes more formally, sometimes more informally. 

Finally, I would mention a meeting such as the Foreign Ministers' meeting that has just occurred at Ottawa. This provides a further opportunity for direct consultation. The term "conciliation" is a more technical term in diplomatic language; however, certainly consultation is there. It is an inherent part of the NATO process and commitment. 

Mr. FRELINGHUYSEN. Thank you.
