U.S. ARMS TO IRAN 

Mr. HAMILTON. General, when Secretary Schlesinger was before this committee he pointed out that a very large proportion of the $8 billion in arms sales in fiscal year 1974 went to Iran-well over half, I believe. 

Along with that fact some of us are concerned about the fact that the price of oil in the world today is bringing the Western economic system very close to great difficulty, if not collapse. I am wondering if there is any relationship between these two facts. Does the United States, as the chief supplier of arms to Iran in simply enormous quantities, have some obligation to exert pressure on Iran which is the chief culprit in keeping the price of oil so high? Do we have any obligation to try to exert pressure on Iran to try to bring down the price of oil, and frankly use the leverage of our arms sales to do it?

General GOODPASTER. These are two very important questions. The heart of your question goes to linking the two in some way. Let me first address the issue of the price of oil.

For a number of years it has been the Iranian view, as stated by members of their government, that there should be a higher price of oil. Interestingly, they have pressed very strongly for less wasteful use

of oil. This seems to have been a strongly held view for quite a number of years.

I also know that the price of oil was discussed recently among the producing nations. There was reported to be a considerable divergence of view. Some feel that it should be raised further. Some feel that it should be reduced.

In general, my understanding is that the Iranians have indeed taken the stand that the price of oil should be relatively high. I say that because there seems to be a conviction of long standing on their part and related not solely to the money question, but to the fast dissipation of this nonreplenishable and very important world reserve. 

With regard to the idea of exerting pressure, I would not have understood that to be a very rewarding approach for a sovereign, independent, proud nation. To that I would add that there are other sources of arms in the world today. American arms that are being provided are well chosen and are being well utilized. There are other places to which a nation could turn if it felt it was being subjected to any kind of coercion.

An approach of continued consultation, which I assume is now going on, would be the right approach. The oil-producing nations must understand that the continued existence of a viable world economic and financial system is in their interest just as truly as it is in the interests of the other nations.

OIL AND U.S. ARMS TO IRAN 

Mr. HAMILTON. General, I can appreciate your reluctance to link the two, and under ordinary circumstances obviously that would not be the path to follow, but in view of the really very grave threat to the Western economic order, because of this price of oil we may be forced to take some action. The United States does have a special standing with Iran, not just because of the arms sales, but because of other reasons as well, and it seems to me we are going to have to do a lot more than just consult in order to get them to understand the impact of that price of oil on the Western economy.

INCREASE IN MILITARY ASSISTANCE TO JORDAN 

Mr. HAMILTON. Could you tell us what are the reasons for the very substantial increase in the amount of military assistance to Jordan? What particular weapons will we be furnishing and the like?

General GOODPASTER. Jordan is a moderate Arab State which maintains close ties with the West. Its location, adjacent to Israel, makes it an important buffer state [security deletion]. Following the Jordanian suppression of the Palestinian guerrillas in 1971, the U.S. undertook to replace Jordan's combat losses and to initiate a military modernization program. [Security deletion.] The Jordanian 

Armed Forces require sufficient modern weapons and equipment to enable them 

[security deletion] and to deter [security deletion] aggression [security deletion]. 

The continued Israeli occupation of the West Bank and the cost of the Jordanian Army-fedayeen confrontation have resulted in the loss of some of the cash subsidies from other Arab States. [Securty deletion.] The fiscal year 1975 security assistance programs proposed for Jordan will assist in meeting the critical modernization needs and help maintain Jordan as a bulwark against disruptive elements seeking to erode the negotiated peace settlement in the Middle East. 

The particular items currently programed for Jordan under the fiscal year 1975 security assistance authorization are set out below. Some adjustment may be anticipated. 

A. Military Assistance Program: [Security deletion] F5E and F5F aircraft, [security deletion] Self-propelled artillery, [security deletion] Trucks, [security deletion] Machine Guns and Submachine guns, [security deletion] TOW missiles.

B. Foreign Military Sales Credit: [Security deletion.] C. Military Assistance Training Program: 63 Students. 

HOMEPORTING IN GREECE

Athens soon?

General GOODPASTER. At the present time this project is in a deferred status. I think Secretary Schlesinger referred to the fact that there were I believe his words were "differing perceptions"-regarding the factors that enter into this issue. Until a better and stronger basis for agreement is found, it would not seem likely that these negotiations could go forward.

OPIUM POPPIES AND U.S. AID TO TURKEY 

Mr. HAMILTON. One other question, if I may, Mr. Chairman.

A number of members are sponsoring an amendment to prohibit aid to Turkey if they allow poppies to be grown there. What would be the impact of such an amendment? 

General GOODPASTER. If that amendment were enacted and as a result aid to Turkey were, in fact, terminated, this would have an extremely serious and harmful effect. Let me just speak in the military area. The forces of Turkey are really excellent forces in terms of their

training, their dedication, the hard work of their officers, and their intense effort in making their forces fully effective. 

They have a common border with the Soviet Union, and also with Bulgaria. The military strength of Turkey is indispensable to a position of security and stability in the eastern end of the Mediterranean. I very strongly would hope, and indeed, urge that this prob lem, too, be dealt with through the process of conciliation and negotiation.

I have had occasion to discuss the dimension of this problem in at least general terms with my senior Turkish colleagues. I have tried to find out the dimensions of the problem from their side as well as to let them know the gravity with which this problem is viewed, not only within our country, but in terms of my responsibilities for U.S. military men in the European area. Anything that leads us in a direction which would reduce our effectiveness in gaining control over this drug problem would have to be deeply deplored. 

They understand that this is a matter which is especially suited to serious, frank negotiation between two allies who respect each other very, very deeply.

Mr. WHALEN. 

TOUR OF DUTY FOR U.S. TROOPS IN NATO 

General Goodpaster, what is the tour of duty of our U.S. troops wilo are assigned to NATO?

General GOODPASTER. This varies, but in general, the established tour is 3 years. For some of our forces, it had been extended to 4 years. 

The tendency now is to move it back to 3 years with possibilities of extension on an individual case-by-case basis. 

U.S. DEPENDENTS IN EUROPE 

Mr. WHALEN. How many dependents do our NATO assigned troops have residing with them in Europe?

General GOODPASTER. The figure is 205,800. 

Mr. WHALEN. General, I am sure that all of the Members of Congress share the hope that our NATO assigned troops meet the combat effective goal that I am sure you are seeking to attain. Nevertheless, I am concerned that our forces, encumbered by approximately 205,800 dependents, may not be achieving this goal.

Would you agree, General, that our troops might be more combat ready, more combat effective, if they were trained and operated under conditions that avoided the distractions which dependents create? 

General GOODPASTER. This, of course, is a matter that has been reviewed and evaluated repeatedly. In fact, it was tried out on at least a limited scale in late 1960-early 1961. That time a ban on dependents was put into effect. 

Mr. WHALEN. May I just interrupt here, General? Was it not that ban put on dependents in order to reduce the impact on the balance of payments which the dependents generated?

General GOODPASTER. That is correct. It was a gold flow action at that time. 

Mr. WHALEN. Yes.

IMPACT OF BAN OF FAMILIES IN EUROPE 

General GOODPASTER. It was reevaluated and has been reevaluated repeatedly since. You have to face this question if you are going to have the forces overseas. What is the impact on readiness of having families versus not having families? You have to consider what kind of force you would have if you could not have families, including the problems that typically arise when you have a force that is separated from the families.

Our experience at that time was that you could not maintain a force without families for long periods of assignment in Europe. You would have to decrease the term of assignment, and even then you would have to expect difficult problems of morale, discipline, and behavior. These are problems that concern us deeply. 

I happened to be there during the 1960-61 experiment. Out of that experience and based upon every analysis that we have made since that time, it has been our conviction that in terms of force effectiveness and readiness, we are actually in better condition with the dependents than if we took all of the consequeces of the alternative. 

REDUCING TIME OF NATO TOUR 

Mr. WHALEN. As I understand what you are saying, General, you are suggesting that we have a difficult choice of having no troops or few troops there versus perhaps a reduced combat readiness with our NATO troops having their dependents along with them. 

I raised the first question for a reason, General Goodpaster. I can appreciate the fact that separation from one's family for 3 or perhaps 

4 years is very difficult. I was wondering, therefore, have you considered the possibility of reducing to perhaps 1 year, or perhaps even 6 months, the assignment to Europe and in that way achieving a greater turnover and minimizing at the same time the separation of the serviceman from his family? 

General GOODPASTER. That was one of the specific options evaluated.

That was the experiment to which I was referring. I had some experience with the problem of bringing troops over for a 6-month period. They were incorporated into the division that I commanded at the time. They were good troops. It took them a number of months to learn the area and the mode of operations within the area and to develop familiarity not only with their own emergency plan and mission, but also with the operations of other forces, including the air forces in the area. Just about the time that this unit was achieving an effectiveness comparable to that of the forces that were there, it was sent back and a new unit was sent to go through the same process. This experiment worked even to this limited degree only, because the new unit was incorporated in a structure in which nine-tenths were there on a permanent basis.

Particularly in the deployed forces, there is a necessity to know the procedures of the allied forces on their right and their left and in the

air. These requirements are such, I am convinced, that we would undergo a very substantial reduction in effectiveness if we were to try to limit significantly tour length.

We are aware of the burden of support in schools, in housing ac commodations, and the like. It is a significant burden, although in terms of its load on the total force, it forms a very small part. A good part of this work is done by civilians, including local civilians. 

Mr. WHALEN. Mr. Chairman, I apologize for straying somewhat from the subject at hand, but I did want to take the opportunity to relate to General Goodpaster my concern about our posture in NATO. 

Thank you very much, Mr. Chairman.

SOVIET NAVAL FACILITIES IN MEDITERRANEAN 

Mr. WOLFF.  

Happy to see you again, General Goodpaster.

General, do the Russians maintain any naval bases in the Mediterranean?

General GOODPASTER. They have no naval bases that you would say are under their sovereignty or control. However, they do have established access to several bases. 

Mr. WOLFF. Where are they?

General GOODPASTER. They make use of Alexandria. They have been operating in and out of Latakia in Syria. Beyond that, they employ anchorages which are in international waters in the Mediterranean. 

Mr. WOLFF. I understand that we have the capability of taking out those facilities if necessary.

General GOODPASTER. I would prefer to put it in these terms: We have the capability of dealing with the Soviet naval forces. The extent to which they would be able and would wish to try to use bases of that kind in an actual emergency becomes very, very questionable. 

Mr. WOLFF. Now in a briefing that I had in your area I was made to understand that we have the capability of closing the Strait of 

Marmara in the Dardanelles. Am I correct in that? 

General GOODPASTER. Yes, we evaluate that we have that capability.

This becomes a matter, however, that requires continuing evaluation, particularly because of the threat that is formed by the large Warsaw Pact forces in the area of Greek and Turkish Thrace. Here the approach is to the west of the Dardanelles, and the chance of bypassing the Turkish Straits has to be recognized.

FRANCE AND NATO Mr. BIESTER.  I am cognizant of the pressure of time and will ask just one question.

General, to what extent do you perceive any gradual change or difference in the attitude of the French Government or France with respect to her commitment to NATO, or her involvement in the NATO process?

General GOODPASTER. First of all, the nature of the relationship between France and particularly the United States over these military issues and NATO issues, has greatly improved in my opinion in the past 6 or 8 years. To the extent it is within my power, I have tried to further that kind of improvement. The practical limits of what can be done are still set by the decisions that were made by General de Gaulle in 1966 and 1967. Of those, I do not see any, nor have I learned of any prospect that those would be modified. Within the scope of those decisions, practical measures of cooperation have indeed been developed. That process continues.

Insofar as the NATO command is concerned, there is considerable value to be achieved through maintaining common procedures. Our forces could operate together effectively in the circumstances where that remains a possibility. The French have said simply that they will reserve until the time of an emergency the decision as to whether or not to stand with their allies. In the event they do, I believe that what we have done and are continuing to work toward, will make it possible for their association to be militarily effective. 

Mr. BIESTER. Thank you, very much.

READINESS OF THE GREEK ARMED FORCES 

Mr. YATRON. Thank you.

General Goodpaster, following on the line of questioning that was started by Mr. Broomfield and Mr. Rosenthal, you give us your impression of the degree of readiness and the importance of the readiness of the Greek armed forces. Now I would like to say that, according to information that has reached me, many U.S. officers who have taken part in bilateral exercises-that is, the United States with the Greek armed forces in the framework of NATO have had excellent impressions about the capabilities of the Greek armed forces. I would like to know if you would like to amplify or comment in this regard? 

General GOODPASTER. I commented earlier about the evaluations that we conduct from time to time affecting particularly the air force. 

I noted the exercises that we conduct in which army and navy units are involved. It is out of those experiences that I have formed this evaluation of the effectiveness and the dedication of the Greek soldier, the Greek officer, the Greek sailor, and the Greek airman. They train hard. They work hard. They are very serious about their military activities and their military obligations. They are very serious about their dedication to the continued independence of their country against any foreign attack.

You sense these factors. You see the result of these factors in the fact that their units are handled well. Their troops perform well. 

They perform excellent maintenance on equipment, much of which I might add, is becoming old and difficult to maintain. These are the tests that a commander and senior staff certainly will be making when they observe forces of this kind.

GREECE AND NATO'S "SOUTHERN FLANK' 

Mr. YATRON. General, one final question. In yesterday's Washington Post there was a syndicated column entitled "Greece: The Conflict in U.S. Views" in which Elias Demetracopoulos, represented as "Washington Greek exile leader," was mentioned. 

Now this article refers also to you, General. Mr. Demetracopoulos is said to have had close contact with Andreas Papandreau, who would like to see Greece expelled from NATO.

Now my question is, how would you see the southern flank of the alliance without the important contribution of Greece?

General GOODPASTER. It is an important contribution. It is an indispensable contribution. Greece gains security because of its membership in the alliance. The alliance gains security because of the membership and participation of Greece in the alliance. 

I am not familiar enough with the views of these gentlemen that you mentioned to be able to comment on those. However, the military and the security facts of the matter lead me to the conviction that we have achieved a stable security situation in that area. Without Greece, it would not be possible to conceive of the maintenance of a balance and stability in the region.

Mr. YATRON. Thank you.

U.S. FORCES IN NATO

RACIAL SITUATION IN U.S. EUROPEAN COMMAND 

Mr. GUYER. At the time we talked with you, then, you indicated that you had greatly reduced the black troop problem. I don't think it is within the language, the fact that it was a little bit difficult to adapt black soldiers to white communities, and you felt that you had made a nice amalgamation in that regard. Is that still a prevalent situation! 

General GOODPASTER. Very substantial progress has been made in the last 2 or 3 years in opening communication and establishing broader and better understanding with our black soldiers, sailors, and airmen, whether officer or enlisted. This progress has contributed in a very valuable way to the effectiveness of the force. I would like to say that I know of no one who thinks that this is an issue or a problem that lost its importance. It must continue to be tended to; it is being tended to. Part of the means by which this progress has been made was the creating of an understanding of its importance. Another part was the necessity to undertake active leadership in this regard by our responsible officers up and down the chain of command. 

THE DRUG PROBLEM IN U.S. EUROPEAN COMMAND 

Mr. GUYER. I believe you also indicated that originally drugs was a problem because of the great amount of leisure time and perhaps lack of combat, and you said they had turned the corner there and that was no longer a major problem. Is that still correct?

General GOODPASTER. I would say that we have turned the corner in the sense that the incidents are down by the measures that we now have in effect. These measures give us a much higher level of confidence that we know what is going on. However, I would not want to leave the impression that there no longer is a major problem. It is a problem. 

So long as any of this continues, it is a problem that is of the deepest concern to us.

One of the grounds of my concern is that the incidents lie primarily among the young soldiers. No commander can feel at peace with his sense of responsibility so long as this continues. We have a multiphase program going on that attempts, directly or through our contacts with other agencies, to attack this problem. At every stage from where the opium or other products are grown, all the way through the manufacturer, the shipment, the selling process, until it comes to the final end, we are trying to overcome the drug situation. What can be reported is progress and a lowering of the incidents. Nevertheless, there can be no ground whatsoever for complacency. 

Mr. GUYER. I think perhaps, as Mr. Wolff indicated, that is more our problem in the Congress than yours, Mr. Wolff is chairman of an ad hoc committee addressing itself to narcotics problems. 

U.S. TROOP REDUCTIONS IN EUROPE 

One final observation. You are going to be bombarded sooner or later with a peppery number of bills to reduce troops, I am sure of that. 

We have had it already this session. Mr. Hays and others have indicated that it is not exactly economy to take people from one place and put them in another. In other words, our just sending people home from 

Europe would not shorten their term of service, it would not particularly make it inexpensive because of the cost of transport. 

I think that sooner or later if there is a troop reduction it might be well, sir, for you to have a figure in mind rather than us trying to solve this by vivisection on the floor of the Congress. I would hope that if economy or cutbacks would come you might have a knowledgeable figure in mind. That would be a whole lot better answer than having a Congressman with a meat ax just saying, "We should take 100,000 away here and 150,000 there." I would hope that you might keep that in your advisement as you go along.

General GOODPASTER. We are approaching this through the route of the mutual and balanced force reduction negotiations. Those negotiations present a wide range of possible cuts on both sides which have been evaluated. That is by far the preferable route because the premise of the mutual and balanced force reductions is that there will be undiminished security on both sides as a result of those reductions. Reductions of that kind actually, in my opinion, can contribute to added stability in the European area.

Just referring to your point about moving the forces out of Europe, it is very questionable, in my opinion, whether if those forces are kept in service, as I think they should be, in the United States, they, in fact, would cost less. My own expectation is that when you consider the necessity of forward stocking, duplicate sets of major equipment in the European area, opening of additional stations in the United States, and the problem of enlarging your capability to get them back

quickly, the net of it could well be an increase in the funds that would be required.

Mr. GUYER. I think the point is well taken because we do have in every man and woman in the service an investment and if they are removed or terminated from that service then we lose part of that investment.

General GOODPASTER. There is no margin for an overall reduction in our forces at the present time. 

Mr. GUYER. Thank you, sir.

SECURITY SUPPORTING ASSISTANCE FOR MALTA 

Mr. FOUNTAIN. General, there is $9.5 million in security supporting assistance for Malta in this bill. What is this money for, and is the United States the only contributor?

General GOODPASTER. The $9.5 million is the U.S. share of an annual rent which the UK and NATO agreed to pay Malta under the terms of the UK/Malta Defense Agreement signed on 26 March 1972. The agreement is for seven years. It basically provides for British use of Maltese facilities and the exclusion of Warsaw Pact usage.

CONTRIBUTIONS TO THE U.N. FORCE IN CYPRUS 

Mr. FOUNTAIN. General, $4.8 million is in the bill for the UN Forces in Cyprus. 

What is this money used for; how many other countries contribute to this Force, what is the total for all, and what is the U.S. share? 

General GOODPASTER. $4.8 million is that amount which the United States has pledged annually to support the 2,500 man UN-Force in Cyprus. Some 54 countries have contributed to this project over the years, but on an irregular basis, thus creating a financial shortfall. To eliminate this deficit, the United States has been urging a RIF which would result in a smaller force with the same capability. The 

United States has pledged $64.1 million as of December 1973, or approximately one-third of the total. The UK, FRG, Italy, Greece, Australia, Belgium, Netherlands, Norway, Sweden, Denmark, Austria and Switzerland are among the contributing countries.

Mr. FOUNTAIN. With that, I have no other questions.

COMMAND RESPONSIBILITY FOR MAP IN MIDDLE EAST 

Mr. BINGHAM. 

General, what is your responsibility as Commander in Chief, U.S. 

European Command, and Supreme Allied Commander, Europe, with respect to these assistance programs in the Middle East? 

General GOODPASTER. With the exception of the Israel program which is not administered by my command, we are the administering agency. The policy determinations are made at the Washington level with inputs, of course, from my command and from the MAAG's in the various countries. The decisions as to what proposals will be made to the Congress are made in Washington. Once the programs have been put in in final form, then we are responsible for actually administering them, carrying them out and providing the assistance and advice in the countries concerned. 

Mr. BINGHAM. And that applies to Iran? 

General GOODPASTER. Yes, that applies to Iran also.

IRAN AND OIL PRICES

Mr. BINGHAM. I would just like to make a brief comment in relation to the matter that Mr. Hamilton raised. I am not sure that I would agree with his suggestion that we try to put the kind of pressure on Iran that he was talking about, but I think the very fact that he asked that question indicates a considerable degree of unhappiness in the Congress and this is something I would like to underline-about the role of Iran in the matter of oil prices. General GOODPASTER. The implication is that this could lead to a change in the way we are working with the Iranians. On the military side, this is a matter of concern to me. We have developed a good relationship; it is sensible; it is very responsible. The Shah takes a direct part in giving very constructive leadership in the development of a defensive posture which is calculated to give stability in the area.

QUESTIONS SUPPLIED FOR RECORD 

Chairman MORGAN. Thank you, General. We are going to submit some questions to you and you can supply the answers for the record. [The questions submitted and the response subsequently received follow:] 

Chairman MORGAN. General, on page 5 of your statement you say that security assistance in Continental Europe is in the form of military cash sales, with token grant training for Austria and Finland. I have two questions about this: Are cash sales really considered to be "assistance"? What would be the impact if a limitation were to be placed upon the level of cash sales which can be made without prior approval of Congress-the so-called Nelson Amendment?

General GOODPASTER. As a matter of law, cash sales are not considered to be "assistance."

I would not favor adoption of any such proposal at this time for the following reasons: 

The flexibility required in order to meet unanticipated and critical needs of our allies would be severely eroded if their needs exceed the threshold. 

The delays inherent in the procedure could, by denying funds at a critical time, prohibit the timely administration of production lines with a corresponding increase in cost.

The public debate of the terms of a pending sale could encourage a foreign supplier to make a "more favorable bid" thus prejudicing a sale which may otherwise be in the best interest of the United States. 

In terms of reporting as distinguished from approving the data is already required and is currently being furnished (see Section 657 FAA 1961 as amended and pages 84-86 CPD).

The Nelson Amendment is itself imprecise and would be extremely difficult to administer.

Reference is made to a memorandum from the Assistant General Counsel, Department of Defense, addressing the Nelson Amendment which was previously supplied (see p. 336).

Today it will be our pleasure to hear from two distinguished colleagues from the House. We have with us today the Honorable Clarence Miller and the Honorable Bella

Mr. Miller, you have a prepared statement. You may proceed, sir.

STATEMENT OF HON. CLARENCE MILLER, A REPRESENTATIVE IN CONGRESS FROM THE STATE OF OHIO 

Mr. MILLER.  

I have with me today my administrative assistant, Mr. Dave Brown, and my legislative assistant, Mr. Dave Jeffery. 

Mr. Chairman and members of the committee, I appreciate this opportunity to testify before you today on a proposal which I believe deserves a place in our foreign aid program. This concept is the "barter bill," H.R. 14041. Basically, it would allow the United States to exchange or barter its foreign aid for raw materials which we lack in this country or which are in short supply. I would like to take a few minutes explaining why I feel this barter idea is necessary; then a little about the bill itself, and finally direct myself to some of the obvious questions and criticism that the bill raises. 

Since the end of World War II the United States has contributed over $158 billion in foreign aid and assistance. During the period immediately after the war up through the mid-1960's an attitude prevailed in this country that since we were the richest country in the world we could give away large portions of our wealth to help the poorer nations. Today, however, this is no longer the case. We cannot afford to continue to give away our wealth with no strings attached. 

Our wealth is limited; our resources are limited. If we are to maintain and improve the quality of life in the United States, we must receive something in return for our foreign aid. (421)

FOREIGN AID: BOUGHT NO LOVE 

Our foreign assistance program has certainly not made the rest of the world love us. Many aid recipients gladly take foreign aid with one hand while slapping us with the other through the promotion of anti-U.S. policies. For example, Ecuador has received $340 million since 1964. They have returned our generosity by seizing U.S. fishing boats that come within 200 miles of their shores. 

Jamaica has received $86 million during that same period. Just last month the Jamaican Government announced that it intends to increase the royalties and taxes it levies on bauxite by more than 500 percent. 

Presently Jamaica is the major source of bauxite ores for the U.S. aluminum industry.

There are, of course, other examples: Peru, Uganda, India, and others. They all serve to illustrate the point that in many instances our aid has not brought stability to some parts of the world. It has not bought friendship for the United States. It has not, in many cases, filtered down to the poor man in the recipient countries. Often it has been wasted on showy office buildings or other extravagant trappings that are monuments to the waste of the American taxpayers' dollars. 

While the United States has spent these billions of dollars in foreign assistance over the past 28 years we have been ignoring the crisis that we are heading for with regard to our own economic stability. 

Each year the Congress is called upon to raise the debt ceiling. Much of that debt is generated by borrowing to meet foreign aid outlays Our balance of payments picture continues to look bleak for the future. 

At the same time that our national economy is saddled with these burdens American industry faces an uncertain future as the critical raw materials necessary to progress become more and more scarce. 

CRITICAL RAW MATERIALS 

Of the 13 so-called basic materials vital to manufacturing, the United States must import all or part of its requirements for 11 of them. 

Unfortunately this picture will not get any better. There are almost no known large reserves of these minerals left in the United Statesand they have been prospected for almost everywhere in the country, So as far as our ability to be mineral self-sufficient, we have reached our limits, barring the discovery in the distant future of substitutes Of course, it is not just these 11 basic minerals that we are forced to import. There are many others that may be equally important such as platinum, cobalt, mica, magnesium-and the petroleum that we all know about now. Even assuming that our demand for these materials does not increase-an unlikely event-the United States will be out of most of these by the year 2000. 

If we want to insure that our children and grandchildren are not brought to their knees by the type of economic blackmail that we have seen in the past year we must take steps now to provide mineral resources for the years ahead. Without such security American industry will be permanently crippled, jobs will be lost, and our standard of living will drop sharply. The longer we wait to take preventive action the closer to economic disaster we move. Just over the past 6 months we have seen the chaotic effect that spot shortages of certain critical

raw materials can have on U.S. industry. Imagine what it could be like if industry had to be at the mercy of foreign mineral cartels for all of its crucial needs. 

UNITED STATES RUNNING OUT OF STRATEGIC MATERIALS 

At the same time that the United States is running out of these strategic minerals, many of our aid recipients are sitting on mountains of untapped or partially developed natural wealth. Looking at a list of the known or speculative mineral reserves in the world you won't find nations such as the United States, France, Germany, or Japan on that list. Instead you will find nations such as Brazil with zinc, Indonesia with copper, Peru with lead, and Jamaica with bauxite. These are the same countries that in most instances receive U.S. aid in one form or another.

With this situation in mind, it seems only right that the United States should begin to receive something in return for its aid. Twenty years ago it was a case of the "developed" nation giving aid to the "underdeveloped." As we run out of our strategic minerals it is time to barter our aid for these minerals we need. The position of "developed” and “underdeveloped" is being reversed.

BARTER BILL PROPOSAL: STEP TO "MINERAL SECURITY' 

I feel that the barter bill I have proposed would be that first necessary step to mineral security. In addition, the American people would begin to get something back for the billions of dollars of foreign aid we dispense. What I am proposing here is a fair exchange for mutual benefit. Last December, the Appropriations Committee stated in its report on foreign assistance that:

Some consideration should be given to the possibility of establishing certain arrangements with the underdeveloped countries receiving U.S. foreign aid concerning the exchange or barter or strategic or critical raw materials in their possession.

As the bill is worded the barter aspect of the foreign aid program would be discretionary. It would be used whenever the President "deems it to be in the national interest." This nonmandatory approach would enable us to continue aid to an especially needy area even when that particular country may be completely without any raw materials that we need.

On the other hand, it is my feeling that under present circumstances the President should be encouraged to use his barter power at all other times. Whenever he would find that a nation receiving U.S. aid does in fact possess a strategic or critical raw material he should exercise the barter option and obtain something in return for our aid. 

ACQUIRED RAW MATERIALS: SALE OR STOCKPILE? 

The second aspect of the bill concerns just what the United States would do with the raw material once it had successfully bartered for it. 

As I see it, there are two ways to approach it. The mineral could be stockpiled by the Government and then sold at a time in the future when the shortages become even more acute. As with the Commodity

Credit Corporation, this sale would be done in a manner which did not disrupt the market or cause problems for U.S. industries. The other avenue of approach is to put the rights to the raw material up for bid. 

The successful bidder would then mine the raw material and sell it, subject only to the stipulation that the mineral must be sold to this country. The barter idea is broad enough in scope to cover either approach or even some third methods.

I frankly admit that I do not have all of the answers as to how the specifics of the program would work in detail. However, with the expertise of this committee and its staff I am confident that the details can be worked out. 

BARTER CONCEPT: CRITICS ANSWERED 

Those critical of the barter concept have mentioned several areas of concern. One criticism has been the idea that the program is unworkable. I don't think so. As I have mentioned, all of the details may not have been worked out but the 30 years of experience in foreign assistance of this committee and the executive departments can surely provide the guidance and answers that are needed. 

If we sit around and wait until every single contingency is covered, the idea will never be put into action. We must take that first step now. 

When the United States began its foreign aid program no one could predict for sure where it would lead-and yet the United States took that first step because it was considered necessary. It is time now to head back up that road. To delay any longer will continue this needless expense of taxpayers' money and jeopardize our industrial future. 

A second question on the barter approach has been that it allows the United States to prey on the poorer countries of the underdeveloped world. I cannot buy that argument. What we are proposing here is a fair exchange. We are not robbing anyone. These nations will also profit as development of their resources leads to increased employment and a stronger economy for them. If we do not follow the barter course, we will pay dearly in 10 or 20 years, even as we are beginning to pay now.

We have already seen the beginning of the formation of cartels by these mineral-rich nations. The longer we postpone facing these facts, the more difficult we will make our future. Admittedly this is a carrotand-stick approach to the problem, but it is the most effective. 

PUT BARTER INTO FOREIGN AID PROGRAM 

I think the time is right to incorporate the barter idea into our foreign aid program. The American public and the Congress are vigorously questioning the giveaway of aid. This sentiment was reflected in the House last January when the IDA authorization was voted down. I feel there is strong support for the barter idea in the House, as evidenced by the 54 cosponsors of this bill. 

The barter proposal is not a plan for continuing the foreign assistance program because my votes of not supporting the program strongly reflect that I would much prefer that we stop giving away the taxpayers' dollars. But each year we find that the program continues,

TEN T: so if it must continue then we should take the necessary steps to receive material of equal value.

Once again I would like to express my appreciation to the committee for this opportunity to testify. I think the barter concept is an extremely valid idea. I urge its careful consideration and inclusion as part of our foreign aid program. 

 We would attempt to answer any questions that you may have.

Mr. MILLER. The Commodity Credit Corporation under the Secre tary of Agriculture did use the barter concept and it was on the same general idea as what we have right now. This was continued until 1967. 

I believe now that we have our problems we will be facing them for some years in the future. As an example, the energy problem that has developed and the lack of fossil fuels only leads us to believe that in the future we will have this strategic metal problem that we are talking about right now.

INDUSTRIAL DIAMONDS FOR FOOD Chairman MORGAN. I definitely remember our country getting some industrial diamonds from the Belgian Congo for food in the earlier years. This was a critical material that we did get under the barter provision of the food program.

Do you feel that this may give the Government too large a role in the materials. market?

Mr. MILLER. Frankly, Mr. Chairman, I am concerned about that because I believe that we should have less government than more, but by the same token when it comes to pass that we would not have the necessary strategic metals and the minerals to keep our industry working, then it is the responsibility, I feel, of the Government to see that we have something coming toward our shores. 

It is in my opinion an idea whose time has come and it undoubtedly would give the Government more authority than now, although the minerals could be put up for bid and private industry could actually mine in some foreign country and then sell them back in this country to other private industry.

FOREIGN AID AND U.S. DEBT 

Mr. FRELINGHUYSEN. Thank you,

Mr. Chairman. 

I would like to join in welcoming Mr. Miller to the committee. I have listened to his testimony with interest. 

I can appreciate the reasons why you, as a long time opponent of foreign aid, are trying to develop alternatives, but I wonder if it is really not stretching the facts a little to suggest as you do on page 2 that much of the debt that the United States has been accumulating is generated by borrowing to meet foreign aid outlays. We are reaching $300 billion expenditure level, and it is difficult to see how much of that can be attributed to foreign aid. It is really a very microscopic part.

I certainly share your concern about the continuing pressures to spend more, but I would think you would look at lots of other programs which are more legitimate culprits than the foreign aid program. It is a very small part, and not much, of the debt that could be by any stretch of the imagination the result of our foreign aid programs.

Mr. MILLER. I guess, Mr. Frelinghuysen, as we look at the program and what has been given to other countries over the years it amounts to $158 billion since 1949.

Mr. FRELINGHUYSEN. But how much is that in comparison with what the country has spent in that time? As I recall, we have run up deficits of about $58 billion in the last 5 years. So when you are talking figures you may make it sound like a lot, but as you look at the actual expenditure levels of the Government and the proposed expenditure for foreign aid you get a better relationship than trying to decide how much we spent in the past, I should think. 

Mr. MILLER. We get a better relationship, this is true, but if we use priorities as to what was spent within our country for our own good compared to what is spent outside we could say that $158 billion would actually be $158 billion of national debt today.

Mr. FRELINGHUYSEN. The State Department does not dispose of the foreign aid money, Mr. Miller.

Mr. MILLER. There is an AID because- 

Mr. FRELINGHUYSEN. I don't see it. As I understand it is going to be a fair exchange, we are going to get material of equal value. We are not going to give anything unless we get an exact equivalent in terms of the raw materials that the country may have? 

Mr. MILLER. We would need that, and we do need it today for our country, but there is something in the barter system that would help the underdeveloped countries. I mention it on page 5 of my testimony. 

DEVELOPMENT OF RESOURCES AS FOREIGN AID 

Mr. FRELINGHUYSEN. That is what I am looking at, too.

They work around the world, and it is possible for them to move the equipment and hire the people from the underdeveloped country which in turn would increase the employment in that underdeveloped country.

Mr. ZABLOCKI.

FORMATION OF RESOURCE CARTELS 

I, too, want to welcome our colleague, Congressman Miller, before this committee.

On page 5 of your statement you point up a matter which, of course, we are all seriously concerned about when you say:

We have already seen the beginning of the formation of cartels by mineral-rich nations.

Apparently, the executive branch is very concerned about the forma tion of these cartels and Secretary of State Kissinger has taken a position that access to raw materials should be worked out on an international basis.

I must admit your proposal has some appeal. Indeed a similar sys tem has worked for the Soviet Union, particularly their barter agreements with satellite states where they have some domination and control. But we do not have such a relationship between the noncommunist countries and ourselves-and I hope it never so develops. 

Does not your proposal have a unilateral quality that might work against administration attempts to reach multilateral agreements on equitable access to mineral resources?

Mr. MILLER. I believe, frankly, that we have gone a little bit too far in our multilateral aid. It appears that many of the nations that are being aided by the multilaterals at the present time, and we are supporting them, obtain a great percentage of their funds from the United States. I believe in turn this lessening of multilateral aid could help a return to a bilateral system where the people in other nations would be aware of where the aid is actually coming from. 

I would hope that as we move along we could go in the opposite direction that many people feel we should go now, and that opposite direction would be staying with the line of bilateral aid. 

AGREEMENT ON RAW MATERIALS ACCESS 

Mr. ZABLOCKI. I join the gentleman in his concern about multilateral aid. But I am speaking about the decision of the executive branch to get some agreement among the nations of the world as to access to world supplies of needed mineral resources. This would be a multilateral agreement, not necessarily for multilateral aid, but to have fair access to the mineral resources.

It is my understanding the executive branch is working toward that kind of an arrangement.

Mr. MILLER. Yes; I understand it is. We have to, of course, at the same time look after ourselves-that we have our fair share. Whether it would create a problem of acquisition under a multilateral system I am not positive, but we must remember that we in the United States are consuming about 35 percent of the world's natural resources, and with only about 7 percent of the world's population. 

Whether the administration is on the right track in working under this type of system I am not sure. If we could start with the unilateral programs that we have, and they amount to quite a few dollars of exchange, whether they be in loan or grant form, and work in that direc tion, I still think that we will be better off.

APPLICATIONS OF BARTER PROPOSAL 

Mr. ZABLOCKI. In your opinion, would your proposal apply to military grant aid, military sales and the Peace Corps?

Mr. MILLER. The Peace Corps would not fit in the particular language we have, but it could be included. 

Mr. ZABLOCKI. As the gentleman knows, we have limitations on the amount of military aid and military sales to given countries and regions. Would those limitations be lifted? Do you believe we should barter as much military material as possible with a given country for commodities we need?

Mr. MILLER. I could not answer that for sure. We would need to get an answer for that under the particular bill that we have right now. 

BARTER PROPOSAL AND PRIVATE ENTERPRISE 

Mr. ZABLOCKI. The chairman touched upon a problem that concerns me. If your amendment were enacted, the U.S. Government would get into the business of buying and selling commodities and possibly interfering with private American commercial transactions. Have you given some thought to that?

Mr. MILLER. Yes; very definitely. As I had mentioned to the chairman, it is very possible that private industry could be involved directly so that the material could be put out for bid in another country, and our private industry would bid for and receive a contract to mine and move that particular material to this country and then sell it again to private industry. 

Mr. ZABLOCKI. Under our present system of private enterprise, can you foresee such a system without going closer to the type of government-managed economy that the Soviet Union has? 

Mr. MILLER. I am concerned about this very much, but by the same token I am concerned that we will be out of the material and the raw materials that we need to keep this industrial nation going. 

Mr. ZABLOCKI. I want to thank the gentleman for his thoughts. They are very intriguing. His proposal has some appeal, but I do find some problems.

Mr. Whalen. 

"QUID PRO QUO" APPROACH TO FOREIGN AID Mr. WHALEN.  

I want to join in welcoming my distinguished colleague from Ohio, Mr. Miller. I too want to congratulate you on your very thoughtful approach to this question of access to resources. 

I am disturbed as to what the quid pro quo is in this, Mr. Miller. 

Are you suggesting that in return for aid we receive a like amount of raw material?

Let me state an example. We say to a country, look, we will give you $10 million in economic and/or military assistance, and in return for this we would like to have an equivalent amount of the particular raw material which you are producing. Am I correct in that understanding?

Mr. MILLER. That is the general idea of the barter system. If the particular country would need our food, fiber, technology, and equipment, then we would be able to barter with them for whatever raw material that they may have that would be in short supply in this country.

Mr. WHALEN. In other words, it could be dollars, it could be finished products, but this then is not foreign aid, is it? Is not this simply a market exchange? Could this not be done outside of the foreign assistance umbrella?

Mr. MILLER. It could be done, and it is done today, not necessarily with our Federal Government but with private industry. The point is that today we are turning over to some 103 countries our technology,' food, and fiber. While we are doing this, we should have something in return for that, and that is the whole purpose of the barter systemto include a repayment from those countries that have the strategic metals and the raw materials that will keep us going in the future. 

BARTER PROPOSAL: NOT FOREIGN AID 

Mr. WHALEN. I can understand your concern about foreign aid and whether or not we are receiving a return on those aid dollars. Apparently we in the Congress and in the executive branch feel that we are. 

What I am simply suggesting is that the arrangement that you are proposing is not foreign aid, it really involves exchanging either dollars for scarce raw materials or finished American products for raw materials.

Mr. MILLER. Well, the whole idea of course is to come up with that payment for something that we are either giving away or loaning at the present time, and it fits right into the aid program. Today many of the AID programs provide loans for 40 years with the first 10 years having an interest charge of 3 percent, and the last 30 years having an interest charge for 4 percent, as I recall. Now this would amount to really a grant of about 70 percent over the 40-year period. 

Mr. WHALEN. Are you suggesting, then, that perhaps in lieu of these loans that we receive raw materials? 

Mr. MILLER. This would be possible. As a matter of fact, if we have a country that needs and wants our assistance, and they have the natural resources, it is possible for us to go the other direction and let them loan us that of equal value. If they do pay for our particular commodity, or whatever we send them, then we in turn could balance it off by paying them for the raw material and by paying with also cheaper dollars.

Mr. WHALEN. I think this is similar perhaps to the Russian Aswan 

Dam deal where the Egyptian Government repaid the Russians in cotton.

THE PRICE PAID FOR RAW MATERIALS 

Let me go to another problem, really the focal point of this issue, and that is the price that we have to pay for raw materials. How would this affect that question? 

Let me explain. Where we have a worldwide shortage of raw materials, this has tended to force the price up, the industrial nations are bidding among each other for these scarce materials. How would this approach reduce the price?

BARTER PROPOSAL: "SOME REFRESHING THOUGHTS" 

Mr. FOUNTAIN. Thank you, Mr. Chairman. 

I want to join others in complimenting you, Mr. Miller, for appearing before this committee and giving us some refreshing thoughts, or at least reemphasizing something we already knew, that in effect we now have a national indebtedness of about $500 billion, and this next year we are going to be paying about $31 billion in interest on that almost $500 billion, and the young people who are sitting out in this audience and countless millions of others throughout America are

182 & ​going to be paying that bill, they and their husbands, and their children.

We have been giving money away for along time, and I think in some cases it has served a useful purpose, but I do think you have presented an extremely meaningful idea. The practical way of handling it may involve a lot of bugs, but that is not your job. You have presented an idea which I think has tremendous merit. Not only can we use it in the foreign aid program, but I see no reason why we cannot use it in other ways.

I happen to know of some private enterprise operations in this country which in the past have engaged in the bartering approach. I assume some companies are still doing it. I don't see anything socialistic about the Federal Government buying from private enterprise in this country those things that are necessary to exchange with other countries for the basic raw materials which they have and which they need. Frankly, I think one of the reasons many countries feel as they do about us or at least the people to whom we give without receiving anything I think they would like to have made a contribution-they would like to feel that they are doing something for what they are getting.

It seems to me that this might well be an approach which could be worked out to enable us to go back, as Congressman Nix said, a little nearer home to the idea of our Founding Fathers and engage in that bartering approach which kept people alive, and which enabled them to exchange among themselves without ever passing a dime or a piece of money. They traded value for value in items they all needed. 

TOBACCO FOR CEMENT IN EGYPT 

I know that a tobacco manufacturing establishment in my own congressional district has engaged in exchanging tobacco for cement, with Egypt, I believe. They did for some time. I don't know about now. 

It seems to me that in these critical areas where the people themselves those in need, as Congressman Miller says, are not getting the benefit of our foreign aid. It is not getting down to the grassroots. 

I want to commend you, and I hope that this committee will give serious consideration to injecting into our program this idea. It does not have to be a completely quid pro quo because we have been giving it away anyhow. If we can get half of it for the whole, or a quarter for the whole, it would seem to me that we will be giving the people who make these contributions, whether it be foreign economic aid or foreign military assistance, the feeling that they are participating, and that this is a partnership operation.

STATEMENT OF REPRESENTATIVE WILLIAM M. KETCHUM 

Chairman MORGAN. We received a statement from Congressman
