Mr. MILLER. Thank you, Mr. Chairman. [The statement of Hon. William M. Ketchum appears in the appendix, p. 732.]

Chairman MORGAN. Our next witness is a distinguished colleague from the State of New York, the Honorable Bella S. Abzug. 

Ms. Abzug, we are glad to welcome you to the committee. You have a prepared statement and you may proceed. 

STATEMENT OF HON. BELLA S. ABZUG, A REPRESENTATIVE IN CONGRESS FROM THE STATE OF NEW YORK MS. ABZUG. Thank you, Mr. Chairman. 

Members of the committee, I am grateful for this opportunity to discuss our mutual concern with the kind of foreign aid the administration is requesting. I appreciate the hard work that this committee has put in over the years to develop a program that will reflect the genuine desire of this country to help others less fortunate and to assist struggling democracies such as Israel in their efforts to survive. 

But despite our best attempts the program seems to have gone awry at many points. Increasingly we are being asked to give more and more money to countries that refuse to grant their citizens even the

most basic civil rights. This year, for example, the administration request for $3.2 billion in foreign economic and military aid is a startling 

72-percent increase over last year's appropriation, and of the 53 countries on the list for and, 34 are governed by civilian or military dictatorships.

This is a policy not contemplated by the original Foreign Assistance Act, and I know that you have made many efforts to redirect it. 

This year I believe you will have the support of many other Members who feel as I do that we must pass legislation expressing our real intent. We must make it known that the United States will help to fill the desperate needs of the world's people and will support the legitimate aspirations of democratic nations, but the Congress through this committee must find a way to separate such aid from military gifts and sales and to channel more economic aid through multinational organizations such as the United Nations. 

FOOD FOR PEACE; FUNDS FOR WAR 

Even the food for peace funds in the agriculture bill were exposed last year as funds for war. Agricultural commodities sold to foreign countries could be resold and the dollar value spent for weapons purchased from the United States. South Vietnam received some $178 million worth of weapons in this way. In order to control the disposition of such moneys, the Congress placed a prohibition on the diversion of funds and established categories for spending such as food and nutrition, population planning, and education, rather than the former loan and grant programs. 

Last week the House voted to limit to 10 percent the amount of Food for Peace funds that any country could receive. While well-intentioned, this may prove to be unfair. Starving people in Africa, for example, may need far more than 10 percent and the Saigon Government may still find ways to convert their 10 percent into war materials despite congressional prohibitions. Even without such diversion, money sent there releases other funds that should have to be spent on domestic needs. Therefore, I feel that no funds at all should go to 

South Vietnam, in any guise, until the Thieu government complies with the Paris Peace Agreements. 

There are two ways, I feel, by which Congress could achieve more effective controls of so-called "foreign assistance" funds. First, this committee could write into its bill a provision for a country-by-country, item-by-item review of all foreign aid authorized. Second, funds intended for humanitarian use could be dispersed through agencies such as the International Red Cross rather than to the treasuries of foreign governments.

NO AID FUNDS UNLESS HUMAN RIGHTS INSPECTION 

Furthermore, no funds should be made available under this act to any country which does not permit inspection to determine its regard for human rights. Chile and Greece, for instance, continue to maintain closed societies while receiving aid from the United States. This must be stopped. Senator Abourezk on June 21 introduced an amendment to this effect, S. 3394, and I hope this committee will adopt it.

It is a complete reversal of American tradition to provide military support to dictatorships-yet each year we do so more and more. 

Fourteen past and present recipients of U.S. arms aid are regimes that have acquired their power by military takeover of nationalist or constitutional governments, or simply by declaring martial law. These countries and the takeover dates are: Argentina (1955), Bolivia (1964), Chile (1972), Dominican Republic (1963), Greece (1967),

Iran (1953), Indonesia (1966), Philippines (1972), Mali (1968), 

Nigeria (1966), Thailand (1969) and Uruguay (1973).

Thirty-four military and civilian dictatorships in Africa, Europe, Latin America, the Mideast and the Far East are on this year's list for military assistance. Almost half of the proposed foreign aid money would go to Indochina where we have supported repressive governments for over a decade.

As you are well aware, nowhere in the Federal budget is there a total figure for military assistance; it is scattered through 17 programs administered by the Department of Defense, the AEC, the State Department, the Department of Agriculture and others. More than $4 billion of it requires no congressional authorization at all and is spent by the military branches with almost no civilian control. 

In addition, Senator Fulbright has shown that $490 million in the 

Department of Defense budget for War Reserve Materials is for the acquisition, storage and maintenance of war reserve munitions for Vietnamese, Thialand, and Korean forces. This is yet another attempt to circumvent the will of the Congress to reduce foreign military aid. 

OBJECTIONS TO FOREIGN AID 

My objections, then, are based on several factors: (1) the Congress has no way of knowing exactly what we are asked to approve; (2) we do know that we render military aid to repressive regimes; (3) we are discovering that we subsidize torture; (4) we sell arms to both sides in several conflicts; and (5) we are robbing our own people to accomplish these dubious aims.

It is not only in the Middle East that we are asked to support both sides of conflicts. Columnist Jack Anderson had his staff research the subject and discovered that:

The U.S. has supported opposing sides in nearly a dozen wars since World 

War II ended. Uncle Sam aided both sides, for example, when Nicaragua invaded Costa Rica in 1955; when Honduras and Nicaragua battled over their borders in 1957; when Morocco and Spain fought over Spanish Morocco in 1958; when France and Tunisia collided during the 1961 Bizerta crisis; when India invaded the Portuguese colony of Goa in 1962; and when Indonesia invaded 

Malaysia during the early 1960s.

The Pentagon gave massive doses of military aid to India and Pakistan, whose armies used U.S. weapons to fire at one another in 1965. American military assistance went to both Arabs and Israelis before they clashed in 1967 and again in 1973; to India and Pakistan before the 1971 Bangladesh war; and to both El 

Salvador and Honduras during their "soccer war" of 1969. 

Certainly no ideological commitment nor desire for "regional stability" inspires us to sell arms to both sides in these conflicts. The motive is money. It has been noted that our said program has become a kind of walfare subsidy for giant multinational corporations. No one else benefits not the people of these countries, who are often

near starvation while their rulers make fortunes; nor the American people, whose taxes pay for all this largesse. 

AID: "HANDING OUT NUCLEAR REACTORS' 

And to this a terrifying new dimension has been added. The administration's idea of "assistance" to other countries now includes handing out nuclear reactors as though they were party favors. 

Though these reactors are authorized by the AEC and not by this committee, they must be considered as part of the total foreign aid program.

Mr. Nixon's sudden agreement with Egypt has made us painfully aware that the United States has already sold nuclear materials to more than 70 nations, including Germany, Spain, Korea, and Taiwan. 

Every one of these plants increases the danger of accidental or deliberate destruction of millions of people. We have learned the hard way that terrorists exist everywhere, and their numbers will grow as the gap in world resources widens.

Theoretically the developing nations want to increase power supplies to compete in the industrial market. But there is as yet no proof that nuclear fission is even an efficient source of power, since as much energy is expended in production as is produced. Why don't we wait for the safe and far less costly development of solar energy and then share our know-how? The sun shines on all-dispensing solar energybut let us pray that meanwhile, lethal doses of radiation will not fall on all.

NO REAL "SAFEGUARD" ON NUCLEAR REACTORS 

There is no real "safeguard" despite much loose talk. The AEC admits to 850 "abnormal happenings" from January 1, 1972, through

May 30, 1973. Multiply this by 30 countries and chances for the survival of humanity diminish rapidly. So long as we give these potential weapons without regard to the kind of government in power, we can expect that they will be used to maintain existing cliques. 

I have just introduced a bill to amend the Export Administration Act to require congressional approval of all agreements with foreign countries providing for the transfer of nuclear materials or technology. I have also introduced a resolution of inquiry to ascertain the conditions under which the agreements with Egypt and Israel were made. The resolution of inquiry has been referred to this committee and I urge you to give it the prompt yet thorough attention it requires. 

One of the most flagrant examples of the abuse of our foreign assistance programs is our continuing support for President Thieu. In addition to the Department of Defense budget of $1.4 billion, the administration wants $917 million in foreign aid funds for something called Indochina postwar reconstruction: $56 million is to go to Laos, $110 million to Cambodia, and $751 million to South Vietnam. The President says this is to help these countries "shift their economies from war to peace." Along with resettling refugees, providing for the disabled, the orphans, and widows, and meeting inflated costs of imports, this aid is supposed to provide investments to create productive jobsand to-

Support the military forces needed to preserve movement toward peace so long as hostile forces continue to be deployed within South Vietnam and supported from outside.

SITUATION IN VIETNAM 

Apparently Mr. Nixon's briefers still aren't giving him the picture. 

Could he really not know that "movement toward peace" is hindered daily by the aggressive acts of President Thieu's forces-who make no secret of their continuing attacks on PRG strongholds? Does he not understand that the Paris Peace Agreements-article 7-permit the Provisional Revolutionary Government to maintain and resupply troops in South Vietnam? It is claimed that the PRG cheats on the supplies, but so does the United States when we send fighter jets far more sophisticated than the original F-5A's and call them "training planes. 

I would be the first to agree that we should help Vietnam to take care of the human misery we helped to cause, but I do not see how military hardware is going to do this.

Even Senator Stennis recently remarked that the military procurement program "has evolved into a military aid program for one nation-South Vietnam." The same might be said of the foreign aid program. Every day we spend $1 million for the 700 tons of ammunition fired by Saigon's troops. Casualties are as high as before the cease-fire.

Despite the billions we have poured into this unhappy land, its people are nearing starvation. The refugees, orphans, and widows are not being helped.

Diane Jones, who spent over 2 years with the Quaker rehabilitation program in South Vietnam, testified recently before a Senate committee that her own visits to refugee camps showed that American economic aid does not reach the people who most need it. In one camp, she said:

People were literally on the borderline of starvation. They were eating chopped up banana stalk-normally used for pig food.

POLITICAL FREEDOMS IN VIETNAM 

And there is still no indication that President Thieu intends to hold free elections, restore civil rights or open his jails to visits by international observers. His administration, and ours, continues to denybut never really to answer-charges that thousands of Vietnamese are being held under barbarous conditions simply because of their opposition to his regime.

I have been to Saigon and talked with relatives and friends of prisoners. I have received letters from religious and professional and student leaders testifying to the conditions of their imprisonment and torture. I believe we, in the Congress, must demand that international inspection of the prisons be allowed before another penny goes to President Thieu.

SITUATION REPORTED IN CAMBODIA 

A comparable situation prevails in Cambodia where American bombs have pounded a fertile land into desert. Once an exporter of 36-333-74- -29

rice, Cambodia must now receive rice from other countries; her ravaged land cannot be cultivated. Nearly half her people are refugees-they need food and shelter, not bullets. 

A special report to the Washington Post by Elizabeth Becker on 

June 21 tells what the problem is: "Corruption here is unbelievable, but it is dangerous to know too much," said a European diplomat. "It is unpleasant for us to think that a small government like the Khmer Republic can defeat U.S. policy through corruption." 

Diplomats, businessmen and politicians here operate on the assumption that generals allied to President Lon Nol, in cooperation with Chinese merchants, make millions of dollars each year by illegally controlling commercial traffic and diverting U.S. aid for their personal use *** Three very different sources said that Lon Nol's younger brother, General Lon Non, left the country after obtaining $90 million illegally. 

Most of the money reportedly is made through the sale of arms and ammunition-which makes up 20 to 30 percent of U.S. aid-and illegal taxes and blackmail of merchants.

In Laos a fragile peace is threatened by U.S. intervention again. Do we really want to continue such involvement?

U.S. MILITARY TRAINING 

One of the more pernicious effects of so-called aid is that it trains military men around the world, giving them the know-how for military coups. From the close of World War II through this June we will have trained 512,000 such leaders. For example, the military group that overthrew the elected Government of Chile last fall included six graduates of our training schools. Over two decades we have trained 14,144 potential leaders of the Greek military regime; 2,881 of Portugal's officer corps; 7,883 from Brazil. They are trained both in the United 

States and in their homelands in such subjects as counterinsurgency and "interrogation." All too often, we have found, interrogation means torture.

TORTURE IS A POLITICAL TOOL 

Torture is a political tool that many Americans find hard to believe. 

To recognize that we subsidize torture around the world is to face a deep moral responsibility. This we must do as we consider the foreign aid bill.

This committee, I am sure, is better informed than I on the ghastly details. You have read the "Amnesty International Report on Allegations of Torture in Brazil" published in 1972. It describes the sophisticated psychological torture chambers where images of the victim's family are interspersed with approaching high speed trains, piercing screams and strobe lights, using equipment far beyond the capacity of ordinary police forces. You have the reports of three 

Uruguayan torturers who told of the involvement of the U.S. Agency for International Development in torture training in Latin America.

The New Scientist, a respected British journal, said in July 1973 that:

Evidence indicates that torture is now routine in over 30 countries*** Primitive methods based on physical force remain common, but as the practice is illegal there is an effort not to leave incriminating marks*** psychological methods use drugs and sensory deprivation ***.

DOTY الية 

The Military Hospital in Montevideo, Uruguay, is renowned for *** a drug (which) produces terrible agony brought on by painful muscle contractions and unless administered under strict medical supervision is fatal * * *. 

A torture colleague is the "lying" doctor * * * a physician whose diagnoses or report is false. International teams of observers have been known, in the face of overt political pressure, to suppress information * * *.

Other physicians include the "authorizing" doctor who certifies that the victim can stand more of the treatment, and the "reviving" doctor who administers treatment either to enable a torture to continue, to prevent death or to maximize the pain.

CHARGES AGAINST THE INTERNATIONAL POLICE ACADEMY 

Evidence is mounting that U.S. agencies are major torture exporters, primarily through training of third world police in the field by AID officials and at the 

International Police Academy in Washington, D.C.

Now these are very serious charges. None of us would knowingly authorize funds for such use, nor would our constituents allow it. But with the curse of secrecy lying over so much of our Government, we must be constantly alert to inquire what our money is doing.

Conditions under the military junta in Chile are described by dozens of reporters but perhaps the most moving is Anthony Lewis' account in the New York Times for May 29. He calls it "The Meaning of Torture" and describes its use as a political instrument. The article has been printed in the Record for June 17, 1974, and should be mandatory reading for every Member before voting on foreign aid. Senator 

Abourezk comments:

The International Police Academy here in Washington, which is funded by U.S. foreign aid money, just graduated another class of students who will return to Uruguay, Guatemala, Nigeria, Thailand, Indonesia and the Philippines to continue to stabilize the dictatorship and support the activities of which we are "officially unaware." 

Yet all these countries are again on our list. Why? And at what cost to our country?

SITUATION OF POOR IN UNITED STATES 

I am sure you are all following the work of the Senate Nutrition

Committee and were stricken, as I was, by the report they released which stated that inflation has reached such proportions that our elderly poor are reduced to eating dog food. 

The report said:

For the poor, there is virtually no flexibility to switch to lower cost food items *** they already are consuming the lowest cost and lowest quality items. 

Therefore, they "eat less *** and switch to foods that are not designed for human consumption, that is, pet foods ***. As much as one-third of the pet foods sold in ghetto areas are being used for human consumption. For areas with high proportions of elderly poor, the estimates (are) even higher. 

Meanwhile we are asked to give military aid to oil-rich Saudi 

Arabia. The logic somehow or other escapes me.

DOES MILITARY SPENDING CREATE JOBS? 

The Pentagon carefully promotes the notion that military spending creates jobs. The overall request for the Department of Defense for fiscal year 1975 includes some $6 billion for padding the economy

according to the admission of the Secretary of Defense in testimony last February. Yet a study by the Public Interest Research Group in 

Michigan shows that for every $1 billion spent by the Pentagon the 

Nation actually loses 20,000 jobs.

Using the Government's own figures, the researchers found that the Pentagon generates fewer jobs per billion dollars than any other form of private or Government spending except the space program. The average Pentagon budget of $80 billion, the study says, results in the loss of 1,600,000 jobs each year across the Nation due in large part to exorbitant salaries paid to higher echelon military personnel. 

A Department of Labor study done in 1972 reaches a comparable conclusion.

Our present assistance has been called "an aid program for big multinational contractors," and it should be noted that the beneficiaries of the nuclear agreements are General Electric and Westinghouse. 

SUMMARY OF RECOMMENDATIONS BY MS. ABZUG 

In conclusion, then, may I summarize my recommendations. I would like to see clearly defined prohibitions in the bill against disguising military aid as economic or humanitarian aid. I believe we should insist that no aid be given to countries that are holding political prisoners without due process and that international inspection of prisons and adherence to the Geneva Convention be required as a condition of aid. 

I would like to see in the bill a prohibition against military aid to any dictatorship, including Chile.

I believe that Congress should have a country-by-country veto power over all funds given under this act. 

I believe we must immediately provide for congressional review of every plan to transfer nuclear materials to other countries and must investigate fully agreements already implemented. 

I believe we must immediately negotiate a comprehensive test ban treaty and not a partial or limited test ban. These reforms could hardly be construed as "interfering in the internal affairs of other nations." 

What we now do by arming and abetting certain military factions within other countries constitutes a far more dangerous interference than the withholding of arms. 

Chairman MORGAN. Thank you, Ms. Abzug. 

RESOLUTION OF INQUIRY ON NUCLEAR AGREEMENTS 

Ms. Abzug, in your statement you refer to a resolution requesting information regarding nuclear agreements with Egypt and Israel. 

Ms. ABZUG. Yes. 

Chairman MORGAN.

I believe you introduced this resolution yesterday. 

Ms. ABZUG. Yes, sir.

Chairman MORGAN. It has a number. I see in the record the number is resolution 1189. However, the resolution has not been printed so the committee has not received a copy yet. Could you tell us what is in the resolution? 

Ms. ABZUG. Yes, certainly, Mr. Chairman.

The resolution requests the President of the United States to furnish to the House of Representatives, within 10 days after the adoption of this resolution, full and complete information on the following: 

1. The steps being taken, in the negotiation of the agreement for cooperation with Egypt and in the negotiation of the agreement for cooperation with Israel for the sale of nuclear reactors and fuel, to comply with the provisions of sections 54 and 123 of the Atomic Energy 

Act (42 U.S.C. 2074 and 2153); 

2. Whether or not the United States has required a commitment by 

Egypt and/or Israel not to construct chemical separation plants to extract weapons-grade plutonium from the fuel elements of such nuclear reactors; 

3. Whether or not any distribution of nuclear materials or of classified nuclear technology will be made to Egypt or to Israel prior to the conclusion of such agreements for cooperation; 

4. What steps, if any, the United States has taken to require as a condition of such agreements that Egypt and Israel sign the Nuclear Nonproliferation Treaty; 

5. The safeguard provisions, beyond those prescribed in the Nuclear 

Nonproliferation Treaty, which the United States has imposed to prevent the diversion of plutonium from fuel to weaponry purposes or to prevent terrorist acquisition of radioactive materials. 

Chairman MORGAN. I expect we will have the resolution before the day is out. 

Ms. ABZUG. I would hope so.

LIMITATION ON USE OF FOOD FOR PEACE FUNDS 

Chairman MORGAN. Ms. Abzug, on page 2 of your statement you say that you are opposed to the 10-percent limitation on food-for-peace funds that any country could receive. You know, of course, that the 

House last week voted for this restriction on the floor. 

Ms. ABZUG. I don't oppose it. I voted for that limitation. What I am suggesting is that really I think it highlights the issue that I am trying to address here and that we do have to have a country-bycountry determination of programs including this one. We are now, as I understand it, giving maybe 40 percent or more of that program to Indochina. 

Chairman MORGAN. How would you propose changing the action the House voted for last week?

Ms. ABZUG. Well, I have some very serious reservations, Mr. Chairman, about the whole Public Law 480 and I would propose that we reexamine that program entirely. You see, the purpose for which it was originally intended has been violated-as has been reported over and over again-by the providing of currency which is then turned into other purposes, counter to our intention. Therefore I am not sure that this program has any more validity. 

Chairman MORGAN. Would you support an amendment on the floor to return Public Law 480 to the jurisdiction of the Foreign Affairs Committee?

Ms. ABZUG. Yes, I would, but would, however, wish to see the whole evaluation of that program at the same time, sir.

ITEM-BY-ITEM REVIEW OF FOREIGN AID PROGRAM

Ms. ABZUG. I believe that unless we change the operation of this program, we are just providing for a total amount of money to each of these countries without getting an enumeration of the breakdowns for the moneys that we are giving. I think it is very important for us to know what each country is doing and what is the nature of its government and what kind of individual liberties it grants to its citizens, before we agree to a general appropriation to each of these countries.

Ms. ABZUG. I am critical of trust violations, Mr. Chairman, whether they are North or South and I have made many statements publicly and on the floor of the House that there are troop violations, I am sure, on both sides. What I am addressing myself to is what I have addressed myself to consistently. One of the basic cores of the Paris peace agreement was that there would be a cease-fire during which there would then be an election. 

CRITICISM OF PRESIDENT THIEU 

General Thieu still refuses to allow elections. His political opponents, the non-Communist opponents, the people who represent democratic potential in Vietnam, are all in prison. There has been over and over the documentation of this. We ourselves I think are violating article 7 of the peace agreement which provides that we can make replacement only piece by piece of the armaments there yet. we are giving the South Vietnamese jet fighters, the F-5E to replace the F-5A. I think there is no question that that is not a piece-by-piece replacement. 

We continue the potential for violations on each side if we prop up the self-perpetuating dictatorship of General Thieu who is preventing any kind of peace agreement. Political leaders, religious leaders, labor leaders, students who are in prison are unable to develop a viable government which could then negotiate a real peace, conduct an election and allow the self-determination of the Vietnamese. 

Our continued aid program is felt by many commentators on the scene, very estimable journalists, to be the major factor which is preventing an agreement there. Why should General Thieu worry about that when he can continue to get this enormous assistance from all

[Article From the New York Times, June 5, 1974] ECONOMIC DISENGAGEMENT FROM VIETNAM By Hubert H. Humphrey 

In a similar fashion, $250 million in American food aid to South Vietnam in fiscal 1974, under the terms of our Food for Peace program, was resold by the Government to its people and the local currency generated was used for military purposes. This type of transaction shows that American aid priorities in Vietnam are overwhelming military.

In 1973, 42 per cent of the entire Vietnamese military budget was provided through local currencies generated by sales under the Food for Peace law and the American commodity-import program. Statistics for fiscal year 1974 show that nearly 45 per cent of our total Food for Peace program goes to Indochina. It is not sound policy to have nearly half of our much-diminished foodaid supply committed solely to this one region while other areas of the world are experiencing widespread famine. 

[Excerpt From the Congressional Record of Feb. 21, 1974, page S1986] SENATE CONCURRENT RESOLUTION 69-SUBMISSION OF A CONCURRENT RESOLU- TION RELATING TO POSSIBLE USE OF FOREIGN CURRENCIES AND AGRICULTURAL COMMODITIES 

(Referred to the Committee on Agriculture and Forestry.) 

Mr. Humphrey.

FOOD FOR PEACE, NOT WAR 

However, now we see the administration turning this respected program into a travesty as administration officials search for ways to covertly support military operations in Southeast Asia. The Congress, having called a halt to U.S. involvement in military operations in Southeast Asia, now must contend with efforts by the executive branch to subvert this congressional directive. 

During Senate consideration of foreign economic assistance legislation last fall, an amendment was adopted to prohibit agreements, without prior approval of Congress, that permit the use of foreign currencies generated by Public Law 480 food commodity sales, for military purposes. As finally enacted, the Foreign 

Assistance Act of 1973, Public Law 93-189, provides under section 40 that, effective July 1, 1974, congressional authorization shall be required for the disbursement of all foreign currencies. This general provision, replacing the earlier specific prohibition, may need to be strengthened to make the intent of 

Congress absolutely clear.

I am seriously concerned that the administration may intend to interpret the law as permitting it to continue agreements-presently limited to just two nations, Cambodia and South Vietnam-for the diversion of Public Law 480generated currencies for military purposes. Congress must not permit the administration to find loopholes in the law to continue actions that undermine the humanitarian intent of the food assistance program. 

If this continues, the administration will only weaken a program that has stood out as one of our most successful in the history of foreign assistance. 

Tables provided by the Agency for International Development indicate that within fiscal year 1974 alone, the estimate of the value of title I Public Law 480 shipments to Cambodia and South Vietnam has more than doubled. Fortyfour percent-almost half of all food for peace shipments from the United States throughout the world in fiscal year 1974 will go to these two nations. 

That works out to a major diversion of local currencies in these countries, through U.S. food assistance, for defense purposes-an indirect but nevertheless substantial addition to American military aid.

Meanwhile, commodity assistance for humanitarian programs by CARE and church-sponsored relief agencies have been cut back. It has been estimated that 

20 million fewer people are being helped to avoid starvation than 2 years ago. 

[From the St. Louis Post-Dispatch, June 10, 1974] FOOD FOR PEACE FUNDS DIVERTED TO ARMS AID (By Richard Dudman) 

WASHINGTON, June 10-Two recently discovered legal loopholes threaten to frustrate efforts in Congress to limit United States financing of the continuing war in Indochina.

Together they could funnel well over $500,000,000 in military aid into South Vietnam and Cambodia beyond whatever formal ceiling Congress finally places on military aid to the two countries. 

Both loopholes involve the so-called Food for Peace program, which now is used in South Vietnam and Cambodia primarily to pay military and police expenses.

Researchers for several anti-war groups organized into the Coalition to Stop Funding the War spotted the loopholes and began a lobbying campaign over the weekend to bring them to the attention of members of the Senate and House. 

Food for Peace, a program for disposing of surplus agricultural commodities, began as a humanitarian device. 

A foreign government bought U.S. farm products, paying for them in its own currency. The foreign government then resold the products to merchants in its own country, who sold them in turn on their local market. 

The U.S. permitted the foreign government to spend the proceeds of its sales to the merchants for specified peaceful purposes, hence the name Food for Peace. 

Several years ago, Congress took into account the military needs of the South Vietnamese and Cambodian governments and permitted both countries to use 80 percent of these local "counterpart" funds generated by the sale of U.S. commodities "to procure equipment, materials, facilities, and services for the common defense including internal security."

As part of the arrangement, the U.S. writes off the local currency debt incurred by the recipients in buying the American commodities. 

Last October, an adjustment permitted South Vietnam to spend 100 per cent of these counterpart funds for "common defense."

To some, however, this seemed to be a perversion of the Food for Peace program. 

Senator Mark O. Hatfield (Rep.) Oregon, succeeded in attaching an amendment to the foreign aid authorization bill last year prohibiting this military use of these counterpart funds unless approved by Congress. This prohibition becomes effective in three weeks-on July 1.

The first loophole involves $309,000,000 in commodity sales agreements signed in the current fiscal year, which ends June 30. Only about $150,000,000 in the commodities will actually be delivered to the government of South Vietnam by then. 

That means that more than $150,000,000 in commodities from these fiscal year 1974 agreements will arrive in South Vietnam in fiscal year 1975. The money they generate for the South Vietnamese can legally be used for military purposes. 

The second loophole involves the method of payment. The Food for Peace legislation says that the U.S. may accept payment either in foreign currencies or in "dollars on credit terms."

These credit terms are extremely lenient. The first 10 years is a grace period in which the foreign government pays nothing on the principal and only 2 per cent interest. Repayment is spread over the next 40 years at 3 per cent interest. 

In recent testimony before the House appropriations subcommittee on agriculture, William Goodfellow, director of research at the Indochina Resource Center, quoted a Department of Agriculture official as saying: "These debts will not come due for another 10 years. Right now in Vietnam and Cambodia they are worried about how they are going to get through next week. They do not have time to worry about 1984." counterpart The same official acknowledge that the prohibition on using funds for military and police purposes would have little or no effect. He was quoted as saying "once they have the commodities, it's their money."

The Administration has committed $309,000,000 in agricultural commodities for South Vietnam and $194,000,000 for Cambodia in the current fiscal year. 

For next year it has requested only $160,000,000 for South Vietnam and $77,- 000,000 for Cambodia, but Department of Agriculture officials expect the actual level next year to be about the same as this year. 

Goodfellow quoted department officials as saying that "strategy security" is the chief standard by which these U.S. farm commodities are scheduled for export under the Food for Peace program. 

He said that the officials told him that priorities and commodity levels were being determined by the National Security Council rather than the Agriculture 

Department of the Agency for International Development. 

Senator Mark O. Hatfield (Rep.) Oregon, has urged that the proposed ceiling on military aid to Vietnam now being considered by the Senate be broadened to include any military appropriations of local currencies generated in the 

Food for Peace commodity import programs.

NOTE: IN REALITY ONLY 2 OF ADMINISTRATION'S PROPOSAL FOR "HUMANITARIAN" OR "RECONSTRUCTION" NEEDS 

1. "Reconstruction and Development" Covertly war-related

Since fierce war rages in South Vietnam, the Indochina Resource Center does not believe that any of the funds designated as "reconstruction and development" for South Vietnam will actually go for that purpose. We would only consider the $39.9 million designated for Laos as fitting this description. 

2. "Humanitarian" 

Covertly War-related

Most of the "humanitarian" funds designated for South Vietnam and Laos are meant to aid in a war-related program designed to keep refugees away from the other side. This includes $116.5 million out of $135 million in South Vietnam ($30 m. for "City to Farm", $86.5 for "Refugee 

Relief", and all $20 million in Cambodia. Therefore, the only truly humanitarian aid we consider is $33.8 million, ($15.3 million for Laos, $10.3 million for Health Care in South Vietnam, and $8.21lion for Child Care in South Vietnam.)

To prevent involvement of U.S. military forces in Indochina; to encourage a political settlement as outlined in the 1973 Paris Agreements; to oppose continuing U.S. military and para-military aid to Vietnam, Cambodia, and Laos.

VIOLATIONS OF VIETNAM PEACE AGREEMENT 

Mr. ZABLOCKI. Ms. Abzug, I would like to pursue the line of questioning concerning the Commission for International Control and Supervision that the Chairman had inquired about. You are aware, of course, that the Canadian member had left in frustration. Do you know why? 

Ms. ABZUG. No, I don't know why.

Mr. ZABLOCKI. Well, because the CICS was not given access to and the freedom to inspect PRG and VC held areas. Yet you say that there is not any ability for the observing of prisons in South Vietnam. Are you aware that the North Vietnamese have infiltrated a substantial number of men and equipment into South Vietnam after the ceasefire in direct violation of the Paris Agreement?

MS. ABZUG. I have already indicated that I am sure there have been violations on both sides of the agreement. I did not suggest otherwise. 

I am addressing myself to what I believe is fundamentally standing in the way of any kind of meaningful peace being developed in Vietnam. Some of the things that the Vietnamese are doing obviously is provided for in the agreement, some are not, on both sides. I realize that and I have said that before.

This does not take away from our responsibility which is to see that what we do in this country is not going to perpetuate the war and prevent the implementation of the peace agreement. 

No enumeration or itemization of each side's violation is going to change the fact that we are contributing directly to preventing the Vietnamese people in South Vietnam from having a say as to what should happen in their government. 

POLITICAL PRISONERS AND VIETNAM'S FUTURE 

If you could get those political prisoners who are neutral opponents of Thieu who represent a different approach to the solutions of problems, being able to function freely, having civil rights, free elections, and so on, there might be a whole new situation developed, and that is what I am addressing myself to.

One man, a dictator, is in power. We give him aid, military and economic, which is being used to maintain him in power, not to help the people. I suggest that is wrong. I suggest we have to do what we can to see that the cease-fire is implemented and not inhibit it and interfere with it. I believe that our continuation of aid itself is a violation of that cease-fire agreement and I continue to make that point, sir.

Mr. ZABLOCKI. I know. 

MS. ABZUG. Others will make the point that both sides are violating the agreement. I have conceded that there is no question that some violations are taking place. That has nothing to do with what our policy should be. 

Mr. ZABLOCKI. Well, if our policy will be, as you maintain, it should be denying assistance to any country charged with having political prisoners, I would submit there is not any country in the world that cannot be charged with the allegation that there are political prisons, including Israel, including the United States. Who is to define a political prisoner is the question. To base granting U.S. aid on whether a country has or has not political prisons, will preclude any aid at all to any country.

UNITED STATES AND PEACE IN LAOS 

But let me go to a very interesting comment you have on page 6 of your statement where you say, and I quote: "In Laos a fragile peace is threatened by U.S. intervention again." 

What are you alluding to? Do you have any evidence that the United

States has in any way obstructed the operations of the new Provisional Government of National Unity in Laos or is violating the cease-fire agreements? Certainly you must be aware that the new Foreign Minister of Laos who is a high ranking member of the Communist Pathet Lao recently signed foreign aid agreements with western nations and said that he wished U.S. assistance and other foreign aid to Loas to continue. 

Are you aware that the new coalition government has made complaints against the North Vietnamese for their failure to take all of their troops out of Laos in violation of the cease-fire? Just what do you mean that the fragile peace in Laos is threatened by U.S. intervention?

Ms. ABZUG. I am suggesting, sir, that the question of whether or not we continue to maintain Thai troops in the area is intended to interfere with the continuation of that very fragile coalition which exists there. I suggest that we have some serious problems about the continuation of the operation of various forces in our Government through the maintenance of troops and military forces in and around those areas and operations of various elements of our Government, including the CIA, do not entirely accept that coalition. I suggest that this committee have some testimony on some of these questions. I will be glad to supply additional information on that as well. 

Mr. ZABLOCKI. I respectfully request that you supply for the record some explanation for that type of broad statement. 

Ms. ABZUG. I certainly will. Sources all over the world, as diverse as the New York Times and the Far Eastern Economic Review, have provided insight into the extent of U.S. involvement in Laos. A few examples suffice.

[The examples referred to follow:] [From the St. Louis Post-Dispatch, Dec. 2, 1973] PEACE SEEMS POSSIBLE AT LAST IN LAOS VIETIANE, Laos, Dec. 1 (UPI)-While an end to the fighting in Vietnam appears no closer, both government leaders and foreign officials are wondering whether Laos finally may be moving toward real peace after more than a decade of war.

Each day contigents of baggy-panted Communist Pathet Lao troops and functionaries arrive aboard Russian planes at the airport on the outskirts of this capital on the Mekong River, their welcome assured under a protocol signed with the government Sept. 14.

Officials voice hope that a joint commission of the two sides will soon open formal talks on the nut and bolt issues of implementing the nine-month-old cease-fire agreement. But, as always, hopes remain fragile in this obscure land of mist-covered mountaintops. 

Prime minister Souvanna Phouma, who engineered the protocol that set up the country's third coalition government in 20 years, continues to profess public optimism that the cabinet will be able to meet in the near future. 

Sources close to Souvanna say he is pushing to get the coalition-already eight months behind the deadline for formation set by the cease-fire agreement-into being and a political settlement far enough along so that widespread fighting in Vietnam cannot involve Laos as it did in early years. 

The sources say his concern over the events in neighboring Vietnam are at least part of the reasons why he recently issued a call for a summit meeting with Prince Souphanouvong, his half-brother and titular chief of the Pathet Lao. 

Laos, Southeast Asia's least developed country and a backwoods kingdom of no more than 3,500,000 persons that lies between Vietnam and Thialand, long has been a pawn in the international power struggles that have racked Indochina. 

Little of the fighting here in recent years was a Laotian affair. It was mostly 

North Vietnamese soldiers against the United States Air Force and troops recruited by the U.S. Central Intelligence Agency, many of them from Thailand. 

In the process one-third of the population became refugees at one time or another.

The United States has played an active role in negotiations between the two sides and already has started to rotate from Laos a number of the 18,000 Thai troops who were in the country in February. Some CIA paramilitary advisers have also left for home, although more than 200 military advisers remain on the job. Air America, the airline that flies for the CIA, has pulled its airplanes out of 

Vientiane and drastically reduced operations.

Events in Laos often stretch the limits of probability. For example, both the 

North Vietnamese and Pathet Lao were allowed to maintain active diplomatic missions in Vientiane throughout the war while fighting went on outside the capital.

Nevertheless, there were some temporary jitters in Vientiane when the first Pathet Lao troops arrived, brandishing AK-47 assault rifles as they got off the planes.

Approximately 1600 of the troops will be in Vientiane to serve as a security guarantee for Pathet Lao officials. So far they rarely have ventured outside their billets, where the intricacies of indoor plumbing have proved insurmountable for many of the peasant troops. 

Diplomatic sources describe the atmosphere between officials of the two sides as good in recent days.

A 1962 coalition government failed when Souphanouvong and other Pathet Lao members left Vientiane for the bomb-proof caves of Lao headquarters at Sam Neua in northeast Laos. But officials and diplomats in Vientiane cited several differences between then and now. 

First, Laos is the only place in Indochina where a cease-fire has held. Fighting tapered off quickly after the agreement was signed last Feb. 21. Since signing of the protocol incidents have reached the near-zero point. 

Secondly, well-informed sources say the Pathet Lao so far have accepted the 72-year old Souvanna's leadership readly as the only statesman capable of negotiating compromises. Otherwise, a provision requiring unanimous cabinet decisions would be unworkable.

Lastly, both government and Pathet Lao officials have stated publicly that the third coalition was the last chance for survival of Laos as an independent coun-

try. The alternative would be a partitioned buffer state, half controlled by the 

North Vietnamese and half under the influence of Thailand. Sources say Souvanna is hoping there is enough nationalistic feeling in the Pathet Lao to resist this. 

[From the Far Eastern Economic Review, Dec. 10, 1973] CUTTING BACK ON AID TO LAOS 

United States economic aid to Laos, running at around US$50 million for the past six years, will probably be reduced by about $5 million or $6 million next year, according to sources in Vientiane. US AID will probably get no more than $45 million this financial year, the sources say, although the money is unlikely to come through Congress for quite some time. US AID economic aid to Laos is provided into three fairly equal parts; one-third goes on refugee relief, one-third on the Foreign Exchange Operations Fund (FEOF) and the remainder on general economic support (schools, roads, public health etc). Total American aid to Laos has been running at $375 million a year (the "Symingtom ceiling" for war aid) in recent years, but only $50 million of this has been for economic support; the bulk has gone on military support for the Royal Laotian Army. [From the Manchester Guardian, Mar. 2, 1974]

AFTER A SECRET WAR AN ENIGMATIC PEACE (By T. D. Allman) 

Laos-the small Southeast Asian country on which the United States dropped 2,080,000 tons of bombs, and at least a million more tons of napalm, phosphorus, and defoliants-last week marked one of its few happy anniversaries since independence in 1954.

A year ago, the Laos ceasefire came into effect, ending nine years of continuous fighting between Communist and CIA forces in Laos. To the surprise of all the countries involved-the U.S. both Vietnam, Thailand, and China-the Laos ceasefire, unlike that in Vietnam, has worked. "We just keep our fingers crossed," said one Western official stationed in Vientiane. "The Laotians have suffered too much for peace to be lost again."

The enormous suffering inflicted on Laos during the Vietnam war is still not widely appreciated, even though the Laos "secret war" became a public one four years ago. At least a third, and probably more than half, of Lao's three million people were made homeless. A ton or more of U.S. explosives and chemicals was dropped for every person in the country. 

Many small villages were much more heavily bombed than Coventry or London, and tens of thousands of Laotians spent years at a time hiding underground. An entire generation of Laotians, often as young as 10 years of age, was conscripted into the CIA forces. Among some tribes, the death rate-including women and children-was 40 per cent.

The Laos war was thus never a "limited war," at least for the Laotians. But the struggle always had two saving graces. The intervening Powers, including both the U.S. and North Vietnam, remained committed in theory to the Laotian neutrality established on paper, but not in fact, by the 1962 Geneva Convention. Laos' own divided factions themselves also remained open to a compromise settlement. The American-backed Premier, Prince Souvanna Phouma-unlike Lon Nol is Phnom Penh, or President Thieu in Saigon-never outlawed his opponents, instead he left the way open for eventual reconciliation. 

Similarly, the Pathet Lao leader, Prince Souphanouvong—unlike the Vietcong and Prince Sihanouk-never declared his Laotian Patriotic Front an independent Government.

A year ago, this Laotian tendency to leave options open came to the country's rescue. Both Hanoi and Washington finally permitted the Laotians to agree to a ceasefire, to be followed by the formation of a provisional coalition Government and the withdrawal of foreign troops.

Over the last 12 months. the Laos peace settlement has been a technical failure, but a success in fact. The coalition Government has not been formed. American, Vietnamese, Thai, and Chinese military personnel remain in Laos. But no bombs have fallen for nearly a year and there have been no communist ground attacks. Casualties have declined from hundreds a week to only a few a month-

mostly inflicted by the delayed explosions of millions of U.S. cluster bombs and other antipersonnel devices that still litter the countryside. 

The most important political-military result of the ceasefire has been the movement, by separate Russian and Chinese airlifts, of nearly 3,000 Pathet Lao troops into Vientiane and the royal capital, Luang Prabang.

Under the ceasefire terms, the Pathet Lao presence is supposed to "neutralise" the two capitals. In fact, the result has not been neutralisation, but a microcosm in both towns of the tenuous military balance that has given Laos its first full year of peace since the nineteen-forties. While the pro-Communist forces with U.S.-supported Laotian units, in fact they serve, as one Laotian put it, as an "insurance policy" against rightwing attempts to destroy the ceasefire. 

In 1958, and again in 1963 and 1964. U.S.-supported right-wing forces destroyed two previous attempts at a compromise solution. With the Pathet Lao now so powerfully entrenched in Vientiane and Luang Prabang, a repetition of such events would be very perilous for the right wing. As one diplomat commented: "The days are gone when you could plunge the rest of Laos into war, while the cocktail parties went on in Vientiane."

The establishment of the "joint police force," however, is an example of how slow and limited Laos' return to normality is likely to be. While the joint force, like the coalition Government, was supposed to have been formed last April, most Pathet Lao forces did not take up their posts until last autumn. And the final accords on the joint force's operation were only approved two weeks ago-eleven and a half months after the ceasefire came into effect. 

And on the first anniversary of the ceasefire, Laos is still without its "provisional" coalition Government. Neither Laotian faction has nominated its equal number of Cabinet appointees. Nor has Prince Souphanouvong even visited Vientiane. But following final agreement on the mixed police force, a prominent Pathet 

Lao negotiator, Phoun Sipraseuth, has resumed negotiations with Prince Souvanna Phouma. 

Officials close to the Prime Minister hope the coalition can now be formed "immediately." With a typically Laotian nuance of meaning, the Pathet Lao say they want the coalition established "as soon as possible." 

In spite of the resumed negotiations, the vaguest predictions are probably the most accurate. According to most sources, Prince Souphanouvong is expected to visit Vientiane, if not assume his office as Deputy Prime Minister, "sometimes later this year."

Even if the coalition Government should be in operation before the second anniversary of the ceasefire arrives, Laos will still be a very long way from returning to normal government. Eventually the "provisional” coalition is supposed to be succeeded by a Government chosen in nationwide parliamentary elections-which, in a free vote, the Pathet Lao almost certainly would win. 

But even Prince Souvanna Phouma, who is usually an optimist, has said only that a return to constitutional government will occur "sometime in the future." 

If all goes well, that might be in four of five years, a period which for a country in Laos's position lies beyond the horizon of prophesy. 

Laos' extremely slow, and largely inconclusive, implementation of the political provisions of the ceasefire, however, is best regarded not as a means to a solution but as a solution in itself.

After decades of division and foreign invasion, it is impossible for any Laotian Government, whatever its composition, to rule Laos as a unitary State. And the details of the UN-implemented political settlement-intricately balanced Cabinet offices; and an entirely separate and "co-equal" council of national unionare so cumbersome that, as one Laotian commented: "I doubt they could work in Switzerland,"

Another Laotian official was equally candid: “Laos,” he said "is probably better off without a functioning Government. There is no point in rushing into a 'settlement' that will bring a whole new set of problems." Continuing peace in 

Laos in fact will depend not on the Laotians but upon the foreign Powers that have been violating Laos' defenseless and contracting frontiers for centuries. 

Fortunately, both Thailand and Vietnam-which once partitioned Laos-now seem eager to let the new settlement work. 

The new Civilian Government in Bangkok, unlike its predecessor, has no ambitions in Laos other than protecting Thailands Mekong frontier. And with 

US troops gone from South Vietnam. Hanoi is intervening less in Laos than in the past; the most promising sign is the construction of a new "Ho Chi Minh 

Trail in Communist-controlled areas of South Vietnam, rather than Laos. 

But Laos' best hope for the future is that the United States for the first time, also seems willing to let a Laos ceasefire work. Even the Nixon Administra-

1 tion, for all its continuing interest in Vietnam and Cambodia, now seems to recognize that there is little for any one to gain in Laos. 

Observers of several persuasions have pointed out that Laos' functioning ceasefire so carefully guards foreign interests in Laos that, under the surface, it amounts to little more than a disguised partition of the country among the 

Thais, North Vietnamese, Chinese and CIA. 

[From the Far Eastern Economic Review, Apr. 8, 1974] LAOS' PRINCES OF PEACE (By Norman Peagam) VIENTIANE.—The return of Prince Souphannouvong to the Laotian capital on 

April 3 signified the return of peace to Laos after a decade of bitter hostilities. In an emotional scene at Vientiane's Wattay Airport, Souphannouvong embraced his half-brother Prince Souvanna Phouma before making a short speech. 

Inside the packed airport building, Prince Souphannouvong said: "I have come today to proceed, together with Prince Souvanna Phouma, with the formation of the new provisional Government of National Union and the Consultative Political Council . . . This is an important event which marks a new development in the political life of our whole people and .. actively contributes towards safeguarding peace in this part of the world [The Pathet Lao side] has the conviction that under the august auspices of His Majesty the King [Sri Savang Vatthana], persisting in a just position and spirit of goodwill, enjoying the support of all levels of the population, and the approval of vast sectors of world opinion, [the new government and Council] will successfully carry out their historic mission with a view to realising a peaceful, independent, democratic and prosperous Laos."

The Prince then made his way through the packed and cheering crowd to a waiting motorcade for a 3-mile drive to the residence prepared for him: a drive 

Vientiane is not likely to forget, as tens of thousands of people following on motorcycles and in cars and massed along both sides of the route gave him a triumphant welcome.

The Prince and his party, which included the Pathet Lao's nominees for ministers and members of the Consultative Political Council, left their mountain headquarters at Sam Neua on March 31 by road for Hanoi. They then flew from the North Vietnamese capital to Vientiane in a Russian Antonov 24-B aircraft which was recently donated to the Pathet Lao by Moscow. The red and white plane, which bears the Pathet Lao flag and is flown by a North Vietnamese crew with Pathet Lao assistants, including blue-uniformed hostesses, touched down in Vientiane at noon.

Prince Souphannouvong, a short, robust figure with a dark moustache and silver hair, was greeted by his half-brother, the entire Pathet Lao delegation in Vientiane, the diplomatic corps (including the US Ambassador) and thousands of young Laotians, some of them carrying banners which read "Long Live Souphannouvong, long live peace."

The new government will be the third attempt in 20 years to establish a neutral Laos: both previous coalition governments collapsed within months of their formation, following US intervention in support of rightist elements, and on both occasions the Pathet Lao ministers were forced to flee into the mountains of northern Laos for their own safety.

This time the 1973 Laotian ceasefire agreement and its protocol stipulate that the two main towns of Vientiane and Luang Prabang are to be "neutralised" to ensure that the new government can function effectively and in conditions of reasonable security. 

During the past few weeks this "neutralisation" has been proceeding smoothly and a number of small ceremonies to mark the change have been held, culminating in the formal transfer of duties from the Vientiane city police to a joint Vientiane-Pathet Lao police force on March 14 and the handover of the city's defence to a joint military command on March 27. Similar ceremonies took place in Luang Prabang.

Police and army units from both sides have now begun working throughout Vientiane and so far there have been no reports of any friction. However, a few points still remain to be implemented including the withdrawal of excess Vientiane troops from the capital (i.e. all those over the numerical limits laid

down in the peace agreement, thought to be around 3,000 according to a source close to the Pathet Lao) and the removal of the former government's air force from Vientiane Airport.

On April 4 the nominees for the new Cabinet and Council flew to the royal capital of Luang Prabang where Souphannouvong and Souvanna Phouma had an audience with the King. The following day the new governmental bodies were sworn in. Although no official list was available when the REVIEW went to press, informed sources indicated that Souphannouvong himself would not be in the Cabinet, but would instead become President of the Consultative Political Council. The Vice-Chairmen of this body were expected to be Phoun Sipaseuth (PL) 

and Prince Sisoumang Sisaleumsak (Vientiane). 

The Cabinet itself was thought to be composed as follows:

Premier, Prince 

Souvanna Phouma; Vice-Premier (Pathet Lao) and Minister of Foreign Affairs Phoumi Vongvichit; Vice-Premier (Vientiane) and Minister of Education Leum 

Insisiengmay; Minister of Defence Sisouk na Champassak (Vientiane);

Minister of the Interior Pheng Phongsavan (Vientiane); Minister of Finance Ngon Sananikone (Vientiane); Minister of Public Health Khamphay Abhay (Vientiane); 

Minister of Economy and Planning Soth Petrasi (PL);

Minister of Information 

Khamsouk Keola (PL); Minister of Public Works Prince Souk Vongsak (PL); 

Minister of Religion Maha Kon Souvannamethi (PL): Minister of Justice 

Khamking Souvanlasy (Vientiane); Minister of Posts and Telecommunications

Khampeng Boupha (RL). For each minister of one side, there is also a secretary of state from the other.

Bordering the wasteland of war that is South Vietnam and Cambodia, Laos is the only oasis of peace in the Indochina peninsula. An 11-year civil war, which began in 1953 and was fought intermittently until 1959 when the fighting escalated with support from North Vietnam to the Pathet Lao, has been wound down. 

A year ago, the Vientiane rightists were adamantly opposed to a genuine settlement with the Pathet Lao. But today, although some opposition persists, there is a great measure of acceptance and most have slowly got used to the idea of working with the Pathet Lao who, as one US official put it, are not the ogres that some people thought they might be. The presence of about 2,500 armed Pathet Lao troops in Vientiane and Luang Prabang has also had a sobering effect on those military elements which might have resorted to force to frustrate the settlement. 

The key factor, however, has been the US Government's decision to end its military involvement in Laos.

The war in Laos ended with the Government's armed forces in a very weak position despite superior numbers and firepower. About half the population and four-fifths of the territory of Laos is in Pathet Lao hands, including all of the strategic Plain of Jars in north Laos, and the Bolovens plateau in south Laos. 

No ceasefire lines were drawn at the close of hostilities but both sides agreed to pinpoint 27 temporary "landmarks" where the opposing forces were close together, and these are relocated along the approximate demarcation lines (see map).

Official U.S. reports say there were about 68,000 in the government sides' armed forces at the time of the ceasefire but this could be much too high owing to the Lao practice of reporting false totals to pocket salaries of nonexistent personnel. This total includes 18,000 special forces integrated into the regular army, at least on paper, the day before ceasefire agreement was signed to circumvent the provision calling for their disbandment. It also includes 42,000 regulars. 

5,800 neutralists, a river flotilla of 330 and 2,050 in the air force which has about 200 planes. U.S. officials estimate the Pathet Lao forces number between 

30-35,000, over half infantry units. About two-thirds of the total are stationed in north Laos. Eventually the two armed forces will be merged but this will be one of the last steps towards national reconciliation. 

The unconfirmed total of US aid to the Vientiane government in the past year is about $110 million, compared with a budget ceiling of $375 million in the last year of the war. Of this sum, something under $50 million was spent on economic projects, and there was a sharp drop in military aid, mainly because most US military support consisted of keeping the Vientiane government's war effort going with basic supplies of ammunition, gasoline, uniforms, etc., which the ceasefire has now rendered unnecessary. This cutback in military supplies has forced the Vientiane

著 ​O side to observe the ceasefire and in the next few months it will oblige them to begin demobilising troops.

There has also been a significant reduction in the number of U.S. personnel in Laos, from around 1,200 at the time of the ceasefire to less than 600 today. 

Further reductions are expected. There are now less than 300 U.S. personnel working for U.S. AID, and around 70 in the embassy, half a dozen with the U.S. 

Information Service, and less than 200 assorted military personnel attached to the so-called Project 404, which coordinated the Vientiane government's military effort during the war. This last category, which U.S. spokesmen say is mainly engaged in administrative and logistics work, was to be withdrawn once the new government was formed, leaving only a Defence Attaché's Office with a staff of about 30, including ratings and communications people. Future U.S. aid plans here are described as highly uncertain, depending partly on the policy of the new Lao government and partly on the attitude of Congress. Many U.S. officials are uncertain whether they will still be here this time next year. 

[From the New York Times, Apr. 6, 1974] LAOS COALITION TAKES OVER (By John Burgess) 

Luang Prabang, Laos, April 5-The Vientiane government and the leftist Pathet Lao today formed a coalition government, bringing a formal end to nearly 

20 years of warfare in Laos.

Shortly after noon, King Savang Vatthana issued a special royal decree to inaugurate a new Cabinet and political consultative council in which the Americansupported Vientiane government and the Pathet Lao each have an equal share. 

Vientiane's Prince Souvanna Phouma remains as price minister, and his half brother, Pathet Lao leader Prince Souphanouvong, will head the council.

Shortly before 3 p.m., Prince Souvanna led the new Cabinet to call on King 

Savang at his palace in the royal capital. Wearing traditional Lao uniforms of white jackets and blue silk sarong pants, Souvanna and the Cabinet reviewed the royal guard and posed for photographs.

Moments later, Prince Souphanouvong arrived with the members of the political consultative council, whom he also presented to the king. On Saturday the government and council are to return to Vientiane, the administrative capital, to conduct religious ceremonies and begin the work of the new coalition. 

The installation of the new government followed a triumphant entry into 

Luang Prabang by Prince Souphanouvong yesterday. Vientiane and Pathet

Lao members of the government arrived in the royal capital yesterday evening aboard separate airplanes, Souvanna and Souphanouvong rode into the city in a black Ford limousine, to the cheers of thousands of students and citizens lining the roads.

At city hall Souphanouvong delivered a short speech and that afternoon the two princes called on the king to pay their respects. In the evening they were guests of the queen at a special banquet.

Today's ceremony_ended more than a year of negotiations since the Laotian cease-fire began on Feb. 22 of last year. In the new government, the Vientiane faction named men to head the ministries of defense, finance, interior, education, and public health. Pathet Lao appointees took over the ministries of foreign affairs, public works, economy and planning, information and religion. Neutralists were selected by both sides to head the ministries of justice and post and telegraph.

Vientiane retained the major figures of its old Cabinet in the new one: Sisouk 

Na Champassak at defense, Ngon Sanannikone, of the powerful rightist family that dominates the capital, at finance, Pheng Phongsavan at interior and Leuam

Insisienmay at education and as vice premier. 

The Pathet Lao vice premier and minister of foreign affairs is Phoumi Vong vichit, a member of the Central Committee of the Pathet Lao. As special representative of Prince Souphanouvong, Phoumi negotiated much of the Laotian settlement.

L Prince Sonphanouvong is chairman of the Joint National Political Council, a special body of 42 people included in the coalition formula at Pathet Lao insistence. Each side appointed 16 members, with the remaining 10 being neutralists acceptable to both sides. 

According to the protocols that the two sides signed last Sept. 14, the council and government are "two independent and equal organizations." The council "has the duty to organize elections and to deliberate and furnish opinions . . . on major questions of domestic and foreign affairs" which the provisional government must take into consideration and "scrupulously implement." In the case of disagreement, the government must provide "clear and adequate explanations." 

The exact function and importance of the council remains unclear, though it is generally felt that the Pathet Lao would try to give it as large a role as possible. Prince Souphanouvong's appointment as chairman, together with Khamsouk Keola, head of the patriotic neutralists, as vice chairman, would seem to confirm this.

The coalition is intended to be only a provisional administration, pending nationwide elections at an unspecified date in the future, probably at least two years from now if all goes well. Until then, the Pathet Lao will continue to administer the four-fifths of Laos they already control. 

A 60-day countdown began today during which all foreign soldiers and advisers in Laos illegally-about 140 Americans, 4,000 Thais and 55,000 North Vietnamese, according to figures provided by Vientiane government and U.S. sources-are to leave and any and all prisoners of war are to be exchanged. "From here on it's an adventure into an unknown realm," commented one observer of the Laotian scene, in speaking of the new coalition's viability. All government decisions are supposed to be unanimous and each minister has a deputy from the opposite side working under him. 

Nonetheless, this coalition is given far greater chance of success than the previous two of 1957 and 1962. The big powers and the countries around Laos seem to want it to work. 

The United States has realized that the Pathet Lao must be allowed to participate in the political process and cannot be excluded by military means. 

Through arm twisting the United States has forced this view on neighboring 

Thailand and the Vientiane rightists.

China and the Soviet Union also seem anxious to see a united peaceful Laos. 

North Vietnam sees the terms of the agreement as a victory for its Pathet Lao allies and is believed that, regardless of the ban on foreign troops, it will have continued access to the Ho Chi Minh Trail to supply the war in South Vietnam and Cambodia. [The U.S. State Department welcomed the formation of the new coalition government and offered to continue economic and military assistance to Laos if requested to do so.]

The two Laotian parties have demonstrated an ability to cooperate, however slowly, and during the last year of negotiations they made steady progress toward a settlement. In addition there are now about 1,700 Pathet Lao troops and police in Vientiane and 800 in Luang Prabang to insure the safety of their members of the government.

The Pathet Lao's dominant position on Laos' mountainous battlefields at the time of the cease-fire enabled them to virtually dictate terms of the settlement to Vientiane. Thus they took half of the seals of the government while retaining exclusive control of their zone, and sent troops into Vientiane and Luang Prabang.

Assuming that the new government is not disrupted by violence, the Pathet Lao apparently expect that their superior ability at political organizing will allow them to do well in the coming elections. The enthusiasm of the welcome accorded their leader, Prince Souphanouvong, indicates that they might succeed. 

[From the New York Times, Apr. 6, 1974] KEY MEN IN THE LAOTIAN COALITION 

A favorite of the royal household since birth, Prince Souvana Phouma was trained to assume leadership, and as a neutralist in the East-West struggle he has long been regarded as the one man who could forge unity among the divergent

Laotian factions. His shrewd and sophisticated continuation of a family tradition of public service has brought his divided country through a decade of recurrent crisis.

He was born at the royal capital, Luang Prabang, on Oct. 7, 1901, to Princess 

Throngsy, the first wife of Prince Boun Khong, a collateral member of the royal family who had several wives and concubines. 

He is one of five half-brothers, another of whom is Prince Souphanouvong, leader of the pro-Communist Pathet Lao. Although rivalries and jealousies between them started almost at birth, they have maintained an almost friendly relationship through more than two decades of war; they met Wednesday after a 10year interval,

STUDY IN FRANCE 

Souvanna Phouman's father packed him off at an early age to French-style schools in Hanoi. He then went to France to study. 

At age 30 he returned to Laos, then a French protectorate, and began a 19-year career in the public work agency. 

After World War II Souvanna Phouma joined with Prince Souphanouvong and another brother, Prince Phetsarath, in setting up a provisional government. This ended when French troops moved back into Laos, and Souvanna Phouma went into exile for three years. He returned after his country gained independent status within the French Union in 1949. 

He then began his long career at the highest levels of government, holding inany ministerial posts. Since then, while serving several terms as Premier, he has been determined that his country should pursue a neutralist course. 

He emerged as head of a coalition government that functioned after an international conference on Laos was held in 1962. But the coalition did not work and the Laotian civil war sputtered on year after year. 

At the age of 72 he is in good health, smokes many large cigars and plays a conservative game of tennis and a deft hand at poker. 

He and his wife, the former Aline-Claire Allard, who is of French and Laotian ancestry, have three children and five grandchildren. She and the children are 

Roman Catholics. 

Prince Souphanouvong, an aristocrat turned Marxist who once grew vegetables in his front yard while others of his class grew flowers, has returned to Vientiane after an 11-year absence to reap another uncertain political harvest. 

In his youth he was among the less privileged members of the Laotian royal family. While he and his half-brother, Prince Souvanna Phouma, the Premier, had the same father, Souphanouvong's mother was a commoner and a royal concubine and was not permitted to live in the palace. The boy was not favored by his father, who did not pay for his education in France. 

Supported by another half-brother, Souphanouyong studied engineering in Paris. He has been described as both brilliant and intellectually arrogant; visitors have also found him serene, scholarly and a passionate reader, with literary tastes that range from Marxism-Leninism to Greek tragedy. 

He had received his secondary education in Hanoi when it was under French rule. After finishing his engineering studies in Paris, he worked for a year on the docks of Le Havre and got to know French Communists. 

Asked years later whether he was a Communist, he replied: "What is a Communist? If being for schools, better health for the people, national independence and an end to corruption in government and opposition to imperialism is Communism, then I am a Communist."

Prince Souphanouvong owes the start of his political career to Ho Chi not long after World War II. 

At age 62 Prince Souphanouvong, who was born in 1912 and is said to have a large number of children by his Vietnamese wife, is 10 years younger than Prince Souvanna Phouma. Many people regard him as a man of destiny in Laos, and there are those who believe that he sees himself as the eventual leader. 

In 1950 Prince Souphanouvong was at a secret meeting in northern Laos at which the Pathet Lao organization was set up, and a decade later he was in the coalition government that resulted from the 1962 Geneva conference. That government broke up and he fled after a brief period of imprisonment. 

The Prince does not appear to have changed much since his last appearance in Vientiane in 1963. He wears Eastern European-styled suits and rather bulky shoes, but he conveys a cool, dignified presence.

FISCAL YEAR 1975 FOREIGN ASSISTANCE REQUEST MONDAY, JULY 1, 1974 HOUSE OF REPRESENTATIVES, COMMITTEE ON FOREIGN AFFAIRS, Washington, D.C. 

The committee met at 10:38 a.m. in room 2172, Rayburn House

Chairman MORGAN. The committee will come to order. 

Today the committee begins its 4th week of hearings on the President's foreign assistance request for fiscal year 1975. We are pleased to have a number of public witnesses. This morning we have before us Dr. James Dornan, Jr., Chairman, Department of Politics, Catholic University. With him are Dr. William Schneider, an aide to 

Senator Buckley of New York, Dr. Donald Senese, former professor and aide to Representative Archer of Texas, and Mr. James Streeter, an aide to Senator McClure of Idaho. These witnesses are appearing as a team. Dr. Dornan, I understand that you will make an oral statement and that you will submit, for the record, a written statement for the group.
