STATEMENT OF JAMES E. DORNAN, JR., CHAIRMAN, DEPARTMENT OF POLITICS, CATHOLIC UNIVERSITY 

Mr. DORNAN. Mr. Chairman, it is a privilege for us to appear before this committee to talk about those aspects of the foreign aid bill which deal with Vietnam.

Although the truce of 1973 substantially alleviated the bitter controversy over American policy on Vietnam which was the Nation's most prominent political problem in the decade of the 1960's, debate over current American aid to Vietnam continues. A large number of our citizens are skeptical about the efficacy and utility of the American foreign aid program in general, particularly during a period when claims on the Federal Treasury are many and extensive. Others doubt the viability of the government of South Vietnam and question on this (477)

the wisdom of ongoing U.S. assistance. Still others express concern about the moral quality of the Saigon government and the degree of popular support it enjoys within South Vietnam and thus wonder whether the United States can, consistent with its own principles and values, continue to support that government's existence. And finally, there are those who believe that South Vietnam is governed by a vicious and corrupt dictatorship which ruthlessly suppresses all opposition and indiscriminately imprisons its political opponents, and which therefore long ago forfeited all claim to American aid. 

In the final analysis, it is the Congress which will pass judgment on the accuracy and relevance of these critiques and determine America's future role in South Vietnam, since it is the Congress which must authorize and appropriate funds for the military and economic aid programs.

Obviously, the extent and quality of the information available to the Members of the House and Senate will be a crucial determinant in the process of reaching a decision. We are therefore pleased to be able to present to you some of our views on the present military, economic, and political situation in South Vietnam based upon a tour there in January of this year.

BRIEFINGS IN VIETNAM 

During our 8 days in Vietnam we were briefed by high government executives and cabinet ministers, as well as by American diplomats and intelligence officials. We toured three of the four military regions, visiting both province chiefs and field commanders for briefings and informal discussions. Our activities included interviews with politicians outside the government, the questioning of imprisoned Viet Cong agents and conversations with common citizens in a great variety of settings. 

No attempts were made to limit our activities or to interfere with our ability to acquire the information we deemed necessary to investigate precisely some of the critiques of the Vietnamese government with which the Congress is most concerned. The following analyses and conclusions are therefore our own, based on our personal observations and the information available to us. Needless to say, in no sense was it possible within these 8 days to conduct an exhaustive examination of the problems presently confronting South Vietnam.

VIETNAM: THE MILITARY CONTEXT 

First, the military context. Since the Paris accords were signed in 

January of 1973 there has been a reduction in the intensity of combat operations in South Vietnam. The heaviest fighting occurred in the first 3 months after the cease-fire. Since that time, the North Vietnamese and Vietcong have taken firm control of much of the area ceded to them by the Paris accords, particularly along the Laotian and Cambodian border, and have conducted a series of military operations designed to probe the extent to which the South Vietnamese would be willing to resist further incursions.

In addition, military engagements have taken place during the rice harvest when Vietcong and North Vietnamese units sought to intercept the grain which was being transshipped from the Mekong Delta

to urban areas throughout Vietnam. There has been no significant change in the percentage of territory controlled by either side since the cease-fire, although both sides have attempted to consolidate their hold on broad areas by eliminating the "leopard spot" areas, or small pockets of enemy-controlled land behind the lines.

Despite continuing heavy casualties on both sides, a relatively stable military equilibrium has existed for the past 18 months in part because of the continued resupply of the South Vietnamese Army by the United States. In addition to insuring that the NVA does not overrun the South, American military assistance serves a very important political end as well: it provides a viable framework within which a political settlement between the two Vietnamese factions might take place in the future.

In that respect, the situation in South Vietnam today approximates that which has existed in Western Europe, the eastern Mediterranean littoral, the Korean peninsula, and the Formosa Straits since the end of World War II. In all these cases a military equilibrium has been maintained as a result of a major effort on the part of the United States. In Western Europe and Palestine, political accommodation on the basis of the military equilibrium is already underway; a similar evolution on the basis of the political status quo in Korea and Formosa-and ultimately Vietnam-can be anticipated perhaps during the next decade. Such an evolutionary political accommodation is clearly in the interest of the United States. Therefore, in pursuit of that objective the United States ought to continue to provide the material wherewithal to South Vietnam as insurance against any effort by the North in the short term to achieve its political objectives by force of arms.

VIETNAM: THE ECONOMIC CONTEXT 

Second, the economic context. As this committee knows, since the end of World War II the use of material and financial assistance to support American interests abroad, relieve friendly nations confronted with security threats, and aid underdeveloped countries in economic difficulty has been a central feature of American foreign policy. Contrary to widespread belief, the successes of this policy have been many: Western Europe immediately after World War II, Greece and Turkey in the same period, South Korea, Iran, Taiwan, Brazil, and other nations since.

Many economic experts, both from the United States and from the international financial community, have asserted that South Vietnam possesses human and material resources comparable to those of South Korea and Taiwan and, given an equal level of American support, could achieve an economic "take-off" similiar to those two nations within 5 years. Nevertheless, in the short run South Vietnam confronts economic difficulties of a particularly acute nature, a consequence of the continuing military conflict, the rapid withdrawal of the American expeditionary force and soaring worldwide prices of fuel and fertilizer. The inflation rate last year soared past 60 percent and may reach 50 percent again this year despite a government austerity campaign. The economy remains heavily dependent on foreign imports.

Despite these facts, optimistic signs are plentiful. South Vietnam is an enormously fertile country whose agricultural potential has barely been tapped. Her people, despite 30 years of warfare, have lost none of their natural resilience and industriousness. Oil is believed to exist in quantity off the southern coasts, and drilling by one of the large international oil companies is scheduled to begin this summer. 

The government has embarked upon a major campaign to attract private foreign investment and is seeking, and already receiving to a limited extent, economic assistance from industrialized countries other than the United States.

No one would argue that massive doses of American economic aid should continue indefinitelv. Indeed, assistance on a large scale should not be necessary beyond fiscal year 1977. Until then, however, it is doubtful that the government can survive without substantial American assistance.

VIETNAM: THE POLITICAL CONTEXT 

Third, the politcial context. Those who would urge that the United 

States terminate its aid to South Vietnam have very often been motivated in their argument by the alleged unpopularity and authoriarianism of the Saigon government. During our stay in the country we discussed this issue with government officials, leaders of the political opposition, the editor if a large daily newspaper and even with those who claimed to be political prisoners. While opposition leaders were naturally critical of government policy in a number of areas, virtually everyone with whom we spoke conceded that President Thieu, and to a lesser extent his political party, enjoy a reasonable degree of popular support. Most expressed satisfaction with the opportunities afforded by the system for political expression, including criticism of the government.

Such criticism of a particularly vigorous nature is frequently heard in the legislature, and of the 15 daily newspapers currently published in Siagon 3 are openly hostile to the government and only 3 are proadministration. Ironically, one of the most frequently voiced demands of the North Vietnamese delegation in Saigon is that the government prevent the press from attacking the Communists. 

The 500,000 man local militia continues to be armed by the government, indicating how little it fears an uprising by its armed citizens, and no one with whom we spoke believes that there is the remotest possibility that the Viet Cong could achieve power in a free election. 

ISSUE OF CORRUPTION IN SOUTH VIETNAM 

It was not possible for us to investigate in detail the corruption issue although we discussed it at length with American officials from AID and the State Department, including several who work at the provincial level. The consensus appears to be that while problems remain in several ministries, there has been considerable improvement during the past year or so. All of us were profoundly impressed by the extraordinary group of able and dedicated young men who are increasingly being selected for positions of responsibility in both the armed forces and the civil service. These men, many of them holding

advanced degrees from America's finest universities, are clearly Vietnam's best hope for the future. 

In summary, then, we found no utopia in South Vietnam. We found instead an able and energetic people attempting to cope with the social and political consequences of more than 30 years of warfare, with the continuing presence of a large foreign army within their country, and with awesome economic problems not of their own making. There is no denying the magnitude of these problems. Nevertheless, we must describe our position as one of guarded optimism, aware though we are of the number of "guardedly optimistic" reports to which the members of this committee have been subjected over the past 25 years on the subject of Vietnam.

When its record is evaluated in the light of the continuing crises which it has confronted, it is our view that the Government of South Vietnam cannot be said to have performed badly in most areas. A wide variety of government programs appear to be administered with reasonable efficiency. There are few signs of overt discontent with 

President Thieu, and even his political opponents concede that he has grown in his job. Much of the unfavorable commentary on his stewardship over the affairs of South Vietnam appears to us to be based on standards inappropriate for judging governments in the war-torn segments of the developing world; moreover, few of the positive achievements of the government have received the attention which they deserve. If the military equilibrium can be maintained and the current economic difficulties controlled, in our view the prospects for political stability in the short run and for considerable economic progress over the longer term appear very hopeful. 

THE UNITED STATES AND SOUTH VIETNAM 

In evaluating the future relationship between the United States and South Vietnam, moreover, it is impossible to ignore our role in the past. Expectations have been created and commitments made, both within Vietnam and in the larger universe of international politics, which ought not to be cavalierly left unfulfilled or abandoned. 

The Secretary of State has recently emphasized this and related points in a letter to Senator Kennedy from which I briefly quote:

We also recognize that we have derived a certain obligation from our long and deep involvement in Vietnam. Perceiving our own interest in a stable Vietnam free to make its own political choices, we have encouraged the Vietnamese people in their struggle for independence. We have invested great human and material resources to support them in protecting their own as well as broader interests. 

We have thus committed ourselves very substantially, both politically and morally. While the South Vietnamese Government and people are demonstrating increasing self-reliance, we believe it is important that we continue our support as long as it is needed.

It is the conviction of this group that, given a reasonable level of American assistance over the next several years, the Republic of South Vietnam can survive and prosper. If it becomes clear, in time, that the government is capable of holding its own militarily and is in no danger of collapse from internal causes, the prospects for an ultimate political solution between North and South should advance concomitantly. 

For a quarter century the United States has been deeply involved

in the affairs of the Vietnamese. That involvement has been inspired by many assumptions and objectives-some valid, some questionable. 

But whatever the merits of our original involvement, one of the most important of our original objectives-the emergence of a viable non- Communist government in the South-now appears close to achievement. We urge the Congress to continue to fund the Vietnam aid program at a level sufficient to insure that end. 

Thank you very much, Mr. Chairman. We will answer any questions that you or the other members of the committee may have. 

Chairman MORGAN. Thank you, Dr. Dornan.

VIEWS OF COMMON PEOPLE IN SOUTH VIETNAM 

You listed, Dr. Dornan, many of the people that you talked to. I am particularly interested in the people on the street or in the villages. 

Many of us have been of the opinion that there were, say, 10 percent that were strongly pro-South Vietnamese and 10 percent maybe or 20 percent strongly pro-North Vietnamese but there was a 70 or 80 percent swing of apathetic people that were just trying to get along and survive.

Did you talk to any of these people down in the street? That is what 

I would like to hear about, No. 1; what their opinion was of their government. 

No. 2, are they aware of American aid? We sometimes hear that the leaders of the nations are well aware of how much help we are giving them, but the people in the streets and in the fields, are they aware of our aid? 

Mr. DORNAN. Mr. Streeter will speak first.

Mr. STREETER. Yes. The political situation is one where the government party of President Thieu is the primary political party and it is based to some degree on the support of the civil service and the soldiers, but beyond that, even if you put that aside, it is clearly the dominant party at least with a plurality in terms of support among the citizens, the general population of Vietnam, partly because of the weakness of the opposition parties. I think of those who have a strong political interest certainly there is nothing that can compete in terms of allegiance of the population at large with the government party. 

As to their feelings toward American aid, I often read that we were very unpopular, but I have spent several years in Vietnam in the Army and on this recent trip and have never seen any genuine hostility that was at all widespread toward Americans. I cannot say to what extent they are aware of the amount of American commitment. I have certainly never seen or heard expressed any hostility toward America. I cannot say that there is a strong political hostility either to the government or America but there is certainly a degree of skepticism. 

I think it might be most accurate to say that the government party has the most support, and beyond that there is a very large measure of acceptance and beyond that a measure of acquiescence. So you add those three characterizations and you get clearly the dominance by the government party.

PRESIDENT THIEU: GROWING IN JOB 

Mr. DORNAN. I think the words "acquiescence" and "acceptance" are far better than "apathetic." It is clear that the President is not a charismatic figure as are certain other third world leaders. He has not been a politician until recently; he is a military man and much is implied in that term. When people talk about President Thieu growing in his job, I think they mean growing in political acumen, and his growing zest to go out and meet people. I believe that has certainly helped the stability of the government and the degree of popularity of his regime.

Keep in mind, too, that politics is always a choice among alternatives, and it is often a choice between evils. It certainly seems clear in all that I have read about Vietnam plus what we were able to observe while I was there that the pinnacle of the Vietcong popularity occurred sometime in the midsixties; and the American intervention in Vietnam played an important role forcing them to behave as occupying armies frequently behave, in the exaction of heavy taxes, and overall oppression of the people. That has certainly had a big impact on the willingness of the South Vietnamese populace to look upon the government in a new light, and that light seems to be not just a negative one as Mr. Streeter indicated but a positive one as well in terms of acceptance or acquiescence. 

Mr. STREETER. The plebiscite is openly commented on, the practice of people voting with their vote. The refugees always flow toward the government, never toward the Communist controlled areas. 

POLITICAL PRISONERS IN SOUTH VIETNAM 

Mr. WINN. You mentioned, and I believe I can quote you correctly, so-called political prisoners that you talked to, something along that line. Why do you say "so-called" and what did you find out when you talked to this group of people?

Mr. STREETER. Well, we said so-called because I think to define them as political prisoners would be to say that acts of terrorism and bombing and so forth are political acts and it is also possible to say that, but they are also criminal acts and acts of war. So while they claim to be political prisoners, when we asked them what specific charges it was never what we would consider a political crime. 

The term "political crime" is so alien to the American tradition that we have trouble even imagining one. In each case of the people we spoke to-and they were definitely VC, they said so proudly-in each case they would admit to having been arrested and tried for a specific act such as a bombing or a hand grenade throwing or illegal weapons possession and so forth. So while they would say that is a political act, I think that stretches the meaning too far for us. 

Mr. DORNAN. I think probably a comparable situation in this country is if someone would claim that because a member of the Weatherman organization or Symbionese Army was jailed for the bombing of the Bank of America, they were jailed for part of their politics. 

Well, in one sense it is obviously true and in another sense that is a travesty of the word. In talking about the Vietcong we are talking about people who are in prison because they have committed acts of violence and terrorism against the government.

PHASING OUT U.S. AID BY 1977 

Mr. WINN. You said that you thought we ought to be able to curtail or complete the physical aid to South Vietnam by 1977. How did you arrive at 1977?

Mr. DORNAN. By talking to people in the Vietnamese Ministry of 

Trade, the Ministry of Finance, and by talking with Americans familiar with the situation in both Vietnams. I should point out, too, that among the former are several individuals who formerly worked for the World Bank and who had run in large part the program of reconstruction and development in Korea, so they are intimately familiar with what is required to enable the economy of Vietnam to reach a so-called economic takeoff point. 

Now one would hope 1977 is an accurate figure but that seems to be a fairly professional opinion and is not something we just pulled out of the air. It was the best we were able to come up with by talking to people who are intimately familiar with the Vietnamese economy. 

AD WORLD BANK AID TO SOUTH VIETNAM

Mr. DORNAN. That might be possible.

Mr. WINN. In other words, not cut off. If we said we are in a depression now or we are in a recession and we cannot give any more money away for 10 years.

Mr. DORNAN. Now, if over time the burden of aid shifts in relation to direct allocations, the World Bank can become involved, along with other industrialized countries such as Japan, France, and Australia which are gradually looking at the situation in Vietnam in a positive way. Obviously that will help the phaseout of our own program.

SHIFTING THE BURDEN OF AID

the financial aid back to the countries is like throwing confetti into the face of a fan or something, it just blows right back at you. 

Mr. DORNAN. Well, in most countries it has not worked that way but the two examples we cited, Taiwan and South Korea, are most analogous to Vietnam in terms of the material we have to work with.

INTENTIONS OF NORTH VIETNAM Mr. LAGOMARSINO. Thank you, Mr. Chairman. 

Dr. Dornan, you apparently think that South Vietnam can survive. 

Mr. DORNAN. Yes, quite definitely.

Mr. LAGOMARSINO. Was there anything from your visit there that would indicate to you what North Vietnam might be thinking about with regard to further operations in South Vietnam?

Mr. DORNAN. We cover this in some detail in the longer statement which we will submit. We are relying on the best information we had available from American and Vietnamese intelligence. No one predicted a major offensive for 1974 and few people seemed to contemplate a major offensive in 1975 although the South Vietnamese are dubious about that second point. I think a great deal will depend on how things go.

If the army continues to perform as effectively as it has since the cease-fire, if the economy remains stable, if the government seems to maintain a reasonable degree of popularity and seems to be able to cope with the problems the nation has, my hope would be that the North Vietnamese would gradually allow their policies to evolve in a more status quo direction as has occurred in other parts of the world under similar circumstances. But there is no way of knowing whether or not they will make one last attempt to seize by force of arms what they seem to be losing otherwise. That is certainly unpredictable. 

AID PHASEOUT IN SOUTH VIETNAM 

Mr. LAGOMARSINO. You mentioned several times that you thought that we could cut off aid in 1977 or a year or so either way. Have you discussed this with the State Department? 

Mr. DORNAN. No, we have not.

Mr. LAGOMARSINO. As I recall their testimony before this committee they are talking about a 5-year phaseout period but have not really submitted that timetable to us yet. Apparently you are somewhat more optimistic about the situation there.

Mr. DORNAN. I think the way I phrased it in my statement was that we would hope that the program could begin to substantially diminish by 1977. Whether it will be completely phased out within 3 years' time

of course is something that would have to be dependent upon circumstances. I simply was attempting to make the point that no one can expect us to continue these massive expenditures forever. At some point every nation which has been a recipient of American aid has got to be able to make a go of it on its own. 

The Vietnamese know this and all of them are keenly aware of the growing American resistance to foreign aid expenditures and they are therefore also aware that they have to get themselves into a position where they can deal with their problems with little or no American assistance at all, and expert opinion seems to indicate that there is a reasonable chance for it. That is all I wanted to say about using that 

1977 cutoff figure.

The first thing I would like to mention is that there is a moral commitment that the United States has made to our allies to keep them free and to give them the supplies that are necessary for them to keep their own freedom. UNDERSTANDING WHAT IS INVOLVED IN VIETNAM 

I think that many Members of this Congress have not really understood all that is involved in Vietnam. There has been a lot of propaganda that things are as bad as a dictatorship. Also that President

Lon Nol had a dictatorship and yet occasionally some of our Congressmen go to Indochina and see what is going on there.

I just would like to quote two lines from a report that Senator Percy made on the economic and political development in the Far 

East on his mission of November/December 1972. He says:

In Saigon I felt that politicians and citizens, even newspapers, were more free in expressing differences with the regime than they were in Indochina.

Also, land reform is showing some success and tax collections are up sharply and enabling the government in Saigon to do more for the individual provinces. 

There are now more aggressive and able members in some of the ministers, exports of rice have already doubled to 24 million in 1972 and are expected to reach the 50 million level in 1973. It is conceivable that South Vietnam could become self-sufficient in even such vital areas as food, fertilizer, and cement. Nevertheless, inflation continues to be a serious problem. Prices rose 75 percent in 1972 and 25 percent in 1973.

I need not point out that because of the embargo in the fall of 1973, the prices for fertilizers and petroleum products have risen tremendously and this hurts South Vietnam where they are using a tremendous amount of fertilizer for their miracle rice, the IR series. This coupled with what Mr. Robinson will mention later about the Communist effect on the rice crops has produced a tremendous inflation in the country.

When I was there in 1970 I saw a tremendous rice crop coming in, the biggest they had had in 10 years. The same was true in 1971. They were on the way to becoming a rice exporter to the rest of Indochina and this was earning them hard currency that they would need to buy other items and to reduce their dependency on the United States for aid. The 1972 offensive wiped out much of the grain they had and they are still trying to recover, especially from the cost of the ricelands and the cost to refugees. 

OIL IN SOUTH VIETNAM 

There is a little bit of hope in the future here and I think that it is going to be the word "oil." Many people have accused the United 

States of economic imperialism in Southeast Asia, especially in Vietnam. What we can get out of South Vietnam we can put on this tablevery, very little outside of say some wood.

There are indications by American oil companies-Mobil, Esso, Shell-that they feel there is a tremendous amount of oil in the continental shelves around the border of South Vietnam, Cambodia, and Thailand. Should this come true, should there be a tremendous strike in the future, this would help solve the problems of economic dependency on the United States and get the hard currency they need. 

I would like to put this into perspective. The June 25 issue of the 

New York Times had the headline "Guatemala Strikes Oil” and this was the first oil-producing well in the country. When I was in 

Guatemala in 1966 as an archeologist I was out in the Yucatan Peninsula and part of my job was to survey the area around the Tikal site. 

What we did was to follow the oil prospectors' trails and to remeasure them for accuracy for our grid maps. They were out there in 1963 prospecting for oil; it is now 1974 and they made their first strike down in Yucatan.

It will probably take another 2 years before that well is actually producing marketable oil. So this is one reason why South Vietnam will need our help if there is oil to be had because if they strike it today it will take approximately 2 years before they can market it and begin to get the currency that they will need to support themselves. 

I have just one major article on this I would like to submit to the record by Philip A. McCombs, "Search for Offshore Oil Quickens in

Vietnam," and it gives a general wrap-up of the situation in that aspect.

[The article referred to follows:] ENVOY TO SOUTH VIETNAM ANSWERS HIS CRITICS 

(Interview with Graham A. Martin ¹)

ARE AMERICANS GETTING A "DISTORTED" VIEW OF THE REALITIES IN VIETNAM? A VETERAN DIPLOMAT-AT THE CENTER OF A BOILING CONTROVERSY-PRESENTS IN THIS EXCLUSIVE INTERVIEW SOME OF HIS OBSERVATIONS ON HOW IT LOOKS AT THE SCENE AT SAIGON 

Question. Going back to the U.S. aid program. In a cable to the State Department in March you stated that Hanoi decided last autumn to launch an all-out campaign to persuade Congress to cut economic and military aid to Saigon. In your opinion has Congress been in any way swayed by Hanoi? 

Answer. What I actually said was that we had long been aware of decisions taken last fall in Hanoi to mount an all-out campaign this winter and spring to persuade the Congress to drastically reduce the magnitude of both economic and military aid to the Government of Vietnam. 

Hanoi's plans called for the Stockholm International Conference on Vietnam to be the main co-ordinating mechanism, and the Provisional Revolutionary Government delegation in Paris-the South Vietnamese Communist representativesto be the principal channel. The remnants of the American "peace movement” would be used in such a way as to bring influence to bear on selected susceptiblebut influential elements of American communications media and, particularly, on susceptible members of congressional staffs. 

The element of timing was important. First, as much material as possible condemning the South Vietnamese Government was to be moved into the "Congressional Record." The hope was that these insertions would show up in-or at least influence-formal reports of congressional subcommittees. These, in turn, could be followed up and given wide circulation by "investigative reporting" which would tend to confirm and, where possible, expand on the distortions already in the congressional subcommittee formal reports. 

When I referred to the Hanoi decision of last autumn I was referring to a special effort designed to particularly affect the authorizing and appropriation process for the fiscal year 1975 aid program for Vietnam. 

Hanoi's campaign was not something new. I watched the same process being used in France in the early '50s when the French were still, here in Vietnam. I became fascinated by its efficiency and pervasiveness. 

Question. But is it really effective in the U.S.? 

Answer. Let me give you an example. Outside the corps of professional Hanoi watchers, I have probably been one of the most regular and consistent readers of the output of Hanoi's principal newspaper "Nhan Dan" and of Radio Hanoi. 

With a background like that you'd think one should be immune to the propaganda. Instead, I find that even I have on occasions accepted as true parts of the "conventional wisdom" so carefully implanted. I believe all Americans havebeen touched by it to some degree, and since the Congress is representative of our people, it is inevitable that Congress would be influenced by it. 

1 U.S. News & World Report, Apr. 29, 1974.

When some of these distortions began appearing in the "Congressional Record" and even in some congressional committee reports, I began to worry more about what was happening to us in the United States than about what was happening in Vietnam. 

"THE PEOPLE MUST HAVE THE TRUTH" 

I deeply believe that when the American people and the American Congress have the whole truth, their decisions are almost always correct. But they must have the whole truth.

Mr. FRIEDMAN. I have prepared for your use documents from the 

World Peace Assembly, the World Peace Council, the Stockholm 

Council of Indochina and from several leading American Hanoi lobby groups showing that over the years they have programed themselves to attack U.S. aid to Indochina. I would like to submit them for the record because I believe this will show that Ambassador Martin is 

100 percent correct. [The material was received as part of the committee records.] 

Mr. FRIEDMAN. I thank you for allowing me to testify.

STATEMENT OF RON ROBINSON, DIRECTOR OF STATE AND CHAPTER SERVICES, YOUNG AMERICANS FOR FREEDOM 

Mr. ROBINSON. 

I first would like to mention that I was in Vietnam last month and visited. 

We appreciate the opportunity to offer the views of Young Americans for Freedom regarding American assistance to South Vietnam in the year ahead.

In recent years much of Vietnam's struggles have been shared by the American people. We agonized as South Vietnam was torn apart by the North Vietnamese's unyielding determination to impose their inhumane ideology upon an unreceptive population. From the earliest days when 1 million refugees gave up their homes and livelihood and fled to South Vietnam, through the systematic assassination of their most capable leadership, the wanton destruction of their towns and cities in the Tet and other offensives, to the recent attacks on their children at Cai Lay and Song Phu, we have witnessed their struggle. 

Through it all the South Vietnamese have suffered heroically. They did not tire when the battle intensified and the end did not appear in sight. They passed no Gulf of Tonkin resolution to tell their citizens they were at war; they knew this when their village leader, relative, or friend was murdered, or their homes were shelled or confiscated. 

Likewise, they have never had the luxury of backing away from it all, to disengage. The peace treaty negotiated by Henry Kissinger, which was done with minimal consultation with their representatives, offered little more than a brief respite from Communist aggression. 

They have been faced with the choice of subjugation or taking up arms and they chose the course that any freedom-loving people would. 

NORTH VIETNAM VIOLATES PARIS PEACE ACCORDS 

We have also shared in this struggle because we recognized the subtle meanings of the war in Vietnam. Another Communist state, this time North Vietnam, was attempting to extend the perimeters of the Bamboo Curtain. As recently as June 4, another deadline passed that illustrates the true nature of this war. On that date the North 

Vietnamese were to have withdrawn their troops from Laos. Once again we witnessed the Communists flagrantly violating a would-be peace accord. In an age of proliferating military technology we can ill afford to ignore continued aggression. Yet that is actually what we will be doing if we discontinue aiding the South Vietnamese. 

We have always been skeptical of those who would legislate away the liberties or property of others. We feel that whenever government takes from one man to bestow upon another, it diminishes the incentive of the first, the integrity of the second, and the moral autonomy of both. But aid to Vietnam is in no way a mere giveaway program. We are simply fulfilling our obligations to world peace and to world freedom. With over 1,200 American servicemen still unaccounted for, with tens of thousands of North Vietnamese troops still active in South Vietnam, and with the Vietcong receiving unlimited aid from North Vietnam, the Soviet Union, and Red China, it is inconceivable to us that Congress would underestimate the need for

this aid. Nonetheless, that is the hope of both the North Vietnamese and those Americans who have an emotional commitment to the defeat of South Vietnam.

AID OPPONENTS: CONTRADICTING EARLIER VIEWS 

Many of those who are currently calling for a reduction or elimination of aid are contradicting their earlier testimony to the American and Vietnamese people.

We were told, in countless statements and publications, that our involvement was destroying the Vietnamese countryside. Yet now we fail to hear those same voices in support of efforts to rebuild the countryside.

We were told we shouldn't have American troops stationed in Vietnam, that military and economic aid would be sufficient if the South Vietnamese supported their government. Yet now we fail to hear those voices on behalf of the aid they implied we would continue. 

We were told the South Vietnamese should accept the Paris peace agreement, despite its lack of adequate enforcement provisions, because we would always be able to give adequate military and certainly economic aid to South Vietnam. Yet we now fail to hear those voices carrying through on their commitments. 

Those who would have us abandon our allies in South Vietnam have never been bothered by consistency. Their blind opposition to the 

South Vietnamese is not unlike North Vietnamese aggression; they are both unabated and unproductive. 

I have recently returned from a visit to South Vietnam. I have witnessed the devastation caused in cities like Hue and Quang Tri, the sights of clearly American war babies in their streets and the hopes of a determined people to recover from a long and costly war. I cannot join those who call upon us to suddenly drop our support before Communist aggression has been stopped or the rebuilding process has moved dramatically forward.

LIMITED NATURE OF CURRENT VIETNAM AID 

Much has been made of the fact that we have already invested billions of dollars and thousands of lives in South Vietnam, yet that argument points up the very limited nature of our current assistance. 

We are not being asked to endanger additional American servicemen. 

Indeed the contrary is true-as long as we have a presence in South Vietnam the hope continues that we will receive an accounting for our missing in action. We are not being asked to pour in any unlimited amount of funds. Indeed, the current recommendation is for less than 

1 percent of our previous support and about one-half percent of our national budget. This seems to be a most modest recommendation in light of the challenges facing our ally.

With an appreciation of what we have done in the past and hope for what can be accomplished in the future, Young Americans for Freedom urges an approval of the administration's appropriations recommendations of assistance to South Vietnam.

[From the Washington Post, Wednesday, Oct. 11, 1972]

HANOI PUSH CUTS SOUTH RICE OUTPUT 

(By George McArthur)

SAIGON, Oct. 10-The North Vietnamese offensive launched six months ago has cost the Saigon government about half a million tons in lost rice production and set back indefinitely the regime's hopes to be self-sufficient in rice. 

Figures gathered from various sources and supported by government statistics indicate that the half-million ton figure for lost production may be low. 

Tran Van Chanh, rice-production expert at the Ministry of Agriculture, estimates that about 400,000 tons was lost in the coastal areas of Binhdinh Province far north of Saigon and in the fields of Binhlong Province just north of the capital. These figures do not take into account lost production in the 

Meking Delta, which is more difficult to ascertain. 

The lost production—which amounts to about 10 per cent of the rice needs for South Vietnam for one year-will be made up by shipments of American rice under the Food for Peace program. 

Under this program, American rice is sold to the Saigon government for piasters and the local currency is then plowed back into the South Vietnamese budget in various American-approved programs. 

The latest such agreement between Washington and Saigon, signed early this month, commits the United States to ship 200,000 tons to South Vietnam in the first three months of 1973. Before the end of this year, the United States will also ship another 200,000 tons. 

MORE U.S. RICE 

With stocks on hand sorely depleted by refugee and war needs, it is likely that South Vietnam will need more American rice before next year is out. 

Local government officials estimate that they need 50,000 tons on hand at all times to maintain some semblance of price stability and to meet emergency needs. 

Despite such measures, ordinary rice is now about 25 per cent more expensive than when the Hanoi offensive began. 

It is a major disappointment to both South Vietnamese and American officials that rice self-sufficiency now appears out of reach for the foreseeable future. 

Officials insist, however, that the goal can probably be attained within 12 to 18 months if the current Hanoi offensive is beaten back.

Up until 1963 South Vietnam's 'lush Mekong Delta produced enough rice to allow considerable exports. Starting the following year, however, the abandoned farms in the Delta sent production plummeting. From 1966 to 1969 the United 

States sent about $100 million worth of rice to South Vietnam every year. 

SCUTTLED HOPES 

Improved pacification and new miracle strains of rice began to send up production up sharply after 1968. The Saigon government hoped to reach a breakeven point in calendar 1972 and to export half million tons in calendar. 1973. 

These hopes have now been scuttled. 

Current production figures are obviously imprecise, with much of the country affected by the Communist offensive. Agriculture Ministry figures show that the government had hoped for a record-breaking harvest of almost 7 million tons for the 1971-72 crop year ending with the October harvest. 

Quite apart from the likelihood that the target production figure was high, the production lost due to the offensive makes the original figure ridiculous. The deni 97

government will probably be fortunate to match the 5.7 million tons harvested last year-the record at the time, and likely to remain so. 

That figure was half a million tons higher than the previous year-the increase being equally due to new rice strains plus land restored to production.

Mr. I. L. Kenen, chairman of the American Israel Public Affairs

STATEMENT OF I. L. KENEN, CHAIRMAN, AMERICAN ISRAEL PUBLIC AFFAIRS COMMITTEE 

Mr. KENEN. Mr. Chairman and members of the committee, I do thank you for the opportunity to appear here today. We represent the American Israel Public Affairs Committee. Mr. Kenneth Wollack, our legislative liaison, and Mr. Aaron David Rosenbaum, our director of research, are joining me here at the table here this morning. 

I am authorized at the outset to inform you that the Conference of Presidents of Major American Jewish Organizations, which includes 31 major American Jewish organizations, supports our proposals. The list appears in the appendix to the written statement which I have submitted to the committee. I have a similar authorization from the American Jewish Committee. 

In the beginning I should like to express our warm appreciation for the vital role this committee has played in helping Israel to develop her economy, to strengthen her defenses, and to resettle both her land and her people over many years. 

INITIATIVES FOR ISRAEL HAVE BEGUN IN COMMITTEE 

Many initiatives began in this committee. I refer to the first grant aid in 1951, the resolution calling for the end of the Arab blockade of the Suez Canal in 1960, the amendment barring the use of any part of the U.S. contribution to UNRWA funds to support terrorists in 

1966-and I wish the U.N. would have adopted that policy-the proposal for desalting research in Israel in 1969, the resumption of grant economic assistance for Israel in 1971, the appropriation to help resettle Soviet Jewry in 1972, and finally, and most impressive, the (507)

$2.2 million emergency security assistance which you approved last

December. 

This year the administration has proposed a $50 million supporting assistance program for Israel for fiscal 1975. We recommend an authorization more responsive to Israel's need to strengthen her defenses and stabilize her economy. 

Earlier this year the Israel Government requested the administration to recommend a supporting assistance grant for $250 million which, coincidentally, is the amount which the administration later proposed for Egypt. We believe that this request merits your consideration. In addition, we suggest that $100 million of the $300 million requested by the administration for military credits for Israel be authorized in the form of grants, the remaining $200 million in the form of credits. This, incidentally, happens to be the amount of grant military assistance scheduled for Jordan. 

LONG-TERM AID TO ISRAEL NEEDED 

We believe that our proposals are conservative and consistent with the intent of President Nixon's affirmations to Israel during his recent visit to the Middle East that the United States will continue the longterm military supply relationship with Israel and "in accordance with congressional authorization will continue to provide substantial economic assistance for Israel at levels needed to assist Israel to offset the heavy additional costs inherent in assuring Israel's military capability for the maintenance of peace."

Our current recommendations are directed to the pending authorization for fiscal year 1975. We believe that developments since October justify the request for aid over and above that proposed by the administration. Israel's arms procurements requests since October already exceed $3 billion. 

The shooting did not end on October 22. It continued for many months in a war of attrition costing many lives. The inability of the U.N. to enforce past U.N.-sponsored cease-fires which the Arabs violated when they attacked last October 6 and which they continued to violate after October 22 certainly bodes ill for the effectiveness or durability of disengagement arrangements. 

Disengagement is not synonymous with nonbelligerence. Who can really be sure that Arab leaders are ready for a genuine peace? In recent days they confronted President Nixon with militant and uncompromising demands for Israel surrender and U.S. subsidy. 

OPERATIONS OF ARAB TERRORISTS 

The Arab terrorists apparently believe that shooting civilians, mostly women and children, is the open sesame to approbation and recognition. They cross Israel's frontiers with never a whisper of reproach from the U.N. and with no curb by any Arab government. 

In this connection may I recall that under the 1949 U.N. Armistice 

Agreement between Lebanon and Israel, Lebanon was obligated to prohibit "paramilitary" and "nonregular" forces from attacking Israel. Lebanon's failure to seal her borders and to prevent terrorist infiltration has been a glaring violation of the armistice agreement,

P 11. and the U.N. Security Council's grotesque failure to censure Arab terrorism-and the Council's knee-jerk condemnation of Israel's response-has been an immoral judgment which rewards and encourages aggressors and denounces those who resist them. 

The new disengagement agreements have weakened Israel's defense capability because they required her to withdraw from strong vantage points to positions of static defense. Accordingly, Israel must maintain strong frontier forces and take new precautions to protect her civilians. In addition, Israel must have more soldiers in her regular army and her armed reserves, equipped with more sophisticated and costly weapons because the arms balance is tilting dangerously against her.

Arab military capability is growing partly because of tremendous Arab oil wealth and partly because of the proliferation of Soviet and 

Western arms in the Persian Gulf area. Israeli officials now estimate that the Arabs have a quantitative superiority of 3 to 1 in planes and tanks, 7 to 1 in artillery. Furthermore, the Arabs demonstrated ability to use their new sophisticated weapons means that Israel's postqualitative superiority has been sharply reduced. 

HIGH COST OF ISRAELIS DEFENSE 

This puts a new strain on Israel's debt-burdened economy. The war cost Israel an estimated $7 billion, almost 1 year's GNP. Defense expenditure rose sharply. In the war year it was $4 billion as compared with $1.5 billion the year before. In 1972, Israel's imports for defense totaled $662 million. The figure rose to $1.57 billion in 1973 and it may exceed $1.8 billion in 1974.

The high cost of defense, soaring inflation, and lowered production have all combined to boost Israel's current account deficit which rose from $1.075 billion in 1972 to $2.475 billion in 1973 and which is expected to exceed $3.28 billion in 1974. Israel economists have predicted that after utilizing all foreseeable sources of foreign exchange, Israel will still be short $587 million this year and $840 million in 1975. 

These calculations are all based on the assumption that the administration would finally allocate $1.5 billion of the $2.2 billion voted last year in the form of grant in accordance with the congressional authorization. We are pleased that the administration did make that decision last weekend. Israel's economic position would have been more critical if the administration's decision had not been favorable. 

ISRAELIS: HIGHEST TAXED PEOPLE IN WORLD 

I must emphasize that our Government never provided Israel with grant military assistance until last October. Israel paid for her defenses, either in taxes or in heavy borrowings. As a result, the Israelis are the highest taxed people in the world. The average Israeli had a per capita income of $2,100 in 1973. Out of this $2,100 he paid $900 in taxes and $300 in loans leaving $900 for living expenses, a sum further reduced by the abolition of subsidies. If one includes city tax rates and social security, the Israelis are contributing 62 percent of the GNP to government treasuries.

The table at the top of page 4 in our memorandum on U.S. Aid to 

Israel shows how Israel's foreign currency debt is steadily rising-

from $4 billion in 1972 to an estimated $5.8 billion by the end of 1974 and $6.8 billion at the end of 1975. Thus, Israel's per capita foreign debt is rising from $1,275 in 1972 to an estimated $1,680 in 1974 and $1,940 by the end of 1975. 

THE NEED FOR ADDITIONAL AID TO ISRAEL 

One further point. Some claim that additional aid is unnecessary. 

We have heard this argument here because of Israel's foreign exchange reserves, which reached a peak of $1.7 billion at the end of 1973, but this was partially because Israel's friends contributed and loaned her large sums during the crisis. That was an abnormal situation. Israel's reserves have already dropped $350 million in the first 5 months of this year and the decline will continue because of the balance-ofpayments deficit.

In 1971, 1972, and 1973 the Congress voted $300 million in military credits and $50 million in supporting assistance for Israel. Now the administration proposes to revert to that prewar, preinflation figure even as it has begun greatly to expand assistance to those who attacked Israel.

There is an anomalous disparity between the $50 million grant recommended for Israel and the $527.5 million in military and economic grants which may be available to Egypt, Jordan, and Syria. 

To many people, this may imply a change in American policy. I do not believe that the administration is diminishing support for Israel, but Arab leaders have extravagantly claimed that the United States now supports their political objectives in the Middle East. 

A dramatic expansion of aid to the Arab States coinciding with a contraction of aid to Israel would be prejudicial to the peace because it would increase Arab strength to the detriment of Israel's security and dangerously inflate Arab expectations that the United States is preparing to abandon Israel in the East-West competition for Arab favor.

Indeed, it is already clear that Arab leaders are sharpening demands. for an imposed settlement which would force Israel to surrender completely to their diplomatic, territorial, and economic terms. If Israel is to win a negotiated peace, she must continue to be strong and the United States must continue to be clear and steadfast in her support. 

I thank you very much. [The written statement submitted-Memorandum on U.S. Aid to 

Israel-fiscal 1975-follows:] MEMORANDUM ON U.S. AID TO ISRAEL-FISCAL 1975 

(Submitted by American Israel Public Affairs Committee, I. L. Kenen, Chairman) THE RECOMMENDATIONS 

The Administration has proposed $50 million in supporting assistance for Israel. We recommend an increase to $250 million. 

The Administration has recommended $300 million in military credit sales for Israel. We suggest that $100 million of this amount be in the form of grants. 

The Senate has voted authorization of $50 million to help Israel resettle Soviet Jews, an amendment to the Department of State authorization. We hope that the House will concur.

We submit that our proposals are responsive to Israel's urgent need to strengthen her defenses and to stabilize her economy.

THE JUSTIFICATIONS 

Israelis were outgunned and outmanned when Egyptians and Syrians, massively armed by the Russians, attacked last October and they suffered heavy losses in life and materiel, as well as economic reverses. Congress then voted the $2.2 billion in emergency assistance recommended by the Administration.

The war did not end on Oct. 22. The shooting continued for seven months. 

Despite disengagement agreements, the area is a long way from genuine peace. 

The continuation of Arab belligerence and a new wave of brutal terror compel Israel to maintain a larger and better-equipped military force and armed reserves. 

Moreover, the arms balance is tilting dangerously against Israel, partly because of continuing Soviet shipments, partly because of Arab oil wealth, partly because of the proliferation of Soviet and Western arms in the Persian Gulf. As a result, Israel's arms procurement requests in the United States have already exceeded $3 billion.

Israelis never received grant military assistance until October 1973 and over the years they went deeply into debt to pay for their security. Per capita, they pay the highest taxes in the world and carry the highest external debt, which will continue to grow unless they receive grant military and economic assistance. 

The high cost of defense, inflation and war-depressed production combine to boost Israel's current account deficit, which may exceed $3.2 billion this year. 

Israel's foreign currency reserves, which reached a peak of $1.7 billion in 1973partly because of borrowing and gifts-have already dropped $350 million this year.

There is an anomalous disparity between the $50 million grant recommended for Israel and the $527.5 million in military and economic grants which may be available to Egypt, Jordan and Syria.

A drastic expansion of aid to the Arab states, coinciding with a contraction of aid to Israel would be prejudicial to the peace because it would increase Arab strength to the detriment of Israel's security and it would inflate Arab expectations that the United States is preparing to abandon Israel in the East-West competition for Arab favor.

MEMORANDUM ¹ 

At the outset, may we express our appreciation for your favorable vote on the Administration's emergency aid program for Israel last fall, when Congress recognized Israeli's peril and helped to assure her survival. 

It is our hope that the 1975 aid bill will serve to promote a genuine peace in the Middle East. The aid program includes requests for $1.37 billion in military grants and economic supporting assistance for 51 countries. 

It recommends $430 million in military and economic grants to seven Arab countries including $100 million in military assistance and $77.5 million in supporting assistance for Jordan, $250 million in supporting assistance to Egypt. 

There may be an additional $100 million for Syria. Other Arab states to receive grant military aid; Tunisia, $2 million; Morocco, $860,000; Saudi Arabia $220,000; Lebanon, $150,000; Sudan, $50,000. The program also includes $23.2 million for UNRWA.

The amount proposed for Israel is $350 million, but of that amount $300 million is for credits and only $50 million is for a grant. These contrasting programs appear anomalous because the Arab states were the attackers last fall and Israel suffered heavy losses in her defense.

I call your attention to an editorial which appeared in The New York Times on April 28, 1974: "The economic aid to Israel is considerably less than had been requested, and both Congress and the executive branch would do well to stay flexible in meeting this country's long-standing interest in preserving Israel's economic and military strength. Unlike the Arabs, Israel has no other major source of investment and economic aid." 

1 The Conference of Presidents of Major American Jewish Organizations, which includes 31 major Jewish organizations, and the American Jewish Committee associated themselves with the AIPAC recommendations (seee Appendix, p. 520).

We ask you to approve an appropriation for Israel which would be more responsive to her need to strengthen her defenses and to stabilize her economy. Earlier this year, Israel requested the Administration to recommend a supporting assistance grant for $250 million, which, coincidentally, is the amount which the Administration has now proposed for Egypt. 

In supporting this request, we are fully aware of, and grateful for the generous assistance approved by Congress last December. But subsequent developments do justify a request for additional aid.

In voting the $2.2 billion last year, Congress provided that the Administration could grant Israel up to $1.5 billion and that the $700 million balance could be in the form of loans. The Administration recently announced an initial allocation under this legislation of $1 billion in grants, the balance in long-term loans at concessionary rates. It is our understanding that the $2.2 billion is to be spread over a three-year period: $800 million for the arms which Israel received during the war; $800 million in the current year; $600 million in 1975. 

But Israel's arms procurement requests already exceed $3 billion. The agreements signed as of the end of March approximated $1.2 billion, and agreements approximating $1 billion were awaiting signature. The remainder were in various stages of negotiation. This means that Israel must continue to go more deeply into debt to pay for her survival, unless Congress approves additional grant assistance.

We submit the following reasons why legislation for additional assistance to Israel is justified at this time: 

The war did not end on Oct. 22. The shooting continued for seven months. 

Despite disengagement agreements, the area is a long way from genuine peace. 

The continuation of Arab belligerence and a new wave of brutal terror compel Israel to maintain a larger and better-equipped military force and armed reserves. 

Israel suffered heavy losses in manpower and materiel. Her economy was shaken by the war and its prolongation and by worldwide inflation. 

Israel's citizens have paid heavy taxes and loans to maintain their security and to amortize the heaviest per capita external debt burden of any people on earth. 

The military balance is beginning to tilt dangerously against Israel, partly because of Soviet shipments, partly because of the ominous proliferation of arms in the Persian Gulf.

A drastic contraction of American aid for Israel, coinciding with a substantial expansion of U.S. aid for the Arab states, may have a psychological impact detrimental to the peace.

THE WAR GOES ON 

The Administration's recommendation last year was made on October 19, just three days before the cease-fire. There has never been a real cease-fire since that time. The Egyptians kept shooting until the disengagement agreement was finally signed on January 17. Syria's war of attrition on the northern front persisted even while Secretary of State Henry Kissinger was in the region attempting to negotiate a disengagement agreement. The Syrians punctuated their demands with shells.

The inability of the United Nations to enforce the UN-sponsored cease-fire and to curb the shooting bodes ill for the effectiveness or durability of the disengagement agreements. Cease-fires are easily violated and disengagement is not synonymous with non-belligerence. 

Nor has the UN been able to censure and halt shocking and brutal terrorist outrages against Israel civilians like the massacres at Kiryat Shemona, Ma'alot and Shamir.

All segments of the Palestinian terrorist leadership deny Israel's right to exist. The recent meeting of the Palestine National Council in Cairo rejected "recognition, conciliation [and] secure borders with Israel," and insisted that any Palestinian national authority which might arise in the West Bank or Gaza be constituted as a "fighting force" against Israel and Jordan. 

These unhappy developments inform Israel that she must continue to maintain adequate defensive strength to guard her frontiers and to take new precautions to protect civilians. She cannot rely on documents or third-party guarantees. 

Throughout the war and for months thereafter, the Soviet Union poured sophisticated military equipment into the arsenals of Israel's neighbors, encouraging them to maintain a belligerent and negative posture toward disengagement and a negotiated settlement.

1 At the same time, the wealthy oil states have financed the Egyptian and Syrian arms purchases from the Soviet Union, and, in addition, have enabled these countries to procure essential commodities to strengthen their home fronts. 

"ISRAELIS ARE THE HIGHEST TAXED PEOPLE IN THE WORLD. 

In the past, the Israelis were always assured that they did not need to maintain a quantitative balance because of the qualitative capacity of their soldiers. 

To some extent, the Arabs have now mastered sophisticated weapons. But the 

Arab military advantage during the October war was due not so much to sophistication as it was to the vast profusion of weapons, financed by oil dollars gleaned from the West and transmitted to the East. 

The disastrous experience of last October, the overwhelming firepower of tanks and missiles, the rapid Soviet arms resupply, the alchemization of Arab oil into weapons, the prolongation of the war of attrition, the new wave of brutal terror-all these compel Israel to maintain a larger and a much better equipped military force.

Before the war, Israel had some six to seven thousand in its mobilized reserves. In 1974, the Israelis estimate that they will need an annual average of 80,000 mobilized reserves, more than eight percent of Israel's labor force. 

THE COST OF THE WAR 

The war struck a hard blow at Israel's economy—an estimated $7 billion dollars almost the equivalent of a full year's output. 

The replacement cost of materiel and damaged property is approximately $4 billion. The loss in production was about $400 million; it may be double that this year.

When the war came, the government moved viftly to absorb purchasing power. It imposed a compulsory war loan of seven to twelve percent and a similar voluntary loan on top of that. Later there were five percent increases in custom rates, five percent increases in sales taxes, increases in cement excise. 

In addition to the reduction of subsidies on essential goods and services there were increases in the price of fuel and electricity. 

The total annual absorption of purchasing power came to 6.495 billion Israel pounds, the equivalent of more than $1.5 billion. 

If 1973 had been a normal year, the Israelis would have paid their government some $3.8 billion. As a result of the October war, the Israelis contributed almost $2 billion more to finance their own security.

ISRAELIS PAY A HIGH PRICE 

The Israelis are the highest taxed people in the world. 

The average Israeli had a per capita income of $2,100 in 1973. On this income, he paid $900 in taxes and $300 in loans, leaving $900 for living expenses. But this was further reduced by additional emergency taxes and by the abolition of subsidies.

An Israeli with an income of $5,000 pays 52 percent in taxes and loans; on an income of $10,000 he pays 66 percent; on an income of $20,000 he pays at the rate of 75 percent.

The new taxes and compulsory loans mean that Israelis will be funneling 54 percent of the gross national product back to the treasury, according to 

Israel's Finance Minister Pinhas Sapir. The New York Times reported, on 

March 15: If one includes city tax rates and social security payments, the

Israelis are actually contributing 62 percent of the gross national product to government treasuries, it was estimated by Mashe Neudorfer, Director of State 

Revenue. 

Israel's defense expenditures rose sharply in 1973. For that fiscal year, the total was $1.5 billion. In the war year, it was $4 billion. In the next twelve months, it is hoped, the figure will drop to $3.6 billion. 

In the last two years, 45 percent of Israel's defense expenditures were in foreign countries, about 95 percent of that amount in the United States. 

In 1972, Israel's imports for defense totaled $662 million. The figure rose to $1.57 billion in 1973 and it may exceed $1.8 billion in 1974.

Along with this tremendous rise in imports for defense, there has been a sharp increase in imports for basic commodities. Inflation, worldwide and domestic, bit deeply into Israel's income. The cost of living rose some 26.4 percent this

last year-about three times the rate in the United States-and an additional 22 percent in the first five months of 1974. Israel must import much of her foodstuff. The tonnage of soybeans, wheat and food grains which Israel required in 

1972 cost $130 million. This year's estimated cost is $290 million. A few years ago, Israel paid about $25 million for wheat at P.L. 480 prices. This year a similar quantity will cost $80 million.

While the cost of imports rose sharply, Israel's exportable goods have not commanded a comparable increase. Israel's largest exports are citrus and polished diamonds and these have not yet risen in price as rapidly as foods and other staples. Tourism, a dollar earner, declined because of the war. Exports have also been hit by dislocations in Israel's economy. Many of Israel's factories have lost production because key manpower and vehicles have been on battle lines instead of production lines. Heavily taxed consumers cannot afford to buy many domestically manufactured products. Manpower must shift to defense oriented industries. The domestic difficulties have been compounded by a worldwide monetary uncertainty. Currency devaluations have hit exports. 

ISRAEL'S DEBT AND DEFICIT 

The high cost of defense, inflation, and lowered production have all combined to boost Israel's current account deficit which rose from $1.075 billion in 1972 to $2.475 billion in 1973, and which is expected to exceed $3.28 billion in 1974, but to drop back to $2.92 billion in 1975, assuming that there is peace and substantial increases in exports.

Aside from her mounting current account deficit, Israel has carried a heavy debt burden because over the years she has borrowed large sums to finance her development as well as to pay for her arms. 

Always concerned lest U.S. aid to Israel should provoke a counterproductive reaction in the Arab world, the Department of State was always reluctant to meet Israel's requests for arms. AID's records show that between fiscal 1946 and fiscal 1973, more than 90 percent of all military assistance was in the form of grants. The United States provided $58.4 billion in grant military aid to more than 70 countries but not a grant military dollar was allocated to Israel. The fact is that Israel never asked for military grants. She wanted to pay her way and she went into debt for her security. Even so, although the United States was providing arms to Saudi Arabia and Iraq in the 1950s, it never sold Israel any military equipment until 1962, and it was not until last October that our Government provided her with grant military assistance of any kind. 

Those who complain that America favored Israel over the Arab states should reflect on this history, particularly in the light of the fact that Israel's neighbors have been at war with her all through this period and have been equipped by all the great powers: England, France, the United States, the Soviet bloc and even, to some extent, by the Peoples Republic of China. 

"THE ARMS BALANCE IS SHIFTING AGAINST ISRAEL 

• • 99 The result has been a steadily mounting external debt. For many years, Israel's per capita external debt has been the highest in the world. (See table on following page.)

Despite her heavy war expenditures and her rising imports, Israel's foreign currency reserves rose in 1973 but that was an abnormal development because Israel went further into debt and because Jewish communities contributed large sums to assist her during the war crisis. These reserves, which stood at $1.7 billion at the end of 1973 have already dropped $350 million this year and the decline is expected to continue because of the mounting balance of payments deficit.

Israel economists predict that after utilizing all foreseeable sources of foreign exchange, Israel will still be short $587 million this year and $840 million in 1975. Accordingly, foreign exchange reserves will drop to $1.1 billion by the end of 1974-or only 17 percent of imports-and to a perilously low $270 million by the end of 1975-or a tiny four percent of imports, less than two weeks' require ments.

This is the somber prospect confronting Israel unless there is an increase in grant military or economic assistance as well as a substantial restoration of 

PL480 surplus commodities.

Like all Americans, we are keenly aware of opposition to foreign aid in this country which has been fed by our own inflation and our heavy tax burdens.

Our own citizens pay a heavy price for civic responsibilities, both in the areas of domestic and international concern, and we would hesitate to ask fellow Americans to contribute additional sums to assist Israel if the Israelis were not carrying such a tremendous burden to defend their survival.
