THE SHIFTING ARMS BALANCE 

The arms balance is tilting against Israel, partly because of the readiness of the Soviet Union to arm Egypt and Syria, partly because of mounting Arab oil wealth, partly because of the alarming arms race in the Persian Gulf. 

We should note that between October 22 and May 1, the Israelis lost 90 men on both the northern and southern fronts. Thus, the Israel death toll in this war exceeds 2,600. Drew Middleton, veteran New York Times military analyst, has pointed out on May 12 that more than 600 of them were officers, who fight in the front lines in the Israel army. He drew the conclusion that the military balance was shifting against Israel.

SOVIET AID TO THE ARABS 

There are conflicting estimates on the military strength of the Arab states when they launched their offensive, but all authorities agree that they had overwhelming superiority over Israel. They suffered heavy losses but the Soviets have more than replenished them.

Syria is believed to have lost at least 600 tanks during the October fighting but it has since received 1,000 from the Soviet Union. The New York Times reported on May 5 that Syria now has 1,590 tanks, many of them T-62s, the heaviest and most advanced Soviet battle tank. Cuban, North Korean and possibly East European crews and technicians are reported to be manning the tanks while new Syrian crews are being trained. Syria also has received 

MiG-21J improved fighters and Sukhoi-20 fighter bombers. 

President Assad asked Moscow for MiG-25 Foxbat high altitude fighters when he was there in April, and Syrian pilots are now training in the USSR to fly the MiG-23 Flogger fighter-bomber, the first line Soviet tactical aircraft. It was recently reported that 16 Floggers have arrived in Latakia, Syria—a dangerous escalation in the arms balance.

Egypt, which began the war with about 1,950 tanks, now has 2,445 according to the May 5 New York Times. These include about 700 T-62s Iraq has also received a number of these weapons, including Tu-22 supersonic medium range bombers.

Egypt has a Soviet-flown squadron of Foxbats flying reconnaissance missions far out of range over Israel. 

Egypt and Syria have received a wide variety of support equipment which even Warsaw Pact countries have not obtained. These include radars, electronics countermeasures equipment (ECM), automatic quad-mounted antiaircraft guns, bridging equipment and night fighting gear.

Scud 1b missiles-presently under Soviet control-are in Egypt and said to be in Syria. This missile has a 185 mile range, is capable of carrying a nuclear warhead and is a fearsome long-range bombardment system. Even with conventional warheads, the Scuds represent a quantum leap in the Arab offensive capacity.

It should be stressed that all the above military estimates are regarded as conservative.

ARAB AID 

The rich Arab states bankrolled the war. 

It is reported that Saudi Arabia and Kuwait donated $675 million to Egypt during the last year for arms and committed a smaller sum for economic aid to enable Egypt to buy food and subsidize officers' salaries.

Debt-ridden Egypt was suddenly able to pay cash for imports to avoid high interest rates and she stockpiled a two-month's supply of wheat. She normally imports 22 million tons a year. 

Qatar gave Egypt $50 million; Algeria sent Egypt two million tons of oil after the war, and Sadat told a German newspaper that Algeria paid $100 million for arms which Egypt received from the Russians. (Algeria did the same for Syria.) Abu Dhabi borrowed $100 million, reportedly for Egypt, in November. 

And in April the Lebanese press carried news of an arms transfer from Saudi Arabia.

Most Syrian defense financing came from Saudi Arabia. Estimates range between one-half billion and a billion dollars. After the war, Syria received $400 million in economic aid from Kuwait and $100 million from Saudi Arabia. Iraq recently announced that it would give Syria $50 million. After Assad's last visit to Moscow in April, Syrian analysts claimed that the Soviet Union would repair all damage to the Syrian economy, estimated at $1.8 billion. 

There is no doubt that Egypt and Syria could not have fought without substantial subsidies.

Production was slowed by the war in Egypt but not at the same rate as in Israel, where a much larger proportion of manpower and vehicles had to be diverted from production to defense; Egypt maintains a large standing army. 

U.S. AID TO EGYPT 

Naturally, our Committee has some reservations about our aid to Egypt and Jordan. We hope that the Administration is correct in the assumption that Sadat wants peace, that he is ready to reactivate civilian life in the Suez Canal area and that he wants to liberate himself from the Soviet mortgage. 

"SADAT MAY ATTEMPT TO RECEIVE U.S. ARMS FROM ARAB ALLIES . . ." 

But, having witnessed the futile and expensive efforts of former administrations to win President Nasser for the West, we are not convinced that our Government can prematurely enter into a partnership with the Soviet Union to revive the Egyptian economy and to raise Egyptian living standards, however desirable those objectives may be. There should be strong assurances, some genuine evidence, that Sadat is really ready to make peace. 

Thus, if the United States and other powers are to join forces to help Egypt open the Suez Canal, the very least Sadat could do to signal his sincerity is to announce his intention to respect the international character of that waterway, as well as the Straits of Tiran and Bab el Mandeb, and the obligation to keep them open to the shipping of all nations.

If the purpose of America's aid to Egypt, Saudi Arabia and Jordan was to procure their assent to disengagement agreements, it should be borne in mind that authoritarian regimes often have a short life expectancy. Experience has also taught that they are short on gratitude and long on appetite. 

U.S. ARMS FOR SADAT? 

Sadat has announced his readiness to turn to the West for arms and cease to be solely dependent on the Soviet Union. 

Obviously, it would take some years before he could free his armed forces from dependency on Soviet weapons. He is aware that the United States does not intend to abandon Israel but he has, nevertheless, suggested that an evenhanded United States might sell him the Tow anti-tank missile and the Maverick, the television-guided air-to-ground missiles which our Government made available to Israel. 

On June 19, the Defense Department announced that high-ranking military officers would soon go to Egypt for "friendly discussions in the context of the newly-established relations with Egypt."

Now that the United States is prepared to supply Egypt with a nuclear power plant, arms shipments may be next. However Secretary Kissinger said on June 

22 that the United States has no plans to sell weapons to Egypt or Syria. 

We do not believe that the American people would favor U.S. military supplies to Egypt or Syria just eight months after Egypt and Syria opened up a vicious war against Israel and before the consummation of a genuine peace. And we hope that the Administration does not intend to use any of the aid funds voted for Egypt to strengthen Egyptian military capacity.

12 

THIRD PARTY CONDUITS 

But Sadat may now attempt to secure American, French and British weapons from his wealthy Arab allies, which they are now buying in great quantity. And whether the American people approve or disapprove, there is really nothing to prevent Egypt from securing American weapons from other Arab states. Since they helped provide Egypt with the means to purchase Soviet weapons, they probably would not hesitate to transfer ownership of American weapons. 

The huge increase in the price of oil has made the Arab states in the Persian Gulf area a superb market for arms. Last year, the United States disclosed that it had offered Phantom jets to Saudi Arabia and other supersonic planes to Kuwait. State Department officials defended the proposed sales contending that the arms were intended to ensure a balance in the Persian Gulf area and that this region was not really involved in the Arab-Israeli conflict. It was argued that Saudi Arabia had, over the years, "stuck to the notion that the question of security in the Persian Gulf, the question of oil, ought not be related to the political question of the Arab-Israeli dispute." 

But just a month earlier, King Faisal of Saudi Arabia had already made it very clear to Aramco officials that he was prepared to use the oil weapon against the West on behalf of Egypt and Syria. There is no doubt that his alliance with 

Egypt was decisive in precipitating the October attack. 

At that time, Rep. Lee Hamilton, Chairman of the House Near East and South 

Asia Subcommittee, said that the United States Navy had a $600 million equipment and training program in Saudi Arabia and that we would sell her an additional $1 billion in arms, in addition to $600 million worth to Kuwait. 

Congressmen were quick to question whether the Persian Gulf states might transfer their planes to Egypt. On June 6, 1973, the Department of State told 

Congress that "none of the equipment can be transferred to any third party without prior approval of the United States." But later, in his testimony, Under 

Secretary of State Joseph J. Sisco said frankly, "I don't think anybody can give a guarantee.” However, he felt that Saudi Arabia "would view the obligation seriously."

As the October war neared, there were reports that Libya had sent its Mirage planes to Egypt. And other French planes were used against the Israelis, who found it difficult to distinguish their own Mirage planes from those flying for Egypt.

As Western nations competed for Arab markets, Arab leaders proclaimed their freedom from restrictions. Last July, Kuwait's Defense and Interior Minister 

Sheikh Sa'ad Abdulla Al-Salem pledged to refuse any arms contract which included restrictions on their use. "We are free to use our arms when and where we want," he said.

When Sadat proclaimed that he no longer wished to be dependent on Soviet weapons and it is reported that the Russians are slowing down their suppliesthere were reports that other Arab states would come to Sadat's aid. 

The New York Times, on April 28, quoted "qualified Arab sources to the effect that, in the interim, Egypt might borrow non-Soviet equipment from other Arab states." 

On April 18, The Times reported from Cairo that: "officials of Saudi Arabia and Kuwait have reportedly said that they are free to put their new weapons at the disposal of other Arab countries. They have been quoted in the Arab press as having said that the manufacturing countries had placed no restrictions on the use of these weapons." 

And Stanley Karnow wrote in The New Republic on March 23: 

"Pentagon spokesmen are . . vague. when asked whether the Persian 

Gulf recipients of U.S. arms may be illegally transferring them elsewhere. 'We consider it unlikely, but we can offer no guarantee' is their routine reply." 

"ARAB RULERS SQUANDER BILLIONS TO SUBSIDIZE WAR. 

99 On June 8, the United States and Saudi Arabia reached a new agreement for economic cooperation and the sale of American weapons. The Saudis have ordered 

200 F-5Es this year. They may purchase A-7 Corsairs and F-14 Tomcats. Saudi

Arabia's national guard, which is established to preserve domestic peace and to guard petroleum installations, is scheduled to receive M-60 battle tanks. The 

Saudis already have the Hawk missile. Americans are training the Saudi na-

tional guard, helping to build a navy of 19 ships as well as ports. Ironically, the aid program includes a gift of U.S. training to Saudi Arabia. 

Saudi Arabia's oil revenues are expected to rise to $17.3 billion this year, as compared with $4.9 billion in 1973 The Economist estimated on May 4. There are reports that it will spend more than a billion on American arms, but this is unconfirmed because the information is classified. 

Saudi Arabia is also negotiating to buy French and British tanks. It is buying weapons from France: 38 Mirage-3 jets, MX-30 tanks, machine guns and missiles. 

Last year, Britain negotiated a five-year $600 million contract with Saudi Arabia for aeronautical equipment and has some deals with the United Arab Emirates. 

Tiny Kuwait, which has always lived in fear of Iraq, has also been in the market for arms. France has reached a deal to sell her 17 Mirage F-1 fighter planes, and Kuwait Defense Minister Sheikh Sa'ad Abdulla Al-Salem claims that France has placed no restrictions on Kuwait's use of the equipment. And 

Kuwait may buy F-4 Phantoms from the United States and Jaguar fighter bombers from the British. France has also sold 14 Mirage jets to Abu Dhabi, which has no pilots; it will borrow some from Pakistan. 

The Economist of April 27 noted that France is arranging to sell more than $150 million of advanced equipment to Arab states. 

The United States is also enlarging its arms sales to two of Israel's neighbors, Jordan and Lebanon.

Jordan, which has received American tanks and planes in the past, is getting the Tow anti-tank missile, which is better-although much more expensivethan the Soviet Sagger missile. (It arrived in Israel after the war ended.) 

Jordan wants the Hawk anti-aircraft missile, but this would be an immediate threat to Israel aircraft flying in Israel's confined air space and Israel has objected. 

And the United States has offered two squadrons of A-4 Skyhawk jet fighters to Lebanon to replace 10 Mirage fighters. The United States has provided the 

Lebanese army with M-16 automatic rifles. 

In the Persian Gulf, the Russians have been concentrating their attention on Iraq, which has nationalized oil and which is in a never-ending battle with Iran over access to the Persian Gulf. It is estimated the Russians have sold 

Iraq arms worth a billion dollars. The Russians also have a military interest in South Yemen and they compete with the Chinese in supporting the rebellion in Dhofar. It has also been reported that Libya will enter into a new arms deal with the Soviet Union. 

All this must surely be of some concern to Israel. Her danger grows because it is obvious that the great powers, anxious to share in Persian Gulf riches, no longer seem to care about slowing the arms race or restricting the proliferation of weapons. Supersonic planes in the Persian Gulf area, like the F-4 Phantoms, are within range of Israel or could be transferred to Israel's hostile neighbors. 

Arab countries which have hitherto held aloof from the war against Israel may be tempted and will have little excuse to refuse to enter it if they have the power.

There are tremendous dangers. Lethal weapons are now being amassed by oil-producing nations which demonstrated their propensity for blackmail and their massive irresponsibility when they wielded the oil weapon in their attempt to hijack the world, economically and diplomatically, just a few months ago. 

In an editorial on Feb. 16, The Washington Post declared that: "never in history have arms been amassed at such a rate volatile region." 

It observed that: "new weapons create their own pressures to use them. "9 in such a "The $2.2 billion for arms which the United States pledged to Israel after the war is a large sum, but it will be overwhelmed by the arms now coming to Egypt and Syria and their Arab allies." 

And the editorial concluded: 

"It becomes all the more necessary for the United States to leave no doubt that its commitment to Israel's security is firm." 

AID FOR UNRWA 

In addition to the funds proposed in the AID program for Jordan and Egypt, the Administration requests a $23.2 million contribution to the United Nations 

Relief and Works Agency (UNRWA). We have never opposed this gift. But it

L SE TL is appropriate to point out that the United States is once again carrying a major portion of the burden.

In 1959, Secretary General Dag Hammarskjold optimistically told the UN that the Arab refugees could be integrated in the Middle East and that they should be regarded not as a liability but as an asset for the future. His study showed that if $1.5 billion to $2 billion in capital could be invested in the area, this sum, together with the capital likely to become available from future oil revenues, could create a demand sufficient to absorb the refugees. 

But, regrettably, the Arab leaders, who were primarily responsible for the displacement of the refugees in the war against partition in 1948, rejected the Hammarskjold view because it implied resettlement in Arab countries. They ignored the humanitarian needs of the refugees. They preferred to turn the UNRWA camps into military training camps and bases for terrorist warfare. 

Despite their rapidly expanding oil wealth, the Arab states have been miserly in their contributions to UNRWA. The record shows that in the 23 years down to 

June 30, 1973, all Arab states donated just $26 million to UNRWA, a minuscule sum when compared with the $549 million donated by the United States and the $849 million contributed by all sources. 

Arab rulers are ready to squander billions to subsidize a war against a hated Israel. But they have never been willing to help the Arab refugees to gain a new life in lands where there is room and opportunity for them. This refusal of the 

Arab states to recognize their responsibility for a tragedy which they created and which they have needlessly prolonged has brought misery, deprivation and violence to many thousands of men, women and children, Arabs and Jews, who might have shared life rather than death.

The indifference to the fate of others is not limited to disregard for the Palestinian Arabs. The record shows that the wealthy Arab states have been similarly callous toward the appeals of UNICEF and the calls for food for the starving millions in drought-stricken African Sahel, whose plight has been further aggravated by the inflated costs of oil-based fertilizers and fuels. 

In an article in The New York Times on April 4, Chester L. Cooper pointed out that approximately $350 million in aid had been contributed to help the stricken countries of Senegal, Mali, Mauritania, Chad, Niger and Upper Volta, The United 

States gave more than a third, the EEC contributed slightly less than a third. 

As compared with these generous contributions, Libya—a rich neighbor of the Africans—contributed a nominal $760,000, Kuwait $300,000 and Saudi Arabia not a dollar in 1973 and only $2 million this year.

An article by Jim Hoagland in The Washington Post of March 15 points out that UNICEF spends about $5.4 million a year in 16 Middle East countries. Arab countries and Iran contributed only $871,000 to UNICEF: Saudi Arabia, where 

UNICEF spends $500,000, contributed a paltry $30,000. 

When will the civilized world begin to call the rolls of those who vote for food and medicine for people and those who are for weapons to destroy them; of those who vote for peace and those who vote for war?

IMPACT OF THE PROGRAM 

We offer some comment on the psychological impact of this aid program. 

In 1971, 1972 and 1973, Congress voted $300 million in military credits and $50 million in supporting assistance for Israel. Now the Administration proposes to revert to that pre-war figure, even as it greatly expands assistance to those who attacked Israel.

To many people in the Middle East, and perhaps to people in Israel itself, this may suggest a retreat in American policy, I cannot believe that the Administration is diminishing its support for Israel, but Arab leaders have made extravagant claims to the effect that the United States now supports their views on the future of the Middle East. 99 

"AMERICANS RECOGNIZE JUSTICE AND URGENCY OF ISRAEL'S CAUSE 

Many of you who have been to Israel since the war have been startled by the mood in that country. Israel's people won a military victory after initial reverses but they were abandoned by many of the governments of the free world and the Third World.

As long as they were on the defensive, no one moved to stop the war. When victory was within Israel's grasp, the great powers interceded to save Egypt and 

Syria from a crushing defeat.

We have not criticized the United States for this action and for the policy it pursued during that period. On the one hand, our country maintained the balance of strength but it also sought to maintain the balance of influence. As a result, the United States has accumulated a substantial reservoir of goodwill in the Arab world. 

If the effect of this new aid bill is to encourage the Arabs into believing that the United States is abandoning Israel in a campaign to win the Arabs away from the Soviet Union, then there is scant hope for the attainment of an Arab-Israel peace. If Israel is to win the peace, she must be strong and the 

United States must continue to be clear and steadfast in her support. 

AID FOR SOVIET JEWS 

Despite and throughout the war, Israel kept her doors open to all Jews in need of sanctuary, in fidelity to her highest purposes. In 1973, Israel received 

54,700 immigrants, most of them from the Soviet Union, at an estimated resettlement cost of $550 million. This epic achievement during a period when the country was threatened with destruction was made possible by a partnership of Israel and Jewish communities throughout the world. The struggle of Soviet 

Jews to win freedom has aroused the conscience of the world, and we are most grateful that the United States Congress has generously responded to their appeal.

We note that the Senate has approved a $50 million authorization to continue this effort as an amendment to the Department of State's 1975 budget and we hope that your Committee will approve this authorization.

CONCLUSION 

In conclusion, we respectfully urge you: To approve an appropriation of $250 million in supporting assistance for Israel in fiscal 1975. To provide that $100 million of the $300 million requested by the Administration for military credits to Israel be appropriated in the form of grants-the remaining $200 million in the form of credits.

We believe that these appropriations will help to stabilize Israel's economy, to strengthen her defense capacity and preserve a balance which will encourage negotiations for peace. The danger of a military imbalance is growing in the 

Middle East and with it the threat of another disastrous war. 

We are keenly aware of the opposition to foreign aid expressed by many Americans in their communications to Congress, but we do not hesitate to advance our requests, for we believe that aid to Israel is in the national interest, both on strategic and on moral grounds, and that this view has been registered emphatically by public opinion in this country. Americans have recognized the justice and the urgency of Israel's cause-in public opinion polls, in editorials, in the media and finally, and most important, in the roll calls of the Congress, which truly reflected the overwhelming support of the American people. We hope this support will continue.

IMBALANCE IN MIDDLE EAST AID QUESTIONED Chairman MORGAN. Mr. Frelinghuysen. 

Mr. FRELINGHUYSEN.  

I am glad to see you here, Mr. Kenen. As the chairman has said, you are a friend of many members of this committee. You have given us a very clear picture of the enormous strain on the Israeli economy because of hostilities and the continuing uncertainty. 

The one message that comes clearly across to me is the necessity for a settlement. There are too many uncertainties for a small country to sustain this kind of strain over an indefinite period so I surely hope that there will be progress, perhaps on a bilateral basis, as the Israelis are now suggesting between Israel and Egypt and presumably not in the Geneva forum. As the Israelis have also pointed out, it might not be easy to come to make progress in that particular forum. 

You mentioned the anomalous disparity-I think that was your expression of the amount proposed for Israel in this bill, and the amount that might be made available to Israel's neighbors. I suppose if we take into account the very substantial amount of grants and the additional $500 million which the President has just made available in the form of grant assistance to Israel, then balance is quite sharply corrected. In other words, if we compare what is being made available and what has been made available to Israel since the recent hostilities with what is being offered for her neighbors, I don't believe it is quite fair to suggest that a serious imbalance is being proposed. 

Mr. KENEN. My point about that, is the fact that the $2.2 billion voted last year was a result of a war in which Israel lost many people and in which her economy suffered a devastating blow. The Israel arms procurement request exceeded the $2.2 billion soon after, within months or within weeks after the war began. 

I did not overlook the $2.2 billion in my statement. I am quite aware of the fact that that money was voted and we are grateful to the Congress for its action. I did make the point that the figures which I have projected here are based on the assumption that the $1.5 billion of the $2.2 billion would be in grant. 

LONG-TERM AID NEEDS OF ISRAEL 

Mr. FRELINGHUYSEN. As the chairman has pointed out, the figures that are being proposed in this bill are a drop in the bucket compared to what Israel's actual needs may be from this country. It may not be a happy coincidence that we can't avoid thinking about the larger sum that is being reported in the press that Israel is going to need from us on a long-term basis. A number of members of this committee did meet with the Defense Minister of Israel and got an indication of the nature of the problem and the fact that there is a long-term need. I

don't think any of us are going to forget the importance of a strong Israel in this kind of a situation, and I hope we can be helpful in bringing about a settlement because it seems to me that there is no reasonable alternative. I hope we respond sympathetically to your suggestions. 

Mr. KENEN. Thank you, sir.

[The information requested was subsequently supplied as follows:]

AMERICAN ISRAEL PUBLIC AFFAIRS COMMITTEE, 

Washington, D.C., July 30, 1974.

Hon. THOMAS E. MORGAN, Chairman, House Foreign Affairs Committee, House of Representatives, Wash ington, D.C. 

DEAR MR. MORGAN: When I testified before your Committee, Representative

Lester Wolff asked me for information on Soviet bloc aid to the Arab states. 

The figures are not easily obtainable but I am offering the best estimates available to us.

The aid to the Arab states from the Soviet bloc for the 19 years from 1955 to July 1, 1974 is about $20 billion. Of this sum, $15.5 billion was for military aid, already supplied, and $5.5 billion for economic assistance committed. The accompanying table shows the breakdown of military and economic aid for the major countries.

The Soviet Union provides assistance on very generous terms. Much of the military assistance has been given as a grant. Loans to the Arab states are repay-

able within 10 to 12 years in local currency and at low interest rates; not more than 2 percent in the case of military assistance; 22 percent in the case of economic assistance. Often, loans appear to be forgiven, as in the case of Syria's debts.

Weapons purchased by Israel from the West cost much more than those furnished by the Soviet bloc to the Arab states. For example: A Mig-21 costs approximately $1.25 million as compared with $3 million for a Mirage; $2.5 million for a Skyhawk and $4.5 million for a Phantom. A Soviet tank costs about $100,000 while an American tank may cost more than $300,000. 

The confrontation Arab states have been able to obtain weapons from the West as well as from the Soviet Union. For example: The Mirage planes which 

Libya purchased from France and transferred to Egypt. 

I hope this information is responsive to your request. Sincerely, Enclosure.

I. L. KENEN, Chairman.

NUCLEAR PLANTS TO EGYPT AND ISRAEL 

Mr. BINGHAM. Mr. Kenen, your statement is very complete and very clear and helpful and I don't propose to ask you any questions about what is in the statement. I would like to ask you about your reaction to the proposed nuclear plants that the President has offered to Egypt and to Israel.

Mr. KENEN. Well, I am speaking here for many organizations and if I go over the documents that some of these organizations have published I find a great deal of concern about these proposals. I am not prepared to make a statement at this moment on behalf of the American Israel Public Affairs Committee or the organizations that have authorized me to speak for them.

As a matter of curiosity I did send out a mailgram to many of the leaders who are on our executive committee and national council and I find that the percentage is about 3 to 1 in opposition, but a good deal of it is qualified. It has to do with concerns which may be allayed by testimony showing that there could be utter and complete safeguards against the diversion of the plutonium. may sound quixotic and utopian but I would like to see a nuclear reactor serve both Egypt and Israel following a peace treaty and policed by both. Now that may not be so quixotic. I would think, however, that the proposals that were made could very well have waited until we were further along the road to peace. This is my real concern. 

We may have been premature, but this is a personal view. 

JOINT ATOMIC ENERGY COMMITTEE ACTION 

Mr. BINGHAM. I think many Members of Congress share your concern, particularly about the timing and concern that the safeguards may not be adequate. As you may have noted, the Joint Committee on 

Atomic Energy has reported out legislation that would require congressional approval of any agreements of this kind. I have felt that, in addition to the Joint Committee on Atomic Energy receiving the reports and making recommendations, any such legislation should require that the Foreign Affairs Committee of the House and the Foreign Relations Committee of the Senate should also receive the reports and should also be asked to make recommendations on the agreements to

their respective full bodies. Would you care to make a comment on that aspect of the matter?

Mr. KENEN. It seems to me that this is more than a problem involving scientific questions and that it certainly has tremendous political and foreign policy implications. If I were a member of the Foreign 

Affairs Committee, I would certainly concur in your view that this is a matter requiring the fullest discussion. I think the major objection to what has happened is that it came very suddenly, and some people think prematurely, without an understanding by the general public, and the media of what was proposed. I would like to see the most exhaustive consideration of these proposals before we go forward. 

Mr. BINGHAM. Well, I certainly agree that the foreign policy implications of any of these agreements are tremendous and that is why it seems to me that any legislation requiring congressional approval should make certain that the recommendations of the two committees concerned with foreign policy be involved. 

I think that is all. Thank you very much.

ARMING BOTH SIDES IN MIDDLE EAST Mr. DU PONT.  

Just two questions, Mr. Kenen. The next witness that is going to follow you this morning is Mr. Snyder, the executive secretary of the 

Friends Committee on National Legislation.

Chairman MORGAN. Senator Tydings will be the next witness and

Friends Committee on National Legislation and in his material which we have at our desks here he comments that we seem to be bent in the Middle East on arming both sides and suggests that maybe the better solution would be to arm neither. I wonder what your reaction to that is.

Mr. KENEN. Well, the world being what it is, I cannot believe that this is a practical proposal. Indirectly, we are arming both sides because we are providing arms to Saudi Arabia and Kuwait, and these countries, as I point out in my memorandum, really cannot be prevented from transferring them if they wish to. I think it is much too utopian to suggest that we could have an end to the arming of both sides. We can't possibly think in terms of an evenhanded policy on arms to both or arms to none so long as the Soviet Union uses weapons as it does cynically and dangerously in order to propagate its own position in the area. 

Mr. DU PONT. And you don't think there is any chance that we might be using arms cynically to propagate our interests in the area? 

Mr. KENEN. Well, I would hesitate to comment on it but we are now sending very substantial weaponry to the Persian Gulf countries, and I think this is one of the most frightening developments. I would like to see a program of energy independence in this country so that we would not have to scramble for aid by squandering weapons. 

Mr. DU PONT. It also seems to me, as you point out, in the arms we are sending to Arab countries that we are sending arms to countries that can have the resources to really provide all their own armaments if they choose.

MORGAN, FRIENDS COMMITTEE ON NATIONAL LEGISLATION, Chairman, House Foreign Affairs Committee, House of Representatives, Washington, D.C. 

Washington. D.C., July 10, 1974. 

DEAR DR. MORGAN: During the July second hearing there was an exchange between Rep. duPont and a witness, Mr. I. L. Kenan, concerning a brief statement in my testimony about the Middle East. 

Since my statement concentrated on military aid in general and aid to Indochina specifically, and since there was no opportunity for questions because of a quorum call, I would appreciate an opportunity to state briefly our position on the Administration's proposed aid to the Middle Eastern nations. It is as follows: 

1. ECONOMIC AID 

We support proposals for economic assistance, especially when aid is used to resolve refugee problems and rebuilt war-damaged facilities, help solve food, nutrition, and population problems, and reach the neediest people in the general population.

We especially hope U.S. economic aid to the Mid-East can be used through international channels to foster cooperation and mutually beneficial projects of river development, transportation, etc. 

2. MILITARY AID 

We oppose U.S. military aid to any country, especially in the Mid-East tinderbox where we arm both sides. We support an area-wide arms embargo. While there may be some exceptions, the record of history shows that arms races end in war more often than in peace. The Middle East has had its share of wars in the last two decades. Our information is that these amounts have been sent or are requested for the Middle East: 

Israel, $300 mil. credit sales (proposed FY 1975).

Jordan, $94 mil. MAP grants-$30 mil. credit sales (proposed FY 1975). 

Lebanon, $10 mil. credits (proposed FY 1975). 

Iran, $2,000 mil. cash sales (FY 1973). 

Saudi Arabia, $180 mil. cash sales (FY 1973). 

3. NUCLEAR ENERGY 

(a) We have strong reservations about the growing use of nuclear fuels for power, both in this country and abroad. The dangers arising from accidents and diversion to unlawful or terrorist purposes are increasing. The crucial problem of disposal of plutonium has not been solved and until it is this program should not be expanded. (b) We oppose the transfer of any U.S. nuclear material or know-how to any country which has not ratified both the limited test ban and the non-proliferation treaties. Our information indicates these countries have taken the indicated action:

What would you think about leaving Israel's at $50 million and cutting Egypt and the others back to $50 million?

Mr. DU PONT. I understand. 

Mr. KENEN. The point is that the Israelis requested that figure but they failed to copyright it, and after they presented it the administration then picked it up and offered it to Egypt. I point this out merely as an interesting coincidence. I am not suggesting that we raise aid to Israel because we have to keep up with aid to Egypt. I am suggesting that the aid for Israel is necessary on its merits because of Israel's tremendous debt and its inability to balance its current account at this time.

IMMIGRANTS TO ISRAEL FROM THE SOVIET UNION 

Mr. YATRON. Mr. Kenen, in 1973, you say in your report, Israel received 54,700 immigrants, most of them from the Soviet Union. What are your projections for 1974 and has this picture improved any or would you care to comment about the Soviet Jews coming to Israel? 

Mr. KENEN. The figure went down substantially during this year and nobody knows why. Whether this was a deliberate Soviet policy or whether it was because of bureaucracy, we don't know, but there is the hope that, as a result of the remarkable support that the Congress of the United States has registered on this issue, the Soviet Union may finally come to the conclusion that it should adopt a more liberal policy. During the last 48 hours we have suddenly seen the announcement that the foremost Jewish scientist in the Soviet Union will be released; he will be allowed to go the end of next year, his son immediately. They are topflight scientists.

We also have the case of the Panovs. So it is just possible that as a result of the current talks the Soviet Union may restore the figure and may go even higher; some people talk about 45,000 or 50,000. 

Mr. YATRON. I am very happy to see that. 

Mr. KENEN. I hope that is true.

KENEN: NO OPPOSITION TO AID TO EGYPT 

Mr. WHALEN. Thank you, Mr. Chairman.

Mr. Kenen, on pages 4 and 5 of your memorandum you indicate some concern about the aid which has been asked for Egypt. As I understand it, however, the organizations which you represent do not oppose this aid, is that correct?

Mr. KENEN. That is right. We are not coming to oppose aid to 

Egypt. But we wish we were further along toward peace. As we do

indicate in this memorandum, in the light of the position that Congress has taken from way back to 1960, there ought to be some signal or affirmation of Egypt's readiness to go along with respect to freedom of navigation in the Suez Canal.

Our country helped to open up the Suez Canal in 1957 with the understanding that it would be open to all shipping. President Eisenhower, on February 20, 1957, said the canal will be open to all and then in 1960 there was the amendment to the preamble of the foreign aid program calling for it, too. We would like to see further progress although there is an understanding in the disengagement agreements that there will be some movement along these lines once the canal is opened, but I would like to see that issue resolved in advance of a final settlement. 

Mr. WHALEN. Would you suggest that we might incorporate language to that effect in this bill?

Mr. KENEN. The Congress has done that in the past and it could either be as a statement in the bill or it could be a recommendation in your report.

THE "SPECIAL REQUIREMENTS FUND" 

Mr. WHALEN. There is also in the bill the so-called Special Requirements Fund, $100 million. Your memorandum does not refer to this. 

As you know, Secretary Sisco indicated that in all probability these funds, or at least part of them, will go to Syria. The organizations which you represent, do they have any position on this particular portion of the bill?

Mr. KENEN. This memorandum which was drafted in May and submitted to a Senate committee preceded the administrations acknowledgement that some of these funds might go to Syria. I must say as emphatically as I can that the organizations we represent may favor economic aid to help these countries raise living standards for reclamation and reconstruction, following the war but we are strongly opposed to a policy of arms for Egypt or arms for Syria at this time. 

We think this would be a very great mistake in advance of a settlement. Once we get the kind of settlement that Mr. Frelinghuysen indicated, we would hope that all of these astronomical figures that have been projected in the press and in my own memorandum, would decline and perhaps we might then reach the stage that Mr. du Pont talked about, where we could stop all arms to both sides. 

AID TO PALESTINIAN ARABS 

Mr. WHALEN. Have you had any thoughts about incorporating funds in this bill for the Palestinian refugees? 

Mr. KENEN. There is a sum of $23.2 million for UNRWA.

We have never opposed economic aid to help the Palestinian Arab refugees in the camps, but I do suggest to you that a long time ago we should have been taking the position that our funds would be dedicated to resettlement projects rather than merely to maintain the status quo indefinitely.

There was the amendment you adopted in 1966 that said, let's not use any of the American funds to support terrorists or guerrilla fighters in the camps. If UNRWA had called upon the United Nations

General Assembly for the establishment of a UNEF to guard the camps and to prevent the infiltration of terrorist groups, we would have been a lot better off in the Middle East today and many, many lives would have been saved.

Mr. WHALEN.  

Thank you, Mr. Kenen.

INCREASING EGYPTIAN STANDARDS OF LIVING Mr. BIESTER. Thank you, Mr. Chairman. 

I have just one question, Mr. Kenen. 

I want to thank the witness for appearing and being here with us. 

My question goes to the matter raised on page 5 of your report. In dealing with the usefulness of increasing the standard of living and the economy and strengthening the economy of Egypt, it has seemed to me that one of the circumstances which may tend to lead toward a more peaceful climate in most regions of the world is for those who form the populace to have a higher stake in peace. 

Where people are poor they have, I suspect, a less high stake in peace than when they feel better off. When an economy is moving forward, there is more reluctance to divert it into sterile military areas. 

I am wondering whether it isn't to the long-term advantage of all the nations in the region for the economy in the region as a general proposition to be raised and living standards to be raised. 

Mr. KENEN. Well, I would agree with you 100 percent. The fact is that one of the proposals with respect to the opening up of the Suez area was advocated a long time ago by Mr. Rabin when he was the 

Ambassador here in Washington. I am not speaking for the Israeli 

Government but one of their reasons for agreeing to an interim arrangement involving their withdrawal from the Suez Canal before the October war was that if the Suez area were reactivated those people would have a stake in maintaining the status quo and preventing the eruption of another conflict.

Undoubtedly this whole area would have been much better off if funds which had been devoted to war could have been used for the resettlement of Palestinian Arab refugees in Arab countries. Mr. Haminarskjold, the U.N. Secretary General, recommended back in 1959 that with increasing oil revenues and investments of $1.5 billion and $2 billion, the Arab refugees could be resettled in all of the Arab countries, which have vast areas and the capacity to put people to work.

Mr. KENEN. I beg your pardon?

Mr. BIESTER. In other words, it is a limited admonition.

Mr. KENEN. Either his intentions or his durability. There is the possibility that you could have another regime in Egypt and I wish we were further along towards the settlement. If I were voting in your committee, I would not vote against the $250 million for Egypt.

Mr. GILMAN. And that Israel's immediate arms procurement request presently exceeds $3 billion? 

Mr. KENEN. That is right.

Mr. GILMAN. Actually then, Mr. Kenen, the $2.2 billion program has been fully committed and expended, isn't that correct? 

Mr. KENEN. Yes.

Mr. GILMAN. And the $250 million that we are now talking about is needed to stabilize the economy and to help bolster perspective defense?

Mr. KENEN. And to prevent a very large shortfall in 1974 in Israel's current account. 

Mr. GILMAN. Thank you.

THE PROBLEM OF TERRORISM Mr. LAGOMARSINO.  

Mr. Kenen, when I walked into the room you were speaking about terrorism in Lebanon. I didn't catch all that you said. You mentioned the United Nations, and again I didn't hear that. I wonder if you could tell me briefly what the situation as you see it is now with regard to the United Nations, the position of Israel and the problem with the terrorists. I know that is a big order but I think it is very important.

Mr. KENEN. Well, the point that I was making earlier was that under the armistice agreements negotiated in 1949, Lebanon, Egypt, Jordan and Syria undertook to bar the use of their territory by the paramilitary forces preparing to cross into Israel. These agreements were made in the negotiation with the Israelies and they were not kept so far as Lebanon was concerned, presumably because Lebanon did not have the power to restrict the movements of the terrorists. 

The regrettable fact which I later referred to was that, since this was a U.N. supported operation, the United Nations could have intervened with some kind of force to protect the UNRWA camps from the infiltration of terrorist organizations and the mobilization of a guerrilla war against Israel. 

Now I believe also that the United Nations has failed to distinguish between aggressor and victim. There never has been a resolution in the United Nations Security Council censuring an outrage like the Olympic games, Maalot, Kiryat Shemona. None of these have ever been referred to explicitly in the U.N. resolution denouncing the terror, but inevitably the United Nations has always come back to censure Israel for its replies, and this has to some extent, I suspect, encouraged the Arabs to maintain the paramilitary forces. 

THE UNITED NATIONS AND TERRORISM 

Mr. LAGOMARSINO. As you understand it is that the same situation now prevailing in the United Nations with regard to terrorism? 

Mr. KENEN. Well, there is not the slightest chance of a resolution condemning the terrorist groups at the United Nations because there is a Soviet veto to prevent it. The Security Council includes many members who don't even have diplomatic relations with Israel at this stage.

Now I happen to be a proponent of the United Nations. I was at the 

San Francisco Conference in 1945 and I believe in it, I believe in col-

i lective security, but I abhor the way in which the United Nations has failed to discharge its responsibilities in this respect. 

Mr. LAGOMARSINO. To your knowledge is there any prospect for assistance to Israel from any other nation at the present time? 

Mr. KENEN. From any other nation? Israel has been acquiring most of its defense imports-95 percent-from this country. I assume there could be credits from other countries. I cannot conceive of grants from other countries. 

Mr. LAGOMARSINO. But there could be credit? 

Mr. KENEN. I would assume so; yes.

POSITION OF ISRAEL'S DEFENSE MINISTER Mr. LAGOMARSINO. When some of us spoke to the Defense Minister a week or so ago, we asked him about economic aid; although obviously he was not in a position to say yes or no, at least to me and to some of us, it seemed that he was much more concerned, greatly more concerned, about military aid than he was about economic aid. My impression is that he thought that Israel could get by economically but that the real need for the next 10 years, as you pointed out yourself, was for military aid to keep up with what he expected the Russians were going to do in that area.

Mr. KENEN. And because of the increasing costs and sophistication. 

Mr. LAGOMARSINO. That is right.

When Secretary of State Kissinger was before this committee several weeks ago he made some comments about the role, or I guess it would be more accurate to say the non-role of Russia with regard to Syria during the negotiations between Israel and Syria with regard to the border, and I gathered from what he said that Russia, while not exactly encouraging what happened, did not intervene and try to prevent it which he said they easily could have done. Do you have any comments on that?

Mr. KENEN. I think there were reports that the Soviet Union during the Kissinger shuttle was encouraging the Syrians not to accept the proposals that the United States was advancing. Now they may have moderated their position and the negotiations continued because of the pressures of the other Arab states on Syria to go along in order to prevent Egypt's isolation.

There is no doubt in our judgment that the Soviet Union has done everything possible to try to maintain its hold in Syria at this time and it recently did send MIG 23's to Syria and it put the SCUD missiles into Syria just before the war or during the war. Their aid continues to Syria. I don't believe we have disengaged Syria from the Soviet Union as much as we might have liked to. 

EGYPT AND THE SOVIET UNION 

Mr. LAGOMARSINO. The Defense Minister seemed to think that while 

Russia is not involved with Egypt at the present time, that he does not expect that the situation will last very long, that he expects that it will be resolved.

Mr. KENEN. The notion that Egypt would turn away from the country which has provided it with all the arms in the past and a

great deal of economic aid, is unrealistic. Just 2 weeks before the nuclear agreements were announced, there was a mission from Egypt to the Soviet Union inquiring whether the Soviet Union would provide nuclear reactors and there were agreements on new electricity projects. 

Mr. Buchanan.

UNITED STATES: KEEPER OF MIDDLE EAST BALANCE Mr. BUCHANAN.  

First, let me commend you on your usual and very able performance here and your good testimony.

Second, is it not the case that we are the only nation that can and will provide the balance that is needed on the Israeli side? 

Mr. KENEN. I think that is true not only because America is a strong Nation but also because of the long relationship between America and Israel and the community of interests and ideals between the two peoples. Quite apart from that, no other nation is ready, as the United States is, to reject the pressures which may come from the Arab world. 

Mr. BUCHANAN. Now for years before this committee and our Near

East Subcommittee witnesses have been telling us we needed to establish a balanced policy in the Middle East. It has been my feeling that we have always had a balanced policy. It would appear to me the fact that the Arab world as well as Israel turned to us in the negotiation toward peace is some indication that we have some credibility on both sides. 

Mr. KENEN. Well, if you were to go over the aid figures, as you probably have over the years, you would see that we have for many, many years provided the Arab states with substantial aid. We provided them with grant military aid long before we provided Israel with any military aid.

We provided Saudi Arabia and Iraq with military aid back in the fifties. We never provided Israel with a sophisticated weapon until 

1962. So anybody who argues that we may have favored Israel over the Arab states during this period is really not cognizant of the facts. 

I think it has been a policy that sought the favor and the friendship of both sides. I don't think we have ever given the Arabs any real reason to believe we have discriminated against them during this period. During the war in October there is no doubt that American policy did save the Arab states, Egypt, and Syria, from what would have been a devastating defeat because, as the war was coming to an end, Israel was on the offensive. 

I have never criticized Dr. Kissinger for this position. On the one hand, he maintained the balance of military strength so far as Israel was concerned, coming to Israel's support. On the other hand, he maintained the balance of influence with the Arab world. So just as you have said, the Arabs turned to the United States because they knew this was the one country that could talk to both. 

STRENGTHENING MODERATE ARABS IN MIDDLE EAST 

Mr. BUCHANAN. Just one thing. You may not wish to comment, but it would appear to me that by strengthening the more moderate forces

among Israel's Arab nations that our country can continue to be a force for peace in this way just as we must, in my judgment, give the assistance that is adequate and necessary on the Israeli side. 

Mr. KENEN. I think it would be a disaster if we had a situation where the United States had only one friend in the Middle East, Israel, and Israel was isolated and we had extreme polarization.

STATEMENT OF HON. JOSEPH D. TYDINGS, FORMER U.S. SENATOR, ON BEHALF OF HON. WILLIAM H. DRAPER, JR., HONORARY CHAIRMAN, POPULATION CRISIS COMMITTEE 

Mr. TYDINGS. Thank you very much, Mr. Chairman.

Gentlemen of the House Foreign Affairs Committee, I am delighted to be here, in a sense pinch-hitting for Bill Draper who is the "first string" in the world population effort. He is in Japan raising money, hopefully, for the United Nations Fund for Population Activities and the International Planned Parenthood Federation, so I am here to deliver his testimony.

If the chairman would so permit, I would ask that General Draper's testimony be now included in the record in its entirety as though read by me. 

Chairman MORGAN. Without objection, it is so ordered. 

[The prepared statement follows:] STATEMENT OF HON. WILLIAM H. DRAPER, JR., HONORARY CHAIRMAN, POPULATION CRISIS COMMITTEE Mr. Chairman and Members of the House Foreign Affairs Committee: For nearly 10 years I have had the honor of appearing almost annually before your Committee. Throughout that time I have been calling attention to the serious potential threat that too rapidly growing population in the developing countries poses to them and to the entire world, including our own country. 

During the past year or two that potential threat has become a present menace. 

World population growth has outrun world food production and starvation is being reported from a dozen countries of Africa, Asia, and even from some parts of Latin America. The steady addition of 75 millions of people each year to the world's consumers of food-200,000 added to the world's population each and every day-together with a poor grain crop in several countries in 1972, despite a record world crop of last year, has now practically exhausted world grain reserves.

The world is now dependent on the vagaries of weather-if nature smiles throughout the farmlands of the world and 1974 provides a record crop of wheat. rice, and corn, as now seems likely but by no means certain, the present bad situation may not get worse for the time being. 

But the outlook is bleak indeed.

The Food and Agricultural Organization of the United Nations has just reported, and I quote, "The world food situation in 1974 remains more difficult 36-333-74- -35

and uncertain than at any time since the years following the devastation of the 

Second World War." 

Norman Borlaug, often called the father of the "Green Revolution" for developing Mexican dwarf wheat, said last week that the "Green Revolution" was never expected to solve the food problems for an expanding world population but rather to "buy time" while governments acted to stabilize what he called this "Monstrous Population Growth." Instead he said governments have frittered away the time gain. He recently predicted that if there was bad weather this year or next year in the United States, such as caused the Midwest Dust Bowl in the 1930s, it would mean that at least 20,000,000 people would die of starvation in those countries dependent on American grain exports and American food aid. 

The vastness of food needs in terms of population increases is not something people grasp easily, he said. He likened annual global grain needs to a highway of grain stretching around the world at the Equator, 55 feet wide and 6 feet deep, each year the population grows by 76,000,000, and that means annually adding a 625-mile link for a second highway. It is becoming more and more difficult for the world to build that second highway. 

Before World War II all areas of the world were food exporters except Western Europe. Today, except for the United States, Canada, and Australia, all areas of the world are net food importers. The world today is dependent on 

North American farmers as never before.

And now on top of this desparate food situation, the energy crisis has struck all of us, and badly. As a consequence, a fertilizer shortage has developed which threatens a shortfall in food production this year in India and in many other developing countries. The Indian subcontinent with its 750,000,000 inhabitants in Bangladesh, Pakistan, and India faces a most critical situation with both oil and fertilizer tripled in price, and often not even available. And the African countries of the sub-Sahara are gradually losing their battle with the desert. 

There are even recent reports of serious hunger in Central America. 

The Director of the Children's Fund of the United Nations warns that 400 to 500 million children are now threatened by serious malnutrition. 

So the world is already experiencing a related food and population crisis, at a time when the demographers are predicting that the present world population of not quite 4 billion will grow to 62 to 7 billion by the end of this century, only 

26 years from now.

Will mass starvation take over to make these predictions meaningless and so prove Malthus finally right?

Clearly, if worldwide disaster is to be avoided, the world must produce more food and less people-and start both actions now on a high priority basis. 

But now let me review the favorable side of the picture and what is still possible.

First, I must commend the Members of this Foreign Affairs Committee and the Members of the Senate Foreign Relations Committee, and in fact, the entire Congress, for the actions taken during the past 7 or 8 years, often under the expressed opposition of the AID Administration, in earmarking funds for population and family planning programs. This earmarking has grown from $35,- 

000,000 to $125,000,000. This action by the American Congress, more than anything else in the world, has provided the stimulation and the support which has attracted similar grants from most industrial countries and encouraged the governments of developing countries representing 60% of their entire population to embark on population and family planning programs. 

I believe that without this action by our own Congress, and without the independent program initiated by the People's Republic of China, with its 800,000,000 people, a few years ago, the present situation would be well nigh hopeless. As it is, I am still an optimist. I believe that the food and population problems can still be solved although many will undoubtedly die of hunger and starvation before birth rates and death rates are brought back into reasonable balance. 

But for this to happen the program of earmarked funds for population activities on which the Congress embarked some years ago must go forward and continue increasing. 

The United States population program and its funding by Congress brought support for population programs from Germany, Japan, Great Britain, Canada, and from Holland, Belgium, Australia, New Zealand and other countries. 

Sweden had made population grants even before we did, and now all of the Scandinavian countries support the population movement generously.

לים 

hen ​sk It was the United States AID program which assured the International Planned Parenthood Federation of 40% of its total budget, which has increased in 8 years from less than $1,000,000 to $40,000,000 this year. During that period its family planning associations have now increased to 84 in 84 different countries-practically a universal world program. 

The United States in 1969 offered to match the contributions of other governments in the newly activated United Nations Fund for Population Activities toward its 1970 budget of $15,000,000. This year more than $50,000,000 is being ds made available to UNFPA with our contribution of at least $20,000,000, or for nearly 40%. Already this year, however, requests for assistance for over $80,- 

000,000 have been asked by developing country governments from the Fund. As 

I have just said only about $50,000,000 are expected in contributions this year so there will be a large and unfortunate shortfall. The United Nations has now become the world leader in assisting governments with their population programs. It has proclaimed 1974 as World Population Year. In August-two months from now-the United Nations will hold a most important World Population Conference in Bucharest, Rumania. It is hoped and expected that a World Population Plan of Action will be agreed upon by the governments of the world at Bucharest, which will lay the groundwork, hopefully, for a humanitarian solution of the world's population problem. However, it will most certainly also generate many more requests for program assistance for the growing population and family planning programs. 

It is vital—now more than ever before-that American support continue and be increased. I understand that the Agency for International Development originally proposed an increase to $150,000,000 for Fiscal Year 1975 and that this request was reduced to $137.5 million by the Office of Management and Budget.

With this background and the present world situation, I cannot urge too strongly at this time when food is running short throughout much of the world, and when the developing countries of the world are faced with their most serious financial crisis as a result of the higher price today for oil and fertilizer-and when population growth in many countries is beginning to respond to growing governmental and private contraceptive programs, that this Committee continue its long and honorable record of strong support. I hope and recommend that the Committee will earmark at least $150 million for population programs for 

Fiscal Year 1975. 

I should add that American support for this cause is being supplemented by contributions from more than 60 governments, both developed and developing alike, to the United Nations Fund for Population Activities, and by contributions from nearly 20 governments to the International Planned Parenthood Federation in the private sector. From next to nothing ten years ago, the amounts being spent this year-1974-for population and family planning programs in the developing countries of Asia, Africa and Latin America will total somewhere between $400 and $500 million, about half contributed by the more developed industrial countries, and the balance coming from the national budget of the developing countries themselves. 

This total is in addition to the nationwide, high priority family planning program now being carried out throughout the People's Republic of China with its 800,000,000 people, since we do not know China's budgetary costs. But from all 

I saw and heard during the three weeks I spent in China last year, the most populous country in the world is carrying on the best and most universal and highest priority program of this kind that I have seen in any large developing country. They told me they had reduced their population growth rate from 22% to slightly below 2% in the past eight or ten years. 

We must realize that in the rest of the developing world most of the governmental programs have been under way only a few years. Many of them are now growing rapidly and with widening public acceptance, as in Indonesia and in the Philippines. 

I attach to my testimony charts recently prepared for AID by the Bureau of the Census which show that very real progress in reducing fertility has been brought about in those countries where programs were started early and have been given high priority-in Korea, Taiwan, Hong Kong, Singapore, Fiji Islands,

Mauritius, Reunion, and Egypt. This is also true of both Chile and Colombia in 

Latin America. Even in Brazil, which has only a private family planning program, the growth rate has been brought down from 32% to 2.8%.

Even India where progress has been slow and difficult has now brought its population growth rate down from over 3% to 22% or perhaps lower. Two weeks ago the Indian government apparently basing its action on a most favorable finding by the British government on the lack of side effects, finally approved the use of the contraceptive pill throughout the Indian program. This should make for much greater progress. 

I am sure that the members of this Committee are aware that the entire developed world-Russia, Japan, Eastern and Western Europe, the United States, Canada, Australia, and New Zealand-are all well on their way toward solving their own population problems, and that many of them, as is true here in the United States, are at or below the so-called replacement level, which means the 2-child family, with all of their average growth rate under 1% each year. 

But even the developing world is making very real progress. Ten years ago almost no governments, except India and Pakistan, had population policies or programs. Now governments representing two-thirds of the developing world's population have initiated both population policies and programs, and all governments are now distinctly aware of the problem. 

The draft World Population Plan of Action, on which agreement is expected at the Bucharest Conference next August, contains proposals that would re-examine the basic human right of every couple in the world to decide the size and spacing of its own family, and also the recommendation that every government in the world should provide its own people with the contraceptive facilities and means so that this human right may be exercised effectively. It is further recommended that this nationwide, hopefully worldwide, family planning program be completely in force within the next 5 to 10 years. 

The discussions now beginning throughout the world relating to the World 

Population Conference and the World Population Plan of Action will most cer tainly increase again the program of developing countries and their requests for assistance. This emphasizes more than anything else the importance of the 

United States government increasing its earmarked population program at least to $150,000,000 for Fiscal Year 1975, and then, hopefully, to increase that program at least $25,000,000 in each succeeding year. 

During the past three or four months the Population Crisis Committee has been cooperating with the United Nations leadership in circulating a Declaration on Food and Population. Copies of the Declaration have been made available to your Committee, containing the names of more than 2,200 distinguished signers from more than 100 countries. The Declaration was officially presented to Secretary-General Kurt Waldheim on April 25 last, to which he responded eloquently and in full agreement. He received messages of support from the Shah of Iran, the President of Senegal, the Prime Ministers of India and Sri Lanka, the Foreign Ministers of Korea and Mexico, and from our own Secretary of State, Henry Kissinger. All of these messages and the Secretary-General's response are included in the Reprint of the Declaration. 

I would like to express appreciation for the fact that a large number of Members of Congress, including Members of this Committee, are signers of the Declaration, and so have indicated great interest in efforts to solve both of these related and serious problems before it is too late. 

Specifically, then, I recommend that the present earmarking of $130,000,000 for population in Fiscal Year 1975 be increased by $20,000,000 to $150,000,000, and that the authorization for Health and Population (now authorized for $145,000,- 000) be increased similarly by $20,000,000, to $165,000,000 which will increase the total AID authorization by $20,000,000. Specific language, I believe, should also be included in the legislation to authorize appropriate population activities from the additional funding recently requested for Indo-China and the Mid East. 

I should point out that the need for increased food aid is being recognized by the Administration, with requests for some $550,000,000 for Food and Nutrition, and for nearly $1,000,000,000 in Public Law 480 food aid-or a total of over a billion and a half dollars for food-certainly badly needed, but representing ten times what I am suggesting for population. 

Only drastic reduction in the growth of world population can lead to any permanent solution of the world's present food problem. 

We must all recognize that our planet Earth is finite-that its resources are not unlimited. While world food production can undoubtedly be further increased, the human race must soon call a halt to its rampant population growth, or hunger and starvation will most certainly take over.

al To help prevent this outcome, I respectfully ask this Committee to support the earmarking of $150,000,000 for Population and Family Planning Programs for 

Fiscal Year 1975.

Mr. TYDINGS. I would like, if I might, to paraphrase the testimony and review it with you since it is a subject with which I am not totally unfamiliar.

Basically, General Draper would be here and I am here to ask you to increase the earmarking in the Foreign Assistance Act for population to $150 million for the coming fiscal year. The world popula-

tion crisis and its twin, the world food shortage, unfortunately have collided sooner than the experts, the demographers, the agronomists had anticipated. That situation is further aggravated by the energy crisis. 

The world population continues to grow at a rate of 75 million new people a year. In 1973, despite the fact that we had the greatest food grain crop in the history of mankind, the world food prices doubled. 

The reason for that is the population increase, 75 million people a year, plus the fact that in 1972 a drought in parts of Asia helped to clean out the world reserves of food in one summer. 

The doubling of world food prices means a lot to the American housewife but imagine, if you would, gentlemen, over 2.5 billion people in Asia who spend 80 percent of their income to buy food. Or 4 million people in Africa who spend 75 percent of their income to buy food. 

THE COMING WORLD FOOD CRISIS 

The FAO this summer in preliminary reports for the World Food Conference in Rome state that there are approximately-and they say it is a conservative figure-400 million people in the twilight zone of starvation. Two weeks ago Dr. Norman Borlaug, the Nobel laureate who developed the so-called "miracle wheat," came back from nine months working overseas in a number of the countries in Africa and India. He was able to spend a day or so on Capitol Hill. Unfortunately the chairman was away at that time. He did have an opportunity to meet with Mr. Rhodes in the House and Speaker Albert and a number of men in the Senate and he had lunch with a number of 

Representatives. 

For the first time Dr. Borlaug is very pessimistic. He says that the time which was purchased by the Green Revolution has not been well used. He pointed out, gentlemen, that in 6 years of the Green Revolution, with miracle seeds and fertilizer, farmers were able to increase wheat production in India from around 300 million bushels to over a billion bushels but next year it is going to drop back by some 200 to 

300 million bushels.

He pointed out in testimony before the Senate Committee on Food and Nutrition that to supply the world's food grain need this year you would need to build a highway around the equator 55 feet wide and 6 feet deep but next year in addition to that band around the equator you would need to add 625 miles of additional food grains. He pointed out that agricultural fertilizer is produced from petroleum. Because of the petroleum crisis, poorer nations are not going to be able to continue to produce the miracle wheat, miracle seed crops, just because of this lack of fertilizer. 

NATIONS "WAKING UP" TO POPULATION PROBLEMS 

One of the results of this has been that many of the nations in the developing world are waking up. In 1965 Mr. Culver, Mr. Tunney, Mr. Kennedy from Massachusetts and myself went to Vietnam and from Vietnam we went on around the world to Thailand, India, and Pakistan. In 1965 in Thailand the Government told us that they were bitterly opposed to family planning in Thailand, that the Thais needed to have a population of 60 or 70 million people to be a force in Asia and that meant an increase in population almost four or five times.

I am happy to report that 3 years ago the Thai government completely changed its position. There is an all out family planning program in Thailand, as in Indonesia. The same is true in the Philippines; the same is true across Asia and into Africa. 

The point I wish to make, gentlemen, is that this committee has been the leader in providing population assistance, voluntary family planning aids to developing countries of the world over the years. 

It is this committee under the leadership of Dr. Morgan who 7 or 8 years ago, often against the expressed opposition of AID, began to earmark foreign aid funds for population assistance. That earmarking has gone up from $35 million to $125 million. 

RAISING FUNDS FOR UNFPA 

Since 1970 when my constituents wanted me back in the practice of law in Maryland, in addition to practicing law in Maryland I have been volunteering about 20 percent of my time to help Bill Draper raise funds from other countries for the U.N. Fund for Population 

Activities and IPPF. The reason we have been able-and, gentlemen, we have to raise the budget in IPPF from $1 million over a year ago to about $30 million and UNFPA from $50 million to $75 million in contributions was because you earmarked funds which AID had to spend on population assistance and we were able to get a 40-prcent matching agreement from AID for the UNFPA and IPPF. 

When we go to the Japanese Government or the German Government with that sort of a proposal we get results. Now the U.S. pro rata share has dropped and the fund has increased 400, 500, 600 percentnot enough. This year the requests for UNFPA aid-and this includes census, maternal and child health, voluntary family planning are almost double the contributions.

NEED FOR INCREASED U.S. POPULATION AID 

This is world population year under the United Nations. There is a conference in Bucharest in August which hopefully will include representatives from over 100 nations, including the Vatican, and hopefully will come up with a world plan of action. It is tremendously important that the U.S. effort not be diminished this year but be increased. We are not asking for a lot, gentlemen. Let me say that in fiscal year 1974, for instance, the combined AID authorization for foreign economic assistance, Public Law 480 authorization, was just over $3 billion. The amount appropriated for population was $112.5 million, only 4 percent of that total, and that does not include any foreign military assistance.

For fiscal year 1975, if $150 million would be provided for population, that would amount to only 3 percent of the total economic assistance. The total proposed AID budget is $1.4 billion, plus the Mideast and Indochina at $1.4 billion, Public Law 480 at $900 million, International Organizations at $900 million, Peace Corps at $83 million, and others at $158 million. We are asking for less than 3 percent of total U.S. economic assistance.

U.N. FOOD AND POPULATION DECLARATION 

Gentlemen, I don't want to dwell on this problem. Suffice it to say, on April 25 a declaration was presented to Secretary Waldheim of the

United Nations on Food and Population signed by representatives of 

100 nations, over 1,500 civic and governmental leaders, 40 Members of the Senate and House of Representatives, including distinguished members of your committee, calling the attention to the world of the impending crises on food and population.

Mr. TYDINGS. This declaration was supported with letters and telegrams from the Shah of Iran, Secretary of State Kissinger, Prime

Minister Indira Gandhi of India and Prime Minister Sirima Bandara naike of Sri Lanka.

I cannot tell you how grave the world population situation is and how vitally important it is that voluntary family planning be afforded for the developing world now that the governments recognize it, now that the people want it I would hope that this committee would seriously consider earmarking $150 million in this year's Foreign Assistance Act.

Let me make one point which might be of some interest to the members of this committee. I wrote a book called "Born to Starve" in 1970 which related to the world population. In the course of this I did some research. In Brazil in the 1950 decade the No. 1 cause of death of women between the ages of 14 and 60 was what they call la sorda. Now that is the butcher knife or the coat hanger, the selfinflicted abortion. I think Mr. Helms would be better advised if he were trying to increase the appropriation and earmarking on population assistance because that is the real way to reduce abortion.

INCREASE IN POPULATION FUNDING Chairman MORGAN. Senator, I see in General Draper's statement, that he is asking for an increase of $25 million in the authorization.

Mr. TYDINGS. Well, the history of it is exactly the opposite. As we have increased the earmarking of our funds over the last 5 or 6 years, the contribution made by other countries, has increased more than ours. 

As a matter of fact, we have been able to reduce the percentage of our contribution to the UNFPA which was originally 50 percent, now it is down to 40 percent.

As we have told Germany and Japan and the Scandinavian countries and others, we are going to bring it down to 30 percent but at the same time that we have been reducing our contribution the U.N. Fund for Population Activities has gone up from $7 million to $50 million even though we have been reducing our percentage share and we are going to continue. Earmarked funds have been a tremendous help. It has been tremendously helpful to have that U.S. support when you raise money from foreign governments.

Although we are unhappy about abortion, we feel the way to avoid it is by voluntary family planning so that it is not necessary.
