MATCHING BASIS FOR UNFPA FUNDS 

Mr. GILMAN. On what basis do we match those funds? Is it dollar for dollar, Senator?

Mr. TYDINGS. We match them in a 40-60 basis. We now put up 40, and we have been reducing our share gradually. The first year when 36-333-74-36

the total amount of the fund was $15 million we contributed $7.5 million and that was a 50-50 match. I think it was that way maybe 2 or 3 years and then we dropped it down to 48 and I think it is now down to 40.

We have told other developed countries that they have to contribute, too. The ideal would be to have Japan, Germany, Britain all contributing the same amount as the United States. Our goal ultimately in this field is a world effort of $2 billion a year, half of it coming from the developing nations themselves and half of it coming from the developed nations, either multilateral or bilateral. 

PROGRAMS OF THE UNFPA 

Now the UNFPA is just one multilateral agency. As you know, there are other organizations that have programs. Population programs are very broad. For instance, about one-third of the UNFPA budget goes into census or demographic projects in the developing nations to give those governments a grasp on what their problems are. For instance, Oman which is a protectorate, a small country on the Persian Gulf, has never had any sort of record of births or deaths in the country. 

They don't even know how many people they have. That is true with many of the countries of Africa which have high population growth rates. Well, one of the areas that the UNFPA concentrates on then is to get these governments to have a census of the population in their country, training local officials on how to take a census so that the government knows what their own population problem is. 

Another approach which is important particularly in countries where you have a strong religious feeling generally not favorable toward any type of family planning-is maternal and child health. 

UNFPA puts I think about one-third of its resources in maternal and child health. This focuses on protecting the mother both immediately before birth and after birth and preserving the life of the child, making sure the mother gets her shots, the child get its shots, and the proper food. Well, in these programs the mother can be told that she can limit or space her family if she wants to, that there are safe ways to do so. This is a type of population assistance which has been very effective in certain areas. 

Mr. GILMAN. Do any of the oil producing nations assist in this endeavor?

Mr. TYDINGS. Yes. As a matter of fact, I have been trying to raise funds myself from oil producing nations. Saudi Arabia contributes; 

Kuwait contributes; Bahrain contributes; even Oman has contributed. 

Abadabi has not come through yet. Qatar promised; they have not contributed what we think they should contribute but then a lot of other countries have not contributed what we think they should.

Well, now, because of the eradication of cholera and what have you, that family of 10 will grow up and survive to be 6 or 7 and the birth rate basically remains constant. That is the basic reason for the population explosion.

Mr. TYDINGS. Yes. As a matter of fact, the world public health programs have been, I think, tremendously successful. What officials will mark down as the cause of death now is diarrhea, chicken pox, measles, cough, and cold, but the real cause of it is that the children don't have enough to eat. They just don't have enough nourishment to throw off a minor illness which we would not even keep our children home from school for.

THE ABORTION QUESTION

South America, the number one cause of death for women between the child bearing ages of roughly 14 to 49 years was infections caused by, as they say down there, la sorda. STATEMENT OF EDWARD F. SNYDER, EXECUTIVE SECRETARY, FRIENDS COMMITTEE ON NATIONAL LEGISLATION

[The prepared statement of Mr. Snyder follows:] STATEMENT OF EDWARD F. SNYDER ON BEHALF OF THE FRIENDS COMMITTEE ON NATIONAL LEGISLATION 

My name is Edward F. Snyder. I am Executive Secretary of the Friends

Committee on National Legislation, an organization which attempts to reflect a general Friends' view on legislative issues but which does not purport to speak for all Quakers because of the democratic organization of the Religious Society of Friends.

For many years we have testified before this Committee when the foreign aid bill was being considered. Because this bill contains so many varied and-in our opinion-contradictory programs, we have tended to indicate our support for some programs and opposition to others. 

This year is no exception. In fact, the contradictions seem intensified. Much of the aid in this bill goes to Indochina and the Middle East. In the Mid-East we continue to arm both sides of the conflict. In Indochina funds for the socalled "postwar reconstruction" program and military aid to Cambodia continue the war instead of beginning a true process of reconstruction and reconciliation. 

INTERNATIONAL AID SUPPORTED 

We want to express our strong support for the several international development and United Nations programs in this bill. The level of these programs still seems pitifully small compared to the needs of the world and the value of carrying out development and other programs through international institutions. 

We urge your strong support for at least the full amounts requested by the 

Administration, and hope you will approve increases. 台灣

While the authorization bill for the International Development Association is not before this Committee, we also hope individual members will vote to support a four-year authorization of new funds for that Association when that bill comes to the floor from the Banking and Currency Committee. 

PROGRAMS TO COMBAT HUNGER ENDORSED 

Current projections of world hunger are so dire that we urge this Committee immediately to increase funds available for food, nutrition, rural development, and population planning programs. We note that the Administration is requesting an increase in the authorization for food and nutrition for Fiscal Year 1975 from $291 million to $546.3 million and we urge this Committee to approve this increase. We hope that you will stress that this money be spent with special emphasis on three priorities: (1) Need, as indicated by current living standards and number of people affected. (2) Reasonable assurance that assistance will improve the lot of the lower and middle classes within the country. (3) Sound development plans which help assure that assistance will be effectively and efficiently used and population stabilized. 

MILITARY AID IN GENERAL 

There appears to be a general lack of public interest and awareness about the foreign military aid programs. The importance of these programs, which comprise about half of all "foreign aid," is seldom realized. Yet in many countries this is the most important United States foreign policy thrust, affecting people more immediately than any other U.S. program. 

Fortunately Congress has recently provided new ways to obtain information about these programs through two invaluable tools, the report required by Section 657 of the Foreign Assistance Act and the report on the "International Transfer of Conventional Arms" prepared by the Arms Control and Disarmament Agency and published as a Foreign Affairs Committee print April 12, 1974. 

Taken together these two reports present a damning picture of United States involvement in the international arms traffic. They show, for example, that: 

In fiscal year 1973 the United States gave away or sold for credit or cash some $8.7 billion in arms.

The United States is the world's chief arms merchant, transferring more than 50% of the world total in 1971. The Soviet Union is a distant second; other countries such as Britain, France, Poland, Czechoslovakia, the People's Republic of China, the Federal Republic of Germany, and Canada trail far behind.

The world arms trade has expanded 112% in the decade 1961-1971, from $2.4 billion to $5.1 billion in constant dollars ($6.2 billion in 1971 dollars).

Much of this arms flow goes to the developing world, thus contributing to the militarization of societies in desperate need of economic and social development. 

In 1961, out of a total of $2.411 billion arms shipments in the world, $1.173 billion or 48% went to developing nations. By 1971 the total had risen to $6.156 billion, of which $4.501 (73%) went to developing nations. This was a percentage increase from 1961 to 1971 of 52%.

The United States was by far the largest supplier of arms to the developing world in this decade. More than half of all United States arms went to developing countries-$15.7 billion of its total $22.7 billion shipments in the decade. 

Huge arms shipments to conflict areas of Europe, Southeast Asia, and the

Middle East in this decade do not account for all of this increase, either. Latin 

American shipments increased 147%, South Asia 285%, and Africa 415% in the same period.

Aside from transfers of arms, U.S. programs of military education and training have far-reaching effects. In 1973 the United States educated and trained future military leaders from forty-six countries at a cost of more than $28 million.

Fourteen past and present recipients of U.S. arms aid are nations that have acquired their power by military takeover of nationalist or constitutional governments or simply by declaring martial law. 

More than 2,200 U.S. military officers are located in forty-six countries under the Military Assistance Advisory Groups and Military Missions. One of their primary roles is to push U.S. arms sales.

Ent La the at 33 This mass dispersion of arms throughout the world with all the consequences which flow from it is not the kind of leadership we want the United States to exert. 

The world is now experiencing a period of unprecedented and rapid social change. New and seemingly insoluble problems are thrust upon national leaders: overpopulation, poverty, food shortages, resource depletion, energy crises, inflation. These are worldwide problems. Only worldwide cooperation can bring solutions. Military aid only fuels the problems instead of providing solutions. It is a fire, building up steam in the world pressure cooker.

It accentuates the gap between the haves and have-nots, internationally and within many countries. It inflames regional rivalries and insecurities. It diverts more than $6 billion a year in resources from desperately needed domestic programs. It reinforces status quo military leadership and repressive policies at a time when new, imaginative, and flexible leadership is required. It encourages recourse to simplistic violent solutions when sober, sophisticated, and mature response to complex economic, social, political, and psychological problems is essential.

Instead of being the world's largest arms merchant, the United States should be devoting its major foreign policy efforts to peaceful purposes-to ending the international transfer of arms and to building up alternative international institutions which will encourage non-violent solutions and provide substantial economic and social justice to the world's people. 

We make these specific recommendations regarding military aid and sales: 

1. The Administration is requesting a huge increase in military grants from $512 million to $985 million, and in credit sales from $325 million to $555 million. 

It is also asking that the $150-million ceiling on Latin American military assistance be removed.

This Committee should retain all regional ceilings, authorize less money than was appropriated last year, and write into the law a phase-out of these programs over the course of the next few years. 

2. In order to give the Congress more notice and control over military cash and credit sales, we urge adoption of Sen. Gaylord Nelson's amendment permitting

Congressional disapproval of any such transaction of more than $25 million or aggregate in excess of $50 million in any one year.¹ 

3. We believe U.S. aid programs should be constructive and benign and should concentrate on positive efforts for economic and social development. We oppose 

U.S. programs which involve our country deeply in internal security, police, prison, intelligence, or surveillance matters of other nations. The potential for abuse, misunderstanding, and charges of outside interference is very great and far outweighs any benefit to the United States. We urge this Committee to amend the bill to prohibit all U.S. funds and local currencies generated by U.S. funds from being used for these purposes. 

4. There is deep concern that U.S. military aid is going to nations which do not recognize and respect fundamental human rights. We urge you to write into this act a provision cutting off all military aid to countries which do not permit impartial international groups access to the recipient country's prisons to inspect alleged violations of human rights.

INDOCHINA FUNDS 

The continuing deep U.S. involvement in the war in Cambodia and the "postwar war" in South Vietnam is distorting U.S. development programs throughout the rest of the world. The Food for Peace program has been corrupted into a food for war program. At a time of starvation in the Sahel in Africa and widespread hunger in South Asia, U.S. officials have indicated development funds may be diverted to make up Saigon's shortages. Administration officials are pressing the International Development Association to approve projects in South Vietnam.

One analysis of U.S. aid proposals indicates that the Administration in Fiscal 

Year 1975 proposes to spend more for Indochina ($3.668 billion) than for the rest of the world combined ($3.542 billion). 

If this money were being used for genuine postwar reconstruction in Indochina, we would strongly endorse it, as we did reconstruction programs in Germany 

1 Senate amendment No. 1399 to S. Bill 3394. See Congressional Record, June 6, 1974, p. S-9851.

and Japan after World War II. But it is not. The lion's share is for military purposes and much of the remainder is for paramilitary or economic uses which only fuel the conflict and buy more time for the corrupt and repressive Thieu and Lon Nol governments at the expense of American taxpayers. 

Only a tiny fraction of these funds go for truly humanitarian purposes or genuine international programs. We would like to see these funds expanded greatly within the context of a real peace agreement. 

VIETNAM 

In many ways the current situation is heavy with irony. For four years we 

Quakers strenuously opposed the Nixon-Kissinger policy of continued U.S. bombing and military presence in South Vietnam and the Vietnamization program. 

Finally, after many hundreds of thousands of lives were needlessly lost, an agreement was negotiated and signed. That agreement provided a formula for removing U.S. forces and moving the struggle in South Vietnam from the military to the political arena. It provided a framework for negotiations leading to a coalition government and elections. 

Now we Quakers are in the position of standing foursquare behind the Nixon- Kissinger-Thieu agreement as the only hope for ending the fighting and providing a peaceful solution. Meanwhile President Nixon, Secretary Kissinger, and President Thieu appear to be abandoning the Paris Accords they so recently signed. 

Thieu has refused to restore the democratic liberties called for by Article 11, and has prevented people from returning to the homes outside his governmentcontrolled areas in violation of the freedom of movement and commerce provisions of Article 11. He has announced that the war has resumed and that the elections called for in the agreement will not be held. 

The U.S. Administration has acquiesced in this repudiation and is doing nothing to encourage Thieu's compliance with the Accords. This is despite the fact that the United States pays the lion's share of his government's expenses. 

In fact, the federal government is requesting more "federal aid" to South Vietnam per capita this year than it spent per capita for the residents of the State of Indiana in Fiscal Year 1973 (the most recent year for which data is available).

According to Dennis Doolin, Deputy Assistant Secretary of Defense for Inter national Security Affairs for East Asia and Pacific Affairs, testifying before the 

Senate Armed Services Committee on April 9, 1974, 

"When you include both the MASF dollars, Mr. Chairman, and economic assistance dollars, we are currently paying some 81.2 percent of the defense of Vietnam."

This fact appears to put the United States in clear violation of Article 4 of the Agreement, which states that "The United States shall not continue its military involvement or intervene in the internal affairs of South Vietnam." 

Indeed, you can search AID's presentation from cover to cover but you will find no mention of the Paris Accords which should be the controlling documents here. The Administration has in fact selected a U.S. Ambassador to South 

Vietnam who seems more an apologist for Thieu than an independent representative of U.S. interests there, a man who advises the State Department that "it would be the height of folly" to give Sen. Kennedy "the tactical advantage of an honest and detailed answer to the questions of substance raised in his letter."

The current situation has a certain "Alice in Wonderland" quality about it. Euphemisms and myths abound. "Postwar reconstruction" funds are requested while military spending requests nearly double. 

Basically it seems to us that, following the Paris Accords of 1973 (which bear a strong resemblance to the Geneva Accords of 1954), we have returned to the Vietnam situation of the late 1950's and early 1960's. And it is only a matter of time before the war heats up again. Recommendations 1. We urge this Committee to launch an intensive investigation of the implementation of the Paris Accords. We suggest you inquire in depth into the allegations of ceasefire violations by both sides. We urge you to examine the relative willingness of the two South Vietnamese parties to accept the terms of the Accords and to publicize the Accords among their own people.

1 2. We urge this Committee to make deep cuts in the so-called "Postwar Reconstruction Fund," authorizing funds only for humanitarian and international programs. Further aid to South Vietnam beyond precisely construed humanitarian and international aid should be contingent upon good faith efforts by the 

Thieu government to comply with the Paris Accords. 

3. Last year Congress enacted the Hatfield amendment to the Foreign Aid 

Appropriations Bill. It prohibited the use of U.S. funds for South Vietnam's police and prison system. But it applied only to funds covered in that bill, not to programs funded in other bills. We urge this Committee to extend that ban to cover all appropriated funds. 

4. There has been a general understanding not written in the law that in 

Fiscal Year 1976 military aid for South Vietnam (MASF) would be shifted from the Defense Department procurement bill and the Armed Services Committee back to the foreign aid bill and the Foreign Affairs Committee, as was done with Laos this year. We endorse that move. There are so many foreign policy ramifications to the South Vietnamese situation following the Paris Ac-. cords that this should be treated as a foreign policy-diplomatic issue, not a military issue. We note that the Senate Armed Services Committee in its Report (93-884) says, in commenting on its new recommended procedures, “In addition, a single appropriation and account would facilitate the transfer for fiscal year 1976 of military support from the regular military appropriations to the 

Military Assistance Program." (p. 161)

LAOS Our sense of foreboding about the viability of the Paris Accords and Administration intentions in Indochina is heightened by recent press reports about Laos. 

After years of travail, the Vientiane agreement was signed February 21, 1973, providing for a Provisional Government of National Union, which was estab lished April 5, 1974. Yet, despite the principle of nonterference in Laotian affairs set forth in Article I of the Agreement, and the importance of acting only through the newly established government, the United States, according to reports on June 24, is sending military aid exclusively to the Royal Lao faction, and economic aid is going almost entirely to areas controlled by that faction. 

It is strange and ominous that the Administration is asking for more than $85 million in military aid for one Laotian faction during the year after a coalition government is set up. U.S. military and clandestine activities in Laos after three previous agreements (in 1954, 1956-1957, and 1961-1962) make us apprehensive for the future. Recommendation

We ask that before this Committee authorizes any military or economic funds for Laos it assure itself that these funds have been requested by both parties of the Provisional Government of National Union, and that all military aid is in compliance with Article 17 of the Protocol in the Agreement which states, "In cases where it is necessary to replace armaments and deteriorated war material, a discussion and unanimous decision by both parties is needed." 

CAMBODIA 

I visited Cambodia many times between 1967 and 1969 while I was Quaker 

International Affairs Representative in Southeast Asia, located in Singapore.

I returned in 1970 just as American troops poured across the border and bombing intensified. The contrast between pre-war peaceful Cambodia and its people and the current war with its killing, maiming, refugees, strife, and corruption is beyond description. Conservative estimates suggest that in Cambodia 350,000 people have been killed or injured, and three million have been made refugees, since 1970, out of a total population of less than eight million. This is the appalling price which innocent bystanders pay when the military juggernaut rolls. "Cambodia is the Nixon Doctrine in its purest form," President Nixon told a press conference November 12, 1971. This claim has become a damning admission in the light of Cambodian casualty figures. It is also a sober warning to other countries now receiving U.S. military largesse. 

In the four years before U.S. intervention in 1970, the United States spent virtually nothing on Cambodia. In the four years since, you in Congress have authorized and the Administration has spent more than one billion dollars, and

the Administration is asking you to make available another $550 million in 

Fiscal Year 1975. 

There can be no doubt of U.S. involvement. It is deep and pervasive. The amount of money the Administration is requesting for Cambodia this next year is more than half that country's entire gross national product.' There is no state in the United States which receives anywhere near this large a percentage of its total resources from Washington. As Philip McCombs reported in the Wash ington Post June 6: "The new U.S. Ambassador in Phnom Penh, John Gunther 

Dean, has in two months made it absolutely clear to Cambodians and foreigners alike in Phnom Penh that he is, in effect, running the country." 

We believe any impartial observer must agree that this level of U.S. involvement is a clear violation of Article 20 of the Paris Accords, which states: (b) Foreign countries shall put an end to all military activities in Cambodia and Laos, totally withdraw from and refrain from reintroducing into these countries troops, military advisers, and military personnel, armaments, munitions, and war materials. (c) The internal affairs of Cambodia and Laos shall be settled by the people of each of these countries without foreign interference. 

We note that Deputy Assistant Secretary of Defense Dennis Doolin is quoted as saying as recently as March 25, 1974, "The United States has not declared the Agreement inoperative, nor do we consider it so. We consider the Agreement binding and comply."

Do members of this Committee know what the goals and policies of our government are in Cambodia? If so, we urge you to make them known to the public. 

We would also appreciate the Committee's citing in its Report on this bill the language of the treaty or executive agreement approved by Congress which requires or permits the level of support requested by the Administration. If authority is derived only from these annual authorization bills, then we urge that the Committee make no further authorization until it is satisfied as to the duration, nature, and extent of the U.S. commitment in Cambodia. As citizens we want to know how many years of death, destruction, and skyrocketing costs we are being asked to support in order to maintain a government which few Americans known about and fewer still endorse. Recommendation

We ask that this Committee prohibit any further military aid to Cambodia until it is assured that there is a valid treaty or executive agreement approved by Congress authorizing such aid, and that such aid is not in violation of Article 20 of the Paris Agreement on Ending the War and Restoring the Peace in Vietnam of January 27, 1973.

THE WORLD ARMS TRADE 

The world arms trade is expanding very rapidly as well, and much of this increase is due to the developing world contributing, in our opinion, to the militarization of those societies which are in desperate need of economic and social development. The United States, we regret to note, was by far the largest supplier of arms to the developing world. This was not just the Middle East and Southeast Asia but the figures for increases in Latin America and South Asia and Africa are startling.

As for the uses to which that aid is often put, we know that 14 past and present recipients of U.S. arms aid are nations that have acquired their power by military takeover of nationalist or constitutional governments or simply by declaring martial law. This kind of mass dispersion of arms throughout the world with all of the consequences

which flow from it is not the kind of leadership which we would like to see the United States exert in the world today. 

We have so many almost insoluble problems-overpopulation, poverty, food shortages, resource depletion, energy crisis, and inflation. 

The military aid adds fuel to these fires and increases the problems rather than providing solutions. It accentuates the gap between the haves and have-nots. It inflames regional rivalries, and reinforces status quo military leadership in many cases. 

SPECIFIC RECOMMENDATION FOR LEGISLATION 

On page 4 we have indicated four rather specific recommendations for legislation in this area. We note that the administration is requesting a huge increase in military grant aid from $512 to $985 million, and an increase in credit sales from $325 to $555 million. In addition, it is asking that the $150 million ceiling on Latin American military assistance be removed. We would hope that this committee would retain all regional ceilings, authorize less money than was appropriated last year and write into the law a phaseout of these programs over the course of the next few years. 

Second, there is a problem which Congress has of trying to understand what is going on in the arms transfer field. Senator Nelson has proposed an amendment which would permit congressional disapproval of any transaction of more than $25 million or aggregate in excess of $50 million in any one year. We would hope that this committee might consider this proposal favorably when it marks up the bill.

Third, we feel there is a definite difference in the quality and kind of aid that the United States gives under the economic aid rubric between genuine developmental aid and aid which goes to the question of internal security of a nation-police, prisons, helping them to improve their surveillance system, how they keep track of their citizens and so on. We would like to see the United States in its development aid have a benign and constructive effect on other countries, and therefore we would hope that you can find some language which will say that the United States will not continue its involvement in public safety programs and these other kinds of programs which have a great potential for abuse and misunderstanding and create charges of outside interference in their internal affairs. 

We are also concerned about the effect of military aid on human rights. There is a proposal that there be a cut off of all military aid to countries which do not permit impartial international groups access to recipient countries' prisons to inspect alleged violations of human rights. Senator Abourezk has some language that he is suggesting to try to meet both of these last two problems I mentioned. 

FUNDS FOR INDOCHINA

If you have specific suggestions with regard to tightening up the prohibitions on the police assistance and so on, I would be very glad to have them. The administration witnesses have assured us that that prohibition has been respected not only by the AID but by other agencies in Vietnam. If you have contrary information, we would be glad to have that. 

Mr. SNYDER. All right.

Responding to Mr. Bingham's inquiry as to compliance with last year's limitations on U.S. aid to police and prison systems in South Vietnam: 

On March 20, 1974, the following exchange took place in the Foreign Operations Subcommittee of the House Appropriations Committee between Mr. Daniel 

Parker, AID Administrator, and Rep. Passman:

Vietnam or on behalf of South Vietnam now?

Mr. PASSMAN. Does the Department of Defense provide any assistance to the police or prison systems in South Vietnam?

Mr. PARKER. The Department of Defense has been providing assistance to the police but not to the prison system of South Vietnam. ate.

DOD has not decided whether it will pick up the responsibilities being terminated by AID. 

Subsequently Senator James Abourezk wrote to the Department of Defense asking clarification of Mr. Parker's statement that "DOD has not decided whether it will pick up the responsibilities being terminated by AID." 

On May 24, 1974, Rear Admiral T. J. Bigley, Director, East Asia and Pacific

Region in the Department of Defense, replied to Senator Abourezk as follows: 

Question. Is the substance of Mr. Parker's statement correct? 

Answer. Yes. At the time of Mr. Parker's statement, DOD had not decided whether it would assume police support responsibilities terminated by AID. 

Subsequently, DOD has decided to assume management reponsibility for the delivery of those commodities in support of the National Policy on irrevocable order. This responsibility will be terminated when the commodity pipeline is depleted. DOD will provide no further funding for police support for the remainder of FY 74 or beyond.

We believe a broad amendment to the authorization bill is still needed to assure that no U.S. funds are being spent for these purposes for two reasons: 

(1) The chief limitation, Sec. 112 of the Foreign Assistance Appropriations 

Act of 1974, was a limitation of appropriations in that bill only. It did not have general or prospective application. Its effect expires when those funds are expended. Rather than add similar provisions to future appropriations bills, it would be better to amend the pending authorization bill. (2) While AID and the Department of Defense have indicated their present intent not to engage in such programs, Congress and the public have no assurance that funds might not be channeled through other programs for South Vietnamese police and prison systems unless a comprehensive prohibition is inserted in the law. (We note that in the confirmation hearings of William 

E. Colby to be director of the C.I.A. in July 1973, the statement appears on p. 174 that in South Vietnam the "C.I.A. maintains liaison and assists the Special 

Police Branch of the National Police in its intelligence functions.")

Laos, as follows: 

(c) No assistance shall be furnished under this part or any other provision of law, and none of the local currencies accruing under this part or any other provision of law, shall be used to furnish funds, commodities, equipment, advice, training, or personnel for the support of detention facilities, prisons, police, other internal security forces, or any program of internal intelligence or surveillance in 

South Vietnam, Cambodia, and Laos.

[The prepared statement of Mr. Block follows:] STATEMENT OF EDWARD L. BLOCK 

My name is Edward Block. I am a former employee of the U.S.

Agency for 

International Development (AID), serving as a Refugee Relief and Rehabilita tion Officer in South Vietnam. I resigned from AID in December 1973 after a 20month tour, and returned to the States to complete my studies for a Ph. D in 

Political Science. 

While in Vietnam I was fortunate to have the opportunity to work in a number of locations, including Binh Dinh and Phuoc Tuy provinces, and the Region I Consulate-General's Office in Danang. My final assignment was in Saigon where 

I assisted the Deputy Director-General of the Office of Land Development and 

Hamlet Building (LDHB), the Vietnamese agency currently responsible for civilian relocations. During the course of my tour, I observed conditions at hundreds of refugee sites in all four regions of the country, spoke with numerous officials in the field, and met many refugees living in camps, return-to-village (RTV) hamlets, and resettlements.

As a result of my experiences in Vietnam, I have formed some rather strong opinions about the impact of AID-sponsored programs on the lives of millions of helpless refugees, primarily women and children, who are caught in the middle of a war that seems to have no end. It is my judgment that the AID-funded relief and rehabilitation program in South Vietnam is a disaster for the refugees involved, a financial bonanza for officials of the Saigon Government, and an insult both to the American people who are being deceived and to the many conscientious American field officers whose reports on these deceptions are routinely suppressed by their supervisors and higher level officials in region and Saigon. 

The so-called "humanitarian aid" program in South Vietnam is as much a scandal as Watergate, and in some ways more serious, since it is a matter of life and death for the refugees who are forced to bear the consequences. I feel I am speaking to you today on behalf of these refugees, who have no political voice in their own country, with the hope that something can be done to put AID out of the "humanitarian assistance" business. 

What is of primary concern to me are the "Refugee Relief" and "City to Farm" programs currently being proposed by AID/Vietnam for FY 1975. The cost of these two programs total $116.5 million or about 87 percent of the entire "humanitarian assistance" effort in Vietnam. The cost of these programs in terms of the human suffering, the loss of lives and limbs, and the unnecessary waste in resources will never be measured-if the Congress allows AID and the Government of South Vietnam (GVN) to pull off this massive hoax.

THE REAL OBJECTIVES OF "HUMANITARIAN AID" 

We should know by now that AID is not requesting public moneys primarily for humanitarian purposes, which comes in, at best, a poor fifth on their scale of priorities. In fact, what AID is proposing to do this year is to continue a refugee program in Vietnam which has failed, by all standards of evaluation, to satisfy even the most basic humanitarian needs. The real objectives of the 

U.S. Mission, for continuing to supply AID funds to the refugee program in 

Vietnam, are strongly political and military in character: (1) to support and maintain in power the Thieu regime; (2) to subsidize the unstable GVN economy. noted for its chronic incapacity to internally generate resources for any sustained growth; (3) to encourage the GVN to hold hundreds of thousands, perhaps millions, of refugees as dependents of the government rather than allowing them to return freely and peacefully to their original villages which may be in or nearby areas controlled by the Provisional Revolutionary Government (PRG); and (4) to help the Saigon Government to occupy additional territory presently contested or claimed by the PRG.

The first two objectives, I believe, should be obvious both from the past record in Vietnam and from the AID FY 1975 submission to Congress which states, "Increased economic assistance is essential to maintain this stability and to provide

the humanitarian aid which is needed after years of war. If assistance is not increased substantially from FY 1974 dollar levels, the consequences could be a collapse of the economies of Indochina." As a rejoinder, I wish to quote from an editorial in the Vietnamese newspaper, Trang Don, appearing in the November 4, 1973, issue and entitled, "U.S. Assistance: A dangerous Drug": "Twenty years have gone by since 1954. During all that time, billions of U.S. dollars have been poured into this land in the form of assistance. In what way have these huge sums of money helped the Vietnamese people? By modernizing the agriculture? By developing the industry? By raising the standard of living of the population? "Some Americans often take on elders' manners, boasting that U.S. assistance has helped this country in many ways, especially in the economic field. I want to tell them flatly to their faces that either they are pitifully mistaken or they 

"*** In plain words, I resent and blame the American assistance for having pushed the economy of this country into a state of inconsistency ** *. "I think it is necessary to point out that U.S. assistance is only a kind of narcotic, no more and no less. The economy of this country resembles the body of a drug addict, 'appearing' healthy when it receives enough of the drug, but weakening immediately as the amount of drug given is reduced and facing inestimable consequences if the drug injections are suddenly stopped altogether." 

The third objective is evidenced by the fact that the GVN continued to keep more than a half million refugees in camps long after the cease-fire agreement had been signed (reportedly, some 180,000 are still unnecessarily stagnating in camps). The refugees remained in camps because the GVN would not give them the opportunity to go back to their original farms, and there was (and still is) insufficient land available to resettle them in areas controlled by the GVN. As one GVN official privately said to me: "It would be politically impossible for us to allow these people to go back to the VC. After all, we have told everyone that they are refugees because they ran away from the Communists. We would look very foolish if we allowed them to run away from us." 

The fourth objective shall be discussed in detail later in my testimony. But it should be mentioned here that gaining a strategic military advantage over the insurgents has always been a primary goal in the GVN's establishment of resettlement sites. Going back to the days of Land Development Centers, Agrovilles, and Strategic Hamlets, a major aim was to deny to the enemy their control over territory. During the middle and late sixties, in order to establish "free-fire zones," huge numbers of civilians were forcibly relocated and held in resettlement/concentration camps, where many still linger today. During the latest resettlement operations, entitled "Land Development and Hamlet Building," refugees have commonly been placed in "marginal" or contested areas in order to establish "security"; that is, to provide a GVN presence in an area where there had previously been none. All of these programs have proved diastrous for the refugees involved-resulting in the death or injury of thousands of helpless civilians. Within the GVN political establishment, military considerations have always taken precedence over any humanitarian purposes. 

THE "REFUGEE RELIEF" PROGRAM 

A major component of the proposed "refugee relief" program is continued support to the GVN for return-to-village and resettlement of refugees through the end of 1975. According to last year's program, only refugees in-camp were scheduled to be RTV'd or resettled, the completion of which would have normally signified a termination of the AID refugee effort in Vietnam. However, for the reasons I have just outlined, AID is now requesting new funds to resettle or RTV an additional 400,000 people. These are primarily destitute Montagnards forced to relocate during the 1968-72 period, and poorly resettled under AID-financed programs in areas where they are now barely surviving. The AID argument for establishing this increased resettlement target is that it provides these additional refugees an opportunity to "earn a living in new resettlement sites" and consequently "achieve self-sufficiency." In reality, this argument is a sham because only a mere handful, if any, of the resettlement projects carried out by the GVN Ministry of Social Welfare (MSW) from 1968 to 1972 and the Office of Land Development and Hamlet Building from 1972 to the present can be considered by any stretch of the imagination to be self-sufficient. As my testimony

will show, refugees resettled between 1968 and 1972 are now living in conditions below even a subsistence level, while the GVN and wealthy Vietnamese landlords are proceeding to take over their original farms. Furthermore, refugees resettled since 1972 are suffering the same hardships, if not worse, as those who came before them.

A 1973 AID survey of 198,000 Montagnards living in 118 resettlement sites established between 1968 and 1971 found that 64 percent of those people did not cultivate a sufficient quantity of land to provide them with even a six months supply of food. Most of those surveyed either worked for wages for other people or depended on forest products in order to survive. It was also found that most of these resettled refugees had been given no land of their own and were usually living and working on someone else's land. At the same time, however, they have land titled to them at their former locations, which they have been unable to use because the GVN will not allow them to return. 

Understood in the context of the present request for funds, this is a revealing indictment of the refugee resettlement program in Vietnam. People who have been living in resettlements for as long as six years or more are totally non-selfsufficient. These Montagnards formerly cultivated their own land until forced out of their original homes and villages by the GVN. Now, they must work for 

Vientamese landlords, serve as day-laborers, or dig for roots and wild plants. 

In the meantime, there are reports that Vietnamese farmers have been allowed to go into the very areas from which the Montagnards were forced to leave. To make matters even worse, the resettlement sites chosen for these Montagnard refugees fall well below minimal standards for physical facilities, required community services, land availability, and opportunities for employment. In short, they are a disgrace.

Additionally, hundreds of thousands of refugees from the 1972 April Offensive are currently being poorly resettled under the same conditions that exist for the 1968-71 refugees. No consideration is given to planting and harvesting seasons when the people are moved; little or no assistance is provided for land clearing; refugees are often placed in resettlements where no land is available; little or no farmland is ever distributed where it is available; and in the relatively few sites where farmland has been distributed, it is totally insufficient to support the refugees.

In many cases, food allowances are arbitrarily cut off, causing widespread hunger and malnutrition. The GVN has set a target of six months for resettlement sites to achieve self-sufficiency, after which food and other support can be withdrawn. It is a fact that this target has never been reached; nor is there any indication that it will ever be reached in the future. From all reports, people living in resettlement sites for a year, two years, or longer are still in dire need of government food subsidies. How can we possibly believe that 400,000 refugees will achieve self-sufficiency in new resettlements next year, when AID and the GVN obviously cannot provide the means for self-sufficiency to the more than two million refugees whom they claim have already been resettled over the last six years.

In its current submission to Congress, AID reports the return-to-village of 355,000 refugees and the resettlement of another 214,000 in 1973. Such figures suggest that the GVN has fully rehabilitated these large numbers of refugees. 

In fact, AID is using a standard administrative ploy to indicate "success" and to deceive Congress and the American public. Most of the refugees reported by 

AID as having been "resettled," were not at all resettled, but rather may have been paid specific amounts of money or given commodities to assist in resettlement. From visits I made to Quang Ngai province last year, for example, I found no indication that means for the establishment of self-reliant and viable communities were even being considered for refugee resettlement sites. Furthermore, I observed that no more than 30 to 40 percent of the reported numbers of people RTV'd or resettled were actually living at the sites. The true number of people who move to resettlements is unknown, because the GVN figures relied upon by AID are usually inflated beyond any reasonable degree of reality. And the true "benefits" provided to refugees in these resettlements, in terms of essential requirements such as agricultural assistance, community facilities, etc. are minimal-in many cases, nonexistent. 

To cite a few more examples, in Binh Dinh province, where over 25,000 refugees had been reported resettled last year, absolutely no land was available for

is da 31 vi farming in six of the first seven sites selected. In Pleiku province, more than 

5,000 refugees were reported resettled last year on land that did not even belong to the GVN. In Lam Dong province, more than 11,000 refugees were resettled in 

June of last year; as of December, the GVN had not even begun to clear land. 

In Binh Tuy province last year, more than 15,000 refugees were reported to be resettled; at year's end, only about 120 hectares or 3 percent of the required amount had been cleared and none distributed. In Long Khanh province, more than 17,000 refugees were resettled beginning in April 1972; yet, a year and a half later, less than 50 percent of the farmland had been cleared and only about 10 percent of the families had received any land other than a few meters to build their homes. To make matters worse, the relatively few people in Long 

Khanh who did receive land have found much of it to be unsuitable for cultivation.

There is good reason to believe that those refugees who finally receive land from the GVN will never be allowed title to that land. In fact, the GVN has never issued ownership papers in land resettlements. Although hundreds of thousands of refugees had been promised ownership to as much as three hectares of farmland, at the end of 1973, not one family had received official title from the government. Influential officials should have little difficulty in reclaiming such lands from the refugees, once American resettlement funds have been depleted (the GVN is already actively engaged in reclaiming land set aside for Montagnard use under the AID-sponsored land reform program, which suffered its demise late last year).

THE "CITY TO FARM" PROGRAM 

There is little substantive difference between the refugee resettlement program and the newly-proposed "City to Farm" program, which offers to relocate 300,000 urban dwellers back to the countryside. Such a program merely adds a major new task to the already overburdened and understaffed GVN agencies responsible for relocations. In its submission to Congress, AID states that "Given the experience and administrative capability of the Office of Land Development and Hamlet Building, we estimate that around 300,000 urban dwellers can be resettlement of 300,000 urban dwellers at the same time it is resettling or returnwe are supposed to be normalizing our relationship with the GVN, is to ignore all our previous mistakes in South Vietnam. Furthermore, to state that the 

Office of Land Development and Hamlet Building is capable of managing the resettlement of 300,000 urban dwellers at the same time it is resettling or returning-to-village 550,000 refugees, and while it continues to support refugee resettlements involving more than a half-million people from the 1972-74 period is absolutely preposterous.

The current administration of the refugee resettlements by the GVN Office of Land Development and Hamlet Building is so mismanaged and inefficient that the refugees resettled under its authority have little hope of receiving the required or promised amounts of land and assistance to give them a chance at self-sufficiency (just as their brethren received too little land and assistance from the MSW between 1968 and 1972). As evidenced by numerous reports AID officials continue to file from the field, no systematic planning is done by the LDHB Office, leading to serious deficiencies in the program. The resettlements are run on an ad hoc day-by-day basis, without any effective planning mechanism; on too many occasions, without any plans at all. In most cases, LDHB officials have no advance data on conditions at proposed resettlement sites, such as land areas available, water, soil quality, crop suitability, etc., in order to properly evaluate the essential requirements for long-term economically viable resettlements. The results of such an operation are what we would expect: The selection of sites is haphazard, site preparation is minimal (in many instances, merely the setting up of tents), and after the refugees arrive, land clearance and distribution do not take place for months and years, if ever.

Because of the extremely large numbers of refugees involved, officials in the LDHB Office have found themselves overwhelmed by the requirements for developing resettlements. There are just not a sufficient quantity and quality of personnel available to properly manage the necessary administrative tasks. 

Although the LDHB resettlement program is operating in twenty three provinces in South Vietnam, at last count, field representatives from that office have been assigned to only four of these provinces. Furthermore, detailed guidelines in resettlement planning and operations had not been prepared. Finally, officials

both in the field and in Saigon are very reluctant to make any decisions without prior consultation with the Minister of State for LDHB. In fact, most officials (including the Minister of State) lacked the proper information and technical data which is needed to make such decisions. All of this has resulted in inadequate planning, sluggish operation, financial mismanagement, lack of coordination, poor logistics services, and numerous other administrative problems. 

The resettlement situation at the Suoi Nghe site in Phuoc Tuy province provides a good illustration of poor LDHB management. This project was originally set up in December 1971 as a model resettlement in Vietnam. Thus, it has received a proportionately greater share of money and attention than any other similar project. Since this is one of the few resettlements where there are at least some outward signs of prosperity, it is included on the itinerary of many visiting dignitaries. But appearances can be highly deceiving without the proper background information. Most dignitaries who tour this site, therefore, are not made aware of the serious problems which exist at Suoi Nghe related to the ever-present land situation-particularly its quantity, distribution, and clearing.

The GVN had promised the settlers at Suoi Nghe three hectares of farmland per family, an amount which many experts feel is barely sufficient to earn a subsistence on dry upland soil. As it turns out, however, even this minimum amount will not be provided. There is only enough land available at Suoi Nghe to distribute, at most, 1.4 hectares per family. This is 55-percent less than the original GVN commitment, and totally inadequate for economic self-sufficiency unless huge and expensive irrigations systems are installed. Despite the fact that, as of November 1973, many of the settlers had been living at the site for almost two years, 60 percent had not received their one-half hectare farm plots, which was only the initial allotment to be distributed. Additionally, after more than two years of developing this site, 18 percent of the initial one-half hectare farm plots still had not even been cleared. Needless to say, the farm income for most of the settlers at this site is minimal, and large numbers of them continued to be dependent on government subsidies for extended periods of time. Once these subsidies are reduced or cut off, the settlers find it difficult, if not impossible, to earn a living from their farms. Thus, it was reported that almost half of the original refugee families abandoned the project to resettle elsewhere on their own. Surely, this is not an encouraging precedent for future attempts to resettle an additional 850,000 people, who would have far fewer benefits and advantages than refugees at the "model" Suoi Nghe site. 

Another area of the LDHB program which should be discussed is their system of financial accountability. Under the present system, controls over the expenditure of AID-provided funds are practically non-existent, leading to some blatent misuses. Funds are usually sent by the LDHB Office based on requests submitted by the provinces (verbal requests are quite common here). However, an examiner of records and major functions in the LDHB Office would soon discover that there are no standard procedures for evaluation of requests and fund allocations, and only superficial controls over the expenditure of funds and commodity usage. Dossiers requested by the LDHB Office to substantiate expenditures are hardly ever submitted, and there is very little followup on such expenditures. The LDHB Office in most cases, relies on the Province Chief's "discretion" to assure that funds are spent correctly. 

Obviously, this is not a very efficient or reliable financial procedure, particularly in a program where GVN officials are well known for abusing the distribution system, cheating both the refugees and the American taxpayer. The latest GAO report on the refugee program in South Vietnam discovered that, in the LDHB Office, "of the 4.2 billion piasters distributed to 23 provinces only 

895 million had been accounted for." Numerous instances of misuse and unauthorized allocations have been identified and brought to the attention of high level AID officials. To give a few rather conspicuous examples, the LDHB 

Office provided some 21 million piasters or $43,000 out of an AID-financed account to various GVN agencies to pay for official parties and gifts during last year's Independence Day celebration. Large sums are allocated to subsidize, additional salaries and "per diems" of GVN civil servants, as well as provide allowances to military dependents who are not the responsibility of the LDHB Office. Expenditures of refugee funds are routinely made for such unauthorized items as installation of telephones, land rental, and even roofing for churches.

5! nd z di Fe 2 This type of activity goes on continuously in Vietnam with U.S. money, and 

American officials do very little, if anything, to stop it. 

Perhaps the most expensive refugee program, in terms of the total amounts lost through corruption, has been the support of between 40,000 and 90,000 "ghost" refugees in the Danang camps. These refugees do not actually exist, but are submitted on the camp distribution lists by GVN officials in order to pad their rolls and thereby gain an additional profit from their normal rakeoff or "tea-money" on food distributions. After a period of more than 18 months, during which time numerous high level AID officials were informed of the situation and several articles were published in the American press, the GVN finally admitted to a ghost refugee population of 40,000 in Danang. What makes this situation even more ludicrous is the likelihood that an undetermined number of these "ghost" refugees are now returning-to-village in Quang Tri or resettling in Thua Thien and other places, adding huge sums to the already bulging bank accounts of various GVN officials.

THE LACK OF LAND FOR RESETTLEMENT IN GVN AREAS 

Another topic for consideration is the availability of unoccupied land presently under GVN control. In Regions I and IV there is a lack of public domain land and most of the abandoned private land which could be set aside for refugee use is either untillable, unsafe, or would require major reconstruction efforts. During an investigation we made in the Delta to assess a GVN proposal to reserve 55,773 hectares for refugee resettlement, we found that only about 4,000 hectares were actually suitable for resettlement (not counting a proposal, which I consider highly impractical, for using 20,000 hectares on Phu Quoc island). After talking with a number of province officials in IV Corps, we concluded that most of them would prefer not to resettle refugees in their areas. 

The available land is very limited, and the best of this has already been set aside for retired servicemen and civil servants. Refugees relocated into Region 

IV would receive small scattered pockets of land requiring extensive renovation to make them economically viable, as well as the protection of large security forces. As we have come to discover in South Vietnam, if an area has good soil, plentiful water supplies, and is safe, there is inevitably somebody farming or claiming it; if an area has poor soil, few water resources, and the GVN would like to make it a buffer zone, then the land is available for refugee resettlement. 

In Regions II and III the GVN has been busy using the resettlement program as an excuse to intrude on land set aside for the benefit of Montagnards. Just prior to my leaving Vietnam, I became aware of extensive GVN plans to resettle ethnic Vietnamese on land belonging to Montagnards. I know of at least one instance, in Binh Tuy province, where such land has already been requisitioned. The GVN claims that the Montagnards are not able to cultivate all of the land titled to them over the past three years, therefore releasing the government from any previous obligations. Such a rationale completely negates the tremendous efforts of American officers in the AID/Land Reform program, who struggled for years to legalize Montagnard landholdings. Thus, we have a situation in 

Vietnam where destitute Montagnard refugees are suffering in nonviable resettlement camps without any land. Yet the Saigon Government, with AID assistance, is in the process of requisitioning land originally set aside for use of the Montagnards in order to resettle ethnic Vietnamese in the Highlands. I can easily foresee the rapid claiming of all Montagnard land for resettlement of. 

Vietnamese "refugees" under the guise of programs such as "City to Farm." It is totally unnecessary for use to repeat a tragic era in our own history by paying, the GVN to open up large tracts of lands for "homesteading"-lands which right-, fully belong to the "Indians" of Vietnam.

A related question, which I urge this Committee to consider very carefully, is exactly where AID and the GVN plan to relocate these 550,000 refugees and 300,000 urban dwellers, for whom funds are now being requested. In order to resettle people on new land or return refugees to their original homes in such large numbers during 1975, it will be necessary for the GVN to militarily occupy, and be able to defend huge amounts of new territory in the countryside. It would be impossible for an occupation of such large amounts of new land to take place without directly violating the cease-fire agreement and without severe consequences for civilians who participate in this scheme. 

In an early draft, which I saw, of the AID FY 1975 refugee program, it was argued that a million hectares of arable abandoned or virgin land should be

considered for resettlement, despite the fact that the GVN did not control these areas and there were no military forces operating in them. The essential rationale of this proposal was that these unoccupied lands could be brought under GVN control by organizing and training refugees to defend themselves against the VC (very much similar to what was attempted in the ill-fated agrovilles and strategic hamlets). The Saigon Government, then, by placing refugees on the one million hectares under consideration, will significantly widen its territorial base and effectively establish authority over a much larger area than it controlled at the time of the Paris Agreement. All under the very convenient aegis of "humanitarian aid" for the refugees of South Vietnam.

CURRENT RESETTLEMENT POLICY 

If there are any members of this Committee who may be skeptical such a policy could exist that would so utterly disregard the safety of hundreds of thousands of helpless civilians and the sanctity of an agreement signed in good faith, you need only look at the most recent record. During the 1973-74 resettlement program, hundreds of thousands of refugees have been forced (in the sense that once food rations are withdrawn in the camps most refugees have no real choice but to take whatever meager land and allowances the GVN offers them, if any) and misled (in the sense that many GVN promises made before the refugees move are never kept) into relocating in areas where the GVN wishes to establish or re-establish control. 

As evidenced by the Region III Consul-General's letter to the GVN Corps Commander, published in a recent document of the Senate Subcommittee on Refugees, the U.S. Mission in Vietnam continues to promote the inhumane GVN policy of moving refugees to "marginal" areas in order to improve "security." 

In fact, most of the areas proposed by the Consul-General for resettlement in Region III were not even controlled by the GVN at the time this letter was written. This policy is in direct violation of the cease-fire agreement which states, "The armed forces of the two South Vietnamese parties shall remain in place." Yet, such a policy has been carried out time and time again over the past year, especially in the provinces of Quang Ngai and Binh Dinh. Almost every resettlement established in those two provinces has pushed the GVN deeper into contested areas; in many instances, areas where the GVN had no military presence prior to the cease-fire. And once the GVN occupies these new areas, it wastes little time in seizing this opportunity to utilize refugees for their own counter-insurgency purposes, despite possible hazards to the people involved. For example, I know firsthand that in resettlements in Quang Nam province, the GVN has been busy recruiting children between the ages of 7 and 14 to perform intelligence and detection work within their villages and the surrounding areas.

Simply because the GVN decides to put helpless civilians into areas in order to "secure" them does not consequently deny the PRG's own claims to these areas or limit the PRG ability to attack at will the military outposts located in many of these resettlements. Within only a ten-week period between July and 

October 1973, in resettlement sites in Quang Ngai province, 20 civilians were reported killed and 38 wounded. When I visited Quang Ngai in June of 1973,

I found that none of these refugees had volunteered to move to the resettlement sites selected for them by the GVN. Furthermore, they were both fearful and unhappy about being forced to relocate in a battle zone where there was almost daily military contact between the two sides. On September 26, 1973, in Tu Cung village of Quang Ngai, 2 civilians were reported killed and 4 wounded-Tu Cung village is the site of My Lai hamlet. You may wonder, as I do, how much death and suffering these unfortunate people will have to endure before they will be allowed to live in peace.

Although the GVN has not hesitated to resettle refugees into hazardous areas, it has done very little to demonstrate any real concern for their safety. As if it wasn't bad enough for the Stieng Montagnards of Binh Long province, many of whom barely escaped from the battle at An Loc, to be concentrated for a year and a half in the squalid An Loi refugee camp where they watched more than 300 of their children die like flies. When the GVN finally decided to resettle them, a newly-occupied site in Lam Dong province was chosen. This site not only has the advantage of putting the GVN presence into a strategically important territory, but the possibilities for lucrative contracts to cut down the prime forest preserves in this area must certainly have been an added incen-

tive. But the GVN failed to take into account the strength of their enemy, and now these Montagnards are subject to continued harassment and attacks by the PRG with no effective protection provided by local forces stationed at the sites. Unknown numbers of Montagnards have escaped or tried to escape from these resettlements back into the forests-it is evident that even these normally docile people can take but so much abuse. 

RECOMMENDATIONS 

Thus, as always in South Vietnam, the refugees are caught in the middlepawns in a political game which the U.S. Mission deceitfully terms "humanitarian aid." I respectfully urge this Committee to reduce to zero the funding for AID "humanitarian" programs. With such funds, the GVN will continue to resettle refugees in territories it does not control, giving their human cannon fodder a minimal amount of land (none in many cases) and allowances to survive on. Without the U.S. relief funds, however, the GVN will be forced to allow these people, most of whom are from villages in PRG-controlled areas, to return if they choose to their original farms in accord with the Paris Agreement. 

AID officials argue that no refugees have come forth to request their return to home in PRG-controlled areas. This argument might as well be, no refugees have come forth to commit suicide, because the GVN still maintains a policy of shooting or jailing anyone caught moving about in areas outside of its immediate control. I suggest that this Committee might want to investigate reports of refugees attempting to return by boat from Danang to Dong Ha, a PRG-controlled area in Quang Tri province. It is a poorly kept secret that no one has heard from these refugees since they were picked up last year by the GVN coastal patrol. I do not know, of course, the number of people who have been involved in such incidents. Nor do I know how many refugees would return to their homes in PRG areas if given the opportunity. But the point is, the United States signed an agreement which allows for free movement of population, yet we are now encouraging the GVN, through support of its refugee resettlement program, to completely disregard this basic right of self-determination-for people to choose where and under which government they wish to live. As long as we continue to pay the GVN for its "humanitarian" aid, the victims of war in South Vietnam will never be able to enjoy that right.

Looking briefly at the larger picture, I would further recommend a detailed review, not only of the humanitarian assistance program, but of all AID programs in Vietnam for FY 1975. While working in Vietnam, it became painfully obvious to me that our socio-economic programs had clearly failed to respond to the problems in that country. The reconstruction of highways and bridges, the building of schools and wells, the resettlement of refugees have little positive impact on the well-being of the rural peasantry of South Vietnam. This is because such programs are remote from and irrelevant to the basic factors which underlay the conflict disrupting their lives. In addition, these programs allow the Thieu regime to ignore the substantive political issues such as land tenure, reform of the military and administrative heirarchies, shifting authority back to local communities, and so on. Our foreign aid has accomplished nothing towards these objectives. Rather, as I have attempted to illustrate in my testimony, AID funds are being used primarily to enhance the military objectives of the GVN, and to pursue a policy directly counter to the Paris Peace 

Agreement. 

It is apparent that as long as he believes he can rely on American foreign aid, President Thieu will continue to stall any political accommodation with the PRG.

And the failure to reach such an accommodation has resulted over the last eighteen months in more refugees, more deaths, and more suffering for the people of South Vietnam. On the other hand, a major reduction in foreign aid at this time would likely force President Thieu to make the necessary compromises, which had originally been agreed upon on January 27, 1973. Once this is accomplished, an effective and long-term solution to the refugee problem, as well as many other problems of reconstruction and development in South Vietnam will be possible. 

Thank you very much for allowing me to appear before you today.

Mr. BLOCK. I will try to summarize this as quickly as I can. 

I am a former AID employee working in Vietnam as a refugee relief and rehabilitation officer. I was in Vietnam from March of 1972 to 

December of 1973.

While in Vietnam, I had the opportunity to work in a number of locations throughout the country. My last assignment was to assist the 

Deputy Director-General of the Office of Land Development and Ham let Building. This is the Vietnamese agency currently responsible for refugee resettlements. During the course of my tour, I observed conditions at hundreds of refugee sites, worked with officials in the field, and met many of the refugees living in camps, return to village hamlets and resettlements.

AID REFUGEE PROGRAMS IN VIETNAM 

As a result of my experiences in Vietnam, I have formed some rather strong opinions about the impact of AID-sponsored programs on the lives of millions of helpless refugees. These people are primarily. women and children caught in the middle of a war that seems to have no end. It is my judgment that the AID-funded relief and rehabilitation in South Vietnam is a disaster for the refugees involved, a financial bonanza for officials of the Saigon government and an insult both to the American people who are being deceived and to the many conscientious American field officers whose reports on these deceptions are routinely suppressed by their supervisors or higher level officials. I feel I am speaking to you today on behalf of these refugees who have no political voice in their own country with the hope that something can be done to put AID out of the humanitarian assistance business. 

What is of primary concern to me are the refugee relief and cityto-farm programs currently being proposed by AID/Vietnam for fiscal year 1975. A major component of the refugee relief program is continued support to the GVN for return to village and resettlement of refugees through the end of 1975. According to last year's proposal, only refugees in camps were scheduled to be returned-tovillage or resettled. However, AID is now requesting new funds for an additional 400,000 former refugees-primarily destitute Montagnards forced to relocate during the 1968 to early 1972 period and poorly resettled under AID-financed programs.

REFUGEE PROGRAMS FAIL OBJECTIVES 

The AID argument for establishing this increased target is that it provides these additional refugees an opportunity to "earn a living in new resettlement sites" and consequently "achieve self-sufficiency." 

But, in fact, this argument is a sham because only a mere handful, if any, of the resettlement projects carried out by the GVN can be considered by any stretch of the imagination to be self-sufficient. What 

AID is actually proposing to do is continue a refugee program that admittedly has failed in the past and is failing even now primarily in order to accomplish four major objectives: (1) To support and maintain in power the Thieu regime; (2) To subsidize the unstable GVN economy, noted for its chronic incapacity to internally generate resources for any sustained growth; (3) To encourage the GVN to hold hundreds of thousands, perhaps millions, of refugees as dependents of the Government rather than allowing them to return freely. and peacefully to their original villages which may be in or nearby areas controlled by the Provisional 

Revolutionary Government (PRG); and

(4) To help the Saigon government to occupy additional territory presently contested or claimed by the Provisional Revolutionary Government.

In a survey done last year by AID the economic conditions of 198,- 000 Montagnards living in 118 resettlement sites were covered. It was found that a great majority of refugees living in these resettlements for as long as 6 years can produce enough food for only a 6-month supply or less. Montagnards who formerly cultivated their own land until the GVN forced them out now must work for Vietnamese landlords in order to survive.

RESETTLEMENT SITES POOR IN VIETNAM 

Finally, most of these sites fall far short of even a minimal standard for physical facilities, required community services, land availability, and opportunities for employment. This is a revealing indictment of past AID-sponsored refugee programs in Vietnam. In my opinion it is a disgrace.

Yet, additional hundreds of thousands of refugees from the 1972 April offensive are being just as poorly resettled under the current program. Many of the new resettlement sites are in danger of collapsing or are already collapsing due to insufficient land and lack of required support from the GVN. In addition, much of the land provided for refugee resettlement is of poor quality with few water resources and the areas are subject to constant military harassment. 

We have come to discover in South Vietnam that if an area has good soil, plentiful water, and is safe, there is inevitably somebody farming or claiming it; if an area has poor soil, few water resources, and the 

GVN would like to make it a buffer zone, then the land is available for refugee resettlement. How can we possibly believe that 400,000 refugees will achieve self-sufficiency in new resettlements next year when AID and the GVN cannot provide the means for self-sufficiency to the more than 2 million refugees whom they claim have already been resettled? 

Chairman MORGAN. Mr. Block, Mr. Bingham and I have to be on the House floor at 12:31 so we have 6 minutes to get there.

RECOMMENDS NO FUNDING OF REFUGEE PROGRAMS IN VIETNAM 

Mr. BLOCK. All right. I will just read my conclusions.

Perhaps the greatest tragedy of all though is the hardship incurred by hundreds of thousands of refugees who are forced or misled into relocating in areas where the GVN wishes to establish or reestablish its military control. The U.S. mission in Vietnam continues to promote the inhumane GVN policy of moving refugees to "marginal" or contested areas in order to provide a GVN military presence in an area where there had previously been none. Despite the fact that this policy is in direct violation to the cease-fire agreement, it has been carried out time and time again over the past year, pushing the GVN forces deeper into contested areas and causing countless deaths and injuries. for the helpless civilians involved-women and young children and older people.

For example, within only a 10-week period between July and October 1973, in resettlement sites in Quang Ngai Province, 20 civilians

were reported killed and 38 wounded due to military action. When I visited Quang Ngai in June of 1973, I found that none of these refugees had volunteered to move to the resettlement sites selected for them by the GVN and they were both fearful and unhappy about being forced to relocate in a battle zone where there was almost daily military contact between the two sides. 

I respectfully recommend that this committee reduce to zero the funding for AID-supported refugee programs in Vietnam. With such funds, the GVN will continue to resettle refugees in territories it does not control, giving their human cannon fodder a minimal amount of land and allowances to survive on. I strongly urge you to consider very carefully the drastic consequences of voting even one more dollar toward continuing the so-called humanitarian aid program in Vietnam. 

I am finished. I would just like to submit a series of documents that 

I collected to include as a substantiation of my testimony.

All the Members have received statements in advance for they were sent to Members' offices yesterday. In order to allow each Member the opportunity for questioning, we ask each witness to limit his opening remarks to not more than 10 minutes. Your full statements, of course, will be placed in the record.
