STATEMENT OF JAMES GRANT, PRESIDENT, OVERSEAS DEVELOPMENT COUNCIL 

Mr. GRANT. Thank you very much, Mr. Chairman.

Following your proposal, if I may, I will put my entire statement in the transcript and then highlight certain parts of it before the question period.

I very much welcome this opportunity to testify again before the House Foreign Affairs Committee, this time on the request by President Nixon that the authorization under the Foreign Assistance Act for fiscal year 1975 for increasing food production, improving nutrition and accelerating rural development be raised by $255 million to a level of $546 million. I understand that the administration also proposes to allocate the majority of loan repayments to these purposes in fiscal year 1975, raising the total to $675 million. 

I think several major questions can be raised quite properly with respect to this request to increase the authorization above that approved by the Congress in 1973 when it voted a 2-year authorization (581)

for the development assistance components of the Foreign Assistance Act. Most important among these considerations is the question: Have there been changes on the world scene of sufficient importance to justify a reexamination of the level authorized last year? There are other important questions and these I will discuss later. 

My recommendation to this committee is that it authorize the full amount of the increase requested for the authorization for food and nutrition assistance. While there are some risks and disadvantages from reopening the existing authorization for fiscal year 1975, the dangers from not doing so are far greater. I also urge favorable action on the closely related House Resolution 1155 introduced by Congressman John Culver and cosponsored by some nearly 70 Congressmen which calls on the United States to take the lead in a cooperative effort to ease the pending critical food crisis both by increasing food assistance to the most seriously affected nations and by taking measures to increase production-including making available more fertilizers for food production by reducing the present substantial use of fertilizers for nonfarm purposes.

Principal among the developments justifying reopening the issue of the appropriateness of the existing authorization are the following: 

ENERGY AND FINANCIAL CRISES 

First the food, energy, and financial crises which have engulfed the world since last year's hearings on the present development assistance authorization have signaled a new order in international and political affairs, one characterized by a new global politics of resource scarcity. 

This new era is marked by widespread scarcities, a shift from the traditional buyers' market to a sellers' market for many commodities, shifts of political as well as economic power to resource-rich countries, a freshly impoverished "Fourth World" (worse off now than the rest of the Third World), global inflation, and a perilous food situation for much of the world.

The hearings on development assistance held before this committee 1 year ago were focused on the need to bring progress to the poor majority in the low-income countries. This need remains but there is the additional need to examine the relevance of the tools of assistance to the new set of global problems, many of which now also affect the daily life of Americans.

Two quite different sets of circumstances brought on the tight supplies and resulting jarring changes of the past year. One of these sets was comprised of short-term circumstances, primarily the business boom of the early 1970's (which caused all the industrial economies to expand at once for the first time since World War II), the unprecedented droughts (which diminished or wiped out crops), and the Mideast conflict (which restricted oil supplies). The second set of circumstances, made up of long-term trends accelerated by these shortterm factors, probably will be seen in retrospect as the main causes of the recent shortage crises. These trends are rapid economic growth within a finite physical system and relatively inflexible political and economic structures. In short, we have had a systems overload. 

The responsive capacity of the world system was pushed toward its limits as global economic activity grew from $1 trillion in the late

Ca 1940's to about $4 trillion in 1974. As the $3 trillion level was reached in the late 1960's, signs of stress appeared everywhere-ecological overloads ranging from massive pollution to overharvesting of fish. 

Food producing capacity was strained as the demand for food grew by 30 million tons a year to keep up with population growth of 2 percent a year and as rising affluence, reflected in 3 percent yearly increases in per capita income, also made itself felt. This 30 million tons annual increase in food demand compares with a rate of increase of about 15 million tons annually just 20 years before. 

In retrospect it can be seen that these trends were well advanced by early December 1973. The doubling of oil prices by the OPEC countries on December 22, 1973—which raised oil prices in 1974 to levels most economists had not anticipated until 1980-has introduced a "system overload" which may be beyond the capacity of the international order to absorb without major chaos. It has also accelerated and brought into stark relief other important trends which must now be taken into account.

THE "FOURTH WORLD" OF POOREST COUNTRIES This I put under the second heading. A new Fourth World of some 

40 of the poorest and slowest growing countries with a total population of nearly 1 billion people is emerging. These countries are so seriously threatened by the combination of soaring food and fertilizer prices on the one hand and of skyrocketing oil prices on the other that they face the prospect of disaster during the next several years unless there is a major, stepped up international effort to assist them in meeting new threats that were not primarily of their own making. Many of these governments can be expected to topple under the new stresses. 

Third, the world food situation is dangerous, particularly for the developing countries, and considerably more so than was expected by most observers 1 year ago. World food stocks are at the lowest level since the World War II era despite the world's largest crop harvest last year. Reserves calculated on the basis of stocks in the major food exporting nations and readily usable land being kept out of production are now estimated at 27 days of consumption-down from 36 days 

1 year ago and 90 days in 1970. Thus, poor weather over any widespread area during the next 18 months would trigger an acute world food crisis.

I might say, by the way, as a footnote that so far the weather in both India and China to date has been poorer than expected or hoped for and the next month will be quite critical on that account. 

SHORTAGES OF FERTILIZER 

Also a shortage of nitrogenous fertilizer production capacity insures an even more dangerous food supply situation for important parts of the developing world for at least the next several years. Under current scarcity conditions for fertilizers, not only have prices trebled and quadrupled for developing country buyers but in addition—and I wish to stress this the industrial countries, including the United States, which produce four-fifths of the world's fertilizer supply, themselves have pre-empted larger amounts and shares of the world's

supply to meet their own increasing fertilizer needs. The result is that some developing countries have very sharply reduced availability of fertilizer. 

The seriously reduced harvest of the Indian wheat crop this spring, which amounted to less than 23 million tons instead of the original estimate of 30 million tons, was due primarily to fertilizer shortages. 

These were due in large part to massive fertilizer contract cancellations by the Japanese and Europeans in the winter months following the oil crisis and following the U.S. embargo on new fertilizer sales introduced in October of 1973. 

SHORTAGES OF OIL 

Shortages of oil for the irrigation pumps on which this Green Revolution crop is so dependent were also a contributing factor, causing a loss of 1 million tons in the Punjab, according to the USDA estimates. The adverse effects of this fertilizer shortage extend far beyond the immediate loss in production in the developing countries. The shortage also threatens to interrupt the whole forward momentum of the laboriously launched Green Revolution which has focused on encouraging farmers to use new rice and wheat seeds whose profitability depends on heavy use of fertilizers. Many thousands of small farmers who have accepted the idea of the Green Revolution in recent years will now be faced with major difficulties. During times of shortages they tend to suffer far more than large farmers. 

With the industrial countries favoring their domestic needs (including low priority domestic needs) over the needs of the fertilizer importing countries, the FAO projects a shortfall of 2 million tons of fertilizer in 100 developing countries from autumn 1974 to spring 1975. This represents roughly 16 to 20 million tons of grains, or the normal consumption of about 100 million people, which will cost these countries some $4 billion in scarce foreign exchange. For food importing countries, each $1 worth of nitrogenous fertilizer they are unable to import now will require $5 worth of high priced food imports a year later. An FAO study concludes: 

In the short run, there is no way of bridging the gap between expected demand and supply capacity additional to that planned so that the world has to live with a worsening shortage in the meantime. 

This will last for several years.

Having embargoed new fertilizer sales because of rising domestic demand and lacking the food surpluses on which its food aid (Public Law 480) program so long depended, the United States the food and fertilizer center of the world-is no longer implementing even the semblance of a global food policy beyond that of maximizing profits for agricultural exports. U.S. food aid this past year was one-third the volume of 2 years ago, and one-half of this greatly reduced amount went to Indochina.

RISE OF GRAIN CONSUMPTION IN UNITED STATES 

Meanwhile, the direct and indirect grain consumption of the average American has risen to approach 1 ton annually, and scarce ferti-

E: PL lizer is used for such nonfarm purposes as lawns, golf courses, and cemeteries in ever increasing amounts which already exceed the total fertilizer shortfall in the developing countries. Against this background, the administration's request to expand agricultural production assistance and House Resolution 1155 takes on a special significance, and neither should be allowed to fail.

House Resolution 1155 is correct in urging the President to restore food aid to fiscal year 1972 levels (approximately 9.5 million tons) and to encourage the American people to reduce their nonfarm uses of fertilizers now requiring nearly 3 million tons a year-to make available increased fertilizer supplies for rising food production in the United States and in the developing world. The lifesaving benefits it would bring to great numbers of people in the developing countries is obvious. The increased availability of fertilizers to American farmers should result both in increased food production in the United States and lower prices in our supermarkets.

Fourth, events of the past year have vastly increased the problems of the poor throughout the world, particularly in the poorest countries whose prospects can be expected to deteriorate over the next several years. Barring major international action, the combination of a doubling to quadrupling of food and energy prices and the cutback on fertilizer exports by the industrial nations dooms millions to premature deaths from increased malnutrition and even outright starvation. The only question-and one which Americans can influence-is: 

How many millions?

NEED FOR IMPROVED GLOBAL MANAGEMENT OF RESOURCES 

Fifth, the new era of increasingly tight supplies brings with it the need for greatly improved global management to increase resource availability if inflation rates of over 10 percent are not to become a nearly permanent fixture. We see this most clearly in the case of food. 

Rising global demand, due to both population growth and affluence, requires a 400-million-ton increase in grain production over the next 10 years, to reach approximately 1.6 billion tons by 1985. If the bulk of the increased food production required over the next decade is to come from the developed countries, the price of food will need to rise very sharply to cover the higher costs of producing it. 

New land can be put under cultivation in developed countries only at substantially increased cost, and increasing production through more intensive use of inputs such as fertilizer is likely to be even more costly. In the developed countries, the use of inputs is at a point of diminishing returns for most crops. Each additional pound of fertilizer applied to an already heavily fertilized acre of corn in Iowa or of rice in Japan now yields only one-half to one-third the increased output per acre resulting from the first applications of fertilizer. 

On the other hand, if the bulk of the increase in production comes from developing countries, there may not need to be an increase in the cost of food over the next 10 years. Because limitations of organizations, financing, and applied technology have kept use of inputs low in most of the poorer countries, there are great opportunities for expanding production at very little, if any, increase in cost in these 36-333-74- -38

countries. An additional ton of fertilizer, for example, will produce two to three times as much additional rice and corn in South Asia as in Japan, Europe, or North America. 

According to one responsible source-Ray Ewell-to increase grain production by 100 million tons in developed countries will require 24 million tons of fertilizer; a comparable increase in developing countries would require only 10 million tons of fertilizer. The same contrast is seen in the use of energy in general. It now takes 10 calories of energy in the United States to produce 1 calorie of food, as compared to a one-to-one ratio 50 years ago. The developing countries, on the other hand, have large pools of underemployed labor which can be put to use.

To ignore the potential of many developing countries for increasing food production at relatively low costs is to insure higher rates of inflation throughout the world. Also worth remembering, as the committee knows, is the fact that increased rural production in the developing countries (relying primarily on smaller farmers) not only would result in maximum production per acre but also would bring many of the ancillary benefits emphasized by this committee last yearincreased rural employment, decreased income disparities, reduced rural to urban migration, and lower birth rates. 

CHANGES IN WORLD POWER STRUCTURE 

Sixth, the world economic and political power structure is changing massively in favor of the resource-rich countries, both developing and developed. 

Going to page 14, it should be clear from what I have said already that there have been vast changes since the Foreign Affairs Committee reached its conclusions with respect to development assistance a year ago. Most of the changed circumstances of the past year, and certainly their net impact, call for an increased international effort to head off the threat of an acute world food shortage which could bring millions more deaths in the poor countries and sharply higher food prices to the American consumer during the latter part of this decade. As indicated earlier, however, some possible negative factors need to be considered and I will just mention these very briefly. 

NEGATIVE FACTORS IN FOREIGN AID 

First, is there a serious danger that this increased assistance will be used primarily for financing major capital projects not affecting the poor majority? I believe that AID is making a genuine effort to accomplish the turnaround that the committee sought last year. 

Second, can AID effectively implement a doubling of its program for assisting rural development, food production, and nutrition? My conclusion is that AID should be able to manage this increase with no major difficulty in part because a substantial part of this increase is to cover the higher costs. 

Third, will this increased assistance worsen inflationary pressures in the United States? Very frankly, it might in the next 12 months if poorly handled. In the longer run, however, it almost certainly should

contribute noticeably in the lessening of inflationary pressures in the 

United States. 

I believe that only in the case of fertilizer might AID's increased purchases be substantial enough to noticeably affect the price level. 

Thus, increased shipments of fertilizers could aggravate the already high prices in the United States if there were not the compensatory moves to decrease U.S. use of fertilizers for low-priority nonfarm purposes as suggested in House Resolution 1155. 

Fourth, will increased U.S. assistance at this time decrease that which will be provided by other rich countries, including notably the richer OPEC countries? My conclusion is it should not. In fact, it now appears that if the United States does not provide increased assistance to the Fourth World countries under the Foreign Assistance Act and under Public Law 480 in the magnitudes proposed by President Nixon and House Resolution 1155, this probably will jeopardize the supply of a substantial amount of increased assistance which other countries now condition on increased assistance from the United States. 

As this committee is aware, the U.N. General Assembly's Special 

Session on Raw Materials, held in April 1974, called on Secretary

General Waldheim to raise emergency assistance to help the most severely affected, or Fourth World, countries tide over the next 12 months. The Council of the European Economic Community has offered to increase its assistance by $500 million if the other rich countries will raise the balance for a fund of at least $3 billion, of which they would expect the OPEC nations to provide some $1.5 billion. My judgment is that if the United States is prepared to provide its share to this fund, the OPEC countries will more than match it. 

RECOMMENDATIONS OF THE OVERSEAS DEVELOPMENT COUNCIL (ODC) 

Finally, turning to my recommendations on page 19, the Overseas

Development Council has recently completed its second annual assessment of the issues involving the United States and the developing countries in its Agenda for Action, 1974, published in mid-April that many of you have had an opportunity to see. In it the council recommends a number of immediate actions, summarized below, which address the urgent problems posed by the energy, food, and fertilizer crises and are relevant to legislation now before this committee. 

First, we urge agreement by food exporting countries to set aside a portion of their food exports for transfer on concessional terms to the poorest countries. This is an issue that the U.S. Government is now debating and is covered by House Resolution 1155. 

Second, a parallel agreement by capital surplus, oil exporting countries to set aside a portion of their oil exports for transfer to the poorest developing countries on concessional terms, or to set aside a small portion of oil revenues for development, or both. This is now in process and, as I indicated earlier, they are likely to match us or more if we are prepared to move, too.

Third, agreement on a global system of increased food reserves to meet future shortages. This is still being debated in the U.S. Government. Hopefully, we will have a positive stance for the World Food 

Congress.

Fourth, a joint effort by the capital surplus oil exporters and industrial countries to help the poorest developing countries with their immediate and expanding needs for fertilizer. The immediate crisis remains with us; the foreign countries still have great difficulty buying here. That again is addressed by House Resolution 1155. 

Fifth, there should be an agreement to launch a worldwide effort to expand low-cost food production, with particular emphasis on the poorest countries, and early action on IDA replenishment. The latter has taken place and the legislation now before you is designed to cover that.

Finally, let me just say in conclusion that there has been some useful rhetoric coming from Secretary Kissinger on this set of problems. 

There is now an urgent need for the United States to support its rhetoric with concrete proposals, as the European Economic Community did in June, on the assistance it is prepared to provide in association with others to meet the critical needs of the most severely affected countries. The increased assistance for food production proposed under the Foreign Assistance Act for fiscal year 1975 and the increased food aid and fertilizer availability proposed in House Resolution 1155 could be the core of an appropriate U.S. participation in a much larger effort. 

[The prepared statement follows:] STATEMENT OF JAMES P. GRANT, PRESIDENT, OVERSEAS DEVELOPMENT COUNCIL 

Mr. Chairman and members of the committee, I welcome this opportunity to testify before the House Foreign Affairs Committee on the request by President Nixon that the authorization under the Foreign Assistance Act for FY 1975 for increasing food production, improving nutrition, and accelerating rural development be raised by $255 million to a level of $546 million. The Administration also proposes to allocate the majority of loan repayments to these purposes in FY 1975, raising the total to be made available to $675 million. This proposal allocates 60 percent (compared to 32 percent in FY 1974) of the total bilateral development program for achieving food and rural development goals. 

Several major considerations can be properly raised with respect to this request to increase the authorization by $255 million above that approved by the Congress in 1973, when it voted a two-year authorization for the development assistance components of the Foreign Assistance Act. Most important among these considerations is the question: have there been changes on the world scene of sufficient importance to justify a reexamination of the level authorized last year? But there are other important questions.

Has there been sufficient acceptance by the Administration of the new concepts of development assistance pioneered by the Congress last year to warrant confidence that these additional funds will be used in accordance with the spirit of the congressional priorities established last year? Can A.I.D. and the recipient countries effectively implement the doubling of A.I.D.'s programs directed at food, nutrition, and rural development? What effect will this expanded assistance effort have on inflationary pressures in the United States? Will this additional assistance make increased assistance by other countries, including in particular the newly rich OPEC countries, more or less likely? 

My recommendation to this Committee is that it authorize the full amount of the increase requested for the authorization for Food and Nutrition Assistance. While there are some risks and disadvantages from reopening the existing authorization for FY 1975, the dangers from not doing so are far greater. I also urge favorable action on the closely related House Resolution 1155, introduced by Congressman John Culver and co-sponsored by some 70 Congressmen, which 1 The views expressed in this testimony are those of the witness, and do not necessarily represent those of the Overseas Development Council, or others of its directors, officers, or staff.

MET חור calls on the United States to take the lead in a cooperative effort to ease the pending critical food crisis both by increasing food assistance to the most seriously affected nations and by taking measures to increase production-including making available more fertilizers for food production by reducing the present substantial use of fertilizers for non-farm purposes. 

The past year has witnessed mammoth changes relevant to the development assistance legislation. In my judgment a significant expansion of U.S. assistance to help increase food production abroad and to provide increased food aid at levels more comparable to those of two years ago should not only be of substantial direct help to developing countries to meet new problems but should also encourage comparable increases in assistance from others, including the richer OPEC countries. Increased assistance from both sources can- 

Save millions of lives, possibly as many as were lost in all of World 

War II, during the 1970's; 

Reduce the rate of inflation in the United States in FY 1976 and subsequent years; and

Contribute significantly to determine whether the relations between the United States and the developing countries in the mid-1970's will be characterized primarily by cooperation or by confrontation. 

Principal among the developments justifying reopening the issue of the appropriateness of the existing authorization are the following: 

1. The food, energy, and financial crises which have engulfed the world since last year's hearings on the present development assistance authorization have signaled a new order in international and political affairs, one characterized by a new global politics of resource scarcity. This new era is marked by widespread scarcities, a shift from the traditional buyers' market to a sellers' market for many commodities, shifts of political as well as economic power to resourcerich countries, a freshly impoverished "Fourth World" (worse off now than the rest of the Third World), global inflation, and a perilous food situation for much of the world.

The hearings on development assistance held before this Committee one year ago were focused on the need to bring progress to the poor majority in the lowincome countries. This need remains, but there is the additional need to examine the relevance of the tools of assistance to the new set of global problems, many of which now also affect the daily life of Americans. 

Two quite different sets of circumstances brought on the tight supplies and resulting jarring changes of the past year. One of these sets was comprised of short-term circumstances, primarily the business boom of the early 1970s (which caused all the industrial economies to expand at once for the first time since World War II), the unprecedented droughts (which diminished or wiped out crops), and the Mideast conflict (which restricted oil supplies). The second set of circumstances, made up of long-term trends accelerated by these shortterm factors probably will be seen in retrospect as the main causes of the recent shortage crises. These trends are rapid economic growth within a finite physical system and relatively inflexible political and economic structures. 

The responsive capacity of the world system was pushed toward its limits as global economic activity grew from $1 trillion in the late 1940s to about $4 trillion in 1974. As the $3 trillion level was reached in the late 1960's, signs of stress appeared-ecological overloads ranging from massive pollution to overharvesting of fish. Food-producing capacity was strained as the demand for food grew by 30 million tons a year to keep up with population growth of 2 percent a year, and as rising affluence, reflected in 3 percent yearly increases in per capita income, also made itself felt.

Economists and foreign offices (other than those in the OPEC world) have been slow to recognize the fundamental character of the change in progress—a change which in a period of less than 12 months has resulted in energy shortages throughout much of the world, soaring food prices everywhere, a host of related shortages, widespread speculation about the possibility of more OPEC-type situations in store ahead, and increased malnutrition and the prospect of an earlier death for many millions of people in poorer countries. 

As the world moves toward a more than $10 trillion gross global product by the end of the century, one can safely predict that- Competition among countries for the earth's limited resources will intensify;

A linkage effect will frequently set in, with shortages in one field limiting production elsewhere (as when energy shortages result in fertilizer production cutbacks, which, in turn, limit food production);

Product substitution will become more difficult; and 

Economic and, therefore, political power will continue to shift markedly from buyers to sellers.

In retrospect, it can be seen that these trends were well advanced by early December 1973. The doubling of oil prices by the OPEC countries on December 22, 1973-which raised oil prices in 1974 to levels most economists had not anticipated until 1980-has introduced a "system overload" which may be beyond the capacity of the international order to absorb without major chaos. It has also accelerated and brought into stark relief other important trends which must now be taken into account. 

2. A new Fourth World of some 40 of the poorest and slowest growing countries with a total population of nearly one billion people is emerging. These countries are so seriously threatened by the combination of soaring food and fertilizer prices on the one hand, and of skyrocketing oil prices on the other, that they face the prospect of disaster during the next several years unless there is a major, stepped-up international effort to assist them in meeting new threats that were not primarily of their own making. Many of these governments can be expected to topple under the new stresses.

International price rises and supply dislocations will require these countries to pay some $3 billion to $4 billion per year more than appeared likely one year ago for essential imports-with some 50-60 percent of this total going to OPEC countries for oil, and some 40-50 percent going to the United States, Canada, Australia, Japan, and other developed countries for the increased costs of food, fertilizer, and other critical imports. Additional amounts, some $1 to $2 billion annually, will be required if these countries are to incease their food production and indigenous production of energy so that they will be less dependent in the future on high priced imports when there are economic, domestic alternatives. 

3. The world food situation is dangerous, particularly for the developing countries, and considerably more so than was expected by most observers one year ago. World food stocks are at the lowest level since the World War II era. 

Reserves calculated on the basis of stocks in the major food-exporting nations and readily usable land being kept out of production are now estimated at 27 days of consumption-down from 36 days one year ago, and 90 days in 1970.

Thus, poor weather over any widespread area during the next 18 months would trigger an acute world food crisis.

A shortage of nitrogenous fertilizer production capacity ensures an even more dangerous food supply situation for important parts of the developing world for at least the next several years. Under current scarcity conditions for fertilizers, not only have prices trebled and quadrupled for developing-country buyers, but in addition the industrial countries, including the United States, which produce four-fifths of the world's fertilizer supply, themselves have preempted larger amounts and shares of the world's supply to meet their own increasing fertilizer needs. The result is that some developing countries have sharply reduced availabilities of fertilizer. The seriously reduced harvest of the Indian wheat crop this spring, which amounted to less than 23 million tons instead of the original estimate of 30 million tons, was due primarily to fertilizer contract cancellations by the Japanese and Europeans in the winter months and to the United States embargo on new fertilized sales introduced in October 1973. Shortages of oil for the irrigation pumps on which this Green Revolution crop is so dependent were also a contributing factor, causing a loss of 1 million tons in the Punjab according to the USDA. 

The adverse effects of this fertilizer shortage extend far beyond the immediate loss in production in the developing countries. The shortage also threatens to interrupt the whole forward momentum of the laboriously launched Green Revolution, which has focused on encouraging farmers to use new rice and wheat seeds whose profitability depends on heavy use of fertilizers. Many thousands of small farmers who have accepted the idea of the Green Revolution in recent years will now be faced with major difficulties. During times of shortages they tend to suffer far more than large farmers. 

With the industrial countries favoring their domestic needs (including low priority domestic needs) over the needs of the fertilizer-importing countries, the FAO projects a shortfall of 2 million tons of fertilizer in 100 developing countries

from autumn 1974 to spring 1975. This represents roughly 16-20 million tons of grains, or the normal consumption of about 100 million people, which will cost these countries some $4 billion in scarce foreign exchange. For food-importing developing countries, each $1 worth of nitrogenous fertilizer they are unable to import now will require $5 worth of high-priced food imports a year later. An 

FAO study concludes: "In the short-run there is no way of bridging the gap between expected demand and supply capacity additional to that planned so that the world has to live with a worsening shortage in the meantime.' 

Having embargoed new fertilizer sales because of rising domestic demand and lacking the food surpluses on which its food aid (PL 480) program so long depended, the United States-the food and fertilizer center of the world-is no longer implementing even the semblance of a global food policy beyond that of maximizing profits for agricultural exports. U.S. food aid this past year was onethird the volume of two years ago, and one-half of this greatly reduced amount went to Indochina. Meanwhile, the direct and indirect grain consumption of the average American has risen to approach one ton annually, and scarce fertilizer is used for such non-farm purposes as lawns, golf courses, and cemeteries in ever-increasing amounts which already exceed the total fertilizer shortfall in the developing countries. Against this background, the Administration's request to expand agricultural production assistance and House Resolution 1155 takes on a special significance and neither should be allowed to fail. 

House Resolution 1155 is correct in urging the President to restore food aid to FY 1972 levels (approximately 9.5 million tons) and to encourage the American people to reduce their non-farm uses of fertilizers-now requiring nearly 3 million tons a year-to make available increased fertilizer supplies for raising food production in the United States and in the developing world. The life-saving benefits it would bring to great numbers of people in the developing countries is obvious. The increased availability of fertilizers to American farmers should result both in increased food production in the United States and lower prices in our supermarkets. 

4. Events of the past year have vastly increased the problems of the poor' throughout the world, particularly in the poorest countries, whose prospects can be expected to deteriorate over the next several years. Barring major international action, the combination of a doubling to quadrupling of food and energy prices and the cutback on fertilizer exports dooms millions to premature deaths from increased malnutrition and even outright starvation. The only question, and one which Americans can influence, is: how many millions? 

Increased food prices are a serious enough problem in the United States, particularly for people on fixed incomes and the poor, but for a majority at least in this country food accounts for a relatively small percentage of total expenditures (some 17 per cent) and it is possible for many Americans to change their diet to lower cost by substituting cheaper but equally nutritious foods when prices rise. Most of us can move from beef to chicken and other products that are cheaper yet give us the same food value. In the poorer developing countries, such as those in South Asia and Central Africa, however, the effect of rising prices is much more serious for the average family which generally spends over 60 per cent of its income on food. In a city such as Bombay, the poorer half of the population spends over 80 per cent of income on food. Moreover, these high expenditures already represent a minimal level of consumption—since the average consumption of grain taken directly and indirectly is only 380 pounds per year, compared to a 1972 level of 1,850 pounds (up from 1,600 pounds in 1964) in the United States, and compared to 1,450 pounds (up from 1,100) in the U.S.S.R. 

Faced with the doubling of grain prices, the poor in Asia and Africa have no- I where to go but "down the nutrition ladder" into more acute malnutrition and greatly increased deaths from their weakened condition. 

5. The new era of increasingly tight supplies brings with it the need for greatly improved global management to increase resource availability if inflation rates of over 10 per cent are not to become a nearly permanent fixture. This is seen most clearly in the case of food. Rising global demand due to both population growth and affluence requires a 400-million-ton increase in grain production over the next 10 years, to reach approximately 1.6 billion tons by 1985. If the bulk of the increased food production required over the next decade is to come from the developed countries, the price of food will need to rise very sharply to cover the higher costs of producing it. New land can be put under cultivation in developed countries only at substantially increased cost, and increasing production through more in-

tensive use of inputs such as fertilizer is likely to be even more costly. In the developed countries, the use of inputs is at a point of diminishing returns for most crops. Each additional pound of fertilizer applied to an already heavily fertilized acre of corn in Iowa or of rice in Japan now yields only one-half to one-third the increased output per acre resulting from the first applications of fertilizer. 

On the other hand, if the bulk of the increase in production comes from developing countries, there may not need to be an increase in the cost of food. Because limitations of organization, financing, and applied technology have kept use of inputs low in most of the poorer countries, there are great opportunities for expanding production at very little, if any, increase in cost in these countries. 

An additional ton of fertilizer, for example, will produce 2-3 times as much additional rice and corn in South Asia as in Japan, Europe, or North America. According to one responsible source, to increase grain production by 100 million tons in developed countries will require 24 million tons of fertilizer; a comparable increase in developing countries would require only 10 million tons of fertilizer. 

The same contrast is seen in the use of energy in general. It now takes 10 calories of energy in the United States to produce one calorie of food, as compared to a one-to-one ratio fifty years ago. The developing countries, on the other hand, have large pools of underemployed labor which can be put to use. 

The potential for increasing yields at low cost in India and Bangladesh can be seen by contrasting their production with that in the United States and Japan respectively. India, for example, has about the same crop area as the United 

States, with many similar characteristics. If India's yields equalled those of the United States, its current annual production would be 230 million metric tons rather than the total of approximately 100 million tons. Similarly, if rice farmers in Bangladesh attained Japanese yield levels, rice production would jump from 10 million to 40 million tons. 

To ignore the potential of many developing countries for increasing food production at relatively low costs is to ensure higher rates of inflation throughout the world. Also worth remembering, as this Committee knows, is the fact that increased rural production in the developing countries (relying primarily on smaller farmers) not only would result in maximum production per acre but also would bring many of the ancillary benefits emphasized by this Committee last year-increased rural employment, decreased income disparities, reduced rural to urban migration, and lower birth rates. 

6. The world economic and political power structure is changing massively in favor of the resource-rich countries, both developing and developed. Countries such as Saudi Arabia and Canada are greatly benefited. Although the United 

States is the world's largest consumer and importer of raw materials, it is also the world's largest producer and exporter of raw materials. Thus the increased income from our higher-priced 1973 food exports approximately equaled our higher import bill for oil. Moreover, the United States dominates world grain exports to a greater extent than Saudi Arabia does oil exports. In 1973, North 

America provided 88 million tons of the 95 million tons that moved in world grain trade between regions-compared to 39 million tons in 1960 and 5 million tons in the mid-1930s. The countries whose economic and political positions are most weakened are countries such as Japan and Italy, which are largely dependent on imports for their raw materials and have no major raw material exports of their own. 

7. The danger of confrontation between rich nations and poor nations has greatly increased during the past year, even as tensions may have eased between the nuclear superpowers-the United States, the U.S.S.R. and China. Global shifts of the magnitude described above rarely take place smoothly. A principal global challenge is whether nations can accommodate to the structural changes required as a result of the progress of the past 25 years, or whether they will, by default, become locked into a pattern of chaos and conflict (analogous to that of the 1930s) which could sentence whole nations and much of mankind to massive suffering.

There is an urgent need for constructive dialogue and cooperation on at least two fronts as a result of this new resource-tight era. First, it is urgent to develop a new set of approaches to the international management of those commodities that are in relatively tight supply. Present practices smack of the law of the jungle and seriously threaten continuation of the rapid global economic progress of the past quarter century. This has been the threat from Arab embargoes on oil to advance Arab political aims in the Mid-East; from collaboration

east 25 

End a! between the Arab and non-Arab oil exporters to achieve a quadrupling of price to increase their income for development and U.S. embargoes on export sales of soybeans and on fertilizer to slow domestic inflationary pressures. 

Second, and equally important, special measures need to be taken to help those resource-poor countries which are most severely affected by the recent changes. The resource-poor group includes developed or nearly developed countries such as Italy and Korea, and, particularly, the new "Fourth World" of poorest nations. As has been graphically illustrated by the events of the past year in the Middle East, countries with major grievances have a frequently unexpected capacity to vent their frustrations on the international order. 

It should be clear from the above that there have been vast changes since the Foreign Affairs Committee reached its conclusions with respect to development assistance a year ago. The Committee's concern with accelerating the progress of the poor majority in developing countries remains as valid today as it was a year ago. Most of the changed circumstances of the past year, and certainly their net impact, call for an increased international effort to head off the threat of an acute world food shortage, which could bring millions more deaths in the poor countries and sharply higher food prices to the American consumer during the latter part of this decade. As indicated earlier, however, some possible negative factors need to be considered. 

1. Is there a serious danger that this increased assistance will be used primarily for financing major capital projects not affecting the poor majority? 

A.I.D. appears to be making substantial progress in reorienting its program to meet the new priorities set forth by Congress last year. Administrator Dan 

Parker is clearly making a major effort to restructure the A.I.D. program in these new directions, and news stories from such diverse countries as Indonesia, Pakistan, and the Philippines have been telling of the impact of these new congressional priorities on the A.I.D. programs in these countries. Equally if not more important, the thinking in the international development community is following the general lines espoused by the Congress under the leadership of this Committee last year. This is evidenced by Robert McNamara's annual address to the Board of the World Bank at Nairobi last September and the new IDA funding priorities favoring rural development and small farmers. While changes of agency actions (as distinguished from policies) usually come considerably more slowly than desired, A.I.D. seems to be making good progress in shifting programs to meet the new congressional directions. 

2. Can A.I.D. effectively implement a doubling of its program for assisting rural development, food production, and nutrition? A.I.D. should be able to manage this increase with no major difficulty, in part because a substantial part of the increase is required to cover the very much higher costs for some of the commodities. The price of fertilizers on the international market has more than doubled since early 1973. Moreover, the greatly increased cost of food imports is already compelling the governments of most developing countries to devote far greater management attention to increasing food production. This increases the opportunity for effective use of American assistance for the rural sector. 

3. Will this increased assistance worsen inflationary pressures in the United 

States? It might in the next 12 months if poorly handled; in the longer run, however, it certainly should contribute noticeably to lessening of such pressures. 

I believe that only in the case of fertilizer might A.I.D.'s increased purchases be substantial enough to noticeably affect the price level. Thus, increased shipments of fertilizer could aggravate the already high prices in the United States if there were not the compensatory moves to decrease U.S. use of fertilizers for low-priority non-farm purposes, as suggested in House Resolution 1155. 

Over the longer run, the expanded cooperative effort to increase agricultural production in the poorest countries called for by President Nixon should ease inflationary pressures. The events of 1973 demonstrated conclusively that it is no longer possible to insulate U.S. food prices from the outside world and that food prices in the United States are now determined by world price levels. As noted earlier, it will be far more cost-efficient for the world over the next 10 years to seek to produce in the developing, rather than in the developed, countries most of the additional 400 million tons of grain that will be required annually by 1985. 

4. Will increased U.S. assistance at this time decrease that which will be provided by other rich countries, including notably the richer OPEC countries? It

should not. In fact, it now appears that if the United States does not provide increased assistance to the Fourth World countries under the Foreign Assistance Act and under PL 480 in the magnitudes proposed by President Nixon and House Resolution 1155, this will jeopardize the supply of a substantial amount of increased assistance which other countries now condition on increased assistance from the United States.

As this Committee is aware, the U.N. General Assembly's Special Session on 

Raw Material, held in April, 1974, called on Secretary General Waldheim to raise emergency assistance to help the most severely affected, of Fourth World, countries tide over the next 12 months. The Council of European Economic Community has offered to increase its assistance by $500 million if the other rich countries will raise the balance for a fund of at least $3 billion, of which they would expect the OPEC nations to provide some $1.5 billion. 

The U.S. Government has affirmed to Secretary General Waldheim that it will participate in this emerging effort, but without specifying any amount or share. A fair share for the United States total should be at least one quarter, probably even a third, given the fact that we are much less hurt by the recent price dislocations than the Europeans or the Japanese. A U.S. contribution in the form of increased food and agricultural production assistance totaling $1 billion will be less than one-half of the more than $2 billion we will receive in 1974 from the developing countries as a result of our higher food prices. 

Canada and Japan are each reported to have offered to put up $100 million, and the Netherlands $30 million. Iran and Venezuela are also reported to have promised $100 million or more each; and Dr. Raul Prebisch has been conducting a round of discussions with the Arab countries in the past two weeks on behalf of Secretary General Waldheim. The Secretary General of OPEC has stated several times recently, but without substantiating detail, that the OPEC countries will provide assistance in 1974 in amounts greater than 1 percent of their GNP, i.e., more than $1.5 billion. This, however, includes assistance to such countries as Jordan and Egypt which, like U.S. aid to Vietnam and Colombia, does not qualify as aid to Fourth World countries.

This raises the issue of the extent of assistance which should be provided by the OPEC countries to meet the needs of the most severely affected countries. 

Most Americans have been pointing the finger at the OPEC countries, saying that these financially liquid countries should pay the increased costs of the developing countries. The OPEC countries have replied that the West ignores the fact that the West is part of the problem too. They have noted that the price of wheat, for example, had gone up almost threefold before the price of oil started going up sharply at all. They claim we should acknowledge that we, too, are contributing to the situation, and that only as we show our own preparedness to respond are they willing to be forthcoming in a major way. A second point they raise is: "What is a fair share?" In Saudi Arabia, even after the great increase in oil earnings, per capita income is about $3,000-compared to $5,000 in the United States. The United States today provides one-third of 

1 percent of its GNP as aid. If the Saudis were to provide the same proportion of their GNP it would come to less than $100 million. Most Americans, when they demand that OPEC countries do something, are really thinking in terms of billions of dollars; but such amounts represent several percent of the GNP of the 

OPEC countries. And this raises the very real question: Do we expect the newly rich Saudi Arabia-which, even with its new wealth is still much poorer on a per capita basis than the United States, West Germany, or Japan-to pay five or six times as high a proportion of its GNP for aiding the poorest countries? 

And if so, on the basis that their abrupt governmental actions jeopardize world order, for how long? There is a major need for an improved dialogue between the 

Western industrialized countries and the capital-surplus OPEC countries on this subject. 

RECOMMENDATIONS 

The Overseas Development Council has recently completed its second annual assessment of the issues involving the United States and the developing coun tries, The United States and the Developing World: Agenda for Action, 1974, published in mid-April. The Council recommends a number of immediate actions, summarized below, which address the urgent problems posed by the energy, food, and fertilizer crises and are relevant to legislation now before this 

Committee:

PI (1) Agreement by food-exporting countries to set aside a portion of their food exports for transfer on concessional terms to the poorest countries; (2) A parallel agreement by capital-surplus, oil-exporting countries to set aside a portion of their oil exports for transfer to the poorest developing countries on concessional terms, or to set aside a small portion of oil revenues for development, or both; (3) Agreement on a global system of increased food reserves to meet future shortages; (4) A joint effort by the capital-surplus oil exporters and industrial countries to help the poorest developing countries with their immediate and expanding needs for fertilizer; (5) Agreement to launch a worldwide effort to expand low-cost food production, with particular emphasis on the poorest countries, and early action on 

IDA replenishment; (6) Agreement on a cooperative effort to help all countries find substitutes for oil, including a) an exchange of information on energy technology, and b) financing by capital-surplus countries; (7) Agreement on such short-term financial support for the price-distressed poorest countries as debt postponement.

These actions would be mutually reinforcing if all or most of them could be secured. Their total impact would go well beyond dealing with immediate problems of the current economic turmoil to hold out the prospect of accelerated development.

CONCLUSION 

Secretary Kissinger, in my judgment, was acting very much in the global interest of the United States when, before the U.N. General Assembly's Special Session on Raw Materials in April, he spoke in favor of increased food aid and of a stepped-up cooperative effort to increase food production in the developing countries, and again reaffirmed the importance he attributes to the World Food Conference that will convene in Rome in November. 

There is now an urgent need for the United States to support its rhetoric with concrete proposals, as the European Economic Community did in June, on the assistance it is prepared to provide in association with others to meet the critical needs of the most severely affected countries. The increased assistance for food production proposed under the Foreign Assistance Act for FY 1975 and the increased food aid and fertilizer availability proposed in House Resolution 1155 could be the core of an appropriate U.S. participation in a much larger effort.

I agree with the statement in the lead editorial in the New York Times yesterday, July 9, on hunger in the world that: "Despite the experts' gloomy forecasts, it is not apparent that the scope of the problem is even now recognized-or admitted at the highest levels of the United States Government. The responsibility for formulating policy is fragmented and diffused. If headway is to be made toward solutions of the problem at the United Nations food conference in Rome in November, significant leadership will have to be exerted by the United States. "Somehow, between now and November, the United States will have to recapture and sustain the level of concern which prompted Secretary Kissinger to propose the conference in the first place. The effort will require the urgency and application of will and ingenuity that have been invested in detente and the Middle East. The problem is that big." 

In many ways, the world in 1974 is at a watershed comparable to that of the mid-1930s, when the world chose the wrong direction and proceeded on to World War II, or that of 1947, when the decisions taken led to a new cooperative world order which, for all its obvious imperfections, has taken the world to unprecedented levels of cooperation and prosperity. The need in 1974 is for a sense of vision and cooperation comparable to that of the late 1940s. 

The past year has clearly indicated what can lie ahead if, by preference or by lack of foresight, the law of the jungle, rather than cooperation, remains the response of nations. Many of the new problems of global scarcity brought on by rising affluence and increasing populations certainly should be amenable to alleviation, and possibly even to solution, through cooperative international action. The United States, the world's breadbasket and the major beneficiary (by over $6 billion) of scarcity-derived higher prices for its food exports, has

a special responsibility for helping the hardest-hit countries at least on the food aspects of the world economic crisis. By skillfully handling the world's most essential raw material-food-whose supply it dominates, the United States might also begin to pioneer and formulate new "rules of the game" for access to supplies, for increasing production to meet demand, and for the establishment of global food reserves-new rules that could be to the benefit of all nations in the management of increasingly tight supplies of essential global resources.

Chairman MORGAN. Thank you, Mr. Grant. 

Mr. Zablocki. 

EFFECT OF CHANGES ON FOREIGN AID Mr. ZABLOCKI.  

First, I know your enthusiasm, Mr. Grant. Though we asked you to limit your statement to 10 minutes, it is very difficult to summarize a program in 10 minutes.

On page 14 of your statement you say that there have been vast changes in the international situation since last year when the Congress enacted the new directions in foreign aid. Mr. Parker, director of AID, also mentioned changes.

Now would you for the record, not necessarily at the present time, specify some of the changes that indeed have been made by AID in order to move in the new direction? I realize that you said actions usually follow policy much more slowly, but if you would for the record give specific instances where the changes have been accomplished.

Mr. GRANT. I shall. 

[The information requested follows:] RESPONSIVENESS OF AID TO NEW DIRECTIONS 

The following are some of the specific instances of which I have been personally aware illustrative of the responsiveness of AID to the new directions set by the Congress last year.

Congress called for a shift in development assistance funding away from large-scale capital transfers toward increasing concentration in those func tional sectors which affect the lives of the majority of the people in the developing countries: food production, rural development and nutrition, population planning and health, education, public administration, and human resource development. AID's increasing concentration on the functional areas cited has meant that the Selected Problems and Selected Countries appropriations, which contained the bulk of the financing for large-scale capital resource transfers, constituted 30 percent of the FY 1974 program, but only 10 percent of the proposed 1975 program. AID also has established a "Task Force on the New Initiatives" composed of senior officials to accelerate the shift and to monitor and assist the shift in the program. 

With respect to the congressional mandate for AID to make greater use of private voluntary agencies in the development assistance effort overseas, and to provide greater support for private initiatives addressing the priority problems identified by the Congress, AID has taken a number of major actions. Thus, in late April AID called a two-day Development Assistance Policy Conference attended by some 150 private voluntary organizations to discuss AID's proposals in response to the congressional mandate and to elicit the response of the private organizations. In addition, AID has set aside some $11 million to assist the private voluntary organizations in expanding their developmental capacity and to enable them to launch new developmental activities overseas. AID will be working with private agencies this fall and winter on a wide range of issues that affect the developmental capacity of private organizations and their relations with the U.S. Government.

HOW DOES CONGRESS ENFORCE REFORMS? 

Mr. ZABLOCKI. If you were in the position of those of us in Congress who sponsored the reforms, what steps would you suggest to assure compliance with the new approaches? 

Mr. GRANT. Two general steps: First, I would recommend that you do as I understand you have been doing which is when you get the administration witnesses up here, hold their feet to the fire after the performance that they are making. I think it is very important to demonstrate to the executive branch that the changes introduced were not just a matter of whim or of transition. 

Second, where the administration does move in the right direction responsive to the earlier directions set by Congress it seems to me very important for this committee to be responsive. Now you called on the executive branch to do far more for rural development, food production, and this is what they now propose to do. With the increased amount of assistance they have asked for it would mean that 60 percent of the total development assistance budget instead of some 30 percent today will be earmarked for this purpose. I think that if you are prepared to provide additional financial support in this direction, it will accelerate the shift toward increased assistance to rural development and agricultural production from the loan repayment proceeds, the use of which are at the administrative discretion of AID. 

COST OF ODC RECOMMENDATIONS 

Mr. ZABLOCKI. Mr. Chairman, if I may ask a further question. 

You suggest seven points for action. What would be the total cost involved in them? For example, take suggestion 3, agreement on a global system of increased food reserves to meet future shortages. On page 9 you state that House Resolution 1155 is correct in urging the President to restore food aid to 1972 levels, approximately 9.5 million tons.

How much would this be in dollars, taking into account the increased cost of food? In your proposals for action, what would be the cost in dollar amounts?

Mr. GRANT. Well, for us to set aside a portion of our food reserves and to go back to fiscal year 1972 levels for food shipments, this would mean an increase of about 6 million tons from the present 3.5 million to 9.5 million and the cost would be approximately, with shipping, about $1 billion. That is one aspect.

On the part to engage in a cooperative effort to increase global food production, the additional costs I think are reflected by the administration's request for $255 million of new money plus greater use of loan repayment for this, an extra $350 million or so for food production.

I think it is worth noting, however, that this extra $14 billion from us will trigger at least $2 billion or close to that from others. 

If we assume that there are all sorts of adverse consequences that would flow from not doing this, it really means that we would be setting up a jointly funded new effort of which our costs would be about $114 billion.

FERTILIZER PRODUCTION IN INDIA 

Mr. ZABLOCKI. That is quite a bit of money.

I have one further question. You state on page 12, giving India as an example, what India could have produced in food if she had the amount of fertilizer that is available to farmers in the United States. 

Is it not true that India's fertilizer industry is operating at 40 to 50 percent of capacity? My question therefore, is, Are India and all other developing countries doing their share in coping with the problems that are confronting them?

Mr. GRANT. This is a very fair question. One of the real difficulties we found with the fertilizer industry in all developing countries is that it is a highly sensitive, highly complex industry of space age technology. The developing countries-whether it is Kuwait, Venezuela, India, Iran-have all had vast difficulties with their fertilizer plants, the urea plants in particular. 

My understanding is that the Indian plants have been running in the last couple of years between 55 and 65 percent of capacity. This compares with the plants here which are running close to 100 percent but for the developing countries generally it is somewhere in the 60 percent range. What this reflects is that when you get falling voltages these plants are very sensitive to it. It is very difficult to make spare parts locally; they have a major spare parts problem. I think AID is absolutely right in launching a major global effort with the World Bank using the TVA to try to get at these problems. 

I think we have to face the fact that the fertilizer plants are just so sensitive that it is unlikley in most developing countries they will operate at anything like our capacity. Given foreign exchange problems, which means oil shortages and the like, they are even more dangerous. The powerplants will run at the low levels and spare parts will be hard to get. So I would think that if we could help them get up to 70-75 percent, that is probably all we can look for in the shortrun. 

Mr. ZABLOCKI. Thank you.

Chairman MORGAN. Mr. Ryan. 

THE WORLDWIDE FERTILIZER SHORTAGE 

Mr. RYAN. Thank you, Mr. Chairman.

In talking about the fertilizer shortage, you quote an FAO study that concludes:

In the short-run there is no way of bridging the gap between expected demand and supply capacity additional to that planned so that the world has to live with a worsening shortage in the meantime.

Can you describe how we got into such a situation, and what is the short term that you refer to?

Mr. GRANT. Yes, sir. I will try to be brief on this one and say that as you may know the world fertilizer industry became badly overbuilt in the late 1960's as a result of the response to the great needs of the mid-1960's. This made the fertilizer industry reluctant to build new plants about 1970 and 1971 when the need began to become apparent again. Just about the time that a great number of new plants were to be built, the price of energy began to soar, and the economics of building plants in Japan, the United States, and Western Europe, which were the principal sources for export, came under question because of excess gas in the Middle East that did not cost anything. To haul it at a high cost to Japan and then manufacture and export it meant that somewhere down the line that plant was going to become uneconomic. 

The next generation of plants should be built for world export, and should be built in the oil countries. However, the big multinationals that have produced fertilizer are very reluctant to put one-half billion dollars into these oil countries at this stage of their own investment equity for fear of subsequent expropriation, which is understandable at this stage, I think.

Second, for the oil countries which have the capital surplus they are not yet enthusiastic about putting it into these plants because, first, as I indicated, they are very fragile plants, with lots of management problems.

Third, the principal market for this fertilizer for world export is the developing countries, and as you know as the result of recent events many developing countries are in great financial distress, not a particularly attractive market. So this is a situation where neither the traditional builders of plants, the multinationals in the Western countries, nor the newly rich oil countries have a real incentive yet to build. 

This is one of the issues that obviously should be considered at the World Food Conference and it has a very great consequence. 

INCREASING FERTILIZER PRODUCTION 

Mr. RYAN. How do we get the production increased to meet the demand?

Mr. GRANT. In the short run, the next 30 months- 

Mr. RYAN. Is that the short term that you refer to?

Mr. GRANT. Yes.-I don't see how we can get the production increased adequately to meet the demand. It is clear that something can be done. The question that Mr. Zablocki raised was: Can there be a massive effort to help the plants in India, the Philippines and elsewhere to move up from the 60 percent range to the 75 or 80 percent range? That would help.

Second, I believe that in the next 12 to 18 months there ought to be a major appeal to the nonfarm users of fertilizers to cut back just as there was an appeal to people to drive the 55 miles per hour and to turn down thermostats. We are using this year 3 million tons in this country, more than all the fertilizer used in South Asia for 800 million people, on our lawns and cemeteries and golf courses, and that sort of thing.

The average American who is using it for these purposes has no idea that this is closing off fertilizer that could be used both by the 

American farmers and by farmers overseas.

As you know, the American farmers have had something like 8 percent more fertilizer this year than last year because they needed it for the increased land that was put under production and because the higher grain prices made it profitable to put more fertilizer on the land. They could have used significantly more than was available, hence the widespread concern about a fertilizer shortage in the United 

States. 

There has been this shortage in the United States even though we have embargoed fertilizer export sales from October through the end of June, so that for food production purposes both here and overseas it seems to me there ought to be a major appeal to Americans to use less fertilizers for nonfarm uses, and I would hope that this committee could very seriously consider this question.

The Indians for the last year have been prepared to pay cash for the fertilizer because they know that for each dollar's worth they cannot buy now they will have to pay $5 out for food next year, and they have been short about one-half billion dollars worth of fertilizer that they want to buy.

INDIA'S NUCLEAR DEVICE Mr. WHALEN.  

Mr. Grant, the measure before us provides $75.5 million for India. 

Now there have been those who have argued that as a result of India's exploding a nuclear device, she has so distorted her priorities that we should cut out these funds. Do you have any comments on that observation?

Mr. GRANT. I must say like many Americans I feel very torn on this. My sense of dismay, frustration, and ire when the explosion took 36-333-74-39

place was really quite high. When one looks at the problem somewhat more dispassionately it seems to me there are two major different parts to it: One is how do we by our actions make less likely further and worsened nuclear proliferation? The second issue is how does any action we take affect our concern in working with India on another set of global problems which are of vital concern to us-the world population problem, the world inflation problem, the Law of the Seas, and the like.

My own conclusion after thinking about this is that on the nuclear proliferation side what we really ought to emphasize is how do we help the Indians keep to their stated promise that they are not going to move into a weapons system. That is interest No. 1. 

U.S. INTEREST: NO INDIAN NUCLEAR TRANSFER 

Interest No. 2 is how do we make sure that the Indians in their, let's say, desperate financial straits, don't transfer nuclear explosion technology to other countries such as Iran or Saudi Arabia which might be prepared to pay a very high price for it. 

We also have an interest in deterring others from doing this. A key question to be asked is: If there is to be a punitive measure, does it not better come out of the Japanese and the Canadians, who have refrained from going nuclear, rather than us who have gone nuclear, have made it quite clear in our foreign policy of the last 3 or 4 years that we consider being a nuclear power is the way you get into the big leagues. 

So I could see a lot of merit in our not taking the lead in closing off aid to India because of the nuclear explosion letting any closeoff's be led by other countries like Canada, and we then consider following if need be but emphasize now that we take the Indians at full faith and confidence that they are not going to go to a weapons system, and we assume that they are going to be internationally responsible, and in fact set a standard for the future. 

I would say that is much more likely to get the Indians to do what we want on the nuclear side than otherwise. 

THE COMING ECONOMIC CRISIS IN INDIA 

Then on these other problems we do have a very real issue here. of whether we should curtail our ability to work with India on them. 

India is a country that is going to face a really mammoth economic crisis in the next 18 to 24 months, and millions in my judgment are going to move down the malnutrition ladder very starkly. Are we really going to tie our hands on this?

Again if you want to deal with the world inflation problem, the potential for increasing grain production in India, 100 million tons. at low cost, is very great. This act proposes to work with them on that and basically will affect the world price of food 5 years from now. 

So my own judgment is that I would hope that there could be some language in the record that would clearly indicate our dismay and concern, and that would really frankly try to deter the Indians from going to the next stage, but do that in a way that would not tie our hands behind our back and prevent us from working with them on

these other sets of problems of food production, population, et cetera, that are really necessary for the global system. One-seventh of the world's people are in that country.

Mr. GRANT. OPERATIONS OF THE ODC 

Mr. Chairman, I understand you have several other witnesses. A number of questions have already been asked Mr. Grant and I won't take any additional time other than to suggest that it might be good for the general public as well as for some of us who are on the committee to have a little better understanding of how your Overseas Development Council operates, how it is financed, what your purpose is, what your interests are, and so forth. 

I understand you are president of the council. 

Mr. GRANT. Yes, sir.

Mr. FOUNTAIN. I wonder if you would give us a little synopsis for the record.

Mr. GRANT. The council was set up a little over 5 years ago by a group of private citizens who were very concerned with the U.S. relations with Asia, Africa, and Latin America, and they felt there ought to be a center of concern that engaged in research and stimulating public discussion and awareness on these issues. So the council has a research program, many writings. We conduct seminars at the council and elsewhere around the United States on these issues and contribute articles to publications like Foreign Affairs and Foreign Policy, as well as putting out our own publications. 

Where there is an interest in a congressional committee, normally it is on invitation that we testify. In other words, we don't seek to push ourselves on congressional committees. I would say that at this stage of time the council has become recognized as an important source of information. The New York Times in the lead editorial the other day said that some of the most serious analysis of the world economic scene today was coming out of the council. 

Mr. FOUNTAIN. I think you have a very impressive array of people on your board of directors, and I think it is good for organizations such as yours to be in existence and to have an interest in this field. 

I want to commend you for the interest you are showing in rural development, in food, in fertilizer, and in things of that kind, which I think are problems here as well as abroad right now, although maybe more so in the underdeveloped areas of the country.

A FOOD SHORTAGE IN THE UNITED STATES? 

What is your prediction, if you are willing to make one, concerning the possibility of a food shortage within this country within the foreseeable future?

Mr. GRANT. I don't see a food shortage in this country. What I do see is the possibility of higher prices. As you know, we are the world's biggest food exporter. In fact, it is not generally known but we dominate the world grain trade, the world food trade more than Saudi Arabia dominates the world oil trade. We and Canada provide something like 88 of the 95 million tons of grain that moved last year, even a higher percentage in the case of soybeans. So what really tends to push up prices in the United States since the food reserves vanished, which used to be a buffer for us, is the world demand for food. We are now at a place where if there is bad weather in the Soviet Union, or bad weather in China, bad weather in South Asia, that bad weather will get reflected in higher food prices here. This is one reason why serious attention needs, in my judgment, to be placed upon reestablishing some kind of buffer food reserve stocks for the world of the sort that we had before.

The earlier stocks were a byproduct of our farm income programs. 

We need a buffer to prevent bad weather in Russia from pushing up the price of food 30 percent in the United States. It seems to me that is an intolerable situation to be in. 

Referring back briefly to your earlier question, I should indicate for the record that our funding comes overwhelmingly from private sources. There are some 35 corporations that provide us with support. 

There are a half a dozen major foundations, and we as a matter of policy take very little money from the Government, and currently none.

[The information requested follows:] OVERSEAS DEVELOPMENT COUNCIL FUNDING 

During the twelve months ending December 31, 1973, the Overseas Development Council received total revenues of $689,792. Of this amount, $17,000 represented income from special projects; $4,820 for subscriptions to Council publications; and $21,842 was earned on investments. The balance ($646,130) was from direct contributions to the Overseas Development Council. The bulk of this support came from five major foundation grants, which totalled $465,000, ranging in amounts from $40,000 to $125,000. Thirty-four corporations or smaller foundations contributed a total of $170,860; and contributions from individuals totalled $10,270.

Mr. GROSS. Do you put out any publications critical of foreign aid?

i Mr. GRANT. Yes; we have put out publications that take negative views toward both foreign aid in general and towards specific aspects of it. This is under our policy that the council will sponsor publications that are worthy of discussion even though many of the people within the council might disagree with a particular point of view. 

Mr. GROSS. Do you get any of your money from importers or exporters?

Mr. GRANT. We get no money from firms that are exclusively importers or exporters. We do get contributions from firms like General
