STATEMENT OF SAMUEL P. HUNTINGTON, PROFESSOR OF GOVERNMENT, HARVARD UNIVERSITY Mr. HUNTINGTON. All right. 

Chairman MORGAN. Your statement will be made a permanent part of the record.

Mr. HUNTINGTON. First of all, Mr. Chairman, let me say I greatly appreciate the opportunity to appear here with you today since I was supposed to be here tomorrow. I know that you were going to be exploring this subject of arms transfers in much greater detail tomorrow with other witnesses and I regret that I cannot be with you then. 

I think it would be appropriate to view the statement which I have submitted to you today and which I will summarize briefly as a general prolog to the more detailed discussion of these issues which you will have tomorrow.

In my statement I would like to focus primarily on the problems of arms transfers to less developed or Third World countries. I would like to identify some significant trends in the overall development of arms transfers in recent years, to highlight what seem to me to be the political and economic actors responsible for those trends, and to discuss alternative general approaches which the United States might adopt toward this complex matter of arms transfer issues. 

Specific American decisions on arms transfers concerning what weapons to make available to what countries on what terms-are inevitably based at least in part on a more general set of underlying assumptions, attitudes, and policies which together constitute an approach to arms transfers. My principal point is that the two ap proaches to arms transfers which have dominated much recent thinking, which I think could be referred to as the "arms control" and "Nixon doctrine" approaches, are no longer compatible with the major changes taking place in world political and economic and military relationships, and that instead a new approach, something which might be called an "open access" approach, is more likely to serve American national interests in the light of these changes in the world. environment. 

PRINCIPAL TRENDS IN ARMS TRANSFERS 

Well, what are the principal trends in recent years in arms transfers?

First of all, there has been a tremendous growth, particularly in the last few years, in the total amount of arms transfers between countries.

Second, there has been a sharply accelerating rate of diffusion of sophisticated weapons, so that in some cases new sophisticated weapons enter the inventories of other states at almost the same time as they do that of the state which produces the weapons. 

Third, there seems to have developed in the past decade a relative stability in the major sources of weapons on the international scene, with the United States and the Soviet Union obviously being the major sources, Britain and France in close competition for a third place, and these four countries being responsible for perhaps 85 to 90 percent of the weapons which enter into global distribution. 

Fourth, there is the phenomenon which has come rather dramatically to attention in the past year or so of the rising importance of middie level powers as arms purchasers. These include not just oil states like 

Iran and Saudi Arabia but also Brazil, India, Taiwan, Argentina,

and other states which are reaching intermediate levels of development and have the incentives and the wherewithal to enter into arms purchases. 

Fifth, there would seem to be a diversification of supply sources on the part of the individual recipient states which are now in a better position to balance their acquision of weapons in a way not to become totally dependent upon any single supplier. 

Sixth, particularly among these regional states, the local regional Leviathans, there is clearly a sharp pattern of increase in their own. arms production. 

TREND: GROWTH IN INTERNATIONAL ARMS TRANSFERS 

All these trends point toward the growth in size and complexity of international arms transfer. It could be argued that this might just be a temporary or a transitory development. It seems to me, however, that this development does reflect the existence of some fairly fundamental, far-reaching, and at least for the foreseeable futureirreversible trends in the structure of global politics. 

These include, first, the economic development of the poorer countries in the Third World which gives them the capability of increasing their arms purchases. It includes, second, the diffusion of power, and particularly the development of local and regional rivalries and conflicts in a way which have not existed before. Third, and paradoxically it also includes the growing patterns of global integration and interdependence. There are striking parallels in many respects to these developments with respect to arms and the development of arms purchases and the way in which other types of capital goods have entered into the world trade and into world production. What is going on in the arms sphere is not all that different from what is going on in other spheres in connection with other commodities. 

U.S. POLICY ON ARMS TRANSFERS 

The question then comes up: Given these general trends and the fact that they seem to be deeply rooted in some fairly fundamental changes: in the world scene, what attitude is it appropriate for the United States to take toward them? As I indicate in my statement, the arms control approach is based upon the assumption that the transfer of arms will in general have bad effects particularly upon the recipient countries. No conclusive evidence exists, however, to demonstrate that these assumptions are valid in terms of the relationships they posit between arms transfers and their deleterious effects upon either stability or development or for that matter the tendency of the military to interfere in politics.

ARMS THE ARMS CONTROL APPROACH 

In addition to being based upon assumptions which seem to be unwarranted, the arms control approach also involves prescriptions. which, with some notable exceptions, have proved generally incapable of realization. The prescription for cooperative action by the supplier states has proved very difficult to achieve and efforts at restricting

DOTI da arms transfers have been almost unanimously opposed by the major recipient states. Unilateral actions to restrict the control of arms transfers generally have been counterproductive and certainly have not had any direct effect upon the ability of the potential recipient states to get arms.

ARMS: THE NIXON DOCTRINE APPROACH 

In contrast to the arms control approach, the Nixon doctrine approach stresses the extent to which arms transfers and particularly military_assistance can play a role in promoting American security as we reduce our overseas deployments of our own troops. The problem here is that, while military assistance and military grants can clearly play such a role in certain limited cases, the Nixon doctrine and the arms transfer corollary to it is really based upon assumptions about the cold war which the diplomacy of the Nixon administration has by and large invalidated. Consequently, apart possibly from the 

Korean Peninsula, Indochina, and a few other areas where the likelihood of Communist aggression seems real enough to pose significant threat to American interests, clearly most of the arms transfers which go on at the present time have only a very distant relationship to 

American security.

This leaves us, Mr. Chairman, with the problem of what attitude to take toward arms transfers given the difficulties in these two other ap proaches. Conceivably the United States could take a unilateral approach of restraining or trying to reduce arms transfers to a minimal level, yet it does not seem that this would work and it would undoubtedly involve certain costs, particularly political, as far as we are concerned.

DANGER: ARMS COMPETITION IN LOCAL REGIONS 

There is, I think, one very great danger which we must avoid. This is the situation where great powers become involved in arms transfers with particular states in local regions of the Third World which are in a highly competitive position themselves. We must not end up supplying one state or states and the Soviet Union or China end up being the exclusive suppliers to other rival states in a Third World region. 

Consequently, I would come down in favor of what is not perhaps an entirely happy alternative or approach, but one which it seems to me avoids the even worse evils of the other approaches and recommend a policy of relatively open access on the part of the United States with respect to arms sales to other countries. 

Chairman MORGAN. Dr. Huntington, we are going to take a short recess in order to answer the rollcall. Then we will be back. 

Mr. HUNTINGTON. All right. 

Chairman MORGAN. Please stay where you are. We will be back in about 6 minutes.

Mr. HUNTINGTON. All right.

Mr. HUNTINGTON. Sir.

RECOMMENDS SCALING DOWN GRANT MILITARY AID 

Mr. Chairman, I was about to conclude my oral statement, and I will conclude it now simply by saying that given the way in which world politics has developed, and particularly the dangers of great power involvement in regional conflicts, that a desirable course for a general American approach to the problem of arms transfers would include. 

First, the continued scaling down of grant military assistance and the restriction of such assistance to a very small number of countries whose defenses are vital to American interests and who lack the resources to purchase arms, or to countries who demand such aid as payments for base rights which are important to our security. 

Second, the removal of legislative and other restrictions on arms transfers.

Third, the articulation of a policy of open and equal access to arms through foreign military sales and commercial sales, recognizing that the specific terms of credit will vary with the particular circumstances of individual cases.

REMOVING LEGISLATIVE RESTRICTIONS ON ARMS 

Mr. ZABLOCKI. Thank you for your statement, Dr. Huntington.

In your closing remarks you reiterated what is contained in your written statement, on page 16, making specific recommendations for the removal of legislative and other restrictions on arms transfers. 

Would you have the Congress remove, for example, the restrictions on the transfer of arms to third parties which appear both in the sections on grant assistance and in the provisions relating to military credit sales, in the basic act?

Mr. HUNTINGTON. It is my impression, Mr. Chairman, that such restrictions are not terribly effective. I can see a somewhat greater case being made for grant military assistance since presumably the rationale for grant military assistance is that it does contribute directly to American security and consequently there should be assurance that the arms which are transferred clearly will be used for the purpose for which the grant was made.

1950 among Britain, France, and the United States to limit arms transfers to the Middle East. That lasted only so long as Britain, France, and the United States were able to dominate the situation in the Middle East, and when the Soviet Union came into the picture, that came to an end.

The Non-Proliferation Treaty has worked up to the present point because the superpowers have been able to dominate the nuclear field until the present time.

ARMS SUPPLY TO LATIN AMERICA

the 1940's and 1950's. In terms of major arms supplies to Latin America during the past 6 years we have only supplied something like 13 to 15 percent, and European countries have supplied 75 percent. The lesson I would draw from this rather dismal set of facts is that if arms control on the part of the supplier states is going to be effective, the supplier states have to be in a position to dominate or exercise some sort of hegemony in the particular arena or situation. Given the way in which the world is developing at the present time with a growing diffusion of power, I just don't see that capability.

[The prepared statement follows:] STATEMENT OF SAMUEL P. HUNTINGTON, FRANK G. THOMSON PROFESSOR OF GOVERNMENT, HARVARD UNIVERSITY ARMS TRANSFER POLICIES I. INTRODUCTION 

Mr. Chairman and distinguished members of the committee: I welcome this opportunity to respond to the Committee's initiative and to appear before you in connection with your consideration of the Military Assistance Program and Foreign Military Sales for FY 1975. These programs are, as you know, two components of a much larger pattern of arms transfers including commercial sales between the United States and other states, and American arms shipments are, in turn, only one component, albeit the single largest component, of an extensive global pattern of arms transfers. In my brief statement before you today, I will focus primarily on problems which come up in connection with arms transfers to Third World countries. I would like to identify some significant trends in the overall development of arms transfers in recent years, to highlight certain political and economic factors responsible for these trends, and to discuss alternative general approaches which the United States may adopt towards arms transfer issues. Specific American decisions on arms transfers, concerning what weapons to make available to which countries on what terms, are based inevitably at least in part on a more general set of underlying assumptions, attitudes, and policies, which constitute an "approach" to arms transfers. My principal thesis is that the two approaches to arms transfers which have dominated much recent thinkingwhich I would refer to as the "arms control" and "Nixon Doctrine" approachesare no longer compatible with the changes taking place in world political, military, and economic relationships and that a new "open access" approach is more likely to serve American national interests in the light of these changes in the world environment.

II. TRENDS IN ARMS TRANSFERS 

1. Growth in total transfers.-The past few years have seen a major increase in the total amount of global international arms sales. In 1971, the world total approximated $6.2 billion; the total for 1973 is estimated at $15 billion. During the 1950s and 1960s such transfers grew at an average annual rate of about 9%. 

Since 1969, the rate of growth has undoubtedly been substantially higher. 

2. Accelerating rate of diffusion of sophisticated weapons. As the major suppliers develop more sophisticated weapons, one would expect these weapons

1 eventually to find their way into the inventories of other states. What is significant, however, is that rate of weapons diffusion appears to be rapidly increasing. 

The gap between the time when a weapon enters the armory of a major producing state and the time when it is sold or otherwise transferred to other states, particularly less developed countries, is becoming less and less. 

3. Stabilizing oligopoly of suppliers.—In the early 1950s the United States and the United Kingdom were the only significant sources of supply of major weapons. 

The Soviet Union now rivals the United States, however, and France has equalled and at times exceeded Britain as a major weapons supplier. The sales efforts by the United States in the early 1960s directed towards Europe impelled the European countries to find markets in the Third World in order to sustain their aircraft and armaments industries. By and large, the United States and the Soviet 

Union each tends to provide about one-third of total arms exports, Britain and France each about ten percent of the total, and the remainder is divided among a large number of smaller suppliers, including West Germany, Canada, Italy, PRC, and Czechoslovakia. This pattern of supply seems to be stabilizing into a classic oligopolistic mold. 

4. Increasing importance of "middle level" powers as purchasers.-The rise in oil prices has only underwritten dramatically a more long range trend involving the emergence of a number of regional powers in the Third World who, because of size, raw material resources, rapid economic development, threatened security, or some combination of these elements, are now able and willing to purchase substantial quantities of sophisticated arms. These include oil states like Iran, Saudi Arabia, and Libya and also countries like Brazil, India, Taiwan, and Argentina. More states are getting more able to purchase arms and are more likely to do so. 

5. Diversification of supply sources on the part of individual recipient states.- 

During the 1950s, Third World states typically received arms transfers from one side or the other in the Cold War, and such transfers often took the form of arms grants rather than arms sales. In more recent years, as the Cold War has waned and as Third World states have become more able to purchase arms, they have also tended to diversify their sources of supply. Obviously, with two supplier states providing over half and four states supplying close to 90% of all arms exports, and with ideological and political factors remaining critically important, this diversification has not and cannot go very far. Yet the dramatic expansion of 

French arms exports in the 1960s and the continued growth of British exports as well as those of some of the smaller suppliers, has been clearly helped by the interest of recipient countries in minimizing their dependence upon any single source. 

6. Increased arms production in Third World countries.-At present, several countries located in Third World areas, such as Israel, India, South Africa, Brazil, and Argentina are in the process of developing substantial armaments industries. Other countries are trying to develop comparable capabilities. In some cases, these countries already have their eye on potential export markets for their products, and in due course Third World suppliers will play a much more significant role in the provision of less sophisticated weapons to their neighbors. 

III. FACTORS RESPONSIBLE FOR THESE TRENDS 

These trends all point towards the growth in size and complexity of international arms transfers. Conceivably, they could be the result of relatively shortterm factors which might weaken naturally or which could be weakened by conscious government policy. Total arms transfers to the less developed countries for instance, peaked in the late 1950s and then declined in the early 1960s, before reaching new heights in the later 1960s. The bulge of the late 1950s was due largely to the appearance of the Soviet Union as a major supplier for the first time, to U.S. stress on military assistance to "forward defense" countries, and to the initial transfers to some countries of sophisticated aircraft. The current bulge in transfers also obviously reflects some time-limited factors such as the initial availability of oil revenues in the Persian Gulf States. While these revenues are not likely to decrease, it does seem unlikely that Iran and Kuwait, for instance, will be able to sustain indefinitely their current levels of orders for military equipment.

More generally, however, it would appear that the trends in arms transfers identified above reflect fairly fundamental changes in the global environment which are both far-reaching and, at least for the foreseeable future, irreversible. 36-333-74-41

1. The economic development of the poorer countries.-While there are some notable exceptions (such as Japan), on a global basis the proportion of a country's peacetime gross national product devoted to military purposes tends to increase with its level of economic development. The relative success of the efforts to speed economic development in the Third World significantly increases the capacity of these countries to purchase or to build arms. The rate of growth of military expenditures in less developed countries has, indeed, been about twice the rate of growth of their GNP. It is, however, the expansion of the latter which makes possible the rapid expansion of the former. 

2. The diffusion of power.-The relative decline of the United States in world politics and the waning of the Cold War have opened up international politics in many regions of the Third World. Local rivalries and tensions are coming to the fore, replacing the dominance of the Free World-Communist World cleavage which tended to freeze and subordinate such conflicts during the 1950s and much of the 1960s. Regional politics in the Third World has been characterized by the rise of "local Leviathans" like India, Iran, Brazil, not to mention Israel and South Africa, which development in turn has stimulated jealousy and counterbalancing efforts on the part of weaker states in the region. Nigeria, Zaire, and Indonesia seem likely to assume comparable roles in Western and Central Africa and Southeast Asia. All these developments, reflecting a broad diffusion of power and influence, furnish the incentive for sustained arms acquisitions by both the local Levia hans and their apprehensive neighbors. 

3. Global integration.-This development is more nebulous but also, if anything, more important than the others. The growth in the arms trade parallels rather nicely the growth in world trade generally, and the pattern of arms acquisition in Third World countries is not unlike that which prevails with respect to other products. At first, a slowly growing market is supplied through imports; then arrangements are made for local assembly of imported components; facilities are then developed for full-scale local production to meet the local needs; and finally the limits on those local needs lead to the search for export markets. At present, the distribution of U.S. arms sales abroad does not differ greatly from the distribution of other U.S. exports. 

In the absence of a substantial decline in rates of economic growth, the reassertion of U.S. and/or Soviet political and military influence in the Third 

World, or a major movement toward mercantilism and national isolation on the part of many states, recent paterns of growth in arms transfers are likely to continue. If these assumptions are correct, what overall approach or perspective should then inform U.S. policy decisions in this area? In recent years, much 

American thinking on this subject has reflected one or the other of two such approaches. 

IV. THE ARMS CONTROL APPROACH 

This approach has basically rested upon the assumption that arms transfers in general are likely to produce more harm than good and that consequently efforts should be made to limit and control them insofar as that is possible. The principal evils seen as resulting from arins transfers, particularly those to less developed countries, affect the recipient countries. Arms transfers, it is held: (1) Tend to increase international tensions in the recipient area, to promote arms races, and to enhance the probability of military conflict; (2) Tend to affect adversely the economic development of less developed countries, by diverting foreign exchange, economic resources, and trained manpower from constructive to nonconstructive purposes; (3) Tend to strengthen the military forces within the polity of the recipient state, thereby increasing the likelihood of military intervention in politics and increasing the government's repressive capability; and (4) Seldom are directly relevant to actual security needs of the recipient state but instead involve "wasteful" investments in prestige weapons. 

The last of these four propositions is in large part justified, although it also appears likely that only in rare instances are less-developed countries induced through coercion or sales pressure by supplier states to invest in weapons they do not "need." More generally, countries buy weapons because they want them, for either foolish or wise reasons. With respect to the first three assumptions which underlie the arms control approach, however, the evidence is quite inconclusive. There is no basis for thinking that any one of these three propositions is generally true, although obviously each may be true in varying degrees in particular circumstances.

15 The arms control approach thus begins with assumptions which are unwarranted by the empirical exidence. It concludes, on the other hand, with prescriptions which are, in general, incapable of realization. These involve restrictions on arms transfers either unilaterally by one supplier or collectively by several suppliers or jointly by suppliers and recipients. The evidence suggests that joint restrictions by suppliers and recipients only occur when they are part of a deal to transfer arms from one state to another and are made by the supplier as a condition of the transfer (e.g., prohibition of retransfer of arms). More general efforts to enlist the support of large numbers of supplier and recipient states in measures which might be interpreted as arms transfer limitations (such as the Maltese resolution on registration of arms transfers) have failed because of the intense opposition of recipient states. 

Collective restrictions have been somewhat more effective. The Tripartite 

Agreement of 1950 to limit arms deliveries to Middle East states was maintained for about five years until the Soviet Union appeared on the scene. The Non- 

Proliferation Treaty has to date been adhered to, but again could fall victim to the activities of France, China, or other states which have refused to sign it. 

In general, any collective effort to restrict or prohibit arms transfers may, at any particular time, be in the interest of some major suppliers, but other suppliers either exist or will come into existence in order to take advantage for either political or economic motives of the unmet demand for weapons. 

Unilateral actions suffer even more dramatically from the same weaknesses. 

Unilateral restrictions could only work where the supplier state is in a politically and militarily dominant position vis-a-vis the recipient state or states. For twenty years after World War II, the United States had for all practical purposes monopolized the supply of weapons to Latin America. In the 1960s, the 

United States attempted through a variety of measures to prevent the acquisition of certain sophisticated weapons by Latin American states. These restrictions reflected, in effect, the assumption that the United States could use its monopoly power to determin what weapons Latin American countries could acquire. The result was almost entirely negative in its consequences. Latin American countries resented the restrictions and reacted by drastically increasing their arms purchases from European states: between FY 1968 and FY 1972, Latin American countries ordered $261 million worth of arms from the United States and $1,320 million worth of arms from European countries. In addition, both Brazil and 

Argentina accelerated their efforts to develop their own arms production capacity, Argentina's taking the form of a "Plan Europa" which was "explicitly designed to seek coproduction arrangements with European arms manufacturers as an initial step toward developing an independent Argentine military production capacity." ." Unilateral restrictions thus may serve the purpose of indicating the supplier state's disapproval of actions taken by the recipient state, and they may also (as in the case of Peru's purchase of Mirages) increase the cost to the acquiring state, but they are unlikely to deter that state from obtaining the arms which it desires, and they may even stimulate it to take more active measures to insure its continued access to arms in the future. In a world characterized by a diffusion of power, the ability of any supplier state to prevent a recipient state from acquiring arms will become less and less likely. 

The arms control approach is thus based on false assumptions about the consequences of arms transfers on the recipient states and false assumptions about the capabilities of supplier states to control those transfers. 

V. THE NIXON DOCTRINE APPROACH 

The arms control approach stresses the harm done by arms transfers to the recipient states. The Nixon Doctrine approach stresses the benefits of arms transfers for American security. The basic rationale here, of course, is that the 

United States must maintain its treaty commitments to assist its allies in their defense. It should do this by providing a guarantee against nuclear threat and by assisting its allies through equipment and training to play the major role in defending themselves against conventional attack. The role of American general purpose forces in meeting this contingency will be, in turn, reduced. "In cases involving other (than nuclear) types of aggression, we shall furnish military and economic assistance when requested and as appropriate. But we shall look to the nation directly threatened to assume the primary responsibility of providing 

1 Luigi Einaudi, Hans Heymann, Jr., David Ronfeldt, Cesar Sevesavas. Arms Transfers to Latin America. Toward a Policy of Mutual Respect (RAND Corp., R-1173-DOS, June, 1973), p. 41.

the manpower for its defense * **" Presumably arms transfers, both under

MAP and FMS, can play a major role in achieving this goal. As American forces overseas are drawn down and as the contingencies in which it is likely that American troops would be committed to action decline in number, arms transfers presumably should increase to bolster the "self-help" and "local initiative" of our allies. 

The Nixon Doctrine approach thus sees arms transfers as a means of providing for the security of the United States and its allies aganst threats of communist aggression. The priority which has been given over the years to aid the 

Greece, Turkey, Iran, Thailand, Taiwan, and South Korea, underlines this point. 'The problem here is that the Nixon Doctrine is, in large part, only a slightly different way of implementing the goals which were central to American policy in the Cold War. It represents a change in means, not a change in purpose or a change in the assessment of the nature of the threat to American security. 

In fact, however, the basis of the Nixon Doctrine has, in large part, been undermined by the diplomatic achievements of the Nixon Administration. Apart from the Korean peninsula and Indochina, the likelihood of communist aggression which would threaten American interests seems relatively remote. The very improvement in American relations with the major communist powers which has made it feasible to reduce American forces overseas also weakens the Nixon Doctrine rationale for providing substantial arms transfers to enhance American security. As Stephen Gibert has rather nicely put it: "An important justification for reducing troops-the diminishing Chinese threat-renders it difficult to justify billions in aid which permits the removal of troops *** the countries that can most affect U.S. security do not need U.S. aid; the fate of the aided countries, with few exceptions, can only marginally affect U.S. security." 

What is true of military assistance is even more true of foreign military sales and commercial sales. It would be extraordinarily difficult, for instance, to defend the current Iranian arms buildup as essential to American security. 

That we have an interest in the stability and security of the Persian Gulf is undeniable, but that these goals require the form of Iranian military hegemony in that region which the Shah apparently seeks is dubious, to say the least. These arms transfers clearly contribute to the expansion of Iranian influence in the Gulf and Indian Ocean areas; they do not make any direct contribution to 

American security, particularly American security against communist threats. 

Given the improved relations between the U.S. and China and the Soviet Union, as well as the predominance of local rivalries in most of the Third World regions, only in rare cases, such as for instance, South Korea, is there a basis for justifying arms transfer in terms of their countering direct threats to the security of the United States and its allies. The only other significant security rationale for military grants is where such grants serve as rental payments for base rights (Ethiopia, Morocco, Thailand, Philippines) which are necessary or convenient to the U.S. in counterbalancing the major communist powers. 

VI. AN OPEN ACCESS APPROACH TO ARMS TRANSFERS 

39 8 Arms transfers, it would thus seem, are unlikely to do identifiable harm to recipient states and unlikely (except in a few cases) to make readily identifiable direct contributions to American security. Yet clearly the basic trends toward economic development, power diffusion, and global integration mean that arms transfers will continue to be a major feature of global politics and probably one of increasing importance. There will be a sustained and probably increasing demand for arms by Third World countries, as their level of economic development improves and as their level of regional rivalry and conflict increases. The question is: To what extent and how should the United States participate in these transfers?

American decisions on arms transfers should be guided, first, by our overall political and security objectives, and secondly, by our economic interests. In terms of U.S. security concerns with respect to Third World regions, one critical factor concerns the local rivalries which are coming to the fore and are likely to come to the fore in these regions. The past few years have seen the emergence 

Richard M. Nixon, U.S. Foreign Policy for the 1970s: A New Strategy for Peace, 

February 18, 1970, p. 56. 

Stephen P. Gibert, "Implications of the Nixon Doctrine for Military Aid Policy," 

Orbis, 16 (Fall 1972), p. 680.

21 in many regions of locally dominant regional powers. In response to this development, the second strongest power in the region usually attempts (a) to develop its own military and economic strength; (b) to ally itself with other regional powers against the locally dominant state; and (c) to promote a global superpower presence in the region to counterbalance the local Leviathan. 

By and large, American security policy towards the Third World regions should be directed to: (a) developing and/or maintaining close relations with the strongest local power, whose interests in protecting the stability and security of the region will often coincide with our own; and (b) developing such close relations with the local Leviathan in such a way as not to antagonize other states in the region and, in particular, so as not to encourage them to become wholly aligned with or wholly dependent upon the support and assistance of the Soviet Union or, when relevant, Communist China. These somewhat conflicting priorities thus involve, on the one hand, a close or even special relationship with the locally dominant power, and, on the other, an even-handed approach to all powers in the regions. The implications of these objectives with respect to arms transfers would appear to favor an open access policy of general willingness to supply arms to those ready and able to pay for them in cash or on reasonable credit terms. 

This would mean the application on a general Third World basis of the policy of "mutual respect" in arms transfers which Einaudi and his associates have recommended for Latin America. In their words, such a policy would involve: 

(1) "The elimination of grant material assistance ✶ ✶ ✶” (2) "The termination of legislative and other restrictions * * *" on military transfers; (3) "The provision of sufficient government credit through the Foreign Military 

Sales system to facilitate the competitiveness of U.S. equipment ***"* 

The facts of the matter are that Third World countries want arms and are, in many cases, increasingly able to purchase them; that they will not lack for suppliers; and that they want such arms not to defend themselves against Communist aggression but rather as instruments in their rivalries and conflicts with other Third World powers. In such a situation, the alternatives for the United 

States are: (a) to provide arms to neither side; (b) to provide them only to one. side; or (c) to be willing to provide them to all parties. 

To follow the first alternative would involve significant loss of political influence for the United States in the affected region and a loss of potential leverage with which to achieve other goals in that region. It would also involve certain small but real economic losses in terms of our balance of payments, a loss which would increase in the future with the increasingly sophisticated weapons. 

The second alternative would, in many respects, produce even more undesirable consequences. For if the U.S. transferred arms to only one side in a local balanceof-power rivalry, the other side would procure its arms elsewhere, and this could well lead to competitive great power involvement in local conflict. It would directly counter American interests in maintaining an even-handed stance with respect to regional rivalries. A policy of open access, on the other hand, does provide a reasonable impartiality, on the one hand, and will, in most cases, have the consequences of favoring the stronger regional power (which will be in a better position to purchase arms), which is also likely to be in American interests. With a view to minimizing their own dependence, the states procuring arms from the United States will in most cases be obtaining arms from other major suppliers also.

In this connection, it is perhaps appropriate to take note of the argument advanced by advocates of the arms control approach that it is "senseless," "ridiculous," and evidence of the "bankruptcy" of policy for the United States to supply arms to two countries which have used or are likely to use them against each other. The classic instances involve, of course, India vs. Pakistan, Israel vs. Jordan, Honduras vs. El Salvador, and, for the future, possibly Iran vs. Saudi Arabia and Greece vs. Turkey. Yet those who make this point invariably fail to indicate which alternative they would prefer. Would conditions in the 

Middle East be better if Jordan were supplied by the Soviet Union and Israel by the United States or if Iran got her equipment from the USSR while Saudi Arbia got it from us? Or would it be preferable for all these countries to secure their arms from the Soviet Union or some other country? The fact that both 

4 Einaudi, et al., Arms Transfers, p. 65.

countries in a regional rivalry get their arms from the same supplier can have and has had a moderating effect on that rivalry, and it is clearly in the interests of the United States that it be in this position rather than one of the other superpowers. As international rivalries percolate up in Latin America, for instance, particularly over the role of Brazil vs. Argentina and Brazil vs. the 

Andean Pact countries, it would obviously be most unfortunate if the United States ended up supplying one side to these disputes and the Soviet Union furnished the other side. 

In general, then, I would urge that American policy towards arms transfers avoid the unrealities of the arms control approach and the Cold War focus of the Nixon Doctrine. This does not mean that these approaches are totally invalid: 

We should do all we can to sustain the Non-Proliferation Treaty and we cannot ignore the security threats which exist in the Korean peninsula and Indochina. 

But in general our policy towards arms transfers should be guided by the principle of open and equal access, except where such access runs clearly counter to the needs of national security. In specific program and legislative terms, this would mean : (1) The continuing scaling down of grant military assistance and the restriction of such assistance to a very small number of countries (a) whose defense is vital to American interests and who lack the resources to purchase arms, or (b) who demand such aid as payment for base rights important to our security; (2) The removal of legislative and other restrictions on arms transfers; (3) The articulation of a policy of open and equal access to arms through foreign military sales and commercial sales, the specific terms of credit, of course, necessarily reflecting the particular circumstances of individual cases.

Mr. BRANFMAN. Well, the major point that I would like to stress in my oral presentation this morning is that I think it is quite necessary (639)

to see the administration's aid request for Indochina in the larger context of what has become one of the dominant phenomena of this latter half of the 20th century, a phenomenon which we chose to call Presidential covert warfare. It is not limited to the United States, of course; other executive branches of other superpowers practice it. I think, of course, the part that does concern us is that done by the U.S. executive branch, which of course is also far more than has been done by any other superpower since the end of World War II. 

We see this Presidential covert war in places like Ethiopia, the Congo, the Philippines, and Iran, but of course the most dramatic example of it is in Indochina. Some of the more obvious signs of it is the fact that the administration is proposing more for Indochina this year than the rest of the world combined. 

FOOD FOR PEACE: ALMOST HALF TO INDOCHINA 

Another example, which you will see in chart 2 of my introductory statement, is that almost half of last year's food-for-peace shipments went to Indochina. This means that 0.8 percent of the world's population received almost as much food as the rest of the world. And this occurred when, for example, 100,000 people were starving to death in Sahel. We sent seven times as much food for peace to Indochina as the Sahel.

Another particularly dramatic example is the fact that 350,000 people are said to have been killed or wounded in Indochina since the cease-fire-far more than all wars in the rest of the world combined in the last 18 months as far as we can tell.

In talking about how this happened, I think it is important to understand how the phenomenon of Presidential covert warfare is working in Indochina. I stress four aspects of this on page 4 of my statement which I would like to explain a little bit more here. 

When we talk about Presidential covert warfare, what we are talking about is the practice by the executive branch of committing large amounts of American materiel and small amounts of American personnel to back up a local administration in a place like Laos or Cambodia or South Vietnam and to try and keep that administration in power. For example, in Indochina the American people, and I think Congress, are tired of waging war. So the Executive has made it covert, which we will define not so much as secret but as disguised and hidden, an attempt to present a war as something else. 

At least 88 percent, if not more, of the budget which is being presented this year as Indochina postwar reconstruction is actually for war. In my paper I present a number of other examples of how the 

Executive covertly disguises what is war-funding by necessarily trying to deceive the American people and Congress, trying to manipulate public opinion in order to obtain its funding. 

VIOLATIONS OF THE CEASE-FIRE IN VIETNAM 

After I go through each of these examples and they are only examples-in some detail, I point out on page 9 that if, for example, the administration admitted that the Government of South Vietnam is taking much of the initiative in violating the cease-fire in South

Vietnam, which as I point out is the case; if the administration admitted publicly to the Congress and elsewhere that it has reneged on a promise made to the other side to withdraw American advisers after 12 months; if the administration admitted that we spent far more money in Indochina than do the Soviets and the Chinese, and in fact they cut their aid last year whereas we increased it; if the administration admitted that Thieu has a great number of political prisoners; if the administration admitted that we are not showing the proper kind of humanitarian concern, for example, by removing the various mines that lay strewn over the South Vietnamese countryside; if the administration admitted that the other side's military pressure on Thieu is relatively minimal, that the other side is interested in a political settlement; if the administration admitted that U.S. aid is endangering a coalition government in Laos, that we are supporting the rightwing faction and not the Provisional Government of National Union, as a number of administration witnesses have testified to this committee; if the administration admitted that Food for Peace moneys are still going to aid the military in Laos and South Vietnam and Cambodia despite a congressional prohibition against doing so if the administration were to admit all these things which are documented in my report, and of course one can come up with many more examples, I think it would not receive the kind of funding it wants in Indochina. 

I think the American people would realize in effect we are committed to war there and would stop it. Therefore, the first aspect which 

I do want to stress is that Presidential covert warfare involves attempting to attain a great deal of funding through a necessary manipulation of the domestic public opinion. 

MILITARY-BASED GOVERNMENTS IN VIETNAM 

The second key aspect that I want to stress is that it involves trying to maintain narrow-based, military, local administrations and power. This is true in South Vietnam; this is true in Cambodia; and it may well be again true in Laos if the coalition government falls apart from our continued unilateral support of the rightwing forces. 

In South Vietnam-our side has been unwilling to engage in political competition with the other side. It has not even tested their offer to do so. As a result, the war continues. The war continues because we won't at least test the other side's offer to negotiate politically. We have a 1.1-million-man army which is not being demobilized. 

We have a huge source of civil servants. We have a huge number of refugees who are not being allowed to return to their homes, most of whom have to be fed from the outside and supported by aid. 

PROBLEM OF CORRUPTION IN SOUTH VIETNAM

This appears on page 13 of my statement. I just listed them there in one paragraph and this is only basically during April, May, and June. 

South Vietnam has very serious economic problems-and no one should underemphasize them. They are causing terrible starvation

in many areas, they are causing hardship, there are reports that they are causing suicides. But these economic problems are not due to a lack of aid, not because we have not given them enough. On the contrary. As I mentioned a moment ago, we gave them as much Food for Peace last year as we gave to the rest of the world combined. The reason is there is an ongoing war and corruption. For example, our 

Food for Peace is not reaching those who need it. 

The third and fourth aspects are fairly obvious and I won't take too much time this morning since we agreed to limit it to 5 minutes.

The first key aspect was funding, the second was a commitment to these narrow-based military administrations. The third aspect is due to the fact that these governments are military oriented, because they have minimal support from their own people. PRESIDENTIAL COVERT WARFARE 

Fourth, and I think really the key to it all, Presidential covert warfare ultimately comes to mean one of the most ambitious attempts to control whole populations of people that we have seen in this century. Originally the emphasis during the sixties was on refugee programs, the result being that now we have 14 million people out of 28 million in the three countries of Indochina who have become refugees.

They use this police force, in a word, to try and control the population. They use this police force to both isolate the insurgents as well

World Bank study because it is an essential document. It contains the most credible statistics now available or at least the most credible detailed statistics possible on the fundamental economic problems. 

But the World Bank accepts some impossible assumptions; for example, that inflation will not get too much worse and that somehow the PRG will just disappear.

Even with such presumptions, the World Bank suggests that the aid needs to Vietnam will be something on the order of $770 million a year until 1980 and $450 million a year or more into the 1990's. The 

World Bank and AID appear to have two different countries and two different sets of economists and I think it is rather obvious why. 

AID also argued that, because the committee and the Congress cut aid last year, development was not possible. In point of fact the total economic aid that went to Vietnam during fiscal year 1974 was much higher than the $475 million originally requested because the Food for Peace total went up and piasters purchases went up. Consequently, aid was raised, not cut. 

There are other problems that stand in the way of development, most particularly the consumption of resources which we document at some length. In addition the kinds of development policies that are pursued by AID are fundamentally not apropos to the economic realities of Vietnam, especially trickle down development, and capital intensive agriculture in a capital poor country. 

Development is not an apropos term because the money does not go for development. The money goes for commodity import stabilizing. 

About $360 million of $400 million of the AID money last year went for commodity stabilizing. 

REFUGEES AND PROGRESS IN VIETNAM 

AID had more specific arguments also. They argue that, for example, the number of refugees declined in fiscal year 1974 and this was an indication of progress while Mr. Block suggested that it was not

so much the number of refugees as what happened to them after they resettled. In addition, if one believes AID and the Vietnamese Government that the number of refugees is down, why is the amount requested for refugees going up?

AID also argued that taxes went up and this was a sign of progress. 

I think if you investigate the tax system you will discover what they are talking about is indirect taxes. This is an unhealthy and inappropriate method of fiscal growth. I think this indicates again the narrow run political base by what is possible to tax and what is not possible. 

The sum of all these AID efforts is what one could, if one were going to be pejorative, call propaganda. I think even a casual look at 

AID's own statistics in Vietnam Economic Data which it publishes quarterly would sustain conclusion very different from what they present to Congress.

There have been quite a lot of what one might call Cook's tours to Vietnam recently, both by staff aides and by Congressmen, particularly on the Senate side. I think the effect of this propaganda is probably kind of mixed. I hope that people who have been involved in this and people who have thought about this will weigh, for example, the impressions that one might get of a refugee camp by visiting it one time against the kind of perspectives that someone like Ed Block could bring by working with all the refugee camps for a period of 12½ or 2 years and knowing the cultural and political context over time and how and why these camps operate as they do.

CONDITIONS IN VIETNAM: "NOT ABSOLUTELY BLACK AND WHITE” 

Conditions in Vietnam, of course, are not absolutely black and white. There are comparatively humane refugee camps and incidents of healthy development. There are terrible refugee camps and terribly institutionalized corruption. What we are arguing is that conditions are sufficiently bad that the Congress, the American people, and the Vietnamese people should be looking for concrete alternatives and we propose two. One could suspend nonhumanitarian aid-incidentally, the humanitarian aid is a very tiny percentage of this so that it is a rather large cut-until certain political provisions, kinds of compromise that are envisioned in the Paris agreement set before you and set before the Vietnamese are carried out. This could be accomplished in a very short period of time. We are not talking about a period of 6 months or a year, we are talking about a period of perhaps several weeks.

Our second proposal is that the Congress could adopt a policy of a substantial cut and put in effect all-inclusive country ceilings for the programs to Vietnam and Cambodia. My feeling is if the Congress wants to pursue an alternative policy it will only do so successfully with a ceiling lower than perhaps $200 million for Vietnam or $300 million total to Indochina which means a cutting from last year's authorized level of $504 million.

I will stop there and if you like I can go into what I have in mind in some detail..

STATEMENT OF FREDERIC R. BRANFMAN, CODIRECTOR, INDOCHINA RESOURCE CENTER PRESIDENTIAL COVERT WAR AND U.S. AID TO INDOCHINA INTRODUCTION 

On of the dominant, if least understood, facts of this latter half of the twentieth century is that we have entered an era characterized by a new form of war-making, a phenomenon we call Presidential covert war. 

By this we mean that Executive leaders of today's superpowers have opted away from conventional or nuclear war and toward war by proxy-"lowprofile" war, in which they rely on intensive use of technology and relatively few technicians to wage clandestine war abroad largely without the knowledge or consent of their own people. 

There are many examples of such Presidential covert war today from our support of Hailie Selassie against his Eritrean opponents, to our interventions in the Congo and Philippines, to our heavy involvement in Iran. The most dramatic we find the Administration heavily involved in war in Indochina. 

Most Americans are overwhelmingly opposed to our continued war-making in Indochina, and gratefully believe that we are out. After years of demonstrations, letter-writing, draft resistance, civil disobedience, editorials and congressional hearings, the U.S. Congress has responded by making clear its desire that we disengage.

Despite this public and congressional mandate for disengagement, however, we find the Administration heavily involved in war in Indochina. 

The Administration is proposing to spend $3.7 billion for Indochina, more than for the rest of the world combined (see Table 1, Appendix, p. 879). This will provide the Thieu and Lon Nol governments with 90% of their total resources, including all of their war materials. 

Food For Peace to Indochina in FY 74 totalled 49% of worldwide shipments, meaning that 0.8% of the world's population received nearly half the world's 

U.S.-supplied food (see Table 2, Appendix, p. 881). Although some 100,000 persons are estimated to have starved to death in the Sahel, for example, Sahel received only 15% or of what Indochina received-because Food For Peace was indirectly used to finance war last year. 

The latest reports indicate that 350,000 soliders on both sides in Vietnam alone have been killed and wounded since the ceasefire (UPI, June 11, 1974).

This figure is more than ten times the total casualties during and after the October Mid-East war. One should also realize that there have been 818,000 refugees in South Vietnam alone since the ceasefire (U.S. Senate Refugee Subcommittee), and many hundreds of thousands of war victims in Cambodia. There were more war victims in Indochina last year than in the rest of the world combined.

The Indochina Resource Center is a church-sponsored private research group which regularly monitors dozens of official documents, newspapers and magazines, and receives personal correspondence from individuals, on the scene in Indochina.

Mr. Branfman's testimony is based on this ongoing research, as well as 4 years' experience in Indochina over the past 7 years. His most recent visit was a post-ceasefire trip to South Vietnam, Cambodia and Thailand from April through August, 1973. He also visited North Vietnam in November, 1972, and spent four years based in Laos as an educational adviser and writer from 1967-1971. 

Such data makes it clear that the U.S. is in fact still heavily involved in the 

Indochina war. If one's memory only runs back five years or so, one may take comfort from the fact that there we are less involved than in 1967 or 68; if one has read the Pentagon Papers, however, one has learned that after 1954 we practiced a covert involvement that led to our finally intervening directly. Our current covert presence there is as indefensible now as it was before 1964, and as dangerous.

The Indochina Resource Center and NARMIC, a project of the American Friends Service Committee would like to submit for the record the first major studies of Administration aid requests for Indochina in the history of the war. 

They analyze in detail the $3.7 billion request for Fiscal Year 1975, giving par- 

1 Fredric Branfman is codirector of the Indochina Resource Center, located at 1322 18th 

St., NW., Washington, D.C., 20036. Its telephone number is (202) 785-3111.

! ticular attention to the $1.39 billion being considered by this committee ($943.3 million for "Indochina Postwar Reconstruction" (IPR) plus military aid of $363 million for Cambodia and $86.1 million for Laos.) 

These studies massively document four major conclusions: (1) U.S. aid in Indochina is not leading to stability, but only demands for more money. In FY 1974, for example, the Administration began with a request for $827.8 million to South Vietnam and Cambodia in economic aid (IPR plus 

Food For Peace). By the end of FY 74 it had allocated $1.052 billion, an increase of 27%. This year it is demanding $1.181 billion, an increase of 40% over last year's request (see Tables 3 and 4, Appendix, pp. 881-82). (2) Since an admitted 88% of this year's $3.7 billion is war-related, and in reality only 2% is truly humanitarian, passage of the Administration's proposal will only bring more war-and an even larger aid request next year (see Table 

5, Appendix, p. 882). (3) Any Congressional attempt to reduce our aid to Indochina must be massive. For the Administration has shown that if it can circumvent congressional restrictions, it will. Last year, for example, "Indochina Postwar Reconstruction" aid was cut from a requested $632 million to an allocation of $450 million. 

By unilaterally increasing Food For Peace shipments from a requested $208 million to an estimated allocation of $502.6 million, however, the Administration has not only restored cuts in economic aid. It has exceeded its original FY 74 request in a blatant violation of congressional will (see Table 3, Appendix, p. 881). 

Indeed, Food For Peace to Indochina last year ($502.6 million) turned out to be more than normal economic aid (IPR funds totalling $450 million). In addition, the Executive possesses a wide variety of other loopholes-including the Food and Forage act, huge amounts of War Reserve material built up especially for Indochina and over which Congress has little control, ceilingless "excess defense article" and "purchase of local currency" categories and an uncontrolled 

CIA budget. (4) Our only moral commitment remaining to the Indochinese people is to see. that the Paris Agreement is observed, so that we may finally reach a political solution to a war which cannot be won on the battlefield. This necessitates congressional action to suspend or reduce aid to military governments in Indochina until they show more willingness to switch the conflict from the military to the political arena.

It is important to understand, however, that a suspension or reduction in aid so as to encourage progress toward a political solution in Indochina has implications extending far beyond that peninsula. 

For it must be understood that the root of the problem in Indochina remains the American Executive branch's decision to wage covert war, and that such covert warfare means untold waste, death and destruction for millions of other foreigners and Americans throughout the years to come. 

The United States Congress, by its pressure on the President to withdraw American ground troops from Indochina and its courageous decision to force the President to stop the bombing of Cambodia on August 15, 1973-as well as its passage of the war-powers act-have given hope to millions that massive and direct U.S. combat intervention in the Third World has become a thing of the past.

It is urgent, however, that Congress now move to stem the evolution of Presidential covert war, whose fullest flowering we now see in Indochina. It will be more difficult. Greater courage and foresight and leadership are called for on the part of those in Congress charged with overseeing our foreign policy. But the stakes could not be higher. 

It is not only that in an era of scarcity, the quality of life for millions now alive is at stake. Presidential covert war is devoted, above all, to the perpetuation of local narrow elites who do not have the tools or interest to meet the needs of their people for food, education and health. 

It is also that their very existence is quite literally at stake. Presidential covert warfare, as we have seen in Vietnam, invariably produces opposition which inevitably has led our Presidential branch to escalate its involvement. 

The result is a decision to bomb or send in ground troops in order to keep local governments in power, leading to the death of millions. 

And, finally, the extent to which Congress will try to curb Presidential covert war is also essential to our survival as a nation. It has become more than

clear that we can neither afford morally nor financially the cost of attempting to fund, direct and eventually fight for unpopular local governments around the world.

The threat posed by Presidential covert war is most clearly understood when we remember that it is through such war that we got involved in Indochina in the first place. Thanks to the Pentagon Papers, it is now officially confirmed that our Presidental branch after 1954, relying heavily on the CIA, sent in numerous covert operatives an hundreds of millions of dollars to impose the Ngo Dinh Diem government upon the people of Vietnam. 

Today, in 1974, the same pattern is repeating itself. The Administration is spending billions of dollars and using thousands of American and Third Country advisers to keep the Thieu and Lon Nol governments in power. This intervention, moreover, is once again covert. Given widespread public and congressional opposition to more U.S. war-making in Indochina, the Administration has chosen to try and disguise its intervention as essentially humanitarian, reconstructive, and peaceful in nature.

As in 1954, moreover, there is little reason to believe that such covert war will succeed. Indeed, if anything is clear at this point it is that present administration policy is directly leading to major new confrontations in Indochina, confrontations which may once again see a Presidential attempt to renew our direct and open involvement. This Administration policy of covert warring is, moreover, ignoring what is an acceptable alternative: accepting the necessity of reaching a political settlement. 

These points will become clearer as we now turn to a consideration of some major strategic goals of Presidential covert war in Indochina: (1) Obtaining funding through manipulation of domestic public opinion-The principal requirement of Presidential covert war is funding. Neither Congress nor the American people would approve continued funding of Executive war.. making in Indochina in violation of Article 4 of the Paris Agreement, which reads "The United States will not continue its military involvement or intervene in the internal affairs of South Vietnam." As a result, the Administration has consistently tried to deceive public opinion about its real involvement in Indochina. Such manipulation of public opinion may enjoy some short-term successes, as when the Administration managed to spend more than $3 billion on war in Indochina in Fiscal Year 1974. Long-term results, however, are counter-productive. It leads to the wastage of billions of dollars our economy can no longer afford; it poisons the political atmosphere as the American people gradually learn they've been deceived. Most importantly, it continues the excessive concentration of power in the Executive which has already proved so disastrous to this country. An informed public and Congress would have kept us out of Indochina in the first place, and would today see us using our resources for healing at home and abroad. (2) Maintaining narrow-based, military-oriented local administrations in power-The Administration has chosen to continue trying to keep in power those who represent a tiny minority of the people: the civilian rich, the top-ranking military officers and, to some extent, the western-educated. The result is either that the Administration fears political competition and opts instead for war, as in South Vietnam; the U.S.-supported side becomes so weak that the other side refuses to negotiate with it, as in Cambodia; or we are forced to accept political compromise, see the other side gain in power, and pressures grow for re-intervention, as in Laos. And the result is also increased corruption and war, leading to declining local economies and armed forces, leading to increased demands for aid from the U.S. Presidential branch. (3) Using U.S. technology and advisers to control local military operations- 

Given the Administration's narrow political base in Indochina, it is forced to try and compensate by extremely heavy inputs of U.S. military advisers, war material and funding to develop and field local military forces. This makes such local forces entirely dependent on American logistics and personnel, and invariably inferior to their guerrilla adversaries. This leads to growing pressures for direct American intervention-e.g., through covert or overt bombing by 

American pilots or U.S. Marine landings-ever-increasing costs, and increased deception at home. (4) Practising population control through police programs and population concentration-Since U.S. Executive-backed local administrations cannot win popular support, the emphasis instead has been on physical control of the

the population. Executive policy has since the 1960s resettled nearly 14 million people in areas closer to U.S. Executive control in South Vietnam, Cambodia and Laos. Under the Nixon Doctrine, however, there has been a noticeably increased emphasis on police operations, ranging from greatly increased surinveillance and national i.d. card programs, to constant arrests, to the physical liquidation of opponents. This practice, however, has also proved counter-producon the tive since it violates the most basic tenets of humanity, leading to world-wide Hola protest, increased lying by American leaders, and the further alienation of a local population constantly subject to mass surveillance, round-ups, summary sentencing, and inhuman torture and prison mistreatment. 1. PRESIDENTIAL COVERT WAR: CONTROLLING U.S. DOMESTIC OPINION 

The Executive branch's recision to switch to a major policy of carrying out covert warfare has led to unparalleled attempts to control U.S. public and congressional opinion. It has also led the Executive either to blatantly deceive 

Congress or violate Congressional law.

In Indochina alone, major examples of Executive deceit include: 

Installing and maintaining Ngo Dinh Diem in 1954, acknowledged within the American Mission as an unpopular dictator who unilaterally cancelled elections in 1956 in violation of the Geneva Accords, while publicly praised as a popular, democratic, sovereign leader (Pentagon Papers); withholding information from Congress and the American people about U.S.-directed commando raids against North Vietnam, thus making the Gulf of Tonkin incident appear unprovoked (Pentagon Papers); funding and directing Thai and other foreign troops in Laos, in direct violation of congressional law; secretly bombing Cambodia for 14 months, and falsifying records so that the U.S. Congress and people would not know; publicly denying the bombing of northern Laos from May 1964 until September 1969 when Congress was first told, and March 1970, when the American people first heard; U.S. cross-border operations into Laos and Cambodia in 1971 and 1972, thus expressly violating congressional law against sending U.S. ground forces into these countries; carrying out rain-making missions over Indochina, while publicly denying that they were being carried out; attempting to cause fire storms, also not acknowledging until years later." 

And, in addition to these now officially-confirmed covert activities, there are a wide variety of other clandestine activities which have been revealed by numerous persons with first-person experience, but are still officially denied by the Executive branch. These include the sending of military personnel into 

Laos and instructing them to wear civilian clothes and carry a card identifying them as working for the Agency for International Development; the dispatch of U.S.-directed intelligence-gathering teams into China and North Vietnam from northern Laos, thus jeopardizing the shaky neutrality of Laos; the use of 

CIA-trained Vietnamese to dress like the NLF and carry out atrocities, in the hope of having these blamed on the NLF; the falsification of documents given to the American and Vietnamese press; U.S.-established quotas which led to the deliberate assassination of tens of thousands of Vietnamese under the U.S.sponsored Phoenix program.

Given this record of Executive deceit stretching back over the past decade, there is substantial reason to believe that the Executive could be continuing its deception over the true scope of American activities since the ceasefire. 

This necessary skepticism is hardly helped by an Air Force announcement on May 15, 1974, that it is legal to disquise military operations through false reports for military of foreign policy reasons. (LA Times, May 16, 1974). This shocking contention has not yet been contradicted by any high-ranking Executive official.

The notion that Executive officials are deliberately deceiving the American people is heightened by the fact that the U.S. Ambassador in Saigon, Mr. Graham 

Martin, has forbidden all contacts between U.S. officials and the U.S. press without his approval, which is rarely granted. The Chicago Tribune on June 9

And, of course, Mr. Martin's famous advice that "it would be the height of folly to permit Kennedy. an honest and detailed answer" to his questions hardly inspired confidence in the truth of what we are getting from Saigon."

In fact, moreover, there is much evidence that the Presidential branch is today again following a policy of attempting to control American domestic opinion by restricting the press, withholding information from Congress, denying true charges, and deliberately giving out misinformation. 

A few major examples follow:

American officials constantly claim that the communists have taken the initiative in violating the ceasefire militarily. Yet Representative Peter Frelinghuysen of this committee, a major spokesman favoring continued aid to the Thieu government, recently stated on p. 4 of his May 1974 report, "Vietnam-A 

Changing Crucible" that: "The GVN has fared well during post-cease-fire maneuvering: Since January 

1973 it has added 770 hamlets to the list of those over which it has dominant control, and it has reportedly reduced the number of disputed hamlets by well over a third. The Communists meanwhile have lost over 90 hamlets that were under their firm control at the time of the ceasefire 

-The Administration had never revealed its secret "assurance" when signing the Paris Agreement that it would withdraw all military or civilian advisers to the Vietnamese armed forces within 12 months. This pledge, revealed in a secret nemo prepared by George Aldrich, State Department deputy legal adviser, states in part that: "Secret-The United States has assured the DRV that we shall withdraw from South Vietnam within 12 months from the signature of the agreement all our civilian personnel working in the armed forces of the Republic of Vietnam." (Wash. Post, June 4, 1974)

When this pledge was revealed by author Tad Szulc, the State Department denied that this "assurance" constituted a firm promise to do so. Today, over 17 months after the signing of the Agreement, some 3800 American civilians continue to work with the South Vietnamese Armed Services." -U.S. Executive branch officials continue to maintain that our military aid to 

Thieu and Lon Nol is designed to balance off Soviet and Chinese aid to the North Vietnamese. In fact, Congressman Aspin revealed on June 3, 1974, that we gave 

18 times as much aid as they did ($5.3 billion to $290 million), and that whereas the Soviets and Russians decreased their aid from $605 million in 1972 to $290 million in 1973, the Administration actually increased our aid. (See Table 6, Appendix, p. 884.)

The Administration continues to stress its humanitarian concern for affairs in South Vietnam, while castigating the other side for its lack of humanitarian concern. On June 26, 1974, however, Senator Kennedy revealed confidential cables from U.S. Ambassador Graham Martin in Saigon advocating that the U.S. hold up its contribution to the International Red Cross in an attempt to pressure them not to invite the Provisional Revolutionary Government (PRG) to an international conference to be held in Geneva in September to discuss limiting weapons which are either indiscriminate or cause unnecessary suffering; on June 23, 1974, the N.Y. Times reported that the U.S. was opposing UNICEF aid to children in North Vietnam and PRG zones.

And, most seriously, the Administration has still not even begun to remove the many mines still maiming and killing numerous Vietnamese peasants in 

Saigon zones. 

On May 28, Secretary Kissinger supported Graham Martin's charge that there is no evidence that Saigon is holding large numbers of political prisoners, and added that "the extensive evidence available to us simply does not sustain the "A Cable From Saigon," Senator Kennedy, Congressional Record, Apr. 2, 1974.

On June 3, 1974, the St. Louis Post-Dispatch reported that at the end of March 1974, 2643 U.S. employees contracted to the Pentagon were working with the South Vietnamese military, 936 were employed directly by the Defense Attache Office in Saigon, and 225 made up the official DAO military contingent.
