S di highly publicized charges that civilian prisoners are subjected to widespread, systematic mistreatment (Senator Kennedy insert, Congressional Record, May 28, 1974) 99 On June 7, 1974, however, Representative Abzug inserted into the Congressional Record (p.E3657) a listing of over 100 articles which emanated from Saigon, from western journalists or residents, indicating widespread mistreatment of large numbers of political prisoners; since the Saigon government has not allowed even the International Red Cross to talk freely with civilian detainees, and since it has also turned down requests for visits by Bishop Thomas Gumbleton of Detroit and other groups and individuals, the closing off of the prisons to the outside world (with the exception of a few guided tours) is cause for alarm, in and of itself. The assertion that the U.S. Embassy has "extensive evidence" on the treatment of prisoners is curious, since an earlier U.S. Embassy study stated that U.S. advisers had been withdrawn from the prisons since the ceasefire, and that Embassy information was based on "internal" GVN records. -U.S. and GVN officials have blatantly attempted to deceive the American people and Congress about the Thieu government's need for economic and military aid. During March and October, 1973, for example, Administration spokesmen trumpeted the idea that a "North Vietnamese offensive" was imminent. To this day, of course, none has materialized.

Even more serious was the transparently false attempt to wangle an extra $474 million supplemental military appropriation for the GVN during the spring of 1974. The U.S. Congress was flatly told that if Thieu did not have this money, his army might collapse. On March 12, 1974, for example, Assistant Secretary of Defense William Clements testified before the Senate Armed Services Committee: "Without additional funds the South Vietnamese forces are going to be in extremely dire straits here in April, May and June. There is just no doubt about it . . . We are going to run out of funds here in the later part of this fiscal year unless we are given additional funds."

In the event, of course, the funding request was denied. Theoretically, the 

ARVN should thus have been near collapse. In fact, however, the Washington 

Post reported on May 9, 1974, after the request had been denied, that: ... "(Pentagon spokesman) Friedheim also appeared to take a less dire view than have some other White House and Defense officials. Friedheim noted that only two months remain in the current fiscal year . . ." -U.S. officials constantly maintain that they support the coalition government in Laos. Testifying before this committee on June 13, 1974, for example, Mr. Robert Nooter stated that "the formation of a Provisional Government of 

National Union (PGNU) this past April represents a bona fide political resolu tion of Laos internal differences. The U.S.

supports this effort 99 On June 23, 1974, however, Senator Edward Kennedy issued a press release, based on a still secret Government Accounting Office report, which revealed that in fact the Administration has not been supporting the PGNU at all. On the contrary. To date, all funds had been going to the right wing Royal Lao faction directly, an ominous throw-back recalling the pattern of past coup-making which has upset political settlements before in Laos. 

Kennedy's charges appeared to gain some substance, moreover, by a NY Times report the next day which indicated that a Vice-Admiral Ray Peet had told this committee that U.S. objectives in Laos were "to maintain the survival of the politically neutral Royal Laotian Government. . . and to encourage pursuit by 

Laos of objectives compatible with the United States." -And there is fresh indication that while pretending to obey a new congressional prohibition against using Food For Peace monies for war, the Administration is continuing to use local currencies generated by the sale of Food For Peace commodities for military purposes in South Vietnam and Cambodia, as it has in the past.

On June 30, the Washington Post, reported that "Congressional efforts to prevent military use of funds generated by the Food For Peace program apparently are being frustrated by some ingenious bookkeeping in Cambodia and South Vietnam."

There are innumerable other such examples of Administration attempts to manipulate domestic opinion in the U.S. since the ceasefire. Even these few examples, however, make it clear that the pattern of Executive deception which existed before January 27, 1973, has extended up until the present day.

The principal purpose of this constant stream of falsehoods is clearly to get more aid out of Congress. One can presume that Congress might substantially cut our aid to Indochina if the Administration admitted that the GVN has taken the initiative in violating the ceasefire, the Administration has reneged on a promise to withdraw American advisers, we spend far more money in Indochina than do the Soviets and Chinese, our Ambassador in Saigon is neither telling the truth about his humanitarian concern nor political prisoners, military pressure on Thieu from the other side is minimal, U.S. aid is endangering a coalition government in Laos, and the Administration is still using Food For Peace monies in violation of Congressional law. 

Deceiving domestic opinion, then, is an integral part of Presidential covert war. For the Executive branch can only receive the funds it wishes to wage such war if Congress and the American people can be placated. 

It is equally clear, however, that such deception does not serve the best interests of the United States. 

Economically, Executive deception of Congress is leading to an annual expenditure of billions of dollars that this nation simply can no longer afford. 

Politically, such deception can only split this nation further. The more the 

Presidential branch lies, the newer and more lies it must create to explain away previous contradictions. Thus, for example, the original lie that we were in South 

Vietnam to build a democracy has helped create today's lie that the GVN has. no political prisoners, which in turn has led to the even greater lie that those who express concern about the prisoners are "dupes of Hanoi”. 

The end result of such a process can only be a heightened atmosphere of bit-terness and spite, making our disengagement from Vietnam all the more difficult. 

Morally, such falsehood at the top can only lead to the continued brutalization. of this society, a process which has become ever-more apparent in recent years. 

It is not only that congressional passage of this year's aid requests will lead directly to the meaningless death of tens of thousands of Indochinese, the maiming of scores of thousands more. It is also that passage of such war-aid will mean that this nation will have delayed still longer the process of coming to ac-cept our obligation to respect international treaties, sovereign nations, and human life.

The international order simply cannot exist unless great nations learn torespect small nations, the wealthy learn to respect the poor. 

Nor can we as a nation survive. For if we have learned nothing from Watergate but that those who lie abroad will lie at home, we have learned enough; let us understand that those who illegally seek power in distant lands will do so hereas well; those who are indifferent to human life in Vietnam will not respect it in Washington, D.C.; those who respect neither the truth nor international law in Cambodia will not obey it here at home. 

Congress' main leverage over Presidential covert war is clearly both to cut Administration aid requests as much as possible, and to close all possible loop-holes. Other steps are desirable, if possible: for example, Congress could thisyear stipulate that no money be given to Laos unless it is agreed to by the- PGNU; it could state that no congressional aides are to travel to South Vietnam any longer at GVN or Vietnam Council on Foreign Relations expense; it could" make a far more determined effort to determine the facts, insisting for example that Administration spokesmen present some evidence to support their mereassertions.

In the long run, however, such steps would seem at best palliative in nature. 

The most substantial way to bring an end to deception institutionalized as partof Presidential covert warfare is to ensure that such deception no longer succeeds: in obtaining money from Congress. 

As long as the Presidential branch finds it profitable to deceive Congress, afterall, it can be expected to continue doing so. 

2. PRESIDENTIAL COVERT WAR: THE LOCAL ADMINISTRATION 

It is no coincidence that the main theme enunciated by Messrs. Schlesinger, Nooter, Kissinger and Moorer, before this committee last month was that our aid to the Thieu and Lon Nol governments is allowing them to become self-sufficient; that by continuing to aid them, we are strengthening them, thereby giving the other side the incentive to negotiate a political settlement, therebymoving towards peace in the region.

Ech Ted 

TO £50

For, in an age of de-colonization, Congress and the American people will clearly only support Administration requests if they are presented as involving foreign aid to an ally which is both important to our interests and reasonably independent.

In actual fact, however, U.S. post-ceasefire aid in Indochina has neither contributed toward stability nor helped the Thieu and Lon Nol governments stand alone. On the contrary. Recent events have made it clear that conditions are deteriorating rapidly-economically, politically, and militarily. Under these conditions, continued aid to the GVN, Lon Nol, or right-wing Laotian elements is actually preventing more than promoting a political solution. 

One of the clearest examples of this is Laos. It was not our massive military and war-related economic aid to the right-wing generals, coupled with one of the most massive bombing campaigns in history and the creation of a Meo "Secret Army" which led to a political settlement in Laos. Quite the opposite. 

Our military funding simply fueled the war, prevented negotiations, and led to -extra years of unnecessary fighting. Indeed, it was only when the Pathet Lao had come out on top-destroying the Meo army and establishing control over most of Laos-that we agreed to negotiate. 

The truth about Laos was that it was we who were the obstacle to a negotiated settlement ever since our Ambassador there was told by the Secretary of State to oppose a coalition "every time it raised its ugly head." 

The result of our finally agreeing to negotiate now, of course, is increased stability, a saving of hundreds of millions of dollars, and the potential end to American involvement in a war that few Americans know very much about. 

Of course, it has meant that the Pathet Lao have done much better, been much more warmly received by the Laotian people, than Executive spokesmen had predicted to Congress. But this is simply a lesson we must learn. I do not sense that it has been overly painful for the American people. 

But though the Administration has for the time being come to grasp with realities in Laos, it has not extended this understanding to South Vietnam or Cambodia. It has not seen that funneling in hundreds of millions for war will not "stabilize" the situation. Indeed, lavish aid to the GVN and Lon Nol government-composed, after all, of military men who have shown little inclination for political compromise-will only encourage them to keep on fighting to hold on to what they have, rather than risk it through engaging in a political struggle. 

The Administration decision to wage covert war through the GVN and Lon Nol government has not brought us any closer to a negotiated settlement in Indochina; it has produced only increasing political, economic and social disintegration in their zones. (a) Saigon zones The major problem facing the GVN today is political and moral in nature, not economic. AID officials try to explain the very serious problems in GVN zones as due to rising world commodity prices, the withdrawal of the American presence, and other factors out of anyone's control. In fact, as a comparison with the frugal, well-balanced economy in PRG zones reveals, the heart of the GVN's economic problem is not financial, and these problems cannot be solved by American aid. In a word, there is enough to go around in GVN zones. The problem is that the rich and the military elite are taking far more than their proper share, leaving the majority-the poor-to go hungry. 

The root cause of GVN problems is the Administration refusal to chance political competition with the PRG.

The primary responsibility for this, of course, lies with the U.S. Executive branch. The U.S., after all, supplies 86.3% of the GVN's income, including all of its ammo, guns and tanks and planes and bombs. (See insert by Senator McGovern, C.R., May 6, 1974. It is fundamentally inane to suggest that despite this preponderant role played by the U.S., we do not have the leverage to ensure that the GVN at least test the PRG's offer to compete politically. 

Such political competition would appear to be in the PRG's interests. The first step toward forming the National Council of National Reconciliation and Concord, for example, would logically be enforcing Article 11 which gives basic democratic freedoms to all Vietnamese. Under Article 11 all Vietnamese would be given freedom of political activity (presumably freeing many political prisoners from GVN prisons), freedom of residence (which would allow the refugees to return home), and freedom to organize (which would allow the Third Force and PRG

to organize in the cities.) At the same time, the PRG would be expected to allow the GVN similarly to organize in PRG zones. 

Perhaps because it fears that the GVN could not stand up to political competition with the PRG, the U.S. Executive has taken no known steps to push for such a political compromise. Instead, it has given uncompromising support to Thieu whose position includes the following points: 

The PRG must set a date for elections before the people can have their democratic rights as outlined in Article 11. (This position violates the Paris Agreement, which sets no conditions on the enforcement of Article 11. It could also only be viewed as an attempt to obstruct any kind of settlement by the PRG, which could hardly be expected to surface its cadre and start campaigning solely on the promise that Thieu will allow Article 11 to be enforced.)

There is no "Third Force", one of "three equal segments" recognized in article 12. (On March 25, for example, GVN spokesman Bui Bao Truc declared that "the third force is merely an imaginary segment," which means among other things that the National Council of Reconciliation could not come into being, since it is to be composed of the three parts.) 

The North Vietnamese must withdraw from South Vietnam before the GVN will agree to elections. (Again, this position is a major violation of the Paris 

Agreement. The withdrawal of such a condition by the United States was clearly one of the major factors which led to the signing of the Agreement, which nowhere mentions the presence of the North Vietnamese. Article 1 of the 

Agreement explicitly states that Vietnam is one country.) 

The Administration, by requesting aid to the GVN despite its stated attitude toward the Paris Agreement-an attitude of setting impossible conditions which it knows in advance the other side will not meet-gives the impression that it is not seriously interested in promoting a political settlement in South Vietnam. 

Instead, it has clearly opted for covert war to keep the PRG from power. 

This war, in turn, is the basic reason for South Vietnam's economic problems, which are enormous. As a result of the war, the US supports a GVN which refuses to allow refugees to return to their native homes in or near PRG areas. This creates a great unproductive mass of millions of people either clustered near cities or resettled in arid, landless sites, millions of people who must be fed from the outside. 

As a result of the war, the US supports a GVN which refuses to demobilize significant portions of its 1.1 million man army, 350,000 civil servants, or 

120,000 police. All 1.57 million of them do not produce and must also be paid, as well as fed.

As a result of the war, South Vietnam has seen a 65% increase in prices last year, a 25% rise this year (Baltimore Sun, May 8, 1974); cash reserves have fallen dangerously low, under $100 million (L.A. Times, May 16); South Vietnam had to bring in imports totalling $795 million in 1973, while exporting only $56 million-producing a trade deficit of $739 million. 

And such economic problems, in turn, have helped increase South Vietnam's corruption problems to epidemic proportions. 

In recent months, Saigon newspapers have reported a major rice smuggling operation out of Vietnam to other Asian countries where prices are higher (Dai 

Dan Toc, 5/11, 5/13 Dien Tin, 5/12); a timber smuggling scandal, which has seen high government officials seize 450.000 acres in the last 6 months, depriving the government of $150-190 million in revenues (Dai Dan Toc, 3/15, 5/18); a scrap metal scandal, which the State Department says involves $20-40 million, Saigon newspapers say it is more like $1-2 billion (Ta Sang, 4/10; Dai 

Dan Toc, 4/15; Chicago Tribune, 6/5); a fertilizer scandal, by which 100-150 high-ranking officials have gotten rich through speculation, hoarding, and price manipulation (NY Post, 5/20; Song Than, 5/30; Hoa Dinh, 5/31); 50–150,000 non-existent soldiers drawing salaries, (Chicago Daily News, 6/4); grass-roots corruption going to the very lowest of officialdom, for example a refugee official who stole money that was supposed to go to refugees to build new homes (UPI, St. 

Louis Post-Dispatch, May 12, 1974) Six ARVN Generals named as war-profiteers, by a Vietnamese Senator enjoying immunity from arrest. (L.A. Times, 6/17).

The combination of this war economy coupled with thoroughgoing official corruption has produced increasing economic hardship for South Vietnam's people. The Baltimore Sun reported on May 8, for example that:

2220 "In the northern part of South Vietnam, people are dying of starvation because speculative rice hoarding has made this basic food too expensive to buy." 

Reports of suicides due to economic pressures are becoming increasingly frequent (e.g., NY Times, 5/1; Dien Tin, 5/23). There are increasing reports of crumbling morale, shortages of basic commodities, massive unemployment. 

The situation has become so serious, indeed, that it is unlikely that even if the Administration's full request was passed this year that it would serve as more than a mere stop-gap measure. No evidence whatsoever has been introduced to support the claim that granting $750 million in Indochina Postwar Reconstruction aid would start South Vietnam on the road to self-sufficiency; there is a general consensus, however, that such a sum would be a mere temporary measure designed to allow the GVN to hold its own for another year-unless it is willing to work towards a political compromise. 

The solution to South Vietnam's quite serious economic problems, therefore, is not simply to give a substantial amount of Food For Peace and/or Indochina Postwar Reconstruction aid. For people are not hungry for lack of food. In FY 

74. for example, the GVN received more Food For Peace ($304.8 million) than all of Africa ($122 million), Latin America ($67.6 million), Bangladesh ($41.4 million) and Pakistan ($38.1 million) combined.

The problem is that the Food For Peace South Vietnam receives costs too much-due to war and corruption-for those who need it most to purchase it. 

Lavish American aid can only encourage war and corruption, and therefore hunger. A massive reduction in American aid will force the GVN to think about finding a political solution, thereby structurally increasing the chances that South Vietnam can become self-sufficient. 

As we look towards the political arena, however, we find that once again U.S. aid is not "stabilizing" the situation, but rather leading to a deterioration in the political climate in GVN zones.

The U.S. permitting Thieu to push through an amendment for him to run for a third term as President caused Senator Nguyen Van Huyen, a leading anticommunist Catholic, to resign as head of the Senate on January 19; Senator Vu 

Van Mau, head of the Buddhist Lotus group, shaved his head in protest, calling 

Thieu a "dictator” and “incompetent"; on January 10, the NY Times reported that politics in GVN zones had been reduced to competition between two palace cliques, one headed by Thieu's cousin, Hoang Duc Nha, the other by a man named Nguyen Van Ngan; Nguyen Van Ngan was then reported arrested 5 months later because, at least according to one commentator, Thieu feared Ngan's rising power (LA Times, 5/31).

Meanwhile, protests-small, but visible, by the few who dare speak publiclyhave continued; a hunger strike by hundreds of Buddhist monks, Cao Daiists, and other third force political prisoners was reported in Chi Hoa prison in March (NY Times, 3/7, 3/12); 20 Hoa Hao Buddhists cut off the little fingers of their left hands in protest against restrictions on them (UPI, 6/7); 300 monks were reported demonstrating in the Delta to protest arrest of 6 monks (Philadelphia Inquirer, 6/13); 19 Buddhists and Madame Ngo Ba Thanh led a march through Saigon calling for the release of Thieu's political prisoners. (Christian 

Science Monitor, 5/7) (b) Lon Nol zones

As bad as the political and economic situation in GVN zones is, however, the situation in Cambodia for the Lon Nol government is even more hopeless. 

Once again, the responsibility for the rapidly deteriorating situation lies with a U.S. Executive branch which has preferred to wage covert war in Cambodia rather than attempt to reach a political solution, no matter how distasteful it might find such a political compromise. 

As the Washington Post reported on June 30, the Lon Nol government is entirely dependent on U.S. funds to continue its day-to-day functioning: "Cambodia's domestically generated government revenues from taxes in fiscal year 1974 amounted to $54 million-not nearly enough to cover its $109 million military and $60 million civilian budgets." And, in addition of course, the U.S. is supplying all transport, arms, ammunition, and other basic commodities. 

As the Washington Post also reported, moreover, the new U.S. Ambassador to Cambodia, Mr. John G. Dean, has openly taken control of the government machinery: "The new U.S. Ambassador in Phnom Penh, John Gunther Dean, has in two months made it absolutely clear to Cambodians and foreigners alike in Phnom Penh that he is, in effect, running the country." (June 6, 1974)

The American responsibility for controlling the fate of the Lon Nol government may well extend beyond its present levels, moreover; I wish this morning to submit for the record a communication we have recently received from Okinawa, indicating that U.S. Marines are being openly prepared for moving into Phnom Penh should it be under siege. 

This U.S. commitment to supporting Lon Nol at any cost has no conceivable justification as far as we are concerned. It has led to an intolerable situation for Cambodians and Americans alike, as we funnel in almost as much money into Cambodia as we do for all of Latin America. 

The basic fact is that Lon Nol controls little more than a few major towns, which can only be supplied by an American airlift or occasional boat: as a result prices are reported to have risen more than 300%, with foodstuffs up 400% in the past year. Speculation and corruption are also reported to have risen tremendously. (Chicago Daily News, 6/12). In a separate report, the Chicago

Tribune reported that millions of dollars of U.S. arms aid has been disappearing into Cambodia, much of it turning up with the Khmer Rouge. 

The basic military and economic weakness is reflected above all in Lon Nol's political problems. His only real base of popular support when he took power was the teachers and students. By now, however, he has long since broken with both. In January, 22,000 teachers went on strike, later supported by students. 

Students continued demonstrating regularly, culminating in a May 31 march of some 1,500 through the center of town; the killing of the Cambodian Minister of Education, after being held by demonstrating students (the identity of the assassin is not yet known) symbolizes the major and perhaps irrevocable break between the Lon Nol government and students and teachers. 

Lon Nol, moreover, has become increasingly isolated, even within the small coterie of politicians with which he surrounds himself. Forced through American pressure to join a coalition with Cheng Heng, Sirik Matak and In Tam about a year ago, Lon Nol has progressively gotten rid of each. This split was finally consummated recently, when Long Boret formed a new cabinet in the aftermath of the Minister of Education's death. Six top cabinet officials quit; Sirik Matak was excluded from the new cabinet, along with all members of his Republican party, which supports Lon Nol; 6 independents; and two army men. Since In 

Tam had long since left, this newest cabinet reshuffle left Lon Nol with his narrowest political base since the U.S. had forced him to take in the others a year earlier.

Under the circumstances, then, it is hard to think of a single coherent reason why the Congress should give any aid to Lon Nol at all, let alone the astronomical sum of $550 million being asked for by the Administration for Fiscal Year 1975.

The major justification for our involvement in Cambodia originally was that it was necessary to protect U.S. ground troops fighting in South Vietnam. 

As American troops were progressively withdrawn from South Vietnam, the Administration changed its rationale to protecting the Cambodians from a North Vietnamese invasion. During the past few years, however, the North Vietnamese have not been involved in the fighting between Lon Nol and Khmer Rouge troops. 

As the N.Y. Times reported on November 25, 1973: "The Government tells them that they are fighting Vietnamese invaders and the soldiers are beginning to discover that that is not true. . . . Nobody sees North 

Vietnamese troops in battle any more. The voices that call to Government soldiers from across the battlefields are Khmer voices, the soldiers say; the bodies are 

Khmer bodies."

The new Administration position that lavish American aid to Lon Nol will show the other side that it cannot win a military victory, thus pushing it towards negotiations. There is no evidence to support this point of view, however, and even less justification for why the United States should be involved in what is now admitted to be a civil war among Cambodians at all. 

In fact, as in Laos, continued U.S. support to Lon Nol will simply lead to more fighting, less likelihood for a political settlement, and increased costs for the United States. Thus it is that Lon Nol has lost territory and people in the past year, despite a giant U.S. military and aid package totalling $631.5 million, more than we gave to all of Latin America last year. 

And thus it is that this staggering amount of money not only accomplished very little last year, but has seen the Administration ask for almost twice as much for FY 75 in Cambodia ($550.8 million) as it did in FY 74 ($287.3 million).

BI 71 27 No, congressional passage of Administration aid requests for Cambodia will bring us further away from, not nearer to, peace. Cambodia, where we support a half-mad field-marshal who has absolutely no observable support from his own people, is the greatest example of our time of what is wrong with the practice of Presidential covert war.

As I have testified this morning, the time has come for Congress to move to terminate such war around the globe. I can think of no more appropriate place to begin than Cambodia.

EXCERPTS FROM: VIETNAM-THE HUMAN COSTS OF THE AMERICAN AID PROGRAMS AN ALTERNATE FISCAL YEAR 1975 FOREIGN AID PROPOSAL FOR INDOCHINA (Guy Gran, Indochina Resource Center, May 1974) AN ALTERNATE FISCAL YEAR 1975 FOREIGN AID PROPOSAL FOR INDOCHINA- SUBMITTED BY GUY GRAN, INDOCHINA RESOURCE CENTER PREFACE 

For fiscal year 1975, the Administration has requested the appropriation of at least $7.46 billion in direct bilateral foreign aid. By the AID presentation figures Indochina could receive $3.09 billion or 41% of the total aid for the whole world. A more precise accounting of total planned fiscal year 1975 expenditures. reveals that the real figure for Indochina would be at least $3.67 billion or about half of the world total. 

Most of these funds are intended to support the Republic of Vietnam (RVN) on the supposition that it can someday become an economically viable state. It would appear, however, that no amount of economic or military aid can ever overcome the essentially artificial nature of this state. The United States supplied 86% of the resources that permitted the RVN to exist in 1973. It is, however, far more than the degree of dependence which merits such a conclusion. The 

RVN state feels obliged to spend enormous sums to maintain a military and police bureaucracy. It is a very expensive way to maintain political control, and it keeps 19% of the work force out of commodity producing jobs. Various refugee and income maintenance programs also permit political control but drain the treasury. These fundamental distortions make the RVN economy structurally unviable.

The same drives for political control and the profits that accrue also destroy the RVN ability to generate substantial new revenue. While indirect taxes did rise last year, the RVN still fears to tax significantly the major pockets of wealth, land and personal income, because it is the rich who support it. With 

AID's urging the RVN pursues capital intensive agriculture in a labor rich country. Even if such processes show some success, agribusiness and trickle down development will add primarily to the wealth of those Thieu chooses not to tax. It is little wonder that such policies continue to create active opposition among the Vietnamese.

The RVN answer to opposition is repression. Totalitarian control over economic transactions and individuals provides enormous possibilities for corruption. The present degree of corruption alone is enough to warrant the conclusion that the RVN government is incapable of acting in the best interests of its citizens. Meanwhile inflation, fueled by corruption, domestic "security" expenses, and world market conditions, is slowly but inevitably destroying the ability of a majority of Vietnamese to survive, let alone prosper. The appalling human costs of such processes are the most persuasive arguments for change. 

The Administration argues that it could perpetuate a status quo and a stability that in reality do not exist. AID's presentations ignore both the political fabric and the enormous human suffering it is largely responsible for. It is bad enough that the Administration's proposals are fundamentally irresponsible and inappropriate in economic terms. But it is totally unacceptable to continue and enlarge the psychological dehumanization, social degradation, poverty, and corruption on the present scale when other choices exist. 

These are sad conclusions to draw from 25 years of American aid programs in Indochina. To reach them requires intellectual energy, curiosity, and empathy,

It takes political courage as well to recognize that the costs of the status quo can be greater than the costs of change. In lieu of the proposed $911 million program of subsidies for the RVN, I propose a transitional aid program of $200 million. For it is substantial pressure on Thieu that offers the best chance that he and the RVN will begin to live up to the obligations of the Paris Agreement. 

Without the substantive political accommodation the Agreement outlines, there will be no peace, no viable government, and no viable economy in South Vietnam. Without peace Congress will be facing another year with 100,000 Vietnamese casualties and 800,000 refugees followed by an fiscal year 1976 request for $3 billion more in aid. The Vietnamese and the American people both deserve better.

INTRODUCTION 

From the wreckage left by Dienbienphu, the French withdrawal and the Geneva Accords in 1954 figures with substantial political and economic power gathered in support of a new Saigon government. The United States made this possible by contributing $550-$750 million in fiscal year 1954 and $320.3 million in fiscal year 1955. In 1955 the government of Ngo Dinh Diem spent $537 million on revenue of $146 million. Much of the $146 million was generated by taxing 

American financed imports. Little has changed in two decades. In fiscal year 

1974 the United States will contribute about $850 million in direct and indirect economic aid to maintain this state: our total aid program supplied about 86% of all the resources used to sustain the RVN in calendar year 1973.2 

Administration spokesmen, ignoring this twenty-year heritage, now speak of two to three years of high level economic aid, perhaps $800 million to one billion dollars, to prevent ultimate communist victory and create the conditions for a stable and relatively independent economy in RVN areas. In early March, however, a Saigon newspaper reported that projected import needs of just gasoline, fertilizer, and rice would reach $900 million for 1974 with total imports scaling $1.1 billion."

In addition the World Bank recently completed two substantial studies of the Vietnamese economy. Imprisoned by Administration political goals and unaware of the gravity of inflation, the World Bank nevertheless destroyed the basis for any euphoria over the RVN economic potential. For the RVN economy "net aid required in 1980 would still be on the order of $770 million a year . . . by 

1990. . . about $450 million." 995 These are considerable contradictions. They suggest more than political duplic ity and fiscal irresponsibility. They point to a policy of permanently substituting material means for political appeal. And they reveal a basically artificial state, dependent upon another to a degree and durability which conjures few historical analogies, except perhaps Laos. In the analysis to follow I shall argue that such dependence has profoundly unhealthy results for the Vietnamese economy, the RVN state, and the people under its aegis. 

The RVN economy, in the manner of a heroin user, is addicted to American aid. This means, in the first place, that the Vietnamese economy we subsidize is extremely ill in ways not apparent to traditional economic analysis and ways not considered in the surface picture of vibrant and healthy potential USAID will present. Most addicts don't appear very ill on the outside. They can carry out most normal functions over a long period of time. But the drug is slowly debilitating them. In like manner U.S. aid to Vietnam is sustaining a certain stability and economic health for some but the econonmy, the society, and the polity as a whole are being slowly destroyed. I shall try to describe the figura-

Toward Peace in Indochina

By the AID fiscal summary the fiscal year 1975 foreign aid requests to Congress contain $7.46 billion in new obligational authority for bilateral military and economic assistance. Of that total the 60 countries of Africa and Latin 

America are to receive $886 million. On an average that is $10.4 million a country in economic aid and $4.4 million in military, a total of $14.8 million. The three countries of Indochina alone are to receive $3.09 billion which is 41% of the total for the world, 29% of world economic aid and 55% of world military aid. 

Such an indication of Administration priorities requires serious contemplation from anyone interested in the merit and continuation of foreign aid in general, never mind the wisdom of the Administration position in Indochina. 

The Administration wishes $550.7 million for Cambodia to prolong briefly this tragic and bloody civil war. State Department officials admit candidly that the only Administration purpose is to save face before its domestic critics as long as possible. Killing Cambodians is preferable to taking any responsibility and accepting the inevitable. By such moral and political cowardice, Congress is given two unpleasant choices. The most responsible position is a $50 million interim program of medical aid, sufficient until a new government can assess the situation. The Administration wishes to intrude another $143.5 million into the fragile new peace in Laos. In view of the existence of a new coalition government, it would appear wise to seek the advice of all of its leaders before deciding what should be done. The long and unhappy heritage of AID and the CIA in disrupting Laotian political settlements suggests that Congress make enormous extra efforts on behalf of the Laotian people. 

Last, but not least, the Administration is requesting $2.4 billion in new money (and $2.5 in spending authority) to support for another year one of the parties in a 40 year old revolutionary war in Vietnam. This is 32% of the total military and economic aid for the entire world, 23% of the economic aid and 42% of the military aid. Without such aid over the past two decades the RVN would not have come into existence and would not have survived. It is an anomalous historical situation. There are powerful emotional and psychological interests, involving personal image and political credibility, which argue for a continuation of such aid. Portions of the Pentagon, State Department, and international business community favor this policy. So naturally do the RVN leaders. 

The optimal scenario envisaged by Thieu and his supporters seems to be the following. First they would have Kissinger's secret diplomatic dialogues with 

Le Duc Tho be successful. To wit Kissinger should venture to Paris and conjure up yet another public relations triumph with a veneer of progress toward peace. 

Whatever actually transpires, a Kissinger diplomatic "breakthrough", peace perhaps "in hand" this time instead of "at hand," is likely to be staged to assist the passage of this aid bill. 

The long range dream for Thieu to retain power takes the following form. 

Because the economic problems are irresolvable with an army of 1.1 million men, Thieu will have to adapt the Paris Agreement to his own uses and make apparent compromises. The first step will be a sign of reconciliation, eliminating Article 

4 from the constitution so "communists" can operate as a legal political party. 

At this point Thieu can hope to begin a negotiated partial demobilization and the PRG will also demobilize. Then Thieu will select secret supporters as members of the Third Force in the National Council of Reconciliation and Concord, so that his forces dominate that body. National election will then be scheduled and held. With Thieu's officials in control of the machinery, the communists can easily be held to 20% of the announced vote. Thieu's forces will remain in power. 

The present political economy, with adjustments for peace, will remain essentially intact. Foreign investors and tourists will flock in, and the need for 

American aid will diminish to far more politically tolerable levels. If this sounds possible to the reader, basic political reality should be remembered. The 

PRG position rests on a political heritage that is 2,000 years old. The present struggle to end foreign domination has been going on for four decades. Dreams of social justice and political independence remain healthy. 

For 24 years in a row the American Executive branch, supported in varying degrees by the legislative branch, has struggled with diplomatic financial, and 13

military means to mold the realities of Indochina to American perceptions and purposes. This Administration would continue such a pursuit. It would ignore the moral and human costs and insist that the American taxpayer support the financial burden to assure the status quo and the Administration's perceptions of Vietnamese reality. Last year Congress, hoping to pressure Thieu toward political compromise and peace, cut the FY 74 aid requests slightly. The Administration ignored the Congressional intent and subsidized Thieu in every way possible.

In this essay I have tried to document what these choices have cost and will continue to cost the Vietnamese people. It is not enough to add up the billions it has cost the American taxpayer and uncover the many domestic programs that have been starved as a result." It is not enough to count the 120,000 to 150,000 

Vietnamese who have been killed or wounded in the last year and the 800,000 to 1,000,000 new refugees which have been created. One must consider whether the political and economic system as a whole functions in the best interests of the people. 

It is not an impossible question, for the empirical evidence from every sector of political and economic activity documents an inescapable answer. The present policies and practices of the RVN and its officials are fundamentally and irremediably contradictory to the basic needs of the Vietnamese people. For the poor it is now not even a question of tolerating this misery, it is a question of sheer physical survival. On March 22 Dien Tin reported that a progovernment Senator Tran 

Tan Tuan had announced that the RVN Ministry of Agriculture was considering the export of 50,000 metric tons of rice. Last year 50,000 tons was "loaned" to 

Lon Nol. Holding up decision was not the reality of PL 480 import shipments, 124,000 tons in the first quarter of 1974, but the possible conflicts with American dealers on the world market! The Ministry of Agriculture said there was plenty of rice, but people were just too poor to buy it. Thieu does not permit them to cross into the PRG areas where rice land is freely available and where much of the Delta rice is now sold in preference to RVN government markets. The production, purchase, and consumption of rice is the heart of economic reality in Vietnam. The RVN government has ravaged the heart as it has every other part of the body politic in its quest for political power and economic wealth. 

Whatever the costs of political change, they are insignificant compared to the magnitude of human misery this Administration would perpetuate for the Vietnamese. 

Congress has another choice. That choice is to force this Administration and the Thieu government to live up to the political obligations they undertook with the Paris Agreement. The PRG has consistently urged this path to a peaceful political settlement. There is every indication that it would abide by its provisions. Thieu knows that the Paris Agreement means compromise and a sharing of the political power his officials find so profitable. He has thus ignored nearly every major element of the Paris Agreement." He will continue this pattern until or unless he is forced to do otherwise. Meanwhile at terrible cost to the Vietnamese the basic structural contradictions of the RVN economy are slowly destroying the RVN state. To change this situation Congress must considerably diminish the resources available to Thieu. 

Such a path will not be without costs and risks, but these costs are far less than accepting the perpetuation of the present kinds of human tragedy, degradation, and corruption, a tiny portion of which I have chronicled herein. Such a path will also involve complex political and economic change in Vietnam which cannot be precisely mapped out. But the continuation of the known is fundamentally irresponsible in every sense of the word. Any decision made in June can be reviewed in December if it needs to be, but money once appropriated becomes inevitably fuel for further tragedy.

275 289 75 639 541 c275 c275 541 350 105 20 475 175 300 475 It is possible to speculate on the general process of loosening political restrictions that would take place. However, such speculation perpetuates precisely the same basic ethnocentric assumption Americans have made for two decades or more. It carries on the basic presumptions that the United States has the ability and the right to program the future of any other country or people. That such a view cannot be defended and that such policies have failed for two decades in Vietnam do not seem to deter this Administration. But Vietnam is the business of the Vietnamese, not the Americans, as the Paris Agreement clearly and repeatedly states.

The military evolution depends on the assumption that the PRG will not launch an attack in the middle of the transition. The PRG and DRV leadership have always been eminently pragmatic. Faced with major economic priorities at home, the DRV does not want to pursue with expensive bloodshed and uncertain outcome a political problem that can be solved with political means. If there is substantive political movement, the PRG and DRV will avoid bloodshed. An in-place military ceasefire could be negotiated fairly quickly. Demobilization, negotiated stage by stage, would mean DRV tanks and troops going north as well as fairly rapid RVN demobilization of 4 to 600,000 troops. With little gas and no technicians, Thieu would be discouraged from offensive air operations. Local commanders could afford peace in part because they could not afford war. 

But the economy will collapse say the defenders of the status quo. I have documented that for most poor Vietnamese, which is most Vietnamese, the economy has already collapsed. The price of food is beyond the means of many poor, and the price and allocation system is controlled by corrupt officials and private speculators. It is hard to imagine how things could get worse. What is most likely to take place would be a slow cutback in certain commodities over six months as the CIP and PL 480 pipelines were drawn down. This is NOT an immediate cutoff. 

It leaves 4 to 6 months at least for adjustments. In 1942 the Japanese conquered 

Indochina and there really was an abrupt cutoff of imports. The Vietnamese economy thrived as never before. It is a most instructive historical parallel.

When a country is cut off a demand exists but no foreign supply is possible. 

Domestic entrepreneurs grab the opportunity. A wide variety of small enterprises would seize upon the scrap iron, for example, for agricultural needs like plows. 

Certainly the living standards of the wealthy would drop, but the Vietnamese in RVN areas rather badly need a more egalitarian society if they ever hope to live in peace in one political community. Three basic imports provide most of the total yearly bill. Petroleum for all RVN uses should be drawn from the military aid monies to insure that both the civilian and the military populations in RVN areas become acutely aware of how much petroleum costs and how little they can afford frivolous military exercises. Rice imports should be limited to the central regions. 

Given its corruption, the RVN will soon be unable to feed urban slum dwellers and refugees. They will vote with their feet. They will insist on returning to abandoned rice lands to begin farming. Hungry poorly paid soldiers on either side will have no incentive to stop them. Such movement is, in fact, already under way. 

Finally, there is the problem of fertilizer. For the long term I propose funding of the urea plant which, by AID's description, would be operational in a year. In the short term there would be considerable movement back to labor intensive traditional agriculture. This provides needed jobs and enormous incentive to rural migration and settlement. In 1974 1.9 million hectares by traditional methods will produce half the needed 6.5 million metric tons. A majority of 900 million hectares now under cultivation in high yield varieties would have to be turned to traditional varieties to cut down on fertilizer needs. If another 800,000 to 

1,000,000 hectares could be planted by traditional methods this fall, the RVN would need no imported rice and could survive on the fertilizer now in the pipeline. If RVN and PRG soldiers were turned to a giant WPA project of unexploded ordnance disposal and canal dredging such a transformation would be quite possible. And if real efforts were made in both the political and economic transformation toward independence, Congress could consider filling any real gaps late this year.

The Administration proposes $910 million in economic aid to the RVN. It cannot demonstrate that such a funding level will avoid another year of war. It speaks not of another 100,000 Vietnamese casualties and another 1,000,000 refugees. It has no answer for the endless suffering of those millions of Vietnamese being ground to death by the institutionalized corruption and inflation of this artificial economy. For the irresolvable economic contradictions it offers fundamentally erroneous approaches to both agricultural and industrial modernization. 

For the social parasites it offers even greater resources to corrupt. For the Vietnamese people it offers the rhetoric of salvation but the reality of further degradation and dehumanization. Such a proposal rests manifestly contrary to any reading of our constitutional and ethical ideals. 

I propose instead a transitional economic aid program of $200 million. Certainly some Vietnamese will remain hungry in this interim. Urban living standards will decline. But if people are hungry with a tangible goal ahead, rather than starving for nothing as many are now, it will be far more bearable. What such a transformation means is the beginning of hope, of dignity, of selfsufficiency for millions of Vietnamese. It appeals to the positive instincts of mankind, not the instincts of fear, hatred, jealousy and aggression. It asks much of the Vietnamese people and much of the American people. But it promises even more. It promises the answer to the immortal question, "Papa, Qu'est ce que c'est la paix?"

POLITICAL CHANGE IN VIETNAM Chairman MORGAN. Thank you, gentlemen. 

Gentlemen, the statements which you submitted to the committee contain heavy criticism of the Saigon government which is headed by 

President Thieu. I have some questions which either of you may answer. 

Would you please tell the committee who you think would be running South Vietnam if President Thieu is forced out? If the United

States reduces its aid to South Vietnam as you propose in your statement, do you think a changeover in the Government would take place? 

And if so, do you expect the leadership change in Saigon would take place without bloodshed, or how would it occur?

Mr. BRANFMAN. As I mentioned in my statement, I was in South 

Vietnam last year and asked these same questions to an awful lot of people, including American Embassy officials. I think one thing to note just before answering the question directly is that when we are talking about the government of President Thieu we are talking about a very special government. We are talking about a government which now receives about 85 percent of its resources from a foreign power. 

That is the only government like that in the world except, of course, for Lon Nol and the Royal Laotian Government. 

So we really are talking about someone whose main constituency is in the United States, is specifically in the U.S. Congress, and who at this point as far as I could tell in South Vietnam has little, if any, support from anyone.

When I said what is the alternative to Thieu, the general consensus was that there were a number of third force leaders who would enjoy some popular support, certainly more than Thieu does; and that the 

Provisional Revolutionary Government, that is the other side, is not interested in taking power immediately; that they realize the force in this country against an open Communist victory, of how people would be upset and, therefore, there would be a kind of a coalition government that would emerge with perhaps President General Minh, perhaps a younger man that we don't know about at this point very well, perhaps some of the other people in Thieu's cabinet. Perhaps a 

Ngo Cong Duc or other Catholics would be key persons in such a government. It would be made up of a kind of coalition of Communists, PRG people, plus third force people, plus some people who are presently in Thieu's cabinet would govern for a period. What would happen after that I don't know. A lot of people thought that the PRG would take over.

EFFECTS OF REDUCTION IN VIETNAM AID 

If we reduce aid, would this precipitate a change in government? 

I think the opposite. I think what will precipitate a change in government will be a continued high level of aid which keeps Thieu in power and allows him to continue refusing to make any kind of serious attempts to seek a political settlement with the other side. 

I think if we reduce aid two things might happen. One is that President Thieu is as popular as his admirers publicly say. In that case I think he would be able to compete politically with the PRG. He would remain in power and would then have to fight it out politically and we would see what would happen.

The other possibility, and frankly I think it is more likely, is that if we reduced aid that there would be other people on the right and in the center emerging who would then compete with the other side for political power. I think that this is possible, but whatever the risks, the main thing I would like to stress this morning is that the alternative is unacceptable. The alternative is what we have now. It is leading to an unacceptable situation which is offering the other side the choice of surrender or a new offensive. If there is a new offensive, it is offering us the choice of seeing Thieu fall or resuming our bombing. 

And it is resulting in, as I said, mass death, mass starvation, and terrible conditions of repression. That is what we have now.

Now the alternative, and this is where I think most people agreed with me, might not keep Thieu in power. It might produce the kind of government you have in Laos in which the other side is playing a dominant role. Almost everyone I talked to agreed that it was preferable to the present situation, that there was a possibility this other way that there could be some kind of peaceful resolution to the situation which Americans could accept. There was general agreement that the present situation will not produce any kind of an acceptable solution. TES! 128 

BLOODSHED AND CHANGE OF LEADERSHIP IN SAIGON 

Chairman MORGAN. How about the last part of my question, which was do you expect this change of leadership in Saigon would take place without bloodshed?

Mr. BRANFMAN. I think the bloodshed that would occur would be far less than we have right now. Let's again remember 200,000-300,000 people officially killed or wounded since the cease-fire in South Vietnam alone. Cambodia, no one knows what the casualties are, but they are quite extensive.

I think that if we went back to the Paris agreement which calls for the formation of a National Council of National Reconciliation and Concord which would plan elections, which would probably result in some kind of coalition government, that the chances for bloodshed would be minimized because you would have the beginnings of a political process. I don't know, frankly. Nobody really knows how much would take place. But as I say, because under the Paris agreement each of the three parts in the political process is allowed to keep its paramilitary and military forces until finally there is some kind of national government in South Vietnam, I think the chances for bloodshed are far less than we have right now and will have for the foreseeable future.

MILITARY MOVES OF NORTH VIETNAM 

Chairman MORGAN. What do you have to say about reports that 

North Vietnam is continuing to send troops to the south? Do you believe that she is?

Mr. BRANFMAN. Well, I have seen so many different figures on this question of North Vietnam's troops. 

Do you want to answer?

Mr. GRAN. I followed this question rather extensively in studying the military aid request. If you followed the statements presented to various committees in Congress, the numbers of DRV troops in the south over the period from the cease-fire until April or May of this year remained around the figure of 140,000 to 150,000. In the press recently, but not the Congress, some estimates have been much higher than that. I don't see any basis for them, and I have not seen any exploration of them by a Defense Department witness before Congress. 

The North Vietnamese quite apparently are replacing troops lost in the south and troops are going home sick and wounded. I have not seen persuasive evidence that there is any kind of extensive buildup of DRV troops. There has been a buildup of roads in PRG areas. 36-333-74- -43

Chairman MORGAN. Isn't that a violation of the Paris agreement? 

Mr. GRAN. Economic development, including roadbuilding, is not a violation. Of the various kinds of buildups the thing that I think is the clearest violation, is that the number of tanks has increased since March or April of 1973. The number of tanks appears to have grown somewhat since that time and that would seem to be the clearest instance of violations. 

THE "MORAL COMMITMENT" TO VIETNAM Chairman MORGAN. Thank you, gentlemen. 

Mr. Frelinghuysen.

Mr. FRELINGHUYSEN.  

Mr. Chairman, I realize that individuals are entitled to their own. opinion, but I must say I find the testimony of these witnesses most unimpressive and indeed astonishing. I was out more recently in 

Vietnam than these witnesses and perhaps the situation had changed by the time I arrived, but I would not recognize it to have been in the same country from hearing these witnesses. 

I was pleased to see though that Mr. Branfman does recognize that the United States has a moral commitment to help the Indochinese people. He says that, "Our only moral commitment remaining to it is to see that the Paris agreement is observed so that we may finally reach a political solution."

Well, I am not sure how directly involved we are, if "we" refers to the United States. I cannot see how Mr. Branfman's recipe for resolving this problem politically is going to bring it about. 

I was pleased to see Mr. Branfman at least recognizes that the Vietnamese people have an economic problem. Economic self-sufficiency may be some time in coming, but for us to turn our backs on people in trouble and in need does not strike me as a way of helping them with their severe economic problems. 

They speak of-or at least Mr. Branfman does, I don't know to what extent Mr. Gran associates himself with the testimony-of deliberate attempts by Nixon administration officials to deceive the American people. Well, I might say, Mr. Branfman, you seem to be engaging in a little manipulation of the facts yourself. 

CONTROL OF HAMLETS AND CEASE-FIRE VIOLATIONS 

On page 6 you quote from my report, and I am glad you have read it, but you read it and use it for what would appear to be illogical purposes. You say that "American officials constantly claim that the 

Communists have taken the initiative in violating the cease-fire militarily." That rings to me as if you were trying to create the impression that the South Vietnamese are trying to continue a military effort when they should be seeking a political solution. That certainly is your argument in other places.

Well, let me say that the fact that there has been an increase in the number of hamlets that are under the dominant control of the South Vietnamese does not mean they have necessarily been acquired exclusively by military means. Dominant control could not be won

and maintained simply by applying military force. If you are a student of this situation, I would think you would know that. 

I don't know why I should be explaining to you if you have been studying this for years. What has happened and what did happen before the cease-fire was that a lot of South Vietnam was not under anyone's control-not the control of the Communists nor the control of the South Vietnamese Government. In addition, the Communists made a massive "land grab" just before the cease-fire went into effect and they have not had either the military force or popularity to hold on to what they took. 

My point is that since the cease-fire there has been a very substantial increase in the dominant control of the South Vietnamese Government which to me represents the fact that the people support this government. I found no evidence, and I wonder where you found it, that these people are not rallying around President Thieu.

I would suppose that your peace proposal-and this Mr. Gran says would only take a few weeks-would be an utter capitulation on the part of the present government of the Government of South Vietnam to what the North may want as a way of bringing about the result. 

If we have a moral commitment to get a compromise here, I don't see how we can justifiably face up to that commitment by pulling the rug from under one of the parties to the cease-fire. 

THE MILITARY PROBLEM IN VIETNAM 

Following up what you see as the nature of our moral commitment, you say on page 3, that this necessitates congressional action to suspend or reduce aid to governments in Indochina until they show more willingness to switch the conflict from the military to the political arena. That might be good advice if we were supporting the North, but we are not supporting the North. The unilateral suspension or massive reduction in aid by us would affect only the South and you do not seem much worried about what the ultimate effect of such a move would be on our friends and allies or of the nature of the compromise we might force as a result. it I would think that the least you could do is to recognize that there really is a genuine military problem creating serious economic dislocation, and not just suggest that in some way the Government of South Vietnam is to be blamed for institutionalizing inflation. You know, is easy to smear both governments and people and to misrepresent situations, but inflation is not the result of a deliberate design of the 

Thieu government.

Moreover, you surely don't think that the Thieu government is not anxious to test its strength politically. Of course, Mr. Thieu would rather move the conflict into the political arena, because that would reduce the necessity of maintaining a great military establishment to defend against pressures from the North. The South Vietnamese are confident they can compete successfully in nonmilitary fields and have repeatedly offered to face the Communists in elections in the south. 

I don't know why I should be telling this to students of Vietnam, but it is the North that has been reluctant to try the political route and it is the Communists that have insisted on the military approach. 

Now I would be glad to get your comments if you have some.

A COMMITMENT: OBSERVATION OF PARIS AGREEMENT

What I mean by "our moral commitment to seeing that the Paris agreement is observed" is our stopping our present violation of article 4 by which we are intervening in the internal affairs of Vietnam by supporting only one side with massive amounts of money. 

Mr. FRELINGHUYSEN. Are you suggesting we should not worry about our relationship and responsibility to provide a reasonable degree of viability for the South?

FREEDOM OF RESIDENCE IN VIETNAM 

Mr. FRELINGHUYSEN. Thank you, Mr. Lagomarsino.

Mr. BRANFMAN. The shreds of evidence is simply this: Under article 

11 of the Paris Agreement there would be a freedom of residence. This would allow the refugees to return back to their villages. As Mr. 

Block testified last week, the Thieu government has been stopping refugees from returning home, resettling them in arid, landless areas in order to claim control over those areas. It would give them basic democratic freedoms.

Mr. FRELINGHUYSEN. You are not talking to the points raised at all, Mr. Branfman. I want to get evidence of the North being willing to engage in political discussion with the South.

Mr. BRANFMAN. The evidence is that you cannot expect them to do more than to offer to negotiate politically. 

Mr. FRELINGHUYSEN. I have not heard anything about an offer to negotiate politically. 

Mr. BRANFMAN. Certainly. On March 22 the PRG offered a sixpoint plan which calls, in part, for the observation of article 11. This would allow the PRG to organize in the cities, to have the refugees go back to where they came from. It would see the freeing of the political prisoners, all of which can only help the PRG. 

Observation of the Paris agreement would allow the PRG to organize in the cities, to move freely. Obviously, it's in their interest to negotiate politically. 

MEANING OF THE ARMS AGREEMENT 

Now let's look at the other side. We say that Thieu is willing to negotiate politically. If this is the case, why has Thieu, for example, recently announced that he will only have elections if the North Vietnamese withdraw from South Vietnam? This is what we fought for 10 years over. We spent 50,000 American lives. We wasted $130 billion. 

We dropped 7 million tons of bombs trying to force the North Vietnamese to agree that they have to get out of South Vietnam. We could not do it.

We signed the Paris agreement which says that Vietnam is one country, an agreement which does not mention the North Vietnamese anywhere, and which allows them to stay in any part of Vietnam. 

It does not allow them to reinforce in South Vietnam. 

Thieu says they have to pull out of South Vietnam. That is the same as saying, I don't really want a political settlement because I am going to set a condition which I know the other side will not meet. 

Thieu states publicly that there is no third force in South Vietnam. 

He has called it an imaginary segment. One of his spokesmen called it that on March 25. 

Mr. FRELINGHUYSEN. You are off the subject again. 

Mr. BRANFMAN. I am trying to explain. You are saying that Thieu is not willing to compete politically, and the PRG is. 

But Thieu said there is no third force. If Thieu were willing to negotiate, he would recognize the third force which is given legal standing under the Paris agreement. He would allow it to organize and stop jailing its leaders. He has not done it.

For these and many other reasons in my statement I think it is very obvious that Thieu has refused to test the other side's offer to negotiate. 

On the military side of things we produced a paper which I will be happy to give you, 1 year after the peace agreement was signed, which had over 150 reports from the Western press of military violations by the GVN. One example is from the Washington Post of September 30, 1973. It says:

In the past month, military officials say, almost 20 square miles of formerly Communist-held territory has been seized by South Vietnamese troops driving westward from Highway 1.

There are dozens of other reports which makes it quite clear, sir, that although you were there you were in South Vietnam. You didn't really have a chance, I am afraid, to see the actual military situation in the battlefield over the past year, and neither did I for that matter. 

But I think these dozens of press reports make it clear that the reason that the GVN has added so many hamlets to its control is that in many cases it has militarily moved into hamlets, which were either not claimed by either side or under PRG control, and has taken them over. 

So I think that the evidence is fairly clear that Thieu has taken the initiative in violating the cease-fire militarily.

[The information requested follows:] INDOCHINA RESOURCE CENTER 

The Indochina Resource Center is a project of the Indochina Education Council. The Indochina Education Council is composed of representatives from the 

Boards of Social Concern of the United Methodist Church, United Church of 

Christ and United Presbyterian Church.

The Indochina Resource Center's budget is roughly $50,000 a year. This money goes toward paying the uniform salaries of $400 month for 9 full- and part-time staff employees and consultants, publishing Indochina Today, a 100-page booklet produced every 1-2 months consisting of news reports and official documents on Indochina, The U.S. and Indochina, our regular newsletter, numerous special reports, and such basis expenses as rent and telephone. 

The Indochina Resource Center's full-time staff and consultants include 2 persons with advanced degrees in Southeast Asian studies who have both lived in Indochina, 1 person with such a degree who has not traveled to Southeast Asia,

1 person who has spent 42 out of the past 7 years in all four countries of Indochina and Thailand, one Vietnamese woman, 1 behavioral psychologist, 1 former editorial assistant.

Well over 200 individuals have contributed money to the activities of the Indochina Education Council over the past year, with average contributions on the order of $50. Most of those who support us have traditionally given money to 

Indochina-related organizations. 

The Indochina Resource Center does not engage in direct lobbying. Like hundreds of other educational and public interest organizations, however, we do make available to congress or any other interested bodies the fruits of our ongoing research into the war, culture, economy, and society in Indochina. 

INDOCHINA RESOURCE CENTER AND LOBBYING 

Mr. ZABLOCKI. I forgot to ask. Is your center registered as a lobbying organization?

Mr. ZABLOCKI. You don't lobby for or against legislation? 

Mr. BRANFMAN, No, we don't. 

Mr. ZABLOCKI. What are you doing this morning?

Mr. BRANFMAN. We are bringing our expertise to bear- 

Mr. ZABLOCKI. Expertise? 

Mr. BRANFMAN. On the subject.

Mr. ZABLOCKI. Yes. 

How would you define expertise?

Mr. BRANFMAN. Well, on a daily basis we monitor 10 U.S. newspapers, the Foreign Broadcast Information Service, the Saigon Press Review, and we are in correspondence with a number of individuals in Indochina. I spent the last 412 years out of 7 years in Indochina itself, and I think we know as much about Indochina as anyone else that we are aware of. I don't want to say we know more, but we know as much about it as anyone. We keep track of what is happening on a daily basis.

Mr. BRANFMAN. As long as the war continues, I don't think we will be able to do anything to really get into the areas where most of them were lost. 

I must be frank with you, Mr. Zablocki, and say that my primary concern at this point is for the living, it is for the tens of thousands of people who are now being held and tortured in Saigon's jails. It is for the refugees.

Mr. Wolff.

SELF-DETERMINATION IN VIETNAM 

Mr. WOLFF. 

I am somewhat disturbed by the colloquies that have taken place here. I think that both the Members of the Congress as well as the witnesses before us have the highest purposes in mind.

At the outset let me say I am opposed very strongly to a Communist takeover in Vietnam. I am also opposed to the Thieu government, which has been opposed to self-determination for the people of Vietnam.

I believe that the reason the U.S. Government went into Vietnam in the first place was to provide for self-determination of the people. I think that the higher purpose that we have in whatever we do in Vietnam is the basic American interest. I feel very strongly that one

of the major causes, if not the major cause, of the economic chaos that we have in the United States today has been caused by our participation in Vietnam.

I think it is about time we thought of the moral commitments of the American people. I feel it appears very strongly that we have humanitarian interests that are very strong, but what about the American interests?

It seems to me that one of the very basic elements in this entire situation is the continued diversion of American assistance outside of the channels for which they were originally intended. I feel that we had as well a very important decision to be made by this Government in the way of continued assistance to Vietnam. I am not for cutting off all aid to South Vietnam, but I certainly am opposed to the continued pouring of dollars into what seems to be a bottomless pit. 

We are told that we can't provide college tuition for Vietnam veterans because the money spent for tuition payments would amount to some $250 million. This we are told is inflationary, and yet it seems we can afford to spend money to help the South Vietnamese Government stem their inflation and that is not inflationary. 

I think that if we talk about priorities in this Nation we have to talk about the priorities of the American people and our ability to sustain answers to the difficult problems we face. 

BLACK MARKET ACTIVITIES IN VIETNAM 

What interests me in your statement, and I should like to find some means of documentation as has been requested here by Members of Congress, are some of the efforts at diversion that have occurred. 

I am just wondering in your trips to Vietnam, or trips the members of your organization have taken to Vietnam, do you have any evidence of the continuing black market that I saw, not as part of the cook's tour, but on my own in Vietnam?

Mr. BRANFMAN. Personally I don't have hard evidence in the sense that most of the evidence that used to get out was never really the kind of proof acceptable in a court of law, because naturally the Saigon government denies it vehemently. No official will come forward and claim it. But I heard of continuing black marketeering from American officials and American civilian technicians. 

Mr. WOLFF. It is very open on the streets of Vietnam. 

Mr. BRANFMAN. That kind of black market, sure; but it is hard to say if you are out in the market looking at things that this or that comes from American aid, or this or that comes from I don't know where. It is hard to prove the source of any given item. 

Mr. WOLFF. American items that are there, are available on the streets. 

Mr. BRANFMAN. Yes, that still goes on..

All I can tell you is that everybody I talked to-and don't take my word for it, but go out and just talk to other people and try to draw a conclusion-even quite pro-Thieu American officials-said that the corruption problem was quite strong. I have listed here various scandals that have been reported in the Saigon newspapers.

FREEDOM OF PRESS IN VIETNAM 

Mr. WOLFF. The Thieu government has been criticized for the fact that they have not permitted the newspapers freedom of the press, yet you have here illustrations of scandals that have occurred in recent months. How do you reconcile the two?

Mr. GRAN. I think the truth is probably someplace in between, as it is in a number of these issues. From reading the translations of the press over the last 6 months it seems to me that certain kinds of topics are permitted to be covered with really almost laissez-faire up to a certain point, and other kinds of topics have to be avoided or slanted, particularly presentations of the military events. There is an unending flow of RVN victories and sneaky, nasty Communist attacks.

That is a very unbalanced kind of reporting. But corruption scandals can be covered up to a point. It is all right to attack members of the assembly and provincial representatives and most businessmen, but the high-ranking officials in the National Bank, or Thieu's own Cabinet people have to be approached through innuendo, or not at all.

If you follow it on a day-to-day basis, you can see where the line is. The press talked about the National Bank scandal, at length in late 

March. On the third day of April, nine newspapers went too far and were confiscated.
