STANDARD OF LIVING IN NORTH VIETNAM 

Mr. GRAN. I think it is slightly less. The average standard of living is probably a little lower in the North. 

Mr. BRANFMAN. It is hard to say though. For example, when I was in North Vietnam we visited remote villages which had health clinics and schools staffed by teachers provided by the government. So that whereas there were, to be sure, less consumer goods in Hanoi, out in the countryside the people had medical care and schooling that the equivalent village in South Vietnam might not have. So it is hard to measure "standard of living."

Standard of living is a funny word. We often tend to think of it in terms of an urban consumer style and not measure in other things that we take for granted that the peasants in the third world don't and can't.

REASONS FOR U.S. ACTIONS IN VIETNAM 

Mr. HARRINGTON. Let me finish by asking your opinion as to what motivates or moves our country to continue for years in this same direction? We have solved the problem of the war's visibility. Most people are indifferent as to whether there are 350,000 or 700,000 slaughtered in the court of essentially a civil war. Without looking for conspiracies what is your own assessment of the motives which keep us pouring more money into the situation?

Mr. BRANFMAN. I think we have to come to the notion of Presidential covert war and say, "What is the motive of the executive branch?" By that I mean the White House, the top leaders in the 

CIA, the State Department, the Defense Department, the Joint Chiefs of Staff, none of whom are elected, except for the President, all of whom are appointed by him, but many of whom remain in power year after year, no matter who is President. 

I think one has to look to their motives to explain why the Executive still this year is proposing spending $3.7 billion for Indochina. more than the rest of the world as a whole. I think that, particularly in foreign policy they have become what Senator Fulbright has called "Presidential dictatorship." I think their motives have more to do with expanding their control, keeping control, and I think they are very sensitive to the needs of the heads of the major corporations. 

For example, there has been a tremendous transfer of resources over the last 10 years out to Asia with corporations buildings out For the record. Mr. Gran subsequently supplied the following information: The 1974 

Information Please almanac shows 18.9 million people in South Vietnam and 22.04 million in North Vietnam.

there and working out there because of the cheap labor supply. I think the executive branch is anxious and is very sensitive to these corporations to an extent that Congress, for example, is not. 

Över the last decade the central problem of our time was Congress coming to grips with the issue of our direct intervention in the third world and finally stopping it. Over the next decade the central problems of our times is for Congress to try to gain some control over this Presidential covert war which, as I say, is going on all over the globe, and I think the reason really is very clear: That we simply cannot afford this any more. 

We heard a man yesterday say that hundreds of millions of people are going to die during the next several years, or at least during the next decade due to mass starvation around the world. I was just at the Naval War College last week at a 3-day conference and heard that there has been an exponential increase in arms payments and that a volunteer Army has turned out to be extremely expensive, and that the military budget as far as they are concerned will have to expand to keep pace with rising weapons costs.

Mr. HARRINGTON. Let me just conclude by suggesting I don't share your feeling that it is a responsiveness to corporate desires which motivates involvement. I think the reasons to be far more complex and subjective, and I would not want my silence to imply that I agreed with that particular part of the theory.

REFUGEES IN VIETNAM: POLITICAL PREFERENCE 

Mr. WINN. Well, if everything is so swell in North Vietnam, how come some of the refugees are heading toward South Vietnam? 

Mr. BRANFMAN. First of all, I think it is a myth that all of the refugees go south. For example, and this was true in Laos where I lived for 4 years, the younger people, the younger men and women go with the Pathet Lao. The refugees who would come out were basically the old and the very young who could not take the bombing, or who were simply forced out. 

Very often in South Vietnam our troops would go into villages and order the people to leave. So I think this is the primary reason. 

Our bombing was the other major factor. In fact, it is amazing the lack of evidence of dissent in North Vietnam, of people wanting to leave it. We are looking for it. We have people up there trying to find out about it. It is quite amazing the lack of dissent in North Vietnam over the last decade that has been reported. I can only think of a few examples which have even been reported. 

WEATHER MODIFICATION IN WARFARE 

Mr. WINN. Another subject. Do you think that rainmaking for wartime advantage is wrong? 

Mr. BRANFMAN. I think it is very wrong because I think you don't tamper with the environment, you don't tamper with nature unless you can control it, unless it is being used to support life and not death. 

I think when you are making war in secret, when the power to change the weather patterns rests in the hands of a small group of people who are really accountable to no one, it is extremely dangerous. 

For example, suppose there were rainmaking attempts over North Vietnam during the war and perhaps such rainmaking had been successful enough to cause the dams to break and we had flooded out and thereby killed or had starved to death several million people. I would not have approved that, and I hope you would not have. I think it is an example of why certainly Presidential or Executive covert rainmaking should be opposed.

Mr. WINN. Not only would I be opposed to that, I would not be opposed to the rainmaking process that would allow them to wash out the roads that are bringing in ammunition, tanks and supplies down to kill human beings by that method. 

Mr. BRANFMAN. Well, I would be opposed to it if it was a war in which we were in the wrong, we had no business intervening in any way. 

Mr. WINN. You are going to set the stipulation of the war? 

Mr. BRANFMAN. Yes; I am saying that in the case where we are competing wrongly, then I don't agree with it.

STATEMENT OF GEOFFREY KEMP, FLETCHER SCHOOL OF LAW AND DIPLOMACY, TUFTS UNIVERSITY 

Mr. KEMP. 

I welcome this opportunity to discuss with the Committee on Foreign Affairs some of the longrun dilemmas implicit in the transfer of large quantities of advanced arms by the industrial powers to conflict areas in the less developed world. 

My basic thesis is that there is a strong relationship between geopolitical conflict over resources, the nature of the nonnuclear balance of power in areas such as the Mediterranean and the Middle East, and the propensity of the United States and the Soviet Union to become involved in the military aspects of a local conflict. For this reason, the dangers of a nuclear war between the two superpowers may be more likely as a result of political miscalculation in the Middle East than because either the United States or the Soviet Union has a few more nuclear warheads or launchers in commission than the other, in which case it is very much in our interests to examine the nuances of regional military problems with the same degree of rigor and depth which we now apply to some of our debates about the central nuclear balance. Specifically, it is my testimony, Mr. Chairman, that we have been very negligent to date in our efforts to understand the consequences of the worldwide traffic in arms.

ARMS TRANSFERS: "STAGGERING PROPORTIONS" 

Over the past 2 years the amounts of military equipment transferred by the industrial powers to certain conflict areas in the less developed world have reached what can only be described as staggering proportions. The demand for a whole variety of arms shows no signs of slackening.

In particular, the recent spate of purchases of very modern British, French, and United States weapons by the oil-rich Middle East countries especially Iran, Saudi Arabia, and Kuwait-suggests that the oil-rich countries are operating in a "buyer's market" for arms and can obtain very sophisticated weapons from several competing industrial countries.

What are the most important implications of these trends? Are the industrial powers engaged in an irresponsible selling spree designed, in the short run, to increase revenue and insure oil supplies but doomed, in the long run, to increase the sources for conflict? Or, are the suppliers behaving in a rational and cautious manner given the uncertainties involved?

If the former proposition is correct, what steps should be taken to defuse or moderate the dangers of the military buildup? Should the 

United States explore with other industrial nations the possibility of more stringent regulations on the transfer of arms? What should the

United States do if the other sellers refuse to cooperate in such matters?

Alternatively, if it is believed that current supplier policies are, in principle, based upon sound reasoning, then what limits, if any, should be placed upon the issue of export licenses or upon credits for sales? 

Should certain types of military hardware be offered for sale in preference to other types? For instance, should the United States sell the 

Shah of Iran any nonnuclear arms he wants or should some attempt be made to impose qualitative controls on his growing arsenal? 

In order to examine some of these options, it is first necessary to say something about the international geostrategic environment in which the military buildup is taking place. Unless this is done, the impact of various types and levels of arms transfer upon regional security and the prospects for war cannot be fully understood. 

SIX MAJOR CHANGES IN INTERNATIONAL SYSTEM 

In my statement I identify six major changes in the international system which, I believe, have contributed to the new strategic environment. Briefly they are: 

1. Changes in the world economic system; in particular the emergence of rich producer countries and a growing gap between these countries and the industrial powers on the one hand and the poor and super poor nations of the fourth world on the other hand. 

2. The effects of rapid population growth upon the demand for scarce resources. 

3. The impact of new technologies upon nuclear and nonnuclear strategies, as well as the impact of the economic exploitation of reserves. 

4. The policies of détente pursued by the United States, the Soviet 

Union. and China. 

5. The emergence of potential regional superpowers such as Iran, Nigeria, and Brazil. 

6. The increasing use of international terrorism by dissident political groups equipped with very exotic weapons systems. 

THE OIL PROBLEM 

I suggest, Mr. Chairman, that the oil problem ties many of these trends together. For example, the world demand for oil, together with its high price, have increased the importance of existing and potential oil supplies located under the sea bed. This, in turn, has already led

to political, and in one case military, conflict between countries competing for the physical control of the sea areas below which the oil is located. Thus, the current Law of the Sea Conference in Venezuela is taking place in an international environment in which most of the littoral states are anxious to reap the maximum benefit from their offshore resources be they oil, minerals or fish. 

The military implications are very clear as witnessed by the increasing emphasis upon the procurement of weapons for maritime missions by countries such as Brazil, Britain, India, Iran, Nigeria, Norway and Saudi Arabia. For instance, Britain and Norway are studying the strategic implications of the North Sea oil and are examining various ways of protecting the oil fields from a host of diverse miltary threats ranging from terrorists equipped with new technology weapons to the 

Soviet Navy. 

ARMS TRANSFERS: CAUSE OF WAR? 

Do arms transfers contribute to the causes of war ?

It is against this background of increasing concern over the eventual supply of raw materials that we should examine the potential effects of continuing high levels of arms transfers to existing and potential conflict areas. However, I argue that we do not know very much about these effects. Why?

NEED FOR COMPARATIVE STUDIES 

I believe that one reason is that the subject is inherently complex and has yet to receive the attention devoted to studies of the dynamics of the strategic nuclear arms race. There has been no comparative study on the military and security effects of weapons transfers to conflict areas in the less developed world that approaches the levels of expertise applied to matters relating to nuclear weapons, such as strategic arms limitations.

What types of studies do we need to make? I would argue that we basically need some sound answers to the following questions. 

1. What is the relationship between political conflict, military force structures and propensities for armed conflict in less developed countries? 

2. If certain categories and numbers of weapons do influence propensities toward or against armed conflict, how important are military assistance and sales programs in achieving these outcomes? 

3. If military assistance and sales programs are a relevant factor, do particular types of weapons have standard effects in all strategic environments? In certain environments? What method of classification can be suggested? 

4. Can meaningful distinctions be made between those weapons and force structures that enhance certain defensive and certain offensive military capabilities of recipients? 

5. If it is possible to come up with some classifications of weapons systems which has some empirically sound methodology, how should this influence arms transfer policies? 

6. What suppliers, other than the United States, can provide these weapons to the third world? What are their current policies? How do

these policies complement or conflict with the stated goals of U.S.

policy? 

CURSORY ANSWERS TO QUESTIONS 

I then proceed in my statement to give some very cursory answers to these questions. With respect to the first three questions I argue that the less developed world is not an homogeneous entity. Profound variations in the nature of the geographical milieu influence the effectiveness of certain weapons to perform certain missions in certain military environments. Similarly, the economic and technical capabilities of less developed countries to procure and operate modern weapons are varied.

Thus, the transfer of highly sophisticated and expensive weapons to technologically backward nations does not necessarily increase military security. Equally, though, there is no conclusive evidence that the transfer of advanced weapons increases the probability of war between political adversaries. What can be said with some certainty is that the transfer of advanced weapons has a profound influence upon the nature and outcome of military conflict should it occur. 

With respect to question 4 I argue that meaningful distinctions between certain offensive and defensive capabilities can be made provided that one specifies the geographical environment in which the forces are to be used and provided the comparative costs of different types of capabilities are taken into account. I point to the use of new precision-guided munitions in the closing stages of the U.S. air war over North Vietnam and the war in the Middle East in October 1973. 

I argue that at any given time the defense may indeed have an advantage over the offense, although I suggest that, at this stage, it is not possible to envisage a situation when the defense will have a permanent advantage over the offense for all important military missions. 

ARMS CONTROL AND U.S. ARMS TRANSFERS 

I then proceed to examine, Mr. Chairman, some of the options available to the United States in pursuing its arms transfer policies. 

I suggest that there are often conflicts of interest between the various objectives of arms transfer policies. Even arms control objectives can be in conflict with each other. I argue that it is difficult to imagine a situation in which arms control perspectives will take precedence over more traditional motives for transferring arms to rich and influential countries.

However, I do suggest some basic questions that both the executive and the legislative branches of Government should ask when requests for arms are made by foreign countries. I then outline in some detail a checklist of questions which you will find toward the end of my statement. I believe that if this range of questions was addressed by, say, this committee, as well as by other bodies, then at least we might have a much clearer idea as to why the request was being made, what possible effects it would have, both on the recipient's and the U.S. interests, and how these effects might relate to third parties, including local powers and other potential suppliers. 

Let me now summarize my conclusions.

RESOURCE DIPLOMACY AND ARMS 

The relationship between resource diplomacy and the demand for sophisticated military forces is best illustrated by the situation in the 

Persian Gulf. An unprecedented military buildup is occurring, funded by oil revenues, with the purpose of protecting the extraction, refinement, and transportation of petroleum and petroleum byproducts. Yet the military buildup itself may eventually increase the prospects for conflict by contributing to a local arms race. If this is a possibility, it poses a dilemma for the industrial powers, including the United States, who need the oil and, in terms of their power to control arms sales, find themselves in a buyer's market.

It is difficult to make recommendations about U.S. arms transfer policy that have applicability to all countries in the less developed world.

This suggests two lessons: First, that attempts to seek general arms control agreements to limit the transfer of arms are likely to fail. Second, that far more analyses are required concerning the short-run and long-run strategic and arms control implications of weapons transfers to specific regions such as the Persian Gulf. It is, therefore, in the interests of all U.S. Government agencies and congressional committees to devote greater effort to examining systematically the effects of military aid and sales upon overall U.S. interests. 

The continued preoccupation of the arms control community with the bipolar United States-Soviet nuclear arms race to the exclusion of serious study of regional military security and arms control, while understandable, has potentially very serious consequences for U.S. security. Nuclear war is probably more likely to occur as a result of escalating conventional war in the Sinai Desert, the Eastern Mediterranean, or the Persian Gulf than because the United States has more MIRV's than the Soviet Union and the latter has more heavy payload launchers than the United States. 

[The prepared statement follows:] STATEMENT Of Geoffrey KEMP, ASSOCIATE PROFESSOR OF INTERNATIONAL POLITICS, FLETCHER SCHOOL OF LAW AND DIPLOMACY, TUFTS UNIVERSITY, AND RESEARCH FELLOW, PROGRAM IN SCIENCE AND INTERNATIONAL AFFAIRS, HARVARD UNIVERSITY THE MILITARY BUILD-UP IN LESS DEVELOPED COUNTRIES: STRATEGIC IMPLICATIONS AND ARMS CONTROL PERSPECTIVES Intoduction¹ 

Mr. Chairman, I welcome this opportunity to discuss with the Committee on 

Foreign Affairs some of the long-run dilemmas implicit in the transfer of large quantities of advanced arms by the industrial powers to conflict areas in the lessdeveloped world. This phenomenon and the problems it creates or helps to solve are linked to two other important geo-strategic issues that will face both rich and poor nations in years to come; namely, increasing competition and conflict over the distribution of scarce resources, especially food and oil, and the spread of 1 This testimony is a revised, expanded, and up-dated version of a memorandum prepared for the Senate Foreign Relations Committee in the Fall of 1972 ("Conflict in the Third World: The Effects of Military Assistance Programs," Views on Foreign Assistance Policy: 

Comments by Individuals and Organizations Concerning United States Foreign Assistance Policy, Committee on Foreign Relations, United States Senate, January 1973. U.S. Govern ment Printing Office, Washington, D.C., 1973). It should be stressed that the original memorandum was not presented as testimony before formal hearings of the Foreign Relations Committee, and it was written before the 1973 Arab-Israel War and its aftermath.

nuclear technology, which, in turn may lead to a further proliferation of nuclear weapons.

As a scholar concerned with the broad trends in international relations, I would like to suggest that the questions I am addressing are as serious as some of the recent developments in nuclear weaponry which have been discussed in great detail in the context of the U.S.-Soviet strategic balance. 

My basic thesis is that there is a strong relationship between geo-political conflict over resources, the nature of the nonnuclear balance of power in areas such as the Mediterranean and the Middle East, and the propensity of the United States and the Soviet Union to become involved in the military aspects of a local conflict. 

For this reason, the dangers of a nuclear war between the two superpowers may be more likely as a result of political miscalculation in the Middle East than because either the United States or the Soviet Union has a few more nuclear warheads or launchers in commission than the other. In which case, it is very much in our interests to examine the nuances of regional military problems with the same degree of rigor and depth which we now apply to some of our debates about the central nuclear balance. Specifically, it is my testimony that we have been very negligent to date in our efforts to understand the consequences of the worldwide traffic in arms.

The military build-up and the new international strategic environment Over the past two years, the amounts of military equipment transferred by the industrial powers to certain conflict areas in the less developed world have reached what can only be described as staggering proportions. The demand for a whole variety of arms shows no signs of slackening. In particular, the recent spate of purchases of very modern British, French, and U.S. weapons by the oil-rich 

Middle East countries, especially Saudi Arabia, Iran, and Kuwait, suggests that the military build-up in that area will continue for years to come. The oil-rich countries are operating in a "buyer's market" for arms and can obtain very sophisticated weapons from several competing industrial countries. 

In addition to the expansion of the transfer of conventional arms to the Middle East, South and South East Asia, and Latin America, the detonation of a nuclear device by India, talks between India and Argentina on future nuclear cooperation, and the U.S. and French decisions to supply nuclear power reactors to Egypt, Israel, and Iran suggests a potentially ominous linkage between countries currently engaged in conflict with their neighbors and the eventual introduction of locally manufactured nuclear weapons into the regional power equation. 

What are the most important implications of these trends? Are the industrial powers engaged in an irresponsible selling-spree, designed, in the short run, to ensure oil supplies, balance budgets, and win friends and influence events, but doomed, in the long run, to exacerbate the existing sources for conflict by stimulating and fueling local arms races, and thereby increasing the risks of war and the disruption of oil supplies? Or, are the supplier countries in general, and the 

United States in particular, behaving in a rational and cautious manner, given the intrinsic uncertainties of politics in highly volatile conflict areas such as the 

Mddle East? If the former proposition is believed to be correct, what steps should be taken by the United States to defuse or moderate the dangers of the military buildup? Should not the United States explore with other industrial nations the possibility of more stringent regulations on the transfer of arms? What should the United States do if the other sellers refuse to cooperate in such matters? 

Alternatively, if it is believed that current supplier policies are, in principle, based upon sound reasoning, then what limits, if any, should be placed upon the issue of export licenses or upon credits for sales? Should certain types of military hardware be offered for sale in preference to other types? For instance, should the United States sell the Shah of Iran any nonnuclear weapons system he wants, or should some attempt be made to impose qualitative controls on his growing arsenal?

The most important aggregate statistics of the arms trade have been well documented in publications such as The International Transfer of Conventional Arms, a Report to the Congress from the U.S. Arms Control and Disarmament Agency pursuant to section 302 of the Foreign Relations Authorization Act of 1972 (Public Law 92-352), printed for the use of the Committee on Foreign Affairs; The Arms Trade with the Third World, Stockholm International Peace Research Institute (Stockholm: Almqvist and Wiksell, 1971); and The Military Balance (various editions), International Institute for Strategic Studies 

(London).

In order to examine some of these options, it is first necessary to say something about the international geo-strategic environment in which the military build-up is taking place. Unless this is done, the impact of various types and levels of arms transfer upon regional security and the prospects for war cannot be fully understood. It is suggested that the fundamental changes that have occurred throughout the international system over the past three years have radically altered some of the basis premises concerning the role of force in international policies. This, in turn, will influence the future roles and missions fof U.S. national security programs, to less-developed countries. At the most general level, these changes can be summarized under six separate but related headings. First, major changes in the world economic balance of power have occurred as a result of monetary inflation in the Western economies and world-wide increases in the demand for raw materials and food. This has led to further price increases and the emergence of two very distinct economic groups in the old Third World, the rich or potentially rich producer countries, and the poor and super-poor consumer countries who have little hope of adequately feeding their populations, let alone raising their living standards over the next decade. Second, and clearly related to the first change, the continued rapid growth of population in less-developed countries will increase the overall demand for these scarce resources, and thereby make today's problems more acute in the near future. Third, improvements in new technologies in the military sector have already had important effects upon the nature of both nuclear and non-nuclear military strategy. Also, technological developments in the civilian sector are now making it possible for the industrial powers to exploit hitherto untapped resources in the oceans. Fourth, the impact of detente diplomacy between the United States, the Soviet Union, and China has buried many of the ideological stereotypes which evolved during the 1950's and 1960's. Fifth, the emergence of new potential regional superpowers, such as Iran, India, Nigeria, and Brazil, may influence the strategic climate of their local regions in much the same way that the United States and the Soviet Union have determined the main streams of international behavior on a world-wide basis since 1945. Sixth, the increasing use of international terrorism by irregular political and criminal groups points to the highly vulnerable nature of many institutions of the industrial countries and the distinct possibility that "rich" industrial and primary producer nations may be held to ransom by dissident groups. 

The oil problem ties many of these trends together. For example, the world demand for oil, together with its high price, have increased with the importance of existing and potential oil supplies located under the sea bed. This, in turn, has already led to political, and in one case, military, conflict between countries competing for the physical control of the sea areas below which the oil is located. 

Thus, the current Law of the Sea Conference in Venezuela is taking place in an international environment in which most of the littoral states are anxious to reap the maximum benefit from their off-shore resources be they oil, minerals, or fish. The military implications are very clear as witnessed by the increasing emphasis upon the procurement of weapons for maritime missions by countries such as Brazil, Britain, India, Iran, Nigeria, Norway, and Saudi Arabia. For instance, Britain and Norway are studying the strategic implications of the North Sea oil and are examining various ways of protecting the oil fields from a host of diverse military threats ranging from terrorists equipped with new technology weapons, to the Soviet Navy. 

Do arms transfers contribute to the causes of war?

It is against this background that we should examine the potential effects of continuing high levels of arms transfers to existing and potential conflict areas. 

Before speculating about the future, however, it is appropriate to ask what can be learned from the history of the past twenty-five or so years. In particular, what have been the effects of past arms transfer and training programs upon the political, military, and economic behavior of recipients? How good is our ability to analyze the effects? What have been some of the costs and benefits of past security assistance and sales programs to United States interests? 

While we can all think of particular examples when the political, military, and economic affects of arms transfers have been obvious, it is not easy to infer general causal relationships between the supply of weapons and military training on the one hand, and propensities in the direction of war or peace on the

other hand. To the best of my knowledge, no one has yet come up with an empirical study that indicates such causation. To be sure, specific examples, such as U.S. military assistance programs to Europe, Israel, and South Vietnam, or 

Soviet aid to Egypt and North Vietnam, have had well-known effects and have been widely debated, but our understanding of these cases should not allow us, at this stage, to pass simple judgments on the entire sweep of military assistance and sales programs since the end of World War II. 

Why is our knowledge so sketchy? I believe that one reason is that the subject is inherently complex and has yet to receive the attention devoted to studies of the dynamics of the strategic nuclear arms race. There has been no comparative study on the military and security effects of weapons transfers to conflict areas in the less-developed world that approaches the levels of expertise applied to matters relating to nuclear weapons, such as strategic arms limitations. The SALT experience suggests that if we wish to have a meaningful dialogue with the Soviet Union about the nuclear arms race, it is necessary to be very detailed about the weapons involved, their relationship to the strategic and political milieu in which they are designed to operate, and the basic economic constraints that determine what numbers of particular weapons systems can be funded.

Unfortunately, we still talk in the most simplistic terms about the military balance and military power relationships in many other areas of the world. 

Very few detailed analyses have been undertaken by Congressional Committees, or, for that matter, by the academic community itself, on the strategic effects of weapons transfers even to such important areas as the Middle East. 

Outside the close confines of government, most discussions on "Middle East arms transfers are couched in political terms. Yet the Middle East is one area that has great relevance for American security policy. It is an area that warrants the most careful and thorough examination by the United States Congress of the military, as well as the political and economic, variables involved. 

Why has there been so little effort to examine the dynamics of non-nuclear conflict? First, in spite of its undoubted complexities, the dynamics of the bipolar U.S.-Soviet nuclear arms race are easier to define, and therefore easier to analyze, than the dynamics of multipolar, conventional arms races. Second, there has been much more government and private funding of nuclear arms control research. Third, the initial impetus to study ways of controlling nuclear weapons came from the scientists who had been personally involved with the Manhattan project. The American scientific community, which has pioneered a great deal of arms control thinking on nuclear matters, has not, by and large, had the same personal stake in questions relating to conventional conflict. For example, the recent anthology of readings on arms control which have appeared in the Scientific American over the past twenty-seven years does not contain a single article on the control of conventional war. 

While it would be wrong to say that too much effort has been devoted to studies of the strategic arms race, it could be argued that relatively too much attention has been devoted to examining exotic scenarios of nuclear war that result from marginal assymmetries in the respective warhead inventories of the U.S. and Soviet strategic forces. Instead, it might be more profitable to study the relationships between the prospects for conventional war in the Persian Gulf or along the Sino-Soviet border and the risks of U.S.-Soviet nuclear confrontation. 

What studies of the arms traffic are required?

Unless and until scholars and statesmen alike are prepared to do justice to the complexities of the arms transfer process and its relationship to the strategic milieu in particular conflict areas. the debate as to what effects weapons transfers will have upon these conflicts will continue to be couched primarily in ideological terms. What we basically need are some sound answers to the following general questions: 

1. What is the relationship between political conflict, military force structures, and propensities for armed conflict in less-developed countries? 

2. If certain categories and numbers of weapons do influence propensities 

Arms Control: Readings from the Scientific American, introduction by Herbert F. York 

(New York: W. F. Freeman, 1973).

1 toward or against armed conflict, how important are military assistance and sales programs in achieving these outcomes? 

3. If military assistance and sales programs are a relevant factor, do particular types of weapons have standard effects in all strategic environments? In certain environments? What method of classification can be suggested? 

4. Can meaningful distinctions be made between those weapons and force structures that enhance certain "defensive" and certain "offensive" military capabilities of recipients? 

5. If it is possible to come up with some classifications of weapons systems which has some empirically sound methodology, how should this influence arms transfer policies? 

6. Given that it is possible to distinguish between various types of weapons and their effects on local strategic questions, what other suppliers, other than the United States, can provide these weapons to the Third 

World? What are their current policies? How do these policies complement or conflict with the stated goals of U.S. policy? 

What do we know?

To provide even cursory answers to these questions would require more space than is available here. Nevertheless, some very general observations can be made at this stage. 

With respect to Questions 1-3, I would offer the following propositions :

The less-developed world is not a homogeneous entity: profound variations in the nature of the geographical milieu influence the effectiveness of certain weapons to perform certain missions in certain military environments. Similarly, the asymmetrical economic and technical capabilities of less developed countries to procure and operate modern weapons is very pronounced. Thus, it is not at all self-evident that the transfer of highly sophisticated and expensive weapons to technically backward nations necessarily increases military security, especially if the opportunity costs of such transfers are weighed in terms of alternative systems. Equally, though, there is no conclusive evidence that the transfer of advanced weapons increases the probability of war between political adversaries. What can be said with some certainty is that the transfer of advanced weapons has a profound influence upon the nature and outcome of military conflict should it occur. This, in turn, has serious implications for donor countries, especially the United States and the Soviet Union, who, if they are supporting different sides, may be increasingly drawn into active involvement in the conflict.

An examination of certain types of military environments in the less-developed regions reveals that in very general terms a technically backward country is more likely to maximize its military potential if it invests in fairly simple, cheap weapons and force structures associated with army units, rather than in expensive aircraft, missile systems, or warships. But not all donors or recipients wish to maximize military security by "rational" procurements of arms. The implications for the major arms donors are many. If it is their objective to improve the overall military capabilities of recipients, then the provision of certain classes of advanced weapons may not be an optimum policy if the opportunity costs are considered. Equally, however, the provision of certain advanced weapons may result in a local arms race based more on prestige than upon realistic calculations of military power balance. 

With respect to Question 4, I would argue that meaningful distinctions between certain "offensive" and "defensive" capabilities can be made provided that one specifies the geographical environment in which the forces are to be used, and provided the comparative costs of procuring different types of weapons are taken into account. For example, recent developments in precision guided munitions (PGMs) suggest that certain "offensive" and "defensive" air missions are becoming relatively more cost-effecctive in certain military environments. In the closing stages of the U.S. air war over North Vietnam, the effectiveness of 

U.S. bombing was greatly improved over previous experiences, primarily due to the fact that the new "smart" bombs were extremely accurate, and, therefore, far fewer aircraft sorties and bombs were required to destroy a particular target. This reduced U.S. aircraft losses considerably. However, at that point in time, the Soviet Union has not supplied the North Vietnamese with its latest surface-to-air missile, the SA-6. 36-333 O - 74 

45

The SA-6 was used in the October Middle East War by the Egyptians and the Syrians. In the initial stages of the war, Israeli losses to the SA-6 were high enough to cause considerable alarm. 

To date there has not been a major war in which the most modern air-tosurface weapons have been used against targets protected by the latest surfaceto-air missiles. Hence, there is considerable uncertainty as to whether the "offense" or the "defense" has gained most from the new technologies.

Nevertheless, it is these types of developments which, at any given period in time, may give the side which has the most advanced weapons and is capable of operating them, a distinct advantage, provided that the costs of buying such a capability for one mission are not so exorbitant that few funds are available for other important missions. This suggests that, at any given time, the "defense" may indeed have an advantage over the "offense." It is not possible at this stage to envisage a situation when the "defense" will have a permanent advantage over the "offense" for all important missions. 

Arms control perspectives and policy options Before attempting to answer Questions 5 and 6, it is necessary to say something about the relationships between the overall goals of U.S. foreign policy and the particular objectives of arms control measures. 

There is a great deal of understandable confusion over the meaning of the term "arms control." One reason is because the objectives of arms control measures not only vary, but can, on occasion, be in conflict with each other. Three generally accepted objectives of arms control are: 

1. To reduce the risks of war. 

2. To reduce the level and intensity of war, should it occur. 

3. To reduce the costs of military expenditure.

It is not difficult to think of several occasions when, in the short run, Objective 1 has been in conflict with Objective 3. In the early 1960's, arms control efforts to reduce the risks of surprise nuclear attack focused upon developing, procuring, and deploying a new generation of relatively invulnerable nuclear delivery vehicles (Minuteman and Polaris). Increases in the strategic budget to pay for these systems were, therefore, seem to be consistent with Objective 1, but obviously not with Objective 3. Similar situations can arise in a non-nuclear environment. For example, in the absence of political settlement, would the risks of war between Israel and its neighbors be reduced if Israel unilaterally reduced its conventional defense budget, perhaps as a result of U.S. pressure? Many would argue that if this occurred, the risks of war would be increased, and that Israel's incentive to build nuclear weapons would be impelling. 

It is possible to think of occasions when Objectives 1 and 2 might be in conflict. A situation could arise when the risks of war are indeed increased if certain arms are transferred, but that if war does occur, the provision of those arms may lead to speedy victory for one side and, therefore, meet the requirements of Objective 2. This could occur in a region where the risks of war were high, irrespective of arms levels. If additional U.S. arms were sent to a friendly country, the effect might be to act as the immediate catalyst for war. However, if the arms were not sent, the war might still break out, and the country supported by the United States might lose or be forced to take drastic dangerous action. If this were to happen, the United States might have to intervene and thereby run the risks of expanding the war. Therefore, if one purpose of Objective 2 is to insulate the United States from possible future military intervention in local regions of great importance to U.S. interests, this may best be achieved by providing the local friendly power with impressive military capabilities even if these capabilities add fuel to the sources for conflict. Obviously, this is not a preferred option. Hopefully conditions would sometimes permit 

Objectives 1, 2, and 3 to be achieved together. Unfortunately, however, the complexities of regional military balances rarely permit such ideal solutions. The problems of "controlling" arms transfers must, therefore, be approached with these difficulties in mind. 

In reality, it is difficult to imagine a situation in which arms control perspectives will take precedence over more traditional motives for transferring arms to rich and influential countries. However, in certain cases, where the political costs of selling U.S. arms clearly outweigh any conceivable benefits (e.g., selling arms to Rhodesia), arms control perspectives will be much easier to justify.

With respect to Questions 5 and 6, it might be assumed that the United States will wish to consider the effects of its arms transfer decisions in three very broad, and by no means exclusive, areas: the effect of arms transfers upon the recipient's military.

If these are at least some of the effects the United States has to consider, then it can in theory influence certain behavior patterns by adjusting its military assistance and sales policies to conform to those expectations. 

In reality the process may be more or less complicated than indicated here. 

In certain cases complex decisions concerning alliance politics, expected behavior of friendly and unfriendly neighbors of the recipient, expected behavior of alternative suppliers, and expected behavior of political elites within the recipient country, together with numerous strategic and economic factors will need to be taken into account. In other cases, decisions may be taken on the basis of much more simplistic calculations of national interest with little regard to future long-run effects of military assistance and sales programs. 

Nevertheless, if these questions are representative of the types of considerations that politically astute suppliers should make, it can be seen that they go far beyond the confines of expected outcomes based solely upon criteria of military efficiency or maximization of economic returns. For this reason, it can be argued that the goals and objectives of U.S. security assistance and sales programs will inevitably vary from time to time and from place to place, that the concept of U.S. "interests" can be approached from many perspectives, and for this reason simple rules about the future nature and direction of programs are not likely to come to grips with the fundamental issues. 

Screening requests for American arms

What kinds of specific questions should both the executive and the legislative branches of government ask when future requests for arms are made by foreign countries? Clearly, the details involved in the following check-list of questions will vary very much according to the political nuances of the particular request. Nevertheless, I believe that if this range of questions was addressed by, say, this Committee, as well as other bodies, then at least we might have a much clearer idea as to why the request was being made, what possible effects it would have both on the recipient's and United States interests, and how those effects might relate to third parties, including local powers and other potential suppliers.

Country A requests weapons system X from the United States 

1. What are current U.S. arms transfer policies toward Country A? 

(a) To improve Country A's military capabilities? To maintain them at about the current level? To reduce them? (b) To improve U.S. political relations with Country A? To maintain them at the present level of intimacy? To disengage? (c) To improve Country A's economy by providing military and economic aid and credits? (d) To sell U.S. arms to help domestic U.S. industry and to strengthen the balance of payments? (e) To guarantee supplies of raw materials, oil, and gas in exchange for arms sales?

Given this range of options, what particular set of policy goals pertains in this case? 

2. Why does Country A want weapons system X? 

(a) Political Factors: 

External Factors: 

(I) A's relations with immediate neighbors. (II) A's relations within regional framework. 

(III) A's relations within Alliance and International Organization framework.

Internal Factors: 

(IV) Bureaucratic and Party rivalry (e.g., inter-service competition).

(V) National prestige. 

(b) Military Factors: 

External Factors: 

(I) "Peace" time situations: 

A. What are immediate neighbors' military capabilities?

B. What is the regional military environment (are most countries well armed or poorly armed?)?

C. What military allies does Country A have? 

D. What military allies do potential adversaries have?

E. What is the present status of Country A's forces? How many weapons serviceable? State of readiness? Morale of forces, etc.?

F. What is the internal security situation? 

(II) "War" time situations: 

A. Is conflict external or internal? 

B. Is military environment "permissive" or "hostile"? 

C. Over what terrain is conflict mainly taking place?

D. How effective have armed forces and weapons systems proved in conflict so far? 

3. What is likely to happen if the United States agrees to supply Weapons 

System X? 

(a) Economic Costs: 

(I) Who pays, i.e., sale or aid? (I) When and under what credit terms are reciprocal trade agreements involved? (III) How much will sale earn, or how much will assistance cost? (IV) How much technical assistance and training required? (b) Possible effects of transfer of Weapons System X on A's capabilities and the strategic environment: 

(I) Domestic and regional political situation. 

(II) A's economic capabilities. 

(III) A's internal military capabilities. 

(IV) A's external military capabilities. 

(V) The local power balance. 

(VI) The alliance power balance. 

(c) Possible effects of transfer of U.S. political and military options: (I) Will transfer be precursor for additional requests? From Country A?

From Country A's neighbors? From other countries? 

(II) Will transfer tie United States to closer political and military involvement with Country A? (III) Will transfer antagonize or strengthen U.S. political and military relations with Country A's neighbors? 

4. Suppose the United States does not supply Weapons System X? (a) Constraints on the United States: (I) Political (current domestic policy on arms transfers). (II) Own military requirements. 

(III) Economic cost. 

(IV) Transfer may lead other local countries to request assistance or sales from the United States, or U.S.'s allies, or U.S.'s enemies. (See also 

(b) Suppose the United States offers to supply Weapons System Y instead?

(I) Country A accepts Weapons System Y. 

(a) What is likely to happen if United States agrees to supply Weapons System Y instead of Weapons System X? (This would need a repeat analysis of Paragraph 3.) (II) Suppose A rejects offer of Weapons System Y? 

Relevant questions for the United States (a) What happens if no one supplies A? 

1. Refer to analysis in Paragraph 2: (a) and (b) 

2. What is A's indigenous weapons production capacity? 

3. Would refusal to supply arms encourage A to expand indigenous weapons production option? What might be the effects of this? In the short run? In the long run? (III) Who else can supply Weapons System X or Y? (a) How many countries? Who are they? (b) Political, strategic, and economic relationship of other potential suppliers with the United States and Country A.

(c) What would other suppliers stand to gain by supply of System X of Y in the short run and in the long run? 1. Economic advantages 

2. Political advantages 

3. Military advantages. (d) How important is it for the United States to prevent other suppliers from gaining advantages?

Of course, this check-list does not provide easy answers for determining whether a particular request for arms should be approved or denied. Such decisions will inevitably have to be based on subjective political judgments which, on occasion, may have very little relationship to the type of rational approach outlined above. 

Nevertheless, my own feeling is that there is more to be gained than lost by examining a particular request for arms in a structured, rational fashion, since during the exercise things may be learned that could be of use in weighing the costs and benefits of future requests.

Conclusions 

The fundamental changes that have occurred in the international system over the past few years have had a major impact upon the nature and direction of U.S. security assistance programs and arms sales to foreign countries. 

The emergence of an international system more concerned with geostrategic, as distinct from ideological, issues suggests that the role of force in international politics will be increasingly bound up with economic and political competition for scarce land and sea resources. 

The relationship between resource diplomacy and the demand for sophisticated military forces is best illustrated by the situation in the Persian Gulf. An unprecedented military build-up is occurring, funded by oil revenues, with the purpose of protecting the extraction, refinement, and transportation of petroleum and petroleum by-products. Yet the military build-up itself may eventually increase the prospects for conflict by contributing to a local arms race. If this is a possibility, it poses a dilemma for the industrial powers, including the United States, who need the oil, and in terms of their power to control arms sales, find themselves operating in a buyer's market.

It is, therefore, difficult to make recommendations about U.S. arms transfer policy that have applicability to all countries in the less-developed world. This suggests two lessons. First, that attempts to seek general arms control agreements to limit the transfer of arms are likely to fail. Second, that far more analyses are required concerning the short-run and long-run strategic and arms control implications of weapons transfers to specific regions such as the Persian Gulf. It is, therefore, in the interests of all U.S. government agencies and Congressional Committees to devote greater effort to examining systematically the effects of military aid and sales upon overall U.S. interests. The continued preoccupation of the academic arms control community with the bipolar U.S.-Soviet nuclear arms race to the exclusion of serious study of regional military security and arms control, whife understandable, has potentially very serious consequences for U.S. security. Nuclear war is probably more likely to occur as a result of escalating conventional war in the Sinai desert, the Eastern Mediterranean, or the Persian Gulf than because the United States has more MIRVs than the Soviet Union, and the latter has more heavy payload launchers than the United States.

GAINING EXPERTISE ON ARMS TRANSFERS 

Mr. GILMAN. Thank you, Mr. Chairman.

Mr. Kemp, I join with my colleagues in thanking you for pointing out some of the problems in arms control throughout the world. It seems to me that what you are suggesting is more of a scholarly study of where we have been and where we are going. 

Some portion of the checklist that you are suggesting, while it is quite complete, seems to cover most of the questions that I usually hear when we have a major arms proposal before us. 

Where do you think such a study would best fit in our structure of government today? Who do you think should undertake this type of study that you are suggesting?

Mr. KEMP. Well, certainly many of those questions are, of course, asked within the executive branch. I know that for certain. I am not suggesting that detailed studies of arms sales should necessarily be done in a congressional committee. What I am suggesting is that the checklist of questions represents a framework for looking at past, present, and future arms sales. The implications of the questions in the checklist should be considered by anyone concerned about the overall magnitude of arms sales, be they U. S. arms sales or Soviet, or British, or French.

Let me put it to you another way. It seems to me that if we had done more analysis on this subject and looked at the military, as distinct from the political and economic implications, of arms transfers in more detail, we would be better equipped to have a national or congressional debate on the military implications of arms transfers similar to the debate we had in 1969 on the ABM. At that time a lot of expertise was brought in, a lot of homework was done, a very serious set of issues was examined, and, generally speaking, scientists and scholars contributed to a very meaningful dialog. 

At the moment we have no equivalent stockpile of expertise in the academic or legislative branch of Government to deal with the questions raised by the continued transfer of arms.

APPRECIATION TO WITNESS Mr. HARRINGTON. Mr. Chairman. 

First, I would like to express my appreciation to the witness and to our rather limited audience on the committee for the chance to extend the duration of this last act in order to get at a subject, which I consider to have been generally neglected by Congress, though it has been a source of peripheral forays by subcommittees of this committee, as well as a source of concern on the part of the press. U.S. ARMS POLICY: LATIN AMERICAN EXAMPLE 

Having listened to Sam Huntington yesterday, and with interest to yourself today, I would like you to comment in general as to the desirability, in your opinion, of some selectivity in a policy of attempting to restrict arms sales on a unilateral basis. As the Nation responsible for an estimated third of the arms dealings in the world, we must take some responsibility for seeking some rather dramatic new initiatives. 

A unilateral posture could go all the way from a willingness to say we we won't engage in this kind of traffic at all—and let vacuum be filledto the argument that other countries will also follow our course, or something in between. Is

I get a feeling that our deadlock with the administration on military sales is best exemplified by the microcosm of the Latin American situation. Congress attempted to set a limit on the total dollar value of sales to Latin America, but then last year we were whipsawed by the idea that we, as well as any other country, might as well go back into the unrestricted sales business again. So in last year's Foreign Assistance Act we called off the constraints which had been imposed for a couple of years, and repealed the regional ceiling. 

Is there some need, as you see it, for the Executive, which is more able in this area than the legislative, to take an initiative in the arms

areas similar to the dramatic efforts to resolve the foreign policy deadlocks in the Russian and Chinese situations of the past few years? Or would you prefer us not to be quite so multinational in the scope or approach of our efforts to limit arms sales? 

Mr. KEMP. Mr. Harrington, I have looked rather carefully at the attempts by the U.S. Government to influence the traffic of arms over the years from a unilateral, bilateral, and multilaterial perspective. 

My feeling is that the record is very mixed. I think there have been occasions when unilaterial initiatives by the United States to restrict or regulate the flow of arms to particular regions has had discernable benefits in the short run. However, I think there have been long-run costs that we would be well to bear in mind. 

You mentioned the Latin American case, and I think that is a good example. I don't want to repeat any of the discussion on that issue. 

Of course there are particular areas where the United States does maintain a unilateral embargo in accordance with international agreements; namely, the United States does not sell or supply arms to 

South Africa or Rhodesia, suggesting that there are selective restrictions imposed unilaterally by the United States even though other countries such as France and Italy have ignored the embargo and have supplied arms.

Now when you come to look at the problem from the perspective of both the costs and the benefits of unilateral, bilateral, or multilateral controls, within both a short time-frame and a long time-frame, the preferred alternatives are sometimes difficult to see. 

1965 ARMS EMBARGO ON INDIA AND PAKISTAN 

Let me give you an example. In 1965 the United States and Britain imposed a bilateral arms embargo on India and Pakistan who were currently engaged in a war, the argument being that the embargo might bring the war to a speedy conclusion since both sides could not afford to fight a protracted war without continuing arms supplies. 

I would argue that in this case the initiative did have some effects in bringing both sides to a speedy settlement. However, the long run effect was that India became very fearful about its future dependency upon external supplies and as a result of that experience increased very dramatically investments in indigenous arms production for the long run and immediately shifted its focus from Western suppliers increasingly to the Soviet Union. 

Pakistan, you will recall, shifted from the United States to China for a period to get its arms. So I think we have to be quite clear that if we take unilateral or bilateral actions that do have some immediate benefits, the long run implications may be that (A) the recipient nation goes elsewhere for arms, and (B), more seriously, develops its own indigenous capacity. That has happened in Africa as well as India. 

The question is, So what?

U.S. ARMS ROLE 

Mr. HARRINGTON. That is exactly the question.

Mr. KEMP. Well, my argument is that I am not prepared to generalize. I am prepared to talk very specifically about particular countries

and particular regions and particular periods in time. For instance, there are certain categories of weapons which only the United States and the Soviet Union can supply. Not even Britain and France can really compete for the very exotic weapons. Also there may be countries which the Soviet Union is unlikely to supply arms to, if the United States refuses to. Therefore in this case, a unilateral decision to deny certain requests for arms would not necessarily mean that someone else would run in and fill the gap. 

One way to reduce the flow of advanced arms is to try and convince the would-be purchasers of American arms that it is not in their interests to buy the most exotic, the most expensive, and the most sophisticated weapons. I don't think the way to do it is to tell would-be recipients that they should not have these advanced weapons because they may use them in a conflict. I think historically this approach has always rebounded, and it is not likely to serve long-run U.S. interests. 

I think the way to approach the problem is to encourage a meaningful dialog about the realistic requirements for security in these countries, and perhaps suggest alternative ways they can spend their money which have more influence upon their long-run security needs, but I think this has to be done on a case by case basis. 

THE UNITED STATES: WHAT KIND OF RECORD ON ARMS? 

Mr. HARRINGTON. Given the rather dismal track record to date of attempts to convince them that their security depends on factors other than deciding whether to buy conventional or more sophisticated armaments, why would it not be useful at this point for this country to seek more dramatic to break through this cycle of historical negatives? 

If we are not looking at arms transfers coldly as an economic benefit, let our 30 percent of the market go elsewhere, assuming that you meet the argument of national security out of our own self-interest. 

Mr. KEMP. Two things. First I think to be fair to the U.S. record, the United States has shown considerably more diligence in exercising control over the use of its arms by recipients than certain other countries. Suppose the United States unilaterally walks out and somebody else steps in, and in the process that country provides weapons that may contribute to an arms race, and that may actually be used in conflict, then the question to ask is: Would the risks of conflict be increased if the United States did not supply the arms; and if they would be increased, would this be more against U.S. interests than the benefits of feeling good about unilateral restrictions?

Again I can't answer that problem unless we look at specific areas at particular junctures in time. Generally I am pessimistic about the beneficial effects any unilateral effort on the part of the United States. 

Mr. HARRINGTON. I would like to go back to it, but why don't I defer? I have had more than my 5 minutes. I yield. 

Chairman MORGAN. Mr. Yatron, do you have any questions?

Mr. YATRON. No. 

Chairman MORGAN. Do you have some additional questions, Mr. Harrington?

Mr. HARRINGTON. I would like to follow up on this question, while avoiding repetition. I am not convinced that the restraint you sug-

gest of American military sales program is really all that admirable, but I will defer to your more specific knowledge in this area. Certainly, American military sales nave been on such magnitude over a long period of time so as to convince me that we ought to at least raise the question of the level of sales, bearing in mind the suggestions of the Secretary of State in Moscow, in the context of the strategic arms limitation question, that we need to have more of a substantive debate than we are used to in the Congress on the hard questions surrounding our policy. For example, just as Secretary Kissinger seems to advocate our taking some risks in the national security context, which, I infer, the Department of Defense does not seem to want us to take, so we might find it desirable to take some risks in unilaterally reducing our military sales program. 

Why not? Assuming that we have met the requirements of legitimate national security needs, why not try to exercise some moral suasion, even if that may sound like a dated term, to inject into the realities of international politics a greater sense of responsibility and restraint on the part of our Nation? When considering our total military sales effort in recent years, I don't think the track record of the United States, while it may appear to be more responsible comparatively with that of some other nations, is one that is altogether clear and commendable-particularly in the context of the drastic expansion of our arms sales in the last 2 years.

Mr. KEMP. I was merely talking about the track record in relationship to other people's track records. I have stressed, and I don't want to repeat myself, that I am all in favor of a national debate on this subject because I am not convinced that we yet know whether the current traffic in arms serves or does not serve overall U.S. interests. 

Until we have had this debate I don't think we are in a position to start suggesting dramatic proposals because we may find ourselves getting into a situation where the cure causes more harm than current policy I say this with particular reference to the potential linkage between conventional arms and nuclear arms.

Suppose the United States unilaterally cut off arms aid to Israelwhich it is not going to do-but supposing it did? This action would be extremely destabilizing because it would not only increase the prospects for war but it would also be a compelling reason for Israel to rapidly develop a nuclear capability assuming it does not already have one.

This is one of the real types of risks we have to bear in mind. So long as we can restrict the spread of nuclear weapons to conflict areas in the third world, then at least the consequences of war-although dramatic-are likely to be less damaging than if nuclear weapons were used. This is one of the reasons why I think we have to be very careful about premature efforts to restrict military procurements when the recipient countries feel that their national interest is at stake.

STATEMENT FROM DR. IKLE 

Chairman MORGAN.

[The statement referred to follows:] STATEMENT OF HON. FRED C. IKLE, DIRECTOR OF THE ARMS CONTROL AND DISARMAMENT AGENCY 

Mr. Chairman and members of the committee, the Secretary of State and the 

Secretary of Defense, along with other Administration witnesses, have already discussed with the Committee the President's proposed FY 1975 Security Assistance program and its role in supporting United States foreign policy objectives. 

As Secretary Kissinger said, the basic philosophy behind the security assistance proposal is to "promote cooperation and to prevent confrontation and pressure on ourselves, our friends, and our allies." Secretary Schlesinger told the 

Committee that the principal purpose of security assistance is to "strengthen deterrence and promote peaceful negotiation by helping our friends and allies to maintain adequate defense forces of their own." 

I share those views. The FY 75 program continues the desirable transition of many of our allies from grant aid recipients to purchasing nations, whereby

they are encouraged to bear the primary burden for their defense. In addition, the program of grant aid and foreign military sales contributes to stability in important areas of the world. In my judgment, Mr. Chairman, the Administration's proposed FY 1975 security assistance program is a realistic approach to promoting a structure of peace in the world at a time when the opportunities for stability and cooperation are closer to realization than they have been within recent years.

The Arms Control and Disarmament Agency participates in the consideration of the security assistance program through the mechanism of the Security Assistance Program Review Committee (SAPRC), one of the interagency bodies in which ACDA insures that arms control and disarmament considerations are taken into account in policy formulation and implementation. 

In our participation in the SAPRC-indeed, in all our actions on arms transfer matters-we are mindful of the concern over indiscriminate arms transfers. 

Both the Foreign Assistance Act and the Foreign Military Sales Act require that decisions to provide assistance or make sales take into account whether such transfers "contribute to an arms race or increase the possibility of outbreak or escalation of conflict or prejudice the development of bilateral or multilateral arms control arrangements." The FY 75 security assistance program now before the Congress was developed with those provisions fully in mind. 

Because no single nation can by itself effectively limit the international arms trade, we in ACDA continue to explore the possibilities for practical international arrangements for control over arms transfers which would insure the security of friends and allies, and at the same time hold promise of being negotiable. To assist us in our efforts in this problem area we held a symposium of government officials and private experts earlier this year to explore various possibilities for control.

Later this summer we plan to publish a compendium of current statistics on world military expenditures and the world arms trade-data which should help to emphasize the nature and scope of the problem. 

At the Conference of the Committee on Disarmament (CCD) in Geneva and at the United Nations the United States has urged that greater attention be focused on the control of conventional arms and has expressed its willingness to consider all approaches which might be suggested. There is not as yet an international consensus on the need for controlling conventional arms transfers or on ways in which such transfers might be controlled. So far it has not been possible to develop control arrangements which would meet the multitude of complex political, military, and economic objectives which underlie the arms transfer policies of suppliers and recipients alike. However, in my judgment the dangers to peace and stability inherent in the uncontrolled flow of arms make it imperative that within the U.S. Government we continue our search for possible approaches which might be pursued in the CCD or other forums to bring about international controls over conventional arms.

Chairman MORGAN. Also, there are two technical experts from the 

Arms Control Agency here today to answer any questions which the committee may have. They are Byron F. Doenges, Chief, Economic and Arms Transfer Division, Military and Economic Affairs Bureau, ACDA; and Edmund S. Finegold, senior technical adviser on security assistance, ACDA.

Gentlemen, please come to the witness table.

I assume proposals for such control agreements will be put forward by the United States in international forums in the future. Could you tell the committee what some of these possible initiatives are, and how soon do you think they will take the form of proposals by the United States to other countries?

WORK OF THE ECONOMIC AND ARMS TRANSFER DIVISION 

Mr. Chairman and gentlemen, I am Byron F. Doenges, Chief of the

Economic and Arms Transfer Division, Military and Economic Affairs Bureau of the U.S. Arms Control and Disarmament Agency. 

My colleague is Mr. Edmund S. Finegold, senior technical adviser on security assistance in the ACDA. 

The Economic and Arms Transfer Division consists of eight officers concerned with the economic aspects of defense spending and the economic impact of arms control proposals and initiatives. We monitor the military budgets and armed forces of each of 133 nations, and we are responsible for the annual publication, "World Military Expenditures and the Arms Trade." Such issues as military pricing, the Soviet and People's Republic of China military expenditures, and global resource diversion caused by military spending are just a few of our concerns in the economics area. 

In the general area of arms transfers, we monitor the international arms trade. We work closely with the Department of State in the review of requests for arms export licenses. We provide technical support to the ACDA representative on the Security Assistance Program Review Committee. We are involved in trying to examine possible international arrangements to control the arms trade. 

Insofar as my own technical outlook on the subject is concerned, our study of the international transfer of conventional arms which this committee has caused to be printed, should serve the general purpose. We will be pleased to answer any technical questions on the arms trade.
