STATEMENT OF HON. C. W. BILL YOUNG, A REPRESENTATIVE IN CONGRESS FROM THE STATE OF FLORIDA 

Mr. Chairman, I appreciate the opportunity to present testimony on behalf of H.R. 14561, legislation to authorize the provision of assistance to foreign countries in exchange for strategic or critical raw materials. 

I cosponsored this bill because of my firm and longstanding belief that the United States should be getting something more in return for the billions of taxpayer dollars that we send overseas than ill-will, riots, expropriations, and other "kicks in the teeth" on the world scene. Since the end of World War II, the United States has provided other nations of the world with over $185 billion through foreign assistance programs, and yet our own national debt is greater than the total national debts of all the other nations in the world put together. 

Uncle Sam has been the "soft touch" for the world over the past forty years, and all we have to show for it now are taxpayers with empty pockets and an economy increasingly short of vital strategic materials. 

H.R. 14561 would make a very constructive revision in our foreign assistance program by allowing the United States to exchange or barter its foreign aid for the minerals and critical raw materials this country increasingly needs. Many of the underdeveloped nations to which we dole out substantial amounts of aid have abundant supplies of materials which are essential for our industries, and it is good common sense to allow these nations to pay for our aid in the coin which they do possess. 

The Arab oil embargo and the more recent Jamaican bauxite price hike have served notice to the industrialized nations that important basic raw materials may be "held to ransom" with increasing frequency in the future. Why, then, should the United States provide foreign assistance free to nations which possess such commodities?

Mr. Chairman, if we examine the current import status of 13 basic raw materials vital to U.S. industry, we find that our country is heavily dependent

on imports. Right now, the U.S. imports more than 50 percent of its aluminum, chrome, manganese, nickel, tin, and zinc. By 1985, we will be importing more than 50 percent of our iron, lead, and tungsten; by the year 2000, more than 

50 percent of our copper, potassium, and sulfur. In addition, more than 99 percent of our rubber is imported, and more than 53 percent of our hardwood lumber comes from developing nations. Our foreign trade balance is perpetually precarious as a result of our heavy dependence on imports. And yet we continue to send foreign assistance dollars to many of the same nations which we pay for essential raw materials.

In view of the recent "blackmail" attempts on the world scene, in view of our increasing dependence on raw material imports, and in view of the ongoing dissolution of our strategic materials stockpiles, I strongly recommend that the Committee adopt this amendment to the Foreign Assistance Act and thereby put our nation in a better position to meet future demands for many basic materials.

STATEMENT OF HON. SAMUEL H. YOUNG, A REPRESENTATIVE IN CONGRESS FROM THE STATE OF ILLINOIS 

I would like to urge the Committee to support amendments to the Foreign Assistance Act of 1961. I refer to amendments which would authorize the provision of assistance to foreign countries in exchange for strategic or critical raw materials. Such a foreign assistance program would afford the United States with a unique way to abate the rapid depletion of our natural resources and supply the critical raw materials this country will need in the very near future. Such an exchange or barter arrangement would also mean a cooperative venture between the United States and foreign countries rather than the United States simply funneling out money with no return. Delinquent international debts and unpaid claims owed to the United States approach $69 billion. The proposed barter and exchange program would reverse the trend of United States foreign aid not paying for itself.

The exchange-barter concept is not a new idea and is supported by precedent. 

First, Public Law 480 set forth this principle, and later the Commodity Credit Corporation under the Secretary of Agriculture used to barter for goods not produced in sufficient quantity in the United States to meet U.S. needs. The 

CCC then sold goods to the General Services Administration which stockpiled them or sold them in a manner which did not disturb the marketplace. 

Such a proposal is very much needed given our acute energy problem and materials shortage situation. According to the Brookings Institute by year 2000 the

United States will be totally dependent on foreign sources for 12 of the 13 basic raw materials used by our industries. The "basic 13" industrial raw materials needed by highly industrialized society are: aluminum, chromium, copper, iron, lead, manganese, nickel, phosphorous, potassium, sulfur, tin, tungsten, and zinc. 

The loss or short supply of any of these raw materials could impose severe economic hardship and disclocations which our country does not need. This problem could be avoided if we utilize the resources of those countries we are giving foreign aid and assistance to. Some of the countries we give aid to are unable to sell all they can produce. Below is a partial list of countries with the resources they have an abundance of: 

Thailand-tin, manganese, antimony: 

Brazil-bauxite, barite, chromium, manganese, titanium; 

Bolivia-oil, iron, tin; 

Ecuador-oil, copper reserves; 

Peru-copper, gold, lead; 

Venezuela-natural gas, oil; 

Malaysia-tin, titanium; 

Philippines-gold, chromium; 

Indonesia-bauxite, natural gas, petroleum; and 

Turkey-chromite, boron, pyrite, copper, manganese.

The list of minerals currently in short supply or that will become scarce in the near future include aluminum, chromium, asbestos, copper, iron, lead, manganese, nickel, phosphorus, zinc and potassium. This exchange of raw materials with the 

United States would guarantee that we no longer send billions of dollars overseas in return for nothing.

Through acceptance of this bill, and in effect providing U.S. foreign aid money and expertise to these countries, the U.S. could not only satisfy its growing mineral requirements, but help provide internal development and employment in the recipient nation, in addition to bolstering our own economy. The bill would grant the President authority to exchange, when he determines it to be in the national interest, the assistance furnished under the bill for strategic materials and fossil fuels which are either in short supply or which cannot be produced in this country to meet our requirements.

There are two reasons for the current materials shortage: (1) increasing demand without commensurate increases in productive capacity; and (2) the shortage of energy. There have been instances where demand trends were relatively clear but were largely ignored. The reason most frequently given for this situation is that profitability has not been sufficient to finance expansion nor to attract new investment capital, a situation further aggravated by price controls. 

Considering the earth as a total resource system, it appears that most world resources will be adequate even for a many-fold increase in consumption demand. 

However, increased demand will undoubtedly mean temporary and localized shortages in some commodities until new sources of supply are developed or until abundant materials are developed as substitutes for scarce commodities. In addition, resources in general may increase significantly in cost, although historical trends to date indicate rather constant resource costs over a long period. 

Thus, the time to act is now, while we are still planning the proper technology and management utilization for these needed resources. The implementation of this legislation would be a step in the right direction.

APPENDIX 3 STATEMENT BY WALLACE J. CAMPBELL, PRESIDENT, THE FOUNDATION FOR COOPERATIVE HOUSING 1 

The Foundation for Cooperative Housing is a private, nonprofit foundation dedicated to the promotion of good housing for families of low and middle income by using cooperative and other forms of ownership. It is the largest private sponsor of cooperative and other nonprofit housing in the United States. Its operating arm, FCH Services, has provided technical and organizational services in the creation of more than 240 developments or communities serving more than 60,000 families with value at the time of construction of more than $800 million. 

The value of these homes now owned by their residents as consumers probably exceeds $1 billion. 

During the last 12 years FCH Services, under contract with AID, has provided technical assistance to the Governments of less developed countries and to cooperative and other institutions in the development of low cost cooperative and nonprofit housing, particularly for families of low to middle income. 

Because of our relationship with AID we have had an opportunity to study at first hand the evolution of the Housing Investment Guaranty Program which is under consideration by your committee as part of the Foreign Assistance Act of 1974. 

EVOLUTION OF A PROGRAM 

In Hollywood an actor or actress is often identified with the first role he or she played in a movie. The actor becomes typecast, the image tends to hold on with the audience long after the actor has performed successfully in many other characters. The acting changes but the image lingers on. So it often happens with institutions particularly with the Housing Investment Guaranty Program. We would like to describe briefly the very dramatic changes which have occurred in the Housing Investment Guaranty Program since it was inaugurated. Beginning as a source of financing for specific projects, it then focused hard on the development and strengthening of thrift institutions, and now is shifting to an emphasis on national housing policies which will assist all citizens, most of whom are in lower income groups. 

The Housing Investment Guaranty Program was initiated by the Congress in response to requests of American builders for the opportunity to build pilot demonstration projects in Latin America as part of the AID program. The first four years of the program was devoted to project by project guaranties in a number of countries in Latin America. Some of the projects were very good; some of them experienced delays and difficulties. By 1965 the Congress and the Executive 

Branch decided to review and revise the program. It was changed at the will of the Congress from a "pilot demonstration" program to one devoted primarily to "institution building" so that American investments guaranteed under the program, would help build the governmental and private institutions in the developing countries which could continue the process of housing development long after the demonstration project was completed. 

NEW ELEMENTS REQUESTED BY CONGRESS 

While the Congress was reviewing the program it added several objectives. 

These included the creation of organizations within the countries to mobilize local capacity for savings to finance housing (this was primarily through savings and loan associations); greater concentration on production of housing for lower income families; projects for labor unions; a higher concentration of cooperative housing and the continued use of private U.S. capital guaranteed by AID. 

1 The following statement is submitted for publication as part of the hearings on the Foreign Assistance Act of 1974. It was prepared at the request of the staff of the 

Committee to provide a firsthand report on and assessment of the Housing Investment Guaranty Program and the work of the Office of Housing of AID which administers the program. (744)

THE WORLDWIDE PROGRAM AND SHELTER POLICY 

In 1969 the Foreign Assistance Act provided substantial increases in housing guaranty authority or Africa and Asia. The Program has been heavily concentrated in Latin America.

It was decided that housing guaranties were to stay in AID, and it was also decided that a single mechanism for guaranty should serve the entire Agency instead of creating a guaranty capacity in each region. AID asked for and Congress granted the authority to create a worldwide program under a single Office of Housing. 

In 1972 AID's Office of Housing began reconsideration of a Shelter Policy for AID as a whole. The Shelter Policy was adopted in August 1973. It is relatively brief and we are suggesting that a copy be made a part of this record. 

An essential part of AID's Shelter Policy, in addition to institution building, is the focus on formulation of national housing policy in each host country. The 

Office of Housing now provides specialists who can work with the potential borrowing institutions in the development of a national housing policy. Such programs are already underway in a number of countries. Since most lesser developed countries are in the very earliest stages of shelter policy development, substantial benefits should result from these activities. 

TECHNICAL ASSISTANCE FOR LOW-COST HOUSING 

Since 1966 the emphasis has been on institution building. With this has come a broadening use of private organizations to supplement the work of governments both here and abroad. Technical assistance is provided, often through private organizations, to assist in the development of programs within the host countries. 

For example, the Foundation for Cooperative Housing which I represent provides a substantial amount of technical assistance under contract with AID. 

The Senate of the United States has asked for a continuous monitoring of the guaranty program; it has also asked for a policy which will reach an increasing number of families in the lower income brackets while continuing to serve the middle income families through unsubsidized programs with capital coming from the private U.S. market. Most of the funding to date has been through U.S. savings and loan associations although a number of insurance companies and other financial institutions have participated in the programs, and the Office of Housing is anxious to encourage a broad base for U.S. insured loans. 

THE NEED FOR ADDITIONAL AUTHORIZATION 

The program has been so successful in its worldwide operations that the Office of Housing is almost at the limit of its authorization and needs additional authorization at this time. The guaranty authority does not require any additional appropriations and no Government money goes into the investments. The administrative and technical assistance costs are paid for by fees from the borrowers. In this regard the Housing Guaranty is a refreshing and exciting program which must operate like a private business covering its expenses from operating income; yet it is directed at basic social and development objectives in the developing world.

SOCIAL IMPACT OF THE HOUSING PROGRAM 

Many members of the Congress are concerned about the social aspects of these housing programs and particularly their ability to reach families of lower income. As one factor in meeting these social obligations. AID has increased its use of technical staff of the Foundation for Cooperative Housing. In recent years, FCH has assisted AID in the development of cooperative housing in Honduras, Venezuela, Jamaica, and more recently Panama. The projects themselves are less important than the creation of a technical service organization in these and other countries to continue to provide good housing for people of limited income. 

Supplementing direct cooperative work FCH has provided advisory service on minimum cost shelter including low cost housing of all types such as sites-andservices development, core housing, assisted self-help, roof and slab schemes, half houses, and other programs. All of these are designed to create low cost housing by involving the people in construction of their own housing. 

In all countries it is essential to help organize savings plans such as credit unions or savings and loan associations. Eventually, the greatest financial re- 36-333 0 - 74 48

sources for housing must come from the savings of the people. The need and financial requirements are too great to be met by direct international financing or by subsidy programs of developing countries. 

As the Office of Housing takes on greater responsibility for housing programs in general, the policy direction is to serve an increasingly greater segment of the low and limited income families. In this connection FCH has provided specialists to serve on the teams for feasibility studies undertaken by the Office of Housing. 

The maximum results in providing low income housing comes when the local governments are motivated to develop overall national housing policies and plans and the institutional delivery system necessary to generate savings and mortgage financing. An excellent example of economic impact is a region-wide program AID is assisting in Central America. Working through the Central 

American Bank for Economic Integration (CABEI), the Housing Guaranty Program has provided funds for an aggressive regional-wide secondary mortgage market program using capital and technical assistance throughout Central America. A significant part of this program is the expansion of CABEI's operation to include, for the first time, mortgage financing of low cost housing. 

In Israel the funds flowing through the Government housing authorities were used in substantial part in cooperative housing development. We in FCH are proud of the developments. In the broadest context of national and international policy we would like to congratulate the Congress and AID for the constructive evolution of a program which now can serve as a continuing source of housing finance without drawing on the U.S. Treasury and can move toward increasing social objectives with modest appropriations for technical assistance and with increasing support from the governments being served.

APPENDIX 4 STATEMENT OF JOHN M. KANE, ASSISTANT DIRECTOR, NATIONAL SECU- RITY, FOREIGN RELATIONS DIVISION, THE AMERICAN LEGION 

Mr. Chairman, Members of the Committee: I thank you for the opportunity to submit to you today the views of The American Legion on the Fiscal Year 1975 Foreign Assistance Program. The period just ahead is a crucial one for many of our allies and our friends around the world. A sound foreign assistance program is urgently needed to help protect those nations and to assist them further in strengthening their economic development and progress. 

The philosophy of The American Legion on foreign aid is contained in our Resolution No. 402-73, which was unanimously adopted by our National Convention held in Honolulu, Hawaii, on August 22, 1973. A copy of that resolution is appended to this testimony for your information. In essence we support United 

States foreign aid to those nations needing our help, who demonstrate a desire to help themselves, cooperate with us in promoting peace and international cooperation, and utilize our aid to enhance the security interests of the free world and to improve the economic and social well-being of their own people. 

For many years, The American Legion has supported United States foreign aid to deserving countries. We have supported aid as part and parcel of United States foreign policy, as well as a major humanitarian program of assistance to developing countries around the world. We have also supported foreign aid because it has contributed greatly to the capacity of our friends and allies around the world to defend themselves against aggression.

I believe we all realize that foreign aid has proven to be an indispensable tool of foreign policy since the end of WWII. Many of the nations we aided in the earlier years of our country's foreign aid programs now are able to go without aid. 

They have developed strong economies and regained the confidence needed to achieve political stability, economic progress, and an adequate defense. This, I believe, is the basic aim of the United States in providing economic and military aid to nations in Africa, Asia, and Latin America today. 

Nations which we are continuing to aid today can look with hope to the examples of other countries which profited by our aid—those democracies in Western Europe, South Korea, the Republic of China and others-and look forward to the day when they too will be self-reliant and no longer need large infusions of capital and technology from us. I hope our government will continue to make it clear that we are not going to substitute our aid for other nations' self-reliance forever and that we will not do for them what they can be expected to do for themselves.

Nevertheless, we realize that millions of people around the globe still lack housing, food and jobs-and that social unrest and economic chaos will threaten their future and ours and give openings for aggressive governments and aggressive ideologies seeking to change borders and institutions by force and civil strife. So long as these genuine threats exist-and it looks as though they will exist for many years, despite talk of detente and cooperation among nations of differing ideologies and different political and economic systems-we must continue to provide that level of economic and military aid that will defeat aggression and subversion.

For these reasons The American Legion supports the President's Foreign Aid Program for Fiscal Year 1975. 

We note that the program provides for special assistance in two major problem areas today-the Middle East and Indochina. We wholeheartedly endorse the Administration's programs in these two vital areas of the world. The United 

States has vital interests in seeing that peace and stability return to both critical areas. In the past we have devoted much money-and in the case of Indochina much American blood-to insure that democratic self-determination shall continue to exist in the Middle East and in Indochina. We cannot rest yet. Forces (747)

are unleashed in both areas that would swamp our friends and lead to further armed conflict, perhaps to an imminent threat of a major conflict between ourselves and the Soviet Union and its Communist allies. We must help our friends there; we also must strive to establish new friendships, especially in the Middle 

East, and to assist Arab and Jew to find a path to peace and cooperation. 

The most dangerous threat to world peace today lies in the conflict between Arab and Jew in the Middle East. Four times in the past 25 years, major warfare has broken out there. Both Israel and the Arab nations have suffered much bloodshed. They have suffered setbacks to their economies and have been forced to spend inordinate amounts of money on modern, sophisticated weapons instead of devoting these funds to the well-being and progress of their peoples. They seem caught in a never ending circle of fighting and sullen truce they cannot break out of without help.

The American Legion is proud of the part the United States is playing, through the offices of Secretary of State Kissinger, to mediate between Israel and its two major adversaries, Egypt and Syria. We are in a critical period, one that may mean at least a limited peace in the Middle East. Egypt has shown a praiseworthy example for the entire Arab world. Syria has also agreed to a cease-fire and a troop withdrawal plan with Israel. We hope that further steps can be initiated at once to insure a general cease-fire and to start negotiations leading to genuine peace throughout the entire region. 

We are therefore pleased to see that the President is seeking to implement a truly even-handed policy toward Jew and Arab alike and is asking the Congress for economic assistance for Arab countries as well as military security aid for Israel. For the first time in many years relations between Cairo and Washington have improved to the point where we can with confidence cooperate with Egypt in repairing the damages of war in the Suez Canal area and help restore and develop Egyptian trade. We are also pleased to note that an additional $100 million may be made available on a contingency basis, as the outlines of a political settlement take shape, for contingency forces, refugee aid and resettlement, and economic development projects in the region. 

We sincerely trust that, as the Administration states, this aid will contribute to the security of all the nations in the Middle East and give them the necessary confidence in the peacemaking process to lead to a lasting settlement. The forces of moderation in the Middle East must take hold and go forward, with our mediation if it is desired by all sides, to establish the basis for a peaceful settlement. 

Second only to the Middle East in importance to the United States today is Indochina. Our nation fought for more than a decade to defeat Communist aggression in South Vietnam and to help give the Republic of Vietnam the opportunity to maintain its independence and its right of self-determination. 

The American Legion firmly believes that the United States has both a political and a moral commitment to the Republic of Vietnam and to the people of South Vietnam. We lost more than 55,000 American servicemen and suffered more than 

320,000 wounded in Vietnam between 1964 and 1973 in defense of South Vietnam's right to self-determination and freedom from communist aggression. We fought in defense of that land against aggression directed and aided by North Vietnam and supported fully by the Soviet Union, Communist China, and other communist nations. We encouraged South Vietnamese to persevere in the struggle for freedom. We encouraged them to seek a democratic solution for their domestic political problems and to oppose with their lives a communist one. 

We of The American Legion remained more than ever convinced that our cause was right, our conduct proper, our goal honorable.

Many Americans no longer feel that we have such a commitment. Or they insist now that we never incurred a commitment. They would deny history and 

American promises-promises supported and in many instances initiated by the overwhelming majority of the Congress of the United States. They want us either to end all military aid to South Vietnam or to cut it back drastically. Their apparent goal is to force President Thieu to agree to a coalition government in Saigon and to halt his military operations-operations designed to keep North 

Vietnamese forces from overrunning South Vietnam.

We firmly believe that, so long as North Vietnam continues to pursue military action in South Vietnam and to reinforce its troops there in violation of the accords reached at Paris on January 27, 1973, the United States must continue to provide adequate military and economic aid to South Vietnam. Not being experts

and having no knowledge of the exact total dollar or materiel requirements of such military aid, we cannot say how much military aid is required. Nevertheless we estimate that no substantial reductions in aid levels can be made at this time. 

The North Vietnamese forces, according to American military intelligence estimates, have more equipment and more troops in South Vietnam now than they did during the 1972 spring offensive there. They continue to receive substantial materiel support from the Soviet Union and Communist China. They have not altered their goal of subduing South Vietnam by political or military means, whichever appears more feasible at any given time. 

Under such conditions, we cannot see how the United States can honestly conceive of eliminating or sharply reducing the levels of our military aid. We oppose such thinking. It can only lead to swift defeat for South Vietnam and the triumph of communism in Saigon. 

The President's FY 1975 aid program calls also for substantial economic aid to South Vietnam. We all know that political stability-indeed, political survival in a nation-is not possible without a strong and stable economic base. South Vietnam is struggling to build that base. It must build a viable economy out of one shattered by more than thirty years of war and it must do so at the same time that it devotes most of its own resources to defense of the nation. South Vietnam has gigantic problems. It must resettle more than one million refugees; it must provide for widows and orphans of servicemen killed in action and help disabled servicemen return to a fruitful life.

Saigon also faces staggering inflation rates attributable to the continued warfare and the sharp decrease in American financial and materiel support. Most of 

South Vietnam's critical imports are jumping in price-petroleum and fertilizer are just two of them. With all of this, South Vietnam is compelled to support over 

1,000,000 armed troops and a heavy defense budget. Only the United States has the resources and the will to provide sufficient economic aid to South Vietnam to prevent its collapse. We must continue this aid for the next several years. 

If the situation in South Vietnam is discouraging, conditions in Cambodia are bleak. The Republic of Vietnam has been able to put up a creditable defense against North Vietnamese and Viet Cong attacks. In Cambodia, the insurgent 

Khmer Rouge have seized most of the countryside and many provincial capitals. 

They terrorize and besiege the capital of Phnom Penh and other large cities-the only areas now effectively controlled by the Lon Nol government. Greatly assisted by North Vietnamese guns, ammunition and training, and backed by the continued presence of thousands of North Vietnamese troops, the Communist insurgents are nearly strong enough to topple the anti-communist government. It is abundantly clear to us that Cambodia cannot long survive as an independent, non-communist republic without large-scale, continuous military and economic aid from the United States.

We must provide that aid in quantities sufficient to help Cambodia retain its independence. If we fail to do so, there is no question that North Vietnam will speedily achieve hegemony over the entire country. 

Laos presents a superficially brighter picture. A coalition government has been established again and is working at the moment. The communist Pathet Lao faction is participating in the central government. Nevertheless, in blatant violation of the Paris agreement and the desires of the present Lao government, North Vietnamese troops remain in eastern and northern Laos. The Laotian government is a fragile one. The Pathet Lao receives ample support from North Vietnam. 

The United States, in turn, is providing economic and military aid to the remaining factions. Without such aid, we are certain that the communist faction would in short order overcome its political opponents and set up an openly communist regime. 

Our military and economic assistance prevents this happening now. Assistance is also needed badly to resettle refugees and to establish a viable economy. Without such aid, Laos, like Cambodia, would fall to North Vietnamese ambitions thus putting almost all of Indochina under North Vietnamese control and intensifying the military pressure on South Vietnam.

The American Legion supports the expenditure of funds sufficient to meet the objectives we have outlined above throughout Indochina. We have seen the Indochinese peoples through many years of hard warfare; it would be folly to fail to see them through the next few years which could lead to a just and hopefully enduring peace there.

The President's foreign aid program for the coming fiscal year provides an expenditure of $1.925.5 billion for security assistance around the world. The

American Legion does not profess to have the detailed knowledge needed to determine whether these are proper and effective levels of expenditure for grant military aid, for military sales credits, and for security supporting assistance. 

Yet we do feel strongly that we must not stint on providing these forms of aid for our allies and our friends in these crucial times. Our security assistance programs are designed to help our friends to develop the capacity to defend themselves against those countries and those forces who would achieve their unlawful goals by force or threat of force. Our security assistance programs are a form of insurance that would-be aggressors do not miscalculate and breach the peace in the Middle East, in Southeast Asia or elsewhere. We would be foolish indeed not to provide such military assistance as an indispensable concommittance to our economic relief and development aid. No nation can remain free without the security of sufficient military force and equipment to defend its freedom. No nation can pursue economic development without military security. Through the security assistance portion of FY 1975 foreign aid program, the United States is striving to provide the security necessary for economic progress. 

The FY 1975 Foreign Aid Program finally calls for the expenditure of $255.3 million for functional development assistance programs throughout the world. 

These funds will be concentrated in such vital fields as food production among the developing nations, family planning and basic health services, improving nutrition, and strengthening education and other human resources programs. In view of the widespread danger of famine threatening much of the developing world at this time, we feel that such aid-provided on a bilateral basis-could be most useful and we support the concept and general thrust of development assistance in the FY 1975 foreign aid program. 

In conclusion, let me reiterate that The American Legion finds the President's foreign aid program generally to be a valuable and praiseworthy approach to foreign economic and military assistance. We support its emphasis upon the 

Middle East and Indochina and upon basic developmental aid to developing countries in the areas of food, health, and education. We particularly favor bilateral aid over multilateral aid-except in the latter case where the United States has a determining voice in apportioning our aid and in its supervision. 

The long-range interests of the United States depend upon helping our friends and allies both economically and militarily, and in assisting the developing nations in the interests of world peace, stability, and development. We of The 

American Legion will continue to fight for these objectives in all appropriate programs.

FIFTY-FIFTH ANNUAL NATIONAL CONVENTION OF THE AMERICAN LEGION HONOLULU, HAWAII, AUGUST 21-23, 1973 RESOLUTION NO. 402-FOREIGN AID 

Whereas, The American Legion position on foreign aid has consistently upheld the principles that: (A) the foreign economic and security assistance programs of the United States should be so designed and administered as to bolster and promote this country's foreign policy objectives; (B) the national interest of the United States should be the primary consideration in determining whether or not aid is to be extended or continued to a particular country or region; (C) adequate stability to facilitate improved economic and social conditions in the less developed countries is in the national interest of the United States, because it would lessen susceptibility to extremism and would enhance prospects for peaceful and constructive international relationships, including the expansion of trades; and (D) the American public has a right to expect, in the absence of exceptional circumstances, that its tax dollars will not go to assist foreign governments having policies or consistently taking actions which are directly contrary to the basic national interests of the United States: Now, therefore, be it 

Resolved, By the American Legion in National Convention assembled in Honolulu, Hawaii, August 21, 22, 23, 1973, that we support the extension or continuation of United States aid only to those countries which- (1) need and request our help,

(2) demonstrate a desire to help themselves in improving their institutional capabilities, (3) do not regularly and purposefully pursue policies or take actions that are detrimental to our basic national interests, (4) actively cooperate with the United States in promoting peace and international cooperation, (5) utilize our aid programs to enhance the security interests of the free world, including the promotion of measures to control illicit narcotics traffic, (6) utilize our aid to improve internal security and thus the economic and social well-being of its people, and grant equal protection to the person of the United States nationals; and be it further 

Resolved, That The American Legion would accept the channeling of United States foreign aid funds through multilateral or international organizations only if The President or The Congress deems that it is in the National interest so to do; and be it finally 

Resolved, That The American Legion oppose foreign assistance programs in countries having policies or consistently taking actions contrary to the basic national interests of the United States, unless The President with the agreement of Congress determines that as a part of a major detente and a serious and promising effort toward achieving world peace such programs are essential to the national interest of The United States.

APPENDIX 6 AN OPEN LETTER TO MESSRS. FULBRIGHT, KENNEDY, MCCLELLAN, MAHON, AND MORGAN MENNONITE CENTRAL COMMITTEE, 

Saigon, Vietnam, May 28, 1974.

We twenty-two members of the Mennonite Central Committee and members of the Mennonite Mission in Vietnam want to express our deep concern regarding the military appropriations pending before Congress, particularly as they relate to Indochina. Our agencies represent a continuous Mennonite presence in Vietnam since 1954. Our present endeavors include the staffing of several hospitals, assisting refugees to return to their native homes, encouraging local educational efforts and lending support to a local church. Among us are individuals with over ten years of service in Vietnam; some have taken graduate level training in Asian affairs. All of us have had training in the Vietnamese language. 

We recognize that there is not only one side to this conflict. Both sides have resorted to violence and destruction. Violence committed by both sides must be condemned. We want our witness of peace and reconciliation to be extended to all parties involved. With this in mind we wish to share the following concerns with you.

We have followed with deep concern the recent discussion of future military and economic aid to the South Vietnamese government in Saigon. It is our understanding that the Administration is requesting substantial sums for appropria tions to South Vietnam for fiscal year 1975. The Defense Appropriations Bill and the Foreign Assistance Act contain increased allocations for Indochina. 

The primary rationale of the Administration for escalating military assistance to the South Vietnamese government, as we understand it, is that the Saigon government must remain militarily strong in order to counter real or perceived military threats from insurgent forces. The argument suggests that augmented military assistance to the Saigon government will contribute to the cause of peace in this war-torn land. 

Our past experience and our present observation here in Vietnam lead us to believe that exactly the opposite is true. Increased military assistance to this country will not bring peace; it will bring increased warfare. We were much encouraged in early 1973 when all the parties to the Vietnam war agreed to sign the Paris Ceasefire Accords inasmuch as the central theme of the Accords was reconciliation between the warring factions. We felt that peace in Vietnam might at last be possible. We anticipated a new era in which the conflict would be transferred from the military to the political arena. The voices of peace and reconciliation, so long muffled by the sounds of war, would once again prevail. 

Our hopes and, we believe, the hopes of the majority of the Vietnamese people risk being crushed again by the machines of war. We see the military power which the United States is supplying to this country being used to thwart the cause of peace and reconciliation. We Mennonite personnel have witnessed that those persons who speak effectively for the cause of reconciliation are put in prison or have their activities tightly circumscribed by a Gargantuan police apparatus. 

We have witnessed U.S.-provided ammunition being employed widely to shell areas under the control of the Provisional Revolutionary Government. Extensive military operations have wrested control of areas long under the surveillance of the PRG. Thousands of refugees are prevented from returning to their homes in contested or PRG areas by threat of arrest or artillery shelling. 

In short, the military force being supplied to this country by the United States is not bringing about a resolution of the political problems facing the Vietnamese people. On the contrary, it is preventing such a resolution. (754)

For this reason we Mennonite personnel in Vietnam appeal to you to do all within your power to drastically reduce the armaments flowing into this country. 

A significant reduction in the level of military supply to this country will, we believe, strengthen the forces of political and social harmony and bring closer the day of peace for this beautiful but troubled land. It is for such a day the 

Vietnamese pray, as do we all. Sincerely, (Signed)

PAUL BUCHER (U.S.), 

(And 21 others).

APPENDIX 7 STATEMENT OF GREGORY HENDERSON, FLETCHER SCHOOL OF LAW AND DIPLOMACY, TUFTS UNIVERSITY, AND EAST ASIAN RESEARCH CENTER, HARVARD UNIVERSITY 1 I. Introduction POLITICAL REPRESSION IN SOUTH KOREA 

Many Americans interested in the foreign affairs of the United States welcome the concerns of Congress over the implications of American aid-especially military aid-for the internal character of the regimes we are aiding and for the effects of such aid on our moral position without which neither nations nor individuals can exercise leadership. Such questions lie at the core of Section 32 of the Foreign Aid Law of 1973-74. 

Concern that American aid, economic but especially military, is being used for the suppression of individuals and institutions favoring participatory government rather than for their defense is now widespread; no misuse of this aid is so blatant and inexcusable today, however, as that to the Republic of Korea. 

II. Korean Security and the Question of Repression 

The measures taken by South Korea repressive of all liberties are now as extreme and institutionally routinized as they were in the classic fascist and communist examples-Hitler's Germany and Stalin's USSR. Only one element present there is so far missing in contemporary Korea; the concentration camp. 

As in the case of Hitler and Stalin, South Korea also uses external threat and theories of external conspirary as an excuse for escalating internal repressions. The excuse for Korea is essentially transparent. South Korea's armed forces remain 50-75% greater than those of North Korea; they have combat experience in Vietnam whereas North Korea's armed forces have had none for over twenty years; the South has the protective presence of 38,000 U.S. troops whereas North Korea has had no foreign troop presence for over fifteen years; 

U.S. air bases within Korea more than make up for any shortfall in Southern air power; finally, though North Korean aggressiveness is to some degree demonstrable, armed incidents have, since 1971, fallen to an almost infinitesimal percentage of what they were between 1967-1969 at which time martial law was not declared in South Korea, rights were not abruptly abrogated and some semblance, at least, of constitutional government was maintained. South Korean propaganda notwithstanding, armed incidents of Northern origin remain sparse and tangential for any essential question of South Korea's security today. 

III. The Laws of Repression 

Exhaustive analysis of present South Korean laws is not feasible here, but basic references are essential. The Korean Constitution has, following approximately 175 amendments forced on it by U.S. arms during the period of martial law following President Park's October 17, 1972, coup against his own constitutional system, been obliterated as an instrument of the slightest valid guarantee of civil rights or judicial process with any degree of independence from the Executive. The intent of justice is, perhaps, adequately expressed by the dropping from the present constitution of old article 10(6): "In case the confession of a defendant is considered to have been made against his will by means of torture, acts of violence, threat, unduly prolonged arrest, and deceit, etc. or if 

1 The author was a Foreign Service Officer of the United States for over sixteen years, over seven of them on assignment to the U.S. Embassy, Seoul, Korea. He has been Acting 

Officer-in-charge of the Korean Desk, Department of State. He is the author of a standard text on Korean politics: Korea: The Politics of the Vortex, Harvard University Press, 1968, the co-author with Amb. Edwin O. Reischauer of "There's Danger in Korea Still". 

New York Times Magazine, May 23, 1973, and is author of over thirty other articles and books dealing with the politics, history and culture of Korea. (756)

the confession of a defendant is the only evidence against him, such confession shall not be admitted as evidence for his conviction nor shall he be punished on the basis of such confession." While a general injunction against torture remains, it is impossible to interpret the elimination of the above provision except in terms of intent to apply duress to legal process. Eliminated from the new Constitution likewise is the old habeas corpus clause. Civil rights now exist only "except as provided by law"; even in this qualified state they are nullified effectively by Article 53 which states that "in case the national security or the public safety and order is seriously threatened or anticipated to be threatened . the President . Ishall have the power to take emergency measures which temporarily suspend the freedom and rights of the people as defined in the present Constitution and enforce emergency measures with regard to the rights and powers of the Executive and Judiciary." Despite the absence of any credible threat to security, South Korea has been for over half a year ruled by such emergency measures without convincing adumbration of their end. Constitutional historians of Germany will not fail to grasp the analogy between the above Article 53 and the risk of Hitler's control over the Weimar 

Republic. 

The new 'Constitution' was the object of study by some twenty Korean and American scholars at Columbia University last year. It was the informal concensus of this study, as it has been of other students, that the present Constitution of South Korea is one of the most illiberal and authoritarian instruments presently known to the annals of national constitutionalism including the constitutions of the Communist nations against whom the United States and other UN members defended at great cost the Korean Republic. It was imposed under martial law enforced by American arms, photographs of American tanks blockading the Korean National Assembly being widely distributed. 

The Emergency Measures of January 8 through April 3, 1974, far surpass in oppressiveness the Korean Constitution: they today effectively control South 

Korean politics. The first Measure, Jan. 8, 1974, makes it illegal "for any person to deny, oppose, misrepresent or defame the Constitution" or "to assert, introduce, propose or petition for revision or repeal of the Constitution." Courts martial are set up under the immediately succeeding Measure 2 to sentence violators to prison terms of up to 15 years for the above "crimes" and "Any person who violates any provision of these emergency measures and any person who defames them shall be subjected to arrest, detention, search or seizure without warrant." "There shall be no limitation on detention period." (Article 11). "When necessary for trial and investigation, an accused or a suspect may be ordered by the presiding judge or the prosecuting officer to be confined (to house arrest) in such facilities as a hospital or a house with appropriate restriction and supervision. Any person who violates the order of confinement shall be punished by imprisonment for not more than five years." (Article 13). Under these and other provisions, courts martial, closed to public scrutiny, now rule 'justice' in South Korea for virtually all political cases, normal civil judicial process becoming increasingly confined to cases of robbery, divorce and routine non-political matters.² 

Park's Emergency Measure No. 4, April 3, 1974, is, so far as any superficial survey can determine, the most extreme suppressive law against students and universities of which we have knowledge in any known state except for measures taken in the presence of armed conflict. "Students' refusal to attend classes and examinations without plausible reasons, and their assemblies, demonstrations, discussions, rallies and other individual and collective activities in and out of school except normal classes and research activities under the direction and supervision of the school authorities shall be prohibited.... The death penalty, life imprisonment or more than 5 years of imprisonment shall be given those who violate (this) provision." "The Education Minister may order expulsion or suspension from the school of those students who violate Emergency Measures; disbandment of student organizations, assemblies or other groups or closing (for good) of any schools to which such measures-violating students belong." 

Under the above and other provisions of this savage Measure, a student cutting classes or discussing or planning discussion of any political matter, even at home with his family or on campus casually among intimates could be court-martialed 2 There are exceptions. Opposition leader Kim Dae-chung is currently on trial before a civilian court-if his case can be called "normal".

and hanged as a criminal. It would be hard to find in any country a measure more flagrantly antidemocratic, more callously disregardful of any human rights or human dignity than Korea's Emergency Measure No. 4. 

The best-and worst-which can be said about the record of arrests and detentions in South Korea in the last months is that they are consistent with these laws. 

IV. The Categories of Arrests, Imprisonments and Incarcerations 

A noted American lawyer, the United Nations representative of the International Commission of Jurists, representing Amnesty International, who returned in the middle of July, 1974, from an investigative trip to Seoul, reports that official American sources confirm that there are currently 1100-1200 Koreans imprisoned as political prisoners in South Korea. 253 of these were imprisoned as a result of the Emergency Measures since January 8; the rest have been held for long periods-many since the late 1972 period but some longer than that. 

Almost all belong to the intellectual elite of South Korea. 

In addition, much as in the Soviet Union, there are a quite unknowable number of persons who disappear from the streets into the custody of the CIA. As 

Korean Christians, in a message smuggled out of Korea bitterly regretting the lack of international support they receive compared to Soviet intellectuals, put it: "We face the daily threat of being arrested, imprisoned and brutally tortured by the secret police . . . without anybody knowing it. Some of us have been arrested and imprisoned with neither warrant nor trial and without our families knowing what happened to us." Since the Korean CIA is an organization with tens of thousands of operatives, no one knows how many thousands have undergone such an experience. No one dares ask.

Some do not live to tell the tale. Prof. Tche Chong-gil, a noted expert on criminal law at Seoul National University and an outspoken and convinced anti- Communist, was spirited away by the CIA after the middle of October 1973 after having complained in a Law Faculty Meeting of the brutal presence on his campus of the Korean armed forces-all armed with American arms. On October 25, a "crackdown on spies" was announced in the course of which the CIA announced that Prof. Tche had "committed suicide" at CIA headquarters by leaping from the 7th floor bathroom (a place to which a detainee would not have had unaccompanied access.) His wife was not permitted to view the corpse. A student under detention at the same headquarters on that evening reported a man outside his cell saying that "someone has to be taken to a hospital right away." Following this announcement, remarkably little further was heard of this "spy case".▲ 

The clause permitting incarceration in a hospital has also not been completely neglected. Korea's most famous poet, Kim Chi-ha, was committed in the summer of 1972 to a government TB Sanitarium near Masan in lieu of jail until a group of determined Japanese intellectuals forced or cajoled their way in, taped a conversation with him and successfully petitioned President Park for his release. 

The closeness of this treatment to that accorded some dissident Soviet poets is startling. The number of such "committed" intellectuals is unknown. 

Others are under house arrest of various sorts, including that in which they are forced to have as semi-permanent, uninvited and unpaying house "guests" members of the intelligence agencies or police guards. The chief opposition candidate, Mr. Kim Dae-chung, for many weeks had such "guests"; so has a Dean of Yonsei University, so has a prominent Buddhist scholar and monk; so have others. The former President of the country, Yun Posun, a respected anti- 

Communist aristocrat, is watched over from a tower incongruously built in a lowlying residential section opposite the main gate to his historic ancestral home. 

But, besides these, no method of surveillance and/or house arrest-all, of course, without legal process or possibility of defense of any kind-has remained untried. The victims are the exact Korean equivalents of the "internal exiles" of the 

Soviet Union, living in their native land yet in a penumbral exile from it. Those visiting them do so at the risk of entering this same half-lit half-life. Frank Lanich and James Otis, "Church-State Confrontation in the ROK", Christianity and Crisis, Vol. 34, No. 5, p. 56, 1974. Though Americans, the authors dare not use their 

Far Eastern Economic Review, Hong Kong, December 24, 1973. 

own names.

Still others live in the ambivalent purgatory of the suspended trial. The Rev. 

Eun Myong-gi of Chonju, for example, a noted Presbyterian pastor, was the first of the waves of arrests marking the late Park era, having been arrested on Dec. 11, 1972, in the midest of a church prayer meeting. He had refused a request that he support the new constitutional revisions in Nov. 1972. Tried on grounds of "instigating persons" and "spreading groundless rumor", the Rev. Eun was neither sentenced nor acquitted after incarceration of at least eight months but has been described by a recently-returned expert on Korean law as remaining in a legally peculiar category, neither guilty nor innocent but subject to minuteby-minute threat of re-arrest on the same charges. His wife's arrest on grounds of not having reported (nor forwarded) a "circular letter" (obviously an attempted frame-up) preceded his. Others, of course, live somewhat similarly under suspended sentences. No one knows their number. 

Others inhabit still different penumbral planets of detention. Japanese businessman Sawamoto, of Korean descent with high Korean connections, was imprisoned on charges of spying in the first half of 1973; but neither the Korean nor the Japanese governments wished to admit the fact since the method of his arrest and his trial without the Japanese lawyer he had retained "raises questions for both governments." Foreigners are, of course, relatively privileged unless, like Sawamoto and Abe Isuyoshi, they have Korean blood and can therefore be tortured into unconsciousness. But even against foreigners threats have been made. Mr. Lee Kyu-hyun, Deputy Information Minister, told foreign correspondents just after the Jan. 8, 1974, measures that "if an American corre spondent quoted a Korean as having made an anti-government statement, 'both the Korean and you would be subject (to arrest and punishment) under the measure.'" "

The numbers of those picked up for demonstration, beaten, sometimes raped, and then released after anything from a few hours to four days are legion: Ewha students (NY Times, Dec. 28, 1973), opposition members of the National Assembly, like Yang Il-tong who, on release, was reportedly "very ill and would have to go to the hospital soon", Kim Yong-sam, a sturdily-constructed representative whose health also rapidly dissolved in jail, or Assemblymen Cho Yun-hyung, Cho Yun-ha, Kim Sam-hyun, Kim Han-suh and Lee Sae-kyu, most of whom were reported tortured, Cho Yun-ha reportedly by electric shock.' Other arrests reported are just plain Korean farmers near President Park's rural birthplace who wished to give him a petition when he visited the area but were held under arrest until he had "cleared the area"-very possibly without even his knowledge. 

The saddest are those whose imprisonments lead to actual execution. These are, fortunately, few but they are invariably political. They include Kim Kyunam, executed July 13, 1972, Park No-su, a scholar kidnaped by the Korean CIA from Cambridge University, England, died July 28, 1972, and two others, including a journalist. Both the prominent first two had awaited death for over two years and had been the subject of many international appeals including, in the case of Dr. Park, a special visit from Lord Caradonx to whom a promise of favorable treatment was made by Prime Minister Kim Chong-pil. Though accused of being Communist spies, study of the use of evidence and witnesses in these trials in no case discloses standards acceptable in the courts of civil law countries even for a prison, let alone a death sentence."

An increased implementation of death sentences in Korea, under current conditions of trial, would obviously constitute a human disaster. 

V. Torture 

If execution is rare, torture is ubiquitous. It spares neither the high nor the low, being in this respect one of the more democratic parts of Korea's penal system. It is, however, especially severe against men of special power and strength. It has been used-apparently repeatedly against the noted and determined poet Kim Chi-ha and also, according to his own evidence, against almost

Chang Chun-ha, one of Korea's best-known intellectuals, winner of the Magsaysay Award in 1962 for "editorial integrity" as founder and publisher for over 15 years of Sasanggye (World of Thought), later a Congressman, has been jailed seven times during the Park regime. A man of absolute honesty, he himself has told of his detention in October 1972 in the infamous Sobing-vo interrogation center where he was subjected to "Genghis Khan cooking", a savory procedures in which one's Korean government captors hang one upside down and burn various body areas with a flame.10 

Other methods are the "telephone" in which one "talks" to the victim through the application of electric wires frequently applied to the genitals and excited by escalated cranking; and the "aeroplane" in which the victim is suspended and either whipped, choked with water or, in the immortal imagery bequeathed by Mr. Ehrlichman, left to twist, twist in the wind. Korean police "frequently have been known to solve cases by encouragement until they confessed." " 

Most torture is almost synonymous with arrest and is not severe or of enduring effect. Some, however, as with Prof. Tche, results in death or, directly or indirectly through inducing suicide attempts, in permanent disfigurement. Attached is a photograph of the ravages of this process on the face of the Japan-born Seoul National student, Soh Sung, in 1971, a handsome and vivid student when he entered Korean prison. In the third hearing of his case on August 27, 1971, his 

Japanese friends saw him on the witness stand and thus describe the sight: "The appearance of Sung in the court gave us a great shock. We cannot help turning our eyes away from this miserable figure because of the serious burns all over his body. The skin from his body to his face was burned like a keloid. His ears and eyelids had disappeared owing to the burns. His fingers adhered together and his lips too . . . It is said that the authorities forced him to seal on the record (the 'confession') with his toe instead of his destroyed finger while unconscious from serious burns." " Too little of his ears remained to hold up his glasses. Many photographs, including some taken by known American correspondents, confirm this description. Mr. Soh remains in jail today under a life imprisonment in a "spy case" the fragility of whose evidence was as notorious as the methods employed to obtain it.13 

While nothing so extreme as this has been evidenced in the last weeks most or all of the 52 persons on trial in July 1974 up to the time of the writing of this report are understood to have claimed that torture was used to extract "confessions" from them.

Though executions are rare, detention camps unknown and political cases of significant but not enormous numbers, the Park regime has, within these limits, practised the gamut of cruelties and repressions of which modern society and the ingenuity of the ruthless and the vengeful are unitedly capable. 

VI. Judicial Procedure 

The Government invariably tries to rest its most serious charges and convictions on grounds of Communist conspiracy. In almost every case, these charges involve Japanese or Korean residents of Japan and the averring of the existence of networks in Japan intermediate to North Korea. The intermediaries cannot be produced in the courtroom nor the networks investigated first-hand. 

Charges of this sort have a long history in Korean politics. It is not possible at this distance at least-to dissect the minutiae of cases now under trial in Seoul most of which take place in secret courts martial. It is possible, however, to recognize recurring features of these trials and to compare them with the far fuller knowledge we have of the similar "conspiracy" trials of the 13 arrested members of the Korean National Assembly, May 1949-April 1950; the abortive trials of seven National Assembly members and seven other defendants, again on charges of "Communist conspiracy", June-July, 1952 in Pusan; the "conspiracy trial of former opposition presidential candidate (and Agriculture Minister) Cho Pong-am in 1959; and the conspiracy trials-quite numerous-of Korean Socialists (most of them decidedly conservative Socialists) following Park's coup in 

10 Christian Science Monitor, Jan. 25, 1974, as told to correspondent Elizabeth Pond, now denied a visa into South Korea. 

11 FEER, Nov. 18, 1972. 

12 "Save the Soh Brothers", Sept. 1972, Shin-ai Gakusha, Tokyo, and Makoto Nishimura,

Kyoto, Japan. 

13 The varied official explanations for his appearance included attempted suicide by falling into an oil stove. Such suicide attempts are, as under the Nazi, usually induced by extreme torture.

1962; and the conspiracy trial of the Soh brothers (vide supra) in 1972 which were more openly-attended than are present trials and have been fairly extensively analyzed."

In all these cases, miscarriages of procedure major enough to have invalidated all these cases in countries of firm civil law procedure existed, even though these trials were mostly far more exhaustive than the ones now taking place in Korea and took place, usually in public, before civilian courts and not closed courts martial. All of them were characterized by absences from the witness stand of the key witnesses indispensable for establishing from first-hand evidence the alleged links with Communists or with North Koreans. As is today the case with Mr. 

Kwak Dong Yee (and perhaps others), then also most key witnesses were in Japan and could not be produced. In their absence, hearsay evidence, often of extreme remoteness, is relied on. Invariably, the chief evidence used consists of confessions by the defendants made outside the courtroom, usually in jail cells, to the prosecutor. Equally invariably, these confessions are described by the defendants in open court as having been obtained by torture and are denied by them. The prosecution is unable to deny these statements by the defendants. Yet judgments continue to be handed down based on written prosecution documents obtained by torture and ignoring the statements of witnesses in open court in blatant contravention of established procedure in civil law countries and courts. The admission of witnesses, entirely at the discretion of the judge, is highly prejudicial to the defense, sometimes all witnesses for the prosecution being allowed with others unilaterally added by the judge while witnesses vital for the case-as well as for the defense are denied, arbitrarily and without adequate grounds. The position of the prosecutor, a government official, is typically far superior to the position of the defense lawyer who is usually reduced to having to plead for mercy from the judge who shows scant heed to any defense whatsoever regardless of its merits in political cases. The charging and trying of a man on political grounds in 

South Korea hence is the equivalent of a conviction and such judicial procedure as exists is reduced very close to meaninglessness. In recent cases, moreover, too little time for cross-examination and elementary consideration is allowed; the complete erosion of judicial independence from the executive and the utter dependence of sentencing on the judge as a government official decimates justice. 

Sentences bear little relation to the gravity of the crime and are frequently set aside by Presidential "clemency" thus casting legal process in the role of warning, not of justice, and affording to the Executive the specious semblance of benevolence. 

All evidence points to these factors being present in aggravated degree since the subjecting, since January 1974, of judicial process to military controls.

Trials are secret, monitoring, even by foreign embassies, is impossible, almost no witnesses for the defense have been allowed, defense lawyer Kang Sin-ok was today (July 19, 1974) described as having been arrested, for the first time in Korean legal history, for words he uttered in court as a defence lawyer, defendants and their lawyers have not been permitted to construct proper defense and sentences of death for giving the equivalent of $465.00 to students by poet 

Kim Chi-ha speak for themselves.

In sentences of imprisonment for less than life terms, political opposition, usually simple desire to reinstitute freedom of speech and democratic process, is the only cause for "crime", the only ground for conviction. Thus Magsaysay Awardwinner Chang Jun-ha and political scientist Paik Ki-whan were sentenced after the Jan. 8, 1974, decree to 15 and 42 years in jail for their 500,000-name signature petition to restore constitutional government in Korea; Kim Kyong-no and other Christians for fifteen years in jail for calling for constitutional changes; many of some 240 recently-arrested students are charged simply with petitioning for repeal of the present repressive Constitution. Students in 1972 were arrested, tortured and convicted for trying to start an inter-campus newspaper (they testified to receiving torture). One man was sentenced to 3 years in prison for writing to an opposition Assemblyman urging a political fight to nullify the President's Oct. 17, 1972 coup against the constitution. Others get sentences simply for removing government campaign posters from the front of their own private houses; or for writing letters to their own families (then opened by the CIA) advising them to vote against the new constitution. Others are arrested and sentenced for "spreading rumors" or for "rumors crticising the October Revitalizing Reforms." The handing down in mid-July 1974 of 14 death sentences and 

77 other stiff sentences including 15–20 for life imprisonment for political opposi- 36-333-74. -49

tion and the trying of the extremely conservative ex-President on similar charges raises current political persecution in South Korea to one of its highest tides in the history of any nation in modern times. 

VII. Conclusion 

Political repression, political imprisonment, political detention and incarceration, political torture and gross miscarriages or justice for the political preservation of the present regime are rampant in today's South Korea. 

Comparative study is beyond the scope of this report. I find it, however, probable and probably difficult to contest that, in proportion to its size and population, there is currently as much or more political repression in South Korea than today in the Soviet Union or in most other Communist countries from whose attempted invasion and control-and in the name of democracy-the United States and the United Nations sought to save South Korea from 1950-53. 

North Korea is, of course, no alternative. If it is possible for a nation to be even more repressive than South Korea is that nation is probably the Democratic People's Republic of Korea (North Korea), though it must be cautioned that our ignorance of that country may prejudice and certainly does not enhance our judgment. North Korea and its actions, however, while in no way praiseworthy when they concern force, constitute no valid grounds for the repressions now rife in South Korea. 

In granting aid to South Korea in 1973-74, the Executive Branch of the U.S. Government has clearly acted in defiance of the wishes of Congress ex pressed in Section 32 of the Foreign Aid Bill. 

The Department of State has clearly failed adequately to defend or advance American policies in Korea during the last thirty months. Its unwillingness to pressure the Park government with requisite strength to deny aid or even to voice its views publicly have severed the threat of U.S. policy to Korea and broken faith with what our highest leaders told young Americans they were giving their lives for.

The students of Seoul National University well expressed what the results of present Executive policies will be: "You must remember that so long as 

America supports the dictatorial regime in our land, our people are bound to become anti-American in the near future. You will surely understand that dictators of many Asian countries are not your true friends and that support for them will not serve your interests." 99 14 The continued supply of American arms and the effrontery to American interests of increased requests for U.S. military aid, not only spiritually and materially supports the present repression in South Korea but makes impossible democratic attempts in our interests to change that regime. Such aid and such arms actively intervene in South Korea against Korean democracy. From the viewpoint of human rights or democracy it is now as unjustified for Americans to give active aid and support to South Korea as it would have been for us to have aided Stalin in his last five years. Nothing we can do as a nation will be more deleterious for our long-term interests than such misplaced official U.S. support; nothing can fuel greater or more justified hatred of ourselves; nothing can more surely serve, in the long run, the Communist cause. 

May I express the hope that Section 30 of the Foreign Aid Law will be continued and that it now will be forcefully implemented and applied specifically and with requisite public articulation to the shocking situation existing today in South Korea. Aid in the coming years should be denied Korea until and unless she can demonstrate that the weapons provided by the American people for the defense and preservation of Korean democracy are not used for its suppression. That 

American arms suppress democracy in South Korea today is transparently clear.
