APPENDIX 8 STATEMENT OF BENEDICT J. KERKVLIET, FOR THE FRIENDS OF THE FILIPINO PEOPLE Mr. Chairman and Members: I am Benedict J. Kerkvliet, a professor of political science at the University of Hawaii and currently, for 1973-74, a Fellow at the 

Woodrow Wilson International Center for Scholars here in Washington. I am speaking today on behalf of myself and an organization of concerned Filipinos and Americans called Frends of the Filipino People (FFP). 

We have been following closely events in the Philippines since President Ferdinand Marcos imposed martial law and curtailed all civil liberties in that country. I, for example, lived in the Philippines from March 1969 through November 1970 while doing research on peasant movements there, especially the Huk rebellion (1946-1954). And since then I have studied political developments in the 

Philippines and other countries in Southeast Asia, partly in connection with my teaching and my own research. My studies and those of others in the Friends of the Filipino People and organizations with similar interests have caused us to be alarmed at trends in the Philippines. We fear increased repression and violence under the present martial law regime. And we fear that the United States will continue to contribute directly to this repression. We want the United States government to show to the world this year that it will no longer continue to support military dictatorships. We want the United States to end all military and military-related assistance to the Marcos regime, the newest dictatorship in Southeast Asia. If the Administration of President Nixon fails to stop this aid, then we want at least the 93rd Congress of the United States to refuse to appropriate any more money to the martial law regime in the Philippines. 

The basis for this position is the following argument. First, the martial law regime in the Philippines is a repressive one. Repression and abusive government practices have been major themes in the country's politics during the last one and one-half years. They far exceed whatever shortcomings the country had prior to martial law. Second, repression and abuses have provoked Filipinos from many different backgrounds and political orientations to resist, often rebel. 

Rebellion is more extensive than before martial law. Third, the response of the 

Philippine government, in turn, has been more repression and further militarization of the government and the entire society. Fourth, this military apparatus, including the country's enlarged armed forces and modernized national police, is heavily dependent upon the United States. Whether or not Congress has approved, the United States government is perpetuating this dictatorship and its repressive policies. This not only makes a farce of our democratic principles and heritage, but it could easily drag the United States into another "Vietnam" type of war in Southeast Asia. That prospect scares me to death, and I should think that it would millions of other Americans and Filipinos, too. 

POLITICAL REPRESSION IN THE PHILIPPINES 

Since September 1972, the Republic of the Philippines has been under martial law. This country, which once was widely known as America's "showcase of democracy" and one of the few countries in the Third World to have any semblance of democracy, has become a dictatorship. The dictator is Ferdinand E. 

Marcos, who is both President and Prime Minister of the Republic. 

The laws of the land under martial law are the Presidential Decrees, Letters of Instructions, and General Orders that only President Marcos or his own ministers can issue. He has proclaimed over 440 Presidential Decrees so far. He has destroyed the legislative and judicial branches of government, silenced the press, ordered the arrests of thousands, and mobilized the military. 

One of President Marco's first acts after declaring martial law was to dismiss the Philippine Senate and House of Representatives. He banned all political (763)

parties and cancelled all elections, including his own. His second, and final term as President should have ended December 1973. He arrested prominent Senators and several delegates to the Constitutional Convention, which was then in session. 

These persons had been Marcos' political enemies and outspoken of the militaristic tendencies of the Marcos administration prior to martial law. 

He also destroyed the previously independent judicial branch. General Order 

No. 3, which Marcos issued the first day of martial law, disrobes the court by excluding all acts, decrees, and other orders of Marcos or his representatives from judicial scrutiny. Also excluded are criminal cases involving such issues as "national security," "the fundamental laws of the State," and "public order." He added four members to the Supreme Court, appointing persons known to be loyal to him. Then, as a journalist recently wrote, "to seal the collapse of the old independent judiciary, President Marcos not only squeezed resignation letters from all judges down to the Court of First Instance level (presided over by district judges); he also made sure the nine carry-over Supreme Court justices took new oaths of office under his Constitution." The President has also formed "military tribunals," one or more for each military region of the country, to try both civilian and military cases involving "crimes" against the government. 

The Marcos government was not content with simply cancelling all elections. 

It has wanted to give the appearance of free choice, especially for the benefit of the outside world. It has called, therefore, two referendums; one to approve a new Constitution, which allowed Marcos to stay in power indefinitely, and the other to approve the programs of the "New Society." For these referendums, the 

Marcos regime created "Citizen Assemblies" throughout the country. People had to vote in public, frequently in the presence of armed police, and with government officials coaching them on the "correct" ballots. As the highly respected Bishop 

Francisco F. Claver wrote recently,

Probably the single most resented aspect of martial law (and this is true among the privileged as well as the underprivileged classes) is the loss of freedom of choice at the polls. The past two referendums have been unparalleled farces, a fact that is not lost on even the regime's staunchest supporters. For a people used to turning out of office unpopular administrations in the past through the instrumentality of the free ballot, having to vote according to "suggested answers" is the ultimate indignity. The people feel the insult deeply, but they also realize they are not going to achieve anything in open demand for their rights.' The New Society prohibits the civil liberties of the "old society." As one recent study concluded, there is no freedom of the press, no freedom of speech, no freedom of assembly, no freedom of arbitrary arrest, and no guarantee of a fair trial." Where there were 15 to 20 daily newspapers before martial law, there are only three now-all of them strictly controlled by the government, and one of them with close ties to President Marcos. The number of radio and television stations has similarly declined. All media must abide by the government's rule of censorship. These rules prohibit any criticism, let alone any dissent, of government policies and the President himself. "The media report virtually nothing but praise for the Marcos administration," wrote one scholar. A correspondent remarked, as others have, "Manila's press after martial law counts among the dullest and most obedient in the world." 

Media people must adhere to government censorship lest they lost their licenses, be imprisoned, or both. Since martial law, the government has imprisoned numer ous journalists, publishers, and broadcasters. At least one of them has been tried on charges of "subversion," and sentenced to several years of hard labor. Under martial law, "subversive literature" is, as Maryknoll priests told a Washington

Post correspondent last November, "any article even mildly critical of the regime even articles from magazines such as Time or Newsweek. "The gov- ernment has banned from the country at least nine issues of Time, for example, because they had stories containing criticism of Marcos's policies. 

The government has outlawed strikes, political organizations, and unauthorized political meetings. "Strikes are a luxury we cannot afford in the 'New Society'," said Alejandro Melchor, the Executive Secretary to Marcos." The regime has also dissolved labor courts and imposed compulsory arbitration in order to suppress labor and peasant unrest that had been common prior to martial law. Peasants, who comprise nearly 75% of the population, can only form associations that have the government's approval. In most localities the government has outlawed chapters of the two largest peasant organizations prior to martial law, the MASAKA (Malayang Samahang Magsasaka, or Free Farmers Union) and the FFF (Federation of Free Farmers).

Fear and force are principal means the government uses to get compliance and obedience. Both the censored Manila newspapers and the foreign press report numerous police raids and mass arrests. During the first three months of martial law, the Philippine Constabulary (PC) stated that 8,261 persons had been arrested. After one year of martial law, the government admitted that it had arrested or, in the government's language, "detained" 11,697 persons.10 The figure must be far above that now because arrests and police raids have continued unabated in the eight months since last September. A common practice of the specially trained "Metrocom" (Metropolitan Command) police attached to the Philippine Constabulary is to surround an entire neighborhood, usually at night, force everybody out of their homes, and arrest people who look suspicious. These are called "zona" raids, named after the similar methods of the military during the Japanese occupation in World War II. In recent months, the police have focused especially on intellectuals and clergy. In December, for example, the PC raided the Baguio City branch of the University of the Philippines and arrested 150 professors and students. The PC released some of them a short time later, but they took the others to a PC prison or "detention center" for interrogation and imprisonment. Among the prominent persons recently arrested are Dr. Nemesio Prudente, former president of the Philippine College of Commerce in Manila; Attorney Charito Planas, a critic of martial law and a former delegate to the Constitutional Convention; and Lorenzo Tañada, Jr., a media executive and son of former Senator Tañada who has been a lawyer for several of those people arrested during martial law." As for the clergy, the government has raided convents, church schools, church universities, and private homes in order to arrest ministers, priests, and nuns. At least 22 priests and nuns had been "detained" as of November 1973, according to a New York Times report. By now the number is larger because the government, angry with those in the Catholic Church who continue to criticize the military for its abuses and martial law in general, has quickened its drive against the clergy despite military assurances earlier that arbitrary arrest of Catholic clergy would stop." 

Frequently, people arrested are never charged with a crime. People suffer, as priests in one Philippine province recently protested, "arbitrary arrests and acts of harassment on [grounds of] mere suspicion of so-called subversive activities.' 

Others, such as Baldomero T. Olivera, a former press secretary to a late Philippine President, are arrested for "rumor mongering,” a punishable crime according to Presidential Decree No. 90.15 Anyone who utters any criticism automati- 12 13 99 14

Still others are accused of specific crimes, including "subversion," but languish in prison for months without trial. From time to time, the government releases "detainees," after they agree to endorse the New Society and to report regularly to assigned police and military officers. Others, however, have been in prison for months. Senators Jose 

Diokno and Benigno Aquino, Jr., for instance, have been in prison since the first day of martial law. They still have not yet been formally charged. Their only offense seems to be that they were strong critics and threatening political opponents of Marcos prior to martial law. 

Inside the prisons, government authorities often abuse the prisoners. A peasant whom the PC arrested, for example, fought the guards at the "detention camp." The guards, in turn, electrocuted his penis. He had fought the guards in the first place because the reason he had been arrested was because he had tried to get the landlord to follow the rules of Marcos's land reform program." A former prisoner wrote that many of those people arrested for subversive activity never make it to prison; "often as not, they are killed at the time of their capture by ambitious military men anxious to report 'battle' victories." Those who escape murder "are taken to secret apartments and at times to military camps where they are squeezed for information through the use of a wide range of crude to sophisticated torture techniques." ." 18 In mid 1973, 27 priests reported in a joint letter that they had documented proof of men who had been "killed in jail even before their guilt could be investigated and established." 19 A pastoral letter of Sulu and Mindanao priests read to hundreds of congregations on Easter Sunday 1974 protested, "That some detainees, according to a growing number of reports, have been subjected to torture in violation of the United Nations Declaration of Human Rights, yet there are no signs that steps are being taken to correct this." " 

A study in November 1973, based on a survey of key informants throughout the Philippines, found that, "There are frequent reports of physical torture from all regions of the country. The families and relatives of prisoners are [also] kept under surveillance."

Outside the prison, too, military officers and other government authorities abuse civilians and continue practices of corruption and favoritism. In the provinces, people report that military authorities get away with everything from murder to stealing funds from relief projects to siphoning gas from civilian trucks into their own vehicles.22 A study of all regions in the country found, for example, In the cities of Central Luzon, the 1st PC Zone Command protects gambling and houses of prostitution. In Cebu and Eastern Visayas, the 3rd PC 

Zone Command protects smuggling and vice, which are reported to be much worse now than before martial law. From Zamboanga del Norte, there are many reports of crimes committed by the military against defenseless Mus- Jim civilians. In Mindoro, the PC are accused of land grabbing from the 

Mangyans (a tribal group).

The study concluded that instead of controlling the abuses of local politicians, who are by and large the same people as before martial law, The military in most of the eleven regions of the country are. . . party to the abuses. There is a marriage of convenience from which both military and politicians profit. The ordinary people are the ones who suffer. There is no one to defend their rights. No one to whom they can appeal their grievances. 

They are intimidated, fearful. They have no recourse from either the abuses of the military or the politicians, and abuses are common.25

A lawyer for recent refugees from heavy fighting in Sulu province said, "The efforts of the President to establish his New Society by martial law have failed because despite the various decrees, the people are still suffering from want, fear, corruption, and iniquitous treatment from the people who have been charged with carrying out his presidential orders.' 

11 24 99 20 Since martial law began, the Marcos regime has increased its budget for propaganda from 3 million pesos to 68 million pesos ($10 million) in order to sell the New Society both at home and abroad. But appearance of reform is not enough, not when repression is so harsh and the "reforms" themselves so empty. 

As a Wall Street Journal reporter wrote a year ago, "Despite a few promising indications, his [Marcos's] 'New Society' remains more a matter of public relations than of profound reforms. Its momentum, moreover, seems to be sagging.' 

Land reform, for example, which Marcos has said repeatedly should be the only guage of success or failure for the New Society, has so far been a failure. And it shows every likelihood of continuing to be so because it excludes most tenant farmers, while those who are affected will probably end up as poor as they were before martial law." Corruption continues, even at the highest levels of government. The major difference is that corrupt military officers have replaced some of the corrupt politicians. The widely advertised claim that "crime in the streets" is wiped out appears to have been only a temporary reality. Even the government censored press reports more stories of crime now than it did a year ago. Last October, the Department of Defense admitted to a delegation of Catholic bishops that the crime rate was on the rise and was fast approaching premartial law proportions." 28 Those who have benefited from martial law include the foreign investors par ticularly large American, Japanese, and multinational corporations.30 Other beneficiaries include Filipino political and economic elites. Talk about redistribution of wealth and undermining the wealthy families notwithstanding, the martial law regime has not posed a threat to the elite as a whole. Only a few of the oligarical families have lost some wealth and political clout. They did because they were political enemies of Marcos, who took his revenge once he had acquired so much power by virtue of martial law. Marcos and his family have benefited, too. Reputed to have been the wealthiest man in Southeast Asia before martial law, Marcos must be one of the wealthiest men in Asia now. He is also, in effect, President for life or for as long as he can hang on to the position. 

GROWING RESISTANCE AND REBELLION 

Social, economic, and political conditions in the Philippines were bad before martial law. Since then, they have become in several respects even worse. But now Filipinos have far fewer legal options in order to express their discontent. 

The result, almost inevitably, has been increased illegal actions, resistance, and even armed rebellion. The authorities characterize the people who do these things as "subversives," "communists," and "Maoists." If there is any truth at all to this, it accounts for only a small number of people. It is the government-its repressive policies and bad economics-that is provoking people to resist and to rebel.

Take wage laborers, for example. Inflation exceeded 30 percent last year and it is still climbing; unemployment is increasing; employers lay off workers in

But the government continues to refuse. Some workers have publically protested and gone on strike, anyway, risking imprisonment or even death." The PC and local police have arrested many of the workers' leaders.

Squatter families, who compose one-fourth to one-third of Manila's population, have been organizing for years in order to protect themselves against forced eviction and government abuses. Now, under martial law, the evictions have been stepped up in order to make way for the regime's "beautification projects," yet the squatters can no longer demonstrate or hold rallies. But because the situation had become so serious late last year, several hundred people dared to march toward the President's palace to protest "the government's violation of an agreement that no squatters would be ejected beyond the six-meter distance from the Manila Bay shoreline." The PC's Metrocom police confronted the squatters, forced them to disperse, and arrested several leaders. The next week, the Metrocom raided the homes of those in the squatters' "ZOTO" organization and arrested more leaders.22 33 

Presidential Decree No. 33 prohibits the "printing, possession, distribution, and circulation" of leaflets, handbills, papers, graffiti, or any other materials that might "incite" people or criticize the government. Despite this decree and the prison sentence it carries, "underground" papers and leaflets continue to appear in increasing numbers. Many university people who were active in numerous nationalist organizations prior to martial law have now resorted to secret meetings and surreptitious methods in order to collect information and publish news that never gets into the government censored press. They do this despite the fact that police and the PC arrest and imprison people for these "subversive" and "communistic" activities.

Meanwhile, there is considerable evidence that the numbers of groups prepared to fight in armed rebellion is increasing. One group, called the Filipino Freedom 

Fighters, pleaded with Marcos in a publically circulated letter last September to lift martial law. When his term of office under the pre-martial law Constitution expired at the end of 1973, the Freedom Fighters stated that Marcos, in their view, was no longer the legitimate president and warned that force may be necessary in order to oust him. The Freedom Fighters reportedly include lawyers, professors, students, some libertarian-minded wealthy families, and even some disgruntled officers in the Philippine military.

In the countryside prior to martial law, organized rebellion was confined mainly to the small New People's Army in parts of the Cagayan Valley and Muslim rebels in parts of Mindanao. But since martial law, organized resistance and rebellion have appeared in most regions of the country. Reports from the 

Manila and foreign press show armed groups have clashed with the Philippine military in several provinces in the following regions: Ilocos, Cagayan Valley, Central Luzon, Southern Luzon, Bicol, Western Visayas, Eastern Visayas, Mindanao, and Sulu-virtually every part of the country. The province of Pampanga in Central Luzon, for example, had a clash last October for the first time in over four years between "insurgents" and the PC." Armed rebels are also appearing again in other areas, such as Bulacan and Nueva Ecija, where the peasant-based Huk rebellion had been strong in the 1940s and 1950s. The island of Panay in 

Western Visayas has become, according to another report, "a veritable powder keg." with 200 or more well armed rebels scattered across the three provinces there. The rebels reportedly have considerable village support. Many students from universities in Manila and other cities have gone underground to join peasants in armed rebellion in different parts of the country. Prior to martial law, 34 85 36

A study last Fall noted, for example, that many of the approximately 100 armed rebels in Davao Oriental and Davao del Norte (in Mindanao) were young people who had been active in the "Khi Rho" before." The Khi Rho was a Catholic youth group that worked especially with peasant associations. Another report tells of four rebels whom the PC recently killed. One had been the secretarygeneral of the SDK, which was a legitimate student political organization prior to martial law. Another had been the editor of the University of the Philippines student newspaper. Two more had been "campus activists." " Several priests and nuns, too, have joined armed peasant groups to prepare for armed rebellion." 

Although the number of rebels may still be small and the degree of cooperation among these various groups may be weak, the rebels seem to be growing in strength-and even in cooperation. Reports recently have said that the various underground groups within the "Christians for National Liberation" are making a "united front" with other underground groups and the so-called "Maoist" New 

People's Army." 

The New People's Army, too, seems to be larger now than it was when Marcos declared martial law in September 1972. A news report on a province in the Bicol region said, for example, "No more than a communist toehold before the imposition of martial law, this southern tip of Luzon has developed in the 16 months since September 1972 into what appears to be a solid spreading base of the... 

New People's Army. The NPA has taken hold of Sorsogon because it is rooted in the community. Its leaders here are former student activists, born here, ... and former Marcos political opponents led by a former local mayor."" The Philippine army has said that the number of "Communist regulars" has increased during martial law from 1,710 to 2,266."

Although the government characterizes most of these rebels and other "subversives" as "communists" and "Maoists," this is not a fair description, as I have tried to indicate here. A few may be communists, such as some of those in the New 

People's Army. But most people are doing things that the government considers illegal, including armed rebellion, first, in order to protect themselves against repression, and second, to work for improved conditions in their country. Most of these Filipinos would prefer legitimate channels of criticism, dissent, and protest, but martial law has closed those off. 

The situation reminds me very much of the conditions in which the large peasant movement in Central Luzon in the 1940s became a strong peasant rebellion that lasted until the mid 1950s. This was the Huk rebellion. Peasants had not wanted to take up guns to fight for economic justice and against the police and landlords' violent practices. But because of officially sanctioned repressionbeginning in 1945 and 1946, peasants had to fight back. They were forced to rebel. 

The government and US authorities at that time, too, called the Huks a "communist" rebellion. But it was not." One would think that government officials would have learned better over the years since then. 

The largest and strongest rebellion during martial law thus far has been the Muslim movement in Mindanao and Sulu, the southern extreme of the Philippines. 

The Marcos regime. has been terribly anxious to portray the Muslim rebels as Maoists." It is in the Marcos regime's interests to do this, first, in order to keep 

Muslim countries, upon whom the Philippines depends for most of its oil, from accusing the Philippine government of waging a genocidal war on Muslim brothers. Second, the Marcos government knows that the United States government is more likely to help in the counter-insurgency if the insurgents are "communists" and "Maoists."

But the Muslim rebellion is far more complicated than communist subversion. "The . . . charge-that the rebels are 'Muslim Maoists'-remains the best illustration, among many, of the Manila [government] failure to see itself, or the problem, as Muslims see it," wrote Harvey Stockwin, a close observer of the situation. "The rebels are no nearer reconciling Maoism to Islam than are, for example, Sabah's Tun Mustapha or Libya's Colonel Moammer Kadaffi."" The first complication is that there are several Muslim rebel groups, not just one. 

They do not want exactly the same thing and they are not under one unified leadership. Second, the current rebellion among Filipino Muslims is part of a long history of trouble between this minority group and the central government in Manila-whether under the Spanish, Americans, or Philippine Republic-and the Christian Filipino majority. The issues go way back: Muslim identity, landownership, and independence or at least an autonomous Muslim state. 45 Although fighting between Muslim rebels and the Philippine military occurred off and on during the 1960's, it was martial law that pushed an even larger number of Muslims into full-scale rebellion. One important reason was the increased presence of the Philippine military itself. The military's reputation is extremely bad among Muslims, and as the military started to exercise its new power under martial law, it easily angered these people. A second important reason was the government's demand that all citizens turn over their weapons to the military. 

Because Muslims have so frequently had to resort to weapons to protect themselves from the encroachments of Christian Filipinos and the central government, this demand was tantamount to surrendering their only means of self-defense. 

This was all the more so in a martial law situation since other legitimate grievance channels were blocked. From the earliest months of martial law until now, the rebellion has been gaining momentum among people in several provinces in Mindanao and in the province of Sulu. According to numerous reports, the rebels controlled much of Sulu. In January and February, the government decided it could no longer tolerate this and launched a series of heavy attacks. 

MILITARY FORCE AND MILITARIZATION 

On several occasions last year, the Philippine military used airpower, naval bombardment, and heavy assaults against Muslim rebel positions in Mindanao and Sulu. A few months ago, in February 1974, the government put their full might behind a sustained attack on Muslim rebels, numbering between 400 and 2,000, who had moved from the countryside to take control of the Muslim city of Jolo in Sulu province. It had been a city of 150.000 people. Afterwards, according to a Manila newspaper, it had only 20,000 people." The city was in ruins, said a New York Times reporter; "it was acres of charred rubble and blasted concrete, from which bodies were still being recovered . . . more than a week after the Philippine armed forces finally took Jolo back from the Muslim insurgents.' ." Another reporter said that Jolo was 90 percent destroyed." Between 

1,000 and 2.000 people were killed." The government's air force had bombed and napalmed the city, its navy had bombarded it with heavy artillery, and its army had fielded 5.000 heavily armed soldiers. This was, in Philippine military language, "a mailed fist approach" to end the rebellion. After the battle, the Marcos regime's Secretary of Defense, Juan Ponce Enrile, reflected on the method: "We should have taught these people a lesson a long time ago. We have been too easy on them. They must be forced to give up this foolish idea of dismembering a por-

Since the large battle in February, the Philippine military has continued what it calls "sanitizing operations" against Muslims beyond the ruins of Jolo."

Several thousand Filipino refugees, both Muslim and Christian, try to find shelter and food in Zamboanga, Cotabato, Basilan, and other places. The Prime 

Minister of Malaysia recently reported that in his country alone, on the island of Sabah, there were 22,000 Filipino Muslim refugees. But reputable observers say, that rather than bringing the war to a halt, the government's military methods have strengthened the Muslim rebellion. As one foreign correspondent wrote recently about Jolo's destruction, "First, and last, it has increased the polarization between Christian and Muslim in the Southern Philippines. 

Some of the younger [Muslims] inevitably feel that joining up with the rebels is the only way out. There are numerous swirling cross-currents, eddying all the more because of Jolo. They add up to vicious, gathering, circles of fear and suspicion, hatred and violence." "

Other government military attacks similar to the one on Jolo have occurred during martial law. In October 1972, for example, a military commander in 

Northern Luzon forced 50,000 Filipinos to move just as they were preparing to harvest their rice crops. The commander said he wanted to "sanitize" the area with a "big military operation." It was an area where the New People's Army was strong. "Everyone who remains in the area is NPA," General Tranquilino 

Paranis is reported to have said as he prepared the attack. Martial law, he added, had helped to persuade local government officials to cooperate with this military method.

I fear that government attacks like this, the one in Jolo, and other repressive methods will continue in many parts of the Philippines as the government continues to militarize and resort to large scale violence in order to rule. 

A major theme in Philippine politics under martial law has been militarization. 

Previously, the military played only minor roles. Now it has the center of the stage. In terms of size, for example, the military numbered between 60,000 and 

65,000 when Marcos declared martial law in September 1972. By late 1973, government news reports said that the Philippine military was about 80,000. By 

May 1974, the number was 100.000. The Marcos regime plans that by mid 1975 the military will number 256,000.5 Some of the new recruits will be volunteers, but the majority will be draftees. For the first time in the Republic's history, it will have a national draft. 

Military expenditures, too, are way above previous amounts, and they continue to rise. Although the regime's budget has been secret, one report said that, “a number of economists. . . believe that military expenditures are far more substantial than the level authorized in the pre-martial law budget." 57 These military expenditures were a major cause for last year's record deficit of 1.2 billion pesos ($150 million).58

Under martial law President Marcos has given this growing military organization increased powers in nearly every aspect of government. Several provinces have had Philippine Constabulary and Philippine Army colonels and generals for governors. In most regions, military officers are in charge of the important 

Regional Offices for Development, which supervise, among other things, public works and parts of the land reform program. Marcos has also made miiltary officers responsible for the management of the Manila Electric company, a steel mill, and other companies that the regime took from rival political families after

martial law. And there are the new military tribunals mentioned earlier that try civilians accused of certain crimes against the state. 50 In addition to the military itself, there is the national police system. The 

National Police Commission, which was established a few years ago, is now making steady progress in bringing all of the country's 1,500 police departments under one integrated police system. The chief of the National Polic Commission is the Secretary of Defense, Juan Ponce Enrile. As the police departments are integrated, the Philippine Constabulary will take control and supervise all police functions. In this way the integrated national police forces will come under the 

Philippine armed forces. Accomplishments of this integration program thus far include, for example, unification of all police forces in metropolitan Manila, centralized data banks and communication systems for police work throughout the country, and training schools for all policemen and police chiefs. The Marcos regime has also released special funds to raise the salaries and add fringe benefits for policemen throughout the country." This comes at a time when wages for most Filipino workers have been declining. 

Another important part of militarization is the government's efforts to watch or, as government reports say, "monitor" people. One part of this is the expanding role of several security, investigation, and spy agencies. In addition to enhancing the role of the National Bureau of Investigation (NBI) and the National Intelligence Coordinating Agency (NICCA), the regime has created related organizations, such as the Civil Intelligence and Security Agency (CISA). The job assigned to CISA is to gather intelligence information on students, teachers, professors, and non-academic personnel at schools and campuses across the country." 

Another method to keep track of people is the compulsory registration system that the regime has begun. This system requires, according to Presidential Decree 278 issued in August 1973, that, "... all citizens of the republic. . . shall be assigned a reference number and issued a national reference card. 

Citizens or nationals of foreign countries resident in the Philippines shall likewise be assigned" a card to serve as "the official identification of the person to whom it is issued." These numbers and the registration information, together with the centralized computer that will store the data, will help the government to track down criminals, subversives, critics, and complement its other surveillance methods.

AMERICAN SUPPORT 

When President Marcos declared martial law, the US Embassy in Manila and the State Department in Washington had "no comment." Since then US diplomatic officials have avoided a categorical endorsement of martial law in the Philippines. But by its actions, the United States does support President Marcos' regime and apparently it plans to continue to do so. 03 For example, when the Philippine Constabulary and other police forces arrested thousands of civil libertarians, prominent Senators, and other critics of Marcos' government during those first weeks of martial law, the United States Navy's Naval Command helped. It provided information to the Philippine police that led to the arrest of Filipinos and Americans who had been providing legal services to American GIs there. More significantly, US military and economic assistance has continued-even increased. Aid under the Military Assistance Program (MAP), which had been going down since the mid 1960s, is now going up again. 

MAP aid increased from $14 million in FY 1972 to $15.7 million in FY 1973, and to $18.9 million in FY 1974. President Nixon's Administration this year is asking for $17.9 million for FY 1975. On several occasions, US Ambassador to the 

Philippines William H. Sullivan has assured the Philippines that US assistance will continue. To the Marcos government and its supporters, this assistance, which exceeds $100 million per year, constitutes both support and approval of martial law. For instance, a report in a government censored newspaper said when the US Senate voted last year for more assistance that, "In effect, the Senate action in committee constituted an unmistakable approval of the New Society

What is so disturbing is that aid from the United States has been the main source of money, materiel, and technical assistance for the buildup of the military apparatus in the Philippines over the years. Now, US economic and military aid have borne fruit-a dictatorship that relies increasingly on its military, which in turn relies heavily on more aid from the United States. It is hardly the kind of legacy that one would expect the oldest democracy in the world would like to leave.

Last year, Secretary of Defense Enrile thanked “our friends from the United States Agency for International Development" for their assistance for police training when he spoke to a graduating class of the new Police Commission Academy. Just recently US AID gave the police department in Angeles City, Pampanga, 10 new motorcycles with radios (previously the department only had 2) and 15 jeeps with two-way radios." US assistance for "narcotics control," too, seems to be helping the Marcos regime build a police state. The Philippine Constabulary's Anti- 

Narcotics Unit, which receives US aid, is known to arrest suspected critics and "subversives" in Manila. In at least one instance, the arrested person, a young 

Filipina named Liliosa Hilao, died while detained at the Anti-Narcotic's Unit's building at Camp Crame (the PC headquarters in Quezon City). According to 

Liliosa Hilao's relatives, the PC officers who arrested her molested her at her home, then tortured her to death at Camp Crame." For FY 1975 the Nixon Administration has requested $250,000 for "Narcotics Control." 

Turning to US assistance designated specifically for the Philippine military, it seems doubtful that without US aid, the Philippine military could have developed to where it is now or continue to expand in the years ahead. According to the 

US General Accounting Office in 1972, "During fiscal years 1964 through 1971, 55 percent of the US military grant aid was used to cover the Philippine Armed Forces' operating costs, and the percentage has been growing during recent years."

CONCLUSION AND RECOMMENDATION 

Democracy and civil liberties are dead in the Philippines. The Marcos regime is a dictatorship. Resistance and rebellion, as a consequence of worsening conditions and political repression, are growing. And the Philippines is developing into a military state. These things are clear from what has happened since martial law.

It is also clear that the United States, through its military and military-related assistance, has contributed immensely to sustaining the Philippine military before martial law. Today it continues to help the Marcos regime build an even larger military apparatus. If Congress appropriates more of the American taxpayers' money to give military or military-related assistance to the Philippines for FY 1975, that money, too, will further support the dictatorship. 

For this reason, the Friends of the Filipino People (FFP) and I recommend that Congress appropriate no military or military-related assistance for the Philippines. This year is an excellent opportunity for the United States Congress to draw the line. It can say now, before the situation in the Philippines becomes worse, that it will no longer be party to the growth of another anti-democratic regime.

We further recommend that Congress conduct a thorough investigation to find out exactly what American military or para-military personnel have done or are doing in the Philippines. I have presented evidence that American military personnel seem to be helping the Marcos government's counter-insurgency efforts. 

I have also reported what I have been told, but have not been able to verify positively, that American personnel in fact are directly involved in counter-insurgency there. This situation is reminiscent of the 1950s and 1960s when there were many hints and unconfirmed reports that the US government was directly in-

This time, hopefully, Congress and all other Americans will learn the truth of the matter before it is too late-before an American President presents a fait accompli and says Congress must appropriate much larger amounts to support "our boys" or "our commitments" in the Philippines.

APPENDIX 9 STATEMENT OF JAMES E. DORNAN, JR., WILLIAM SCHNEIDER, JR., DONALD J. SENESE AND JAMES R. STREETER 1 

It has by now become a commonplace to observe that the Viet-Nam War has constituted one of the most traumatic experiences in the history of the United States. A limited program of aid to a European colonial power seeking to retain its empire led, over a fifteen-year period, to the introduction of a massive American expeditionary force into Southeast Asia, and to our involvement in an unusually cruel war of indefinite duration and uncertain outcome. The ensuing popular discontent drove a president from office, and inspired a vocal minority of Americans to challenge the very legitimacy of our system of government itself. 

Today, twenty-five years after the United States' involvement began, the struggle endures and so does the American participation in it. To be sure, the operational American role is over, the result both of the Nixon Administration's "Vietnamization" policy and the Paris Accords. But American military and economic aid remains a vital factor in sustenance of the continuing South Vietnamese effort, and several thousand Americans are serving Saigon in a variety of capacities. 

The controversy over American involvement in Southeast Asia likewise continues. Although the "teach-ins," mass peace marches, and annual spring Viet- 

Nam riots on American campuses are now part of our past, contentious debate on the issue within the Congress is spurred and buttressed by strongly-held opinions vocalized by many segments of American society. A large number of our citizens are skeptical about the efficacy and utility of the American foreign aid program in general, particularly during a period when claims on the federal treasury are many and extensive. Others doubt the viability of the government of South Viet-Nam and question on this basis the wisdom of ongoing U.S. assistance. Still others express concern about the moral quality of the Saigon government and the degree of popular support it enjoys within South Viet-Nam, and thus wonder whether the U.S. can, consistent with its own principles and values, continue to support that government's existence. And finally, there are those who believe that South Viet-Nam is governed by a vicious and corrupt dictatorship, which ruthlessly suppresses all opposition and indiscriminately imprisons its political opponents; and which therefore long ago forfeited all claim to American assistance.

In the final analysis, it is the Congress which will pass judgment on the accuracy and relevance of these critiques and determine America's future role in South Viet-Nam, since it is the Congress which must authorize and appropriate funds for the military and economic aid programs. 

Obviously, the extent and quality of the information available to the Members of the House and Senate will be a crucial determinant in the process of reaching a decision. We are therefore pleased to be able to present to you some of our views on the present military, economic and political situation in South Viet-Nam, based upon a tour there in January of this year. 

During our eight days in Viet-Nam we were briefed by high government executives and cabinet ministers, as well as by American diplomats and intelligence officials. We toured three of the four military regions, visiting both province chiefs and field commanders for briefings and informal discussions. Our activities included interviews with politicians outside the government, the questioning of Viet Cong agents imprisoned at Can Son, and conversations with common citizens in a great variety of settings. No attempts were made to limit our activities or to interfere with our ability to acquire the information we deemed necessary to investigate precisely some of the critiques of the Vietnamese government with which the Congress is most concerned. The following analyses and conclusions are there- 

1 Biographies appear at p. 783. 

(778)

fore our own, based on our personal observations and the information available to us; needless to say, in no sense was it possible within these eight days to conduct an exhaustive examination of the problems presently confronting South Viet-Nam. 

I. THE MILITARY CONTEXT 

One of the major subjects of interest in our trip to Vietnam was the nature of the military situation which existed subsequent to the signing of the Paris Accords in January of 1973 as it affected U.S. policy in the region. As is by now well known, the terms of the Paris Accords permitted North Vietnam to maintain a formal military presence within South Vietnam. The size of this deployment is subject to widely varied estimates. Some South Vietnamese Army Commanders appear to over-estimate the magnitude of the North Vietnamese presence by a factor of two. The actual size of the force is probably in the 100,000-150,000 troops, or approximately 50 percent of the North Vietnamese standing army. In addition, the Paris Accords require a one-to-one replacement of expended military material, but the Accords prohibited modernization. 

Since the signing of the Paris Accord, there has been considerable military activity in all four military regions of South Vietnam. The most costly fighting took place in the months following the signing of the accords, which served to establish the de facto territorial limitations of each side's territory. Most of the large-unit engagements have taken place in the border regions in the II and III Military Regions along the Cambodian border. The purpose of these engagements has been an attempt by the North Vietnam and Viet Cong to solidify and extend their control over these regions, and effort appears to be directed to maintaining control over a continuous strip of territory along the Cambodian Border to support a road which is being constructed to serve as a substitute for the Ho-Chi- Minh Trail (situated considerably west of the present North Vietnamese and Viet Cong positions.) During the rice harvest, daily military engagements took place in the major rice-growing provinces in the Mekong Delta, a consequence of North Vietnamese and Viet Cong attempts to divert the flow of rice from the provinces to the populous urban areas of South Vietnam for their own use. 

These have subsided and the major recent engagements have taken place in Tay Ninh province in the II Military Region and in the Central Highlands (II Military Region).

We detected evidence of substantial efforts by the North Vietnamese to reinforce their military position in South Vietnam by the modernization of their existing forces in the area. This is particularly true with respect to anti-aircraft defense in the I Military Region, where SA-2 sites and supporting tube AA artillery have been constructed in the North-western portions of Quang Tri province around Khe Sanh. Moreover, there appears to have been a substantial replenishment of armor in South Vietnam, especially in the II and III Military Regions following the heavy losses which the North Vietnamese incurred in 1972. It is our impression, however, that the constraints placed on North Vietnam re-supply by the Paris Accords are difficult to police because of the limited reliability of available reconnaissance techniques now that the United States no longer maintains a large military establishment in South Vietnam. 

Whatever the details on re-supply, it appears certain that there has been a substantial expenditure of munitions and materiel on both sides. 

Despite this substantial expenditure, however, the military situation remains in a state of equilibrium. It is this equilibrium which provides most of our optimism about the viability of the Paris Accords. Several members of the group had previously visited South Vietnam (some as recently as 1972) and were astonished by the extent to which demilitarization has taken place in urban areas. 

As recently as 1972, virtually every major intersection in Saigon contained one or more sandbagged pill-boxes and occupied by several heavily-armed troops. 

Now, with the exception of a few key government installations such as the Presidential Palace and the National Police Headquarters, the phenomenon of militarized cities has almost entirely disappeared. 

The key to maintaining this equilibrium is the willingness of the United States to re-supply the South Vietnam army as materiel is expended. No one seriously expected the cease-fire of January 1973 to terminate all military activity. Rather, the accords provide a framework for (hopefully) more limited military conflict so that a political settlement between the North and South Vietnamese govern-

ments might be worked out in the future. While it is not reasonable to hold out much hope for an early political settlement, the maintenance of the military status quo is essential if the energy for settling the conflict is to be directed into political rather than military channels. From the perspective we were able to gain during our visit, it appears crucial for U.S. policy objectives that neither side be permitted to develop the notion that it can gain a change in the terms of the cease-fire through military activity. The nature of the re-supply of the North 

Vietnamese appears to reflect a willingness on the part of their Soviet and Chinese suppliers to make sure that the North Vietnamese are able to support their objectives, which appears to be directed towards maintaining the political and military integrity of their currently-held territory and probing the willingness and ability of the South Vietnamese to resist further incursions. The South 

Vietnamese have been capable of doing so because they have been re-supplied by the United States as they expended their materiel in fire-fights with the North Vietnamese in defending their territory against such probes. 

We are concerned about the prospect of the consequences of serious reduction in military assistance to South Vietnam. Important U.S. policy interests in the status quo in Southeast Asia could be upset by the failure of the United States to provide military assistance to balance the Communists' resupply efforts. 

The nature of the military threat facing the South Vietnamese requires rather substantial expenditures of munitions and materiel. The military engagements are spread throughout the border areas of nearly a 400-mile front. Moreover, the highquality Soviet-made artillery supplied to the North Vietnamese, particularly the 27-kilometer-range 130mm. howitzer, means that the South Vietnamese are certain to become involved in munitions-consuming artillery engagements. In addition, a major mobility capability for the South Vietnamese is requred if they are to be able to respond effectively to massed assaults directed at a few selected points along the entire front. The South Vietnamese thus far appear to be capable of maintaining this fragile military equilibrium. The effectiveness of this means of maintaining peace has proved to be significant in other parts of the world in recent years. The peace elsewhere in Asia, ea., Korea and Taiwan, has been maintained by retaining the military assistance. Similarly in Europe, the peace has been maintained through burdensome investment on the part of most of the nations of Western Europe in their own defense as well as by a substantial independent U.S. investment and military presence. Certainly no military analyst would have the slightest doubt that Israel would have fallen but for American military assistance during the first twenty-five years of her existence. 

The evidence available to date from South Vietnam clearly suggest to us that a continuing investment by the United States (modest) when compared with our post-war investment in Western Europe, Korea, Taiwan, or Israel in military assistance will provide the framework within which a political settlement of the kind we have seen in Germany and the Middle East, and may soon see in Korea, might eventually become feasible. 

II. THE POLITICAL CONTENT 

A reason given by opponents of continued aid to South Viet-Nam is the alleged unpopular and authoritarian nature of the government. During our stay in Viet 

Nam we discussed this issue with government officials, with leaders of the political opposition, with the editor of a daily newspaper, and even with those who claimed to be political prisoners. As in most developing countries, the Republic of 

Viet Nam has a major party-closely tied to the government-and several minor parties. The dominant party is the Democracy Party. Its strength results from a broad degree of support and acceptance among the general populace plus the strong allegiance of the civil servants and military personnel. None of the opposition parties seem likely to challenge successfully its strong position any time soon.

Even in countries with a strong republican tradition the position of the opposition during war or times of stress is uncertain. We have had the experience of Alien and Sedition Acts and major abridgements of civil liberties under Lincoln and FDR. Even England-the mother of parliaments-suspended elections during World War II. Seen in historic perspective, it is remarkable how essentially free Viet Nam is. Loyal opposition is tolerated-even supported. To qualify for public financing, a political party must demonstrate broad based support throughout the country. This requirement encourages Vietnamese parties

which are often regional or based on small religious factions to form coalitions, and thus experience the healthy political act of peaceful compromise. In the legislature, approximately one-third of the members are active opponents of the Thieu government-some quite vigorously so. Elections are held regularly and, except for the exclusion of the communists, are considered essentially free. Provincial and municipal elections will be held this summer-except, of course, in communist-held areas. 

There are fifteen daily newspapers published in Saigon. Three are pro-administration; three are hostile; five are independent; the others, non-political. Although military stories are censored, the papers retain considerable freedom to criticize the government. Ironically, one of the common demands of the North 

Vietnamese delegation in Saigon is that the government prevent the press from attacking them.

An interesting measure of the relationship between the government and the people of Viet Nam is the fact that the government has distributed arms to its five hundred thousand man local civilian militia-force equal in size to its standing army. Sure no government which fears and oppresses its people would allow its citizenry to be armed to this extent. 

Not one of the political leaders we spoke to, whether pro-Thieu or anti-Thieu, believed the communists have any chance of gaining power through honest elections. 

We concluded that South Viet Nam can continue to develop into a stable, democratic society if given a reasonable level of support sufficient for her to meet the military and economic challenges of the next few years. 

III. THE ECONOMIC CONTEXT 

The United States has historically, extended aid and assistance to nations which have suffered great natural disasters, need assistance for economic development, and require defense against aggression. This aid, extended for a combination of humanitarian and strategic reasons, has strengthened other nations in the world community. South Vietnam is one of those nations which desperately need and in our view deserves continued United States economic and military aid.

Our post-World War II experience comes readily to mind. We aided two powers defeated and devastated during the war-Germany and Japan. Both of these nations soon recovered and have become important and strong economic partners of the United States. Military aid from the United States prevented both Turkey and Greece from falling under Communist control in the late 1940's. The United States also aided two nations in Asia-South Korea and the Republic of China (Taiwan)-to become strong militarily and economically. Both of these nations bear a strong resemblance to the situation we face in South Vietnam at present.

Korea and Taiwan suffered from occupation by a foreign power during World War II. After the war, South Korea experienced a major Communist attack in 1950 and Taiwan had to absorb refugees from the Mainland when the Communists seized control in 1949. Both of these powers had to face the possibility of imminent attack from powerful Communist neighbors. There appeared to be little hope that these nations would survive for long as independent states. In response the United States extended both military and economic aid, and now, almost twenty-five years later, we find two strong and dependable allies of the U.S. in Asia. South Korea was able to assist the U.S. in Vietnam by both military and economic aid. Taiwan reached a position where it no longer needed 

U.S. aid in the 1960's and is presently the second largest market in Asia, after 

Japan. With continued U.S. assistance, perseverance, and confidence, South Vietnam could easily repeat the success stories of Korea and Taiwan in Asia. 

South Vietnam is a major rice producing area and has many natural resources. 

The people are hard working. Explorations have been made in regard to establishing industries in South Vietnam. Experienced observers on the Asian scene believe that, if South Vietnam can survive immediate problems stemming from the effects of thirty years of war upon the economy and the threat of an aggressive enemy on and within its borders, South Vietnam will reach an economic "taking off" point similar to South Korea and Taiwan. Despite the fact that the 

United States has expended nearly 50,000 lives and a total of $133 billion dollars in an effort to maintain South Vietnam as a non-Communist country, continued

economic and military aid is desperately needed to help the Vietnamese government bridge the gap between the military and economic consequences of the American withdrawal and the economic "taking off" point on the way to an independent and viable economy.

The short-run agricultural potential of Vietnam has been reduced by continuing Communist military pressure, but the government of South Vietnam has been successful in securing more and more villages and towns in rural areas. The land reform program has been a success in distributing land to almost one million farmers throughout Vietnam. The "miracle rice", introduced by the U.S., has made it possible to raise three rice crops a year in some areas where beforehand only one rice crop was grown. Security and aid will be needed for the Vietnamese people to realize the full potential of their land. 

The security problem has also made foreign investors hesitant to risk investment in this area. U.S. assistance and a recently-secured loan from France have aided the South Vietnamese economy. Vietnamese laborers are hard-working, skillful, and offer favorable low cost to investors. A growing agricultural sector if enhanced by foreign investment will greatly aid the stability of the country. 

The present government, which has secured the support of the majority in the South, has shown that it is stable and can conduct the affairs of the nation. 

Serious problems still remain. U.S. withdrawal reduced the amount of money the Vietnamese have been receiving to import rice, fertilizer, sugar, cement, steel. and petroleum products and these have risen rapidly in price. Between mid-1972 and 1973, these commodities experienced an 80% increase in cost; this is especially damaging since these six commodities make up 34% of Vietnam's imports. 

This price increase has helped to spur the tremendous inflation affecting this Asian nation. Prices increased last year an average of 64% and it has been estimated that two-thirds of this increase can be traced to the results of higher import prices. It is essential for Vietnam to halt this rate of inflation, spur the agricultural section to full production, and attract foreign investment to promote a strong industrial base. 

We have visited South Vietnam and have been profoundly impressed by the people of this struggling nation. When the United States has spent so much already in South Vietnam, the easy answer appears to be merely to terminate aid. 

Yet, it would be unfortunate that after spending billions of dollars on this nation we should decide to turn our back on this brave country and refuse to spend an additional billion or more for the next few years when victory is so close. 

Secretary of State Henry Kissinger has noted that North Vietnam still desires to seize control of the South and has strongly urged Congress to continue to provide aid and assistance to South Vietnam. Secretary of Defense James R. Schlesinger has stated that the U.S. is committed to send the tools of protection to 

South Vietnam because we promised that we would. The U.S. Ambassador to 

South Vietnam, Graham Martin, has also raised his voice in support of the aid request, stating that he firmly believes that South Vietnam can survive and achieve an economic taking-off point only if we continue to provide aid in the next few crucial years. We who have been to South Vietnam concur in this assessment. The investment of aid-economic and military-for the next few years could secure the future of a non-Communist South Vietnam, a situation which could stabilize the situation in Asia in future years. If we cut off aid to 

South Vietnam, we may be snatching defeat from the jaws of victory. If we substantially cut that aid, we may encourage its enemies and discourage our friends in South Vietnam. We urge that this committee and the entire Congress vote to provide the necessary aid to secure a non-Communist South Vietnam so that this nation will be able to stand on its own and become a self-suppporting fully viable and independent member of the international political community. 

CONCLUSION 

In summary, then, we found no utopia in South Viet-Nam. We found instead an able and energetic people attempting to cope with the social and political consequences of more than thirty years of war, with the continuing presence of a large foreign army within their country, and with awesome economic problems not of their own making. There is no denying the magnitude of these problems. Nevertheless, we must describe our position as one of guarded optimism-aware though we are of the number of "guardedly optimistic" reports to which the Members of this Committee have been subjected over the past twenty-five years on the subject of Viet-Nam.

When its record is evaluated in the light of the continuing crisis which it has confronted, the government of South Viet-nam cannot be said to have performed badly in most areas. A wide variety of government programs appear to be administered with reasonable efficiency. There are few signs of overt discontent with 

President Thieu, and even his political opponents concede that he has grown in his job. Much of the unfavorable commentary on his stewardship over the affairs of South Viet-Nam appears to be based on standards inappropriate for judging governments in the war-torn segments of the developing world; moreover, few of the positive achievements of the government have received the attention which they deserve. If the military equilibrium can be maintained and the current economic difficulties controlled, the prospects for political stability in the short run and for considerable economic progress over the longer term appear hopeful. 

In evaluating the future relationship between the United States and South Viet-Nam, moreover, it is impossible to ignore our role in the past. Expectations have been created and commitments made, both within Viet-Nam and in the larger universe of international politics, which ought not to be cavalierly left unfulfilled or abandoned. The Secretary of State has recently emphasized this and related points in a letter to Senator Kennedy:

We also recognize that we have derived a certain obligation from our long and deep involvement in Viet Nam. Perceiving our own interest in a stable 

Viet Nam free to make its own political choices, we have encouraged the Vietnamese people in their struggle for independence. We have invested great human and material resources to support them in protecting their own as well as broader interests. We have thus committed ourselves very substantially, both politically and morally. While the South Vietnamese Government and people are demonstrating increasing self-reliance, we believe it is important that we continue our support as long as it is needed. 

It is our conviction that, given a reasonable level of American assistance over the next several years, the Republic of South Viet-Nam can survive and prosper. 

If it becomes clear, in time, that the government is capable of holding its own militarily and is in no danger of collapse from internal causes, the prospects for an ultimate political solution between North and South should advance concomitantly.

For a quarter century the United States has been deeply involved in the affairs of the Vietnamese. That involvement has been inspired by many assumptions and objectives, some valid, some questionable. But whatever the merits of our original involvement, one of the most important of our original objectives—the emergence of a viable non-communist government in the South-now appears close to achievement. We urge the Congress to continue to fund the Viet-Nam aid program at a level sufficient to ensure that end.

THE EDITOR. 

PROLOGUE 

As U.S. Ambassador to Vietnam from 1957 to 1961 and as a member of an independent fact finding mission to Vietnam early this year, I read this report with a somewhat critical eye. 

I am, therefore, pleased to express my almost complete agreement with the facts, findings, and conclusions.

Unfortunately, as the report emphasizes, there would seem to be a deliberate, well-orchestrated effort either to play down developments in Vietnam, or studiously to distort and undermine all the many positive achievements in that still war-ridden country. The few shortcomings and partial failures have been greatly exaggerated by much of our media. Few, if any, of the many positive achievements have been afforded recognition. 

The fact that fighting is still going on has been attributed to the alleged "aggressive activities" of the Government of President Thieu. Actually, even a casual observer could easily learn that it is Hanoi and its Viet Cong clients in the South who are steadily building up their forces and carrying out raids and attacks on Government-held areas. The Government's counter-attacks against these hostile communist moves are usually depicted in the media as "aggressive action" by South Vietnam in contravention of the Paris Ceasefire Agreements. 

That the contrary is the case should be clear from the following excerpt from a 43-page report by the Canadian Delegation on the International Commission for Control and Supervision (ICCS) just before the Canadians withdrew their representatives in July 1973, in frustration and disillusionment. "From the testimony of the captured North Vietnamese Army soldiers, it can be concluded that there never was the slightest indication during the four and (785)

one-half months following the ceasefire that the Democratic Republic of Vietnam has modified its infiltration policy. This policy of unrelenting infiltration down the Ho Chi Minh Trail System is graphically illustrated by the piling up of 7, 12 or even 20 infiltration units of approximately 500 men each in Cambodian rest stations when the infiltration pipeline was blocked for 15 days during the month of April."

That this is still going on is shown from recent aerial photos of bumper-tobumper lines of trucks moving south.

I agree particularly with the statements in the report on the need for continued infusion of foreign economic and military assistance to assure that in the shortest possible time South Vietnam can "go it alone" economically and militarily. United States Ambassador to Vietnam, Graham A. Martin, emphasized the need for stepped-up economic and military aid for a few years, at a press conference in Saigon on March 14, 1974.

If President Thieu is the ruthless hated dictator his small but vociferous American critics claim, he must be a very naive dictator. Otherwise, he would not have distributed over 500,000 World War II type weapons to the part-time soldier-peasants who are in the Peoples Self-Defense Forces as defenders of their villages. Nor would he have distributed over 500,000 M-16 rifles and 

M-79 grenade launchers to the Regional and Popular Forces (a sort of provincial Home Guard). Arming over a million of the local population is not what dictators do!

I repeat my almost complete agreement with the facts, findings and conclusions of this well reasoned and detailed report. 

ELBRIDGE DURBROW, 

American Ambassador (Ret.).

INTRODUCTION 

Gentlemen may cry, "peace, peace," but there is no peace; the war has only begun. (Patrick Henry, Address Before the Virginia Convention, 1775.)

Such is the situation in South Viet Nam one year after the promulgation of the Nixon-Kissinger "peace with honor" in January 1973. To be sure, the massive and direct United States involvement has ended, and Vietnamese affairs, when covered at all by our nation's leading newspapers, are now relegated to the inside pages; it is in the largest sense true, as an unnamed State Department official recently asserted, that this is now "their war."¹ 

The struggle nonetheless endures, despite the disinterest of the American public, and on a fairly impressive scale. According to most accounts over fifty thousand people have died in South Viet Nam since the signing of the truce.² and military contacts between the two sides have averaged at least three thousand per month. American intelligence figures indicate that cease-fire violations by the North Vietnamese Army and the Viet Cong (NVA-VC) in the past twelve months have totaled more than thirty thousand. 

Moreover, although all American combat forces have been withdrawn from South Viet Nam as a consequence both of the "Vietnamization" policy and the Paris Accord, the United States retains a highly significant-and controversialrole in the conflict. More than 4,000 Americans continue to serve the South Vietnamese government in a variety of capacities, and U.S. military and economic aid during FY 1974 will reach at least $1.2 billion, with even larger totals to be requested for 1975. In his State of the Union message on the 30th of January, the 

President reiterated his conviction that both past American sacrifices and the global position of the United States preclude any attempt on our part to "wash our hands of the affair," and he insisted that we must not abandon our "responsibility" for the future of Southeast Asia.³

Under these circumstances of continued military conflict and continued American involvement in Indochina, then, it is imperative that the United States Congress and the American public obtain the most accurate information available from as many sources as possible concerning the prospects for South Viet Nam. 

Policy-making cannot proceed in a vacuum-or on the basis of the quality of reporting about Viet Nam commonly found even in our major newspapers. Moreover, if the history of the past half-decade tells us anything at all about the present state of the American policy, it is that politics in the United States no longer stops at the water's edge. If few Americans should believe in the likelihood of South Viet Nam's survival, the current popular scepticism toward all international entanglements, coupled with continuing hostility toward the South's cause among influential segments of the Congress, will result in a speedy termination of the remaining American effort. Indeed, even strong popular sentiment for the continuation of aid to the Vietnamese will not in itself be sufficient if backing for U.S. policy toward Viet Nam continues to erode within Congress. 

This report, therefore, originated in the need for accurate information about the situation in South Viet Nam, particularly to assess the existing military and economic situation.

Subject to the limits imposed by time-we spent eight days in Viet Nam, from January 6th to January 13th-and the varying degrees and areas of expertise possessed by the writers of this report, we sought at least partial answers to the following questions: (1) What are the prospects for a general offensive in 1974 or thereafter? (2) Can the ARVN hold its own in the face of the continuing NVA military buildup? (3) In which areas is the military situation most serious, given current troop dispositions and capabilities on both sides? 

1 New York Times, January 17, 1974. 

2 Republic of South Viet Nam figures list 11,194 killed, 50,294 wounded, and 3,462 missing from the South Vietnamese armed forces, with an estimated 1,907 civilian casualties; the ARVN estimates 39,853 enemy dead for the same period. Viet Nam Press dispatch.
