(4) Are there opportunities for the ARVN to recover territory now held by the NVA-VC? (5) What are the prospects that South Viet Nam can achieve economic selfsufficiency within this decade? (6) Can the current inflation and balance-of-payments crises be controlled? (7) How long will South Viet Nam require substantial foreign aid? (8) Is there any likelihood that other industrialized nations will assume part of the aid burden? (9) Has the Thieu government acquired sufficient "legitimacy" to constitute a viable alternative to the communist forces? (10) Is South Viet Nam governed by a "vicious and corrupt dictatorship," which ruthlessly suppresses all opposition and indiscriminately imprisons its political opponents?

During our eight days in Viet Nam, we were briefed by high government executives and cabinet ministers as well as by American diplomats and intelligence officials. We toured three of the four military regions, visiting both province chiefs and field commanders for briefings and informal discussions. We interviewed political figures outside the government while in Saigon, spoke with common citizens in a variety of settings, and interrogated VC agents in Con Son prison. No attempts were made to limit our activities or to interfere with our ability to acquire the information we deemed necessary. The following analyses and conclusions are therefore our own, based on our personal observations and the information available to us; needless to say, in no sense was it possible for us to conduct an exhaustive examination of the problems presently confronting 

South Viet Nam.

I. THE MILITARY SITUATION 

As previously indicated, the 1973 truce is a cease-fire in name only. Whether 

Messrs. Nixon and Kissinger truly expected the Paris agreements to bring the 

Indochina Wars finally to an end and to produce a political settlement among the various contending forces cannot at this point be known. Several high South 

Vietnamese government officials have been told by their American counterpartsin one case, apparently by Mr. Kissinger himself-that the ultimate solution to the Viet Nam problem lies with detente and the global "structure of peace" being pursued by the Administration. According to this argument, Soviet and Chinese eagerness for an accommodation with the United States far 'transcends their interest in suppporting North Viet Nam's military effort in the South; as detente proceeds, the communist superpowers will be persuaded to reduce their extensive aid to the Hanoi regime, and the continuation of a major effort by the North to topple the Saigon government will be rendered impossible. We found no one in an official position in South Viet Nam who is persuaded by this reasoning. As 

President Thieu has put it several times, "we knew from the beginning that the cease-fire would end the formal war but bring no peace." 

The communist attitude toward the Paris Accord has of course been apparent from the beginning; one cadre from a coastal province expressed it well to the 

American reporter James Markham: “Either Thieu implements 'the Paris agreements and loses, or he refuses to implement them and he loses." For Hanoi and her VC allies, the purpose of the truce was to eliminate American air power from the war, speed up the withdrawal of U.S. ground forces, and restrict if possible the flow of American military aid to the Saigon government. If political arrangements which would ensure the triumph of the People's Revolutionary Government could be forced on Saigon, so much the better; if not, the war could be resumed whenever and at whatever level seemed most likely to topple the Thieu government and bring a Hanoi-dominated communist regime to power. 

In line with that overall strategy, Hanoi has been steadily increasing her troop strength in the South since the cease-fire. In a briefing conducted for the Washington press corps last December, a Defense Department spokesman estimated total NVA strength in the South at 240,000, with 200,000 organized in units of the Army of North Viet Nam and the rest serving with VC forces. At least 50,000 and possibly as many as 70,000 troops have been sent to the South during the past thirteen months.5 U.S. intelligence figures provided us in Saigon were quite similar; only some American diplomatic personnel place the totals somewhat 

4 Markham, "Where Viet Cong's Roots Go Deep," New York Times, February 18, 1974. 

5 See Baltimore Sun, December 16, 1973, for a report on this briefing.

lower. All sources, incidentally, scoffed at Secretary Kissinger's claim, enunciated after the signing of the cease-fire, that NVA forces in South Viet Nam numbered no more than 145,000 at that time.

Total NVA-VC strength is now in the neighborhood of 270-300,000, a record for the war and a force substantial enough-even without further reinforcement, according to American military observers-to conduct extensive operations for over two years. This large fighting force, moreover, has been substantially reequipped since the 1972 offensive, a consequence of the continued flow of Soviet aid to Hanoi. At least 150 130mm. artillery pieces have been brought south, and as many as 400 tanks and amphibious vehicles. Aerial photography has discovered a major truck park just south of the Cam Lo River in the I Corps region which at times has accommodated nearly 400 military vehicles of various types. East of the 

Laotian and Cambodian borders, extending south from the former Demilitarized Zone to Darlac Province, runs a virtually-completed road network of impressive quality, and older supply networks in Laos and Cambodia have been refurbished." 

An oil pipeline to the South has been constructed alongside the road network, with a spur thrusting into the Ashau Valley. Henceforth it will be far easier than in the past for Hanoi to supply its southern armies. 

Finally, as many as 14 former South Vietnamese airfields now in communist hands are being repaired; that at Khe Sanh-which American intelligence analysts say is now protected by Soviet SA-2 Guideline missiles-is already capable of accepting MIG aircraft. (Some communist units in the South are equipped with the new SA-7 Grail anti-aircraft missile, and there are reports that a small number of SA-6 Gainful mobile missiles have been deployed as well.) Other major fields are located at Dong Ha, which like Khe Sanh is in Quang Tri Province within the I Corps area; near Dak To in Kontum Province in the Central 

Highlands; and in the key areas northwest of Saigon, near the Parrot's Beak and Fishhook salients extending from Cambodia.

No one in South Viet Nam views these developments with equanimity, although Hanoi's immediate strategy remains a subject to debate. Few observers with whom we spoke either Vietnamese or American-believe that a full-scale offensive of the 1972 variety is likely this year (although the South Vietnamese high command is unwilling to rule out the possibility). COSVN Directive No. 4, obtained late in 1973 by U.S. intelligence, orders the VC only to attempt to expand their sphere of territorial control through local operations and to await further instructions; such orders normally remain in effect for a six-month period. At the meeting of the North Vietnamese National Assembly in Hanoi in mid-February virtually all of the principal speakers emphasized the need to concentrate on economic development and "social renewal" in the North during 1974. In fact, the keynote address by Vice Premier Le Thanh Nghi listed the military effort in 

South Viet Nam and Cambodia last on a long list of policy priorities for North 

Viet Nam this year."

U.S. intelligence sources report no step-up in conscription in the North, and although at least 11,000 NVA troops have been sent south since September, over 40,000 had already arrived during a comparable period prior to the 1972 offensive. 

One analyst estimates that at least 60,000 additional NVA would be necessary to mount an assault on a 1968 or 1972 scale, given the improvement in the South's military capability which has occurred since the cease-fire. Hanoi's intentions were possibly further revealed in late January, when the 367th NVA Sapper Group, consisting of at least 1,000 troops trained in rocket and mortar tactics, was pulled out of Tay Ninh Province northwest of Saigon to aid in the siege of Phnom Penh. Finally, there is little reason to believe that either the Chinese or the Soviets are anxious for a major Hanoi military effort at present." 

Nevertheless, it is clear that the North has no intention of abiding by any of the terms of the 1973 truce except when it appears to its advantage to do so. 

If a major offensive does not occur in 1974, the reason will have to do with Hanoi's assessment of the probabilities for major gains, and not with any altera- For U.S. Air Force reconnaissance photos showing various aspects of the North Vietnamese military build-up in the South, with particular attention to airfield reconstruction, see Aviation Week and Space Technology for September 17, 1973, pp. 12-17; October 8, 1973. pp. 20-21; and February 25, 1974, pp. 14-17. 

See the report on the Assembly contained in the Washington Post, February 18, 1974. 

8 Washington Post, February 2, 1974.

Chinese statements dealing with the situation in South Viet Nam have been quite restrained for at least four months, even during PRG President Nguyen Huu Tho's visit to 

Peking in November. See New York Times, November 11, 1973.

tion in objectives. As one analyst told us, Hanoi fundamentally is seeking a strategy which will work; and the activities of the NVA since the cease-fire reflect that search. Between January and April of 1973 the communist forces concentrated on “land-grab” operations, attempting to seize control of territory and population in areas of ARVN military weakness. The onset of the rainy season brought about a period of consolidation characterized by minor local engagements, while in recent months NVA efforts have been reduced to attempts to capture and stockpile rice, due to difficulties encountered in feeding their large army. 

Obviously, however, the NVA is capable of causing major mischief at any time, and certain areas in the South bear particular watching. One is Quang 

Duc, a thinly-populated province 90 miles north of Saigon on the Cambodian border, where the NVA 375-mile network through the Central Highlands now terminates. The North Vietnamese 9th Division has been operating here since early 

November, facing a thin line of ARVN troops and Rangers. The NVA overran a series of posts along the border and the dusty district capital of Kien Duc in November, and at one point surrounded the provincial capital of Gia Nghia. 

ARVN and U.S. military analysts believe that the communist objective is to gain control of enough of Quang Duc to complete their road network through to Phuoc Long Province. Here they might attempt to seize control of Route 14, which runs through Phuoc Long to Binh Long Province and joins Route 13; Route 13, in turn, leads eventually to the major NVA-VC administrative center at Loc Ninh, 10 miles north of An Loc (still held by South Vietnamese Rangers) and 50 miles due north of Saigon. The NVA would then hold an uninterrupted supply network from Quang Tri in the north to Tay Ninh Province at the very core of the 3rd Military Region, vastly simplifying their logistics problem. Achievement of this objective, however, would require major acquisitions of territory in these provinces (Quang Duc, Phuoc Long, and Binh Long), and it is doubtful that the NVA presently possesses the capability to seize and hold an area of this size. 

In addition to the 9th Division, only the 5th NVA Division (now in Tay Ninh, moved last year from the Delta) and the 7th NVA Division in Bing Long are presently supporting the VC units in this region. 

An operation of this kind, it should be noted, would fit in well with a "Third Viet Nam" strategy, often discussed as a possible interim policy for Hanoi. Capture of a major portion of Quang Duc Province, plus additional advances in Phuoc Long and Binh Long, would give the communist forces control of a broad belt of South Viet Nam stretching from the Parrot's Beak region to the former DMZ. 

This area could then be administratively consolidated with the extensive contiguous territories in eastern Cambodia and Laos now controlled by the NVA, and the existence of a new state formally proclaimed.10 Diplomatic recognition might subsequently be more readily obtained than under present circumstances, and a functioning political alternative to the Saigon government with full international status would be established. It is perhaps with this end in view that 

Hanoi has recently resettled 40,000 civilians in areas near I Corps and farther south along the Cambodian border.

As part of such a strategy it is possible that Hanoi might direct the seizure of a provincial capital, perhaps Tay Ninh, Gia Nghia or Kontum, as a potential capital of the new political unit. The seizure of Tay Ninh would afford the additional advantage of proximity to Saigon, thus increasing the threat to the capital region. Saigon residents have already been rendered somewhat nervous recently by the rocket attack on Bien Hoa airfield in November and by the spectacular fire at the Nha Be oil depot. Some observers with whom we spoke, however, doubt that the communists would proclaim a relatively minor city as the formal capital of their area, since this would be taken as an admission that they cannot capture Hue or Saigon. In any event, the North Vietnamese continue to infiltrate troops eastward to Phuoc Tuy Province on the coast, only twenty miles east of Saigon ; while the city itself seems amply protected in this area by the ARVN 25th Division, the possibility of a spectacular raid designed to demoralize the capital-in the manner of the continuing rocket attacks on Phnom Penh-cannot be ruled out. 

10 Ho Chi Minh long ago proclaimed that his "revolution on the Mekong" was to include Laos and Cambodia as well as a large portion of Thailand. Interestingly, unconfirmed reports have recently reached American intelligence indicating efforts by NVA units to clear Khmer Rouge forces out of large sections of Cambodia east of the Mekong.

The Delta continues to be an area of concern, although in the main the security situation there has improved somewhat since the cease-fire. Parts of the region, such as the Hoa Hao Province of An Giang, where we spent the better part of a day during our tour, are among the most war-free in South Viet Nam. Other provinces continue to be troublesome, either because of a long history of VC activity or the presence of significant NVA troop concentrations at the time of the truce. Principal among these are An Xuyen, Kien Tuong, Chuong Thien and Dinh 

Tuong. Three NVA divisions have been moved out of the Delta since the ceasefire, however, and the 7th ARVIN Division of Gen. Nguyen Khoa Nam, with responsibility for the security of all or parts of six provinces, now faces only 18,500 regular NVA troops, organized in six regiments. Three of these are stationed in Dinh Tuong, but the NVA-VC have only a small political apparatus in the province; in fact, of the seven million people in the Delta only 17,500 live in 

NVA-VC areas. While NVA attacks on small ARVIN outposts and efforts to capture rice and other foodstuffs will continue, the Delta does not appear at present to be in serious difficulty.

The same cannot be said for parts of the coast, in both the I Corps and II Corps areas. As previously noted, a large part of Quang Tri Province has been controlled by the NVA since the offensive of 1972, although Quang Tri City itself was even tually recaptured by the South Vietnamese Marines. At least 5 NVA divisions remain quartered just above or below the old DMZ. They face some of the best troops and field commanders in South Viet Nam's armed forces, however, and a frontal assault on ARVIN positions here would almost certainly fail. More worrisome is the possibility of an assault toward Hue from the Ashau Valley area, or a drive from the highlands to the coast in an effort to cut the nation in two. Parts of Binh Dinh and Quang Ngai provinces, along Route 1's famed "street without joy" on the coast, have long been centers of revolutionary political activity and thus of VC strength, and might afford NVA main force units a viable base of operations during and after a major attack. 

In any event, the greater part of the NVA Army in the South is now confined to a somewhat ambiguously demarcated area along the Cambodian border, the outermost extension of which can be viewed almost as a "front" in the traditional sense. Recovery of this "Third Viet Nam" area is clearly beyond the military capability of the ARVIN for the present, but this in itself should have little effect upon the survivability of the nation. Both American and RVN sources agree that an overwhelming proportion of the population of the South lives in Saigon-controlled areas: although the NVA-VC may occupy as much as 25% of the landarea, most of this is located in the unpopulated Highlands. Thus, possibly as few as 200,000 people out of a total population of 19.2 million are controlled by the communists; hamlets and villages in enemy hands are probably no more than 

400. Even the VC propaganda machine itself claims no more than 12% of the people in the South live in areas under their control. 

Moreover, American intelligence sources state that the strength of the Viet Cong infrastructure in the countryside is at its lowest level in eight years; this assertion seems to be substantiated by the marked decline in terrorism during the course of 1973, from 1,700 incidents in January to 900 in October (followed by a rise during the dry season rice-acquisition campaign this winter). It may therefore be correct, as one analyst insists, that "over the long run, the NVA is hurting." With a declining proportion of the Southern population to exploit for refuge, food and recruits for the VC units, and with a reduced political apparatus to bestow legitimacy upon their enterprise, Hanoi's troops more and more assume the aspect of an allen, occupying army, holding foreign territory purely by force of arms. In this sense, the cease-fire may well prove to have mitigated signifi cantly the RVN security problem.

As we have indicated, however, by no means can it be said that the military problem has even approached solution. The ARVN is now spread quite thinly along the "front" and the initiative continues to rest largely with the NVA. 

Should another major offensive occur, for example, it might well assume the form of a feint in the I Corps region, followed-and/or preceded-by the swift redevelopment of several NVA divisions south along the new road network for an assault toward Saigon. A successful defense by the ARVN would require a strong effort by its 3rd Corps, and possibly a rapid counterdeployment of crack forces from the Quang Tri area. Given the reluctance of the Saigon government to risk the capture of Hue, such a strategy by the NVA would provide the RVN

decision-makers-not to mention the South's transportation system-with their sternest test.

Moreover, "leopard spots" of NVA, VC and contested areas remain throughout South Viet Nam. Assuming either the lack or the failure of the major MVA offensive, the fate of these areas may have far more impact upon the future of RVN than that of the territory behind the "front." Hanoi obviously plans to use the "spots" as secure base zones for the expansion of its political apparatus; 

Saigon, conversely, hopes that the zones can be increasingly isolated from the NVA Highland forces and gradually eliminated. It may well be that continued truce violations by the NVA-VC, therefore, will provide the ARVN with a golden opportunity. Although thus far reluctant to directly challenge the trucerisking thereby a fanning of anti-Viet Nam sentiment abroad, especially in the United States-by taking the offensive on its own initiative, the ARVN has in recent months increasingly used enemy attacks as a pretext for carrying the war to NVA-VC zones.

All observers agree that the "other side" has been taken aback by this development, and the results of the ARVN initiatives have often been impressive. 

Most of the Delta areas which were rated as "contested" in the period immediately following the cease-fire, are now in ARVN hands, including all of the 140 hamlets seized by the NVA during the January-February "land-grab" operations. All 27 "land-grab" hamlet losses in Quang Tri Province have been recovered, and even VC raids now draw a response: the day after the rocket attack on Bien Hoa air base in November, e.g., South Vietnamese F-5s attacked the communist administrative center at Loc Ninh, causing substantial damage. Without doubt the departure of the Americans has had a highlybeneficial effect upon the pride and sense of purpose of the ARVN, and this, with the resulting increase in its effectiveness, is clearly among the most hopeful developments thus far.

To summarize, then, the military situation is obviously improved over that of 18 months ago. While the huge NVA army presents a constant threat of the most serious proportions, for a variety of reasons a major offensive does not seem probable now; should one occur under present conditions it is unlikely that it would result in the permanent capture by the communists of major cities or much new territory, whatever temporary advances might be achieved-and widely publicized-in the opening phases. The effectiveness and morale of the 

ARVN are improving, and the armed forces of the South appear to have the capability to isolate and reduce the significance of many of the "leopard spot" zones during the months to come. All of this, of course, depends on a continued flow of military aid from the United States, about which we shall have more to say.

II. THE ECONOMIC SITUATION 

We have concentrated in some detail upon the military prospects because they are for several reasons pivotal. The military problem obviously is directly and intimately related to economic and political development. In addition, military concerns have tended to be most prominent in U.S. press coverage and in the minds of Congress and the American people, having dominated the ongoing debate over the U.S. aid program to the South for more than a decade. 

The major crisis facing South Viet Nam in 1974, however, may well concern the economy. Rampant inflation, combined with a continuing balance of payments problem and an alarming decline in foreign reserves, clearly threatens the stability of the nation's economic structure to an extent unparalleled in the last decade. The official inflation rate for 1973 was 45%; the actual figure probably exceeded 60%, and few realistic observers expect much improvement in 1974. 

Important contributing factors to the 1973 increase were the sharp increases in import prices, the world rice shortage, lower actual and prospective real imports, and higher RVN taxes on less essential imports. The most striking domestic price increases were registered by gasoline (213 percent), kerosene (196 percent), cooking oil (195 percent), laundry soap (198 percent), and brown sugar (195 percent). Excluding these five commodities plus rice and condensed milk, the index rose 43 percent. The Imported Commodity Price Index rose approximately 93 percent in 1973.

As indicated above, a major factor in the Vietnamese inflation appears to be the price of rice, itself affected by such variables as the weather, the accessibility and effective utilization of "miracle rice" strains, the success of NVA-VC "rice 36-333 0 - 74 - 51

raids," and the cost and availability of fertilizer. It is in connection with the latter problem that the energy shortage is having its greatest impact on the poorer nations. Since the rice yields per acre drastically increase with the new strains of miracle rice, agricultural experts have been encouraging their use, and plantings of the new varieties are increasing in South Viet Nam at the rate of 10% per year. South Viet Nam's paddy production 1973/74 is estimated at 5.9 million metric tons or about 37 percent above the estimated 4.3 million metric tons for North 

Viet Nam. Estimated yields per hectare are also higher in South Viet Nam, 2.2 metric tons or 16 percent above North Viet Nam's 1.9 metric tons. The difference in average per capita production between the two countries is believed to be greater than for total production since North Viet Nam's population is estimated to be five percent greater than that of South Viet Nam. Before hostilities began, North Viet Nam was a rice deficit area and made up its deficit by imports from the Delta region of South Viet Nam. South Viet Nam was then a net rice exporter. Both countries now are net rice importers. 11 The new varieties of rice require substantially greater amounts of suddenly scarce and expensive fertilizer. The price of urea (the most commonly used form of nitrogen fertilizer world-wide) has increased from $70 to $250 per ton in the past 25 months, a consequence of both rapidly-escalating demand and shortages in the supply of natural gas." These factors are clearly beyond the control of 

South Viet Nam. Thus, despite the production increases of recent years, Saigon was forced to import nearly 200,000 tons of rice last year, most of it from the United States. When one adds to the fertilizer shortage the effects of the heavy storms in November and December which caused severe damage to rice fields in the coastal provinces, the NVA-VC rice raids of this past fall and winter, and the need to feed a constantly growing refugee population, there seems to be little hope for a substantial reduction in that total for 1974. This, in turn, will increase the pressure on foreign reserves; these were down to $191 million in January, a net loss of $54 million during the past twelve months. 

A viable economy for South Viet Nam clearly depends not only on the cultivation of sufficient rice to feed the nation's 19 million people at reasonable cost, but also upon the production of a surplus for export. While this ambition will not be achieved for several years, the agricultural potential of the nation is virtually without limit. Ba Xuyen and An Giang provinces each produced more than 85,000 tons of rice in excess of local needs in 1972 (the last year for which final figures are available); this record, if duplicated in only several more Delta provinces, would bring South Viet Nam only over the brink of self-sufficiency in rice. With an eye to that eventuality, the government has begun to push again, results have been promising, although budget restrictions and the continuing warfare have thus far limited the resources available for these purposes. 

The economic plan for 1974 calls for a sufficient level of investment to produce 6.5 million tons of rice, as well as investment in other agricultural areas (and also in cottage and handicraft industries, again with an eye toward economic 11 For an excellent brief survey of the world-wide fertilizer shortage, see David Brand, "Fertilizer Industry Warns of a Shortage," Wall Street Journal, February 19, 1974.

diversification and the export trade) at twice the level of 1973. With 45% of the national budget devoted to defense out of a total of RVN$630.6 billion (the official exchange rate is RVN$550 to the dollar), and an anticipated deficit of RVN$176.7 billion even in the face of a budgeted foreign aid total of RVN$186 billion, it is unlikely that these goals can be achieved. 

Indeed, actual foreign aid receipts will surely fall short-perhaps considerably short of the projected aid total of RVN $1860 billion (more than U.S. $3.38 billion). U.S. military assistance totaled $813 million FY 74, and economic assistance $400 million more. For fiscal year 1975 the Nixon Administration has requested $648 million in economic aid from Congress for all of Indo-China (far short of the $850 million recommended by United States Ambassador Martin), and $1.6 billion in military aid. While some progress has been achieved in persuading other industrialized nations, particularly France and Japan, to extend financial assistance, the sums committed thus far have been small. In December the French signed an agreement granting Saigon 30 million francs (4.5 francs= $1.00) for 1974, with an additional soft loan of 35 million, bank credits of 35 million, and 10 million francs for the study of future economic development projects. Thus far Japan has made limited investments in several specific projects (we flew over a generating facility in the Delta constructed with Japanese funds, itself not far from an Australian-built water treatment plant); although 

Tokyo has promised grants and credits, a final agreement has not yet been reached. Here the Saigon government faces another dilemma: each time a leading spokesman calls attention to the military threat, foreign investors, public and private, become concerned about the nation's viability; to avoid mention of the military problem, conversely, is to risk reductions in American military assistance.

It is clear that South Viet Nam faces a long road to economic self-sufficiency, and that continued infusions of foreign assistance, especially from America, will be necessary for five years to come. In the interim, the people appear well-fed, and as resilient and hard-working as any in Asia; neither are there any signs of damage and destruction, either in the cities or in the countryside, on a scale wide enough to interfere with economic development. Over the long term, if the effects of the enduring warfare can be minimized, continued increases in agricultural productivity coupled with development of an export trade in wood, glass, shrimp and other fish products, and ultimately oil, as well as the cheap, abundant and technically skilled labor supply, hold out legitimate hope that the economic miracles of Taiwan and South Korea can be repeated. 14 A major step in this direction could come if the Overseas Private Investment Corporation were allowed to extend its investment insurance to the Republic of Viet Nam. OPIC would guarantee U.S. investors against war damage, currency incontrovertibility and expropriation. But OPIC has been directed by Congress not to extend its investment insurance to the Saigon government. As a result, American private capital, and that of other advanced industrial nations, is not readily available for Viet Nam.

Questioning the unavailability of OPIC aid for South Viet Nam, William Peterson has asked of it is "wise to extend aid at some $1.5 billion a year, while in effect denying the recipient country adequate access to American business investments?" It was, after all, with the OPIC coverage that the economies of 

South Korea and Taiwan were able to prosper to the extent that they are no longer dependent upon American economic aid and that they have achieved healthy and vital economies. Thus, if Congress persists with its present policy of denying OPIC guarantees to South Viet Nam, the paradoxical result will be that Saigon will become more, not less, dependent on U.S. economic aid. 

III. THE POLITICAL SITUATION 

Virtually since the inception of the American aid program to South Viet Nam in 1955, opponents of the U.S. involvement have dwelt upon the authoritarian as- 

12 Exports in just three areas reached U.S. $74.2 in 1973, and there are not-unwarranted hopes that the total can be raised to $100 million this year. Drilling for South Viet Nam's first oil well is expected to begin in late 1974. 

18 For a recent analysis of the future prospects of the economy of South Viet Nam. see 

Patrick M. Boarman (ed.). The Economy of South Vietnam: A New Beginning (Los 

Angeles Center for International Business, 1973). 

14 OPIC is a Government-administered agency which promotes and guarantees private investment in "friendly" develoning countries. 

15 William Peterson, "South Vietnam, OPIC, and American Business," National Business, March 1974.

pects of various Saigon regimes as the core of their argument. Such criticism has if anything increased in recent years, despite the evident stability of the government of President Nguyen Van Thieu. To deal at length with this critique would require an extended analysis of the nature and characteristics of the South Vietnamese political system and of the current regime, which would be far beyond the scope of this report. Let it suffice to note here that Anglo-Saxon style parliamentary democracy is a rare flower, in which practice often fails to conform to theory and which even then flourishes almost exclusively in advanced industrial nations with republican roots of long duration. There is an obvious air of unreality in the implicit expectation that politics in South Viet Nam should reflect the writings of John Stuart Mill as well or better than, for example, electoral competition in Chicago, South Viet Nam is a country torn by war, many of whose finest young men have perforce been summoned to a military career and thus have been unable to contribute to their nation's political life. Her internal security problems have for decades been sufficiently acute to engender justifiable fears for survival. It is not surprising that such circumstances breed restrictions upon what in the West are called civil liberties, and certain of these curbs are acknowledged as necessary even among the most libertarian-minded South Vietnamese.16 

During our stay in Viet Nam we saw none of the outward manifestations of the totalitarian state so visible, for example, in China, the Soviet Union, or Eastern Europe. Travelers are required to present identity cards where asked; we observed two such requests, both put to young men, and both were allowed to move swiftly on their way. The military presence is quite visible, but the reasons for that are obvious. Few of the citizens with whom we spoke seemed bitterly opposed to the government. Indeed, more than 560,000 South Vietnamese have been armed as part of the Popular Self-Defense Force program, with a loss rate of only one to five weapons per thousand distributed-impressive figures for a society supposedly governed by a "small, externally imposed and increasinglydespised elite." " Significantly, there has been no indication of revolutionary stirrings even from an armed populace. 

The continued flow of refugees from the NVA-VC areas and the persistent refusal of the communists to agree to negotiations to establish a time-table for holding competitive elections are testimonials to the relative popularity of the government and the declining acceptability of the VC. In general, we found no reason to dispute the judgment of U.S. Ambassador Graham Martin (expressed to us during a briefing) that "there has developed in recent months a pervasive sense throughout the country of the legitimacy of this government." He further asserted, "The Viet Cong are now largely regarded as intruders, tolerated or resented." The highly-respected Saigon newspaper publisher. Bui Diem, once 

Ambassador to the United States, while aware of the government's limitations in certain particulars, also believes that opposition to the government is fading. He expressed some confidence in the future evolution of the regime in a more democratic direction should peace become a reality. 

We were profoundly impressed by the extraordinary group of able and dedicated young men who are increasingly being designated to fill high posts in the armed forces and in civil agencies up to the ministerial level. While in Viet Nam we were able to speak at some length with men such as the newly-designated Minister of Information, Hoang Duc Nha; a principal aide to the Minister of Finance, Pho 

Ba Quan; the Minister of Trade and Industry, Nguyen Duc Cuong; Director of the Government Press Center, Nguyen Ngoch Bich; and the Minister of Tourism, Pham Luong Quang. It is in the hands of these men-often U.S.-educated, with graduate degrees from institutions such as MIT, Harvard, Columbia University and Johns Hopkins, among others, who are thoroughly committed to the cause of a better and non-communist South Viet Nam-that the future of that nation rests. 

Since we were in Viet Nam, an additional cabinet reorganization has occurred, as well as several changes in the armed forces and among the province chiefs. 

Such shifts seem designed to further improve the administrative efficiency of the government and reduce the incidence of corruption." There has been significant 

16 Such restrictions upon civil liberties in wartime are not unknown even in the United States, as students of the Lincoln, Wilson, and FDR presidencies ought to remind us more often.

Ngo Dzo. who has occupied a minor post since his poor performance as III Corps commander during the 1972 offensive.
