APPENDIX 13 COMMUNIST GUIDANCE ON "NEW PHASE" OF THE "REVOLUTION" IN SOUTH VIETNAM 1 INTRODUCTION 

This report reviews a Communist "political reorientation and training" directive which was captured in late February 1974 in Binh Thuan Province on the central coast. The document, dated 5 February, provides a summary of current Communist strategy in South Vietnam. Its format, complete with an historical review and projections for the future, is along the lines of a Communist policy "resolution," which is the highest-level guidance issued to troops and cadre in the field. Communist soldiers, who have recently rallied to the Government of Vietnam (GVN), report that Hanoi and the Communist command in the South are circulating several new "resolutions" based on decisions of the 

Central Committee of North Vietnam's Lao Dong (Communist) Party. Al though the directive appears to have been drafted at VC province level for distribution to subordinate elements, earlier accounts indicate that the Binh Thuan province guidance is a distillation of these latest policy directives and was probably taken from COSVN Resolution 12. Full texts of COSVN-level resolutions and directives generally are not disseminated below region level; each subordinate element receives a somewhat abridged version based, apparently, on need to know. The broad nature and applicability of the document's content is verified by its resemblence to an "NLFSV-PRGRSV Appeal" issued on the occasion of the 24th anniversary of "National Anti-U.S. Day," March 19, 1974. Although the Binh Thuan document is somewhat more candid in its assessment of Communist weaknesses and GVN strengths, the "tasks" and "missions" outlined in both the Binh Thuan document and the "Appeal" are remarkably similar in substance and tone. 

According to the rallier reports the Communists currently view the cease-fire agreement as merely a convenient "means of postponing the war so as to facilitate their preparations for another war." In a similar vein the training document emphasizes that the Paris Agreement-which is described as a great "victory"has created "conditions (for us) to advance . . . and has weakened the enemy." 

It adds: "We should take the initiative and prepare to wage a violent and critical war of revolution to defeat the enemies and to overthrow their cruel and fascist regime in case they risk expansion of the war." 

Like the Communist "resolutions" reflected in the recent rallier reports, the reorientation guidance candidly identifies the strengths and weaknesses of both Vietnamese sides. Although the Saigon government is said to be suffering economically, it is also described as having "temporarily the upper hand," with "puppet soldiers" plentifully supplied with "strong and abundant equipment." The government's main assets are listed as its "control of the populated areas" and of communications routes; the effectiveness of its police force and of the local administrative agencies; and its ability to utilize manpower and resources in its areas of control. 

The Communists' main advantages are said to be the continuing aid from abroad and their "well trained, well equipped" regular military forces which "are remaining close to critical areas (and are) strong enough to attack and eliminate the enemy." On the debit side, the guidance concedes that the "liberated areas" are largely unpopulated, the Communist Party structure is weak, and the guerrilla movement is almost nonexistent.

The document leaves no doubt as to the ultimate solution for Communist difficulties: "Our basic policy has not changed. . . . We should grasp the standpoint: 

1 Source: Viet-Nam Documents & Research Notes, issued as a research service by the U.S. Mission in Viet-Nam. 

(810)

the revolution in South Vietnam can only be won by means of armed violence in close coordination with the political violence of the masses." As if to drive home the point, the document ignores the usual Communist propaganda developed for foreign consumption regarding establishment of the National Council of National Reconciliation and Concord and the holding of general elections. Recent ralliers state that the Communists have given up the idea of trying to manipulate the Paris Accords to realize these objectives and have decided to concentrate on imposing a favorable solution by force. They add that Communist negotiating strategy is now designed simply to destroy public confidence in the GVN-particularly inside the U.S.-and thus to ward off the foreign trade and aid needed to reinforce South Vietnam. This reassertion of Hanoi's traditional talk-fight strategy is reflected in the reorientation guidance which notes that "we must coordinate to stage struggles on three fronts, political, military and diplomatic, to force the enemy to carry out the Paris Agreements (as the Communists interpret them)."

In discussing immediate Communist tasks in the South, the document outlines a program for mobilization and military pressure that runs directly counter to the spirit and letter of the Paris Agreement. Cadre are admonished to build up the party and guerrilla forces, particularly "secret guerrillas" who operate behind GVN lines, and to "push our attacks" everywhere to expand Communist control over "areas occupied by the enemy" as well as disputed areas. Wherever the Communists already are in control, a concerted effort is to be made to develop a governmental structure and an economic system that can compete with the GVN. 

Elsewhere, in GVN territory, the Communists are to expand their terrorist and subversive activities to weaken the GVN from within. "Enemy hamlet and village governments should be neutralized," the document states. "The armed forces should take the initiative in eliminating despicable persons (read GVN officials)." 

Similarly, "political penetrations should be consolidated and developed." Cadre also are advised to "be sharp in covering up and maintaining our force" inside 

GVN territory.

In sum, the strategy set out in the reorientation guidance represents an elaborate effort to exploit the "less fire" resulting from the Paris Agreement and to lay the groundwork for a Communist take-over. Ideally, the Communists would prefer to see the GVN collapse economically, and their continued pressure and build-up in South Vietnam, as well as their reversion to a talk-fight strategy in the negotiating arena, is designed to contribute to that end. One Communist headquarters recently advised its cadre to be ready to take advantage of "sudden developments" since the economic situation allegedly might deteriorate to such an extent as to allow them to "destroy" the GVN. Short of this, as the document point out, "we must incessantly hold and develop the revolutionary forces in all areas and disrupt all enemy plots; we must weaken the enemy gradually and build up our strength in order to defeat the reactionary regime under any circumstances. As the rallier reports indicate, cadre are being told that the political settlement envisaged at Paris is in fact an illusion. This and the conspicuous lack in the orientation document of even a nod toward the political clauses of the Paris Agreement suggest that the Communists regard these as of propaganda value only.

POLITICAL REORIENTATION AND TRAINING MATERIALS FOR INFRA- STRUCTURE CADRES AND PARTY MEMBERS 

The basic victory of the anti-U.S. national salvation resistance and the Mission of the revolution in the South during the new phase. 

PART I-VICTORY AND THE REASONS FOR VICTORY OF THE ANTI-U.S. NATIONAL SALVATION RESISTANCE 

Since World War II, the U.S. imperialists have become international gendarmes and have attempted to carry out a neo-colonialist policy. In Vietnam, following the defeat of the French imperialists, the Americans threw out the French and invaded South Vietnam, plotting to eradicate the Southern revolution, transform the South into a neo-colony, prevent the development of the socialist North, and to surround, oppress, and obstruct the socialist revolutionary movement and the national liberation movement. Vietnam became a battlefield between the factions of revolution and counterrevolution in Vietnam and in the world.

The Vietnamese people heroically fought and gloriously won the biggest, longest, fiercest and cruelest aggressive war of the U.S. imperialists, forcing them to withdraw their troops and to recognize the sovereignty, unity and territorial integrity of Vietnam, and to recognize the South Vietnamese people's right of self-determination. That great victory has created fundamental, favorable conditions to advance toward completing the national and democratic revolution in the South, and has weakened the enemy, strengthened the world revolution, and made realistic contributions to the struggle for preservation of peace, national independence, democracy and socialism. 

REASONS FOR VICTORY 

1. The guiding role of our Party, headed by Chairman Ho, which has a correct line, unanimity, and experience in struggle; an always firm revolutionary line; close coordination of the three-pronged offensive (military, political and military proselyting) and continuous offensive throughout the three areas and three aspects (military, political and diplomatic); the ability to defeat the enemy at each step and to seize each stage of victory and succesfully consolidate the revolutionary position to advance toward complete victory. 

2. Politically, the resolute and unsubmissive will of the people of both North and South, and close unity on the solid foundation of the allied worker-peasant bloc. 

3. The strength of the great rear area in the North assisted in the establishment of socialism without oppression and exploitation and contributed to the vigor of the people's democratic regime in the South. 

4. The strength of unity in struggle of the three Indochinese peoples draws tighter day by day. 

5. Sincere support has been provided by the socialist faction, the international Communist movement, the national liberation movement, and peace- and justice-loving forces throughout the world. 

PART II.-CURRENT SITUATION AND MISSION OF THE REVOLUTION IN THE SOUTH IN THE NEW PHASE I. THE SITUATION IN THE SOUTH 

1. Enemy plot.-The U.S. imperialists were defeated and forced to sign the agreement, remove their troops from South Vietnam, and end their war of destruction and blockade against the North. But they have not discarded their long-term, sinister plot. They continue to use puppet troops and authorities as tools with which to carry out their neo-colonialist policy in the South and to prolong the partition of our country. They have undermined the agreement in a systematic manner and have intensified efforts to exploit and suppress the people in their areas of control. They continue to launch police operations in contested areas and to attack and occupy liberated areas, producing a situation in South Vietnam in which there is no real cease-fire, no genuine restoration of peace. This situation is unstable and drags on. 

Our basic policy has not changed; we must understand the nature of the enemy. 

2. Strong points and weaknesses of the enemy and ourselves.-(a) The Enemy: The enemy temporarily has the upper hand. Although U.S. troops have been withdrawn, puppet soldiers are still plentiful; their regular units are being strengthened with strong and abundant equipment; regional and popular forces still have the capability of replacing regular units on several battlefields; U.S. aid, although it is decreasing, is still being given to the puppets. 

The enemy is still able to control populated areas and communication routes and to utilize manpower and property of their area of control. 

Police, local administrative, psychological warfare, and espionage apparati, and the reactionary and depraved culture will continue to oppress, dupe and poison many people in the areas under their control. However, the enemy has very basic weaknesses which are becoming more pronounced every day and which he cannot overcome.

The withdrawal of U.S. and satellite troops and the decrease in aid have made things much more difficult for the puppets.

Most puppet troops are the children and brothers of workers and have been forced to join the army. They do not want to die and their morale has decreased seriously, especially since the signing of the Paris Agreement. 

The enemy policy of prolonging the war, undermining the agreement, terrorizing, repressing, exploiting, looting, etc., has made their politica land economic situation worse. The masses have come to hate the enemy more deeply and dissidence has increased in the internal ranks of the enemy. (b) Our Side: We still have several shortcomings and weaknesses, which include:

Our liberated areas are large, but have few people. 

Our Party Chapters are not yet close to the masses and have so far failed to become the nucleus to guide the in-place movement. 

Our in-place forces are still weak and undermanned; the guerrilla warfare movement is not yet strong.

Our three-pronged offensive is still weak and uneven. 

However, we still have some fundamental strong points: 

We have large liberated areas which are being strongly developed and are geographically linked to the liberated areas of Cambodia, Laos, and the socialist North. We also control numerous penetration bases and contested areas adjacent to enemy-controlled areas. If we hold, expand, and strongly develop those areas we will threaten and besiege the enemy.

Our revolutionary forces have survived, developed and been tested in several areas.

The masses are proud, enthusiastic, and confident because of the U.S. defeat and troop withdrawal.

Enemy control in many areas has been checked and production has increased. 

In urban and rural areas under temporary enemy control the life of the masses is growing worse every day while the movement against the puppet authorities is becoming broader. 

Although our guerilla warfare movement is quite strong, it is still being developed. Main force and regional force troops have been well trained and well equipped. They have a high fighting spirit, and remain close to critical areas, strong enough to attack and eliminate the enemy. 

We should be determined to make an all-out, active effort to overcome difficulties and weaknesses; to strive to develop our fundamental strong points; to deeply exploit the enemy's weak points; to strengthen the struggle on the three fronts of military, political and military proselyting activities, in coordination with the legality of the agreement in three areas; to strive to improve ourselves in all aspects; to push the enemy back step by step and seize victory in stages so as to advance toward complete victory; to wipe out the cruel, warmongering, treacherous, and traitorous fascist regime of the Saigon authorities. At the same time, we should take the initiative and prepare to wage a violent and critical war of revolution to defeat the enemies and to overthrow their cruel and fascist regime in case they risk expansion of the war. 

II. MISSION OF THE REVOLUTION IN THE SOUTH 

1. Basic mission.-The U.S. imperialists were defeated and forced to sign the 

Paris Agreement. Yet, they have never given up their plot to transform the Southern part of our country into their neo-colony. The Saigon puppet authorities are still serving as U.S. henchmen to oppose the people and betray the country. Therefore, we must continue fighting in order to complete the people's national and democratic revolution and struggle against the U.S. imperialists, mercantile bourgeoisie and landlords; we must concentrate our thrust against the U.S. imperialists, the mercantile bourgeois authoritarians, and the militarists and fascists who are now ruling in the enemy controlled areas. We must eliminate the 

U.S. lackeys and their neo-colonial administration. We must form the people's national and democratic government, achieve national concord and create an independent, national, democratic, peaceful, neutral, and prosperous South in order to achieve peaceful national reunification. 

Our principal enemies are the U.S. imperialists and the ruling capitalists, bureaucrats, militarist fascists and active lackeys of the U.S. imperialists, who represent the rights and privileges of the merchantilist bourgeois class and the reactionary and corrupt landlords. The U.S. imperialists are the enemy instigators

who provide support to the puppets; the ruling mercantilist bourgeois, authoritarian militarists, and fascist groups are the direct foes whom we should concentrate on overthrowing. 

2. In order to carry out the above-mentioned basic missions, we should increase our efforts to accomplish our immediate missions and tasks: 

We must coordinate to stage struggles on three fronts, political, military and diplomatic, to force the enemy to carry out the Paris Agreement on Vietnam; we must incessantly hold and develop the revolutionary forces in all areas and disrupt all enemy plots; we must weaken the enemy gradually and build up our strength in order to defeat the reactionary regime under any circumstances, even if the enemy stubbornly risks resuming the war. Specifically, we should: (a) Use the slogan of peace, independence, democracy, improved living conditions and national concord in order to accomplish national reunification and assemble the revolutionary forces, consolidate the worker-peasant alliance, widen the national united front, isolate and defeat the ruling mercantilist bourgeois, authoritarian, militarist, and fascist Nguyen Van Thieu. (b) Push our attacks strongly in all areas; combine three types of forces in three areas in a three-pronged offensive; foil all enemy mopping-up and landgrabbing operations designed to seize liberated areas and penetration and pacification bases in contested areas; resolutely defeat the enemy plot to occupy and pacify contested areas; and, at the same time, regain areas occupied by the enemy in order to liberate the people from oppression and exploitation. (c) Strongly promote the political struggle in order to gradually reach the high-tide of revolution in urban areas and, together with the revolutionary movement in rural areas, promote a struggle to gain control of the population and seize the people's mastership rights, push back and defeat all military, political, economic and cultural schemes of the enemy; and advance the revolution step by step. (d) Strengthen our three-pronged offensive of military, political and militaryproselyting activities, coordinating with the legality of the agreement; strive to pay close attention to both attacking the enemy and building our forces in three areas; defeat the enemy step by step in order to achieve victory in stages and be able to eliminate the reactionary lackeys and traitors of the Saigon puppet government and eliminate U.S. neo-colonialism in South Vietnam. (e) We should grasp the standpoint: The revolution in South Vietnam can only be won by means of armed violence in close coordination with the political violence of the masses. We must maintain the absolute revolutionary spirit of the working class and always initiate attacks to defeat the enemy. We must be strong in the military, political and diplomatic aspects and in the three strategic areas (liberated, contested and urban areas) to defeat the enemy. Our political, military, and military-proselyting attacks to seize the government for the people will make us strong, weaken the enemy, and lead to his defeat. 

PART III-SOME PRINCIPAL MISSIONS 

To satisfactorily carry out our immediate missions and to create conditions for accomplishing our basic political objectives we should understand and faithfully fulfill the following principal tasks: 

1. We must maintain the armed forces and strongly develop our militia and guerrilla forces; strengthen the people's guerrilla warfare movement, and the movement to motivate the people to join the army; always initiate attacks against the enemy in order to advance the revolution. At the same time, we should strengthen our security and armed security forces and promote the secrecypreservation and counter-espionage movements. Guerrilla and security forces are two violent tools of the masses in hamlets and villages. They must be quickly developed and well handled. 

2. We should concentrate our efforts in the contested and weak hamlets and villages and carry out comprehensive attacks. Special attention should be given to propaganda, education, and organization of the masses so that we can seize the people's mastership rights and frustrate the new pacification program of the enemy. We should expand liberated hamlets and villages and gain control on many levels, from weak hamlets and villages to strong, from strong hamlets and villages to liberated ones. 

3. Strive to motivate the masses to build revolutionary bases and broaden the struggle movement against oppression, exploitation, and to protect the right to

live, etc.

, in order to create conditions for promoting the rising struggle in cities and towns. 

4. Strive to develop the liberated areas (including base areas) and safeguard and protect large and small liberated areas and penetration and base areas, which are to be used for support in attacks at the front and serve as a banner appealing to the people living in the enemy-held areas to support the revolution. 

5. Increase motivation and organization of workers, farmers, petit capitalists and other classes. We should pay attention to mobilizing the masses, religious sects, and refugees in order to strengthen unity in rural areas. We should strongly promote the Front's mission and the establishment of authority and election of administrations in hamlets and villages, for the purpose of making our government truly represent the people's mastership right. 

6. We should intensify the operations of the Party and Group on two fronts: 

Ideology and organization in order to comprehensively and firmly guarantee that the activities of Party chapters and members adhere to the broad masses; determine their aspirations and strive to propagandize, educate, and lead them in struggle and mutual affection in order to advance to liberate hamlets and villages and, along with the entire people and army, rise up to topple the reactionary regime, liberate the entire South and complete the people's national and democratic revolution. 

The above-mentioned missions must be satisfactorily carried out at each echelon of different areas as follows: 

I. MISSIONS OF HAMLETS AND VILLAGES IN EACH AREA A. Liberated Hamlets and Villages 

1. Liberated hamlets and villages are the result of the people's struggle. Therefore, a regime controlled by the people must be established to bring to the people freedom as well as happiness. The liberated hamlets and villages must be wellprotected from enemy seizure. A strong liberated area will be a source of manpower and material for it will be a stable support for attacks at the front and will be a banner rallying the people in enemy-held areas. Building and protection of liberated hamlets and villages are missions of extreme importance. These missions should be carried out under any circumstances. 

2. The demands on liberated hamlets and villages are the unification of the entire people, production, development, and fighting. The liberated hamlets and villages must be strengthened in political, military and economic aspects, highlighting the people's democratic regime. 

3. What must a Party Chapter do? (a) Politically, a strong Party Chapter should be set up and the Chapter must be truly close to the masses; organize and develop an administration of the people, by the people and for the people which takes care of the people's livelihood, and manages the economy, culture, health, education, society and order and security; actively build and strengthen revolutionary groups; and ceaselessly increase the people's political awareness. (b) Militarily we must urgently build and develop militia, guerrilla, security, and armed security forces; the people's guerrilla warfare movement must be promoted; combat villages must be established and be prepared to counter the enemy with three-prong attacks determined to eliminate his land-grabbing and mopping-up operations; actively conduct a conscription campaign to build up and strengthen our forces. (c) Economically, we must actively step up production and protect production, gradually raise people's living standards, and supply the revolution. A comprehensive long-range plan must be worked out as a large and stable basis from which to proceed to socialism. (d) As for culture, education, public health and social welfare, every possible effort must be made to satisfy the people's pressing demands in these areas. In the meantime, we must correctly carryout the policy toward the wounded, the dead, revolutionary families and families of war victims. 

B. Contested Hamlets and Villages 

1. These are populated areas with abundant resources. They are also a stepping stone to the city. They are the perimeter safeguarding the liberated areas. 

They are areas under constant decisive dispute between the enemy and ourselves and have changed hands many times.

2. The requirement in a contested area is to struggle against oppression and exploitation and protect our own interests, thus changing the movement into a three-pronged attack. The people should be motivated to eliminate traitors and tyrants; loosen enemy grips; actively build and develop revolutionary bases and lead the masses to become masters at various levels. People should then remove outposts (conditions should be created to remove the enemy's outposts because these are the support points of his restrictve force); increase political penetration activities; and expand liberated areas. With the political penetration activities and liberated areas, we must demonstrate our efforts to satisfactorily maintain and develop all aspects. 

3. What should a Party Chapter do? (a) A political motivation campaign must be conducted far and wide among the people so that the people will be made to realize that the Thieu clique, backed up by the U.S. imperialists, undermines the 

Paris Agreement, continues pacification and continues the fighting, pressganging, robbery of rice and property, massive killings and repression. With the continued existence of the Thieu regime, there can be no peace, national concord or improvement of the people's livelihood. There must be struggle unity to advance toward overthrowing the Thieu regime and establishing a new people's democratic regime with freedom, comfort, peace, independence, etc. People should be made to be masters. Enemy hamlet and village governments should be neutralized step by step beyond the elimination of spies, removal of outposts, opposition to land-grabbing, the establishment of people's revolutionary administrations, and the building and maintaining of liberated hamlets and villages. 

The people should be made to have confidence. The above mission can be surely fulfilled with united struggle. Many areas have accomplished this already. (b) The military-proselyting operation should be pushed forward, in order to neutralize and disintegrate enemy ranks and weaken the enemy's basic authority day by day. The military-proselyting mission must actually become a mass movement and must closely coordinate with the soldiers' political struggle movement. 

Soldiers' dependents (miserable families) must be educated and mobilized to unite and join the whole people in daily motivating the soldiers and calling upon their own relatives to desert enemy units and return home to earn their living, gradually take part in the revolution and be determined to give up the life of mercenary soldiers who betray the country. (c) The armed forces should take the initiative in eliminating despicable persons; breaking the enemy's grip; and attacking and frustrating police operations, pacification, land-grabbing and re-occupation operations in support of the people's struggle movement; enlarge our controlled areas and liberated hamlets and villages; and broaden solidarity among people of all age categories participating in the people's guerrilla warfare movement. However, the legal status must be maintained. We should launch the political, armed and military-proselyting struggles in varying degrees according to the capabilities of each area. We must actively build militia and guerrilla forces; especially secret guerrilla. Note: 

Contested hamlets and villages have different strengths and weaknesses. The 

Party Chapter must base itself on the situation in carrying the movement from low to high. Leadership in struggle must be extremely flexible, using all public, clandestine, legal and semi-legal forms. The political struggle must be directed in close coordination with the military one. 

In ethnic minority, religious, refugee, etc., areas, it is necessary to thoroughly understand the policies for religions and ethnic minorities, concentrating on the central slogan and going deep into the life, aspirations and wishes, knowledgeability and capabilities of each circle and each religion. We must be patient in disseminating propaganda and in motivating and leading the mass struggle from low to high and from political struggle to political struggle with violence for self-defense. Thus, we can develop hard-core cadres and forces, particularly secret guerrillas and Party and group members. 

C. Areas Under Enemy Control (including towns, cities and urban areas) 

1. These are the lairs where the enemy has located restrictive machinery to oppress, undermine, and deceive the people and to exploit and develop his reactionary forces. But here the masses of all strata are repressed and exploited. So, in many cases, the people themselves oppose enemy reactionary schemes and policies. With good leadership and organization and strong coordination with the rural movement and with military attack, the movement here will play a direct role in toppling the enemy authorities from central down to local levels.

2. The requirement in enemy-controlled areas is to lead the masses' legal struggle to oppose all forms of repression and exploitation and to demand the fulfillment of the masses' urgent needs, democratic freedom, freedom of travel and enforcement of the Paris Agreement. Thus, we can develop our forces. 

Traitors and despicable persons must be eliminated to support the masses' struggle movement. The struggle must go gradually from low to high and from the participation of a small number of people to a large-scale struggle when the opportunity permits. Propaganda should be actively used to organizing the struggle, but we must be sharp in covering up and maintaining our force. We must be clever in concealing and conserving our forces. We must ceaselessly develop and expand our forces in order to continually elevate the movement. 

3. What must a Party Chapter do? (a) Efforts should be made to have the masses take part in the daily struggle movement to oppose enemy reactionary, dictatorial, fascist, and exploiting policies and schemes in combination with the demand that Thieu be overthrown, that a new government be formed, that the implementation of the Agreement be guaranteed, and that people's life be safeguarded. (b) We should further motivate the working masses and the urban poor, organize and build stable forces, and at the same time, broaden the front through the participation of the classes mentioned above. Public newspapers, should be utilized to create conditions to broaden the political front aimed at isolating Thieu and the lackeys in the local area and then overthrowing their reactionary, country-harming regime. (c) Political penetrations should be consolidiated and developed. We must gain control of the bases, especially in worker's quarters and the outskirts of cities for the protection of the movement; secret organizations must be developed, strengthened and protected. A subtle, simple, clever and strong plan should be worked out for the operation, concealment and motivation of the people publicly, semi-publicly and under cover. The masses must be assembled and used for struggle with the enemy. In order to carry out missions in enemy-controlled areas, the Party Chapter must thoroughly understand the following: 

1. Through mass struggles a central slogan should be used correctly to show clearly the obstinate, belligerent and cruel nature of the U.S. and its running dogs, thus heightening the masses' awareness. 

2. Cadres and Party members must go deeply into the lives of the masses, especially the basic masses. The masses should be rallied under many public and semi-public forms to unite and help one another in the masses' struggle. Only then, can we develop key cadres, secret organizations, the Party and the group. 

3. Special attention should be paid to the leadership of the struggle movements and to the slogans about people's life and democracy (opposition to taxation, the demand for rice and for pay raises) in coordination with the struggle against terrorism, conscription, etc. These are the slogans which now are rallying a large part of the masses and which have great political significance. 

III. THE PARTY'S MISSIONS 

The important conditions for achieving victory in the new phase are that the Party Chapter must be strong and that political ideology and organization must be genuinely close to the masses. 

1. Mission of political ideology.-Cadres and party members should be made to thoroughly understand that the new situation and tasks and the struggle principles in the new phase are to increase the ideology of revolutionary violence, enemy-attack spirit; heighten vigilance; oppose rightist tendencies, pacificism and rest; raise fighting determination and internal unity and be ready to attack in order to defeat the enemy under all circumstances. We must eliminate personalism, selfishness and the intention of resigning to earn our own living. We must pay strict attention to taking care of and helping the poor families of our comrades with a spirit of solidarity and affection in order to fulfill missions. 

2. Organization missions.—The Party Chapter should be motivated to become genuinely close to the masses; rally and guide the masses so that they will take the initiative in carrying out their missions. 

For example: (a) The Party Chapter must thoroughly understand its own responsibilities: Always understand the 6 tasks of the Party chapter (according to the regulations), which are to hold to directives and instructions from upper echelons, to operate on the situation between the enemy and ourselves, to be self-

reliant, to respect the aspirations of the masses, to review the mission, and to carry out decisions. 

Through the groups and hardcore cadres, resolutions and propaganda campaigns should be disseminated for the masses to perceive and sympathize with the resolutions of the Party Chapter meetings, each comrade should report on the results of propagandizing and motivating the masses so that other comrades will observe, comment and draw experiences. This is called operational review. After that, new resolutions will be worked out and Party members will be assigned missions to implement the new resolutions. If such a process is carried out on a regular basis, the knowledgeability of Party members as well as the quality of the Party Chapter will be enhanced. It is best for the Party Chapter to continue the above task. 

It is most important that the Party Chapter cling to the people and link closely to them. There will be a revolutionary movement only when we clearly understand the masses' life conditions and when the masses are propagandized, motivated and organized. (b) The quality of activity of the Party Chapter should be actually increased: 

Regular activities should be maintained; Complete preparation should be made for activities. Each resolution must consist of a plan of attack on the enemy, a development plan, a plan of development of forces; a plan to take care of people's lives; a plan to develop new Party and group members, etc. The collective development of resolutions and the implementation of self-criticism and criticism must be guaranteed. (c) Cadre-improving and training mission: Plans must be made for improving and training cadres of all kinds. First of all, Party Chapter secretaries, Party cell leaders and Party members should know how to lead guerilla security and military-proselyting activities. At the same time, assistance should be provided to Party members in discovering, leading and improving key and hardcore cadres under all circumstances and to rally and lead the masses in villages. Young cadre and female cadres should be promoted from the movement. 

In the past, our cadres and Party members made concrete contributions toward the great triumph of the present revolution in the South throughout all phases. 

Most important, we should all realize our glorious and great responsibility and motivate one another to overcome difficulties; endure sacrifice and hardships and fulfill the immediate tasks in order to complete the people's national democratic revolution in the South and lead to the peaceful reunification of the country. This also reflects the greatest determination to carry out Uncle Ho's testament: "Our people's anti-U.S. war for national salvation will call for many more difficulties and sacrifices. Nevertheless, we will score complete victory. This is a certainty. . . . The U.S. imperialists must withdraw from our country. Our fatherland will be reunified. The people in both the South and the North will be reunited under one roof."

APPENDIX 14 DECLARATION ON FOOD AND POPULATION ¹ TO GOVERNMENTS, ORGANIZATIONS AND MEN AND WOMEN EVERYWHERE WE, THE UNDERSIGNED, ADDRESS THIS DECLARATION ON FOOD AND POPULATION 

No link unites the family of man more than his need for food. For food is an essential condition of life, common to all people; wherever they are, whatever they do they share alike in this need. 

The stark truth is that man's ability to produce food is not keeping pace with his need. Despite efforts by governments and the international community to solve world food problems, more people are hungry today than ever before. 

Hundreds of millions of the world's people are undernourished. Population growth is adding 75 to 80 million more people each year, 200,000 each day. Within the next 25 years or so our present numbers of nearly 4 billion will be nearly 

7 billion. They must all be fed.

The world food situation took a sharp turn for the worse in 1972 and 1973: 

1. Stocks of grain have hit an all-time low since the end of World War II. 

Surplus stocks formerly held in reserve have nearly been exhausted and no longer offer security against widespread hunger and starvation. 

2. Food prices have reached new highs. Last year, despite a record world harvest, escalating demand nearly doubled grain prices. The increasing cost of food threatens to cause serious hardship for many people already spending most of what they have on food. 

3. Less of the cheaper protein foods, which normally supplement grain diets, is available. The world's fish catch and per capita production of protein-rich legumes, the staple diet in many countries, have declined. 

4. Food shortages have created serious social unrest in many parts of the world and are particularly severe in countries where hunger and the diseases that thrive on under-nourished bodies are prevalent. This scarcity has been aggravated by the consumption of more and more grain to produce meat, eggs and milk. 

5. Mounting fertilizer and energy shortages are reducing food production in certain areas and increasing food prices. 

In this new and threatening situation, a bad monsoon in Asia (which could occur in any year), or a drought in North America (like those in the 1930's and 1950's), could mean severe malnutrition for hundreds of millions and death for many millions.

This dangerously unstable world food picture, when seen against an unprecedented population increase, has created an immediate sense of urgency. The dangers of food shortages could remain a threat for the rest of this centuryeven if, hopefully, bumper crops in some years create temporary surpluses and even if the trend toward reduced birth rates becomes general throughout the world.

World food production in the years ahead must rise at least 2 percent a year to keep pace with the present rate of population growth. But it must rise a good deal more if the world's people are to be provided with an adequate diet. This required annual increase in food production is considerably greater than that which occurred during recent decades-and seems to be increasingly harder to achieve each year. But unless there is this necessary and continuous increase in food production, there will be even more hunger and malnutrition and soaring food prices.

The need to seek solutions is pressing. The nature of the problem, the precarious state of world food production made critical by predicted expectations 

1 This Declaration on Food and Population was presented to Secretary-General Kurt Waldheim of the United Nations on April 25, 1974. Food and Population is a Program of the Population Crisis Committee. 

(819)

of continued population growth, calls for concerted action by the world community. There is only one cure for hunger and that is food. No palliatives or panaceas in the form of reports or resolutions can alleviate the pain of empty stomachs that must be filled. International resolutions, however high-minded, are a mockery if they do not have a tangible impact on the human condition. 

The United Nations is now providing leadership on both these problems. In 

August the United Nations will convene the World Population Conference in Bucharest. In November it will convene the World Food Conference in Rome. 

These are the first occasions when governments have agreed to meet to consider these crucial questions and to consider taking action on them. 

With these two conferences only a few months away, we urge governments, acting before, at and after these two global conferences, to consider realistic and purposeful measures such as the following: 

1. Give high priority to programs in each country which will increase the production of grains, legumes and other staple food crops; ensure the availability of protein-rich foods, particularly to the more vulnerable population groups; expand the production of fertilizer; and improve the opportunities for small farmers to make a reasonable living. Develop a comprehensive and constructive 

World Food Plan for adoption at the World Food Conference. 

2. Support sound population policies relevant to national needs with respect national sovereignty and the diversity of social economic and cultural conditions; accept and assure the human right of each couple to decide for themselves the spacing and size of their families; and recognize the corresponding responsibility of governments to provide their peoples the information and the means to exercise this right effectively.3 Embody these policies in a World Population Plan of 

Action to be agreed upon by governments at the World Population Conference. 

3. Recognize that the interdependence of the world community creates an obligation to assist in the necessary funding of food and population programs by both the developing and developed countries. This calls for the elaboration and implementation of a global strategy by the United Nations and its family of agencies, including the Food and Agricultuture Organization of the United 

Nations and the United Nations Fund for Population Activities. 

4. Establish sufficient food reserves through national and international efforts to provide continuing vital insurance against food shortages. 

5. Recognize that, in our finite world where resources are limited, the family of man must one day, and hopefully fairly soon, bring birth rates into reasonable balance with the lowered death rates that have been achieved. Many governments see the need to guide national policy toward this objective. 

A solution to the present world food crisis must be found within the next few years. The social transformation which can lead to reduction in the world rate of fertility, along with lowering the rate of mortality, will take decades to accomplish. But a start must be made now because the millions of people being born each year place a heavy burden on the resources available to many nations for education, health, employment and the maintenance of evnironmental quality. 

A reduction in population growth could help alleviate this burden. Effective measures toward resolving both the world food and population problems must come within a total strategy of development. Not only is social and economic development desirable in itself, but also it contributes to moderating population growth.

In this Declaration, we focus on food because it is the most critical of the pressure on the world today. It is the greatest manifestation of world poverty, which has many aspects. The absolute number of desperately poor are far greater today than ever before in history. The need to eradicate acute poverty is being recognized more than ever as a collective responsibility. It is a task which global partnership and the demands of social justice make imperative. 

We repeat, food is crucial because literally tens of millions of lives are suspended in the delicate balance between world population and world food supplies. 

Growing populations, denied sufficient food needed for survival, resist all efforts to secure a peaceful world. With increased production and more equitable distribution of food, the future could provide a prospect of less misery and more hope for countless people now deprived of the basic necessities that are their right. 

2 United Nations Teheran Declaration of Human Rights, 1968 (para. 16). 

3 Resolution 1672 (LII) of the United Nations Economic and Social Council, 1969.

The World Food Conference represents a unique opportunity. This opportunity must not be missed. Comprehensive international agreements must be reached to assure at least minimal food supplies, with sufficient annual carry-over stocks. 

Disastrous breakdowns in the world food supply can thus be avoided. All nations may then rest secure in the knowledge that this, the most critical of their immediate problems, is being attacked with wisdom, vigor and unity of purpose. 

In the name of humanity we call upon all governments and peoples everywhere, rich and poor, regardless of political and social systems, to act-to act together-and to act in time.

STATEMENT BY UNITED NATIONS SECRETARY-GENERAL KURT WALDHEIM ON RECEIVING THE DECLARATION ON FOOD AND POPULATION FOLLOWING IS THE TEXT OF THE STATEMENT MADE BY SECRETARY-GENERAL KURT WALDHEIM ON RECEIVING THE DECLARATION ON FOOD AND POPULATION PRESENTED BY A GROUP OF EMINENT INTELLECTUALS AND SCIENTISTS AT A CEREMONY AT UNITED NATIONS HEADQUARTERS, APRIL 25, 1974 

I am grateful to be given this Declaration. It is marked by a profound concern for the improvement of the human condition. The Declaration is important of itself by virtue of the authority of the signers whose standing in all walks of life is reflected by the stature of those who have come to the United Nations today, to bear witness to it.

I have recently described the times we are living in as being characterized by mass poverty, food shortages, an energy crisis, a continuing oppressive burden of military expenditure, inflation exacerbated by world monetary instability, and the prospect before us of a doubling of human numbers by the turn of the century. 

The Declaration addresses itself primarily to the dramatic depletion of available food reserves and the shortfall in world food production. There is no more immediate task than that of rescuing the world from a situation which, for many, has always been precarious and is now even more hazardous. Short-term measures, while essential, must not be allowed to become palliatives, for the coming years will increase our vulnerability.

Virtually in no other area is it more pressing than in the one to which your Declaration addresses itself: the need to assure that the men, women, and children of Africa, Asia, Europe and the Americas, whatever their origin, their religion, their political philosophy, their age, their social condition have the basic foods which are the one essential and undebatable pre-condition of a life of dignity and decency. Without an assured supply, all our other aspirations for peace, for social justice, for growth and creativity, both as individuals and as nations, lose their meaning and take on a hollow ring. 

I cannot but be sharply and painfully conscious of the dangers posed by the Declaration, having recently returned from the Sahel. There, the suffering provoked by a six-year drought is resulting in premature death, disease and a dreadful sense of helplessness. The tragic spectacle of dying cattle and their owners fleeing the encroaching desert induces a sense of desperation into what should be the objective analysis of the world's food situation and prospects. 

It is no accident that this Declaration is presented at the United Nations. This body was established in the final phase of the most devastating war in history not merely to embody the highest aspirations of mankind, but to provide an operational vehicle for global action. The present crisis and those that we can see looming ahead can be overcome. They are indeed a serious challenge to use all our forces, our determination and ingenuity to provide a better life for future generations.

This is a year in which the international community, with some brutally abrupt reminders of what the future may hold, is facing up to the situation. At its present special session, the General Assembly is devoting its attention to finding the basis of a more equitable and workable economic system-a system which takes into account not only the needs of all nations, but also the imperative interrelationships of the several parts of the problem; poverty, the conservation and just apportionment of natural resources, the preservation of the environment, and the problems of trade and monetary system. Food and population, the two urgent issues to which your Declaration addresses itself, form an integral part of this whole.

In August, in Bucharest, for the first time Governments will hold a world population conference. Shortly afterwards, in Rome the World Food Conference will offer Governments the opportunity to tackle the world food problem. Your call therefore for international co-operation to ensure supplies of food comes at an opportune moment. The World Food Conference will present the Member

States of the United Nations with the unique opportunity to take immediate practical and urgently needed steps to redress a tragic situation which we can no longer afford to ignore.

The unprecedented growth of the world's population is compounding man's difficulties in feeding himself. The time at our disposal is very short. You point out that the world's food production has barely kept pace with population increases. Our goal is not mere survival but a life of dignity and peace with hope for each new generation to improve the conditions of life for the billions of men, women and children who will inhabit the earth in the coming decades.

Whether or not we can increase food production depends, as the Declaration states, not on a torrent of words and resolutions, but on adopting new and tangible objectives, hammering out the global strategies needed and revitalizing the machinery to achieve them. In spite of its ideological complexity and the political and other constraints that must exist in any global body, the United Nations can and will respond. 

It is in this same spirit of commitment and determination that I receive this Declaration. I am confident that the international community can and will find humane solutions to the serious problems of food and population which confront mankind. 

MESSAGES TO THE SECRETARY-GENERAL IN SUPPORT OF THE DECLARATION ON FOOD AND POPULATION MESSAGE FROM HIS IMPERIAL MAJESTY, THE SHAHANSHAH ARYAMEHR OF IRAN, TO HIS EXCELLENCY KURT WALDHEIM, THE SECRETARY-GENERAL OF THE UNITED NATIONS 

I have learned with pleasure of the Declaration on Food and Population signed by a group of distinguished people which will be submitted to the Secretary 

General of the United Nations Organization on the 25th of April, 1974.

It is my sincere hope that this Declaration will create a sense of urgency and contribute to a greater awareness among nations of the grave problems facing mankind in view of the rapid population growth on the one hand and the precarious state of the world food production on the other. 

Priority must be given by governments to implementing sound population control and environmental protection policies, to devising methods of increasing food production especially that of grains, to encourage increased cooperation between developing and developed countries in order to provide aid for population control and food production programs and to making provisions for sufficient food reserves to guard against famine. 

I earnestly hope that the World Population Conference and the World Food Conference organized by the United Nations and to be held in August and November, respectively, will help to promote a concerted effort on behalf of all the nations of the globe to seek wise solutions to these crucial issue which will have a vital bearing on the future of mankind.

A MESSAGE FROM HIS EXCELLENCY, LEOPOLD SENGHOR, TO UNITED NATIONS SECRETARY- GENERAL KURT WALDHEIM ON THE OCCASION OF THE PRESENTATION OF THE DECLA- RATION ON FOOD AND POPULATION, DELIVERED BY AMBASSADOR MÉDOUNE FALL, PER- MANENT REPRESENTATIVE TO THE UNITED NATIONS FROM SENEGAL, ON APRIL 25, 1974 

Mr. Secretary-General, Ladies and Gentlemen. On behalf of the President of the 

Republic of Senegal, His Excellency Leopold Senghor, I come to bring you the support of my country and of my government for this Declaration on Food and Population, and also on my President's behalf to extend congratulations to those who undertook this generous and opportune initiative. I thank you. 

Ambassador Samar Sen, Permanent Representative to the United Nations from 

India, at the ceremony on April 25 when the Declaration on Food and Population was officially presented to Secretary-General Waldheim, speaking on behalf of the Prime Minister, Indira Gandhi, expressed her support of the Declaration on Food and Population and her hope that this worldwide initiative dealing with the two important and related problems of food shortages and too rapid population growth would be successful. The Ambassador concluded by stating that in 

India, as the Prime Minister herself has stated publicly that family planning is at the base of our whole endeavor of national development. 

PRIME MINISTER SIRIMA BANDARANAIKE OF SRI LANKA CABLED HER SUPPORT OF THE DECLARATION ON FOOD AND POPULATION TO WILLIAM H. DRAPER, JR., WEDNESDAY, APRIL 24, 1974 I thank you for inviting me to join a group of leaders to present a Declaration on Food and Population to the Secretary-General of the United Nations. I regret my inability to accept the invitation due to other commitments. 

I have noted with great satisfaction the initiatives taken by you and other distinguished world citizens to focus attention through this Declaration on one of the most crucial problems facing mankind today.

We of the developing world are particularly conscious of the gravity of this problem.

I am happy to associate myself with the Declaration. 

My government will support all international action to avert a world food and population crisis.

HIS EXCELLENCY KURT WALDHEIM, Secretary-General, United Nations. 

APRIL 25, 1974. 

On behalf of the Government and people of the Republic of Korea, I take great pleasure in expressing our firm support for the Declaration on Food and Population signed by distinguished individuals from around the world. It is our sincere hope that, under your prominent guidance, the said Declaration will receive the prompt attention of all governments and peoples regardless of political and social systems, and be translated into concerned action in order to mitigate misery and create more hope for mankind in the future.

DONG-JO KIM, 

Minister, Foreign Affairs,

Republic of Korea. 

APRIL 25, 1974. 

HIS EXCELLENCY, KURT WALDHEIM, Secretary-General of the 

United Nations, New York.

DEAR MR. SECRETARY-GENERAL: The Declaration on Food and Population pre sented to you today vividly portrays the connected global problems of food supply and rapid population growth.

It is a timely call by distinguished citizens of many countries for urgent attention to two central problems of human welfare. It recognizes that in this increasingly interdependent world there is no acceptable alternative to nations working together to solve global problems, of which food and population are among the most pressing. It reminds us that the individual nations and the 

United Nations must approach the World Population Conference and the World Food Conference with the determination to seek and agree on common approaches.

As I stated in my address to the Special Session of the General Assembly, the United States will do its part. We strongly support a global cooperative effort to increase food production and have removed all domestic restrictions on our output. We will endeavor to increase the quantity of our food aid to needy countries, give technological and material help to efforts of developing countries to expand their food output, assist in the production of more fertilizer and in its more effective use, and join other governments in a worldwide effort to rebuild food reserves.

We hope that other countries able to do so will make similar contributions and that all countries will take active measures to bring population growth and food production into better balance.

The food and population crisis threaten the welfare and stability of peoples and nations. We must act together with the purpose, the mutual confidence and the determination to overcome them. 

Best regards,

HENRY A. KISSINGER, 

Secretary of State,

United States of America. 

1 

LADIES AND GENTLEMEN : 

SECRETARY OF FOREIGN AFFAIRS OF MEXICO, 

May 20, 1974.

I am pleased to refer to the Declaration on Food and Population signed on April 25 by distinguished persons in connection with the effort which the United Nations has undertaken in the search for effective and immediate solutions to two of the most critical problems now confronting humanity-demographic growth and food shortages.

I would like you to know, and I request that this information be communicated to the signers of the Declaration, that I fully share their concerns and viewpoints. I also think that it would be well to emphasize that the President of the

United States of Mexico, Luis Echeverria Alvarez, and the Government which he directs, are aware of the magnitude of these problems. 

We think that disorderly and unrestrained population growth should be avoided. We are led to the conviction that it is necessary to give all possible cooperation in order that the United Nations may successfully hold the next World Population Conference. To this end, a number of very highly qualified 

Mexican experts have been appointed to participate in the preliminary meetings and to contribute from the Mexican national experience at the Conference. 

The National Council on Population was recently created with the mandate to conduct a broad informational program in order to achieve adequate family planning. To this end, the main tenet of the program is that family planning is a fundamental responsibility of parents, who should exclusively determine the number of children they wish to have. For its part, the State limits itself to making recommendations and to making available to Mexican families the necessary information and the most suitable scientific means to practice family planning.

Mexico has supported from the beginning the proposals made at the Algiers 

Conference of Non-Aligned Countries; in the last Regular Session of the General 

Assembly of the United Nations and at the Seventeenth General Conference of the Food and Agriculture Organization (FAO), in which the need to convene a World Food Conference was pointed out, since it was felt that such a Conference might be the most suitable mechanism for coordinating those efforts which, at the international level, have become imperative for effectively solving the present food crisis. 

Prominent Mexican specialists are studying the problems which are to be discussed at the Food Conference in Rome. They participated in the First Preliminary Meeting held last February and will take part in the Second, which will be held during June in Geneva.

The traditional nutritional deficiency of the Mexican people has always motiated the appropriate authorities to conduct long term research in the technology of food production-in both qualitative and quantitative aspects. These efforts have borne considerable fruit. This is evidenced by the fact that high-yielding seeds and plant varieties have been developed which have resulted in the so-called "Green Revolution", in which an outstanding part was played by one of the signers of the Declaration, Norman Borlaug, who was deservedly awarded the Nobel Peace Prize in 1970. 

Mexico has shared her modest achievements with the other Latin American countries, providing them with genetic materials and basic corn seed. Mexico has sent improved varieties of wheat seeds to certain nations of Africa and the 

Near East.

The signatories' suggestion that an international food reserve be created in order to make provision for times of shortages is a point which coincides with Mexican policy. In addition to our cooperation through the World Food Program and through bilateral assistance to nations affected by natural catastrophes, during President Luis Echeverria's visit earlier this year to FAO headquarters he restated the need to create a World Bank for Food and Agricultural Research, the basic purpose of which would be to alleviate as rapidly as possible the consequences of natural catastrophes and to establish a permanent international cooperation fund for people suffering from chronic hunger. 

Mexico's activities in these and other areas help one to appreciate the scope of Mexican initiatives toward adoption of a Charter of the States' Economic Rights and Duties, since we cannot fail to recognize that the present crisis has its immediate origins in the irritating imbalances existing between the rich nations and those which are struggling to achieve total development. 

To supply adequate food for the whole human race, it is vital to have an infrastructure of appropriate agriculture and industrial technology; sufficient credits; equitable marketing systems for raw materials; and a series of other elements which can only be obtained with the establishment of a just world economic structure.

In closing, I wish to express my gratitude for this altruistic effort which demonstrates human solidarity. The Mexican Government shares the concerns expressed in the Declaration and will make definite efforts to see that the World Population and World Food conferences produce results advantageous to all peoples. 

EMILIO O. RABASA.

APPENDIX 15 CONGRESSIONAL RECORD EXCERPTS SUPPLIED BY HON. Bella Abzug CONCERNING POLITICAL PRISONERS IN SOUTH VIETNAM ¹ 

The SPEAKER pro tempore. Under a previous order of the House, the gentlewoman from New York (Ms. Abzug) is recognized for 60 minutes. 

Ms. Abzug. Mr. Speaker, it is not only by the White House scandals that the honor and good name of the United States are being shamed. It is long past time that we all became fully aware of what our country is helping to do to hundreds of thousands of political prisoners in South Vietnam. There is a coverup going on now of atrocious tortures of people whose only crime is that they want true peace for their country. We cannot pretend that we are not deeply implicated in crimes against humanity, crimes against civilization, crimes against common decency.

The regime of President Thieu may be the instrument of repression for its own citizens, but it is our money, our technical aid, our penal know-how, our connivance, which makes it possible for the Thieu administration to use the most savage means imaginable to repress political prisoners of all walks of life in South Vietnam-farmers, physicians, government officials, students, lawyers, businessmen. We must share responsibility equally with the Thieu regime for the crimes against humanity that we are paying for surreptitiously, and have been participating in actively for years. 

It is time we acted, swiftly and decisively, to terminate these acts of barbarism which have as their only purpose the preservation in power of the dictatorial and repressive regime of President Thieu.

ARE WE THE GOOD GERMANS OF TODAY? 

Mr. Speaker, it was more than 25 years ago that the Nazi leaders stood in the stock at the Nuremberg trials and heard our own Associate Justice Robert H.

Jackson excoriate them in his eloquent closing address as prosecutor. With shattering, remorseless detailing of facts, Justice Jackson enumerated their crimes against humanity.

The infamous tiger cages and prisons of the Thieu regime in South Vietnam raise similar moral questions about our responsibility for what is happening there. We must not be the good Germans who pretended that they did not know the obscene things done to other Germans and other human beings in the concentration camps. We must not look the other way. We too must examine with honesty what horrors are being committed daily with the connivance of our own military and civilian officials.

We cannot plead unavailability of the facts. They are readily available. No one can honestly plead ignorance. What is needed now is that we face up to these facts and at long last insist that something be done to terminate once and for all the imprisonments, tortures, and barbarisms inflicted upon South Vietnamese civilians with the full knowledge of our own Government. 

Let me, Mr. Speaker, advise my colleagues in the House where they can readily find the facts. 

On November 28, 1973, the distinguished Senator from South Dakota (James

Abourezk) dealt forcefully with the issue of the political prisoners in South Vietnam in an address to the Senate. He detailed the shocking instances of torture and inserted into the Record an open letter dated August 8, 1973, from students and intellectuals now being held as political prisoners in South Vietnam. 

I hope all Members of the House will read his remarks. 

A second source for learning details is a report called "Political Prisoners in South Vietnam." It is published by Amnesty International Publications, 53 Theo- 

1 Congressional Record, April 9, 1974.
