A rank-ordering of nutrition program goals might place emphasis on alleviaring conditions which interfere with maintaining or elevating a populations' nutritional level, e.g., educational/motivational work on changing infant feeding practices; control of intestinal parasites; availability of basic food supply; food enrichments and supplements and treatment programs for specific problems with high incidence. Family planning goals might give priority to motivation of and/ or direct delivery of services to special target groups, with emphasis or selective barriers to understanding and successful and continued use of contraception methods of their choice (i.e., post-partum, teenage, and regular health center clients); and such barriers as those presented by other family members including those reflecting needs for personal discipline and those related to an economic/culture support for life style changes. 

Analyzing the causes of "quality of life" constraints is equally important in program priority determination. The prevalence of certain diseases and malnutrition may be readily apparent and directly related to attackable conditions: impure water, faulty midwife practices, disease-bearing vectors, weaning customs, etc. In other cases the chief causal factors may be further removed (housing conditions, production practices) or may suggest activities indirectly associated with "quality of life" deficiencies-for example, the possibility of effecting positive changes in popular customs through the influence of social leaders within a target population. In such cases, a multifaceted program may offer an optimal solution for each of the problems individually. (In other situations where a solution seems precluded by resource constraints, the nature and cause of the deficiencies should be spelled out.)

Cost estimates of the proposed actions should then be made in order to determine whether LDC budgets can sustain them. Those estimates may range from simple per capita costs for programs affecting a single goal to more complicated estimates for multi-goal programs. Estimates of unit or per capita cost should be multiplied by the size of the entire target population (taking into account any economies of scale) in order to ascertain whether an extended program is within the host country's financial capability. In this context, it is important to ultimate acceptance and continued support by the host country that total program costs, both capital and recurring, be projected as far as possible into the future. Recurring cost estimates in particular should reflect anticipated changes in prices of consumable supplies: salary adjustments necessary to attract and retain suitable manpower under foreseeable labor market shifts; costs of equipment maintenance; energy costs; inflation factors and similar elements. If the program under consideration is pilot, the Mission should also ascertain the most likely total recurring cost burden if the program eventually were to be extended to similar target populations throughout the country. 

2. Determination of Available Resources-Generating Improvements at Low- 

Cost "Quality of Life" benefits are generally regarded as end-products of economic development, but they may also contribute to the success of general development effort, or in turn be amplified through coordination with other development effort.

When considering low-cost approaches to integrated health/nutrition/family planning delivery systems, one should inquire into other types of development efforts to which delivery systems might be added. Incorporating elementary infor mation services into another kind of activity may permit greater number of people to be reached at a lower cost than would be possible by building a completely new delivery structure. Options permitting services to be added onto existing structures should be thoroughly examined. For example, could curricula in health and sanitation, nutrition, and family planning be combined into expanding school programs? Could wells and latrines be dug at lower costs as part of other construction projects where similar equipment and construction material are used.

Cost-effectiveness and other comparisons of alternative routes for achieving "change in health status" objectives need not necessarily require large investments of time and money, nor precise health sector analyses. Often valuable information can be sifted out of routine local data, basic information gathered for project action, baseline data generated for unrelated projects, agriculture sector analyses that may have been underway, and UNICEF, WHO, IBRD and other international organization studies of the target area, and needs merely to be supplemented with very specific analyses or household surveys. 

What collaborative planning is now in operation? What is the interdisciplinary input (each agency) in the planning and program development? What community input has been developed, especially in respect to problem analysis definition of needs, interests and attitudes of the public? 

Is there a system which assures continuity for planning and program development at each level from national planning to local, and from local to national? 

Does this information reflect all interests and viewpoints involved? 

DEFICIENCIES IN PLANNING, ORGANIZATION OR ADMINISTRATION 

Established health delivery systems are often constrained in their ability to deliver health services by deficiencies in planning, administrative, and/or supervisory capability. This may be evidenced through circumstances like conflicting spheres of influence within command channels; logistical shortcomings such as irregular or inadequate delivery of drugs and supplies to health stations, procurement and warehousing difficulties or lack of transport for construction teams, technical advisors, debilitated patients, etc.; lack of communication and referral; failure to provide for maintenance and depreciation of equipment; ill conceived or poorly executed personnel policies; inefficient coordination amongst key personnel or operating units; and so on. Circumstances like these may constrain utilization of existing health resources to a level substantially below actual capacity. Alleviation of such constraints may succeed in expanding service delivery at a cost considerably lower than the cost of equivalent expansion through increase of resources; or it may attract contributions from other donors which were being withheld because of such difficulties. Missions should be attentive to opportunities for significantly enhancing service delivery to target populations, by improving a system's efficiency or increasing its absorbtive capacity, at relatively small cost in technical assistance. 

3. Possible Program Approaches—Persuasion and Motivation 

Many health and nutrition problems are avoidable. Often they are rooted in, or aggravated by, practices and customs amenable to improvement. It is particularly important that mothers be persuaded to make simple behavioral changes which have a bearing on their health and their existing or expected children. Control of many health and nutrition problems depend on comprehension and motivation, therefore, the uses and potential of behavioral stimuli should be explored among a target population. 

Attempts to assess the behavioral influences of persons and media within target populations and their potential usefulness in affecting changes in health status should be explored. For example, would the tribal or social leaders in a target population be willing to attend short courses directed toward nutrition, family planning and health education; and if so, how effectively could they communicate their learning through their tribe or community? What institutionsreligious, educational, voluntary-function in the area; what part of the population do they reach; and how persuasive are they? What would it take to interest such institutions in participating in an integrated delivery program; what commodities and materials would be required for their success; would additional manpower be required, and would they need training? 

What measures would be incentives to self-help projects beneficial to health, nutrition or family planning? Simple latrines require about $3 in materials; what proportion of households would undertake their construction if materials and instructions were supplied? A simple, durable pump could be mass-produced for about $18: what demand could be generated for such a pump? Would it be sufficient to justify local production; and what inputs would be required to stimulate production? Is family planning a sensitive subject at village level? If so, can social leaders within villages be encouraged to organize various groups to desensitize inhabitants and to disseminate family planning information?

In this regard, the concept of interdisciplinary teams for sector analysis is now fairly well established; but the interdisciplinary teams that have been assembled to date have been notably lacking in behavioral scientists. The inclusion of experts in motivation might be a worthy addition to future consultant teams charged with recommending integrated delivery programs. 

MEDIA 

In some LDCs, radio and other mass media are available to villages and rural areas as well as urban areas. Where radio (or TV or movie theater) time or published media space can be co-opted for public service messages, the cost of disseminating information on health, nutrition and family planning subjects can be quite low-often merely the production cost. Questions to be addressed are: to what extent do target populations believe information that reaches them through existing media? Are there ways of improving the credibility of such information such as endorsements by popular and religious figures, respected experts and organizations enjoying close rapport with target populations? Traditional media (puppet shows, etc.) may also be promising. How do these media compare in cost-effectiveness with other types of delivery systems? 

UTILIZATION OF INDIGENOUS PRACTITIONERS 

Rudimentary health care and childbirth assistance have evolved out of necessity in many LDCs. Native midwives, curandaros, herbalists and other indigenous practitioners constitute networks for treatment and communication in areas where scientific care and education do not reach the people. The major advantages in the use of indigenous practitioners is that they already cover large portions of populations, that some systems cost little or nothing to resource-constrained governments since the practitioners are paid by their clients, and, in some cases, that their advice is listened to more than that of the official health workers. It is worth investigating the extent to which this indigenous cultural and social network can be utilized, by provision of training (and possibly commodities or financial incentives), to provide greater access to the integrated health/nutrition/family planning services that the host country is able to support. Should such an effort be used in areas where it is not now feasible to cover the target population with clinical services or as a supplement to clinical services? In what ways can this be done? What would be the cost of expanding the services and information that indigenous practitioners are able to offer? Which of the indigenous practitioners would be interested in augmenting their present expertise by disseminating information on preventive health, nutrition and child spacing? Do they still attract significant numbers of clients among target populations? Do any legal restrictions constrain their involvement? Can these be changed? What combination of advice and services can they deliver for the purpose of maximizing impact on health, nutrition and family planning goals? 

In what ways should indigenous practitioners supplement, substitute for, a clinicbases system? What would be the training costs, per practitioner, and per "client" reached? What fees, if any should the government pay to the practitioners, e.g., referral fees for sending clients for long-term or terminal contraceptive measures? How well would indigenous practitioners accept coordination with physicians, and physicians with them?

What objections to use of indigenous practitioners can be expected from elements within medical associations, health ministries, or others? How can these objections be overcome? For example, can leading doctors or medical institutions be involved in designing or implementing training for indigenous practitioners? 

How can attention be drawn to the harsh facts in many countries about how long it will take to expand government clinics to cover the total population? Would a study by a respected local health figure of the advantages and disadvantages of using indigenous practitioners be helpful? If there is concern about appearing to give an official stamp of approval to indigenous practitioners (who, in many countries, are likely to continue recommending many ineffective and even harmful remedies), how can training be provided to them without appearing to give such official approval?

UTILIZING PRIVATE VENDORS 

Distribution of family planning supplies, information, nutrients and some health supplies may be facilitated at low cost through arrangements with com-

mercial vendors-tea shops, fuel outlets, etc.—serving the target area. Where such possibility exists, an assessment should be made of whether the target population is likely to use purchased commodities more effectively or less effectively than free commodities. Estimates should also be made of (a) price levels for the selected commodities necessary to stimulate broad demand; (b) profit margins necessary to assure aggressive merchandising; (c) subsidies that may be deemed necessary to meet these criteria; (d) cost-effectiveness of distribution through available commercial and non-commercial channels. 

Where subsidies are favored, Missions should indicate possible sources of funds and should estimate the likelihood of this burden shifting to the host country. 

If merchants are to be paid for distributing informational material or subsidized for distributing commodities, some sort of control or audit may be appropriate to assure their actually reaching the target population. Proposals for subsidizing private vendor distribution channels should include plans for control. 

Many societies draw on central processing at some point in their food supply. 

In Central America it may be a village maize grinder, in Iran a regional baker, and so on. Arrangements can often be made for including nutrition supplements in processing, and for utilizing the processing plant as a channel for education in food preparation, sanitation, preventive health and family planning. In some cases processing may be done individually for customers, permitting voluntary test and control populations for purposes of evaluation. [Airgram]

FOR MISSION DIRECTORS FROM THE ADMINISTRATOR I. PURPOSE 

In the FY 1975 program planning message (ref. A), I indicated that we have decided to intensify our program concentration on basic human problems of the developing countries. Among the most important of the priority areas determined by this emphasis is food production and nutrition. The draft foreign assistance legislation currently being considered by the Congress further underlines the central importance of activities to increase the production of food and to avoid malnutrition. This message provides the strategy and planning guidance that the Agency will follow in the nutrition area of this effort. In order to help move things along, nutrition was included among the priority areas for which a portion of the FY 75 budget is being reserved in a process of accelerated program development.

II. STRATEGY STATEMENT 

Transmitted herewith as attachment A. is the A.I.D. nutrition sector strategy statement that I recently approved after discussion by the Administrator's Advisory Council. I urge that it be read by all Mission Directors, Deputies and 

Program Officers, and all officers involved in agriculture, health, food for peace, and family planning. Briefly, the strategy directs: 

Concentration upon improved nutrition for pre-school age children and pregnant and nursing women as target groups; 

Pursuit of nutrition goals through incorporation of nutrition considerations in analyses of the agriculture, health, and education sectors and in programming and implementation for family planning, food improvement, and child feeding; and

Priority attention to activities designed to achieve the integration of nutrition factors and goals into host country national planning. 

The goal of A.I.D.'s nutrition program is to increase the capacity of LDC's to: 

Carry out accurate analysis of the nature and magnitude of their malnutrition problem and of the food production-distribution-processing-consumption pattern; 

Determine the most effective methods for addressing these problems through the planning in the relevant sectors; and 

Implement nutrition-relevant programs and projects effectively and monitor and evaluate their effect.

A. Program Planning III. IMPLEMENTATION 

Inasmuch as almost all of the LDC's have serious nutrition problems, AID missions generally are encouraged to discuss nutrition with their LDC counterparts and to provide them with information about the opportunities for effective action in this field. Where there is interest and priority for a national nutrition program, A.I.D. should be prepared to respond. Among the approaches available to stir interest or respond to initial interest: (a) travel to places where key component elements of nutrition programs are in effective operation; (b) travel to observe laboratory work in the United States and to discuss possibilities with various supporting American institutions; (c) participation for key officials in either short or long term training in nutrition (four-week, AID-organized workshops on nutrition methodology and on planning, scheduled for 1974; occasional special conferences and workshops; professional society meetings; the annual Gordon Conference on food and nutrition; specialized academic programs of 4-6 months at M.I.T., Cornell, or Stanford); (d) visits to Missions by AID personnel or consultants knowledgeable in this field; (e) distribution of key publications, which will be sent to missions from time to time by TA/N; and (f) small, special-purpose workshops, tailored for key target audiences. 

Where a government decides that it does wish to develop a national nutrition strategy, and requests AID assistance in doing so, the appropriate AID response will generally be to field a sector survey team assembled by a contractor, followed up where appropriate, by providing a long-term advisor backed up by shorter term experts in different fields. For example, a sector analysis-planning person could be made available to work in-residence within the LDC planning body and could call on specialists in fortification, nutrition education, food service, etc. as needed. Three U.S. universities (M.I.T., Stanford and Cornell) are geared to do this, and two private consulting firms are also lined up with their own people, who have already worked for us, plus a number of qualified university staff members they have identified.

Where there are existing AID programs either in nutrition or related fields, they offer an opportunity for a different approach to the overall issue. A mission with a substantial agricultural program, for example, may propose adding a nutrition dimension to either a completed or planned agricultural sector study. 

The result should be a good part of a national nutrition plan. This is already initiated in Colombia and should become standard practice in agricultural sector studies.

Similarly in health sector studies, the nutrition dimension should be explicitly included. The large scale experimental program with low cost delivery of combined health, nutrition and family planning services will require careful planning of the nutrition elements and will identify the issues that need to be faced in elaborating a national nutrition program in the particular LDC involved. 

This is a particularly important vehicle for nutrition efforts because it concentrates on the principal target groups for nutritional improvement, and because the new high priority given by AID to these multi-purpose delivery systems should expand opportunities to work on nutrition through this channel. 

Steps have already been taken to require a framework of national nutrition analysis for the major Title II programs. Many voluntary agencies have a strong interest in nutrition work and have some programs of their own in this field. 

The Agency is concerned to enable the extensive personnel and other resources of these agencies to participate fully in future nutrition activities, in both AID

projects and their own projects which may be proposed in the future. It is planned to provide training for voluntary agency personnel in nutrition under a proposed centrally funded project beginning this fiscal year. The process of refocussing Title II programs on priority nutrition objectives represents yet another way of approaching the general question of nutrition planning. 

A boost to the early implementation of field-based nutrition programs will be given by the current process of accelerated program development for "new initiative" areas.

Of course, nutrition activity should be included in the DAP and other aspects of the overall program planning process. Bureaus and Missions can work out on a case-by-case basis the manner and timing for including a discussion of nutrition strategy in program planning documents. 

The TA/N centrally funded program includes a number of activities to develop and test methodologies in the field. These activities may provide an opportune basis for program development in your countries. In addition, the TA/N program will provide opportunities for training and for sharing of new techniques and technologies which will provide additional momentum to LDC efforts. 

The following types of activities are considered appropriate for AID support as part of a nutrition project: (a) Short-term or long-term in-residence technical assistance to national planning bodies (or agriculture or health sector planning entities). (b) Technical assistance in establishing systems to monitor nutritional status of the population. (c) Technical assistance to planners in conducting nutrition, food consumption, and other related surveys. (d) Technical assistance in evaluation of nutrition related projects. (e) Assistance in training manpower in the U.S. or locally. (f) Assistance in expediting the greater utilization of new higher protein cereal varieties, traditional protein crops such as food legumes, or less conventional protein foods such as oilseed crops. (g) Assistance in establishing food fortification projects which aim to improve the food supply or meet specific nutrition deficits. (h) Assistance in developing low cost protein foods, particularly weaning foods, and foods which may be used to replace high protein foods supplied under the Food For Peace program. 

(i) Nutrition motivation and education programs, using mass media or innovative techniques (e.g. use of indigenous health practitioners as nutrition educators) to reach the low income masses. (j) Assistance in developing, extending, or strengthening the nutrition component of Maternal-Child Health (MCH) programs, including supplementary feeding activities.

Attention should be given in the project submission to describing the role of other donors, which, hopefully, will be complementary and related to a single country strategy. In this regard, missions should keep in mind the potential for program financing by the international financial institutions. A.I.D. assistance in analysis and planning may better enable LDCs to identify and define program needs which may be suitable for IFI's loans. In addition, consideration should be given to provision of A.I.D. sector loans to finance key areas of recipients' nutrition strategies. 

B. Staffing

Missions in some circumstances may need a full-time direct hire nutrition programmer and/or project manager. The responsibility in other cases can be assigned to a multi-sector officer or combined with other appropriate functions. 

It needs qualified professional attention and cannot simply be made an add-on duty for the junior member of the staff, as often has been the case in the past. 

Training can be provided to equip qualified existing personnel with the specific analytical and planning skills required. See Section III, C. below. An effort is underway to identify Agency employees who have the qualifications needed for nutrition programming-monitoring-evaluation assignments. It is believed that specialized expertise is available through contract and PASA arrangements to provide both short term and resident personnel to supplement Mission staff for program and project planning and to implement approved projects. We would welcome your indication of your staffing plans and possible requirements. Any new direct-hire positions for nutrition personnel would be made available pri-

marily through the elimination of lower priority positions within each Mission's present allocation.

C. Training 

The Third Agency-Wide In-Service Workshop will be held in October (ref. 

D.). This will offer an opportunity for orientation of selected USAID personnel and will permit field inputs into strategy and implementation. A four-week training program for A.I.D. personnel (tentatively planned for next February), will help train officers who will have the major nutrition programming responsibility in the USAIDs. This will be followed in March by a similar program for volagency staffers. Training for LDC personnel is scheduled for 1974, with a workshop on current state-of-the-art methodology for senior planners in May and a four-week session on analysis, planning, and implementation for mid-level people in July.

D. Timing 

Actions have already been initiated to strengthen the Agency's capability through both direct hire and contractor staff, to assist missions with sector analysis, training, and other technical backstopping. A roster of backstopping services will be distributed to missions in October. On the basis of country and 

Mission interest, assistance will be provided with the nutrition component of sector assessments and with nutrition program development. Detailed planning of program response should be underway in the field in the Spring of 1974. It is expected that by the beginning of FY 1975, 8-10 countries will have integrated nutrition programs planned and their proposals will have been submitted for approval. Another 8-10 countries will have added nutrition components elsewhere in their programs. Most of the completed agriculture sector analyses will include nutrition issues and most Title II-supported child feeding programs will be related to country nutrition strategies. During FY 75, implementation should be well underway on these new projects and program components.

To: AIDTO Circular A-346 From: AID/Washington DEPARTMENT OF STATE

Subject: Private and Voluntary Organizations. 

FROM THE ADMINISTRATOR FOR MISSION DIRECTORS, AID REPRESENTATIVES AND AID AFFAIRS OFFICERS 

This message is to advise you of the Policy Determination that AID will encourage greater participation by private and voluntary organizations¹ in development assistance. This new program emphasis stems from our conviction that greater PVO participation in the development process is merited and our recognition that both public opinion and the initiatives directed by the Congress support increased participation. An Overseas Development Council survey has reported the confidence which the American public has in voluntary agencies as channels for assistance. The Congressional view is contained in broad context in the Foreign Assistance Act of 1973. 

As a first step toward increasing PVO participation, I directed that AID, jointly with the Advisory Committee on Voluntary Foreign Aid, convene a Development Assistance Policy Conference with U.S. private and voluntary Organizations in Washington, D.C. This took place April 29th and 30th, 1974.

The presentation and discussions of the conference focused on AID's emerging policy to increase its collaboration with the private and voluntary organizations in meeting development needs. The conference went a long way to working out the guidelines for PVO participation in development programs. A report on the Conference will be transmitted to you in the very near future. 

The FY 1975 budget request proposes that funds be set aside to enable AID to finance increased PVO activity pursuant to the authorizing language. 

NOTE: Private and Voluntary Organizations (PVO's) are U.S. and other organizations which are philanthropic or public service oriented. non-profit, non-political and non-governmental. Coonerative organizations are included. Not included are universities and other primarily educational institutions, and research organizations which are being meaningfully engaged in development assistance through existing AID program arrangements.

In the FY 1975 budget request we propose to administratively earmark $6 million to fund new projects to be implemented by PVO's. In this case "new" means either projects that are new or on-going projects which bring in PVO's as implementors for the first time. Projects related to employment creation and equitable income distribution, and projects in the priority areas of food and nutrition, family planning and health, education and human resource development which engage the resources and capabilities of a private and voluntary agency will be eligible for consideration. These are expected to be within national or regional priorities agreed to by A.I.D. and the host LDC, as well as applicable agency and regional bureau program guidelines, although you may wish to consider re-examining these with a view to raising the priority of a particular project which, where executed by a PVO, will have the benefit of significant private resources, human and material, mobilized by that organization. The principles of sound development assistance project design would apply. 

In addition, funds are also being reserved in the FY 1975 budget request for Development Program Grants. These grants will be made available to eligible 

PVO's to assist them in improving their capacity to plan, design, manage and evaluate programs and projects consistent with the objectives of the new foreign assistance legislation. These grants will also enhance the capability of PVO's to work with LDC's in identifying development needs and planning projects to meet those needs. 

I recognize that both the increased involvement of PVO's and the process of considering possibilities for their involvement may initially impose additional burdens on our overseas Missions. It is an indication of the importance I attach to this effort that I am asking you to turn your attention to it. As the PVO's become more experienced and their development capabilities are increased by grants for that purpose, the requirements for U.S.A.I.D. monitoring will diminish.

DEPARTMENT OF STATE From: AID/Washington Subject: Program Planning for FY 1975 and Beyond. 

Date Sent: 4/21/73

FOR MISSION DIRECTORS FROM ADMINISTRATOR I. INTRODUCTION 

As we begin hearings on the FY 1974 AID presentation to the Congress and you begin work on the FY 1975 Development Assistance Field submissions, I want to briefly restate the importance of the U.S. aid program for achieving President Nixon's foreign policy goals of an enduring world peace and an expanding international economy in which all nations, rich and poor, can benefit. 

The importance of the developing countries is incontestable. They comprise 

70 percent of the world's population and therefore will continue to be a major factor of the world's political and economic condition. Despite substantial economic growth during the past decade, millions of people in the developing countries are still caught in the cycle of poverty including malnutrition, ill health, illiteracy and the whole catalog of human misery inherent in underdevelopment. 

No enduring structure of peace can be built on this base of dissatisfaction. 

The United States and other industrialized countries are also linked to the developing countries by mutual interests of trade and investment as well as critical resource needs. The solution of such world problems as environmental protection, narcotics control and restructuring of international monetary and trade arrangements requires broad cooperation among nations. 

Meeting of the challenge of underdevelopment is one of the major requisites for an expanding international economy and for promoting a more stable world peace. The response to this challenge of underdevelopment requires an international system of expanding world trade and investment supplemented by the flow of development assistance from the industrialized to the poor countries. 

Our development assistance efforts in FY 1975 and in future years, as described below, will be aimed at enhancing the ability of poor countries to mobilize

their resources and determination for providing a better life for their people and make the world a more desirable place for all people. 

This guidance builds upon : (a) the FY 1974 Development Assistance Planning 

Guidance per AIDTO CIRC. A-543, dated April 15, 1972, which contained the major elements of the AID Reform Plan and (b) the FY 1974 program submissions from the field. 

The main purpose of this guidance is: (a) To continue our movement forward of concentrating and integrating AID resources on a limited group of development problems, emphasizing a a collaborative style of assistance and operating within a multilateral assistance framework. (b) To indicate to the Missions our conclusions to date as to the priority programs which AID in its worldwide and country assistance programs will be focusing during the coming years. (c) To discuss how these program priorities and objectives relate to Mission programming and submissions to Washington including the DAPS, annual budget requests and project approval requests. 

Two Annexes are attached. The first describes the contents and development of the DAP in some detail; the second describes our plans to integrate and expedite the Washington review and approval process of these submissions from the field.

II. PROGRAM CONCENTRATION AND PRIORITIES 

AID has been working for almost two years to concentrate its efforts on basic human problems of food production and nutrition, population and health, education and human resource development. Despite substantial growth in gross economic terms in the LDCs over the past decade, hunger, malnutrition, ill-health, illiteracy and unemployment pervade the lives of the people living at the lower end of the economic ladder in the developing world. The World Bank estimates that roughly 40 percent of the total population in all the developing countries are entrapped in conditions of poverty beyond the reach of market forces and without minimal levels of nutrition, health services and literacy. The problem is to reconcile the need for more rapid economic growth with improvements in employment and income distribution.

It is our conviction that the Agency's priorities, as stated above, offer a better opportunity to help the LDCs to meet basic human needs, and to reduce poverty, as well as to foster economic growth. Economic growth clearly remains the primary requisite of development. But development policies aimed at rapid growth need to be balanced with other important development objectives. The Agency's 

Policy Determination on Employment and Income Distribution examines in de tail these problems and the relevant policy options including pricing of the factors of production, institutional reform and appropriate technologies. 

Program concentration will also enable AID to strengthen its analytical and response capacity and to improve the linkage between our research efforts and our operational programs in the field. Our 211(d) institutional grants to strengthen U.S. institutions' response capability and support of international research networks are increasingly geared to these same priority sectors and problems. Existing institutions, delivery systems and technology are often not relevant to LDC problems of population growth, nutrition, mass unemployment and lowcost health and education systems. This deficiency requires a concentrated problem-solving approach by AID in which field programs are backed up by research and pilot programs in the LDCs as well as the continued expansion of U.S. and international expertise in their areas. 

Finally the scarcity of AID funds dictates concentrating on a limited number of development problems which address basic human needs and offer the best prospects for promoting both growth and development. 

The decision to focus on priority development problems in these sectors does not mean that requests in other areas will not be supported. In the first place, some of the priority problems, as indicated above, are pioneering efforts which need more time and research to develop relevant technologies and delivery systems before we can proceed on a large scale. Second, in certain countries and regions, transportation and power can be high development priorities, e.g. for the small farmers an all-weather road that would allow them to get their harvest to market when the demand and prices are good. However, in the coming years we see infrastructure programs either increasingly financed by other donors or

becoming part of more comprehensive sector programs (e.g., farm to market roads or rural electrification as elements of AID agricultural or rural development sector loans).

There will also continue to be individual activities outside country areas of concentration (e.g., urban development, science and technology, public safety, export development, labor). Some of these activities will be geared to researching new problems or possible areas of concentration for the future as in the case of science and technology. They all should demonstrate that they are supportive of the Agency's main concern for accelerating economic growth and social development.

We also expect to continue program lending in a few key countries. However, in some countries where program lending has been utilized as a major vehicle for resource transfers, there may be opportunities now in terms of the host country priorities to give serious consideration to development of sector programs which will more precisely focus on basic human development problems. 

We are not abandoning program lending as a development tool nor do we intend to force program lending artifically into a sector mold. But we do not want to use past levels of program lending as justification for future program lending or as a reason for not moving AID's country program to the priority sectors. We realize that sector lending raises specific problems in certain country contexts, and we will provide additional guidance on sector lending in the near future. 

Missions that propose continued program lending or other major programs outside the above priorities will be asked to justify these exceptions fully in their DAP submissions.

As stated in AIDTO CIRC. A-1332, a series of policy papers is being prepared outlining AID strategy in each priority sector. Brief comments on the priority sectors follow below.

Food Production and Nutrition 

Food production is important to the development effort because agriculture contributes a major share to the GNP of most LDCs and provides the basic staple on which the welfare of people depends and is the main source of employment and income for a large part of the population. But despite impressive gains from the application of new technology in agriculture for some crops in some areas, inadequate food production remains a major development problem. 

Population growth in LDCs will continue to put pressure on food supplies. 

While new technologies have been successful, these successes have not been sufficiently widespread in terms of the crops involved, the geographic areas involved, or the size of farms involved. For the foreseeable future, AID will continue to give high priority to agricultural assistance programs. 

The quantity of food is essential, but it is increasingly clear that the quality of food is a major factor in improving well-being. We believe AID food production efforts should increasingly be concerned with producing crops which are high in protein as well as increasing the protein content of major cereals. (This is not to deny that in many countries increased calorie intake may be just as important for the nutrition of many people.) The food quality goal requires more attention to nutrition planning as well as to the problem of meeting the nutrition needs of particularly vulnerable groups such as pregnant and nursing women and pre-school children. Nutrition goals can be supported also by the use of PL 480 Title II commodities which represent a significant resource to the Agency.

Relating employment and income distribution questions to food production leads to concern about those segments of rural populations not benefiting adequately from the new foodgrain technology. These are the small farmers and landless laborers. The small farmer situation is complex, particularly as many institutional and credit programs designed in the past for this group appear to have failed. We look forward to the results of the Spring Review on Agricultural 

Credit to provide insight and new approaches to small farmers. 

We also need a careful look at the problems of landless laborers. In some places, their wages appear to be rising, while in others their labor is less needed due to subsidies on capital (e.g., tractors). Their problems may therefore suggest changes in government policies or, perhaps, special programs such as employmentcreating rural works or non-formal education projects to build salable skills. 

The persistence of rural poverty in the LDCs underscores the relevance of the concept of "rural development." In sector analysis and sector studies we should 36-333 - 74-61

be taking a comprehensive look at the problems of rural people in the development process, including those of production, nutrition, access to public health and education, land tenure, etc. Such analysis should include a focus on the rural poor-who are they, what are their problems, what can governments do? 

This kind of analysis can and should lead to focused and integrated assistance programs (sector loans, technical assistance, food-for-work) aimed at breaking the cycle of low-end rural poverty. 

Population and Health 

AID will also continue to give high priority to population and family planning assistance programs. We intend to complement these activities with greater attention to health assistance programs emphasizing low cost systems that extend services to large segments of LDC populations which do not now have access to or cannot afford such services. 

Family size, poor health, low nutrition and poverty are interrelated. In some cases the availability of health or nutrition services along with family planning services may help increase the "demand" for family planning services. Health care and nutrition programs help enhance children's chances for survival and may thus ease the perceived need for large families. Reductions in morbidity and mortality offer an important means of improving the quality of life, and productivity, of the disadvantaged groups on which AID wishes to focus increasingly. 

The developing countries have made progress in providing the means for and information about controlling fertility and for improving health. However, it is estimated that family planning services still are available only to 10-15 percent of couples of reproductive age in the developing countries. Likewise, even rudimentary health services are non-existent in many areas. 

Therefore AID is experimenting with various approaches to expand and improve the delivery of family planning, preventive health, and nutrition services, in combination or separately, to greater numbers of people at costs that limited LDC budgets can absorb and maintain. We do not wish to invest in highcost Western style medical systems which could not possibly reach most segments of LDC populations. For all but the highest income LDCs, even an extensive clinic-based health system may be too costly to provide effective assistance to most of the population. On the other hand, almost every LDC has some sort of indigenous health delivery system in place. In many cases these systems can be upgraded and/or used to assist in meeting health, nutrition, and population objectives. We do encourage strengthening of LDC health planning capability so as to add a health element to national planning and improve the efficiency of resources invested in health. Building on our experience, AID will intensify its efforts to determine which approaches promise lowest cost, greatest reliability, and wide adaptability at an early date.

Environmental sanitation is a specialized area of public health which could have high benefit to LDC populations at relatively low cost. Activities such as cleaning up water supply, improving waste disposal, and protecting against food contamination also tend to be labor-intensive. AID may have opportunities to assist in these areas based on careful prior assessment. 

In addition to increasing emphasis on the extension of low-cost family planning, MCH, preventive health, and nutrition services, AID will also give more attention to research, pilot and operational projects designed to influence and gain greater knowledge of the numerous factors which affect motivation and willingness to limit families. Individual interest in family planning tends to increase when more effective and convenient family planning services are made available. But we also recognize that interest in or actual resort to family planning in general depends on a variety of other influences-economic, legal, social, cultural-which may affect the attractiveness to parents of large or small families. We know these influences on demand for family planning are still poorly understood, but there is ample evidence that pressure for family planning service grows quickly when people actively want them. Though it is difficult to do much in the short run about some influences on demand, there are feasible public policy measures in such areas as taxation, social security, law, etc., that can have major impacts on family attitudes toward limiting fertility. 

Nutrition and family planning can also be important components of health delivery systems. In some cases the availability of health or nutrition services along with family planning services may help increase the "demand" for the

family planning services. Thus we wish to encourage family planning objectives in programs in health and nutrition and to encourage mutual support between health and nutrition programs.

Education Despite greatly increased LDC outlays for education in the past ten years, progress has been limited. Serious questions have been raised about the economic, social, and educational impact of strategies for education that were widely accepted in the 1960's, particularly the emphasis given to rapid expansion of higher education and vocational secondary education. The Agency needs to seek ways to improve the development impact of education, particularly its impact on low-income groups.

Areas in which we would particularly like to encourage carefully evaluated experimentation include: employment-related non-formal education (ranging from apprenticeship programs to literacy training for farmers); non-formal and formal programs in population, nutrition, and health; and changes in educational technology, with emphasis on "software" and on outputs, rather than just on hardware (we define educational technology broadly to include such things as increasing teacher-student ratios or mimeographed self-teaching materials, as well as sophisticated electronic equipment). All activities in the education area should take note of questions of cost-effectiveness, capital and labor intensity, and impact on income distribution. This does not mean that all earlier approaches to education which the Agency has supported should be abandoned. It does mean, however, that the Agency will increasingly look for new educational patterns and be reluctant to support investments in traditional education systems which merely expand outmoded and irrelevant forms of education and which cannot possibly reach the masses of the people because they are too expensive. 

III. GENERAL POLICY CONSIDERATIONS 

AIDTO Circular A-543 last year stressed several over-all policy considerations that under the Administrator's Reform Plan are relevant to program planning and resource allocation. We believe these points are important enough to be repeated here. 

1. Definition and Analysis of Priority Problems.-In preparing DAPS and in proposing individual assistance projects, it is essential to focus on the priority development problems which offer the best possibility that AID can have a significant impact in terms of improved growth, employment and income distribution effects and/or in terms of significant policy, institutional or technological impact. As indicated in AIDTO Circular A-543, a problem should not be defined so broadly as to obscure the specific steps required to solve it nor so narrowly that the solution is of marginal significance to the development of the country. 

A DAP that simply proposes to assist the "agriculture sector” or focus on "rural development" is not acceptable; further definition and analysis of the specific constraints being attacked within those broad categories is required. Similarly, a project to build an agricultural institute is not responsive to the new directions unless it is made clear how this particular undertaking contributes to the solution of a major problem that has been identified. 

2. Integrated use of resources.—In focusing on priority problems, it is essential to consider the range of resources available to AID-loans, grants, PL 480 commodities, Housing Investment Guaranties-and how they may be effectively integrated into an attack on the problem. Obviously, not all types of resources will be required for each problem, but we must be alert to the possibilities for integration when allocating resources. To cite two examples, we need to continue to apply PL 480 Title II resources to an effective nutrition strategy in many countries rather than treating Title II commodities as a simple transfer of resources (as recommended in the FY 1974 PL 480 Title II Guidance), and give more attention to the use of other AID resources, technical assistance and loan funds in support of Title II nutrition programs. Similarly, in our efforts to develop integrated low cost health, nutrition and family planning programs, we should broaden our programming to include other types of AID resources to be applied in conjunction with Title X funds. AID funding allocations could recognize this type of multiple purpose programming. 

In implementing our programs, we need to give continued attention to maximizing the use of U.S. contractors, universities and U.S. private voluntary agen-

cies. In addition, LDC institutions and technicians should come into a more effective partnership in planning and managing aid programs. 

3. Differences among countries.-In focusing on development problems and the 

U.S. response thereto, we need to consider carefully the range of difference among 

LDCs from nearly self-sufficient to least developed-and tailor the U.S. approach accordingly. This involves the overall allocation of our limited resources between different categories of countries, the types of resources provided to the different categories, and the style of providing assistance. We have issued a policy determination on the Least Developed Countries and plan to provide more specific guidance on the more advanced LDCs.

The implication of this is that individual field missions should be alert to these questions in considering the appropriate U.S. response in each case. We need a dialogue with you on such questions as loan-grant mix, appropriateness of different assistance tools (sector loans, project loans, traditional TA, bloc TA grants, reimbursable TA, etc.) and the degree to which a collaborative style is possible. 

4. Multilateral coordination.-With the growth of other bilateral and multilateral donor programs during recent years, it is essential that our assistance continue to take into account activities of other donors, the financial and personnel resources available, and reflect the fact that the U.S. is a participant in a multilateral development effort in most countries. The DAP as well as specific project proposals should reflect the fact that we are seeking to foster greater coordination on policies and programs, thereby optimizing the use of scarce resources among donors. Difficulties encountered in achieving this objective should be indicated.

To the extent feasible, Missions should use or draw upon analytical material already prepared by the multilateral agencies. Whenever feasible, we should relate our programming to that of the multilateral agencies. 

5. Research, innovation and development.-As stated in last year's guidance, we are attempting to relate agency centrally-funded research more closely to priority development problems of the LDCs and to the concerns of AID Missions in the field. In committing AID funds to research, we are convinced that, despite differences among LDC countries, they have many problems in common, and new approaches to these problems can be discovered through international efforts, combining research in LDC institutions and the private and public sectors of the developed countries. 

AID has financed research leading to innovations which hold considerable promise for the LDCs, including a number of new corn varieties of improved protein quality (Opaque 2), which have promise for early application in Africa and Latin America; an improved fertilizer called sulphur-coated urea, which regulates more effectively the rate of nitrogen released to crops; and a biodegradable pesticide (II-4-D), which promises to do the work of DDT without harmful environmental effects. In addition, AID-financed research is underway on problems of income distribution (Rice University), choice of technology (Yale University), and other social and economic problems of development. 

AID/W will provide periodic reports on the results of AID research which will be of importance to country program activities. 

In developing country programs according to this guidance message, Missions are urged to enumerate and describe those gaps in information and understanding which inhibit the host countries from addressing development problems effectively. Only by building a view of LDC research needs from the bottom up, i.e. based on the actual needs of countries, can AID gear its own research programs to development problems of highest priority. Missions are also encouraged to submit assistance proposals supporting research on development problems in LDC institutions, particularly on food production and nutrition, population and health, and education-areas where innovation appears to be critical for most of the LDCs.

ANNEX A DAP CONTENT AND BUILDING PROCESS The Development Assistance Program (DAP) is the principal Agency planning and programming document that fits together country priorities and U.S. priorities into an action plan for U.S. assistance that is relevant to country needs. 

A.I.D. plans to have approved DAPs for each country where we expect to carry on a significant A.I.D. program over the next few years. DAPS will not be required in countries where this is not the case. Obviously the contents of individual 

DAPS will vary depending on the country situation.

While the following discussion is couched in terms of individual countries, a single DAP may cover several countries in a sub-region if that makes more sense.

The DAP is focused analytically on priority sectors and problems within or among them rather than on aggregate development issues. The DAP is a multiyear document that reflects broad agreement between the recipient country and the U.S. on those areas where A.I.D. will concentrate its attention over the next several years. The DAP is submitted at any time and, when approved, continues in effect until such time as it needs revision. An approved DAP forms the substantive basis for annual resource allocations and individual program and project proposals. The DAP should be consistent with CASPS, country policy papers, and similar documents. 

Set forth below is a discussion of what a DAP should contain and the process for building a DAP.

Contents of the DAP 

The DAP contains two basic parts: (a) a summary narrative statement discussing the country development situation and the rationale and strategy for U.S. assistance, and (b) sector assessments (discussed in AIDTO Circular A- 

1583 and outlined more fully below) for each of the sectors in which major U.S. assistance inputs are contemplated. Ideally, the required sector assessments should be completed before the summary narrative statement is put in final, but in some cases this may not be practical. This problem is discussed below. 

The DAP Summary Narrative Statement 

While the length of the summary narrative statement that constitutes the first part of the DAP will obviously vary depending on the country, we would normally expect it to be on the order of 30-60 pages depending on the number of sectors in which major U.S. assistance inputs are contemplated. The summary narrative statement should contain the following basic elements: 

1. A development overview of the country (possibly 10-20 pages) discussing where the country has been and where it is going, including: 

Examination of economic and social development over the past several years, including the economic and social factors (including demographic factors) affecting development.

Past and present development priorities of the Government and likely development priorities for the future. Mission judgment on the development rationale of these priorities.

Ongoing and planned Government programs and overall levels of financing, including a discussion of the Government Budget and external assistance from all sources. 

Institutional strengths and weaknesses. 

2. Sectoral discussions (possibly 3-5 pages per sector) of those sectors in which major U.S. assistance is contemplated. Ideally, these discussions should where possible be based on the sector assessments described below and should provide summary information on:

Historical trends in the sector over the past several years. 

Past, present, and likely future Government policies, priorities, and programs in the sector.

Economic factors which affect development of the sector, including employment and income distribution. 

Institutional strengths and weaknesses in the sector-both public and private (including domestic voluntary organizations). 

Relevant legislative, budgetary, manpower, attitudinal, and technological considerations. 

Other donor programs, existing and anticipated. 

Include a short section on why these sectors were chosen for USAID concentration as opposed to other sectors. 

3. Proposed U.S. assistance within the above sectors (possibly 10-15 pages) based on country and A.I.D. priorities, and describing priority development problems to be addressed. This section should also include, where applicable, an indication of proposed U.S. involvement in any areas outside the areas of major involvement. A short justification for program lending should be included here, if such assistance is proposed. Cite liberally from World Bank macroeconomic studies.

4. Likely U.S. assistance requirements over the next several years (5-10 pages). 

This should be in terms of both dollars (loans, grants, PL 480, HIGS) and manpower (Direct-hire, PASA, Contract) and should set forth major magnitudes only-remember, the DAP is not a budget request. What is needed at this stage is a general indication of what we are getting into in the way of resource requirements over the next few years. 

5. A.I.D. Manpower Resource Requirements. The DAP should also discuss the organization and manpower implications associated with the projection of assistance requirements. What is needed is some general indication of the number and major categories of U.S. manpower required to execute the program and the principal functional areas in which such manpower is to be deployed. We do not expect the DAP to say with precision what the Mission will require as manpower allocations but it should indicate a general order of magnitude, e.g. 15 to 25 people. The U.S. requirements should be expressed in terms of direct-hire, PASA, and contract staff with the latter two categories to be preferred for most direct technical advisory assistance.

The DAP Sector Assessments 

Sector assessments form the major analytical base for the proposed U.S. effort in a country. Sector assessments will obviously vary in length and content depending on the individual situation-some are apt to be quite extensive, others quite short. The length and methodological approach should be commensurate with the complexity of the development problems being addressed and the magnitude of U.S. assistance which might result. Country-specific guidance, which will follow this general guidance message, will discuss assessment requirements for each country, particularly in those countries where major assessments are indicated. Please note that this country-specific approach to guidance on assessments differs programmatically (but not in analytic definition) from previous guidance contained in AIDTO A-1332 (11/18/72).

In many cases, we would hope and expect that sector analytic work already performed by the recipient country, World Bank, or others could serve our needs as well, and we encourage you to draw on these sources wherever possible. The 

LDC should be fully involved as a participant in the analytical portions of all sector assessments. Following is a list of the types of questions that might be focused on a sector assessment; this list is not necessarily all inclusive, nor do all points mentioned need to be covered in a particular case. 

The economic relationships which determine current performance within the sector or sub-sector. Also, population growth factors. 

Non-economic factors which give the sectors its traditional characteristics; these factors become more important as the country seeks to extend the benefits of development to groups who may respond less vigorously to economic incentives.

Institutions-both public and private (including domestic voluntary organizations)—which influence, either for good or ill, the development of the sector or sub-sector.

The specific problems of underemployment and income mal-distribution within the sector, and the source of these problems within existing economic, non-economic (social, cultural, political), and institutional relationships. 

The top two or three constraints on development within the sector or sub-sector (priority development problems). 

Government planning for the sector: the realism of its stated goals, the desirability of objectives in terms of A.I.D. policy. 

Government development programs in the sector: can they overcome the principal constraints on development within the sector so that planning goals can be achieved?

Alternatives to government plans and programs: what other plans and programs have the host government considered? Form a judgment as to their reasons for rejecting these courses of action. 

Relation of the sector being analyzed to other sectors in terms of developing priorities. Is the government over-stressing or under-stressing the sector in question? Or is the emphasis about right?

What role can foreign assistance play in assisting the government to promote development of the sector or subsector by addressing priority development problems. This will depend upon the nature of the principal constraints on development-there are some problems foreigners cannot and

should not try to solve and upon the adequacy of the government's development program-is it worth supporting? 

What are donors already doing in the sector? Is this sufficient outside help?

What does the Mission propose in the way of assistance (dollars, PL 480 and HIG's, as appropriate) in the sector? Links between the assistance proposed, the government's development plans, and the priority development problems should be described in detail. 

Individual activity descriptions are not expected in the sector assessment, but the statement of priority development problems should be specific enough so that subsequent review of proposed activities and budget levels can refer back to it. A sector assessment of livestock development, for example, could identify animal disease control, small farmer credit and farm-to-market roads as priority development problems, and could conclude that the last of these could be appropriately addressed with A.I.D. resources. The general approach would thus be developed without actually proposing an A.I.D. activity (note that an A.I.D. activity might also address only a portion of a priority development problem, such as a loan for farm-to-market roads, or A.I.D. might address more than one problem, via a livestock sector loan those proceeds would be used to attack all three problems mentioned above).

The Process for Building the DAP 

We would expect the DAP building process in the Mission to include the following steps: 

On a very "rough cut" basis, determine the major areas for A.I.D. concentration based on (a) the country's priorities, (b) A.I.D.'s global priorities, and (c) the Mission's judgment of what can be accomplised. We recognize that the Country's priorities and A.I.D.'s global priorities may not always coincide; that is where Mission judgment is most needed. 

Based on the above identification, begin a rough draft of the DAP Sum mary Narrative Statement described above. 

Perform sector assessments (or collect assessments already performed by others) for areas of major A.I.D. concentration. Request help from 

AID/W as necessary. 

Revise the rough draft DAP Summary Narrative Statement as necessary following the completion of sector assessments. 

Submit the DAP (summary narrative plus sector assessments) to Washington for review and approval.

In cases where sector assessments already exist, the above process would be somewhat shortened. 

ANNEX B THE PROGRAM REVIEW PROCESS IN WASHINGTON 

We plan to improve AID/W's review processes relating to program planning and resource allocation by a better integration of the DAP review, the annual budget review, and the project approval process. Each of these is discussed below.

The DAP Review Process 

The DAP is the place where the overall Agency priorities (described in Part II of the airgram) and the specific requirements of individual country programs come together. An approved DAP constitutes an action plan for a particular country or area which reflects the application of the overall Agency priorities to a particular country situation. 

DAP is intended to be a comprehensive statement of development assistance strategy for a particular country or region. It is to identify priority problems. 

The solution of which would have a significant growth and developmental impact and therefore warrant A.I.D. resource inputs on a multi-year time span. By definition such priority development problems and the multiplicity of economic and social objectives involved will require substantial analysis and professional skills to design programs geared to meeting these objectives. This means a major effort by the field missions with help from AID/W. But the DAPS, once completed, should provide a multi-year, agreed development assistance strategy which will give missions more time for implementing their programs and for increased attention to evaluating program performance.

When a DAP arrives in Washington, a date for completion of Washington review of the DAP will be established and communicated to the mission. The DAP will be reviewed simultaneously by the regional bureau, FPPC, TAB and/or PHA, and SER, plus other offices as appropriate. The regional bureau will take the lead shepherding the DAP through the review process. These bureaus will then meet at a formal session chaired by PPC to discuss the DAP, and if they agree either that the DAP is adequate as submitted or that certain changes are required, the field mission will be notified of the decision. If there is major disagreement among the bureaus, PPC will submit the issues to the Administrator or the Deputy Administrator for decision.

As you will note from Annex A, a DAP has two basic parts: a summary narrative statement and sector assessments for each of the sectors in which a major U.S. effort is planned. We recognize that sector assessments cannot be completed overnight. As a general rule, we do not necessarily plan to hold up Washington review of a DAP until all the sector assessments are completed. We will consider each country situation individually and may in some cases wish to proceed with Washington review of a DAP when the most important of the sector assessments are ready. In such cases, Washington approval of the DAP will obviously be conditional pending receipt of the remaining sector assessments. 

The Annual Budget Review Process 

Unlike the DAP, the annual budget submission and review process is well established within the Agency and will be continued essentially as is except for the modifications noted below. 

Annual budget submissions from the field will continue to be requested on a time frame no later than that established last year for the FY 1974 budget. While we are considering some adjustments, the documentation required will generally follow the pattern established last year in the FBS/MOB instructions. Where approved DAPS exist, we would expect the budget submissions from the field to be largely tabular, with narrative requirement focussed primarily on (a) new loan or grant projects not yet submitted to Washington under the project approval process described below, and (b) any request for budget resources that represents a significant departure from the approved DAP. Until an approved 

DAP exists, the annual budget submission for a country will have to include additional narrative to that described above. 

In the future, it is likely that we will be requesting somewhat more information in the budget submission on (a) sectoral splits in relation to overall A.I.D. priority areas, (b) implementation schedules for individual activities, and (c) projections of requirements beyond the budget wear in question (this latter change reflects increasing interest in such information on the part of the Office of Management and Budget).

Budget submissions from the field will be reviewed in the normal manner in Washington first by the regional bureaus, then by PPC and the Administrator, with participation by other interested bureaus and offices. The process leads to the A.I.D. budget submission to OMB about September 30. As usual, the regional bureaus will keep you informed of the status of your request as the process proceeds through submission to OMB, determination of the President's budget request for A.I.D., Congressional Presentation, and finally issuance of the Op erational Year Budget following Congressional enactment of appropriations. 

As already indicated, once approved DAPs exist, we will rely on them heavily as the substantive basis for the annual budget process, and therefore concentrate on the issues that are relevant in the budget context: (a) does the mission's budget request specifically and clearly reflect the action plans that the approved DAPs represent; (b) are the amounts of money requested for individual activities correct from the standpoint of Agency fiscal guidelines and likely project implementation pace; (c) are the individual activities for which funds are requested achieving their intended purposes i.e. a greater effort will be made to evaluate the program performance. 

The Project Approval Process 

The process for approval of individual projects (defined broadly as any assistance activity) in Washington is reasonably well established and understood, particularly on the loan side, but we plan to make changes that will systematize the process more clearly, speed up decision making, and reduce the distinction between loan and grant project reviews.

As with the budget process, the DAP can be instrumental in making the project approval process work more effectively. We expect that eventually approved 

DAPS will form the same substantive underpinning for review of individual projects as they will for the budget process. This approach will allow us to unclog the project review process and focus it on relevant questions such as technical soundness, implementation requirements, benefit incidence, and relation to the DAP plan instead of rehashing our rationale for assistance to a country each time an individual project is submitted. If AID/W technical personnel are needed to supplement work of mission staffs they should be involved at early stages (see AIDTO Circular A-50) in the project formulation. Early AID/W involvement in the IRR and PROP helps expedite the project review and approval process.

The DAP of course is likely to include only general information on the specific projects to be undertaken over the multi-year time frame, and even at the point of the annual budget process individual new project proposals are often not yet documented in detail. (Once approved DAPs exist, we expect that projects will be developed and submitted earlier than now, and hopefully ahead of the budget cycle.) Whenever a project is ready to move forward, detailed documentation should be prepared and the proposal should be submitted to Washington. 

Documentation requirements for individual projects are already well established in the Agency and we do not propose change for the sake of change. However as we move forward with the A.I.D. reform plan, it is likely that we may consolidate some of this documentation, particularly unifying the different types of documentation requirements for loans and grants, so that the emphasis can be more clearly focussed on priority areas and problems rather than the type of assistance involved. (Obviously some separate requirements for loan and grant documentation will continue to be needed.) As we work on these changes, you will be kept informed.
